title: Damilola: The Untold Story review – John Boyega’s trauma after losing his childhood friend is haunting | Television | The Guardian
description: The actor and his sister were with the 10-year-old on the night he was murdered. For the first time, along with the caretaker who found him bleeding, they share their terror – and celebrate their friend
Author: Hannah J Davies
Headline: The actor and his sister were with the 10-year-old on the night he was murdered. For the first time, along with the caretaker who found him bleeding, they share their terror – and celebrate their friend
Content: Wrong place, wrong time … Damilola Taylor.Photograph: Tunde Taylor/BBC/Optomen TVView image in fullscreenWrong place, wrong time … Damilola Taylor.Photograph: Tunde Taylor/BBC/Optomen TVTV reviewTelevisionReviewDamilola: The Untold Story review – John Boyega’s trauma after losing his childhood friend is hauntingThe actor and his sister were with the 10-year-old on the night he was murdered. For the first time, along with the caretaker who found him bleeding, they share their terror – and celebrate their friendHannah J DaviesMon 5 Oct 2026 17.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNext month marks 26 years since the killing of 10-year-oldDamilola Taylorprompted a wave of grief and incredulity across the UK. Damilola had arrived in London from Nigeria just a few months earlier, with his mother, Gloria, his brother, Tunde, and his sister, Gbemi. His father, Richard, remained in Lagos, intending – like the patriarchs of many diasporic families – to join his wife and children at a later date. But that reunion would never come.On 27 November 2000, while en route from the local library to the family’s home on the NorthPeckhamEstate in south London, Damilola was set upon by the brothers Ricky and Danny Preddie, 13 and 12 respectively. He was attacked with a glass bottle, severing the femoral artery in his left leg, and was found bleeding heavily in a stairwell. Shortly after, Damilola was pronounced dead at nearby King’s College hospital.This one-off documentary opens with recollections from the friends – then children, now adults in their 30s – who were among the last people to see Damilola alive. Among them is John Boyega, appearing here not as an A-list actor, but as a peer who felt the intense emotional toll of losing Damilola. He says he was “frightened out of my mind … I didn’t know kids could die”.View image in fullscreen‘I didn’t know kids could die’ … John Boyega in Damilola: The Untold Story.Photograph: BBC/Optomen TVThe Boyegas are also of Nigerian heritage; John’s sister Grace recalls sticking up for Damilola at school when other pupils tried to pick on him, at a time when African names and accents could still attract derision from other children (“it was my duty to help him,” she says). Later, Grace would blame herself for not walking her friend to his door that night, crying herself to sleep from grief: “I don’t think, at 10, you understand [what has happened].”These days, Peckham is gentrified in a way that would have been unimaginable in 2000, even as Blair-era neoliberalism made the UK an outwardly more comfortable place to live. Here, however, the North Peckham Estate is not reduced to a cliche of misery and deprivation. Caleb Femi, who grew up on the estate and is now a successful poet, film-maker and photographer, says it was a place that “didn’t sound chaotic; it sounded like everything was working in harmony”. There were working-class families from around the world who had made the area their home, but who were “all North Peckhamers”, he says. Femi remembers Damilola joining their ranks, running and smiling as he explored his new home.It’s a refrain that is repeated by different interviewees here: Damilola running, skipping, carefree, seemingly unfazed by bullying at school and – of course – unaware of the dangers that lay ahead and a crime that would frequently be labelled as an appalling example of “wrong place, wrong time”. The Preddie brothers had been known to the police from a young age and were feared in North Peckham. As Femi says: “The worst [was] possible when they were involved.”View image in fullscreenCaleb Femi in Damilola: The Untold Story.Photograph: BBC/Optomen TVDamilola: The Untold Story swerves true-crime cliches of graphic reconstructions and psychological profiling. Instead, the scenes it chooses to recreate are stylised but disquieting, with Damilola imagined not in bright primary colours, but as a fast-moving figure whose blurry face we never properly see. There is also grainy archive footage of the Boyega kids and Damilola at the then newly opened Peckham library. There is no attempt to sharpen this up, to zoom in or make it more forensic. The fuzzy indistinctness seems to be the point: this is footage that had little meaning at the time, but would later take on a disturbing dimension.Star Wars actor John Boyega on the day his 10-year-old school friend Damilola Taylor was killed: ‘It kept me up at night because I was just with the guy’Read moreThere are stark testimonials not just from the North Peckham kids, but also from the people who would become professionally and personally enmeshed with the case. The caretaker who found Damilola, Bill Casale, says it felt as if the boy “was dying in my arms … I knew he was dying”.Sandra Laville– now a Guardian journalist, then at the Daily Telegraph – speaks to the wider difficulty of getting the media to pay attention: “If it had been a kid in Hampshire, it would have resonated.” That was, until the smiling picture of Damilola in his school uniform, which would become the defining image of him, was released.As shocking as Taylor’s killing was, it was just the beginning of increasing fear and violence in Peckham, of young people feeling that they would be at risk if they didn’t carry weapons. Today, Tunde Taylor is the chair of the board of trustees forthe organisation set up in his brother’s name, a role previously held byhis late father. Distressingly, he says that Richard held him accountable for not protecting his brother and – he adds, blinking back tears – “I still hold myself responsible for it”. If Damilola: The Untold Story makes anything clear, it’s that these adults – once innocent kids – could never have prevented the killing that has haunted them ever since.It hasbeen notedthat the documentary doesn’t interrogate the background of the Preddie brothers – but that is another kind of film, one that doesn’t centre Damilola and his friends. What is clear is that, while his killing may have pushed Boyega and others to better themselves, it also terrified them, haunted them and made them fear that they, too, would lose their lives to senseless violence.Damilola: The Untold Story aired on BBC Two and is available on BBC iPlayerExplore more on these topicsTelevisionTV reviewDamilola TaylorDocumentaryPeckhamLondonFactual TVreviewsShareReuse this content

title: To state school alumni starting university, I say this: be proud of your background | Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett | The Guardian
description: Accusations of classism chime with my experience 20 years ago. So all hail the Bristol graduate awarding state schools red plaques, says Guardian columnist Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett
Author: Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett
Headline: Accusations of classism chime with my experience 20 years ago. So all hail the Bristol graduate awarding state schools red plaques, says Guardian columnist Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett
Content: Students at St Andrews University.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenStudents at St Andrews University.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianOpinionUniversitiesTo state school alumni starting university, I say this: be proud of your backgroundRhiannon Lucy CosslettAccusations of classism chime with my experience 20 years ago. So all hail the Bristol graduate awarding state schools red plaquesMon 5 Oct 2026 08.22 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 14.45 EDTShare“So, where did you go to school?” On the face of it, it doesn’t seem likea loaded question. I was mostly bemused when I first started university 20 years ago and found myself being asked it repeatedly by other students. Why were they so interested? Surely no one would have heard of the north Wales comprehensive I had attended? When they countered my baffled reaction with “Charterhouse” or “Marlborough”, how was I supposed to respond? When one student said, of another, “He went to Winchester, you know”, I stared blankly at him, not understanding why he was telling me about someone else’s day trip to a city in Hampshire (“Oh, did he have a nice time?”). It was strange, new territory.Asking someone where they went to school is often not an innocent question. It is a way of “placing” you on a social scale. As thousands of freshers settle in to their first terms at university, a significant proportion will be battling with this dawning awareness that Britain runs on a network of private schools whose alumni often seem to know, or know of, one another. State-school students might have been dimly aware of it before, but nothing puts it into sharper focus than freshers’ week. It’s clear that little has changed since my own student days. I was saddened to read recent reports ofclassism at St Andrews, which led to a student’s announcement that she would not return this academic year: “Working-class students have been made to feel ashamed of their home life at university,” she said.The pervasiveness of private school culture, as I suppose you could call it, remains nationwide and deeply embedded.It’s a shock, as a young person, to go from being the majority – state-educated – to suddenly feeling like the minority, and in some stark cases being made to feel “less than” as a result. It’s why I admireSophie Pender’s 93% Clubso much. Pender set up the initiative while she was at Bristol University, where she was mocked for her working-class background, to bring renewed focus to the fact that the vast majority of people educated in the UK – 93% in fact – attended state school, and to offer them a professional career mentoring and networking alternative to the “old boys” that is a de facto benefit of private school attendance.Pender’s new campaign, Made in State School, aims to shift attitudes by issuing red plaques to celebrate some of the nation’s finest state school alumni – from David Attenborough and Jacqueline Wilson to Jessica Ennis-Hill and Marcus Rashford. She evenpresented a plaque to Andy Burnhamat the Labour party conference last week. She is right when she says that state schools have a PR problem. They are often framed, in rightwing media especially, as dystopian, rough, a hardship that has to be overcome, as opposed to what they actually are: symbols of British excellence, innovation and creativity.So often the media conversation takes the default assumption that private schools are inherently better than state schools, and that it is always in a child’s best interests to attend one. When you hold opinions like mine – that in rejecting the local state school, you are choosing a form of segregation – they can sometimes feel uncomfortable to express. My industries, media and publishing, are dominated by people who went to private school (half of newspaper columnists are privately educated). Education is a sensitive topic, and this can sometimes have a silencing effect.So allow me to lay my cards on the table. Sending your child to private school encourages them to believe that they are better than other children.We have seen where this leads, in the behaviour of some of ourleading politicians.Thecultures of abusethat have been able to thrive at boarding schools that prioritised reputation and prestige over safety have left many victims in their wake.We should be lauding the benefits of state schools. Being moresocially mixed, they teach children openness and confidence. Being able to interact with people from a huge range of backgrounds is a vital life skill. State school kids are often hilarious – there is a unique sense of humour that comes from inclusion; from having seen it all. In the case of mixed-gender schools, they give you a far more developmentally appropriate understanding of the opposite sex. Perhaps due to a combination of socially repressed poshness or a lack of exposure to girls, the ex-public schoolboys at my university often seemed genuinely terrified of the working-class young women they were now expected to study alongside.I wouldn’t go as far to say that it’s impossible to be cool and to have gone to private school, but let’s be honest, it’s harder. University was the first place I went where privilege was a status symbol, and it was discombobulating to be treated with derision by someone who wouldn’t have lasted two minutes in the roasting competition that was your morning registration. Well, you might say, “cool” shouldn’t matter – but as the Made in State School plaques demonstrate, cool people often go on to do radical, groundbreaking, culture-defining things.I won’t rehash some of the toxic attitudes I experienced that first term, mostly from public schoolboys, but the scales fell from my eyes. Someone with less confidence and weaker politics might have put on a voice and tried to fit in. Which is why I want to say to any university fresher who feels that way now to hold their head high. These people’s parents chose to purchase educational advantage for their offspring – which was their prerogative – but that doesn’t make them better than you. You’ve still ended up in the same place, without the astronomical costs of private school tuition fees and largely off your own back! Being made in state school is something to be proud of. Become comfortable owning it, and using it to lift others up. We’re the 93%, after all.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionRhiannon Lucy Cosslett is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsUniversitiesOpinionPrivate schoolsClass issuesStudent experienceSocial mobilityFreshersHigher educationcommentShareReuse this content

title: ‘I spat in Sean Connery’s face 16 times’: Ron Perlman on making The Name of the Rose | Movies | The Guardian
description: ‘When I couldn’t do the spitting scene, Sean took me aside and said: “Ron, if you don’t actually spit in my face, we’ll be here all day.” So I let one fly – and kept having to redo it’
Author: Chris Broughton
Headline: ‘When I couldn’t do the spitting scene, Sean took me aside and said: “Ron, if you don’t actually spit in my face, we’ll be here all day.” So I let one fly – and kept having to redo it’
Content: ‘I opened the door to find Sean there. He said, “Listen, boy …”’ Connery with Christian Slater in the medieval murder mystery.Photograph: Cinetext/Constantin Film/AllstarView image in fullscreen‘I opened the door to find Sean there. He said, “Listen, boy …”’ Connery with Christian Slater in the medieval murder mystery.Photograph: Cinetext/Constantin Film/AllstarHow we madeMovies‘I spat in Sean Connery’s face 16 times’: Ron Perlman on making The Name of the Rose‘When I couldn’t do the spitting scene, Sean took me aside and said: “Ron, if you don’t actually spit in my face, we’ll be here all day.” So I let one fly – and kept having to redo it’Interviews byChris BroughtonMon 5 Oct 2026 09.53 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 12.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJean-Jacques Annaud,directorI read an article about a curious book that had great reviews in Italy, a murder mystery about monks in the middle ages fighting for the fictional missing part of Aristotle’s Poetics. I said: “This is for me.” Since childhood, I had been fascinated with medieval and religious architecture, and Aristotle’s Poetics is my favourite literary work.I learned that Umberto Eco, the author, was going to be in France for one night and agreed to meet me at his hotel and that I would drive him to Charles de Gaulle airport. The first thing I saw was his shadow on the hotel staircase, which looked like the silhouette of Sherlock Holmes – Umberto was a man of great humour, and he met me wearing a deerstalker, with a pipe in his mouth. In the car, I asked questions: what sort of shoes would the Franciscans have been wearing? Would the monks have had beards? What colour would the pigs have been? He said: “I don’t know, I didn’t have to write any of that.” I ended up hiring medievalistJacques Le Goffand seven of his colleagues to make sure we got all the details right – costumes, architecture, liturgy and so on.double quotation markA big piece of timber fell on Feodor. ‘I’m 80 years old,’ he said, ‘I don’t mind dying. Was the take good?’I wanted an unknown to play William of Baskerville, the friar who investigates the deaths, and travelled the world to watch plays featuring great actors in their 50s. Meanwhile, agent Mike Ovitz kept calling, saying: “Sean Connery would love to make this movie.” Eventually, there was a knock on my door and I opened it to find Sean with the screenplay under his arm. He said, “Listen, boy …” and started reading. I had goose bumps. The way he said the dialogue was exactly what I’d been hearing in my head while reading the book.I flew to Vienna to look at paintings byBruegel the Elder. I wanted to be inspired by the real people of the period, people who had no dentists or doctors, but I did cast some good-looking monks, too. Christian Slater turned up to audition for the young novice, Adso, and said: “I didn’t learn the lines, I got drunk.” The casting director, Mary Jo, was furious and tried to send him away, but he was the one I wanted. He was only 16, but looked 14. It turned out he was Mary Jo’s son. I had three women selected to audition for the part of the nameless girl from the village, but Christian fell in love with the first, Valentina Vargas, as soon as he did a screen test with her, so I never saw the other two.We built a vast set on a hilltop near Rome for the monastery and village. During the scene at the end where the library tower burns, Sean’s cowl briefly caught fire, and a big piece of real timber fell on Feodor Chaliapin Jr, who played the blind monk, knocking him to the ground. “I’m 80 years old,” he said, “I don’t mind dying. Was the take good?” He went to hospital and we had to change the schedule because he then had a scar.After four months in Rome, I went back to my production office in Munich and couldn’t find it. I discovered the film’s producer, Bernd Eichinger, in the cellar with his feet on a table. He said, “JJ, I didn’t want to disturb you during the shoot, but I sold the building to help pay for the movie.”View image in fullscreen‘For my dialogue, I just went: eenie, meenie, miny, moe’ … Ron Perlman with Christian Slater in The Name of the Rose.Photograph: TCD/Prod DB/AlamyRon Perlman, playedSalvatoreMy very first film, Quest for Fire, was directed by Jean-Jacques. I played a caveman. Transforming myself into something completely foreign was an incredibly rewarding exercise and a phenomenal introduction to the world of cinema, so when I read that Jean-Jacques had attached himself to The Name of the Rose, I went through the book and found a character named Salvatore – an intellectually challenged hunchback who spoke in a jumble of seven languages – who would embody a similar challenge. I told Jean-Jacques that this part would be a dream come true.Jean-Jacques gave me complete freedom to figure out my dialogue. The Name of the Rose had been published in 80 languages, so I got copies in the seven thatUmberto Ecohas Salvatore referencing, and circled every time Salvatore spoke. Then I just went, “Eenie, meenie, miny, moe – OK, this word is Latin, this word is Spanish, this word is Italian …” and so on. That was the genesis of Salvatore’s communicative skills.I worked with a dialect coach who was also a historian with particular knowledge of the period. He suggested thelullabythat Salvatore sings when he’s burned at the stake. Jean-Jacques had this idea that Salvatore was so out of touch with reality that he was initially amused to be in that situation. The lullaby gave a sense of childlike wonder at the fact he’s involved in this ceremony, but doesn’t realise he’s about to lose his life.I only had to wear the prosthetic hump once, filming the scene where Salvatore is about to be tortured by F Murray Abraham as the inquisitor, Bernardo Gui. I was in the makeup chair for more than 13 hours and by the time I got to set, they had almost run out of time. My hair was shaved so it looked like I had mange. They said: “Good luck with your personal life, my friend.”I spent every moment I could with Sean Connery, watching him act and listening to his stories. He was my hero, the real deal. When it came to the scene where I had to spit in his eye, I just couldn’t do it. Sean took me aside, and said: “Ron, if you don’t actually spit in my face, we’ll be here all fucking day.” So I finally just let one fly. The problem was, you don’t film from just one angle, you have to recreate in profile, medium shot, closeup, over-the-shoulder … I must have spat in Sean Connery’s face 16 times that day.The Name of the Rose is available now on digital and limited edition 4K UHD and Blu-ray (Second Sight Films)Explore more on these topicsFilmHow we madeSean ConneryChristian SlaterRon PerlmanJean-Jacques AnnaudUmberto EcoFilm adaptationsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘I don’t know how I cooked without it!’: 15 everyday items that make your life a teeny bit better | Life and style | The Guardian
description: Breathable bedding, slanted tweezers and an indispensable garlic press … here are the buys you wish you’d discovered sooner. Plus, the best walking poles, tested
Author: Lucy Pavia
Headline: Breathable bedding, slanted tweezers and an indispensable garlic press … here are the buys you wish you’d discovered sooner. Plus, the best walking poles, tested
Content: A recipe for an easier life: the best buys our readers swear by.Photograph: Giselleflissak/GettyView image in fullscreenA recipe for an easier life: the best buys our readers swear by.Photograph: Giselleflissak/GettyGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The Filter UK newsletterLife and style‘I don’t know how I cooked without it!’: 15 everyday items that make your life a teeny bit betterBreathable bedding, slanted tweezers and an indispensable garlic press … here are the buys you wish you’d discovered sooner. Plus, the best walking poles, testedDon’t get the Filter delivered to your inbox? Sign up hereLucy PaviaMon 5 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSometimes a product changes your life – or, more likely, just makes your day 10% better.Whether it’s something small-but-mighty (a gadget that helps you open a jar without swearing, tweezers that get every hair) or a more expensive item that has proved its worth over the years (a much-loved designer dress, a garden mulch-maker), we asked you to tell us about the buys that have made your life just alittlebit better.And no, none of you has any commercial links to these – we always check.Sleep savers and gym buddiesView image in fullscreenRuff night? Breathable linen sheets could make bedtime more comfortable.Photograph: Evgeniya Pavlova/GettyReaderJanetwishes she’d known about linen sheets fromPiglet in Bedbefore she hit menopause: “All those sweaty nights tossing and turning could have been avoided,” she says. “They are soft, comfortable and, being a natural fabric, keep you cool on hot nights and cosy in the winter.” She also loves hermattress protectorand pillows from Woolroom – “expensive but worth the money”.“I bought a Lanvin dress from its summer 2009 collection,” saysCarolyn Richardson. “It’s never out of fashion and takes me everywhere as it’s unfussy, classic and beautifully tailored.”Stuart Hatcherrecommends three life-changing items: “I bought thisgarlic pressand haven’t looked back – no need for time-consuming chopping,” he says. The second is a pair ofwrist wrapsfor weightlifting. “They cost virtually nothing by comparison with other exercise kit and are so effective.” Finally, thistiny pumpearns him “envious looks at festivals when I effortlessly get my inflatable mattress ready”, he says.View image in fullscreenPressing matter: a good garlic crusher saves time – and your fingers.Photograph: Anna Mardo/GettyMartin Millmorehas also found an indispensablegarlic press. “It minces unpeeled garlic, swipes the garlic off with its plastic blade, and auto-ejects the skin. Best of all, no garlic smell on your hands. It’s life-changing (slightly).”“My George at Asda changing robe (now out of stock) has proved indispensable for city breaks and dog walks,”Diana Lovelocktold us. “It is wind- and waterproof, insulated, and my old-lady phone case fits in the inside pocket. I bought it for a trip to New York, and I felt invincible! The dog is [also] happy because we can go out whatever the weather.”For readersLindsayandLyn, the search for the perfect pair of tweezers is over: “I am the happy owner of a £15blue mini slant pairby Tweezerman,” says Lindsay. “Excellent value for money and quality. I highly recommend.” Lyn says Vitry’sstainless steel slant-end tweezersare “perfect for removing everything from unwanted hair to splinters”.Francesrecommends her Vitrycosmetic pencil sharpener: “For decades I’ve been using regular pencil sharpeners for my brow, lip and eye pencils – usually found in my children’s discarded school pencil cases – which left them blunt and pulverised. Now I don’t have to experience the torment of scraping badly sharpened pencils across my skin.”Kitchen heroes and garden helpersView image in fullscreenWhisk taker: a Danish dough mixer can make light work of bread dough.Photograph: Katelin Kinney/Getty/iStockphotoAnn swears by herDanish dough whisk: “It is so much stronger and easier to use than a wooden spoon, allows me to make no-knead dough with ease and is excellent at whisking. It also makes my cheese sauces lump-free.”For speedy breakfasts,Amanda Nieurzyla-Johnloves her egg cooker: “I use it five to six days a week for all my egg cookery. It can do six hard-, soft-, or medium-boiled eggs, or two poached. It takes the guesswork out of cooking while you concentrate on the rest of the meal. I don’t know how I have cooked all these years without it.” We found a similarSalter egg cookerthat can boil up to six eggs or poach two at a time, and it costs less than £20.If you always struggle to open jars? Get ajar key, saysJennie: “No more RSI. Every home should have one.”And finally, for gardeners, one anonymous reader recommended investing ina shredderto help clear up the mess made by clipping and pruning: “It’s a must-have for generating mulch for flower beds, disposal of branches and hedges.”This week’s picksIs tech the secret to a more analogue life? How gadgets, apps and tips could actually reduce your screen timeJess Cartner-Morley’s October style essentials: glam jeans, an irresistible coat and my shoes of the yearThe best dehumidifiers: 14 favourites to beat damp and cut bills, tested‘It could get an orgasm out of a cabbage’: the best vibrators, tested‘A hefty umami punch’: the best (and worst) supermarket light soy sauce, tasted and ratedTime to ditch the iron? I spent six months testing the best clothes steamers – here are my favouritesThe perfect everyday coffee machine: De’Longhi Magnifica Start review‘I’m in my early 50s. Where do I shop?’: The Guardian’s fashion stylist answered your questionsEditor’s pickView image in fullscreenField work: Sian Lewis testing walking poles in the countryside.Photograph: Jacob Little/The GuardianWalking – or trekking – poles aren’t just for serious mountain-goers. Whoever you are, they can reduce strain on knees and hips, improve balance, and help spread effort across your upper body. They’re especially handy on rocky descents. As autumn kicks in and we head for the hills, our outdoor expert, Sian Lewis, put 10 models to thetest. She hiked at least 10 miles with each across a mix of trails, inclines and surfaces, including mountain tracks in the Lake District and more relaxed rambles on theCotswold Way.Hannah BoothEditor, the FilterIn case you missed it …View image in fullscreenAir apparent: a dehumidifier can help tackle damp and get laundry dry fasterIt’s the season of mist, colour and … damp. A dehumidifier can tackle condensation and musty smells – and it is also great at drying clothes for a fraction of the cost of a tumble dryer, something to bear in mind as we bid farewell to the washing line for a while. Caramel Quintested 14 modelsand rated them on aspects from how well they did the job to how much energy they used.Get involvedView image in fullscreenWishlist: tell us what you’d most like to unwrap this Christmas.Photograph: ArtistGNDphotography/GettyHow old are you and what would you like for Christmas? Whether it’s a Legami pencil case, theatre tickets or a new coffee machine, we want to hear about the one thing you’d love to unwrap this year, whatever your age – from gen alpha to baby boomer. Let us know your age and gift choice (and the reason you want it so much) by emailing us atthefilter@theguardian.com.Explore more on these topicsLife and styleThe Filter UK newsletterHomesBeautyGardensFoodGadgetsKitchen essentialsnewslettersShareReuse this content

title: Badenoch is trying to match Farage step for step – but it’s a dance of death for the Tories | Polly Toynbee | The Guardian
description: At conference here in Birmingham I found a small battalion of centrist remainers with a vision for the Conservative party to come, says Guardian columnist Polly Toynbee
Author: Polly Toynbee
Headline: At conference here in Birmingham I found a small battalion of centrist remainers with a vision for the Conservative party to come, says Guardian columnist Polly Toynbee
Content: Kemi Badenoch addresses the main hall audience on the first day of the Conservative party conference in Birmingham on Sunday.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianView image in fullscreenKemi Badenoch addresses the main hall audience on the first day of the Conservative party conference in Birmingham on Sunday.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianOpinionConservative conference 2026Badenoch is trying to match Farage step for step – but it’s a dance of death for the ToriesPolly ToynbeeAt conference here in Birmingham I found a small battalion of centrist remainers with a vision for the Conservative party to comeMon 5 Oct 2026 12.46 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 17.52 EDTShareYou can walk all the way from Somerset to Sussex without crossing a Tory-run constituency, if you wish. You could also travel through each of the counties of Wiltshire, Hampshire, Dorset and Surrey without setting foot in Tory lands. They are now mainly Liberal Democrat, and there’s not one Tory MP in all of Oxfordshire.Is Kemi Badenoch bothered? Everything she does seems cleverly designed to keep those places lost to her for ever as she woos Reform voters, unsuccessfully. The more she leans right, the more she repels home counties moderates. Those Reform voters are not coming back, psephologists say. Without reclaiming the old “blue wall”, there is no hope, ever, of a Tory majority, say both ProfsTim BaleandRob Fordand just about every political authority you care to ask.Shooting the breeze at the party’s Birmingham conference, you might never guess the Tories still poll four percentage points belowthe last election, the worst resultsince theDuke of Wellington was dismissedin 1830 for rejecting electoral reform and defending every rotten borough.Spot that Wellingtonian legacy inthe interviewBadenoch gave ConservativeHome. “I march to the beat of my own drum,” she says. Indeed she does, but out of step with the public, not condescending to care what it might be thinking and allowing no shade of disagreement. Removing theLords whip from Gavin Barwell, Theresa May’s chief of staff, was a deterrent message to anyone taking part in the “festival of ideas” here, a festival of one idea only. Barwell opposed Badenoch’s edict barring any candidate who supports net zero carbon emissions or staying in the European convention on human rights. “I haven’t left the Conservative party. It has left me,”Barwell tweetedplaintively. It has left a great many others, too.Margaret Thatcher, still holy here, never did that: she had“wets” in her first cabinetand never expelled them from the party. Her ideological obduracy over the poll tax only overcame her later on, and it did for her. But Badenoch is starting out this way. The adulation showered on her by Tories and their press must come from some alternative wonderland where they are notpolling in third place at 19%, while their leader, though improved, scores net -15 – compared withAndy Burnham on +7. In polling, more call her “nasty” or “rude” than “strong” or ‘intelligent”.What demographic is she for? Giving free childcare toparents earning over £100,000will strike most as a grotesque gesture. Only 4% make £100,000 or more:they don’t think themselves wealthy, but the other 96% of people do. The £700m cost of that policy should go to the dwindling number of deprived two-year-olds getting early years support, according to theInstitute for Fiscal Studies. Already, the children of the best-off are eight times more likely to benefit from funded childcare hours than the most disadvantaged,says the New Economics Foundation. Children arriving at school unready are tomorrow’s Neets (16- to 24-year-olds not in education, employment or training). This should have the education secretary, Lucy Powell, rampaging: it’s not about parents, it’s about children’s futures. Badenoch’s pledge to cutsome benefits to “subsistence” leveldeliberately implies the4 million children below the poverty lineare living the life of Riley.Her responses to Burnham are also out of touch with the times – and even withthe Times. While70% want closer relations with the EU, her party shockingly pledges torip up any agreement Burnham makes, sabotaging any trade pact on agri-foods or freedom for the young to travel across Europe. Negotiations are at risk of failure if the EU fears Europhobes might ever regain power and reverse it all.Austerity is still raw in public minds, with overflowing prisons, blocked courts, NHS waiting lists anda million Neets, alongside the housing crisis. What a time for Badenoch to propose£47bn in cuts, with her shadow chancellor now planning even more “in every part of government”.Instead of beckoning back those moderate-minded home counties, she competes punch for punch with Nigel Farage. Last week, she strippeddown the aid budget to £1bntoequal Farage’s policy. Look at their arms race to demolish the civil service: Badenoch started last year by pledging to cut132,000 civil service jobs, return it to pre-Brexit levels (before all the mundane EU agencies we quit – medicines, chemical safety etc – had to be replicated). Farage was due tocut a mere 68,500until Danny Kruger upped theante last month to 250,000in his “Storm and Sunshine” policy. The latest? The Tories just pledged to kill offthe Environment Agency, Natural Englandandthe Climate Change Committee. What do the home counties think of that?This contest for lowest taxes, smallest state, toughest stance on migrants, harshest welfare cuts and deepest loathing of young people will spiral downwards towards something new and dangerous. Modern British politics has never before had rightwing parties competing as equals. But locked in this dance of death, the politics of bile carries them further from most voters. Tories are dying out:63 is now the median ageof Badenoch’s voters, while Labour’s is 46.If nothing improves by next conference, the mirage of Badenoch’s rock-solid support will melt away. But what would replace her? Waiting in the wings there is a model of what a Conservative revival might look like –Prosper UK, launched in January.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIt tiptoes, praising Badenoch loudly, yet it is running seven events at this conference. That included a small Sunday night rally for electoral reform. It was addressed by former West Midlands mayor Andy Street, now co-chair of Prosper UK with Ruth Davidson It is backed by a formidable array of what was once the One Nation group, now defunct in parliament – or dormant under Badenoch’s rightwards march. No MPs back Prosper UK in public, but the group claims a third of them do secretly, alongwith 30,000 declared supporters. David Gauke, vice chair, has crept back into the party – he thinks by accident when the membership computer processing his re-application didn’t register he’d been ejected in 2019. In returning, he joined a battalion of remainer luminaries of the centre-right who’d had the whip suspended at the same time, including Kenneth Clarke and Dominic Grieve.Gauke travels the country speaking to Conservative associations and others. Prosper UK is pro-EU, pro-migration for skilled workers and foreign students, pro-net zero and against the pension triple lock – and Gauke says that “Conservatives should be truth tellers on all these”. But though socially liberal, he’s dry as a bone on fiscal discipline, campaigning for low business taxes, a smaller state and enticing back non-doms – all Hayek, no Keynes. “No one speaks for some 7 million people centre or centre-right,” he says.Indeed, the country needs a plausibly electable Tory party to put up a fight against Faragism, not a carbon copy of it. If Badenoch is not for turning, to survive it will need to turn her out.Polly Toynbee is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsConservative conference 2026OpinionKemi BadenochAndy BurnhamcommentShareReuse this content

title: ‘I didn’t know what to do’: collapse of providers of high-end digs leaves students in shock | Student housing | The Guardian
description: Cost of living crisis and drop in international students hits market for purpose-built accommodation
Author: Julia Kollewe
Headline: Cost of living crisis and drop in international students hits market for purpose-built accommodation
Content: A string of tower blocks known as purpose-built student accommodation, targeted at more affluent students, have run into financial difficulty.Composite: Guardian Design/AlamyView image in fullscreenA string of tower blocks known as purpose-built student accommodation, targeted at more affluent students, have run into financial difficulty.Composite: Guardian Design/AlamyStudent housing‘I didn’t know what to do’: collapse of providers of high-end digs leaves students in shockCost of living crisis and drop in international students hits market for purpose-built accommodationJulia KolleweMon 5 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 14.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“It was dead in the middle of summer, it was a shock,” says Nathalie Sriwiboonrattan. The fourth-year game design student at Abertay University was at home with her family thousands of miles away in Thailand when she discovered the owner of her Scottish studio flat had abruptly gone bust.“I was like, my hands are tied. I’m not in the country. I don’t know what to do,” she says. Sriwiboonrattan was forced to act quickly to secure new housing for the academic year, which has just begun, paying £850 to have her possessions moved.Her sudden upheaval was emblematic of the wider crisis in student housing. While UK universities facea financial crisis, providers of accommodation are grappling withfalling international student numbers, a cost of living squeeze and higher borrowing and build costs, exacerbated by the Iran war, affecting upgrades at older properties.A string of tower blocks known as purpose-built student accommodation (PBSA), targeted at more affluent students, have run into financial difficulty.It had been touted as the ultimate student living: smart city centre blocks with gyms, cinemas and rooftop terraces have sprung up across the UK. A world away from the traditional image ofdirty and dingy shared digs, the flats have offered a spacious alternative for their relatively affluent residents – often international students. Now, some sit half empty, andseveral schemes have gone bust.Sriwiboonrattan was among nearly 70 students in Dundeewho were left scrambling to find accommodationin late July after the collapse of the owner of Marketgait Apartments, a 116-room city centre block that had a concierge and a shared games lounge with a pool table.Despite the boom in housing developed by financial institutions in recent years, many students heading off to university this term faced a different dilemma. Rents at the tower blocks have grown much faster than maintenance loans for British students, leaving PBSAs financially out of reach.Meanwhile, the cost of living crisis has putfinancial pressure on studentsseeking university-owned or managed accommodation, while rising rents have hit those wanting to live in shared private rentals. Underlining the scale of the shortage of affordable housing, the students’ union in Bristol included an emergency support number for the housing charity Shelter in an email to new students.At PBSAs, the national average rent, excluding London, is £191 a week including bills, according to the website StuRents.At the top end,en suite rooms in Manchester command a weekly rent of £170 to £320, whereas in London,en suite rooms are £250 to £650 a week, and studio apartments in Bloomsbury cost between £550 and £800 plus.“I wasn’t able to get into PBSA because it is very expensive in Birmingham,” says Soham Chougale, 23, a student at University College Birmingham. “I am an international student, so my working hours are capped at 20 hours [a week in term time], which means I can’t afford to live in PBSA,” says Chougale, the education officer at UCB Guild ofStudents.He lived in university-owned dorms for the first two years of his aviation management degree and now shares a two-bedroom privately rented flat with a friend. On campus, he paid £660 rent including bills a month during the first year, which rose by 10% in his second year; now he pays £700 rent a month, excluding bills.View image in fullscreenSoham Chougale ‘wasn’t able to get into PBSA because it is very expensive in Birmingham’.While living on campus “gave me the best feeling of community” and “I still have those friends that I met on the first day”, the wifi was patchy, some facilities were broken and there was a mouse infestation, he recounts.“PBSA can be quite pricey,” says Matthew Pointon, a real estate analyst at Capital Economics, but adds: “Normally professionally managed buildings are better in terms of quality.”In London, which attracts the richest students, there is still demand for upmarket accommodation, but outside the capital, there is an oversupply in some cities, such as Coventry, Leeds and Nottingham.This week, university staff beganstrikes in Dundee, Edinburgh and Nottinghamover budget cuts, with the industrial action threatening to wipe out a term of teaching for many students.In Nottingham, demand has fallen from a pandemic peak of 46,295 beds in 2022-23 to 42,290 beds in 2025-26, while 7,700 more PBSA beds came on to the market, the student housing charity Unipol calculated.The number of students arriving from China has stagnated, and those from the new growth countries India, Pakistan and Nigeria aremuch more cost-conscious than the pre-Covid students from China, says Martin Blakey, an adviser on student living and the former chief executive of Unipol.Deniz Yalçın, the chair of the Newington-Meadows branch of the Living Rent union in Edinburgh, says: “In Edinburgh, we’re seeing an explosion of PBSA despite the fact that this type of development is not needed and actually fuels the housing affordability crisis here.“Many of them lie empty during most of the year,using the Fringe [festival]to bolster profits. Some have even been bought by the council to become temporary housing.”graph showing rise in loan balances 2021-2026Richard Ward, the head of research at StuRents, says the key issue is the big gap between maintenance loans and rents, after double-digit rental growth at PBSA blocks and shared houses in recent years.Maintenance loanshave declined in real termsbecause of below-inflation increases and frozen parental income thresholds. “And what have we seen?More students commuting,” Ward says. “Outside of London, you’re talking about £300 rent a week to make a new PBSA scheme viable. Well, your average British student is paying about £160 a week.”Occupancy rates at the tower blocks range between 71.3% in Glasgow, 69.9% in Coventry, 89.7% in Bristol and 95.3% in Exeter, as of August, according to StuRents.Student housing providers are increasingly focusing on the cities with the best universities. Unite Group, the UK’s largest developer and manager of student accommodation, has stepped up sales of unwanted sites.The loss-making group aims to slim down its portfolio to 55,000-60,000 beds in 20 cities compared with 72,000 beds in 29 cities at present, “to increase alignment to the UK’s strongest universities, where student demand is robust and growing”. Unitereduced rents and tenancy lengthsin Nottingham, Leicester and Sheffield, the “most challenging” cities, earlier this year, and rooms start from £99 a week in Coventry.About 95% of new student beds are being built in cities with Russell Group universities, up from 81% last year, according to the property agency Knight Frank, by investors such as Blackstone, KKR and Greystar. The Russell Group is an association of 24 established UK universities including Cambridge, Oxford, Durham, Edinburgh, Manchester and King’s College London.Smaller PBSA operators are struggling, with average occupancy levels of 85% across the sector, Unipol estimates. The housing association Sanctuary has been trying to sell student assets of more than 5,600 beds, across 21 properties in eight locations across the UK, for nearly two years, and in July said the buyer had “sought to revisit pricing assumptions” citing changes in economic and market conditions.Investors poured £164m into the PBSA sector between April and June, one of the lowest quarterly levels on record, although total investment of £2.3bn in the first half was ahead of 2025, according to Knight Frank research. Only 13 deals were completed during the second quarter.In response to the sector’s headwinds, several PBSA owners plan to rent some floors to young professionals, while one block in Leeds that is only 50% fullcould partly be used for short-term hotel stays.In Dundee, Sriwiboonrattan has found alternative accommodation – a studio in the nearby Parklands block – which has a sky lounge with city views, gym and rooftop terrace – where she is paying weekly rent of £240, with financial support from her family. At Marketgait, she says the “walls were thin” with noise coming in from neighbours and lifts unreliable, so she prefers her new surroundings now the initial shock has dissipated.GraphicOthers still face a bleak picture, with the freshers’ week parties fading into the memory and the academic year now in full swing. Lewis Wilson, the vice-president for higher education at the National Union of Students, says: “The whole system is broken around student finance and student loans. Some students are going homeless, some students are relying on food banks.” A quarter of student unions now provide a food bank or food pantry.Wilson, who graduated from the University of Sussex two years ago with a law degree, argues that PBSAs need to be better regulated, and become more affordable. “For the students on lower incomes like I was, I would never have been able to afford a PBSA,” he says.The government says: “We expect higher education providers to consider the supply, and affordability of student accommodation in relation to their anticipated student intakes and across all years of study at least five years ahead.“Recognising the inherent uncertainties in student demand and housing delivery timelines, providers should engage with the local planning authority on need.”Explore more on these topicsStudent housingHousingUK cost of living crisisStudentsHigher educationUniversitiesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Green party of England and Wales facing international ostracism over ‘Zionism is racism’ vote | Green party | The Guardian
description: European Green party says motion goes against its policy, with German Green co-leader calling it ‘intolerable and unacceptable’
Author: Aletha Adu
Headline: European Green party says motion goes against its policy, with German Green co-leader calling it ‘intolerable and unacceptable’
Content: Zack Polanski speaking at the Green party conference in Brighton.Photograph: Phil Lewis/SOPA Images/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenZack Polanski speaking at the Green party conference in Brighton.Photograph: Phil Lewis/SOPA Images/ShutterstockGreen partyGreen party of England and Wales facing international ostracism over ‘Zionism is racism’ voteEuropean Green party says motion goes against its policy, with German Green co-leader calling it ‘intolerable and unacceptable’Zack Polanski may rue lack of leadership when Greens needed him to actAletha Adu,Peter WalkerandDeborah ColeMon 5 Oct 2026 15.10 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe English and Welsh Greens are facing international ostracism after adopting a policy declaring Zionism as a form of racism, which has drawn dismay from the group representing European Greens.Head of Jewish Greens says she may leave party over ‘Zionism is racism’ voteRead moreThe co-leader of the German Greens separately said the policy was “intolerable and unacceptable”, running contrary to its belief in the right ofIsraelto exist.The binding policy motionpassed in a vote at the Greens’ conferencein Brighton on Sunday. Four of the party’s five MPs opposed it.The policy saysZionism, the movement for a Jewish state, should be “treated as any other form of racism”, and backs a single democratic Palestinian state across historic Palestine “with equal rights for all”.The EuropeanGreen party, which represents 47 parties, including the Green party of England and Wales (GPEW), said it supported a two-state solution for Israel and Palestine, and the new motion went against this.The alliance “will immediately demand clarity from the leadership and parliamentary group of GPEW, to understand the official party policy of GPEW, how they position themselves towards the self-determination of Israelis and Jews as well as the protection of Jewish people and members in the party”, it said in a statement.View image in fullscreenFelix Banaszak, the co-leader of the German Greens, said the policy ‘runs counter to what the European Green party stands for’.Photograph: snapshot/Future Image/M Behrens/ShutterstockFelix Banaszak, the leader of the German Greens, known formally as Alliance 90/the Greens, told a press conference the motion was “intolerable and unacceptable”.“It runs counter to everything that Alliance 90/the Greens stands for inGermany, and it also runs counter to what the European Green party stands for,” he added.Banaszak said: “There is a widely held view within the European Green party that Israel has a right to exist and that this right must not be undermined.” His party would “approach our partner parties in Europe to clarify how to deal with this”.Sandy Ruthven, the chair of Amnesty International UK’s charitable trust and a longstanding Green member, resigned over the motion and accused the party of failing to confront antisemitism.The fallout from Sunday’s vote has also intensified a debate over whether the Greens’ highly decentralised policymaking structures remain suitable for a party whose membership has expanded rapidly.View image in fullscreenEllie Chowns, who opposed the motion, said the party’s policymaking ‘urgently needs to be modernised’.Photograph: Ellie & Adrian 2025/PAPolicy is made at the party’s two annual conferences, which generally involve a small proportion of members. The Zionism motion won just over 1,000 votes, approximately 0.4% of the total membership.Ellie Chowns, a former co-leader, said the party’s governance and policymaking “urgently need to be modernised”.“As a party we pride ourselves on our democratic member-led policymaking process, but I do think we need to ask ourselves some searching questions when less than 1% of our members actually participate,” Chowns, the Green MP for North Herefordshire, told the Guardian. “This is long overdue and has become even more urgent with the huge expansion of our membership.”Chowns said she understood the concerns of European Greens, which she shared, but stressed: “There is still much more that unites us than divides us.”One source in the party said the criticism from European Greens, especially those in Germany, was understandable given their differing stances on Gaza and Israel.They said: “The German Greens support arming Israel, opposed a ceasefire to Israel’s onslaught on Gaza, backed the suspension of funding to Unrwa and co-sponsored a Bundestag resolution describing the arguments and methods of the peaceful, Palestinian-led BDS campaign as antisemitic.”Any change to internal party structures would be hard to implement. One Green insider said that to give MPs greater authority over members would undermine the party’s commitment to grassroots democracy. However, they said the existing model could produce a lack of coherence and strategic direction, while giving a disproportionate influence to members with the most time to participate in policymaking.They suggested members could determine broad strategic priorities, with smaller bodies developing detailed policy while remaining accountable to the membership.View image in fullscreenThe Green party leader, Zack Polanski,who missed the vote himself, earlier addressed the conference alongside the MPs Hannah Spencer, left, and Siân Berry, right. Berry opposed the motion.Photograph: Sean Smith/The GuardianAnother senior Green defended the party’s model of direct democracy, arguing that allowing members to determine policy was fundamental to the party’s character.What is Zionism and why do some critics describe it as racist?Read moreDaniel Schuster, the regional director of the Simon Wiesenthal Center’s European office, said: “The British Green party’s decision to formally classify Zionism as a form of racism is absurd, not based on any logical basis and is itself racist. And timing, just days before the third anniversary of the 7 October terrorist Hamas attacks, is designed to inflict pain on a deeply solemn occasion.“Branding Zionism itself as racism crosses a profoundly consequential line. It takes a movement for Jewish national self-determination and transforms it into something for which Jews are expected to apologise. We will not.”In a statement, the Green party leader in England and Wales, Zack Polanski, said: “Antisemitism and criticism of the Israeli state are, and must always be, completely distinct – blurring the line between the two is not only wrong but antisemitic, and makes Jewish people less safe. It’s our role as a movement for justice to protect both the rights of Palestinians and our Jewish communities here in the UK. As leader I will not accept any exclusion, or refusal to engage with anyone, because of the religious or communal body they are part of.”He added: “Through the Green party’s unified stance and dedicated pressure, we have begun to shift this government away from its complicity with the Israeli government’s atrocities in Gaza, with the foreign secretary now taking the long overdue step of ending trade with illegal settlements.”Explore more on these topicsGreen partyRaceAntisemitismGermanyEuropeIsraelJudaismnewsShareReuse this content

title: Jeffrey Archer, former Conservative politician and novelist, dies aged 86 | Jeffrey Archer | The Guardian
description: Publisher says author died peacefully at home ‘between writing sessions’
Author: Harry Cockburn
Headline: Publisher says author died peacefully at home ‘between writing sessions’
Content: Jeffrey Archer in his penthouse suite on the Albert Embankment, London in September 2018.Photograph: Geoff Pugh/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenJeffrey Archer in his penthouse suite on the Albert Embankment, London in September 2018.Photograph: Geoff Pugh/ShutterstockJeffrey ArcherJeffrey Archer, former Conservative politician and novelist, dies aged 86Publisher says author died peacefully at home ‘between writing sessions’Harry CockburnMon 5 Oct 2026 18.31 EDTFirst published on Mon 5 Oct 2026 16.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJeffrey Archer, the bestselling author and former MP whose political career ended in disgrace when he was imprisoned for perjury, has died at the age of 86.Archer, who was a Conservative MP for five years before serving as the party’s deputy chair, died “suddenly and peacefully” at his home “between writing sessions” on Monday, his publisher HarperCollins said.He had a successful career as an author and was made a life peer in 1992.During a run to become mayor of London for theConservativesin 1999, his political career was in effect ended when it emerged he had lied in court over a decade earlier when a newspaper accused him of paying money to a sex worker. He was convicted of perjury and perverting the course of justice and imprisoned for four years.An Old Bailey jury found that he had lied in a libel action he had brought against the Star newspaper in 1987 in which he had been awarded £500,000 in damages.View image in fullscreenJeffrey Archer with his wife, Mary, arriving at the high court for the eighth day of his libel action against the Star newspaper and its editor, Lloyd Turner.Photograph: PAHe was released early in 2003 and returned to the House of Lords until he retired in 2024.Kate Elton, HarperCollins UK’s chief executive and Archer’s editor, said: “It has been one of the great privileges of my publishing life to have been Jeffrey Archer’s editor.“He was the master storyteller and an editor’s dream – phenomenally hard-working, utterly committed to completing draft after draft to get every word as perfect as possible, and a true champion of the team nature of great publishing.”Archer’s death came just one day before the publication of his new novel, Adam and Eve, on Tuesday 6 October.His first novel, Not a Penny More, Not a Penny Less, was published in 1976, two years after bankruptcy marked the end of his time as a sitting MP. This marked the beginning of an enviable writing career. Archer spent a total of 14 years and five months on the Sunday Times bestseller lists and over five years on the New York Times bestseller lists, selling 300 million books in 119 countries in 49 languages. His 1979 novel Kane and Abel remains among the best-selling books in the world, having sold more than 30 million copies to date.View image in fullscreenJeffrey Archer arrives for the funeral of Katharine, Duchess of Kent at Westminster Cathedral, London on 16 September 2025.Photograph: Karwai Tang/WireImageHis death came less than 24 hours after Archer had met and signed books for hundreds of fans at a sold-out event with broadcaster Gyles Brandreth at the Leicester Square Theatre in central London on Sunday, HarperCollins said.Writing on X, Brandreth said: “Just yesterday I did a show with Jeffrey Archer to celebrate his new novel –he said it was to be his last.“He was in the most wonderful, ebullient form and had such a great reception from a packed house. He was funny, engaging and self-deprecating – a great storyteller to the last.”Archer was first elected an MP in a 1969 byelection for the constituency of Louth in Lincolnshire when he was 29 years old, having already worked as a Conservative councillor for Havering in north-east London, a period during which he also ran a Mayfair art gallery.Archer cast himself as a centrist in parliament, frequently rebelling against the right wing of the Conservative party, but his political career stalled when he became the victim of a fraudulent investment scheme, which left him almost half a million pounds in debt. He said he would therefore not stand in the 1974 election “due to financial difficulties”.His first novel was a direct effort to regain financial control – a move that paid off, and Not a Penny More, Not a Penny Less was adapted for radio, and later, for TV. By the mid-1980s Archer had written several successful novels as well as short stories, plays and children’s books.As his literary career bore fruit, Archer returned to politics, becoming a popular speaker at grassroots events, leading Margaret Thatcher to appoint him deputy chairman of the Conservative party in 1985.But in October 1986 he became embroiled in scandal when the News of the World claimed he’d spent £2,000 to pay off a “vice girl”, a story immediately followed by a more detailed story in the Star alleging Archer had paid a woman named Monica Coghlan for sex. Archer sued the Star, and the case came to court the following year, winning £500,000 in damages but sowing the seeds for his downfall over a decade later.When the allegations broke, the leader of the Conservative party at the time, William Hague, expelled Archer from the party saying: “This is the end of politics for Jeffrey Archer. I will not tolerate such behaviour in my party.”At the time he was charged in 2000, he was also making headlines by starring in his own West End play The Accused, which ran at the Theatre Royal Haymarket in London, and in which Archer’s character played an alleged murderer on trial and in which the audience voted on whether they believed Archer’s character was guilty or innocent at the end of each performance.Archer’s perjury trial began on 30 May 2001, a month after Monica Coghlan was killed in a road traffic accident.Following sentencing he was imprisoned at Belmarsh, a category A prison in London but later moved to four other prisons before his release in 2003, having served half of his sentence.Despite retaining his seat in the House of Lords, Archer did not take an active role in the upper chamber of parliament and gave up his seat in 2024.The former Tory minister, Nadhim Zahawi, paid tribute to Archer, writing on X: “Jeffrey Archer was a dear friend and an extraordinary human being. His gift for storytelling was matched by his wit, warmth and boundless energy. Life was never dull in Jeffrey’s company.”Archer had been due to be at the Cheltenham festival later in the month to discuss his forthcoming novel.Archer is survived by his wife, Mary, and their sons, William and James.Explore more on these topicsJeffrey ArcherConservativesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Flávio Bolsonaro poised to win Brazilian presidency after shock first-round victory | Flávio Bolsonaro | The Guardian
description: Progressive voters and supporters of incumbent president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva left reeling after far-right surge
Author: Tom Phillips
Headline: Progressive voters and supporters of incumbent president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva left reeling after far-right surge
Content: Flávio Bolsonaro received 47% of the vote – 56.1m votes – compared with Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s 45% (53.8m).Photograph: Diego Herculano/ReutersView image in fullscreenFlávio Bolsonaro received 47% of the vote – 56.1m votes – compared with Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s 45% (53.8m).Photograph: Diego Herculano/ReutersFlávio BolsonaroFlávio Bolsonaro poised to win Brazilian presidency after shock first-round victoryProgressive voters and supporters of incumbent president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva left reeling after far-right surgeTom PhillipsandTiago Rogeroin Rio de JaneiroMon 5 Oct 2026 16.06 EDTFirst published on Mon 5 Oct 2026 12.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFlávio Bolsonaro is in pole position to win Brazil’s presidential election, after a far-right tsunami propelled him to a shock first-round victory over the incumbent,Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, leaving progressive voters reeling.The 45-year-old rightwing candidate received 56.1m votes to Lula’s 53.8m – 47.03% to 45.16% – meaning the 80-year-old leftwinger has a mountain to climb if he is to bounce back in the second round on 25 October. Never, since the return of democracy toBrazilin 1985, has the first-round runner-up managed to turn the game around and win the second ballot.“Miracles are possible in politics. But I don’t see that happening,” the political scientist Miguel Lago said of Lula’s chances of snapping back. “I don’t see Flávio losing this election now.”Speaking outside the White House on Monday, Donald Trump told reporters: “Well, it’s a big victory: close but a very, very big victory. Amazing, actually.”Trump, who is a longtime ally of the Bolsonaro family, predicted the runoff would be “a very close election”.The far-right surge was a triumph – albeit an incomplete one – for the Bolsonaro clan and its 71-year-old patriarch,Jair Bolsonaro.View image in fullscreenSupporters of Flávio Bolsonaro celebrate the first-round results in Porto Alegre on Sunday.Photograph: Sílvio Ávila/AFP/Getty ImagesThe disgraced ex-president, who is serving a 27-year sentence for plotting a coup after losing the 2022 election to Lula, saw four relatives elected to congress. His 44-year-old wife, Michelle Bolsonaro, won a seat in the senate, as did his second son, Carlos Bolsonaro, who is 43. Bolsonaro’s youngest son, 28-year-old Jair Renan Bolsonaro, and the ex-president’s 62-year-old brother, Renato Bolsonaro, both won seats in the lower house of congress.Across Latin America’s biggest democracy, key congressional and gubernatorial races were also won by staunchBolsonaristasincluding Tarcísio de Freitas, who was re-elected as the governor of São Paulo state, and Sérgio Moro, who was elected governor of the southern state of Paraná. Both men were ministers during Bolsonaro’s 2018-22 government.Bolsonaro’s Liberal party (PL) will now boast the largest caucus in the senate with 28 of its 81 seats. Combined with the seats of other hard-right parties, that number rises to 43, giving the movement an upper house majority.A map graphic breaking down the results by municipalityMeanwhile, pro-Lula senate candidates, including the former environment minister Marina Silva, the leftwing veteran Benedita da Silva, and the centrist former planning minister Simone Tebet, suffered bitter defeats.Nikolas Ferreira and Lucas Pavanato, two youngBolsonaristasocial media warriors, became the best-voted congresspeople in Brazilian history, securing more than 3m votes.“We are experiencing a revolution …The far rightis growing in a very consistent way, election after election,” said Lago, calling the election the worst for progressive and moderate centrist parties since the late 80s.View image in fullscreenNikolas Ferreira, a 30-year-old congressman from Minas Gerais, is seen as one of the most influential members of the Bolsonarista right; he has more than 5 million followers on Instagram.Photograph: Alan Lima/The GuardianLago believed Lula had managed to interrupt the advance of Bolsonaro’s populist movement in 2022, thanks to positive voter memories of his first two terms, from 2002 to 2010. Back then, a global commodities boom allowed Brazil’s first working-class president to fund major social welfare programmes that helped millions escape poverty. “Butit was just an interregnum,” Lago said.Control of the senate should allow pro-Bolsonaro politicians to approve an amnesty for their movement’s charismatic leader, allowing the former president to emerge from the Brasília mansion where he is living under house arrest and reassert his leadership of the far right.A bar graph showing the proportion of votes won by candidate“I think he will be freed and I think he will be very important during Flávio Bolsonaro’s [presidency],” said Lago. “Flávio will be running the country and [Jair] Bolsonaro will be doing what he has always done: leading the revolution.”The senate majority may also help Bolsonaro’s third son, Eduardo Bolsonaro, return from self-imposed exile in the US. The 42-year-old, who has close ties to Donald Trump’s Maga movement, was sentenced in absentia to four years in prison earlier this year for coercion – the result of his lobbying the Trump administration to interfere in his father’s coup trial. Eduardo Bolsonaro reportedly hopes to become foreign minister if his brother wins the presidency.The result is good news for Trump, who has been accused of trying to sway the election in Bolsonaro’s favour, and his attempt to expand the conservative “orange wave” sweeping Latin America to its biggest democracy and economy. Recent years have seen a succession of pro-Trump presidents win power in the region, from Costa Rica, Honduras and El Salvador to Chile and Colombia.View image in fullscreenEduardo Bolsonaro, seen here at the Conservative Political Action Conference (Cpac) in Buenos Aires in 2024, reportedly hopes to become foreign minister if his brother wins the presidency.Photograph: Juan Mabromata/AFP/Getty ImagesOne of Trump’s most enthusiastic regional cheerleaders, the Argentinian president, Javier Milei, celebrated Bolsonaro’s “historic” victory against “the communist Lula”. “The American continent belongs to citizens who want to live in freedom,” Milei wrote on X.The prime minister of Israel, Benjamin Netanyahu, wished Bolsonaro “good luck in the final” and celebrated his “great victory”. He wrote on X: “I look forward to restoring the extraordinary friendship between Israel and Brazil.”Speaking after Sunday’s result was confirmed, Lula put a brave face on what analysts called a catastrophic night for the left. “From tomorrow we will launch a new campaign: [and in] a campaign with only two candidates we will be able to show the difference between our proposals for Brazil,” he said, vowing to expose his rival’s “dark past”, which involves well-documented ties to members of Rio’s underworld and corruption allegations, which Bolsonaro has denied.View image in fullscreenLuiz Inácio Lula da Silva said his Workers’ party ‘will launch a new campaign’.Photograph: Xinhua/ShutterstockBut the mood at Lula’s post-election event wasreportedly funerealand Bolsonaro goes into the second round as the firm favourite. He is likely to be boosted by the migration of votes from the election’s other rightwing candidates – Ronaldo Caiado, Renan Santos and Romeu Zema – who, between them, won more than 5.5m votes.Santos quickly announced he would endorse neither candidate, considering both Lula and Bolsonaro to be “crooks”. Zema has vowed to vote against Lula’s Worker’s party (PT) in the runoff, while Caiado has yet to declare his intentions.Lula’s best hope may be convincing some of the record 33 million Brazilians who did not vote to turn out next time. “He will need to mobilise these apathetic voters who, in a sense, have already abandoned politics, which will be an extremely difficult task,” said Camila Rocha, a political scientist who studies Brazil’s new right.Rocha has spent recent months interviewing undecided voters and identified “a great deal of voter apathy, especially among those who are not aligned withBolsonarismo, and who could potentially vote for Lula”.Although Flávio Bolsonaro has held political office for more than 20 years, “for undecided voters, his main positive characteristic is this idea of ‘renewal’, despite his possible involvementin corruptionand withparamilitary groups,” Rocha added.Lago believed only a dramatic shift from Lula’s campaign – such as changing the candidate, or a severe scandal involving Bolsonaro – could change the election’s outcome. But he was doubtful that would occur.Explore more on these topicsFlávio BolsonaroLuiz Inácio Lula da SilvaBrazilThe far rightJair BolsonaroAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: Tory shadow minister claims Luton has ‘no-go zones’ where ‘white people won’t go’ | Conservative conference 2026 | The Guardian
description: Blake Stephenson tells fringe meeting at Tory conference that the town is ‘a very dangerous place’ with ‘ghettoes’
Author: Rajeev Syal
Headline: Blake Stephenson tells fringe meeting at Tory conference that the town is ‘a very dangerous place’ with ‘ghettoes’
Content: Blake Stephenson was appointed to the Tory frontbench two weeks ago.Photograph: Roger Harris/Roger Harris PhotographyView image in fullscreenBlake Stephenson was appointed to the Tory frontbench two weeks ago.Photograph: Roger Harris/Roger Harris PhotographyConservative conference 2026Tory shadow minister claims Luton has ‘no-go zones’ where ‘white people won’t go’Blake Stephenson tells fringe meeting at Tory conference that the town is ‘a very dangerous place’ with ‘ghettoes’Rajeev SyalHome affairs editorMon 5 Oct 2026 14.06 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA shadow Conservative Home Office minister has claimed there are “no-go zones” inLutonwhere “white people won’t go”.Blake Stephenson, the MP for Mid Bedfordshire who was appointed to the Tory frontbench role two weeks ago, claimed the town was “a very dangerous place” where some communities “live in ghettoes”.His comments,made at a fringe meetingat the Conservative party conference, mirror claims by far-right activists including from the terrorist mass murderer Anders Breivik, who have also said Luton has “no-go zones”. These claims have been denied by the local police force as well as local Muslim and Christian groups.Speaking at a Centre for Policy Studies meeting in Birmingham, Stephenson claimed to know Luton well because he lives in a neighbouring constituency. “I know Luton reasonably well because I live 10, 15 minutes away and represent Mid Bedfordshire, I live in a village just over the border.“I think the town is a shadow of its former self. There are parts of that town – and unfortunately the police will tell you this – it can be a very dangerous place. There are parts where white people won’t go. They are like no-go zones. It is not alone, there are other towns across the country in a similar situation. It is dreadful where we have got to.“But we can move on from it but it requires deep levels of integration and we need to break apart these, erm … this is where it gets icky, but we need to make sure we don’t have ghettoes where there are no-go zones for anybody. The country is for all of us not just certain communities,” he said.“It does get icky for some people, but I think there is a consensus, certainly on the right, that mass migration has been an absolute disaster.“So it’s up to us to put a plan together and deliver. We’ve got the borders plan. You know, some of that may feel a bit icky for some people, but we’ve got to face into it, lean into it,” he said.In a statement delivered to court in Oslo in 2012, Breivik asked his audience to look at Luton “and the more than 1,000 Islamic no-go zones where police do not dare pass through”. The city was, he said, living in “warlike conditions”.Bedfordshire police said in a statement at the time that “no-go areas do not exist in Bedfordshire”.Tommy Robinson, whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, co-founded the far-right English Defence League in Luton in 2009, and claimed there were “no-go zones” for white people in the town.Stephenson, who was elected as an MP in 2024, studied industrial relations with politics at the University of Kent, followed by law at the University of Law in Guildford. He was called to the bar in 2007.He was appearing at a fringe meeting entitled From Boriswave to Brain Drain: How Can We Fix Migration?Earlier in the discussion, Stephenson said the Equalities Act had created a framework where “white young men” were being discriminated against, and claimed the government was reserving internships for racial minorities.“You know, equality should be equality for all. It’s a fairly, fairly simple concept, but it’s actually become quite a complicated construct. And the people that are losing out are white young men,” he said.He claimed that some government schemes did not allow young white men to apply. “I’m not surprised that young white men feel like the system is rigged against them, particularly with the government coming out with schemes that won’t allow them to apply for internships. That is state-sponsored racism and it needs to stop,” he said.The Conservative party has been approached for comment.Sarah Owen, the Labour MP for Luton North, said: “It is deeply irresponsible for any politician, let alone a senior Conservative, to peddle the same rightwing nonsense about Luton that we see from the likes of Yaxley-Lennon and Reform.“It is simply untrue and the shadow Home Office minister should get off social media and get to know the fantastic Lutonians I’m proud to represent and call my neighbours. I’d also call on the new Lib Dem/Tory/Green coalition-run council in Luton to disown these comments from their colleague.”Explore more on these topicsConservative conference 2026LutonConservativesImmigration and asylumnewsShareReuse this content

title: Trump approval ratings plummet to new low, polls show | Donald Trump | The Guardian
description: President says ‘I’m doing great’ despite polls showing 32% approval rating and loss of support from 2024 voters
Author: Cecilia Nowell
Headline: President says ‘I’m doing great’ despite polls showing 32% approval rating and loss of support from 2024 voters
Content: Trump speaks to the media before he boards Marine One to travel to Nebraska.Photograph: Eric Lee/ReutersView image in fullscreenTrump speaks to the media before he boards Marine One to travel to Nebraska.Photograph: Eric Lee/ReutersDonald TrumpTrump approval ratings plummet to new low, polls showPresident says ‘I’m doing great’ despite polls showing 32% approval rating and loss of support from 2024 votersCecilia Nowelland Guardian staffMon 5 Oct 2026 18.15 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 18.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDonald Trump’s approval ratings reached a record low on Monday, according to new opinion polls.Anew Reuters/Ipsos pollshows Trump’s approval rating at a record-low 32%. That polling included the president losing support among independent voters and Latinos, who had backed him in 2024. The dip could prove dire for the Republican party a month ahead of the midterm elections that will determine control of Congress.Before boarding a flight to Nebraska on Monday,Trumpshrugged off questions about his approval ratings.“I’m doing great,” Trump told a reporter, who’d asked about recent polls showing the president losing support among Latino voters, before blaming CNN and the media.But according to aNBC News/Telemundo pollrelease Sunday, 59% of Latino voters prefer a Democratic-controlled Congress, double the number that supported the party two years ago. According to that poll, just 24% of Hispanic Americans approve of Trump’s performance.Trump has spent the past few days campaigning across the country for Republican candidates, despiteeven conservative statesstarting to show the loss of support.
