Some Republicans have also started todistance themselvesfrom the president over issues like immigration as they attempt to hold onto local support.With Americans souring on the economy, the war with Iran, and other key issues they attribute to the administration, the impact of the negative sentiments could reach far and wide.Explore more on these topicsDonald TrumpUS midterm elections 2026newsShareReuse this content

title: Saudi-backed forces recapture key areas around strait from Houthis in Yemen | Yemen | The Guardian
description: Government offensive launched under air cover by Saudi military coalition aims to retake all Houthi-held territory
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Government offensive launched under air cover by Saudi military coalition aims to retake all Houthi-held territory
Content: A commercial vessel is anchored off Yemen's coast at Bab al-Mandab on 12 September 2026.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA commercial vessel is anchored off Yemen's coast at Bab al-Mandab on 12 September 2026.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesYemenSaudi-backed forces recapture key areas around strait from Houthis in YemenGovernment offensive launched under air cover by Saudi military coalition aims to retake all Houthi-held territoryGuardian staff and agenciesMon 5 Oct 2026 15.44 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 16.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleForces of the Saudi-led coalition fighting inYemenhave recaptured several key areas around Bab al-Mandab strait from Iran-backed Houthi rebels, Yemeni officials said on Monday.Yemen’s Saudi-backed government launches military drive to retake all Houthi-held territoryRead moreThe officials said forces allied with the internationally recognized government have retaken the crucial town of Dhubab just north of the strait. They also captured the towns of Bab and Hadeid, said the officials, who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak to reporters. Witnesses said they saw government tanks and forces entering the towns.The government push came as part of a major offensive launched early Monday under an air cover by a Saudi military coalition, aiming to retake all territory held by theHouthis.However, the offensive came just after the rebels said they had captured more territory in the south-western part of Yemen, taking the key town of Turbah in a blow to the Saudi-backed forces as they advanced toward the strategic provincial capital of Taiz, Yemen’s third-largest city.The Saudi-led coalition spokesperson, Maj Gen Turki al-Malki, said 100 fighter jets were providing support to the forces of Yemen’s internationally recognized government fighting against the Houthis. He said the coalition had secured “air protection” of the strategic Bab al-Mandab strait and destroyed hundreds of Houthi targets as part of the ongoing campaign.Marco Rubio told reporters that it was expected that the Saudi-backed government in Yemen would hit back at the rebels to reclaim territory. Asked if the Saudi-led coalition coordinated the action with the United States, the US secretary of state said thatSaudi Arabiaand the US had a defense agreement but would not offer more details.He said the Yemeni government was ousted from some of its territory by a Houthi campaign and the Saudis had come under attack, and “they have a right to defend themselves”.The new push sets an ambitious goal for the embattled government, which recently lost swathes of the country’s Red Sea coastline and areas around the Bab al-Mandab strait – a chokepoint for international shipping – after alightning offensiveby the Iran-backed Houthis.Yemen’s internationally recognised government has struggled to roll back the surge, even with the military support of Saudi Arabia. The Houthis have increasingly targeted Saudi Arabia in recent weeks, and on Sunday said they had attacked oil infrastructure in the capital again.Saudi Arabia urged to reconcile with UAE to drive back Houthi separatists in YemenRead moreThe statement came just hours after the Houthis cut a vital supply route linking thebesieged city of Taizwith the government’s interim capital, Aden, according to four security sources.The Houthi advance followed days of heavy fighting in and around the city.“We were informed that the Houthis had taken control of the al-Safiya area, where they cut the main road and took control of the police station,” a police source in the area said.Three sources with the Yemeni military also confirmed Houthi control over the area and the supply route, with traffic along the road halted and the group now surrounding Taiz city. Fighting in the area was ongoing, they added.Sources from both sides told AFP on Sunday that fighting in and around the western province of Taiz had killed more than 70 people over the past day.Sources from the internationally recognised government reported that 34 government troops were killed – 20 on the edge of Taiz province in neighbouring Lahj – while Houthi military sources said 39 of their fighters were killed in fighting across Taiz and in border areas with Lahj.Children forced to give up school for work as fighting upends daily life in YemenRead moreTaiz city itself remains under the control of government forces but has long been besieged from the north, east and west by Houthi fighters and remains one of the main fronts in Yemen’s long-running civil war.A Houthi military spokesperson, Yahya Saree, said on Sunday the group launched ballistic missiles and drones at the Saudi energy company Aramco’s sites in Riyadh and in the Khurais area in the east, causing large fires.The attacks were in response to what the Houthis claimed were 50 Saudi-led ‌air and missile strikes in Yemen in the past 12 hours.There was no immediate confirmation from Saudi Arabia.Saudi oil exportswere already under pressure due to Iran’s blockade of the strait of Hormuz in the Gulf.The Houthi’s Al-Masirah TV channel reported Saudi strikes on Sunday in the northern governorates of al-Jawf and Saada, saying at least two people had been wounded.With Reuters and Agence France-PresseExplore more on these topicsYemenHouthisMiddle East and north AfricaSaudi ArabianewsShareReuse this content

title: France braces for national day of school protests as boy loses hand | France | The Guardian
description: Thousands expected to join marches of support on Tuesday across the country as concerns grow over police response
Author: Angelique Chrisafis
Headline: Thousands expected to join marches of support on Tuesday across the country as concerns grow over police response
Content: Police officers face a protesting student from the Gustave Eiffel secondary school in Bordeaux on Monday.Photograph: Ugo Amez/SIPA/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenPolice officers face a protesting student from the Gustave Eiffel secondary school in Bordeaux on Monday.Photograph: Ugo Amez/SIPA/ShutterstockFranceFrance braces for national day of school protests as boy loses handThousands expected to join marches of support on Tuesday across the country amid growing concerns over police responseAngelique Chrisafisin ParisMon 5 Oct 2026 11.50 EDTFirst published on Mon 5 Oct 2026 08.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFrance is bracing for a national day of protests and high-school blockades as a youth protest movement gathers pace amid a growing debate over the scale of the police response.In one incident, a 15-year-old protesting against what demonstrators said were France’s dilapidated ⁠and understaffed ​schools ‌had his hand ‌blown off outside a high schoolin the northern town of Lens, said François-Xavier Lauch, the prefect of Pas-de-Calais.Lauch declined to comment on the exact circumstances, but said between 150 and 200 protesters had been hurling a series of objects at police when riot officers intervened. It was uncertain if the incident had involved a police stun grenade or how the injury happened. Lauch said ​an investigation had ​been opened.The family of a 16-year-old school pupil in Tours also filed a complaint about police violence after he lost sight in his right eye last week.The state prosecutor said the boy’s injuries were in line with the impact from a police rubber bullet. A police investigation is under way.The French prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, had earlier attempted to calm the protests by accepting schoolchildren’s grievances as “legitimate” and saying the government must listen.View image in fullscreenClashes between student protesters and police in the 12th arrondissement of Paris on Monday.Photograph: Raphaël Lafargue/ABACA/ShutterstockLecornu ordered ministers to tackle the students’ five major demands. These include organising the replacement of absent teachers, in recognition that pupils in some areas miss months of teaching because of staff absences – even in key exam years. Lecornu also called for a review of France’s lengthy school days, which are among the longest inEurope.The government will also look at repairs to dilapidated school buildings. Children on blockades across France have described water leaking into classrooms during class, cockroaches, collapsing ceilings andunbearable heat in summer. Lecornu said ministers must come up with proposals by the end of the month.Sophie Binet, the head of the leftwing CGT trade union, said the government had been late in offering to tackle the schoolchildren’s demands. She said the number of absent teachers who were not replaced had doubled in 10 years and class sizes were at a record high.“Amid such anger, a few measures just for show aren’t going to satisfy demands,” Binet said. She called for the government to instead stop all budget cuts as well as cuts to teachers’ positions.Student unions have called for a national day of protest on Tuesday with more schools expected to be barricaded. Thousands of trade unionists, teachers, public sector workers and parents’ groups are expected to join marches of support in cities and towns across France.View image in fullscreenProtesting students blockade the Turgot secondary school in Paris.Photograph: Raphaël Lafargue/ABACA/ShutterstockBinet said trade unionists would march to ensure there was no violence on the edge of any protests on Tuesday, as she criticised heavy policing. “We’ve been appalled by what we have seen over the past 10 days and by the unprecedented crackdown that the government has organised against the protests by high school students,” she said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionUniversity students continued to support the school protests on Monday, with up to 40 university buildings blockaded across France. Philippe Baptiste, the minister for higher education, told French radio he felt student and high school protests could intensify with the national protests due to take place on Tuesday.Between 400 and 500 high schools are expected to remain completely or partly closed on ⁠Monday out of a total of 3,700, the minister said.A government spokesperson, Maud Bregeon, told CNews television on Monday: “Our priority is to restore order.”The protests began in late September ‌at a high school ‌in a Paris suburb over teacher shortages. The government was taken by surprise as protests then spread nationwide, amid anger at social inequality and a lack of investment in the education system.Since last Monday, about 5,000 people, mostly ‌teenagers, have been arrested across France and dozens injured.Teachers have also been injured. Damage to property is estimated in the tens ​of millions of euros.Explore more on these topicsFranceEuropeProtestYoung peoplenewsShareReuse this content

title: London to Chicago BA flight declares emergency after dropping 28,000 feet | British Airways | The Guardian
description: British Airways Boeing abruptly lost altitude over Ireland due to ‘technical issue’ and returned to Heathrow
Author: Harry Cockburn
Headline: British Airways Boeing abruptly lost altitude over Ireland due to ‘technical issue’ and returned to Heathrow
Content: One of British Airways’ fleet of Boeing 777-200ER aircraft. In the incident on Monday the passenger jet deployed oxygen masks.Photograph: Bayne Stanley/Zuma Press Wire/Rex/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenOne of British Airways’ fleet of Boeing 777-200ER aircraft. In the incident on Monday the passenger jet deployed oxygen masks.Photograph: Bayne Stanley/Zuma Press Wire/Rex/ShutterstockBritish AirwaysLondon to Chicago BA flight declares emergency after dropping 28,000 feetBritish Airways Boeing abruptly lost altitude over Ireland due to ‘technical issue’ and returned to HeathrowHarry CockburnMon 5 Oct 2026 16.33 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 17.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA flight from London to Chicago declared an emergency after a sudden and steep descent of 28,000 feet over Ireland and was forced to turn back to Britain.British Airways flight BA295 was bound for Chicago’s O’Hare airport but after a “technical issue” during which oxygen masks were deployed from the ceiling, the plane landed safely back at London Heathrow.The aircraft, a Boeing 777-200ER, had departed Heathrow at 12.14pm on Monday for its scheduled transatlantic flight, and an hour into the journey had ascended to its cruising altitude of 37,000 feet.According to passengers, the plane then encountered turbulence moments before the masks dropped, prompting “uncertainty” among those on board.Pilots descended to below 10,000 feet and issued a 7700 emergency squawk to air traffic control – the international general emergency code – and made a U-turn to head back towards England.Flight-tracking services showed the aircraft flying in a looping holding pattern over the Bristol Channel between Pembrokeshire and North Devon as the plane burnt off fuel in order to lower its weight, allowing the pilots to make a normal landing just after 5pm.Passenger Tom Nichollssaid there was a “sudden bit of turbulence”before the emergency was declared and that the quick descent to 9,000ft hadn’t been too uncomfortable.He said: “The plane adjusted but it didn’t feel like it was descending rapidly. I’d say the pilots did a very good job.“The oxygen masks popped out soon after and there was a bit of uncertainty onboard. The couple in front couldn’t get to theirs but by the time they’d found a spare seat with a mask, the captain announced we were below 10,000ft so they were not needed.”A spokesperson for BA said: “The safety of our customers and crew is always our top priority, and the aircraft landed safely after our highly trained pilots returned to Heathrow following a technical issue.“Customers disembarked the aircraft normally and our teams are working to get their travel plans back on track as quickly as possible.”Photographs taken by passengers and shared on social media showed oxygen masks dangling from the ceiling as the plane made the return journey.A rapid descent to below 10,000 feet and a 7700 emergency squawk are routinely associated with aircraft experiencing cabin depressurisation but the official cause of the emergency has yet to be confirmed by BA.The Boeing 777-200ER is one of BA’s oldest planes in service, having been delivered to the carrier almost 30 years ago – in July 1997. Live streams showed the aircraft making its descent and safe landing back at Heathrow.Many passengers have been booked on to new flights departing on Tuesday.Explore more on these topicsBritish AirwaysHeathrow airportAir transportAirline industryTransportnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘A God-almighty punch-up’: rare footage shows Battle of Hastings (the 1966 one) | English Heritage | The Guardian
description: English Heritage acquires film of first re-enactment, ‘a lot of pushing and shoving’ between Kent and Sussex students
Author: Esther Addley
Headline: English Heritage acquires film of first re-enactment, ‘a lot of pushing and shoving’ between Kent and Sussex students
Content: 1:05Unseen footage of the first Battle of Hastings re-enactment in 1966 – videoEnglish Heritage‘A God-almighty punch-up’: rare footage shows Battle of Hastings (the 1966 one)English Heritage acquires film of first re-enactment, ‘a lot of pushing and shoving’ between Kent and Sussex studentsEsther AddleyMon 5 Oct 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt the top of a hill in a field near Hastings, a group of defiant English combatants awaited the invading army of William the Conqueror, brandishing their spears and shouting “Harold! Harold!”.Unfortunately, the Norman army had been held up in traffic on the A27 from Brighton, meaning the most significant battle in English history had to be delayed by 20 minutes while the French got into their costumes.On 14 October 1966, when a group of 500 students from Kent and Sussex universities met to re-enact the Battle of Hastings to mark its 900th anniversary, not every aspect was strictly historically accurate. Yes, the event was being staged on the same fields outside Battle in East Sussex where the original clash happened, but the English were wearing belted sacks and their swords and axes were made of wood and hardboard that had been painted silver.View image in fullscreen‘A pleasingly Monty Pythonesque record’: university students in combat at the first Battle of Hastings re-enactment in October 1966.Photograph: Keystone Press/AlamyThe rivalry between Kent and Sussex universities was real enough, however, according to Peter Sampson, a Sussex fresher who had been persuaded to sign up by the prospect of “a grand day out” and the promise of free beer. Once the two sides met, he says, it turned into “a God-almighty punch-up”.“There was actually a lot of real pushing and shoving, a lot of fighting going on in there … My friend John got a big whack around the head with the end of a [fake] spear, which hurt his face quite a lot.”Sixty years after that first re-enactment spawnedan annual eventwhich still attracts thousands of visitors each year, English Heritage has acquired rare colour footage of the inaugural event, at which a bemused French foreign minister attended, Queen Matilda was played by Miss World and health and safety was a far-off dream.View image in fullscreenChaps in fake chainmail bonking each other on the heads with fake weapons: Battle of Hastings re-enactors in 1966.Photograph: Keystone Press/AlamyIt was filmed by Alan Wootton, aninnovative manufacturer of electronicswho lived in Hastings and had been invited to capture a film record of the celebrations by Hastings town council. The film came to light when Alan’s son Cliff, who had helped out on the day as a 12-year-old, recently visitedBattle Abbey, the medieval foundation that was built on the site of the skirmish and is today overseen by English Heritage. He mentioned to a volunteer that he had 300 reels of film of the event, and would the charity be interested in seeing them?The result – condensed into a 12-minute film – is a pleasinglyMonty Pythonesquerecord of chaps in fake chainmail bonking each other on the heads with fake weapons while others ride around a bit on horses and 30,000 highly partisan (ie anti-French) spectators look on. (Though the era-defining British comedy, pedants will note, did not air untilthree years later.)“When Cliff showed me the footage, I was blown away by it, it was really, really impressive,” says James Witcombe, the site manager of Battle Abbey.View image in fullscreenRe-enactors marking the 950th anniversary of the Battle of Hastings in October 2016.Photograph: Jack Taylor/Getty ImagesThe film is, he says, very much of its time – and very different from the event which the charity has continued to stage every year since. “Looking at it from a modern perspective – yeah, it is a little bit of an interesting watch. I think the thing that’s very obvious is that it’s a load of amateurs getting together and really having fun … From our point of view, that’s the atmosphere that we want to preserve, just making sure we’ve got a few more sort of boundaries in place and nobody actually gets hurt.”Present-day crowds still tend to back “the home side”, he says, though “it’s a bit less partisan than it used to be”. This year’s event will be staged on 10 and 11 October, with a full battle run-through each day (though the result, sadly for England fans, does not change).View image in fullscreen‘It’s a bit less partisan than it used to be: thousands of visitors now attend the annual event (October 2018 pictured).Photograph: Jonny Weeks/The GuardianToday’s re-enactors– 1,000 combatants are expected this year – pay rather more attention to historical details, says Witcombe. “Whereas in 1966, there were knitted outfits and all that sort of stuff, the re-enactors today take it very seriously. It’s all about authenticity and, actually, experimental archaeology – [the idea that] living the experience gives you a much greater insight.” Withthe Bayeux tapestry’s presence in Londonhaving driven up interest in all things Norman, English Heritage is expecting bumper crowds – and is inviting any of those involved in the original 1966 event to come along.As Sampson recalls, while the battlefield itself was certainly “edgy”, once hostilities ended after 25 minutes of fisticuffs, things became much more convivial. After the promised free beer did not materialise, “we took matters somewhat into our own hands and, shall we say,liberateda couple of beer kegs from the back of the refreshment tent.“We cracked them open and then sat down with the Kent lads and lasses, and in the warm afternoon sunshine, just discussed the events of the day. So it became very friendly at the end of the day.”Explore more on these topicsEnglish HeritageHeritageBayeux tapestryWest SussexnewsShareReuse this content

description: The US withdrew its bombers from RAF Fairford after an investigation into an alleged planned terrorist attack on the base. Lucy Hough speaks to Dan Sabbagh, the Guardian’s defence and security editor
Author: Zoe Hitch
Headline: The US withdrew its bombers from RAF Fairford after an investigation into an alleged planned terrorist attack on the base. Lucy Hough speaks to Dan Sabbagh, the Guardian’s defence and security editor
Content: 9:05Today in Focus: The LatestUS militaryWhy did the US rush to withdraw bombers from RAF Fairford? - The LatestThe US withdrew its bombers from RAF Fairford after an investigation into an alleged planned terrorist attack on the base. At least 10 B-1 bombers used by the US military in the Iran conflict flew out of Fairford on Sunday, suggesting US officials were taking the threat seriously. title: Tories are united behind Badenoch, but MPs want focus on economy over culture wars to win back voters | Conservatives | The Guardian
description: Party has common enemy in defectors, while Nigel Farage’s woes have given some insiders reason to hope
Author: Pippa Crerar
Headline: Party has common enemy in defectors, while Nigel Farage’s woes have given some insiders reason to hope
Content: This time last year, mutinous Tory MPs were privately predicting Badenoch’s demise. Now, she is the longest serving leader since Boris Johnson.Photograph: Ian Forsyth/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThis time last year, mutinous Tory MPs were privately predicting Badenoch’s demise. Now, she is the longest serving leader since Boris Johnson.Photograph: Ian Forsyth/Getty ImagesConservativesAnalysisTories are united behind Badenoch, but MPs want focus on economy over culture wars to win back votersPippa CrerarPolitical editorParty has common enemy in defectors, while Nigel Farage’s woes have given some insiders reason to hopeMon 5 Oct 2026 14.57 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 21.31 EDTShareDuring a quick-fire Q&A at the Conservative party conference this weekend,Kemi Badenochwas asked who she would pick between Robert Jenrick or Suella Braverman.“Why do you keep offering me these? It’s like asking if I’d rather be shot or drowned,” the Tory leader responded with her trademark directness.The Tories appear more united than they have done in years. Part of that is because they have a common enemy to unite against: Tory defectors.It is not lost on Badenoch’s team that this time last year, it was a matter of when, not if, Jenrick, her erstwhile leadership rival, would try to oust her.View image in fullscreenA year ago it seemed a matter of when, not if, Robert Jenrick would try to oust Badenoch. He was kicked out the party weeks later.Photograph: Guy Bell/ShutterstockMutinous Tory MPs were privately predicting her demise. But after a successful conference, Badenoch limped on – and Jenrick emerged a diminished figure who weeks later would be kicked out of the party.His presence, however, lives on, with shadow ministers openly sharing their relief that he is no longer among their number.“Nobody knew how much we hated Robert until he left,” said one shadow cabinet member. Others were less polite. “Rob going was like pulling out a splinter,” one said. “I miss him like I miss an abscess in my molar,” another added.But while the unity comes, in part, from a mutual dislike, there are of course other factors: Badenoch’s strength as a leader; the country’s yearning for stability; the constant threat ofReform UKto the party’s right.Badenoch has been running the show for almost two years – the longest serving Tory leader since Boris Johnson – and has begun to set out her principles, writing a 30,000 word pamphlet titled The Right Way before the conference.Tory MPs also seem to have finally realised that voters take a dim view of the party cycling through leaders at such breakneck speed, with five in the past eight years.Nigel Farage’s woes have also given them reason for hope: while the Reform leader believes his party will recover from a difficult summer, some Tory MPs are confident that his party has peaked.View image in fullscreenKemi Badenoch believes she can beat Labour and Reform on the issue of the economy, insiders say.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianOther party insiders – possibly more plugged into what is going on in their constituencies – concede that Farage still represents a huge threat. They are among those concerned about Badenoch pitching to the right.Instead, they say that she needs to do more to win over centrist voters for the party to stand a chance of winning another election. Part of that is by focusing more on the economy and less on culture wars.“There’s no point telling Kemi not to do anything. But we do have to be careful with our language,” one MP said. Another added: “That’s not Kemi’s instinct. But she does finally seem to understand it all has to be about the economy. That’s where we win.”Badenoch believes she can “shrug off” the Liz Truss anchor and beat Reform and Labour on the economy, MPs say. Andrew Griffith, her shadow chancellor who has previously worked in business, helps the party’s credibility, they add, and Badenoch will speak more about the topic this week.The Tory leader also polls ahead of her party, which insulates her from much internal criticism. One adviser said the Tories do better when their leader is in that position – citing David Cameron and Boris Johnson – but worse when they’re behind, as Rishi Sunak was.Badenoch has told her top team that they have to work “day by day” to restore the party’s fortunes. Yet there is no escaping that almost two years after she was elected as leader, the Tories are still polling lower than they did in 2024 with their catastrophic general election defeat.“You won’t hear much from us on that,” one senior aide said. “The qualitative stuff is good but it’s not backed up yet by the numbers. We need to put on three or four points in the polls. If we do that and gain momentum we’re back.”Others are hopeful that the exposure of their conference week can give them enough of a lift in the polls to help them maintain the narrative that they’re on the march.The spectre hanging over the whole affair, however, is the prospect of a snap general election. Andy Burnham’s political away day at Chequers on Monday has got many Tories spooked, even though the prime minister has ruled out calling an early election.Perhaps more in hope than expectation, shadow cabinet ministers said they did not believe Burnham would call an election. “He said it would be irresponsible and it’s hard to walk that back,” said one.However, Badenoch told a bash for Tory MPs on Sunday night the party was getting ready for an election regardless. But while she sounded bullish, her closest lieutenants are anything but. “If there is one, we’re all fucked,” they said.Explore more on these topicsConservativesKemi BadenochReform UKConservative conference 2026Conservative conferenceEconomic policyConservative leadershipanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Aphrodite review – a trashy way to treat the goddess of love | Exhibitions | The Guardian
description: She’s the ultimate female nude, a Greek goddess who inspired centuries of artists. Yet despite some world-class loans, her story here is jumbled
Author: Jonathan Jones
Headline: She’s the ultimate female nude, a Greek goddess who inspired centuries of artists. Yet despite some world-class loans, her story here is jumbled
Content: When sex goddesses ruled European art … Michelangelo Pistoletto’s Venus of the Rags.Photograph: Tate and Michelangelo PistolettoView image in fullscreenWhen sex goddesses ruled European art … Michelangelo Pistoletto’s Venus of the Rags.Photograph: Tate and Michelangelo PistolettoExhibitionsReviewAphrodite review – a trashy way to treat the goddess of loveAshmolean museum, OxfordShe’s the ultimate female nude, a Greek goddess who inspired centuries of artists. Yet despite some world-class loans, her story here is jumbledJonathan JonesMon 5 Oct 2026 10.58 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 10.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBotticelli’s Venus has parked her shell outside your house and come to pay a night-time visit. The glowing strands of her hair glitter against blackness as she looks past you at a mystery only she can see, while your eyes follow those river-like locks down to a hand that gathers a looping cascade between her thighs. She is, unmistakably, the goddess fromBotticelli’s The Birth of Venusin the Uffizi, Florence. This very similar painting from about 1490, also by Botticelli and his workshop, suggests his Uffizi masterpiece was already such an icon that someone commissioned this version without the zephyrs and green sea, just that goddess body.So it goes. Venus, in art, is just a word for “female nude”. Botticelli started a modern appetite that has never ended. From his hypnotic paintings a host of lush sex goddesses rose up, or reclined, to rule European art through to Michelangelo Pistoletto’s ironic 1967 assemblageVenus of the Rags, also here, in which a heap of old clothes overflow from a corner around a marble nude seen from behind, the mix of beauty and chaos resembling a rubbish-strewn Naples piazza.View image in fullscreen‘No exploration of its impact’ … Crouching Aphrodite.Photograph: Royal Collection Trust/The Royal Collection/ HM King Charles III © Royal Collection Enterprise/ British MuseumBut this exhibition is not called Venus. And it doesn’t tell her artistic story except in bits with vast lacunae. Instead, it sees Venus as a cheap Roman substitute for the original Greek love goddess Aphrodite, who in turn is exposed as a ripoff of a matriarchal deity once worshipped on Cyprus. The result is a mixture of world-class loans and an archaeological hobbyhorse.Both the quality and gaps hit you straight away with a classical marble Crouching Venus (sorry, Aphrodite), lent from the royal collection. There’s no exploration of its impact on later art. In fact, this Roman copy of an ancient Greek original was sold by Cromwell’s republican regime after the beheading of its royal owner, Charles I. It was acquired by the artist Peter Lely who painted his own mysterious, nude, anti-Puritan masterpiece Nymphs by a Fountain. After the Restoration he also portrayed Nell Gwyn nude – his interest in this Venus was perversely creative. Before that, Rubens saw this same statue and based his painting Venus Frigida on it.Which is another way of saying that the story of Aphrodite/Venus in art is massive, epic and complex. Perhaps the comparatively small size of the exhibition can’t hold all that, yet a lot of space is wasted. Still, it has to start somewhere and the first room displays the many ways Aphrodite was depicted in ancient Greece, including a Red-figure vase with a scene of her and rival goddesses, Hera and Athena, preparing for the beauty contest she will win, leading to the Trojan war. So many stories, and this room seems almost breezy with them. The marriage of Aphrodite to the smith-god Hephaestos and her adultery with Ares, god of war, is told in a yada yada way and illustrated by a minor 16th-century print. Then suddenly you are plunged way, way back to encounter what this show claims was the real, original Aphrodite.View image in fullscreenEgyptianised statuette of Aphrodite-Astarte Golgoi-Ayios Photios, Cyprus c. 600-550BC.Photograph: Louvre Museum/Musée du Louvre, ParisIn classical mythology, Aphrodite has a special relationship with Cyprus: it is to Cyprian shores that her shell wafts in The Birth of Venus. That is because the Greek Aphrodite, we’re told here, is an appropriation of a female deity who was once all-powerful on the island. Prehistoric totems with abstract bodies, and in one case a bird’s head, attest to the centrality of this cult. Terracotta figures of childbirth and motherhood may have been offered by women to this nameless deity. Other images mix her with Egyptian and Phoenician deities. But I wasn’t convinced that any of this explains the Greek and Roman love divinity. Either way, it is crushingly out of sequence – why didn’t they start here then go forward in time?What’s inescapable is that the ancient Greeks made nudity their thing. It embodied (literally) their sense of being different from other cultures. But you don’t want to be caught looking too long at the Capitoline Venus. This second-century AD Roman marble statue is a copy of a lost work that was an ancient scandal: the Venus of Knidos by Praxiteles. Before Praxiteles, the Greeks didn’t portray Aphrodite nude, so people were powerfully struck by its intimacy when it was unveiled in the fourth century BC. Aphrodite has stripped for her bath and is trying, failing, to cover herself with her arms. One besotted admirer allegedly entered her sanctuary by night and rubbed himself against the statue’s cold hard thigh, leaving a semen stain.It’s troubling to see this after you’ve encountered the evidence for the ancient Cypriot Aphrodite. It looks as if the Greeks took a matriarchal deity and turned her into a sex toy. The Romans borrowed that nude image and spread it throughout their empire: a raw, graffiti-like relief from a fort north of Hadrian’s Wall of a naked Venus bathing is a funny, fascinating delight.For me it’s Botticelli who is the true believer in Aphrodite/Venus. For 1,000 years, ever since the fall of the Roman empire, she was cast out by Christianity. Her worship was revived in the Renaissance. When you gaze at the unfathomable eyes of his Venus, you too believe that love is a holy thing that deserves its own deity.Aphrodite: The Making of a Goddess is atAshmolean museum, Oxfordfrom 8 October 2026 to 11 April 2027Explore more on these topicsExhibitionsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Is the US becoming a nation of cat lovers? | Cats | The Guardian
description: Dogs have long been more popular, but for the first time more households own kittens than puppies. Some believe it’s all down to economics
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Dogs have long been more popular, but for the first time more households own kittens than puppies. Some believe it’s all down to economics
Content: But could it see off an intruder?Photograph: Voren1/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenBut could it see off an intruder?Photograph: Voren1/Getty ImagesPass notesCatsIs the US becoming a nation of cat lovers?Dogs have long been more popular, but for the first time more households own kittens than puppies. Some believe it’s all down to economicsMon 5 Oct 2026 12.05 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 12.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleName:The kitten index.Age:The debate has probably raged since animals have been domesticated.The debate being?Dogsversuscats. Not in a fight, but as in which to get as a pet.Well, that depends on whether you want a warm, loving, loyal friend that gives you unconditional love …Or a beautiful, non-needy but still loving animal that doesn’t require constant attention and walking … But we’re not having that argument here.What are we doing?Looking at some interesting new statistics about cat and dog ownership.I already know this –dogs win, every year.True; in the2026 UK Pet Foodsurvey, the dog population (15.5m) is slightly ahead of the cats (13m).Two and a half million ahead!But crossing the Atlantic now …Still more dogs, surely? I’m thinking Lassie, Toto, Snoopy,Eddie Crane from Frasier…Granted, there currently are more dogs, but maybe not for long. The market research firm Packaged Facts reports that, for the first time since it started looking at this stuff, more US households own kittens than puppies. The ratio reached 1:1 last year, and now it’s 1:0.94.But that’s just kittens and puppies.Guess what kittens and puppies grow up to be?Hmm. Have Garfield, Looney Tunes’ Sylvester and Alien’s Jonesy become the hot new pet icons of film and TV?To be fair, it’s less about boom time for cats, more about dog ownership in decline.Because?Maybe because kittens are a bit like lipstick.Excuse me?So the lipstick index was a phrase coined in the 00s, referring to the idea that consumers buy less expensive luxury goods in times of economic hardship, such as lipstick instead of, say, an expensive purse.But the president says the economy’s going great.He alsosaid people were eatingcatsanddogs, remember. Truth is, the property market is sluggish, because of real estate prices, high mortgage rates and stagnant wages.But what’s that got to do with cats and dogs?Packaged Facts says homeowners are nearly twice as likely as renters to have a dog.Bottom line, it’s all about the budget?It calculates the average dog costs its owner $1,300 (£985) a year. For an average cat: $750 (£570). But,writing in the Washington Post, the chief executive of Packaged Facts, Robert Granader, is keen to point out it’s not about cats replacing dogs. “It’s about America becoming more like cats: living in smaller spaces, valuing independence and preferring to be left alone.”And where the US goes, the rest of us follow?While ratiosdiffer throughout Europe, the UK Pet Food survey actually points to slightly more dogs than cats compared withthe last time they published it, two years ago.Woof!But the UK is facing the same economic global headwinds as the US, so watch this space.Do say:“Just a goldfish, please, until I’m on the property ladder.”Don’t say:“Whichever, cat or dog, it’s just for Christmas, right?”Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick hereExplore more on these topicsCatsPass notesPetsDogsAnimalsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Snakes, bobcats, mountain lions: the secret animal world beneath the Hollywood sign | Los Angeles | The Guardian
description: An international symbol for the city, the sign is also hallmark of the region’s environmental richness
Author: Katharine Gammon
Headline: An international symbol for the city, the sign is also hallmark of the region’s environmental richness
Content: A cyclist rides along a hillside path above the Hollywood sign at dusk in Los Angeles.Photograph: Mario Tama/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA cyclist rides along a hillside path above the Hollywood sign at dusk in Los Angeles.Photograph: Mario Tama/Getty ImagesLos AngelesSnakes, bobcats, mountain lions: the secret animal world beneath the Hollywood signAn international symbol for the city, the sign is also hallmark of the region’s environmental richnessKatharine Gammonin Los AngelesMon 5 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 13.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAtop Mount Lee, in the heart ofLos Angeles, the wind is quiet. Two red-tailed hawks sail above, barely flapping as they coast the thermal air like surfers on a wave. Standing beside the giant letters of the Hollywood sign, the city seems peaceful. On a clear day, blocks and blocks of homes unfold beneath and the skies reveal sights all the way to Catalina Island – 10 miles out, across the Pacific.That’s the beauty seen from the Hollywood sign.The sign sits on a hillside in Griffith Park, which, at about five times the size of Central Park, is the largest municipal park in the city. The letters have long been an international symbol for human residents in the metropolis – of dreams, film-making ambition and success. But it’s also a hallmark of the region’s environmental richness.Because the area is closed off from the public, it has become a favorite of animals seeking respite from the city. There are birds nesting in the sign, snakes curled up at its base, bobcat roaming around the letters. It was the backdrop that made the famous wild mountain lion P-22 into an LA icon when a 2013 National Geographic photograph captured him prowling at night with the illuminated Hollywood sign in the background.View image in fullscreenA remote camera captures a radio-collared cougar in Griffith Park, Los AngelesPhotograph: Steve WinterNow, a team of scientists is preparing to outfit the letters with cameras, able to capture any fire outbreaks that the basin may experience. The sign’s caretakers are collaborating with Torch Systems, a technology company that uses solar-powered sensors, on an AI fire-detection service that can identify smoke from miles away. Fire is considered the area’s largest anticipated risk, particularly as visitors may bring lit cigarettes into the park.On a recent Wednesday, the Guardian hiked up the mountain with the team to survey the environment of the sign. As we don gloves, skirt a steep trail and rappel down a private trail to the letters, mounds of coyote scat are a constant reminder of who has walked these paths before us.“Los Angeles is butted up against nature,” says Diana Wright, official caretaker for the Hollywood Sign Trust. She gestures around the hillside, part of the 4,310 acres, or about 6.5 sq miles, that exist in the shadow of the sign. “We’re inside this huge natural park – way bigger than Central Park – and also much more native. And then you’ve got this man-made sign of it that’s meant to withstand rockslides and landslides and winds.”The park is home to many creatures. The Educational Research Center at the University ofCalifornia, Los Angeles, has designated Griffith Park a Significant Ecological Area, in part for its crucial role “as a corridor for any gene flow and species movement between the Santa Monica, San Gabriel and Verdugo Mountains”. Researchers have documented about 200 species of birds in the park, along with 50 species of butterflies and 40 species of mammals.Like many parts of Los Angeles, the sign was originally a publicity stunt – and a temporary one. It was originally constructed of tin and telephone poles in 1923, to advertise a local housing development called “Hollywoodland”. Eventually, the “land” section was dropped. Over the years, the structures deteriorated. Hugh Hefner led a campaign in 1978 to replace the letters with massive steel beams set in concrete foundations.Over the century, it became a real anchor point for life in the city. Wright points to streetlights in downtown Los Angeles that are designed to resemble New York, and other parts of the city where Parisian city scenes are filmed.“Much of the city is designed to look like other places due to our filming background,” says Wright. “The sign offers that sense of place that so many parts of the city lack.” She thinks that is why it is often the sign that is blown up in movies – or photographed when something unusual, like a once-in-a-decade snowstorm happens.View image in fullscreenFirefighters work on hot spots after a brush fire burned in Griffith Park in Los Angeles, California, on 20 January 2025.Photograph: Ringo Chiu/ReutersThe sign may have stronger footholds in the earth now, but it is also facing challenges. Mount Lee is steep, and the hillside, and the animal habitat it is home to faces risks from earthquakes, climate change, changing rainfall and events such as El Niño. The conservancy caregivers have ongoing projects to clear brush to keep fire dangers down, but they have to balance erosion control, fire concerns and unobstructed views of the sign.Wright and the other caretakers are also developing a plan with the city to plant more native California flora and potentially create a native flower super bloom near the sign. “The Hollywood sign is such a celebration of California,” Wright says. “It should be beautiful and stunning in its natural glory.”Will the letters still be here in 100 years? And what will the wildlife surrounding it look like then? Wright says it all depends on the land beneath. “The hillside is going to define what the sign is like in the future,” she says, pointing out that the whole city could look different after a big environmental shake-up like an earthquake. “I think that’s a real metaphor for Los Angeles in general.”But on that day, it was only blue skies and lizards scuttling away from our footsteps, in the shadow of giant letters.Explore more on these topicsLos AngelesCaliforniaAnimalsWest CoastUrban wildlifeWildlifeWildfiresfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: My sister Nicole married OJ Simpson. This is what I wish I had known | Domestic violence | The Guardian
description: Since Nicole Brown Simpson’s murder in 1994, Denise Brown has devoted herself to ending domestic violence. She talks about her beloved sister, the trauma she witnessed in the couple’s marriage and how lives can be saved
Author: Emine Saner
Headline: Since Nicole Brown Simpson’s murder in 1994, Denise Brown has devoted herself to ending domestic violence. She talks about her beloved sister, the trauma she witnessed in the couple’s marriage and how lives can be saved
Content: ‘I told her so many times to leave him’ … Denise at her home in Florida, US.Photograph: Mikaela Martin/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘I told her so many times to leave him’ … Denise at her home in Florida, US.Photograph: Mikaela Martin/The GuardianHow we surviveDomestic violenceInterviewMy sister Nicole married OJ Simpson. This is what I wish I had knownEmine SanerSince Nicole Brown Simpson’s murder in 1994, Denise Brown has devoted herself to ending domestic violence. She talks about her beloved sister, the trauma she witnessed in the couple’s marriage and how lives can be savedMon 5 Oct 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 13.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe last night Denise Brown spent with her sister Nicole Brown Simpson was at a restaurant for a family celebration. Nicole looked out of the window. “All of a sudden she goes, ‘Oh my God, there he is.’Hewas driving by.” Brown looked out, trying to get a glimpse of her sister’s ex-husband, the former American football starOJ Simpson. “I saw these headlights. She said, ‘He’s constantly following me.’” They went back to talking about their plans for the summer.The following morning, 13 June 1994, Brown was up early at her parents’ house in Orange County in southern California, when the phone rang shortly after 6am. “I heard my mom scream a scream that I had never heard from a human being,” says Brown. “It was so guttural. Just awful.”She ran to her parents’ room and took the phone from her mother’s hand. It was a detective from the Los Angeles police department, who explained that Nicole, who was 35, had been found dead, along with her friend Ron Goldman, stabbed outside her house. He finally did it, she told the detective, who asked who she meant. “I said: OJ Simpson. I knew in my heart, in my gut, in my soul that he killed Nicole. Everything started flashing back into my head. Everything about her relationship, everything over the 17 years.”View image in fullscreen‘She was a kid’ … Nicole (left) with Denise.Photograph: Courtesy of Denise BrownSimpson was acquitted of the two murders in a trial the following year, though a civil trial in 1997 found him liable. Later, he would be convicted of armed robbery and kidnap, andserved nine years in prison. Released in 2017, he died in 2024.After her sister’s murder and the evidence of long-term abuse that emerged during the trial, Brown became a campaigner against domestic violence. Now she is about to publish a book, For My Sister Nicole. “I feel like after 32 years I’ve learned a lot, and I thought it was time,” she says, when we speak over Zoom. “I want this book to save lives.”As well as a memoir of her relationship with her younger sister – and her sister’s relationship with Simpson – Brown includes advice and resources for people experiencing domestic abuse (the vast majority of whom are women), or their family and friends. This includes recognising abuse, putting together a safe plan for leaving, and custody of children. “I said all the wrong things to Nicole: ‘You’ve got to leave him. You’ve got to get out of this situation. What are you doing?’ That was not being supportive. I want people to get educated and be supportive, and I want victims to know they’re not alone in this situation, and it’s not their fault that this is happening to them.”In the days after Nicole was murdered, Brown stated that she didn’t think Nicole was a “battered woman” (a term commonly used in the 1990s). “I didn’t know anything about domestic violence,” she says now, and gives a pained smile when she adds that her impression was that it only happened to women in poverty. “Like a lot of people even think today: ‘This kind of stuff happens to poor people, people that have their teeth knocked out, people that don’t have a loving family.’ That’s what I thought a victim of domestic violence was.”View image in fullscreen‘I want victims to know it’s not their fault this is happening to them’ … Denise Brown at home in Florida.Photograph: Mikaela Martin/The GuardianNicole came from a close and loving family – she was the second oldest of four sisters, growing up in an affluent Orange County coastal city – and was a sparky, confident person. The scale of the abuse only became clear after her murder, when Brown and her family found and read Nicole’s journals, where she had detailed beatings and controlling behaviour. They had seen signs, sometimes blatant ones, but Nicole always minimised it. “I did not know that this was something that happens as a cycle,” Brown says, “over and over again.”When Brown first met Simpson, her sister had already been with him for eight months. Nicole was 18 when they met; he was about 30. “What people have to remember is that she was very much head over heels in love with this guy, and she was a kid. She was young; he could mould her into whatever he wanted, and that’s exactly what he did.” Nicole took Brown and their younger sister Dominique to watch Simpson, one of the NFL’s biggest stars, in a football game. That evening at Simpson’s home, Brown heard raised voices and then saw Nicole in tears. He had seen her, from the football field, kiss a mutual male friend on the cheek, says Brown. “She comes back [upstairs], and goes, ‘Everything’s OK. I embarrassed him.’ She blamed herself.” The next day, feeling uneasy, Brown tried to get Nicole to come back with her to New York, where she was working for a modelling agency, but Nicole refused.Worse was to happen another night, when Brown and a friend went out for dinner with Nicole and Simpson in Los Angeles, and continued drinking back at Simpson’s house. Nicole had been living with him for several years by this point. He asked Nicole to get them some food, and Brown pulled him up on it. “I said, ‘You really take her for granted. She does everything for you.’”View image in fullscreenFrom left: Nicole Brown Simpson’s mother, Juditha, and sisters Tanya and Denise stand next to her grave in California in 1995.Photograph: Marilynn Young/AFP/Getty ImagesSimpson became angry, went upstairs and started pulling photographs off the wall and smashing them on the floor. “Then he goes into her closet. He takes her clothes, he starts throwing them down into the foyer. He comes running back down and he grabs Nicole by the throat, up against the kitchen door, and she’s about six inches off the ground. I run over and I am pounding on him, yelling and screaming. He finally lets her go, and he throws her out the door. She’s all bloodied.” He shoved Brown out, too.The following morning, Nicole went back to the house. Brown thought she would be getting some of her things, leaving him, but she stayed. “She goes, ‘It was just too much drinking. Everything is OK.’”How did she feel about her sister going back to him after that? “I figured she’s an adult, and she knows better. I thought it was an isolated incident. I decided he’s crazy, he’s an asshole, and I saw a side of him I did not like. Could I explain what it was? No. I just knew I didn’t like it.” But in the years after that – after Nicole and Simpson got married and had two children, and she learned more about his behaviour – Brown says, “I told her so many times to leave him.”After Nicole was killed, Brown learned that it’s rarely simple to leave. It’s not just that abuse can destroy victims’ self-esteem: “They are the only ones that know how dangerous their [abuser] can be. I’m not saying this happened in Nicole’s relationship, but batterers usually threaten to take children away, threaten family members. When you are in a cycle like Nicole – like a lot of victims of domestic violence – was in, you are the only one who realises how dangerous that situation can be.” That danger peaks when you actually leave.View image in fullscreenOJ Simpson and Nicole Brown Simpson in 1994.Photograph: Vinnie Zuffante/Getty ImagesNicole once asked Brown to photograph bruises on her body, and in 1989 Simpson was sentenced to community service for spousal abuse. “But she never wanted to talk about it.” It can take several attempts to leave an abuser, and many women return. It can be frustrating to friends and family members watching this, Brown acknowledges. “But don’t give up on them.” When she goes to speak to law enforcement officers, “I always say, ‘You may go to 50 calls to the same residence, but that 51st call may be the one where you actually save her life.’”Brown was pleased when Nicole finally left Simpson, but she says he continued to stalk her sister even after their 1992 divorce. (Nicole made a phone call to the police eight months before she was murdered to say Simpson had broken into her house.) Five days before she was killed, she phoned a shelter. “It’s the hardest call a victim of domestic violence will ever make, and that’s why I want people to take them seriously,” says Brown. “Because when they make that call, it’s a desperate plea for help. They need to get a safety plan because a victim of domestic violence is in more danger [when leaving] the situation.”The murder of Nicole and Goldman became a global news story, and the media scrutiny of the families was intense. It helped that Brown was living at her parents’ house in a gated community, together with Nicole’s children, Sydney and Justin, but helicopters would circle overhead, trying to photograph the kids. “It was a time of chaos. It was absolutely horrific.” She was so angry, she says, that she would go for long runs every day, “until I just finally collapsed. That was the only way I could deal with it.”View image in fullscreenDenise at a candlelit vigil to mark the second anniversary of Nicole’s death.Photograph: Andrew Shawaf/Getty ImagesThe day after Nicole’s funeral, Simpson was scheduled to turn himself in to the police, but went on the run. The car chase, with Simpson in a white SUV, was televised live, with millions watching, until he was arrested back at home that night. Brown and Dominique even joined in the chase. “We were out of our minds. We got on the road, but he was so far ahead of us. I mean, come on, really?” She laughs at herself, but says, “It was a time of our lives that was insane.”The trial, which ran for most of the following year, was also televised and became a huge spectacle – it played a big part in sparking the true crime genre. Brown and her family were driven to the courthouse and entered underneath the building; they weren’t confronted by Simpson supporters outside, or by people selling merchandise. Brown took to the stand, but says prosecutors wanted “to educate the jurors about domestic violence, and that was nixed. Afterwards, I remember jurors saying, ‘This wasn’t a domestic violence case. This was a murder trial.’ Well, the ultimate form of domestic violence is murder.” How did she cope with the jury’s not guilty verdict? “I didn’t, not very well. But not guilty does not mean you’re innocent.”View image in fullscreenDenise (left) and Nicole.Photograph: Courtesy of Denise BrownBrown never saw Simpson again after the 1997 civil trial, in which he was found liable for Nicole and Goldman’s deaths, and ordered to pay the victims’ families $34m. But he didn’t disappear. In 2006 it was announced he had co-authored a book called If I Did It, about how hypothetically he could have murdered his ex-wife and Goldman. It was cancelled after an uproar. “He wasn’t around me,” says Brown. “I still continued doing my advocacy work, I still continued my life, and I paid him no mind. He does not exist in my space. He didn’t then, and he doesn’t now.”The murders and trial are still the subject of documentaries. “When I see something on TV, I usually just switch the channel,” says Brown. She is in contact with Sydney and Justin, who lived with their father, but she doesn’t want to talk about them. “They’ve got their own lives. They’ve had a tough upbringing, and I want people to respect their privacy.”Now 69, she plans to be campaigning for the rest of her life. “This is something that I feel the need to do. When we started the foundation [in Nicole’s name, but since closed], I thought, ‘Great! Domestic violence is going to end.’ Well, we’re still at it.”In the US, an estimated one in three women have experienced physical or sexual violence, or stalking by an intimate partner.There and elsewhere, shelters “are on the verge of closing”, she says. “They are not getting the funding that they need from our government.”View image in fullscreenDenise with a copy of the book she has written, For My Sister Nicole.Photograph: Mikaela Martin/The GuardianThe murder and abuse of Nicole highlighted domestic violence and helped push through the Violence Against Women Act three months later. Does Brown hope it will continue to be supported and funded under a president who is not known for his commitment to women’s rights? She holds up two crossed fingers. We speak just after US policereopened an investigation into the alleged rapeof a woman by seven men at Cornell University in 2024. “It’s just horrific,” Brown says.I called her Joybell, my soulmate since I was eight. Then her partner killed her and blew up their homeRead moreHad she known then what she knows now about domestic abuse, she says, “I’m hoping that I could have saved Nicole’s life. When I saw the very first thing that happened to her, I would have had the knowledge to realise that it’s going to continue, not just think it was an isolated incident.” She hopes her book will help educate, and save, others.“I’m hoping that my sister is proud of me, and all the things that we’ve done. I truly believe that if the roles were reversed, Nicole would do the same for me.”For My Sister Nicole: Love Shouldn’t Hurt – What to Know About Domestic Violence, by Denise Brown, is out in the US on 6 October (Blackstone, $29.99)In the UK, call the nationaldomestic abuse helplineon 0808 2000 247, or visitWomen’s Aid. In the US, thedomestic violence hotlineis 1-800-799-SAFE (7233). In Australia, the nationalfamily violence counselling serviceis on 1800 737 732. Other international helplines may be found viawww.befrienders.org.Explore more on these topicsDomestic violenceHow we surviveOJ SimpsoninterviewsShareReuse this content
