title: No queues, empty seats and the worst speech ever heard: welcome to the Tory conference | John Crace | The Guardian
description: Birmingham event is like a safari park attraction where we get to see the remnants of a party in a protected habitat
Author: John Crace
Headline: Birmingham event is like a safari park attraction where we get to see the remnants of a party in a protected habitat
Content: Witnessing Andrew Griffith’s speech was like watching a less sentient version of the PG Tips monkey.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianView image in fullscreenWitnessing Andrew Griffith’s speech was like watching a less sentient version of the PG Tips monkey.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianThe politics sketchPoliticsNo queues, empty seats and the worst speech ever heard: welcome to the Tory conferenceJohn CraceBirmingham event is like a safari park attraction where we get to see the remnants of a party in a protected habitatMon 5 Oct 2026 13.34 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 21.31 EDTShareAt the Labour party conference in Liverpool last week, Andy Burnham floated the idea of electoral reform. This week in Birmingham, the Tories have come up with a plan of their own: voting with their feet.How to put this nicely? Let’s just say that the Conservative party conference is extremely civilised. No queues for the food concessions. No queues to get into any of the halls. In fact, the organisers are delighted that anyone has turned up at all.This doesn’t feel like a high-octane meeting of a party preparing for government. More like a home counties meeting of the Rotary Club. On current evidence, if there is a general election next year – as Kemi Badenoch is trying to convince us there will be – then the Tories won’t be active participants. More like vaguely disinterested observers. For these four days, Birmingham is a city where you can sit and watch the world pass you by.Tories to pledge to scrap Environment Agency and Natural EnglandRead moreNot that those who have turned up seem unhappy. Rather, they are thrilled to find themselves still alive. This time last year, there was a possibility that they faced extinction: under threat from left and right and with a leader in Kemi who looked unlikely to last six months. Since then things have stabilised as Robert Jenrick has been stopped from pulling out their ventilator in the intensive care unit. They are now merely an endangered species. The conference centre is a safari park attraction where we get to see the remnants of the Tory party in a protected habitat.The morning’s activities take place in what is optimistically called the main hall: a hard-to-find side room with a capacity of about 200. These are way more seats than any of the acts require. First up was shadow transport secretary, Richard Holden, who managed to bore even himself. Still, at least the hall was about a third full. Which, for Rich, is a major result. I’m guessing most of the people there were family and friends.It was no fuller for the shadow health secretary, Damian Hinds, who stumbled over his notes for five minutes. Weirdly, there were 24 people watching an empty stage online after he had left, while only 17 had been online when he was talking. Or maybe that’s not so weird.For the afternoon offering we were moved to a slightly bigger hall. This could have been a mistake. It had come billed as a “major speech by the shadow chancellor”. Only we were made to sit through an hour and a half of nothingness – an opportunity to deliberate our own and the Tories’ existential futility – before the main event.By now at least another third of the audience had left. A wise choice. They clearly had some idea of what was coming. Even 20 minutes of Andrew Griffith can rip your soul in half. If only I had joined them.Not that the hall was anywhere near full to begin with. First up was the shadow Defra secretary,Victoria Atkins, who had sensibly worked out that no one in their right mind would stay to hear her talk. So instead she positioned herself as a cable TV presenter – there were 53 people watching online – chatting to her guest, Jeremy Clarkson.This did at least lift the mood in the hall. A genuine celeb was among them for 15 minutes. However, it doesn’t say much for your conference when your most popular speaker is someone who openly says he’s not a Tory party member and has only turned up because he will go anywhere people will have him to talk about farming.“Wow,” said Jezza. “There’s an awful lot of people here dressed as seats!” Vicky giggled nervously. The rest of the chat came and went perfectly amiably. Jezza did what he does best, giving his best impression of a multimillionaire held back by the incompetence of government. Still, at least he injected some fun. Vicky wanted to know how the farming summer had gone. He replied that the Diddly Squat farm had produced several ounces of hen food because of the extreme heat.Someone should have told him that Griffith was about to get rid of the Climate Change Committee. If you missed any of this, you will be able to watch extended highlights on the next series of Clarkson’s Farm.From then on, the conference became one long car crash. A panel with a couple of rightwing hacks droning on about nothing and then another panel in which one businesswoman congratulated herself on not getting stabbed on the train to Brum – apparently all her friends refuse to use trains – and then a businessman sobbing at the thought of billionaires being asked to pay inheritance tax. Some of them are so sick with worry they can no longer sleep.Finally the main attraction. What would turn out to be a landmark occasion for all party conferences. Because Griffith proceeded to give the worst speech ever heard. Not just in content but in delivery. It was like watching a less sentient version of the PG Tips monkey. Constantly applauding himself and ending his sentences with “Yeah”. What was left of the audience didn’t know where to look.If Andy really is the future chancellor, then we are truly fucked. Even Mel Stride wasn’t this hopeless. We might as well all pack up now. He was going to build more homes that were uninsulated and might fall down because they were cheaper. He would cut taxes and regulations the Tories had themselves introduced.“This is our destiny,” he said. And then he dematerialised. It was as though he had been primitive AI and his controller had seen quite enough and decommissioned him. Andy didn’t know he had finished. And neither did anyone else.Explore more on these topicsPoliticsThe politics sketchConservative conference 2026Conservative conferenceVictoria AtkinsConservativescommentShareReuse this content

title: How did some City fans become aggressive defenders of a nation state’s regime? | Manchester City | The Guardian
description: The Manchester City case is one example of how fandom has warped beyond previous boundaries in online spaces
Author: Sean Ingle
Headline: The Manchester City case is one example of how fandom has warped beyond previous boundaries in online spaces
Content: The Etihad Stadium has not hosted a men’s match since the Premier League’s verdict was announced.Photograph: Adam Vaughan/EPAView image in fullscreenThe Etihad Stadium has not hosted a men’s match since the Premier League’s verdict was announced.Photograph: Adam Vaughan/EPAManchester CityHow did some City fans become aggressive defenders of a nation state’s regime?Sean IngleThe Manchester City case is one example of how fandom has warped beyond previous boundaries in online spacesMon 5 Oct 2026 17.29 EDTFirst published on Mon 5 Oct 2026 16.08 EDTShareAvideo of Liam Gallagher playing in a 1996 charity football match resurfaced on social media recently. Dressed in Manchester City blue and a bucket hat, in truth he appears to be in a fug of cigarettes and alcohol. But then, out of nowhere, he hitsa shot into the top corner. Since last week, though, the Oasis singer has preferred to defend the honour of his club with his studs up.As the fallout from thebiggest scandal in British football historyheaded into a second week, Gallagher was asked what he made of rival fans wanting City tolose all their trophiesafter being found guilty of all the serious charges against them. “There all NEUROTIC little GIMPS,” came the reply on social media. It was one of dozens of sweary, punchy, and often amusing responses, all built on a solitary article of faith: that City will somehow find a way to wriggle free.Let there be blanks instead of Manchester City’s name on trophies: there was no honour there | Jonathan WilsonRead moreBut Gallagher is hardly standing alone. Over at Bluemoon, the biggest City forum, the tone has been just as defiant – albeit with a sprinkle of gallows humour. “Have we been blamed for the Titanic hitting the iceberg yet?” asked one user. “Manchester City shot JFK,” wrote another. “This isn’t just a fight between the PL & City. It’s a fight for the heart, soul & future of football,” reckoned a third.Staggeringly, the forum now has over 192,000 posts since the initial charges against City, dating back to 2023. Naturally the Premier League, jealous rivals and the media all come under heavy fire. Yet there remains a curious reluctance among fans to accept wrongdoing – or to criticise the club’s owners.How might we explain that? I am not sure it is down to pure tribalism, or a determination among City fans to wait for the club’s appeal to play out. It’s more complicated, and more interesting, than that.Let us try to get into the head of the most vociferous City fan since last Tuesday. For decades they were in United’s shadow, then everything changed. Their city did too, given how much Abu Dhabi United Group pumped into it. You can forgive them, then, for not wanting to believe that it was all built on sand during the legal process.But now? Now there is no excuse. So what might explain the reluctance to accept what the independent commission report lays out in great detail? According to the Irish academic Colm Kearns, one reason is because the United Arab Emirates has not only brought unprecedented success and forged emotional bonds with City fans “but have also co-opted elements of the club’s fanbase as aggressive defenders of their regime”.In 2023 Kearns and his colleaguesanalysed huge numbers of postsfrom City fans, going back years, and found that some of them would not only “overlook ethical violations by the Group, but decry and – in some cases – attack the Group’s critics.”In other words the club’s owners had successfully leveraged the tribal loyalty of City fans into being Manchurian Candidates – or, rather, Manchesterism Candidates.Kearns tells me that some sports journalists had even self-censored because of the impact of online abuse from City fans. “We had people talking about how fans would go online and try to find their troll through their personal social feeds, and it sent that on to their editor to get them in trouble,” he says.There is another massive factor here: social media, and the way we now consume sport and communicate with other fans. Thirty years ago, most City fans would live near Manchester and see fans from other clubs at work and in the pub. Nowadays, they can dwell in an online space made up entirely of people who support their own club.View image in fullscreenSocial media has created tribal online spaces for sports fans.Photograph: Lee Smith/Action Images/Reuters“I think it makes fans perhaps more tribally myopic than they would have been before and less likely to look outside of their own club’s perspective,” says Kearns.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAcademics also talk of “sports fandom circles”, in which supporters across the globe increasingly mobilise and fiercely defend athletes or their teams. That phenomenon, which came out of east Asia with popular culture and music, leads supporters to be laser-focused on their own tribe. But it hardly encourages lighthearted banter, common ground, or compromise.In City’s case, Kearns suspects that some fans are putting the club above the wider game, citing a Reddit post that said: “I am a City fan first and a football fan second.” Although, as he concedes, it is impossible to know how many online posters do not live in Manchester, or go to games, and therefore feel the need to prove their bona fide credentials by sticking up for the club at all costs.Either way, where we could go next is interesting. If you were a far-right tech billionaire, why wouldn’t you want to buy a successful sports team – especially if you knew there was an army of potential defenders of your reputation among your new fanbase?Over the weekend I went through the fan forums of other clubs to see what their supporters made of the guilty verdict against City. The overwhelming majority welcomed it, of course, even if some questioned whether City would really get properly punished for their crimes, given the relationship with Abu Dhabi and the British government.“Once you lose faith that the rules apply equally, football becomes something else,” one wrote. “Every title, every match, carries a question mark. I feel cheated. I’m one of the victims. And for that, I hate Manchester City.”Some will agree with that sentiment. Others will raise their eyebrows. I do wonder, though, would that poster feel the same way if the boot was on the other foot, and their club was in the line of fire?Explore more on these topicsManchester CitycommentShareReuse this content

title: BT’s purchase of TalkTalk is cosy – but probably politically sensible | Nils Pratley | The Guardian
description: For all the howls of a ‘stitch-up’, it’s hard to see what ministers were supposed to do, as the alternatives risked worse outcomes
Author: Nils Pratley
Headline: For all the howls of a ‘stitch-up’, it’s hard to see what ministers were supposed to do, as the alternatives risked worse outcomes
Content: On Monday, the culture secretary, Lisa Nandy, intervened ⁠after BT’s TalTalk acquisition ⁠was confirmed, invoking a public interest intervention notice.Photograph: SFL Travel/AlamyView image in fullscreenOn Monday, the culture secretary, Lisa Nandy, intervened ⁠after BT’s TalTalk acquisition ⁠was confirmed, invoking a public interest intervention notice.Photograph: SFL Travel/AlamyNils Pratley on financeBTBT’s purchase of TalkTalk is cosy – but probably politically sensibleNils PratleyFor all the howls of a ‘stitch-up’, it’s hard to see what ministers were supposed to do, as the alternatives risked worse outcomesBT to buy broadband supplier TalkTalk in £400m rescue deal, saving 900 jobsMon 5 Oct 2026 12.40 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 21.31 EDTShare“All the characteristics of a stitch-up masked as a rescue deal in the public interest,” thundered Virgin Media O2. It’s not an unreasonable view ofBT’s hurried weekend acquisition of TalkTalk. Once upon a time, TalkTalk was seen as a plucky upstart performing the useful role of irritant to BT’s giant Openreach broadband operation. Now the challenger is being consumed by the dominant player via a pre-pack administration that minimises short-term political headaches.Here’s the problem, though, with the cosy stitch-up thesis. For all the howls of outrage, it’s hard to see what the culture secretary, Lisa Nandy, who gave her blessing by issuing a little-used public interest notice, was supposed to do differently. Alternative approaches, notably a chaotic collapse ofTalkTalkwithout a rescue plan for the customers, risked worse outcomes.OK, perhaps the worst fears of GP surgeries and hospitals being disconnected at a stroke, and thousands of vulnerable customers losing their internet connection, were overdone. But, in Nandy’s shoes, you probably wouldn’t take the risk. TalkTalk, after all, had had months to find a buyer but failed to land a credible deal even when its retail division and its wholesale unit, PXC, were up for grabs separately.Disappointed would-be buyers blame the reluctance of BT, as the critical supplier to TalkTalk, to extend financial support to a new ownership vehicle. From BT’s point of view, however, one can see why another private equity backer for TalkTalk wouldn’t feel like an improvementon the last one. As it is, BT will be booking £100m as a non-payment of a debt even as it takes control.The deep problem here is that TalkTalk – Sir Charles Dunstone’s creation more than 20 years ago – hasn’t been doing much real challenging work of late. After going through the refinancing wringer more times than is healthy, it was a financially distressed company. At the last count, borrowings were in the region of £1.5bn, a staggering sum for a loss-making business with only 1.5 million retail customers and 1 million wholesale ones. Telephony, remember, tends to be a low-margin game even when things are going well.That is not to say the politicians get a free pass. Successive governments have been told many times by the regulator Ofcom that a “supplier of last resort” regime should be in place in the broadband market, just as it is in energy and water. The logic is simple: in extremis, there should be a way for a government-supported operation to step in to prevent sudden disconnections and look for an orderly permanent solution.The unavoidable fact, though, is that such a regime didn’t exist with TalkTalk. That glaring hole in the regulatory setup needs to be addressed for future cases. But a weekend arrangement withBT, however objectionable in theory, at least has the advantage of not drawing on a penny of public money.The medium-term regulatory test will be to ensure BT and Openreach can’t abuse the advantage of gobbling TalkTalk. There was a theatrical public exchange of letters between the BT chief executive, Allison Kirkby, and the Ofcom boss, Dame Melanie Dawes. The former pleaded for regulatory mercy, in effect, for removing a political problem; the latter replied that applying the regulatory framework was a statutory duty.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIt’s anyone’s guess how that will work out in practice since the wriggle room would seem to be enormous. But the guiding principle hasn’t changed – wholesale operators need to have access to Openreach’s network on reasonable commercial terms. TalkTalk couldn’t make it pay but that, in the end, seems primarily to be a story of its own perilous financing. Wrapping the business into BT is very far from being ideal – but it’s not the worst pragmatic fudge.Explore more on these topicsBTNils Pratley on financeTalkTalkTelecommunications industrycommentShareReuse this content

title: Preppers used to be ridiculed – but we’re all stockpiling now | Zoe Williams | The Guardian
description: The UK government urging households to prepare for unknown threats with a three-day supply of food and water doesn’t feel like an overreaction, writes Zoe Williams. But is there a bigger plan to go with it?
Author: Zoe Williams
Headline: The UK government urging households to prepare for unknown threats with a three-day supply of food and water doesn’t feel like an overreaction, writes Zoe Williams. But is there a bigger plan to go with it?
Content: ‘The household solution hinges on the emergency being short-lived.’Photograph: Noel Bennett/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘The household solution hinges on the emergency being short-lived.’Photograph: Noel Bennett/AlamyOpinionEmergency planningPreppers used to be ridiculed – but we’re all stockpiling nowZoe WilliamsThe UK government urging households to prepare for unknown threats with a three-day supply of food and water doesn’t feel like an overreaction. But is there a bigger plan to go with it?Mon 5 Oct 2026 11.47 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 15.14 EDTShareThere is no national food stockpile and there hasn’t been since it was wound up in the 1990s. It feels like a metaphor for the delusions of that era: nothing bad can possibly happen again; no two countries with a McDonald’s have gone to war with each other (according to the journalist Thomas L Friedman,also in the 90s). Now, we all have a McDonald’s and wars regularly disrupt food supplies. The problem with metaphors is you can’t eat them – not even satisfying ones.For people who remember the second world war, or feel as if they do, there is always enough muscle memory to do topical household stockpiling. My mum kept a trunk of food that was mainly filled with condensed milk in case of a nuclear war, all the way through the 80s. When the Berlin Wall came down, we should have had a ceremonial toffee-sauce-making event where we ate it all, but we didn’t; in 1990, she was stockpiling again, to mark the Gulf war.The spectre of Y2K saw a large amount of bottled water enter the house, but by then I’d left home. When 9/11 happened, the water had gone off, but it was still fine for washing, apparently, so all she needed was a load of new water – and all that remained for the wider family was to call her mad and occasionally steal her anchovies.The 2008 financial crash may have brought almost 20 years of roiling turmoil to the world, but the period spent wondering whether the cash would stop coming out of the wall was only a couple of days, during which if you had got your arse into gear enough to buy beans, you would have been considered hysterical. It would be dispiriting to go through all the events since that have made stockpiling seem like a good idea and impossible to pinpoint the date on which having a three-day food stash went from “crazy prepper idea from someone who probably also keeps a crossbow” to “something any sensible person who reads the news and listens to the authorities would do”.The UK government’sresilience campaign, urging households to prepare for threats unknown, doesn’t feel like an overreaction. But nor does it feel realistic.A record number of households –one in eight, or one in six with children – experience food insecurity already, which is to say can’t be sure they have enough even without external events. The range of possible disasters is so wide that it’s hard to consider them practically without freaking out: are we planning for crop failures in the UK or for the collapse of the global food supply, which would mean us relying on our own crops? Are we anticipating a hostile foreign act such as a cyber-attack, or something more meat-world?Power outages, extreme weather, floods – they all seem possible, but none of them seem as if they’d be over in three days. You can see that having a torch would be better than no torch, but a stash of tinned pineapple wouldn’t meet the moment. The advice is to have three litres of drinking water a day for each person, but can you seriously imagine having that and not sharing it? There is no household solution that doesn’t hinge on the emergency being very short-lived and a collective response being ready to go within only a few hours. The more you think about emergencies, though, the less likely they seem to be short-lived. The chance of inoculating yourself household by household seems vanishingly small.The essence of old-school prepping – the reason people who did it were mocked and viewed with suspicion – was that it was implicitly off-grid, or rather planning for a world without a grid and without meaningful order. The modern preppers’ problem is that stockpiling for your own household – even having a workable first aid kit and some non-perishables – feels ridiculous unless you believe there’s a bigger plan under way. The government has the unenviable task of asking us to trust the future less while trusting its authority more. It’s enough to make you want to do something helpful – more helpful, even, than buying a gigantic bag of rice.Zoe Williams is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick hereExplore more on these topicsEmergency planningOpinionFoodFood povertyDefence policyNatural disasterscommentShareReuse this content

title: What happens to a dog when its owner can’t leave hospital? | Ranjana Srivastava | The Guardian
description: Our relationships with pets matter to wellbeing. But concern for an animal’s welfare can also become a practical barrier to healthcare
Author: Ranjana Srivastava
Headline: Our relationships with pets matter to wellbeing. But concern for an animal’s welfare can also become a practical barrier to healthcare
Content: For many older people, an animal is their most constant companion, writes Ranjana Srivastava.Photograph: Eva Blanco/Getty Images/iStockphotoView image in fullscreenFor many older people, an animal is their most constant companion, writes Ranjana Srivastava.Photograph: Eva Blanco/Getty Images/iStockphotoOpinionHospitalsWhat happens to a dog when its owner can’t leave hospital?Ranjana SrivastavaOur relationships with pets matter to wellbeing. But concern for an animal’s welfare can also become a practical barrier to healthcareMon 5 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 18.22 EDTShare“Doctor, do you know I have a little dog?”My team exchanges a glance. It’s my turn today.“Tell me about your dog.”Her face lights up. “Well, he is just a lovely little thing. When I am knitting, he curls up on my lap and keeps me company. We are very happy, the two of us.”Complaining about healthcare can feel like an act of betrayal. But there is a real cost to silence | Ranjana SrivastavaRead moreIt is unlikely that our patient has knitted in the last year, during which a series of mishaps has brought her in and out of hospital. But the rest of her account rings true.For as long as possible, she stayed at home, managing miraculously well despite her cognitive impairment, with little help beyond an occasional carer. But now, a fall has brought her undone. For weeks, she has been waiting for residential care, one more statistic in the familiar story of “bed block”.From our medical perspective, she is waiting for a facility. But from hers, she is waiting to see her dog. She can recall very little about her life but, when it comes to her pet, her descriptions are unwavering. Her words paint a small brown dog, quietly following her around her apartment. Jumping into her lap when she settles into her armchair. Ready to do it all over again tomorrow.Sign up for a weekly email featuring our best readsThe paramedic who rescued her from her garden noted that the neighbour had offered to take the dog until the patient’s return. But this time, the patient is not going home.Seeing how much she enjoys the nurses fussing over her – and because she has never once asked to go home – we have not mentioned her living arrangement. But she longs for her dog – and our decision not to lie is far easier in principle than in practice.There is no easy provision to reunite her with her dog. The neighbour can’t bring the dog in. The hospital won’t let the dog in. (“Imagine the other patients.”)What if seeing her dog proved distressing afterwards? What if it created a safety risk? And if we made an exception for her, what would we do for the next patient who pined for her turn?The more frequently I encounter the problem, the more I see it as an emblem of the things medicine considers peripheral to patient care, even when they may not be peripheral at all.Our relationships with pets matter to wellbeing. They provide physical activity, psychological comfort and social connection. For some older people, an animal is their most constant companion.But concern for a pet’s welfare can also become a practical barrier to healthcare. Patients may delay seeking care, worry about coming to hospital, or discharge themselves because there is a pet at home.A recent essay in the New England Journal of Medicine onhuman-animal relationshipspoints to a perhaps delayed recognition of something we have understood for years: the wellbeing of humans and their pets is intertwined.When I was an intern, just two questions often formed the social history: Does the patient smoke? Does the patient drink?Today we do better. We ask: Where does the patient live? What services exist? Is there a history of falls? Is the family involved?skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFive Great ReadsEach week our editors select five of the most interesting, entertaining and thoughtful reads published by Guardian Australia and our international colleagues. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Saturday morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionPerhaps we should add another question: Are you concerned about a pet?It is a deceptively easy question to ask. Because what happens when the answer is yes?Who will feed the cat? Who will walk the dog? What if the patient cannot return home?The solution can’t be another mental responsibility casually added to the medical worklist. Yet ignoring the issue doesn’t obscure the problem.We have fact sheets for many health conditions. Why isn’t there one for ‘What to do on the day your loved one dies’? | Ranjana SrivastavaRead moreMore of us are starting to notice what we have traditionally neglected – not only where a patient lives but also which animal lives with them and what will happen to that animal if the patient doesn’t go home.For many people, pets are part of the social determinants of health.Hospitalscannot take on this responsibility alone. But it’s time to ask how hospitals can work effectively with community services and animal welfare agencies to care for the whole patient.Know thy neighbour – and thy neighbour’s dog.For as long as we cared for her, one doctor from our team sat down with our patient and heard her retell the story about her dog. We never let our interest drift, even when our hearts slightly broke each time. Every one of us would have brought in her dog – if only we could.One day, all of us rotated out. We left her in the hands of another team, hoping they would continue the ritual.Ranjana Srivastava is an Australian oncologist, award-winning author and Fulbright scholar. title: Is your partner on their phone and ignoring you? I’ve got a buzzword for that | Emma Beddington | The Guardian
description: From microcheating to quiet quitting to weaponised incompetence, new terms to describe relationship failings are abundant. But that doesn’t mean there’s not space for some more ...
Author: Emma Beddington
Headline: From microcheating to quiet quitting to weaponised incompetence, new terms to describe relationship failings are abundant. But that doesn’t mean there’s not space for some more ...
Content: Who are you calling dead-eyed?Photograph: jacoblund/Getty Images/iStockphotoView image in fullscreenWho are you calling dead-eyed?Photograph: jacoblund/Getty Images/iStockphotoOpinionRelationshipsIs your partner on their phone and ignoring you? I’ve got a buzzword for thatEmma BeddingtonFrom microcheating to quiet quitting to weaponised incompetence, new terms to describe relationship failings are abundant. But that doesn’t mean there’s not space for some more ...Mon 5 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 13.48 EDTShareAre you committing “attention infidelity”? TheNew York Timesalerted me to this expression, coined by the public opinion researcher Daniel Cox in a new book on the “crisis of human connection”. It’s exactly what you’d expect: failing to focus fully on your partner because you’re indulging in what the NYT calls, rather judgily, “the banal distraction of dead-eyed scrolling”. Who are you calling dead-eyed? Thisreel of an armadillo in a paddling poolhas my animated attention!Surely we’re all a bit attention-unfaithful – only saints don’t sometimes absent-mindedly thumb throughmedieval manuscript hedgehog memeswhile their partner relates a boring anecdote about how they thought they saw a strange bird that turned out to be a plastic bag. What I find more interesting is how we seem now to need a lexicon of relationship bad behaviour.Why are so many people stealing from restaurants?Read moreThis summer, there was debate around what constitutes “microcheating”; last year, I read about women“quiet quitting” relationships; the “mental load” has been striking chords for a couple of years, with its companion concept of “weaponised incompetence”. It’s reminiscent of the proliferation of negative phrases around work that emerged post-pandemic –resenteeism,fauxductivity,coffee badging,polygamous working(quiet quitting, of course, also originated in the work context). Maybe it reflects the fact that relationships are also (hard) work, or maybe we just love a bit of pop psychology.Assuming it’s the second, I’ve been trying to think up other highbrow phrases to conceptualise the age-old business of being a bit of a dick to your partner, so that I can turn them into a book myself. So far, I’ve invented “cultural pre-emption betrayal” (sneaky solo viewing of the next episode of a show you’re watching together), “premium resource caching” (hiding good food), “semi-hostile infantilising” (telling your partner how to do something with the exaggerated patience you’d show a two-year-old) and “fiscal obfuscation” (when you say something was “not very dear” when it was, in fact, very dear).I reckon some of these may have legs, but I’ve had to stop for now, because my husband wants to tell me about our energy tariff – time to demonstrate some attention fidelity.Emma Beddington is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The Guardian view on sexual abuse in schools: teachers cannot deal with this alone | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: Politicians must redouble their efforts to tackle a disturbing pattern of pupils assaulting classmates
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: Politicians must redouble their efforts to tackle a disturbing pattern of pupils assaulting classmates
Content: ‘As well as the severity of the offences, the youth of many victims is disturbing.’Photograph: Peter Lopeman/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘As well as the severity of the offences, the youth of many victims is disturbing.’Photograph: Peter Lopeman/AlamyOpinionSchoolsThe Guardian view on sexual abuse in schools: teachers cannot deal with this aloneEditorialPoliticians must redouble their efforts to tackle a disturbing pattern of pupils assaulting classmatesMon 5 Oct 2026 13.45 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 17.53 EDTShareThe Guardian’s findings about theextent of sexual abuse in schoolsrequire an urgent, calibrated response. Data revealing multiple rapes committed each year on school premises in England and Wales is hard to comprehend. Yet this is what freedom of information requests to police forces, covering the period from 2021 until last year, have revealed. As well as the severity of the offences, the youth of many of the victims is disturbing. More than 8,500 sexual offences at or near schools were committed against under-13s, most of them girls.Data about perpetrators contains gaps, including their age and sex. While the overwhelming majority of such acts are carried out byboys, we don’t know the exact proportion, nor if there is an age gap between those carrying out abuse and those being targeted. Only 33 out of 43 police forces shared their data, meaning that large areas including Scotland are not represented. But whatever the exact details, and allowing for the fact that these are reports, not convictions, the findings are deeply dismaying.View image in fullscreenOnline safety laws are one tool to tackle the problem.Photograph: True Images/AlamyThe suggestion by the acting chief constable Becky Riggs, who leads on child protection and abuse investigation for the National Police Chiefs’ Council, that the figures could reflect an increased willingness to report sexual abuse rather than more abuse taking place, must be taken seriously. At the same time, an unknown number of assaults continue to go unreported. Exact comparisons with the past are not possible since there is no equivalent dataset. What can be said, 10 years after a committee of MPs recommended that ministers should make sexual abuse in schools an “immediate policy priority”, is that the problem has not gone away; some experts believe that it is getting worse.The response to the problem so far has relied on three main tools. One is the promotion of sex and relationships education. The scale of image-based abuse in schools requires further investigation, but Monday’s warning of ahuge rise in AI child sexual abuse materialglobally points to the need for a curriculum that keeps abreast of technological change. The second tool isonline safety lawsincluding age verification, tighter restrictions on pornography, and the pledge by Sir Keir Starmer’s government to placesmartphonesoff-limits for under-16s. The third is the criminal justice system, and ongoing efforts to improve the way that police and prosecutors deal with victims.Ministers will need all these to work if they are to have any chance of meeting their goal ofhalving violence against women and girls. But acute resource and capacity problems are hampering courts and prisons, while pornography regulation needs to be enforced as well as discussed. While campaigners are hopeful, effects need to be measured. In relationships education, good intentions must not be confused with effects. To make a difference, schools need investment, training and evaluation.This problem cannot be left to teachers to deal with;parentsshould also discuss these issues with young people. And politicians will have to be brave. The focus on sexual crimes by rightwing and far-right parties in many countries places liberals in a difficult position, with some fearful that by talking about them, they risk adding to a narrative thatsows discord and scapegoats immigrants. The abuse of children by other children is an upsetting subject, but looking away is the worst of all options. As a society, we owe it to young people to deal with it.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The Guardian view on Tory economics: Britain’s future needs more than Thatcher’s past | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: The Conservatives blame their failures on abandoning their 1976 principles. But the country needs investment and resilience rather than another round of spending cuts
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: The Conservatives blame their failures on abandoning their 1976 principles. But the country needs investment and resilience rather than another round of spending cuts
Content: Margaret Thatcher in 1983. ‘It is hard to see how restoring Thatcherite principles will help the party.’Photograph: Jane Bown/The ObserverView image in fullscreenMargaret Thatcher in 1983. ‘It is hard to see how restoring Thatcherite principles will help the party.’Photograph: Jane Bown/The ObserverOpinionConservative conference 2026The Guardian view on Tory economics: Britain’s future needs more than Thatcher’s pastEditorialThe Conservatives blame their failures on abandoning their 1976 principles. But the country needs investment and resilience rather than another round of spending cutsMon 5 Oct 2026 13.46 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 17.53 EDTShareThe Conservative party wants to go back to the future under Kemi Badenoch. In her foundational text,The Right Way, released at the weekend, the Tory party leader makes its intellectual lineage explicit, repeatedly invoking Margaret Thatcher’s1976 policy statement The Right Approach. The 2026 economic framework is familiar: only private enterprise creates wealth; taxes, regulation and spending can obstruct growth and competition; markets make the country stronger. The speech by her shadow chancellor, Andrew Griffith, made it clear that Conservative failures over its 14-year spell in charge were the result of the party straying from Thatcherite principles.One might argue that, on the contrary, errors were because the party slavishly followed such a creed. When Rough, a depleted North Sea gasfield that once provided around 70% of the UK’s gas-storage capacity, was judged uneconomic by its private owner, a Conservative government in 2017 accepted that international markets could provide the UK with adequate energy security. That proved to be a big mistake when Russia invaded Ukraine, sending fossil fuel prices upwards. Britain was particularly exposed as a net energy importer and highly dependent on gas. Tory ministers had to bring back Rough into operation in 2022. Mrs Badenoch puts its closure down to “false economies”. But what was wrong was putting private profitability ahead of the country’s needs.View image in fullscreenAndrew Griffith.Photograph: James McCauley/ShutterstockIn his speech to conference, Mr Griffith attempted to distance himself and his party from the chaotic Liz Truss administration, although he was amember of its disastrous Treasury team. But his diagnosis today appears similar. Britain, in his telling, is supposedly more of acommand economythan a market‑based one. To kickstart it, he argued, will require lower taxes, welfare reform and deregulation.The difference, Mr Griffith was keen to stress, is that tax cuts will now come through spending cuts rather than additional borrowing. Why shrinking the state would strengthen growth enough to offset its effect on demand and productive capacity is unanswered. Just how big those cuts might be was revealed by the Guardian. Mr Griffiths admitted when he was the shadow business secretary that the Tories were planning to make sweeping cutsbeyond the £47bnthat the party had announced if it won the next election.This might be seen as the kind of clear blue water that the Tories need to put between themselves and Labour. But the real enemy is further right. As the pollsterJohn Curticetold a Demos fringe event, the voters most dissatisfied with high rates of immigration, the performance of the economy and the NHS are disproportionately moving to Reform UK. The perceived failures of Labour are not automatically benefiting the Conservatives. Prof Curtice said that either the party was “still getting the blame” for its record in government, or Reform was “simply speaking a language” that appeals more to those voters. It is hard to see how restoring Thatcherite principles will help the party here.Mrs Badenochrecognisesthat the world has changed. She acknowledges that insecure supply chains and economic coercion may require the state to step in. But public investment must remain a special case, and, she says, “help to an individual firm should be exceptional and, where possible, temporary”. The real problem with her prospectus is Britain’s future requiring permission from 1976.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Medicine shortages will result if drug prices are driven too low | Pharmaceuticals industry | The Guardian
description: Letter: Amanda Cole says the government needs to weigh the cost of medicines against the damage that a shortage can cause to the NHS and patients
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letter: Amanda Cole says the government needs to weigh the cost of medicines against the damage that a shortage can cause to the NHS and patients
Content: ‘Brexit has made us even more vulnerable as we no longer have access to EU medicine reserves.’Photograph: Muhammad Aqib/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Brexit has made us even more vulnerable as we no longer have access to EU medicine reserves.’Photograph: Muhammad Aqib/Getty ImagesPharmaceuticals industryLettersMedicine shortages will result if drug prices are driven too lowAmanda Colesays the government needs to weigh the cost of medicines against the damage that a shortage can cause to the NHS and patientsMon 5 Oct 2026 12.50 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 12.51 EDTShareWithout decisive government action, the reported medicine shortages in hospitals will only be the tip of the iceberg (Hospitals in England hit by shortages of common drugs such as paracetamol, 29 September). Medicine supply chains are complex and global, with multiple points of potential failure that are especially sensitive to geopolitical shocks. Brexit has made us even more vulnerable, as we no longer have access toEU medicine reserves, and cross-border logistics are further complicated.Ourresearchshows that these shortages tend to be concentrated in (off-patent) generic and biosimilar markets. It’s true that low prices for off-patent medicines are important in driving health system savings and promoting affordability. The problem is that when prices are driven an unsustainable low, manufacturers exit, leaving markets with too few suppliers and dangerously exposed to any supply disruption or demand spike. The NHS bears the cost when a shortage does occur, in the form of higher prices, expensive substitutes and a heavy staff burden in managing emergency procurement and, sometimes, rationing. Patients pay the highest price in delayed treatment and worse outcomes.The government needs to weigh pricing controls against the costly damage that a drug shortage can cause. The answer lies in using regulatory, pricing and approval decisions to encourage competition and nurture supplier resilience. There is a critical balance between affordability and medicine security that needs to be struck.Amanda ColeDirector, Office ofHealthEconomicsHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? Author: Guardian staff reporter

Content: A degree in content creation, otherwise known as the ‘influencer degree’, got readers thinking.Photograph: Getty/Posed by modelView image in fullscreenA degree in content creation, otherwise known as the ‘influencer degree’, got readers thinking.Photograph: Getty/Posed by modelUniversitiesLettersInfluencer degrees may be worth liking. Mickey Mouse qualifications have valueBill Gabbettrecallsteaching media, communications and cultural studies, whileMichael Fullerstudied under the influenceMon 5 Oct 2026 12.50 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 13.24 EDTShareI enjoyed Emma Brockes’ piece (Would I want my child to study for a social media influencer degree? No, but it’s the way of the world, 1 October). It reminded me of the last 30 years of my working life spent teaching media, communications and cultural studies in two great university departments peopled with superb colleagues, and spending my time with bright and inquisitive students.I got used to them being called Mickey Mouse degrees, mostly by people who seemed unaware that Mickey Mouse was one of the global top 10 recognised images, or even that the Walt Disney Corporation was valued at billions.I consoled myself then, and do so now, with knowing that my Mickey Mouse acolytes seemed quite averse to wrecking the economy, global or national, treating people as ciphers, or being intent on exploitation come what may. title: A shedload of trouble for the neighbours | Homes | The Guardian
description: Letters: Jane Whitehead believes neighbours should be heard, not seen, while Paul Burton says the capacity of neighbours to take offence is limitless. Plus a letter from Joyce Corston
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Jane Whitehead believes neighbours should be heard, not seen, while Paul Burton says the capacity of neighbours to take offence is limitless. Plus a letter from Joyce Corston
Content: ‘Someone’s making a lot of money out of aiding formerly civilised people to thieve their neighbours’ privacy and natural sightlines.’Photograph: Sirimo/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Someone’s making a lot of money out of aiding formerly civilised people to thieve their neighbours’ privacy and natural sightlines.’Photograph: Sirimo/Getty ImagesHomesLettersA shedload of trouble for the neighboursJane Whiteheadbelieves neighbours should be heard, not seen, whilePaul Burtonsays the capacity of neighbours to take offence is limitless. Plus a letter fromJoyce CorstonMon 5 Oct 2026 12.50 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 13.24 EDTShareThank you to Emily Retter for exposing the curse of the prefab garden shed (‘Just look at this monstrosity!’ Inside Britain’s bilious back yard shed wars, 29 September). Perhaps these luxury sheds should come with a health warning: “Do not assemble if you value good relations with your neighbours.”In our street, shed wars have been fought with ghosting, poo emojis and sinister, overly loud laughter in back yards. In London, it seems that the more open-plan a house is inside, the more likely it is to have a sealed, square-eyed “room” outside in the garden. After all, we all need walls and doors sometimes.However, neighbours should be heard (faintly, reassuringly), but not seen. It is disconcerting to open your curtains and see your neighbour looking back at you from their garden pod 5 metres away. Someone’s making a lot of money out of aiding formerly civilised people to thieve their neighbours’ privacy and natural sightlines, and their precious peace and air. Planning regulations shouldn’t allow it.Jane WhiteheadLondonHaving lived in Australia for the last 18 years, where I continue to research the popularity and regulation of tiny houses, I can assure you – writing from my shed/office at the bottom of the garden – that the issue raised by Emily Retter is not peculiar to the UK.While there is clearly a need to regulate sheds as much as any other development, the capacity of neighbours to take offence at pretty much anything knows no bounds. And while many are happy if the full force of the law (or the local council) is brought to bear on their neighbours’ “monstrous” intrusion, they will also complain bitterly if their sunlounger or potting shed falls foul of the same regime.Trying to manage these disputes might be why some planners leave the profession in frustration.Paul BurtonEmeritus professor of urban management and planning, Griffith University, Brisbane, AustraliaEmily Retter fails to mention that garden sheds are increasingly being used to house Airbnb guests, with all the intrusions and friction that that can bring. Planning laws need to get to grips with what happens at the back of houses, rather than adopt an “it’s at the back, so what does it matter?” approach.Joyce CorstonEast Molesey, SurreyHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: The vapourware of the airline industry | Heathrow third runway | The Guardian
description: Brief letters: v
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Brief letters: v
Content: ‘The “prototypes” endlessly showcased by the airlines, which never get beyond the artist’s impression, are nothing but “perceptionware”, designed to solve political problems, not technical ones,’ wrote George Monbiot.Photograph: Aviation Images Ltd/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘The “prototypes” endlessly showcased by the airlines, which never get beyond the artist’s impression, are nothing but “perceptionware”, designed to solve political problems, not technical ones,’ wrote George Monbiot.Photograph: Aviation Images Ltd/AlamyBrief lettersHeathrow third runwayLettersThe vapourware of the airline industryHeathrow’s third runway and aircraft emissions | Taking the hint | Editorial mischief | Girls and ladies | The bleeding obviousMon 5 Oct 2026 12.50 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 13.24 EDTShareGeorge Monbiot coins the word “perceptionware” for technology trailed but never trialled, and only intended to impress the credulous (The expansion of Heathrow would be an expensive disaster for Britain and the world. Burnham needs to block it, 3 October). But the IT industry has long had a word for this: “vapourware” – which seems apt when discussing aircraft emissions.Robin HughesWorrall, South YorkshireIn the 1960s, my friend Linda shared a room in Paddington, London, with her friend Cynthia. Two beds in the living room, a kitchen and a shared bathroom. Normal in those days. If I went there for supper, Cynthia would get undressed and into bed at 9pm on the dot. It was difficult not to get the hint, with her head on the pillow and her eyes screwed shut. I went home (Letters, 4 October).Mary FinchDitteridge, WiltshireI smell the whiff of editorial mischief in Monday’s Guardian print edition, with the juxtaposition of the headlines “I don’t want my Celebrity Traitors flatulence to define me, says Imrie” on page 3, followed by “‘The smell suffocates’: The huge methane leaks…” on page 4.Roland WebsterBrighton, East SussexLike Elle Hunt, as an adult woman I hate being called a girl (The hill I will die on: not everything is a ‘girl’ thing – stop gendering and infantilising it all, 3 October). Even worse, though, is being called a “lady”, as in “not in front of the ladies”. As if to be a woman is to be a delicate innocent in need of protection.Julie BakerGloucesterA further example of the bleeding obvious (Letters, 4 October), at least to physicists, is a sign in an Ilkley store explaining that “Helium balloons are now upstairs”.Paul KennedyIlkley, West YorkshireHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Jude awakening: how a more fluid England are ‘unlocking’ Bellingham’s full potential | Jude Bellingham | The Guardian
description: Assistant coach Anthony Barry says new structure means their key attackers are not ‘caged in’ after 7-0 rout of Croatia
Author: David Hytner
Headline: Assistant coach Anthony Barry says new structure means their key attackers are not ‘caged in’ after 7-0 rout of Croatia
Content: Jude Bellingham is enjoying a greater licence to drift in his No 10 position under Thomas Tuchel.Photograph: Marko Perkov/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenJude Bellingham is enjoying a greater licence to drift in his No 10 position under Thomas Tuchel.Photograph: Marko Perkov/AFP/Getty ImagesJude BellinghamJude awakening: how a more fluid England are ‘unlocking’ Bellingham’s full potentialAssistant coach Anthony Barry says new structure means their key attackers are not ‘caged in’ after 7-0 rout of CroatiaDavid HytnerMon 5 Oct 2026 14.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAnthony Barry knows the hunt is on. The England assistant coach has been through the debriefs. He has mulled over the minutiae with Thomas Tuchel to such an extent he is allowed to make a joke at the boss’s expense. “He’s doing my head in,” Barry says with a smile. What is the missing piece of the puzzle? After all the emotion ofEngland’s semi-final finishat the World Cup, how can they take the decisive step to glory?It is early days in the Nations League campaign, which everybody at the Football Association wants to use asa slingshot into Euro 2028when England will co-host, but Barry can see the genesis of an answer. It comes down to liberation, enabling England’s top players to fully express themselves, and there is a reason why he finds himself talking about Jude Bellingham.Bournemouth unhappy over Scott injury but Tuchel says England took ‘zero risk’Read moreThe Real Madrid player was sensational in Saturday’s7-0 win over Croatiain Rijeka, just as he was in the3-2 defeat against Spainat Wembley on the Saturday before that. Playing in the No 10 role but with greater licence to drift, to overload on either side, there were times when Bellingham seemed to be playing with his own ball.The story about why he wore the No 22 shirt at his first club, Birmingham, is well told. Because he was a No 4, a No 8 and a No 10 rolled into one. Tuchel appears to have reached a conclusion, the basis of which was formed at the World Cup when Bellingham excelled: when a talent like him can play in so many positions, perhaps it is better not to give him one at all.“The structure [now in the Nations League] allows Jude to play more from his intuition,” Barry says, “and less from being locked down or caged in a certain position. It allows him to roam and operate in spaces in which he thinks he can be dangerous and so far it’s brought out the best in him.“It is a challenge because Jude can play in any of those positions comfortably and on a high level. So the challenge is to give him a space where he can do it all at once inside of one game. Right now, in a short sample, it seems like we found a solution to unlock all of the potential that Jude has. But we have to continue.”The point is that it is not just about Bellingham, even if he has drawn the eye almost inexorably so far this season. The blueprint was there for all to see against Croatia and it is one in which plenty of players were encouraged to push into new zones away from those traditionally dictated by their positions. Hence Tuchel had the full-backs extremely high, the wingers making zipping runs off the sides.It is about the combinations, the slicker the better, but also about players dropping into unusual areas to provide cover and using their footballing intelligence to ensure the overall structure retains its shape. Hence there was the sight of Harry Kane dropping into defensive spaces out of possession, the kind where most No 9s would never tread.View image in fullscreenJude Bellingham takes on Luka Modric during England’s thrashing of Croatia.Photograph: Raddad Jebarah/ShutterstockIt was impossible to ignore the ferocity of England’s counterpress; how if one player lost the ball, he and his teammates sought to regain it within two or three seconds. Croatia were overwhelmed, especially in the first half, which ended with England four goals up. The intensity has to endure. But it is the proactive add-ons that the management hope will drive the new tournament cycle,continuing against Czechiain the Nations League at Wembley on Tuesday night. It is no longer a positional style. The idea is that it is freer. Is it a reaction to the inhibitions England came to feel in the World Cup semi-final defeat against Argentina?“We have moved to a more principle-driven approach, which allows for more flexibility and fluidity,” Barry says. “But fluidity only looks good if it’s anchored by real principles. There is always a danger in international football with such a lack of time to prepare that if you go for this fluid model it can look quite messy. With the IQ of the players we have, it’s been quite natural for them to work together, operate in different spaces.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“It’s not about starting new, it’s about continuation and adding stuff on top. It’s less prescribed, less fixed in the idea of: ‘You play here, you play there.’ It’s more interchanges of position. We feel it suits this group of players and is the best way to break down opposing blocks.“When you have players like Harry and Jude on the frontline that are really better at moving, that have this deep intuition and IQ for the game … [it is] to trust them, open up spaces for them to operate. It’s also part of the model that we’re moving forward with. We have elite penetration on the last line, whether that comes from our wingers or our full-backs. And we have fluid midfielders with Elliot [Anderson], Alex [Scott] and Declan [Rice], who are happy to move for miles.”Kane is primed to win his 125th cap on Tuesday night and equal Peter Shilton’sEnglandmen’s record. It is a time for tributes and Barry was effusive in his praise of Kane’s professionalism and leadership, his selflessness, his lack of ego; how he is happy to “track back and do the dirty work”.Barry had a better line. “He’s the best ball-striker I have ever worked with,” he said. It is worth noting Barry worked with Cristiano Ronaldo during his time with Portugal as the assistant manager to Roberto Martínez. It is one key reason for Barry’s sense of optimism. There are many others.Explore more on these topicsJude BellinghamEnglandNations LeaguefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Mamardashvili saves penalty as Georgia hold Northern Ireland in Nations League | Nations League | The Guardian
description: Isaac Price saw his second-half penalty saved as Northern Ireland failed to convert their chances in a goalless draw with Georgia in Belfast
Author: Ewan Murray
Headline: Isaac Price saw his second-half penalty saved as Northern Ireland failed to convert their chances in a goalless draw with Georgia in Belfast
Content: Isaac Price covers his face after failing to convert his second-half penalty.Photograph: Liam McBurney/PAView image in fullscreenIsaac Price covers his face after failing to convert his second-half penalty.Photograph: Liam McBurney/PANations LeagueMamardashvili saves penalty as Georgia hold Northern Ireland in Nations LeagueEwan Murrayat Windsor ParkMon 5 Oct 2026 17.08 EDTFirst published on Mon 5 Oct 2026 17.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis game concluded with mutual irritation and a touch of chaos. It is an indicator of Northern Ireland’s progress that scoreless parity led to wincing from players, management and fans alike. Isaac Price’s 84th-minute missed opportunity from the penalty spot added to the sense of annoyance.Michael O’Neill’s team are atop B2 after a window which, going by the players’s physical condition in the dying stages, has been exhausting. Northern Ireland and their youthful setup are a fascinating international story. They are a team on an upward curve, with standards elevated accordingly. O’Neill bemoaned “immaturity” in the second half, saying: “The disappointing thing is we have eight points instead of 10.”Nations League roundup: Olise leads late charge as France bowl over BelgiumRead moreGeorgia were reduced to fury with seconds of the five minutes of stoppage time remaining. The visitors were adamant they should have been awarded a spot-kick of their own as Saba Sazonov toppled under a challenge from Callum Marshall. Ramaz Svanadze, theGeorgiacoach, diplomatically said he would have to view the incident again.The difficulty for Northern Ireland related to a rising expectation. The superb performance duringFriday’s 3-0 win over Ukrainebacked upvictory away to Georgiaanda draw with Hungary. O’Neill’s men were yet to concede a goal in this section. A team quietly tipped to peak around qualification for Euro 2028 was blossoming earlier than anticipated, and this without the long-term absentee Conor Bradley. Northern Ireland’s oldest starter for Georgia’s visit was the 28-year-old Ciaron Brown.Georgia are a curious case, outside the top 70 in the world yet containing one of its finest players. Clearly Khvicha Kvaratskhelia cannotcarry a nation on his own. Indeed, the superstar’s first act was to pass the ball straight to Ethan Galbraith in the Northern Ireland midfield. During the nondescript early exchanges, Kvaratskhelia also gifted possession to Jamie Donley.What football existed in the first half came from the hosts. Ruairi McConville came closest to opening the scoring with a header from Justin Devenny’s cross, Giorgi Mamardashvili not at all convincing in denying him. Georgia responded, an excellent save from Pierce Charles necessary to deny Zuriko Davitashvili. The let-off triggered a sweeping Northern Ireland move which culminated in Devenny overhitting a low cross.View image in fullscreenKhvicha Kvaratskhelia was kept relatively quiet, but even so came close to scoring a fantastic goal.Photograph: Cathal McNaughton/ReutersNorthern Ireland were frustrated by the wasting of umpteen set plays during that first period. That Davitashvili moment aside, Georgia offered nothing in an attacking sense. Northern Ireland should have edged ahead four minutes before the interval, Patrick Kelly instead fluffing his lines having evaded the Georgia defence from Trai Hume’s through ball. Kelly appeared in two minds over whether to shoot or play in a teammate, with the visitors seizing upon his indecision. The half ended with Price curling a free-kick into the wrong side of the side-netting.Price, born in Yorkshire, exemplifies Northern Ireland’s diligence in sourcing players through bloodline eligibility. The Manchester-born Charles brothers – Shea, the captain, was once again classy in midfield as Pierce kept goal – do likewise. This is, however, no team pulled together from afar; Galbraith was a boy wonder in Belfast before being coaxed to Manchester United as a teenager. His imaginative playmaking will surely one day be worthy of a grander stage than Stoke and the ChampionshipThis big-picture stuff was irrelevant as Georgia stood firm. This was a game of intrigue, where Northern Ireland were superior while lacking a ruthless touch. Georgia’s threat was understated but real.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionGalbraith limped off with 25 minutes to play, in what constituted a blow to O’Neill. The game by now was tense and scrappy. While against better opponents that may have suited Northern Ireland, that was patently not the case this time. Georgia were managing to sap energy from the home support.With fatigue apparent across the pitch, O’Neill turned to a 36-year-old who plies his club trade at Stevenage to beef up the attack. Josh Magennis edges ever close to 100 caps, this was No 93.Kvaratskhelia had been strangely subdued for 79 minutes, but striding forward from midfield, the Paris Saint-Germain forward cracked a 20-yard drive just over the bar. What an outstanding goal it would have been.Magennis was handed a golden chance but Mamardashvili saved. A melee from the subsequent corner led to the crossbar being struck but, more significantly, the video assistant referee’s attention drawn towards a kick in the face of McConville by Budu Zivzivadze. A spot-kick was correctly awarded. Up stepped Price, whose penalty was saved, low to his right, by the Liverpool goalkeeper. Northern Ireland had passed up their moment. Georgia believed they should have been given scope to rub salt into wounds.Explore more on these topicsNations LeagueNorthern IrelandGeorgiamatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Nations League roundup: Olise leads late charge as France bowl over Belgium | Nations League | The Guardian
description: France scored four goals in 14 minutes to triumph against their rivals, two coming from Michael Olise, while Italy saw off Turkey and Hungary edged out Ukraine
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: France scored four goals in 14 minutes to triumph against their rivals, two coming from Michael Olise, while Italy saw off Turkey and Hungary edged out Ukraine
Content: Michael Olise embraces Désiré Doué after scoring France’s third goal of the game.Photograph: Benoît Tessier/ReutersView image in fullscreenMichael Olise embraces Désiré Doué after scoring France’s third goal of the game.Photograph: Benoît Tessier/ReutersNations LeagueNations League roundup: Olise leads late charge as France bowl over BelgiumFrance score four goals in 14 minutes to triumphItaly see off Turkey, Hungary edge out UkraineAgenciesMon 5 Oct 2026 17.31 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 18.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMichael Olise came off the bench to inspire France toa 4-1 win over Belgiumin the Nations League, handing Zinedine Zidane his first home victory since taking charge.Dodi Lukébakio putBelgiumon course for their first competitive win overLes Bleusin 45 years when he fired the visitors in front in the first half at the Stade de France. But the hosts turned the match on its head in a blistering finish, scoring four times in 14 minutes to preserve Zidane’s unbeaten start and move closer to the quarter-finals.Mamardashvili saves penalty as Georgia hold Northern Ireland in Nations LeagueRead moreDésiré Doué hauledFrancelevel in the 77th minute with a low drive from the edge of the area before Olise teed up Rayan Cherki to fire them ahead four minutes later. Olise then put the result beyond doubt with a third goal before adding another in stoppage time to cap a stunning French comeback.France, who also beat Belgium 1-0 in Brussels last week thanks to a late goal from Olise, moved three points clear of Italy at the top of Group A1, with Belgium another point back.ItalybeatTurkey3-1 in Bologna to condemn their opponents to a fourth straight loss, goals from Gianluca Scamacca, Riccardo Calafiori and Pio Esposito doing the business.Zidane heavily rotated his team for the last match of this three-week long international window, with only Ousmane Dembélé keeping his place among the 10 changes. The Manchester United defender Leny Yoro and the Toulouse goalkeeper Guillaume Restes made their debuts, with Dembélé again captaining the side in the absence of the injured Kylian Mbappé.Belgium were without the suspended duo of Kevin De Bruyne and Youri Tielemans but caught France cold when Roméo Lavia’s superb ball split open the home defence, allowing Lukebakio to race clear and produce a clinical finish. Maarten Vandevoordt, making his debut in goal for Belgium, kept out efforts from Esteban Lepaul and Cherki as France pressed for an equaliser, but the dam eventually burst.Doué gathered the ball and shot on the turn, beyond the reach of Vandevoordt, to haul France level. Cherki then turned home a cutback from Olise to give the hosts the lead as the Bayern Munich winger stole the show late on.Olise scrambled in a third in the 88th minute and rolled in a fourth after skilful work from Doué to complete a remarkable turnaround.“That’s football, that’s what we love. There were ⁠difficulties, but that’s part of the game, part of the kinds of matches you can have,” Zidane told TF1.“It’s good to put things right, and ​that’s what we did with an extraordinary second half. We were ‌just missing that final few metres in ‌the first half, but then we turned the match around, it was good.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenMark Csinger punches the air after scoring Hungary’s winner against Ukraine.Photograph: Tibor Illyes/MTI/APIn Group B2, Mark Csinger’s late goal earned second-placedHungarya 2-1 win againstUkrainein Trnava.Viktor Gyökeres scored in his seventh consecutiveNations Leaguegame asSwedenearned a 1-0 win againstRomaniain Group B4, while Ivan Basic’s late penalty gaveBosnia and Herzegovinaa 1-0 victory overPoland. The Burnley striker Marcus Edwards scored a stoppage-time winner asCyprushit back from behind to beatLatvia2-1 in Group C2.Explore more on these topicsNations LeagueFranceBelgiumItalyTurkeynewsShareReuse this content

title: Daniil Medvedev disqualified from China Open semi after hitting fan with ball | Tennis | The Guardian
description: Daniil Medvedev was disqualified from his China Open semi-final with Novak Djokovic ⁠after hitting a rebounding ball into the crowd
Author: John Brewin
Headline: Daniil Medvedev was disqualified from his China Open semi-final with Novak Djokovic ⁠after hitting a rebounding ball into the crowd
Content: A spectator is injured after Daniil Medvedev hit a ball into the crowd during his semi-final match against  Novak Djokovic at the China Open.Photograph: Tingshu Wang/ReutersView image in fullscreenA spectator is injured after Daniil Medvedev hit a ball into the crowd during his semi-final match against  Novak Djokovic at the China Open.Photograph: Tingshu Wang/ReutersTennisDaniil Medvedev disqualified from China Open semi after hitting fan with ballPlayer struck rebounding ball into Beijing crowdDjokovic advances to final against De MinaurJohn BrewinMon 5 Oct 2026 10.35 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 15.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDaniil Medvedev was disqualified from his China Open semi-final with Novak Djokovic on Monday after hitting a rebounding ball into the crowd that struck a ​spectator in the eye.The Russian world ‌No 5 was ‌trailing 7-5, 5-3 and had lost a point ‌when, in frustration, he struck a ball that had come off the back wall. The spectator, sitting in the first row, clutched his left eye and appeared in pain as he left the gallery, assisted by the stadium’s ‌staff.“Terribly sorry to the spectator, first of all,” Medvedev said, adding it was “100% an accident” and that he wished to apologise in person. “The ball was bouncing back so I tried to just hit it anywhere so it doesn’t go out from the court. When I saw the result I felt horrible.”View image in fullscreenDaniil Medvedev is disqualified from the match.Photograph: Jessica Lee/EPAThe incident added further to a fiery reputation for the 2021 US Open champion, three times a losing finalist at the Australian Open, born of a series of incidents where Medvedev’s temper has flared. In April, at the Monte Carlo Open,he smashed his racket several timesand placed the remnants in a courtside dustbin during his 6-0, 6-0 loss to Matteo Berrettini.At the 2025 US Open,he received a $42,500 fineafter losing his temper when a photographer interrupted Benjamin Bonzi’s serve for match point. Play was held up for more than six minutes as Medvedev riled up the crowd and insulted the umpire. “What I say and what I do, in my head, I want to do worse and I cannot because there are rules, because we’re on a tennis court,” he said.View image in fullscreenDaniil Medvedev speaks to the media after being disqualified.Photograph: Andy Wong/APAt the 2025 Australian Open,he was fined £54,000, one of biggest sums in grand slam history, after breaking a net camera by repeatedly smashing it with his racket. He also had to pay for the camera.“I was shocked. I hope that person is not badly injured,” said ​Djokovic, who wasdisqualified from the US Open in 2020under similar circumstances. “On the other hand, I also feel sorry for Daniil because I know exactly how it feels to be disqualified in a big match. I’m sure Daniil didn’t ​want to do this intentionally.”Both ​semi-finals in Beijing ended prematurely as Hubert ​Hurkacz retired with ‌an adductor ​injury. Australia’s Alex de Minaur was leading 6-4, 3-2 when his opponent, who had struggled with movement throughout the match, retired.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |FortnightlySign up toThe HotspotA new fortnightly newsletter covering the intersection of sport and the climate crisisEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionQuick GuideHow do I sign up for sport breaking news alerts?ShowIn the Guardian app, tap the Profile settings button at the top right, then select Notifications. Turn on sport notifications.If you already have the Guardian app, make sure you’re on the most recent version.If you don't have the Guardian app, download it from theiOS App Storeon iPhone or theGoogle Play storeon Android by searching for 'The Guardian'.Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Elsewhere, the defending champion, Carlos Alcaraz, overcame early wobbles on his serve to outclass fellow Spaniard Jaume Munar 5-7, 6-3, 6-1 and reach the Japan Open final, taking a step towards his first singles title after ​his comeback from a wrist injury. He will face Jiri Lehecka in Tuesday’s final.The ​23-year-old, who moved through the gears ‌duringTeam Europe’s triumphant ‌Laver Cup campaign last month, looked comfortable against the qualifier in Tokyo at ‌5-4 before gifting him the opening set with two shaky service games.“I don’t know what happened,” said Alcaraz, who dropped 16 consecutive points at the end of the first set. “I started the match well, got a break and was serving for the set.“It seems like I’m struggling every first set. But the way I come back every time, ​I’m really happy about it. Jaume’s a pretty tough player and these conditions suit him pretty well. I just tried to stay there as much as I could.”Explore more on these topicsTennisDaniil MedvedevNovak DjokovicnewsShareReuse this content

title: F1 looks amateurish and incompetent after farcical scenes in Sepang | Formula One 2026 | The Guardian
description: Review is under way, but there will be no quick fix for misconceived regulations that resulted in cars being unable to run in the rain
Author: Giles Richards
Headline: Review is under way, but there will be no quick fix for misconceived regulations that resulted in cars being unable to run in the rain
Content: Heavy rain delayed the race in Sepang and led to chaos as software in the cars was unable to cope with the conditions.Photograph: I-Hwa Cheng/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenHeavy rain delayed the race in Sepang and led to chaos as software in the cars was unable to cope with the conditions.Photograph: I-Hwa Cheng/AFP/Getty ImagesFormula One 2026AnalysisF1 looks amateurish and incompetent after farcical scenes in SepangGiles RichardsReview is under way, but there will be no quick fix for misconceived regulations that resulted in cars being unable to run in the rainMon 5 Oct 2026 11.13 EDTFirst published on Mon 5 Oct 2026 08.12 EDTShareFormula One has gone to no little pains this season in insisting the new format is more popular than ever, despiteoverwhelming disapproval from the driversregarding engine regulations. In short, there is nothing to see here.But the farcical scenes that accompaniedthe opening to the Bahrain Grand Prixin Malaysia on Sunday were all too visible and left some drivers expressing open mockery.‘Insane’: F1 drivers unite over engine regulations after chaotic Bahrain GPRead moreMax Verstappen won the race, held at Sepang to replace thecancelled Bahrain GP. It was a dominant drive for his first win of the season, but overshadowed by the sport – that styles itself as the pinnacle of motor racing – looking at best amateurish and at worst incompetent.The race was delayed because of heavy rain and the track was still very wet as the field lined up for the first time this season in such conditions. They ran behind the safety car to conduct two formation laps before the proposed start.As they toured round at low speed in low-grip conditions, the engines’ software, now an integral part of the application of power in engines using an almost equal split of electrical and combustion energy, found itself in a scenario beyond its parameters. Chaos ensued. First, Verstappen announced he could no longer accelerate, thenLewis Hamiltonslowed and came to a stop before having to do a forced reboot of his car to get moving again. A number of drivers reported the same problem as they crawled around and one Haas and one Cadillac ground to a halt. The field was in disarray and the start had to be suspended.The problem was caused by a combination of low engine speeds, low grip and the circuit layout coming up against the wet-weather management of the power-delivery software. An unanticipated bug, as the governing body, the FIA, described it. There was a 53-minute delay while the FIA wrote and applied a software update. Verstappen and Hamilton mockingly compared it to the time they had driven in Lego cars as part of the pre-race entertainment at Silverstone in July.“These engines are so complicated and a lot of software is implemented,” said Verstappen. “When there is some kind of error or glitch, that’s the problem.
