I triggered it first, then I look in my mirror and I just see everyone … I was, like, wait, are they waiting for me?”“It was like the Lego race,” said Hamilton. “Yeah, we had the same speed,” said Verstappen. Both drivers were, by now, laughing at the absurdity of the situation.The FIA said it will conduct a review with the teams and the power-unit manufacturers, but the damage has been done, once more highlighting the foibles of these engines and how much has been taken out of drivers’ control.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |FortnightlySign up toThe HotspotA new fortnightly newsletter covering the intersection of sport and the climate crisisEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionQatar and Abu Dhabi grands prix to go ahead despite Middle East conflict, says F1 chiefRead moreThe debate on the engines has raged all season. Addressing questions about why, for example, battery-usage data was not part of F1’s broadcasts, amid accusations it would demonstrate how hamstrung drivers were by battery management, F1’s chief executive Stefano Domenicali cited a conversation about the sport’s accessibility with the Star Wars creator George Lucas, himself a noted car enthusiast.“He gave us an incredible chance to see how we can really simplify things because the new fans are not understanding … what is behind the scenes. They are fascinated on the fact there is a lot of action.”F1 clearly believes the force is strong with its product the way it is and will doubtless point to the fact that when the race did eventually get under way it was an entertaining affair.Hamilton came back from dropping to 17th to third place, Verstappen was at his imperious best out front, while George Russell’s dramatic late retirement all but put paid to his title hopes.Yet even the new fans cannot fail to have observed the reality that was laid bare in Sepang: drivers reduced to furiously pushing buttons on a steering wheel, hostages to software over which they have no control, then deriding and condemning the situation afterwards.Moreover, F1 might also consider it dodged a bullet. Had the race started in the dry and then a downpour arrived, the failure would have happened as the cars circulated mid-race behind the safety car.The finger should not be simply pointed at the FIA. These rules were agreed with full input from F1, the teams and the power unit manufacturers.As Carlos Sainz perceptively asked: “My only question is who, five years ago, decided this was the direction to go?”No quick fix is coming, but what happened in Sepang emphasised how misconceived these regulations were, regardless of how they are perceived by fans of every persuasion.View image in fullscreenMax Verstappen won the race, but mocked the situation that unfolded before the start.Photograph: Eric Alonso/DPPI/ShutterstockExplore more on these topicsFormula One 2026Formula OneMotor sportMax VerstappenLewis HamiltonanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Ronaldo’s break with Portugal is sad, fitting, and long overdue | Cristiano Ronaldo | The Guardian
description: The star’s rift with Jorge Jesus is an unfortunate affair. But the forward has been holding his national team back for years
Author: Jonathan Wilson
Headline: The star’s rift with Jorge Jesus is an unfortunate affair. But the forward has been holding his national team back for years
Content: Cristiano Ronaldo and Portugal coach Jorge Jesus were at odds during this international window.Composite: Getty, ShutterstockView image in fullscreenCristiano Ronaldo and Portugal coach Jorge Jesus were at odds during this international window.Composite: Getty, ShutterstockSoccer with Jonathan WilsonCristiano RonaldoRonaldo’s break with Portugal is sad, fitting, and long overdueThe star’s rift with Jorge Jesus is an unfortunate affair. But the forward has been holding his national team back for yearsSign up for our free newsletter hereJonathan WilsonMon 5 Oct 2026 11.30 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 11.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIf this is to be the end forCristiano Ronaldoat international level, at least it can be said that he left the stage as he bestrode it: with monumental self-regard. Ronaldo has always been a preening, self-absorbed player, but for a time, when he was one of the best in the world, it could be tolerated. For the past four years, though, he has actively and obviously held Portugal back. There is a great generation of technical talent here weighed down by the monstrous albatross of his ego.To recap the basic details of the past couple of weeks. Ronaldo played 67 minutes ofPortugal’s scratchy 1-0 win over Wales. Portugal coach Jorge Jesus, who replaced Roberto Martínez after the World Cup, said he had a verbal agreement with Ronaldo that he would not start the following game against Norway but would perhaps come off the bench. Early in the second half, Ronaldo went to warm up – although whether that was on his own initiative or because Jesus had told him to is unclear. The game was tight, Portugal ultimately winning 2-1, and Jesus did not bring Ronaldo on.Cristiano Ronaldo’s Portugal walkout divides a nation as Jorge Jesus asserts controlRead moreTo Ronaldo and his army of apologists, Jesus was guilty of an unacceptable provocation. Jesus’s view was that winning the game took priority over the extremely delicate feelings of a 41-year-old forward.Ronaldo walked out on the squad, and perhaps on his international career, although only three days later, seemingly after Jesus had refused to pay penance for his blasphemy. Which is sad, although perhaps not quite in the way Ronaldo thinks it is.It’s possible Jesus, who also coached Ronaldo at Al Nassr, could have handled the situation differently. He is not, it’s fair to say, a diplomat. After Martínez’s soft-pedalling, that is, though, perhaps exactly what was needed. Jesus is 72. His vision of management is old-school, which is to say that he is a dictator and he takes orders only from the club president, and then only if he feels like it. His career has been characterized by rifts with players who have resisted him. In a sense the only surprise is that his falling out with Ronaldo took until the second game of his reign.View image in fullscreenCristiano Ronaldo was left on the sidelines against Norway.Photograph: Grzegorz Wajda/SOPA Images/ShutterstockOthers might have been cowed in the face of Ronaldo’s sulk, the online backlash and criticism from some of the Portuguese press, certain elements of which Ronaldo owns, but not Jesus. He is a man of great eloquence and is always quotable but, even by his standards, his response to the furore has been remarkable as he has insisted on the primacy of the team over any individual. “I can say to any player that you’re starting on the bench: if I need you for 30 minutes you’re going to play, if I don’t need you, you’re not going to play,” he said. “The way I was reading the game he didn’t come on. Because it’s not Cristiano, just like it will never be any player that will change my ideas as the coach. Never! Not him, not anyone in football. Not him, not anyone, not any president. Never! Zero!”His hardline approach might have backfired had Portugal then lost to Denmark, but they won 4-2, playing superbly. Gonçalo Ramos, who might have thought he had already settled this argument by replacing Ronaldo at the 2022 World Cup for the last-16 game against Switzerland andscoring a hat-trick in a 6-1 win, set up the first and scored another against the Danes, having already scored the winner against Norway. “The new manager is a great help,” Ramos said. “We have clearer ideas; we know exactly where each teammate is, both in defense and attack. We’re improving day by day, and it’s all part of a process. We’re very happy with the win, once again against a good team.” Ramos was on target Sunday as Portugal came from behind to beat Norway at home, making it four wins out of four in this window.The tendency until now has been for the otherPortugalplayers to back Ronaldo, to insist he was an icon and that they didn’t mind his superannuated lumbering. Bruno Fernandes has been notably diplomatic, but others are starting to break cover. Ramos’s former Paris Saint-Germain teammate Vitinha, for instance, who has seen at club level how beneficial a purge of egos can be, observed that Portugal’s improvement has been “the work of the coach … I think beyond the win, the content of our game was great.”Jesus has offered Ronaldo another meeting to try to resolve the situation, but the Portuguese football federation seems already to have accepted how the affair will end, beginning plans for a farewell game for the country’s record scorer. Both Jesus and Ronaldo have indicated they will say more this week.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice weeklySign up toSoccer DeskJonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBut the truth is that this is a break that should have happened long ago. For three tournaments, Ronaldo has undermined an extremely talented Portugal. This is a sad story. It is sad Ronaldo’s career should have ended this way. But the saddest element is that a great player could be so deluded about his own fading ability that a national team’s hopes and dreams should have been sacrificed to his quest to break goalscoring records.This is an extract from Soccer Desk, a newsletter from the Guardian US.Subscribe for free here.Explore more on these topicsCristiano RonaldoSoccer with Jonathan WilsonPortugalUefafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Jake Connor is shock omission from England squad for Rugby League World Cup | Rugby League World Cup 2026 | The Guardian
description: Brian McDermott said he wants players who ‘can best stick to the gameplan’ after leaving Leeds Rhinos’ Jake Connor out of Rugby League World Cup squad
Author: Aaron Bower
Headline: Brian McDermott said he wants players who ‘can best stick to the gameplan’ after leaving Leeds Rhinos’ Jake Connor out of Rugby League World Cup squad
Content: Jake Connor will not be involved when England start the tournament in Australia on 17 October.Photograph: Jess Hornby/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenJake Connor will not be involved when England start the tournament in Australia on 17 October.Photograph: Jess Hornby/Getty ImagesRugby League World Cup 2026Jake Connor is shock omission from England squad for Rugby League World CupMcDermott wants those who ‘can best stick to gameplan’Hull KR’s Lewis in but no Wakefield players includedAaron BowerMon 5 Oct 2026 09.41 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBrian McDermott, the England head coach, has justified his surprise decision to omit Jake Connor from England’sRugby League World Cupsquad by insisting the players selected are better suited to his plans to defeat the world’s best.For the second consecutive year, Leeds Rhinos half-back Connor is the major talking point in a squad that has no players from thenew Super League champions, Wakefield. He was left out by Shaun Wane for last autumn’s Ashes despite winning Super League’s Man of Steel award. England lost that series 3-0 after a string of limited attacking displays.Sam Walker tops off NRL glory with Kangaroos call-up for Rugby League World CupRead moreConnor has been in impressive form this year for Leeds, but once again he has been overlooked. McDermott has made no secret of his desire to introduce a more off-the-cuff and exciting brand of rugby rather than attempting to go toe-to-toe with Australia and New Zealand, and has selected Hull KR’s Mikey Lewis rather than Connor.He did not shy away from explaining why Connor did not fit his philosophy. “We can’t do the usual things,” he said. “We’ve got to play with a point of difference. I’ve got a squad of players of how I want England to play. Jake Connor missed out on selection by a small margin, it came down to who I think can best stick to the gameplan.”Lewis has been one of Super League’s best players in recent seasons, but he had a disappointing year for Hull KR in 2026, punctured by off-colour performances and disciplinary problems. But McDermott appeared to suggest he can get the best out of the half-back.“Mikey still won a World Club Challenge with Hull KR and guided them to a cup final this year,” he said. “I get he wasn’t in the best of shape in the back of the year and incurred a couple of bans, but I’ll point everyone to the attack plan and the game model I think England needs to have to compete with the bigger nations.”Quick GuideEngland's Rugby League World Cup squadShowMatty Ashton, AJ Brimson, Ben Currie, Zach Eckersley, Herbie Farnworth, Ethan Havard, Max King, Morgan Knowles, Mikey Lewis, Jez Litten, Junior Nsemba, Brad O’Neill, Kai Pearce-Paul, Victor Radley, Hugo Savala, Harry Smith, Morgan Smithies, Luke Thompson, Sam Walters, Ben Talty, Jack Welsby, George Williams, Dom YoungWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.McDermott has been hindered by a number of withdrawals, not least from Wakefield. It is understood they would have had four members of their squad on the plane to Australia this week: winger Tom Johnstone, half-back Jake Trueman and forwards Mike McMeeken and Caleb Hamlin-Uele, but they have opted to undergo post-season surgeries. “I’m really disappointed, it’s a real shame the Wakefield boys aren’t available,” he said.There are further significant absences across the backline in Rhinos’ Ash Handley and Wigan’s Jake Wardle. That has led to surprising call-ups for Australian-born players including Brisbane Broncos forward Ben Talty and Sydney Roosters’ utility Hugo Savala, who will now probably start at centre against Tonga in England’s first game of the tournament in Perth on 17 October.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThere is a heavy NRL influence, with 10 players based in Australia selected. That includes the debutant Max King, who was born in Huddersfield but has excelled for Canterbury Bulldogs. Herbie Farnworth, arguably the best centre in the world, is also included and will be critical to England’s chances of qualifying from their group.After facing Tonga, England play France the following week before a showdown with Papua New Guinea in Wollongong that could well decide whether they make the semi-finals or face an early exit.Explore more on these topicsRugby League World Cup 2026England rugby league teamRugby League World CupRugby leaguenewsShareReuse this content

title: Police occupy Djibouti FA headquarters amid attempt to oust Fifa council member | Soccer | The Guardian
description: Attempts to oust Souleiman Waberi as the president of the Djibouti football federation reached a dramatic climax on Monday
Author: Romain Molina
Headline: Attempts to oust Souleiman Waberi as the president of the Djibouti football federation reached a dramatic climax on Monday
Content: Souleiman Waberi (centre) pictured at a Fifa council meeting last October.Photograph: Marcio Machado/Fifa/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSouleiman Waberi (centre) pictured at a Fifa council meeting last October.Photograph: Marcio Machado/Fifa/Getty ImagesSoccerPolice occupy Djibouti FA headquarters amid attempt to oust Fifa council memberGroup of clubs wants FA president Souleiman Waberi outWaberi has faced mounting opposition for weeksEd AaronsandRomain MolinaMon 5 Oct 2026 13.36 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 17.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAttempts to oust Souleiman Waberi as the president of the Djibouti football federation (FDF) reached a dramatic climax on Monday as police occupied the federation’s headquarters after a group of club presidents called an extraordinary general assembly aimed at removing theFifacouncil member and his executive committee.The FDF said police first occupied its national technical centre at about 5.30pm on Sunday, without presenting an administrative document or court order. According to the federation, on Monday a much larger police contingent ordered Waberi, members of the executive committee, staff and other federation members to leave the premises.Nations League roundup: Olise leads late charge as France bowl over BelgiumRead moreThe FDF said 16 club presidents then entered the building under police escort and proceeded to hold what it described as a “purported” EGM. The federation rejected the meeting as illegitimate, saying it had not been properly convened and that the notice periods and procedures required under its statutes and electoral code had not been respected. It declared any decisions taken “null and void”. But sources in Djibouti have insisted the number of delegates required by the statutes was present. They unanimously voted to remove Waberi and the executive committee before establishing an interim committee to oversee the federation.Quick GuideHow do I sign up for sport breaking news alerts?ShowIn the Guardian app, tap the Profile settings button at the top right, then select Notifications. Turn on sport notifications.If you already have the Guardian app, make sure you’re on the most recent version.If you don't have the Guardian app, download it from theiOS App Storeon iPhone or theGoogle Play storeon Android by searching for 'The Guardian'.Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.The confrontation follows weeks of mounting opposition to Waberi, a member of the Confederation of African Football (Caf) executive committee as well as Fifa’s council and a close ally of Gianni Infantino. At the start of September, a coalition of 27 clubs announced its intention to vote on the removal of the executive committee and insisted it had secured the two-thirds support required under the federation’s statutes.The FDF disputed that calculation, saying it has 67 members and that 45 – not 27 – would be required to trigger an extraordinary assembly. The dispute escalated as additional clubs and delegates joined the campaign against the executive committee. The government then intervened, with the secretary of state for sport, Fatouma Ali Abdallah, ordering the FDF to convene an extraordinary general assembly within 72 hours.The FDF has appealed to Fifa and Caf, arguing that the use of state security forces to remove elected officials could constitute interference in the affairs of a national football association. It warned that the consequences could include suspension, exclusion of Djiboutian clubs and national teams from international competitions, and a freeze on development programmes and funding. The Guardian has requested a comment from Fifa.It is understood Waberi and several other officials could be facing charges this week after a police investigation of the FDF related to suspected embezzlement and money laundering was completed. They were arrested in September 2024 after a government inspection of the FDF identified financial and administrative irregularities, including weaknesses in procurement, cash management and financial controls. The government’s investigation also raised concerns about anomalies in payments to third parties, failure to pay tax on salaries and wages and “misuse of cash payments” totalling almost £500,000. The police then carried out its investigation.Waberi has denied wrongdoing. He said in August after the FDF was accused by a club official of misusing funds that Fifa’s “monitoring mechanisms have revealed no indication of wrongdoing regarding the funds it disbursed”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSport in FocusOur picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown inEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFifa, which along with Caf contributes more than $1m (£760,000) a year to the FDF through its forward development programme, has financed football infrastructure and youth-development programmes in Djibouti, including the Douda academy and artificial-pitch projects in Arta and Dikhil. But it is understood that various tenders are under investigation because they did not comply with standard procedures.Several foreign workers who were not in compliance with immigration regulations were sent back to their home countries, meaning construction was halted. According to several Caf and Fifa employees and contractors, the projects in Djibouti are “a complete farce”. “We pass on the information but nothing happens,” said one contractor. “The money has gone missing, the projects are never finished – or if they are, it’s just a bare-bones version – and nobody says a word. It breaks my heart for the young people who just want to play football.”Explore more on these topicsFootballFifaFootball politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Daryz’s Arc reputation secure but retirement would rule out folk-hero status | Sport | The Guardian
description: Back-to-back wins is a huge achievement, but Daryz’s owners have more to think about than unprecedented third Arc
Author: Greg Wood
Headline: Back-to-back wins is a huge achievement, but Daryz’s owners have more to think about than unprecedented third Arc
Content: Daryz, like so many Classic-winning three-year-olds, is destined never to be seen on a racecourse again.Photograph: Martin Dokoupil/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenDaryz, like so many Classic-winning three-year-olds, is destined never to be seen on a racecourse again.Photograph: Martin Dokoupil/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockTalking HorsesSportDaryz’s Arc reputation secure but retirement would rule out folk-hero statusBack-to-back wins is a huge achievement, but owners have more to think about than unprecedented third titleGreg WoodMon 5 Oct 2026 13.24 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 14.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt was, as the moderator of the post-Arc press conference put it, the “difficult question everyone wants to ask”, but Princess Zahra Aga Khan, the owner ofthe winner, Daryz, did not seem to find it difficult at all.“Look, we’re breeders,” she said, “and you get to the point where you’re taking a risk every time you run the horse. Would we want him to train on for another year? I’m not sure. I think he has other things to do.”Daryz makes history with back-to-back Arc de Triomphe triumphsRead moreFor many of those at Longchamp on a memorable Sunday afternoon, it will be a frustrating decision at best. For those who prefer the winter code it could further support the regular claim that Flat horses are never around long enough to earn true folk-hero status.Daryz, after all, did not run at two and seems set to retire – like many Classic-winning three-year-olds – after a couple of seasons on the track. Althoughtwo Arc victoriesis a huge achievement, a third would be unprecedented and secure Daryz a place not just among the great Arc winners, but in the conversation about the greatest of all. Having seen off the best from the 2026 Classic crop, a fit, fully mature five-year-old Daryz would surely be a very short price to see off the best of 2027 next October.Set that against the small risk of a serious injury while racing and it could seem inexplicable not to tilt for racing immortality. France Galop, the sport’s governing body, does not publish detailed statistics on fatal injuries while racing in the manner of the British Horseracing Authority or the Equine Injury Database in the US, but the fatality rate on the Flat in most major jurisdictions is about one for every 1,000 starts. A four- or five-race campaign for Daryz focused squarely on a return to Longchamp would be roughly 200-1 to end with a catastrophic injury.From a racing fan’s perspective, the risk-reward reckoning of keeping Daryz in training could seem like a no-brainer. From his owner’s point of view, though, the calculation is entirely different since it factors in what would be lost – to the Aga Khan Studs breeding operation most obviously, but also to the sport as a whole – in the unlikely event the worst were to happen.Quick GuideGreg Wood's Tuesday tipsShowLeicester1.31 Shark Two One 2.06 Woodvale 2.41 Ma Fille De Reve 3.16 Caelans Rose 3.51 Forager (nb) 4.26 Percy’s Daydream 5.01 Red SnapperBrighton1.38 Jenson Benson 2.13 Son Of Light 2.48 Rainbow Sign 3.23 Bug Boy 3.58 Berning Hot 4.33 Beach Partee 5.08 Roman SpringHuntingdon1.56 The Wise Traveller 2.31 Broadway Honey 3.06 Dancing Dame 3.41 Clever Relation 4.16 Delpotro 4.48 Bran GaladSouthwell4.55 The Pug 5.30 Jahami 6.00 Piazza 6.30 Maxton 7.00 Insuspense 7.30 Tommie’s Angel 8.00 Cliff Danger (nap) 8.30 Spec Of LightWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Princess Zahra’s family has been breeding and racing thoroughbreds since the third Aga Khan, her great-grandfather, made his debut on the British turf in the early 20th century. Hers is the fourth generation to own an Arc winner – there have now been nine in the famous silks – but the first to own a dual winner of the race.It is worth remembering that Aga Khan Studs is not a commercial operation in the manner of, say, the Coolmore Stud in Ireland. It has five stallions on its roster, sends few of its home-bred yearlings to the sales and still operates in many respects like the traditional owner-breeders that were the bedrock of the turf from its earliest days until the Coolmore-led transformation towards a full-on commercial model in the 1970s.On that basis, Daryz’s value to the operation goes well beyond what can be summed up on a balance sheet. For his owners, the decision to send him off to stud is every bit as clearcut as the choice to race on at five might seem to be to Daryz’s supporters in the grandstand.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |FortnightlySign up toThe HotspotA new fortnightly newsletter covering the intersection of sport and the climate crisisEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenPrincess Zahra Aga Khan has hinted Daryz will retire after Sunday’s success.Photograph: Abd Rabbo Ammar/Abaca/ShutterstockBut while the fans and Longchamp seem sure to be denied the spectacle of Daryz lining up for a third Arc, another abiding memory of Sunday’s action, alongside the winner’s brilliant surge to victory, is of a race and an event that has rediscovered its confidence and poise.In the first couple of years after its €150m rebuild, there were plenty from Britain and Ireland – who account for at least 25% of the attendance – saying “never again” as huge queues for toilets, food concessions and betting windows spoiled their days.But there were no queues – that I could see, at least – on a half-hour walk around Longchamp in the hour between the Prix de l’Abbaye and the Arc itself. The weather – not just warm, but hot – undoubtedly added to the general air of contentment and allowed the crowd to spread out and explore the space, but the sense of a special day in the sporting calendar was back.Daryz will be elsewhere on the first Sunday in October next year, but many, if not most, of those who were there to see him win his second Arc may well have it inked into their calendars already.Explore more on these topicsSportTalking HorsesPrix de l'Arc de TriompheHorse racingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Fuel from South Korea being shipped to Russia as Ukraine war grinds on | South Korea | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Guardian analysis finds more than 150,000 tonnes of fuel was shipped to Russian ports in July and August, some using sanctioned tankers
Author: Raphael Rashid
Headline: Exclusive: Guardian analysis finds more than 150,000 tonnes of fuel was shipped to Russian ports in July and August, some using sanctioned tankers
Content: Drone Aerial View of an Oil Tanker Ship Sailing under a bridge in Busan, South Korea.Composite: Guardian DesignView image in fullscreenDrone Aerial View of an Oil Tanker Ship Sailing under a bridge in Busan, South Korea.Composite: Guardian DesignSouth KoreaFuel from South Korea being shipped to Russia as Ukraine war grinds onExclusive: Guardian analysis finds more than 150,000 tonnes of fuel was shipped to Russian ports in July and August, some using sanctioned tankersRaphael Rashidin SeoulMon 5 Oct 2026 19.50 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 21.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFuel is being shipped fromSouth Koreato Russia via sanctioned tankers as Moscow scrambles for supplies amid the war in Ukraine, a move one expert said “undermines” Seoul’s public backing for Kyiv.Guardian analysis of port records and ship-tracking data found that in July and August over 176,000 tonnes of fuel, mostly diesel, was loaded at several South Korean ports on to seven tankers that made 14 voyages to Russia’s far east.Three of the vessels were under sanctions by the UK and EU, and one took on its cargo through aship-to-ship transferin South Korean waters – a method that can obscure where a cargo came from and lets ships avoid calling at port terminals.“It is shocking that EU-sanctioned tankers loaded fuel at South Korean ports and carried it to Russia”, said Isaac Levi, an analyst at the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA), a Finnish thinktank. “This undermines the sanctions regime and South Korea’s support forUkraine.”British armed forces intercept Russian shadow fleet oil tanker in ChannelRead moreSeoul has sent Ukraine humanitarian aid and non-lethal military supplies such as helmets, body armour and demining vehicles, and in 2023 pledged $2.3bn in support, most of it in loans.ButSouth Korea has long sought to balance its support for Ukraine with its desire to improve ties with Russia. Throughout the war, Seoul has ruled out sending weapons directly to Ukraine, in line with its practice of not supplying lethal arms to countries at war. Moscow has signalled an interest in restoring relations with South Korea, including trade ties.While the fuel trade involves vessels sanctioned by some of Seoul’s western partners, it does not appear to breach South Korean law. South Korea’s own measures against Russia rely mainly on export controls on goods such as industrial machinery, electronics and vehicles.The shipments, however, risk making Seoul look like a weak link in western efforts to pressure Russia, as relations with Kyivcome under strainover the transfer of two North Korean prisoners of war to South Korea, which Seoul says was meant to remain secret.It is unclear who owned or sold the fuel, which South Korean port records do not show.The largest carrier, the sanctionedLayla, made two voyages from the south-eastern port of Ulsan to Vladivostok leaving on 19 July and 10 August and carrying 57,000 tonnes of diesel in total. On the first trip, it told South Korean authorities its destination was Vladivostok, but on the second it said it was bound for Niigata in Japan.Korea-Russia mapAnother sanctioned tanker, the Russian-flaggedAstoria, which is also under Australian sanctions, loaded nearly 11,000 tonnes of fuel at Ulsan on 1 August, declaring Japan as its destination, before sailing to Vladivostok.Russia and North Korea open first road bridge across their shared borderRead moreThe third sanctioned tanker, theChongchon, never berthed. It took on about 26,000 tonnes of fuel from an unsanctioned tanker, the Celeste I,at an anchorage off the southern South Korean port of Yeosu in early August, then headed to Vladivostok after declaring Singapore as its destination.The owners and managers of the four tankers did not respond to requests for comment.Russia’s capacity to refine oil has beenseverely disruptedby Ukrainian drone strikes. Its refinery throughput fell in June to its lowest level in more than 20 years, and diesel output is down nearly 30% on last year, according to the International Energy Agency.Ukraine’s military intelligence agency, the HUR, says Moscow has been forced to import fuel products to feed the “Russian war machine”.According to data from the maritime analytics firm Kpler, the buyers included Rosneft, Russia’s state-controlled oil company, which is underUK, US, EU and Australian sanctions, and NNK, a Russian oil group whose owner,Eduard Khudainatov, and one of its companies, NNK-Oil, are under UK sanctions.In August, Russia imported 368,000 tonnes of oil products by sea, more than seven times the previous month and the highest monthly total since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, according to Kpler data analysed by CREA. South Korea accounted for 112,000 tonnes, or 31%, of that amount, second only to India.Loadings at South Korean ports began to surge in July, just as the country’s president, Lee Jae Myung, pledged $100m for Ukraine’s reconstruction at aNato summitin Turkey.A 2025 trade association survey found that nearly 80% of South Korean firms that had stopped exporting to Russia since the war began were open to resuming trade.In March, as thewar with Iranshut the strait of Hormuz, South Korea capped exports of certain fuels and imported Russian naphtha under a US sanctions waiver.On 1 October, the UK temporarily exempted South Korea’s existing gas contracts from a ban on maritime services for Russian LNG that takes effect in January 2027.When contacted, South Korea’s foreign ministry did not address the shipments or the sanctioned tankers. In a statement, it said that as “a responsible member of the international community, the government supports, and is actively taking part in, international efforts to help end the war in Ukraine and bring about a peaceful recovery.”It said ithad expanded its export controlson Russia under the Foreign Trade Act “beyond strategic items to 1,402 non-strategic items with a high potential for diversion to military use” and was “strictly enforcing” them.The government “continues to monitor the implementation of its export controls on Russia and, where necessary, takes action in accordance with the relevant laws and regulations,” the ministry said.The UK Foreign Office did not answer questions about the UK-sanctioned tankers using South Korean ports, or say whether the shipments had been raised with Seoul.A spokesperson said: “The UK remains firmly committed to the effective monitoring of our sanctions and to working with international partners to increase economic pressure on Russia and reduce the revenues funding its illegal war against Ukraine.”Explore more on these topicsSouth KoreaRussiaUkraineAsia PacificOilCommoditiesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Spain’s PM Pedro Sánchez calls snap election after housing law fails to pass | Spain | The Guardian
description: Election called after rightwing parties voted down emergency legislation aimed at tackling housing crisis
Author: Sam Jones
Headline: Election called after rightwing parties voted down emergency legislation aimed at tackling housing crisis
Content: 1:06Spanish PM Pedro Sánchez calls snap election – videoSpainSpain’s PM Pedro Sánchez calls snap election after housing law fails to passElection called after rightwing parties voted down emergency legislation aimed at tackling housing crisisSam JonesandAshifa Kassamin MadridMon 5 Oct 2026 10.09 EDTFirst published on Mon 5 Oct 2026 03.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSpain’s socialist prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, has once again staked his political future on a snap general election called afterrightwing parties torpedoed emergency legislationto tackle the housing crisis.Sánchez, who has been in office since 2018, used a televised address to communicate his decision, which had been widely expected. The next general election had been due before the end of next summer.Announcing on Monday morning that an early general election would be held on 29 November, the prime minister defended his government’s social, environmental and humanitarian record – and admitted it had made mistakes – but said it was time to let the Spanish people have their say.Spain’s Sánchez calls snap election amid national housing crisis – Europe liveRead more“It’s up to you now,” he said. “A glance at the horizon shows us that the world is in a very complex era of transformation and transition. It’s a time of great tension, of climate emergency, and of social and technological changes – including highly disruptive advances in artificial intelligence. It is, therefore, a time of great dangers, but also – if we know how to seize the moment – of great opportunities. You, the Spanish people, must decide what role you wish to play in this era, and what role you wantSpainto play as well.”Sánchez’s gamble is being seen as a pragmatic move from a seasoned political risk-taker. His minority coalition government with the small, leftwing Sumar alliance has faced a turbulent time in parliament since the prime ministersecured his return to office by striking a controversial deal with Catalan pro-independence partiesin the aftermath of the inconclusive snap general electionhe called three years ago.Unable to pass a budget since 2023, with his party and inner circle beset by corruption allegations and his government facing enduring pressure over its handling of the mass crossing into Spain’s north African enclave of Ceuta over the summer, he appears to have decided another snap vote is his best chance of survival.View image in fullscreenDemonstrators gathering in Madrid city centre during a housing rights demonstration on Saturday.Photograph: Enrique Romanos Tardío/NurPhoto/ShutterstockSánchez repeated his familiar assertion in Monday’s address that the choice was between his progressive government and a Spanish right that would curtail freedoms and turn back the clock on hard-won advances.“You, the men and women of Spain, must decide whether you want to join the far-right wave that rolls back progress wherever it governs, or to ensure that Spain remains a bastion of openness, social justice, and environmental responsibility,” he said.“You must decide whether you want our country to move backwards or continue moving forwards, and whether you prefer a government that works for the interests of the majority of society.”The government’s efforts to tackle the housing crisis were set out in two decrees that contained a range of measures – from a ban on evictions until 2030 to the regulation of temporary lettings and lettings by room – but were voted down in congress last Friday by the conservative People’s party (PP), the far-right Vox party, and the rightwing Catalan pro-independence party Junts.The PP, which is leading the polls but which may need to rely on Vox’s support to form a national government, said it believed construction, and not regulation, was the best way to tackle the crisis.The votes were met with an angry response from the crowds who had gathered outside congress, eliciting boos and cries of “Shame” and “Your profits, our misery”.The PP welcomed news of the snap election. “At last, the Spanish people will decide,” said the party’s leader, Alberto Núñez Feijóo. “This isn’t an election like previous ones. This is about Spain beating Sánchez.”2:50How an 87-year-old Spanish woman became the face of the fight for affordable housing – explainerVox, which already governs with the PP in four Spanish regions, hailed the decision. The party’s leader, Santiago Abascal, said Vox would fight to ensure that Spaniards “are not discriminated against in their own homeland” when it came to housing and benefits. He also said his party would focus on“remigration”in order to reverse what he called “the migrant invasion”.Long-brewing fury over the high cost of renting and the precarious nature of many tenancies exploded late last month followingthe eviction of Maricarmen Abascal, an 87-year-old woman who was removed from the home in Madrid where she had lived for 70 years. Abascal said she could not possibly afford the 230% rent hike demanded by the investment fund that bought her apartment.Her plight prompted tens of thousands of people to take to the streets to protest, and sawa huge tent camp reminiscent of the 2011indignadosmovementspring up in Madrid’s central Puerta del Sol square.Over the weekend,large demonstrations were held across the countryas protesters stepped up their demands for urgent action on the housing crisis. Authorities said 70,000 people had taken part in a protest in Madrid on Saturday, while organisers put the figure at 500,000.Sánchez will be hoping that the focus on housing, and the right’s rejection of his government’s plans to address the crisis, will mobilise voters.View image in fullscreenThousands of people marched through central Madrid on 23 September after the eviction of Maricarmen Abascal.Photograph: David Canales/NurPhoto/ShutterstockThe housing issue has served to deflect attention from the government’s much-criticised handling of thecontinuing crisis in Ceuta, which was sparked when about70,000 people crossed into the territoryfrom neighbouring Morocco in the space of 48 hours.Members of Sánchez’s administration, his party and his inner circle have also been battling a series of corruption allegations over the past two years.In July this year, the prime minister’s brother,David Sánchez, was banned from holding public office for nine yearsafter being found guilty of administrative misconduct relating to his hiring by a socialist-led council in the south-western region of Extremadura.Meanwhile, Sánchez’s wife, Begoña Gomez, is due to face trial aftera judge charged herwith embezzlement, influence peddling, corruption in business dealings and misappropriation of funds at the end of a two-year investigation.David Sánchez and Begoña Gómez have both denied any wrongdoing, and the prime minister has previously accused his political and media enemies of launching a “harassment and bullying operation” against his family.Explore more on these topicsSpainEuropePedro SánchezThe far rightnewsShareReuse this content

title: UK threatens to expel Israeli diplomats over planned East Jerusalem consulate closure | Israel | The Guardian
description: Tit-for-tat expulsions expected after relations deteriorate as a result of UK ban on goods from illegal settlements
Author: Patrick Wintour
Headline: Tit-for-tat expulsions expected after relations deteriorate as a result of UK ban on goods from illegal settlements
Content: Israel is expected to close British consulate in East Jerusalem this week.Photograph: Ahmad Gharabli/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenIsrael is expected to close British consulate in East Jerusalem this week.Photograph: Ahmad Gharabli/AFP/Getty ImagesIsraelUK threatens to expel Israeli diplomats over planned East Jerusalem consulate closureTit-for-tat expulsions expected after relations deteriorate as a result of UK ban on goods from illegal settlementsPatrick WintourDiplomatic editorMon 5 Oct 2026 13.53 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe UK has threatened to expel one Israeli diplomat for every British diplomat forced to leave Israel as a result of Israel’s decision toclose the UK consulatein East Jerusalem later this week.This could mean as many as 27 Israeli diplomats being expelled from the UK, a step that would arguably mark the lowest point in British-Israeli diplomatic relations since the formation of the state ofIsrael.The mass expulsion threat – more reminiscent of British-Russian diplomatic relations – was first reported by the Israeli newspaper Ynet, citing a message sent to Israeli officials. The UK Foreign Office said it would not comment on speculation, rather than denying the report outright.Israel has threatened to close the UK consulate in East Jerusalem in protest at the UK decision toban trade in goods from illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bankand to impose sanctions on British firms that aid, support or facilitate the construction of further illegal settlements.Israeli forces overwhelmed by violent settlers in ‘terrorist attack’ on Palestinian familyRead moreThe Foreign Office has been advised informally by the former UK attorney general Dominic Grieve that Israel is acting unlawfully if it closes the consulate on the basis it is sited in East Jerusalem, which is recognised by the United Nations and most of its members, including the UK, as being occupied Palestinian territory.Israel’s foreign minister, Gideon Sa’ar, has said that Britain’s ‌decision to impose sanctions was “morally distorted” and accused Britain’s ruling Labour party of being hostile towards the country.The consulate, which Israel’s foreign ministry has said will close on Thursday, is separate from the UK embassy based in Tel Aviv and has a distinct diplomatic role, covering East Jerusalem, the rest of theWest Bankand Gaza. It is located in the Sheikh Jarrah neighbourhood of East ​Jerusalem.An Israeli diplomatic source said: “There is no reason for us to respond to speculation about decisions that other countries may or may not take in the future.“We have already demonstrated that any step taken against Israel will be met with an appropriate response, and that will continue to be the case.”The UK national security adviser, Jonathan Powell, travelled to Jerusalem last week in an effort to persuade the Israeli government to rescind or defer the closure of the consulate but the talks failed.It has been reported that Powell opposed the decision of theUK foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, to press ahead with the settlement trade ban decision, fearing that it might play to the advantage of the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, in the national election on 27 October as he seeks to bolster his case that only his brand of leadership can bring Israel security. There is no evidence yet that the UK decision has featured in the campaign, but tit-for-tat expulsions of diplomats may raise its profile.The ‌incident highlighted growing frustration among Israel’s longtime allies over its settlements in the occupied West Bank, viewed by much of the world as illegal under international law. In his statement to the UK parliament, Miliband said settler terrorists, supported by Netanyahu’s government, arecommitting ethnic cleansingin the West Bank. Israel disputes this.Diplomats from other western countries have been very worried about the closure setting a precedent, and suggest that Britain had to respond strongly to the Israeli move because it has implications beyond the immediate dispute.Shutting down the consulate involves Israel claiming authority in Jerusalem that it does not have under international law, so it is effectively a challenge to the status quo.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“We are all concerned because if this (closure of the consulate) goes ahead it would be an incredibly damaging precedent for the status of missions in Jerusalem, which are monitoring the status quo,” said one western diplomat, speaking on condition of anonymity.“It would be inconceivable for the British government to accept (the closure) because they don’t recognise the authority of the Israeli government over Jerusalem under international law. Particularly as Israel is taking this step over British measures which are simply applying international law.”Israel has also said it is to revoke the credentials of Dutch diplomats from the country’s mission toPalestine, in response to the Netherlands’ ban on imports from illegal Israeli settlements. Israel’s military occupation of the West Bank, East Jerusalem and Gaza means diplomats need Israeli accreditation to operate in Palestine. The decision also in effect bars them from Israel-controlled East Jerusalem.France and Canada, which also joined the UK in the settlement trade ban, have not had action taken against them.Miliband received a very warm reception at the UK Labour party conference last week during a speech in which he highlighted his decision to get tough with Israel over illegal settlements.UK-Israeli relations have deteriorated steadily during the war in Gaza begun by Hamas’s 7 October 2023 massacre of Israelis as the UK became increasingly critical of the way in which Netanyahu seemed prepared to tolerate the death of thousands of Palestinians in a bid to render Hamas inoperative, a task both the Conservative and Labour governments thought was unachievable through his methods.The UK has rescinded a large number of arms export licences to Israel as a result and Miliband has spoken of evidence of war crimes in Gaza. He has declined to accuse Israel of genocide on the grounds that he believes this is a matter for international courts alone to determine.Explore more on these topicsIsraelWest BankForeign policyBenjamin NetanyahuMiddle East and north AfricaEd MilibandnewsShareReuse this content

title: No 10 insists RAF Fairford is safe after US withdraws its bombers from base  | US military | The Guardian
description: A dozen B-1s stationed at Gloucestershire base redeployed over concerns about possible threat from Iran
Author: Dan Sabbagh
Headline: A dozen B-1s stationed at Gloucestershire base redeployed over concerns about possible threat from Iran
Content: A B-1 bomber taking off from RAF Fairford. US officials told the New York Times new information about an Iran-backed plot against the site had been received.Photograph: @CraigYoungMedia/ReutersView image in fullscreenA B-1 bomber taking off from RAF Fairford. US officials told the New York Times new information about an Iran-backed plot against the site had been received.Photograph: @CraigYoungMedia/ReutersUS militaryNo 10 insists RAF Fairford is safe after US withdraws its bombers from baseA dozen B-1s stationed at Gloucestershire base redeployed over concerns about possible threat from IranAsk our reporters your questions about the Iran war and the US midtermsDan SabbaghandAletha AduMon 5 Oct 2026 14.07 EDTFirst published on Mon 5 Oct 2026 09.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDowning Street has insisted RAF Fairford is secure a day after theUS air force suddenly withdrew a dozen B-1 bombersfrom the Gloucestershire base over security concerns about a possible threat from Iran.The prime minister’s spokesperson, speaking during a scheduled briefing, said “yes” when asked if the military site was safe – contrasting with the concern theUS militaryrevealed during the hasty redeployment the day before.Pointing to comments made last week by the defence secretary, Wes Streeting, the official said there were “tried and tested approaches to defend our bases around the country and throughout the world”.Aircraft trackers reported that an entire squadron of 12 B-1 bombers based at Fairford had redeployed from the British base to the US on Sunday, a rapid movement that the Pentagon confirmed on Sunday evening.9:05Why did the US rush to withdraw bombers from RAF Fairford? - The LatestUS officials told the New York Times commanders had received new information about an Iran-backed plot against the base, which has been on high alert for more than a week. Some of the bombers left so quickly that refuelling aircraft had to be scrambled to support their flights to the US.A report on ITV News said the US feared a multiple drone attack, similar to Ukraine’sOperation Spiderweb, in which cheap small drones launched from trucks destroyed 10 Russian bombers in a coordinated attack in June last year.But UK sources cast doubt on whether Iran had the capability to launch such a complex operation 2,700 miles away. The Ukrainian operation took about 18 months to plan.Donald Trump said on Monday that the US had withdrawn the bombers from the base because of “some threats”, without saying what they were.“There were some threats, and rather than tempting the enemy – we’ll capture the enemy and beat the enemy, but why should we leave them there? So we moved them around a little bit, not very far,” Trump said.UK sources indicated they were not aware of a new terrorism threat to the base and that they would be surprised if Iran could orchestrate a fresh attack, a week after five men from London were arrested late at night having driven to a village near the base in white vans with an unclear purpose.The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said on Monday that the redeployment of the bombers was not tied to the arrests and tried to downplay any discrepancies with the UK. He said the US was confident in the security of all its bases and “with the Brits, we’ve worked very closely for a long time, including on this investigation, and they couldn’t be more cooperative”.Downing Street’s comments were the first made by the UK in the light of the US withdrawal. Neither the Ministry of Defence norGloucestershirepolice commented when asked if there was any additional threat to residents near the base. Other UK officials indicated they had not been briefed on US thinking.RAF Fairford has already been on high alert for several weeks amid heightened US concern that Tehran could try to instigate an attack on the base, which was used for US air force bombing runs against Iran earlier this year. Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said in July that the base was a legitimate military target.The hasty redeployment arguably represents a victory for Iran, forcing US bombers to retreat without any kind of attack taking place, though some experts said Washington was engaging in a wider redeployment that could lead to a scaling up of operations against Iran after the US midterm elections in November.It is unclear what level of threat Tehran could pose to a base in the heart of the UK, thoughIran destroyed a US Awacs radar plane on the tarmacduring fighting in March. Missiles fired from Iran may be able to reach the UK but would be likely to be shot down first, and a drone attack would be a high-risk operation close to the base.Experts cautioned there remained a lack of information. “Airfields are hard to defend, but the US could be making a point or just being very cautious,” said Matthew Savill, an expert with the Royal United Services Institute.Developments in the UK have not so far matched the apparent level of US concern. The five men from London were arrested in Whelford, next to the base, on suspicion of carrying explosives, but they were not charged.No explosive devices were found in the search of the vans or the men, though a barrel of petrol was recovered. All five were released on bail a day later.Trump said afterwards that he was surprised they had been allowed out on bail. “We know everything about them, we would not have released them,” he said.The prime minister, Andy Burnham, has been more muted. He said last week that there were “strong indications that Iran played a part” in the incident, but developments in the British investigation, led by counter-terrorism police, have been limited.A sixth man, a dual UK-Iranian national, was arrested in London on Thursday on suspicion of preparing acts of terrorism, but he was also released on bail on Saturday. Investigations into the circumstances surrounding the events in Gloucestershire were continuing, counter-terrorism police said.Explore more on these topicsUS militaryMilitaryGloucestershireEnglandIrannewsShareReuse this content

title: Revealed: the methane mega-leaks from UN climate summit host Turkey | Greenhouse gas emissions | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Cop31 leader calling for global curbs on climate-heating gas has landfills producing some of world’s worst plumes
Author: Damian Carrington
Headline: Exclusive: Cop31 leader calling for global curbs on climate-heating gas has landfills producing some of world’s worst plumes
Content: Satellite monitoring captured this image of a huge plume of methane detected over the Silivri landfill site near Istanbul.Photograph: Carbon MapperView image in fullscreenSatellite monitoring captured this image of a huge plume of methane detected over the Silivri landfill site near Istanbul.Photograph: Carbon MapperGreenhouse gas emissionsRevealed: the methane mega-leaks from UN climate summit host TurkeyExclusive: Cop31 leader calling for global curbs on climate-heating gas has landfills producing some of world’s worst plumesDamian CarringtonandRuth Michaelsonand Ayça Aldatmaz in IstanbulMon 5 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 09.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTwo or three nights each week, the smell descends. Residents of villages on the rural outskirts of Istanbul don’t know what the smell is, but they have been plagued by it for years: a smell so bad they have to sleep with their windows closed even during hot summer nights. They know the source, too: the huge Silivri municipal waste dump a few miles away that is belching out stinking gases as food and other organic waste rots.“The smell is not subtle. It suffocates you,” said Kemalettin Özenç, sitting outside a tea shop in the village of Yolçatı. “It’s worse when the air is still: sometimes families linger until midnight out here. Even when you go inside it’s inescapable.”These gases are more than a local problem. They include methane, a potent climate-heating gas, pouring out of the site in such vast quantities that the plume is visible from space. Satellite surveillance shows that the Silivri landfill is Turkey’s worstsuper-emitting waste site.View image in fullscreenA methane-capture power station near Seymen waste dump, another Istanbul landfill near Silivri, also run by İstaç.Photograph: Bradley Secker/The GuardianIn fact, its average emission rate of 7.4 tonnes an hour makes it one of the worst identified anywhere in the world by a team of expert researchers at the University of California (UCLA). The planet-warming impact of this single leak is equivalent to 1.5m gas-guzzling SUVs gunning their engines and there are more super-emitting dumps acrossTurkey. They stretch from İzmir in the west, to Ankara in the centre and Antalya in the south, many with “mind bogglingly large” leaks, the UCLA researchers said.The revelation that Turkey has some of the world’s worst landfill methane leaks comes at an awkward time: in November, the country will host the next UN global climate summit, Cop31, and has put cutting methane emissions at thetop of the action agendait wants all nations to agree on. Turkey’s first lady, Emine Erdoğan, has been a prominent campaigner for zero waste and methane cuts on the global stage – despite the super-plumes now revealed at home – and the president, Recep Tayyip Erdoğan,saidwaste management was a priority in a speech he made in June.View image in fullscreenKemalettin Özenç is among those seeking an end to the smell caused by the Silivri landfill site.Photograph: Bradley Secker/The Guardian‘They have the power’On the ground, the problem has festered for some time. Özenç and a growing crowd of disgruntled people in his town and others around the Silivri landfill have spent years looking for someone to intervene, but the notion of contacting the Istanbul municipality who operate the facility did not cross their minds. Some took to the internet to leave outraged messages about the smell underneath the dump’s listing on Google maps, while Özenç tried to rally people to sign a petition intended for the forestries ministry which oversees several nearby mines.But in the end, too many were afraid to sign. “They have the power and can say whatever they want,” he said, in a sweeping reference to the authorities. Turkey’s most notorious maximum security prison looms 30 minutes from Yolçatı: the mayor of Istanbul, Ekrem İmamoğlu, was accused of corruption and detained there in 2025. Özenç and others in the community feared what might happen to them if they were seen to complain too publicly.Staff from the Istanbul metropolitan municipality’s waste management division, İstaç, at the site in Silivri appeared surprised when shown satellite images of the massive gas leak emanating from a spot visible from their office windows. Methane, also known as natural or fossil gas, is transparent, and so the plume coming from the site is invisible to the naked eye.Fatih Arslan of İstaç cleared his throat while staring intently at the satellite images presented to him by the Guardian. “Well there’s not much to say,” he said, initially blaming the emissions on areas of the waste site not yet covered with clay after the dumping process. “It’s inevitable that this is happening … of course we have to make improvements,” he ventured.View image in fullscreenA major plume of methane detected by the Tanager satellite at the Menemen landfill site on 23 December 2025.Photograph: Carbon MapperTheir priority, he explained, was to cover exposed areas of the dump as quickly as possible and trap the methane produced by the rubbish for use as fuel. An on-site facility extracts 6,000 cubic metres of methane an hour from the landfill to burn for energy: letting methane leak into the atmosphere, he said, is therefore a waste.For the head of the facility, Ebu Bekir Ikinci, the current situation is actually a vast improvement on the past. He showed newspaper headlines from Istanbul in the 1990s, when the streets were piled high with rubbish and, in 1993, methane trapped at a dump exploded, killing 39 people. A year later, Erdoğan became the mayor of the city with a promise to bring in better waste management.“The baseline scenario we use for emissions from waste is what would happen if the waste was not stored at all,” said Arslan, pointing to the deadly scenario from the 1990s. “Compared to that, the emissions now are way better. This is actually very good.”View image in fullscreenEngineers monitor energy production at the power plant near the Seymen site.Photograph: Bradley Secker/The Guardian‘Mind-bogglingly large’ ratesSilivri is the largest landfill in Turkey, processing 10,000 tonnes of waste every day. Anotherwaste dump in outer Istanbul, on the other side of the city in Şile, is also a source of huge methane leaks, pouring 4 tonnes of methane into the atmosphere every hour, the global heating equivalent of about 800,000 SUVs. The UCLA team used satellite data from the Carbon Mapper portal to identify the 10 highest-emitting landfill sites across Turkey.“Many of these sites have mind-bogglingly large methane emission rates, even in a global context,” said Cara Horowitz, who leads theUCLA Stop Methane project, whichcarried out the analysis, and is executive director at the Emmett Institute on Climate Change and the Environment. “These are huge leaks, some of the largest single manmade sources of methane emissions in the world,” she added.Landfills mapMethane emissions cause a quarter of all global heating and there has been a “scary” surge since 2007 that risks triggering catastrophic climate tipping points, scientists have said. However,cutting methane emissionsis often relatively easy to do and has a rapid impact because the gas is naturally removed from the atmosphere far faster than carbon dioxide. Some experts call cutting methane the climate “emergency brake”.Turkey says that as the Cop31 host, zero waste and methane reductionare the highest priorityon its action agenda. Murat Kurum, Turkey’s environment minister and the Cop31 president-designate,wrote to the 196 nationsdue to attend the summit in Antalya, saying: “Reducing methane emissions is among the fastest and most effective strategies for slowing near-term temperature rise. The waste sector therefore represents a critical opportunity for delivering immediate climate benefits.”However, Turkey’s environment ministry declined to comment when contacted by the Guardian about the nation’s methane super-emitters.The Istanbul municipality also declined to answer questions about the methane emissions at Silivri and refused permission to photograph the site.Reducing emissions from waste disposal has also been described as the “personal project” of Emine Erdoğan, who is thehonorary president of Turkey’s Zero Waste Foundationandchair of the UN Advisory Board on Zero Waste. While opening a “zero waste forum” in June, she noted that some landfills in the world were filled with discarded food while people went hungry, and thatfood waste causes enormous methane emissions. However, Turkey is not among the 159 countries to have signed theGlobal Methane Pledgeto achieve a 30% reduction in these emissions by 2030.View image in fullscreenÖzenç studies a map showing methane pollution over Yolçatı.Photograph: Bradley Secker/The GuardianWaste opportunityTurkey could become a global leader in cutting methane emissions, Horowitz said, if it managed to clean up its many polluting landfill sites. A suite of tried-and-tested solutions exists across the world, ready for adoption, which start with being aware of the leaks. “Landfills are a significant proportion of the top global methane super-emitters, so just making sure we’re accurately understanding the scale of these emissions is an important first step,” she said.The official record of greenhouse gas emissions submitted to the UN by Turkeyacknowledgesthat a major contributor to its emissions from the waste sector “is the uncontrolled release of methane gas from landfills into the atmosphere”, and that such gases are meant to bemonitored by the environment ministry. However,legislation enacted last August– intended to launch a monitoring mechanism for emissions from select Turkish private interests – only monitors carbon dioxide emissions, and excludes any facilities “using biomass” like landfill.Methane gas coming off landfills can be captured and used as fuel, as at Silivri. However, Dr Tia Scarpelli, waste sector lead at Carbon Mapper, said: “Not all sites that have gas collection are created equal. It does come down to the design and efficiency of the system and day-to day management practices.” Causes of major leaks can include poor maintenance, failure to keep flares alight when burning off excess methane, or collecting only good quality gas and venting the rest.View image in fullscreenThough methane can be captured relatively easily, it can still leak from facilities unless they are properly maintained.Photograph: Bradley Secker/The GuardianA more foolproof way of halting methane leaks is to stop organic waste going into the landfill and rotting in the first place. In South Korea,close to 100%of the country’s food waste is now recycled. “Getting at the real source of the problem is an even better opportunity to reduce methane leaks,” Horowitz said.Stopping the massive methane leaks in Turkey is a climate imperative, but may yet fall victim to politics: Istanbul, Ankara, İzmir and several other big cities remain under municipal opposition control, despite a prolonged crackdown on Turkey’s largest opposition party. Imamoğlu and hundreds of other former employees from the Istanbul municipality are on trial on corruption charges, and the government in Ankara is eager to claim the opposition are incapable of running Turkey’s largest city, including its waste management.After his petition went nowhere, Özenç said he and other communities in Silivri living with the unbearable smell feared another instance of what he saw as a “cover up”.“It’s not like we have a say anyway,” he added. “What can you do? The moment you talk about this, there is silence.”This article was amended on 5 October 2026 to remove an incorrect reference to Istanbul as Turkey’s capital.Explore more on these topicsGreenhouse gas emissionsClimate crisisTurkeyCop31WastefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: To cull or not to cull: Greenland debates fate of world’s slowest shark | Sharks | The Guardian
description: As trawlers compete with Greenland sharks for halibut and cod, conservationists and fishers clash over what to do about misunderstood species
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: As trawlers compete with Greenland sharks for halibut and cod, conservationists and fishers clash over what to do about misunderstood species
Content: Greenland sharks can live for more than 400 years but as they only reproduce after 150 years, plans for a cull could devastate the population, say conservationists.Photograph: Eric Ste MarieView image in fullscreenGreenland sharks can live for more than 400 years but as they only reproduce after 150 years, plans for a cull could devastate the population, say conservationists.Photograph: Eric Ste MarieSeascape: the state of our oceansSharksTo cull or not to cull: Greenland debates fate of world’s slowest sharkAs trawlers compete with Greenland sharks for halibut and cod, conservationists and fishers clash over what to do about misunderstood speciesSupported byAbout this contentAnnaliese Smith in GreenlandMon 5 Oct 2026 00.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘When I accidentally catch a shark, I bring it to my dogs,” Henrik Jensen, a 27-year-old from Greenland’s west coast, says casually. “I don’t let it back down because [the sharks] bully me and cut my lines.”Jensen has fished for halibut in Ilulissat, Greenland’s third largest town, for a decade. He works an hour north of the town’s main iceberg-laden fishery, which sustains the livelihood of nearly 400 fishers. There, the halibut are bigger and more plentiful, but so are the Greenland sharks.“This year I’ve lost around 6,000 hooks in total. Sometimes we lose 30,000 Danish krone [£3,440] a day,” says Jensen.The Greenland shark is one of the least understood species on the planet. As well as being the world’s slowest shark, it is the second-largest carnivorous species, after the white shark, according to theShark Trust. Reaching about six to seven metres in length, they can live for more than 400 years. For a long time they were thought to be completely blind, althoughscientists have recently discovered this may not be true.The sharks inhabit a vast range across the deep and cold waters of the north and west Atlantic, but their attempts to feed on the northern fisheries’ main catch – Greenland halibut and Atlantic cod – often see them tangled in gear and brought in as bycatch.View image in fullscreenCleaning cod on a fishing boat off Kapisillit, south-west Greenland.Photograph: Marko Đurica/ReutersThis acrimonious coexistence has been documented ever since targeted fishing for the sharks’ liver oil ceased in the 1960s, but it came to a head earlier this year. The Avannaata municipality, of which Ilulissat is the administrative seat, approved a controversial plan to cull 1,000 sharks, offering 300 krone for every heart of a Greenland shark.Lars Erik Gabrielsen, mayor of the municipality, says: “We need to safeguard the income of fishermen and the catch so that we can continue to eat the foods that we have relied on for generations.”For many fishing inshore, working in small teams on dinghies, it brought a longstanding issue to a head. Timotheus Petersen, chair of the fishing association in Kullorsuaq, says: “Our longlines are expensive – one costs 1,599 krone. When the sharks cut our lines, we cannot finish fishing. We have to spend more money and buy new gear.”The plan was eventually dropped after the government questioned its legality, but the prospect of a future cull remains.In its decision to approve the cull, Avannaata council cited a similar scheme from the early 2000s in the former Aasiaat municipality, where a bounty of 200 krone was offered. According toa 2007 reportfrom the Danish Technical University, another scheme between 1986 and 2001 in the former Uummannaq municipality brought in 19,697 hearts.But the marine conservation group Oceans North Kalaallit Nunaat (ONKN) argues that culls do not resolve the issue, highlighting the migratory nature of the species, which can swim up to 1,200 miles (2,000km) a year. “Sharks removed in north-west Greenland would quickly be replaced by individuals arriving from other regions,”ONKN warned.Many fishers also do not consider 300 krone worth the effort of hauling a shark onboard. “It’s difficult to catch them,” Jensen says. “You need bigger hooks and chains for the lines, so I don’t think anyone wants to try.”View image in fullscreenA Greenland shark pulled in as bycatch by an Atlantic trawler.Photograph: Juan Vilata/AlamyBut the debate around a possible cull is alarming conservationists. “If somebody says, ‘I’m going to cull a couple of thousand Greenland sharks’, that’s a disaster in my opinion,” says Prof Nick Dulvy, a marine conservationist at Simon Fraser University in British Columbia.The Greenland shark is believed to become sexually mature at 150, which means the species replaces itself extremely slowly and will not rebound from a cull quickly. It is still recovering from targeted fishing throughout the 19th and mid-20th centuries, when, at itspeak in 1948, 58,000 were landed.“They are probably – biologically – the most sensitive species in the ocean to overfishing,” Dulvy says. Globally, it is estimated that 3,500 sharks are caught every year as bycatch and the population remains in decline.Greenland’s fishing community highlight their longstanding problem with the sharks, but do not say why it has suddenly escalated. Jenseeraq Poulsen, the director of ONKN, suggests it is due to mounting pressures within a fishing industrythat accounts for about 25% of Greenland’s GDP.“If every Greenland shark in Baffin Bay vanished tomorrow, the inshore fishery in Avannaata would still face too many boats working a quota under pressure, rising costs and no alternative employment,” he says. “When margins are narrow, a longstanding nuisance becomes intolerable.”Even though the price of halibut continues to rise, according to the Greenland Institute of Natural Resources, the average size of the fish is decreasing annually. While Jensen maintains he can still make a good living from fishing, he describes putting fewer hooks out and bringing in fewer fish, suggesting this is due to overfishing by offshore trawlers.View image in fullscreenGhost gear recovered from Arctic waters around Ilulissat, Greenland.Photograph: Ilulissani Aalisartut Piniartullu Peqatigiiffiat (IAPP)For some of those fishing these waters, however, the shark is not the leading cause of losing gear. “There are more and more ‘ghost lines’ and they are too heavy to pull up by the machine we use,” Jensen says. Ghost lines are discarded or lost gear that can get entangled with new lines, breaking equipment and trapping marine life.Halibut Greenland, a cooperatively owned fish-processing company in Ilulissat, provides funds to clean up ghost gear in the area, which ONKN views as more effective than a shark cull. Poulsen also proposes a gear-loss compensation scheme, as well as funded trials of acoustic shark deterrents.Rebekka Nygård Bak, an adviser to Greenland’s Ministry of Fisheries, Hunting, Agriculture and Self Sufficiency, suggests new bycatch-friendly equipment regulations could be a solution. She says a campaign for better bycatch reporting will also be key to any next steps.For Poulsen, the sharks and those fishing these waters are two components of the same ecosystem, facing growing pressures in changing seas. “The shark is the visible, tangible version of a problem whose real drivers are structural,” he says.Explore more on these topicsSharksSeascape: the state of our oceansFishingFishMarine lifeGreenlandConservationWildlifefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: US supreme court hears big oil’s bid to block climate damage lawsuits | US supreme court | The Guardian
description: How the court will lean is unclear amid Suncor Energy and ExxonMobil’s attempt to stop lawsuits at state level
Author: Hilary Beaumont
Headline: How the court will lean is unclear amid Suncor Energy and ExxonMobil’s attempt to stop lawsuits at state level
Content: Suncor Refinery in Commerce City, Colorado, on 26 July 2023.Photograph: Hyoung Chang/Denver Post/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSuncor Refinery in Commerce City, Colorado, on 26 July 2023.Photograph: Hyoung Chang/Denver Post/Getty ImagesDemocracy, climate and justiceUS supreme courtUS supreme court hears big oil’s bid to block climate damage lawsuitsHow the court will lean is unclear amid Suncor Energy and ExxonMobil’s attempt to stop lawsuits at state levelDemocracy, climate and justice is supported byAbout this contentHilary BeaumontMon 5 Oct 2026 15.57 EDTFirst published on Mon 5 Oct 2026 09.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheUS supreme courtbegan its new nine-month term hearing arguments on Monday in a majorcasein which big oil companies attempted to strike a fatal blow against lawsuits that seek to hold them accountable for theclimate crisis.After the almost two-hour hearing, while it was not yet clear which way the justices were leaning, experts said the court may find it challenging to write a majority decision siding with industry.InSuncor Energy Inc v County Commissioners of Boulder County, local officials in Boulder are suing Suncor Energy and ExxonMobil in state court to force the companies to share a portion of the costs that the climate crisis has imposed on local taxpayers. However, Exxon and Canada-based Suncor are arguing that federal law prevents state courts from hearing Boulder’s climate change lawsuit.If the supreme court justices side with Boulder or decide that the case is not in their jurisdiction, then it would continue in state court. But if the fossil fuel industry convinces the justices, the decision could apply not only to the Boulder case, but also to dozens of other climate cases brought by state and local governments around the US.As a result of Justice Samuel Alito’srecusalfrom the case, there are only five conservative justices weighing in, so Boulder county must only convince one conservative justice to win, assuming the three liberal justices back Boulder. Some noted that the justices focused their questions primarily on the merits of the case rather than askingif the court had jurisdiction to hear it, suggesting they will make a decision on the question of whether federal law pre-empts Boulder’s state climate case.Kannon Shanmugam, a lawyer for the fossil fuel companies, told the justices that climate change was a pressing issue, but state cases such as the one filed by Boulder were the wrong way to resolve it, and the issue should be left to lawmakers. He argued that if the cases were heard in state courts, it would allow a high number of lawsuits to be filed. “The breadth of Boulder’s argument is astonishing,” he said.Samuel Alito steps aside in a major climate case amid scrutiny over oil stock holdingsRead moreShanmugam argued that climate change is different from other interstate pollution cases “because the claim runs through global climate change” and involves anyone who uses fossil fuels worldwide.Kirti Datla, the director of Earthjustice’s strategic legal advocacy program, said the industry lawyer needed five justices to agree with him. “Some of the justices seemed to be persuaded by the idea that climate change is different, or the sheer number of these suits creates a problem of a different kind,” Datla said.
