But she added that the justices were struggling to come up with reasons based in law that would support the industry arguments. “It’s always been Suncor’s task to provide them with clear answers to those questions, and I didn’t hear clear answers to those questions in argument.”Dennis Fan, the founder and director of the Appellate Litigation Clinic at Columbia Law School who wrote an amicus brief in the case, said it was too close to call, but he was concerned for the future of the climate cases. “They focused more on the merits,” he said. “That had me much more worried for Boulder.”Fan said the industry hopes this case is going to be the “death blow” to this type of lawsuit.“The industry is going for the home run … They’re thinking, ‘If we win this argument, there will never, ever be climate change litigation again.’”Boulder officials filed a lawsuit inColoradocourt in 2018 arguing that Exxon and Suncor concealed and misrepresented to the public what they knew about the damage that burning fossil fuels would do to the climate, and that they should pay for the resulting costs of disasters. Initially, the firms sought to have the case moved to federal court. Then when the Colorado supreme court allowed Boulder’s case to make its way toward trial in state court, Exxon and Suncor appealed that ruling up to the supreme court, arguing it should be dismissed on grounds of federal pre-emption.Typically, cases must be decided by lower courts before reaching the supreme court, but the justices agreed to hear this case while the state case is ongoing. “That’s an incredibly weird thing to have happen,” Fan said.The supreme court considered whether it had proper jurisdiction to hear Boulder’s case right now, and whether federal law pre-empted Boulder’s case from being heard in state court.Congress has the power to pass federal laws that invalidate state laws, but the question is whether there are any federal laws that invalidate state climate cases. “They’ve had a little bit of difficulty identifying exactly what that source of federal law is,” Fan said. For instance, the fossil fuel companies claim that the federal Clean Air Act pre-empts Boulder’s case from state court, even though the law specifies that “air pollution control at its source is the primary responsibility of states and local governments”.So the fossil fuel companies in their brief claimed that supreme court decisions from a century ago suggested that federal courts have power to hear environmental cases, even without federal laws on the books, and that these decisions created a “federal common law” governing environmental lawsuits across state lines. They asserted that this federal common law was still in effect and existed in the “structure of the Constitution” even though the federal Clean Air Act has since declared states have primary jurisdiction over local air pollution.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionShanmugam presented the constitutional theory to the justices on Monday, but Kevin Russell, Boulder’s attorney, repeatedly drew their attention back to the constitution. Russell argued that the industry attorney was asking them to “jump through a number of hoops” to answer a complicated question. “Instead, I would suggest that the court can and should directly answer the question: what in the constitution implicitly prohibitsColoradoor any other state’s law from applying to these claims?”Datla of Earthjustice said some conservative justices appeared to agree with Boulder on this point. “Chief Justice [John Roberts] and Justice [Neil] Gorsuch seemed to ask questions that indicated that they thought that broad constitutional rule was complicated at a minimum,” she said.Datla said the reaction of the conservative justices suggested they would find it difficult to write a decision supporting Suncor. “The fact that there wasn’t a clear position that the conservative justices seem to coalesce around as to which one of Suncor’s arguments was right is, I think, telling that maybe they don’t all think this is a foregone conclusion.”The supreme court has not historically agreed with the argument the oil companies are making, Fan said. He pointed to the tobacco and opioid companies that previously faced state public nuisance cases. “For decades, the tobacco industry tried to get the supreme court and other courts to stop state court litigation from happening against the tobacco industry, and they failed every single time,” he said.US states and cities sue over Trump EPA’s repeal of emissions rulesRead moreClimate advocates and wildfire survivors rallied on Monday morning outside the supreme court in Washington DC.Daryl McCool, an artist wholost her homewhen the 2021Marshall firedestroyed her neighborhood in Boulder county, Colorado, is not involved in the case but planned to attend the rally. The fire caused damage estimated atmore than $2bn, and a recent report estimated that the climate crisis could cost Colorado up to$37bnby 2050. “The case itself is meaningful because it affects every single human, every single creature, it affects everyone that is on this earth,” McCool said.TheTrump administrationhas sided with the oil companies and has carried out a series of pollution regulations, includingrevokingthe 2009 bedrock scientific determination that gives the government the ability to regulate climate-heating pollution.A ruling is expected next summer.Explore more on these topicsUS supreme courtDemocracy, climate and justiceClimate crisisLaw (US)Samuel AlitoOil and gas companiesOilGasnewsShareReuse this content

title: Extreme heat warnings issued for parts of southern California | California | The Guardian
description: Temperatures in US state forecast to hit high 30s this week, while parts of Indonesia grapple with wildfires
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Temperatures in US state forecast to hit high 30s this week, while parts of Indonesia grapple with wildfires
Content: A vendor walks with a cooler of waters during high temperatures at Venice Beach in Los Angeles, California.Photograph: Caroline Brehman/ReutersView image in fullscreenA vendor walks with a cooler of waters during high temperatures at Venice Beach in Los Angeles, California.Photograph: Caroline Brehman/ReutersWeather trackerCaliforniaExtreme heat warnings issued for parts of southern CaliforniaTemperatures in US state forecast to hit high 30s celsius this week, while regions in Indonesia grapple with wildfiresJames Michelin for MetDeskMon 5 Oct 2026 04.20 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 13.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe National Weather Service in the US has issued extreme heat warnings for parts of southernCalifornia, including Los Angeles, until Thursday, as temperatures are expected to hit the high 30s celsius. Burbank, a suburb north of Los Angeles, recorded 39C on Saturday, a few degrees shy of the October record for the region set in 1987. A persistent area of high pressure will remain in place this week, leading to further hazardous hot weather and increased fire risk.Parts of Indonesia are in the midst of an extreme wildfire season, which has peaked over the past month. Western Kalimantan (Borneo) and southern Sumatra have been particularly badly affected. The lack of rainfall has dried the usually water-logged tropical soils, meaning that fires have been able to spread quickly, above and below the surface. Indonesia’s soils are also extremely rich in peat, meaning that the smoke produced from the fires contain higher levels of toxic gases such as sulphur dioxide and carbon monoxide. Cities in surrounding areas and as far as Malaysia and Singapore have experiencedreduced air qualityin recent weeks as a result. Drought and wildfires are more common in this part of the world duringEl Niñoevents owing to suppressed thunderstorm activity.View image in fullscreenIndonesian firefighters work to extinguish wildfires near a residential area in Palembang, south Sumatra.Photograph: Muhammad Fajri/NurPhoto/ShutterstockOn the flip side, El Niño is contributing to an extremely active period for tropical cyclones in the Pacific Ocean. After recent hurricanes in the eastern half of the basin, Super Typhoon Choi-Wan is now active and a category 4 typhoon to the south-east ofJapan, while on a strengthening trend. After developing on 30 September, Choi-Wan moved through the Northern Mariana Islands as a tropical storm, causing power outages on the island of Tinian, forcing the closure of schools and government offices. Choi-Wan underwent rapid intensification after clearing the islands on Sunday, and as of Sunday night has sustained winds of 150mph, and gusts of up to 180mph. The system is expected to curve away from mainland Japan and areas affected by Typhoon Dujuan last month, while steadily weakening over the coming week.Explore more on these topicsCaliforniaWeather trackerExtreme heatWest CoastIndonesiaAsia PacificEl Niño southern oscillationExtreme weathernewsShareReuse this content

title: Burnham urged to ‘end cycle of harm’ after scale of child-on-child sexual abuse revealed | Violence against women and girls | The Guardian
description: Nearly 90 organisations write to PM urging him to take decisive action to end violence against women and girls
Author: Sally Weale
Headline: Nearly 90 organisations write to PM urging him to take decisive action to end violence against women and girls
Content: An average of close to five sexual crimes against children aged 12 and younger were recorded by police every day in schools in England and Wales from 2021-25.Photograph: SanyaSM/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAn average of close to five sexual crimes against children aged 12 and younger were recorded by police every day in schools in England and Wales from 2021-25.Photograph: SanyaSM/Getty ImagesViolence against women and girlsBurnham urged to ‘end cycle of harm’ after scale of child-on-child sexual abuse revealedNearly 90 organisations write to PM urging him to take decisive action to end violence against women and girlsFrom unwanted touching to rape: the scale of child-on-child abuseSally WealeandRachel HallMon 5 Oct 2026 09.56 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA coalition of nearly 90 organisations has written to the prime minister calling for “decisive action” on violence against women and girls after a Guardian investigation revealed the scale of child-on-child sexual abuse in schools inEnglandand Wales.The groups urged Labour to redouble efforts to deliver on its manifesto promise to halve violence against women and girls (VAWG) and “end this cycle of harm once and for all”.Guardian analysis of police datafor 2021-25 found that an average of close to five sexual crimes against children aged 12 and younger were recorded by police every day in primary and secondary schools in England and Wales.The figures include reports of almost 2,000 rapes and attempted rapes, which equates to police receiving an average of one allegation of rape at a school every day. More than a third of the rape victims were children under 13.It also showed at least 8,500 sexual offences against under-13s were recorded by police as having occurred on school premises or nearby between 2021-25, equivalent to 4.7 reported offences a day.While most of the police reports did not specify the age of the alleged perpetrator, lawyers and experts say they are likely to be fellow pupils. Most of the victims were girls.From unwanted touching to rape: the scale of child-on-child abuse in English and Welsh schoolsRead moreThe letter to the prime minister said: “The publication of this data once again shines a light on the harrowing reality of sexual violence in education and among young people.“All children should have the right to access education without facing abuse, and this data is only the tip of the iceberg given that most abuse is unreported.“For far too many children, particularly girls, their childhoods are adversely affected in what should be a place of safety. And this doesn’t even account for child sexual abuse in the home, which represents the majority of cases.“We know that sexual violence can devastate victims’ lives, influencing their physical and mental wellbeing, and at school, their attendance, educational attainment and outcomes.”Awareness of child-on-child sexual abuse in schools has been growing since an inquiry in 2016 by the women and equalities committee established that sexual harassment and violence were endemic in English schools.Lawyers and campaigners condemned the “horrifying” scale of child-on-child sexual abuse revealed in the Guardian’s research.The letter to Burnham has been signed by 87 academics and campaign organisations working in the field, including the End Violence Against Women Coalition, Rape Crisis, Women’s Aid, Refuge, the National Education Union and Everyone’s Invited.“There is a long history of governments being alerted to such crises,” the letter said. “We have women and equalities committee reports dated from 2016 and 2023, mass testimonials from young people via the Everyone’s Invited movement in 2020, and the subsequent Ofsted review, which concluded that every school and college leader should act on the assumption that sexual harassment and online abuse are problems for their children and young people.“Once we know better, we must do better,” it went on. “These should have been watershed moments that led to meaningful change, and we are urging you to make this difference today.”A Department for Education spokesperson said: “The scale of abuse and harassment shown in these figures is truly appalling. No child should ever feel unsafe at school, and we are totally clear that every school must take incredibly seriously its legal duty to act on sexual violence and harassment.”They said the education secretary, Lucy Powell, had set out a new whole-school approach to tackle misogyny head-on in the last month.“Schools will have the practical tools, training and support they need to challenge harmful attitudes and push back against toxic influences before they take hold,” they said.Explore more on these topicsViolence against women and girlsChild protectionSchoolsChildrenRape and sexual assaultSexual consentPrimary schoolsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Former Panorama editor Rachel Jupp appointed as head of BBC News | BBC | The Guardian
description: Appointment of experienced troubleshooter follows internal disquiet over delay in replacing Deborah Turness
Author: Michael Savage
Headline: Appointment of experienced troubleshooter follows internal disquiet over delay in replacing Deborah Turness
Content: Jupp says she wants to ‘champion our vital, independent and impartial journalism’ and ‘deepen the trust people have in the BBC’.Photograph: BBC/PAView image in fullscreenJupp says she wants to ‘champion our vital, independent and impartial journalism’ and ‘deepen the trust people have in the BBC’.Photograph: BBC/PABBCFormer Panorama editor Rachel Jupp appointed as head of BBC NewsAppointment of experienced troubleshooter follows internal disquiet over delay in replacing Deborah TurnessMichael SavageMedia editorMon 5 Oct 2026 11.19 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheBBChas brought in one of its most trusted troubleshooters to oversee BBC News, as it battles concerns about a crisis in trust in mainstream television news coverage.Rachel Jupp will start her new job almost immediately, after internal frustrations over the time it has taken to replace Deborah Turness, who resigned last year following thefallout from claims of BBC bias.Turness’s departure came after it had emerged an episode of Panorama had spliced together two parts of a Donald Trump speech. The US president has since launched a $10bn legal suit,though the BBC has saidthe edit did not defame Trump.Jupp’s elevation confirms her status as one of the corporation’s most trusted figures on difficult editorial issues. Her most recent role, as the BBC’s director of news documentaries and long-form journalism, was created after the broadcaster found a documentary about children inGazabreached its editorial guidelines for accuracy by failing to disclose its child narrator was theson of a Hamas official.Jupp has spent less than a year in that role, and has now been tasked with overseeing the newsroom, which faces constant questions from all directions over political bias and story selection. She has previously handled politically difficult topics for the BBC, including editing a 2019 edition of Panorama that examined allegations of antisemitism in the Labour party.At a time when trust in mainstream news has fallen, she was seen as the best candidate to retain it. Trust in the news has slumped to an all-time low globally,according to the Reuters Institute. In the UK, it has fallen to 30% of the public, a 20-point fall from a decade ago. But the BBC remains the most trusted news organisation in the UK.Jupp has also been at the heart of the BBC’s strategy for the use of AI. Transforming the newsroom at a time when short-form video platforms are being increasingly used as news sources will be another major element of her job.Jupp said that as director of news she wanted to “champion our vital, independent and impartial journalism, deepen the trust people have in the BBC and meet our audiences wherever they are”.Matt Brittin, the BBC’s director general, said Jupp was “widely regarded for her news judgment, fairness, and high standards”. He said: “In a world of infinite choice, audiences are fragmenting, trust is scarce and facts are contested. BBC News remains the most used and most trusted news provider around the world and across the UK. It is our duty to recommit to the BBC’s distinctive journalistic mission while reinventing how we serve audiences, and to rise to these challenges.“In Rachel, we have someone who can do both, with a fresh perspective to lead BBC News into a new era.”Jupp was picked from a shortlist of four candidates, which included Jonathan Munro, who had been acting in the role since Turness’s departure, and the Channel 4 News editor, Esme Wren.Explore more on these topicsBBCThe news on TVnewsShareReuse this content

title: A former poet laureate and a Pulitzer winner lead TS Eliot prize shortlist | TS Eliot prize for poetry | The Guardian
description: 10 poets are in the running for the prestigious £25,000 prize, with collections that ‘remind us why it’s to poetry we turn to reorient ourselves’
Author: Emma Loffhagen
Headline: 10 poets are in the running for the prestigious £25,000 prize, with collections that ‘remind us why it’s to poetry we turn to reorient ourselves’
Content: Andrew Motion is on the shortlist for the TS Eliot prize.Photograph: JQB57/Aisha Butler PhotographyView image in fullscreenAndrew Motion is on the shortlist for the TS Eliot prize.Photograph: JQB57/Aisha Butler PhotographyTS Eliot prize for poetryA former poet laureate and a Pulitzer winner lead TS Eliot prize shortlist10 poets are in the running for the prestigious £25,000 prize, with collections that ‘remind us why it’s to poetry we turn to reorient ourselves’Emma LoffhagenMon 5 Oct 2026 12.15 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 17.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe former poet laureateAndrew Motionand Pulitzer prize winner Jorie Graham are among the 10 poets shortlisted for this year’s £25,000 TS Eliot prize, the UK and Ireland’s most prestigious award for a single volume of poetry.Motion has been selected for Gravity Archives, while Graham, who was previously shortlisted in 2012, is on the list for Killing Spree.Motion was the UK’s poet laureate between 1999 and 2009, and has written more than 15 poetry collections, alongside nonfiction books including biographies of Philip Larkin and John Keats. In aGuardian review, Sandeep Parmar wrote that Gravity Archives showcases Motion’s “rooted and resolute eye surveying the mortality of others as well as his own”.Graham, who has published 16 collections, won the 1996 Pulitzer prize for poetry for The Dream of the Unified Field, a book of selected poems. In 2012, she was shortlisted for the TS Eliot prize for the collection PLACE, which won the Forward prize for best collection.Along with Motion and Graham, this year’s shortlist features the British poet and writer Keith Jarrett, whose second collection, Hide Me Under the Blood and I Shall Be Satisfied, is also shortlisted for this year’s Forward prize. He is a poetry slam champion, and his work has previously been projected on to the facade of St Paul’s Cathedral.Other shortlisted poets include Imani Mason Jordan, whose PIVOT is their debut collection; the Canadian poet Sylvia Legris, shortlisted for Sleep Gate; and Shara McCallum, whose collection Behold is her seventh.“Though very different in voice, style and preoccupation, these 10 collections share a determination to meet the challenges faced in difficult times with closer attention to language,” said chair of judges and poet Leontia Flynn. “Each of these books reminds us why, when nothing else makes much sense, it’s to poetry we turn to reorient ourselves.”The remaining poets on the list are 2022 Forward prize winner Kim Moore, for The House of Broken Things; Holly Pester, for Cafés; Jana Prikryl, for The Channel; and the Irish poet Billy Ramsell, for Render. Mason Jordan’s PIVOT is the only debut on the shortlist.Flynn appeared on the judging panel alongside the poets Ishion Hutchinson and Daisy Lafarge. The 10 collections were selected from 174 submissions by 65 British and Irish publishers.The prize was established in 1993 by the Poetry Book Society to mark its 40th anniversary and honour its founding poet, TS Eliot.The winner will receive £25,000, with each shortlisted poet receiving £1,500. Last year’s prize was won by theCanadian poet Karen Solie for Wellwater. Other recent winners include Joelle Taylor, Jason Allen-Paisant, Anthony Joseph and Bhanu Kapil.The shortlisted poets will read from their work at the Southbank Centre’s Royal Festival Hall in London on 17 January, with the winner announced at a ceremony at the Wallace Collection the following day.Explore more on these topicsTS Eliot prize for poetryAndrew MotionnewsShareReuse this content

title: Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor takes legal action against police and Old Bailey over Epstein raids  | Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor | The Guardian
description: Former prince to challenge whether Thames Valley force and central criminal court of England and Wales acted lawfully over searches relating to his arrest
Author: Kevin Rawlinson
Headline: Former prince to challenge whether Thames Valley force and central criminal court of England and Wales acted lawfully over searches relating to his arrest
Content: Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor is taking police to court over his arrest in February.Photograph: Toby Melville/PAView image in fullscreenAndrew Mountbatten-Windsor is taking police to court over his arrest in February.Photograph: Toby Melville/PAAndrew Mountbatten-WindsorAndrew Mountbatten-Windsor takes legal action against police and Old Bailey over Epstein raidsFormer prince to challenge whether Thames Valley force and central criminal court of England and Wales acted lawfully over searches relating to his arrestKevin Rawlinsonand agencyMon 5 Oct 2026 14.40 EDTFirst published on Mon 5 Oct 2026 03.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndrew Mountbatten-Windsor is taking action against Thames Valley police and the central criminal court to challenge the legality of search warrants that led to his arrest this year, a judicial spokesperson has said.A private high court hearing is scheduled to take place before Mr Justice Hilliard on Thursday to determine whether documents related to the former Duke of York’s call for a judicial review can be made public, with Thames Valley police and the central criminal court of England and Wales in opposition.The legal fight stems from the issuing of warrants by an Old Bailey judge that allowed police to raid Mountbatten-Windsor’s residence on the Sandringham estate, and his former Windsor home, Royal Lodge, in February. Mountbatten-Windsor was arrested on suspicion of misconduct in public office, in the wake of information that emerged from theJeffrey Epsteinfiles.A high court judge subsequently granted him permission to challenge the legality of the force’s actions over the searches.According to the Daily Telegraph, which first reported Mountbatten-Windsor’s legal challenge, it represented the first time a member of the royal family had challenged the lawfulness of criminal proceedings against them since the trial of Charles I in 1649.Mountbatten-Windsor was arrested on his 66th birthday in relation to allegations that when he was the UK’s trade envoy he shared sensitive information with Epstein, a convicted child sex offender.Late last year, King Charles stripped his brother of his right to be a prince and of his dukedom over his association with the late financier.Mountbatten-Windsor was arrested on 19 February and interviewed under caution before being released under investigation.Misconduct in public office can cover a wide range of conduct, including sharing confidential financial information, financial misconduct, wilful neglect of duty and sexual misconduct. It also covers corruption and improper interference, conflict of interest, perverting the course of justice, dishonesty or fraudulent conduct, and misconduct leading to personal gain.Thames Valley police said: “While our investigation into misconduct in public office continues, we are engaged in legal proceedings in relation to warrants previously obtained from the central criminal court. As these legal proceedings are currently ongoing, it would be inappropriate for us to comment further.”Mountbatten-Windsor has been approached for comment.Explore more on these topicsAndrew Mountbatten-WindsorMonarchyJeffrey EpsteinPolicenewsShareReuse this content

title: Obama to appear at Abdul El-Sayed rally in critical Michigan Senate race | Democrats | The Guardian
description: Former president to visit 10 days before election day as victory for progressive challenger could tip Senate balance
Author: Joseph Gedeon
Headline: Former president to visit 10 days before election day as victory for progressive challenger could tip Senate balance
Content: Barack Obama and Abdul El-Sayed in this composite picture.Photograph: Getty Images, APPView image in fullscreenBarack Obama and Abdul El-Sayed in this composite picture.Photograph: Getty Images, APPDemocratsObama to appear at Abdul El-Sayed rally in critical Michigan Senate raceFormer president to visit 10 days before election day as victory for progressive challenger could tip Senate balanceAsk our reporters your questions about the Iran war and the US midtermsJoseph Gedeonin WashingtonMon 5 Oct 2026 16.29 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 19.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBarack Obamawill head to Detroit this month to rally withAbdul El-Sayed, a show of establishment support for a progressive insurgent inMichigan, one of the most consequential Senateracesin the country.The former US president will appear with El-Sayed and the gubernatorial nominee, Jocelyn Benson, on 24 October, the state’s Democratic party announced on Monday. The rally falls on the first day of the state’s in-person early voting period and 10 days before election day.“Get. Ready,” El-Sayed wrote on social media as he confirmed the appearance.The US midterm races that will decide control of Congress – mappedRead moreThe event is a significant endorsement for acandidate who survived tens of millionsin an out-of-state ad blitz to beat the congresswoman Haley Stevens by less than a percentage point in August, making the contest a national proxy battle over the party’s direction.El-Sayed, a doctor and former Wayne county health director, ran on Medicare for All and a refusal to take corporate Pac money, and was backed by Bernie Sanders and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez. He madeoppositionto US military aid to Israel and criticism of its conduct in Gazacentral to his campaign, and has described Israel’s actions there as genocide.Aipac and its allies as a result spent arecord-breaking $30mtrying to stop him, and in total Stevens and her allies outspent El-Sayed’s side nearly nine to one on advertising,according to AdImpact.Stevens, a moderate, was backed by the Senate Democratic leader, Chuck Schumer, incumbent senator Gary Peters, and the party establishment.Obama’s presence matters most in Detroit, where Black residents make up more than three-quarters of the population and where he is still highly popular. Stevens won Wayne county, which includes the city, with about 51% of the Democratic primary vote to El-Sayed’s 45%. Some ads backing her used old footage of Obama praising her, which critics called misleading because he had not endorsed in the race.Kamala Harris, the first Black and south Asian vice-president,campaignedwith El-Sayed last month, and Obama phoned him after the primary.Kamala Harris returns to Michigan to campaign for Abdul El-Sayed for SenateRead moreEl-Sayed is running for the seat being vacated by the retiring Democrat Peters, against the Republican former congressman Mike Rogers, and the contest is one of ahandful that will determine Senate control next year. Rogers was the Republican nominee in 2024, and lost that race against Elissa Slotkin, despite Donald Trump winning the state. AMarist pollof registered voters from late September had El-Sayed ahead 51% to 44%.Still, El-Sayed, who hassworn offcorporate donationsand made hisoppositionto big money in politics a theme of his campaign, traveled to New York for a fundraiser where top “all-star” donors were asked to give $57,800, split among his campaign, the Michigan Democratic party and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, with Ocasio-Cortez and the city’s mayor,Zohran Mamdani, expected to attend, theNew York Times reported.Obama has kept a relatively low profile this cycle, but is preparing a broader push. He has recorded about two dozen advertisements for Democratic candidates for governor and Senate, to be released in the coming weeks, and further stops are to be announced.Earlier this year hecampaignedin Texas with the Senate nomineeJames Talaricoand the gubernatorial nominee Gina Hinojosa, and featured in an ad for Josh Turek, the Iowa Senate candidate. This week he will headline a Washington fundraiser for the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, his first with the group this cycle.Explore more on these topicsDemocratsBarack ObamaMichiganUS SenateUS CongressUS politicsUS midterm elections 2026newsShareReuse this content

title: Hundreds of Australians, including war veterans, are being buried in unmarked communal graves | New South Wales | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Guardian Australia investigation reveals state governments use shared graves to bury those deemed too poor to pay for funerals. ‘It’s unspeakable,’ one relative says
Author: Christopher Knaus
Headline: Exclusive: Guardian Australia investigation reveals state governments use shared graves to bury those deemed too poor to pay for funerals. ‘It’s unspeakable,’ one relative says
Content: Christine Halpin was buried in an unmarked pauper's grave in Sydney’s Rookwood cemetery in 1989.Composite: David Maurice Smith/Guardian designView image in fullscreenChristine Halpin was buried in an unmarked pauper's grave in Sydney’s Rookwood cemetery in 1989.Composite: David Maurice Smith/Guardian designUnmarked gravesNew South WalesHundreds of Australians, including war veterans, are being buried in unmarked communal gravesExclusive:Guardian Australia investigation reveals state governments use shared graves to bury those deemed too poor to pay for funerals. ‘It’s unspeakable,’ one relative saysFind more from theUnmarked graves investigationhereGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastChristopher KnausandAriel BogleMon 5 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 15.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleVietnam veterans, rough sleepers and other impoverished Australians are being buried in unmarked communal graves often holding four or more people, a practice relatives have described as “unspeakable” and “a disgrace”.A Guardian Australia investigation has identified more than 100 unmarked graves acrossNew South Wales, and some in Queensland, that are being used by state governments to bury those deemed too poor to afford their own funerals.Using evidence from family, friends and the homelessness sector, together with analysis of cemetery registries and aerial imagery, the Guardian has established that the NSW government is using bare stretches of earth between dirt walkways and old headstones at Rookwood cemetery inSydneyto bury the remains of four to six strangers together in communal graves.Among those being buried together are war veterans, cancer sufferers, people with gambling addictions and severe mental illness, and migrants from developing countries whose families cannot afford exorbitant repatriation costs.Peter and Maria were mourned by people who loved them. So how did they end up in unmarked communal graves?Read moreIn at least six cases, the Guardian has identified failures by authorities that meant friends, family or support workers were either not contacted or not told of the use of unmarked and common graves. The failures are likely breaches of a NSW policy designed to “avoid causing unnecessary distress to people who may have wished to make other funeral arrangements”.Shocked family and friends say they have been left feeling robbed.View image in fullscreenRoger Davies was buried in an unmarked communal grave at Rookwood cemetery“It’s unspeakable,” said Chantel Dubsky, whose brother Roger Davies, a rough sleeper, was buried in an unmarked grave with four strangers at Rookwood without her knowledge. “He should have had the opportunity to be laid to rest with his mother, his grandparents and the people he loved, at his home in Adelaide.“He wasn’t just someone off the street – he was someone’s son, he was someone’s brother. He was my brother.”By crosschecking names with homelessness services in Sydney, Guardian Australia has also identified a further 18 individuals in the communal graves who had experienced homelessness.The homelessness sector is outraged by the revelations.Two leaders in Sydney’s homelessness sector say they were never made aware of the practice of using unmarked communal graves and are not being given the chance to intervene on behalf of their clients to fund a proper burial.A third service, the Rev Bill Crews Foundation, an inner-city Sydney homelessness charity, says it has repeatedly raised concerns with the state government about the possible use of unmarked and communal graves but has been ignored.The Rev Bill Crews, who runs the foundation, identified three of his clients as being among those in the communal graves but said he had not been told about their deaths and impending burials.“It’s outrageous,” Crews said. “We did not know – they would all have had a dignified funeral and a proper cremation, and their ashes would have been scattered in the sea.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailThe foundation regularly uses its own funds to conduct funeral services for rough sleepers when it becomes aware they have died. It was given no notification in the three cases.“For us, it’s frustrating. Incredibly frustrating.”Guardian Australia has also established that two veterans of the Vietnam war, who both served in the Royal Australian Navy, were buried in unmarked communal graves in 2024 and 2025.The pair were buried despite the availability of a federal funding program run by the Department of Veterans’ Affairs to help pay for the funerals of impoverished veterans. NSW policy recommends state health authorities approach DVA in such cases.DVA was never asked for funding for the 2024 and 2025 burials. A spokesperson said it has “not been approached to help fund the burials of destitute persons since 2020”.Aerial imagery shows new graves appearing at Rookwood cemetery between 2025 and 2026 - NearmapThe Guardian’s investigation has prompted an apology from NSW Health, which has flagged changes to improve the process, and criticism from the health minister, Ryan Park, who described the failings as “unacceptable”.In the first half of this year alone, a 17-metre stretch of earth adjacent to a dirt pathway at Rookwood has been dug up and used to bury the remains of more than 40 people in unmarked communal graves, including a rough sleeper who was well-known to most major homelessness services.Nothing has been left to mark the 17-metre stretch of graves. Inspections of the sites of hundreds of other burials at Rookwood since 2010 show only about a dozen are marked by crosses or plaques.The vast majority have no crosses, plaques or headstones to name the groups of deceased in each plot. There are also no signs to indicate the presence of graves.Older sites, where the earth has settled, appear simply as long stretches of grass.Markings are generally not used inQueenslandfor the smaller number of people buried under its scheme. The use of communal graves is much rarer in that state.The situation contrasts sharply with the process embraced byVictoria, where each individual is given their own grave and a simple marking, identifying who is interred below.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe NSW government has previously pledged to stop the use of unmarked graves for destitute burials.View image in fullscreenThe site where Roger Davies was buried in 2015. The unmarked graves are beneath the grassed area to the right, between the walkway and the old headstones.Photograph: Christopher  Knaus/The GuardianThat came after lobbying by Barbara Davis, who was never told that her foster daughter Christine Halpin had been buried in Rookwood in 1989.Davis and Christine’s biological daughter Jayne say they weretold by the NSW government in 2013that the use of unmarked graves would cease. The cemetery erected a “path of remembrance” that allows people to pay more than $800 to put a plaque on a rock, about 1km from some of the gravesites, but this has been used in a few dozen cases since 2020.Christine’s gravesite remains unmarked. Davis and Jayne are both furious.“It is a disgrace,” Davis said. “Whether you’re a prince or a pauper, you deserve a decent burial site, even just with a wooden cross with your name on it.”In another case, a young Fijian who came to Australia to play rugby in Leeton, in NSW’s Riverina region, was buried in a communal unmarked grave after dying of cancer in 2022.After eight months, the body of Bikram Lama – Sydney’s ‘birdman’ – is finally going homeRead moreA former Leeton mayor, Paul Maytom, now president of the Leeton Multicultural Support Group, said he had previously helped raise funds from local Solomon Islander and Vietnamese communities to provide repatriation or proper burials.He was not informed about the Fijian’s death.“There should be a point of contact when this type of thing happens,” Maytom said. “And you should never have a situation where someone ends up in an unmarked grave, particularly when there are community members who are willing to help pay.”A NSW Health Pathology spokesperson apologised for the failings, acknowledging they meant the dead and families and friends were not always treated with dignity and respect.“Families and friends who have lost a loved one face many challenges managing arrangements during a time of grief, and all deceased persons should be treated with dignity and respect, regardless of their financial circumstances,” a spokesperson said.“It is clear this has not always occurred with respect to the burials or cremations for deceased people without the financial means to pay for a funeral, and NSW Health apologises for the distress this has caused to those who have lost someone they love.”NSW Health said it had made changes to the process in 2025 and in recent months to improve the way the funerals were handled. That includes giving NSW Health greater control, in place of police, and creating a dedicated six-person team within NSW Health Pathology to provide “alternative funeral arrangements and alternate sources of support for families and friends that may be willing to assist”.It also flagged improving its relationships with “religious, cultural, charitable, community, and government organisations” to find funding for funerals after deaths.Two NSW ministers, Park and the homelessness minister, Rose Jackson, said the dead and their families should be treated with respect, regardless of their financial circumstances.“Previous arrangements have meant that this has not always been the case, and that is unacceptable,” Park said.“Since early 2025, NSW Health has made significant changes to establish a more comprehensive and person-centred approach to ensure all deceased persons are treated with the respect and compassion they deserve.”A spokesperson for Metropolitan Memorial Parks, which operates Rookwood general cemetery, said the NSW government did not fund it to provide grave markings for persons without means.MMP said destitute burials were not the only burial type that used multiple interments in a single plot, and rejected any suggestion that those buried through the process were being placed between individual headstones, under walkways or in trenches.It also said it had identified no legislation or regulation that had given effect to the government’s 2013 promise to mark graves.Explore more on these topicsNew South WalesUnmarked gravesQueenslandVictoriaHomelessnessPovertySocial exclusionSydneynewsShareReuse this content

title: Pennsylvania faces largest measles outbreak in decades as case count rises to 1,000  | Pennsylvania | The Guardian
description: Neighboring states are also reporting hundreds of cases, with over 3,800 recorded across the country
Author: Edward Helmore
Headline: Neighboring states are also reporting hundreds of cases, with over 3,800 recorded across the country
Content: The US is enduring its worst year for measles since 1991.Photograph: efired/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe US is enduring its worst year for measles since 1991.Photograph: efired/Getty ImagesPennsylvaniaPennsylvania faces largest measles outbreak in decades as case count rises to 1,000Neighboring states are also reporting hundreds of cases, with over 3,800 recorded across the countryEdward HelmoreMon 5 Oct 2026 17.09 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 19.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePennsylvania has surpassed 1,000 measles cases this year, state health officials calculate, making it the largest state outbreak in more than three decades. The benchmark comes as neighboring New York declared a state of emergency about measles rates there.Pennsylvania’s health department said Monday 1,004 cases of measles had been confirmed. Five Pennsylvania residents ⁠have died ⁠after ​contracting the disease, with 198 hospitalizations.Lancaster county, with sizeable Amish and Mennonite populations, remains the hardest hit, with 391 cases,according to official figures.Cases numbers have risen over the past three months, with the highest number of infections in the 24-49 age range.Pennsylvania health officials brace for expected spread of measles outbreakRead moreThe numbers, however, are not included in a CDC count due to an ongoing dispute between Pennsylvania’s governor, Josh Shapiro, and the US health secretary,Robert F Kennedy Jrover how to classify measles-related mortality.Shapiro has called Kennedy “incompetent”, and Kennedy has publicly questioned whether the state’s recorded fatalities were directly caused by measles. The CDC – which Kennedy oversees –currently lists two measles deaths in the US this year.Shapiro has expanded access to the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine in affected communities.“I want every Pennsylvanian to know this: measles does not care about your county, your faith, or your social circle,” he said in August. “I urge everyone to take this seriously and to discuss any concerns with their trusted health care provider.”In New York state, governor Kathy Hochuldeclared a state of emergencyon Monday as well, citing 108 cases in the state as of 3 October.Ohio, which also shares a border with Pennsylvania, has also reported advancing numbers of cases, with more than 200 this year. Like in Pennsylvania, Ohio has a significant Amish population.The US is enduring its worst year for measles since 1991. As of 1 October, the CDC reported 3,887 confirmed cases this year, along with the highest number of measles-associated deaths in decades.In addition to Pennsylvania, outbreaks have been reported in several states, including Texas and Utah, as well as South Carolina, which had the largest outbreak with 997 cases reported.Health officials in Pennsylvania have said the state’s current outbreak started in April, west of Philadelphia and attributed the outbreak to low vaccination rates.According to the Associated Press, the most recent outbreak to surpass 1,000 cases occurred in New York Cityin the early 1990s. That outbreak infected more than 4,500 people. During the 1989 and 1991 resurgences, 55,000 infections and 123 deaths ⁠were recorded, according to Reuters.The domestic US spread of measles was eliminated in 2000 by high vaccination rates, but those rates have fallen in recent years tobelow the 95% coverageneeded to prevent outbreaks.In November, international health officials will meet to determine if the US and Mexico havelost their measles-free status.Explore more on these topicsPennsylvaniaMMRHealthInfectious diseasesVaccines and immunisationRobert F Kennedy JrnewsShareReuse this content

title: Accept ‘bad things’ in return for benefits of AI, says Sam Altman | OpenAI | The Guardian
description: Boss of OpenAI calls for a regulatory light touch because of the ‘good stuff’ the technology can deliver
Author: Robert Booth
Headline: Boss of OpenAI calls for a regulatory light touch because of the ‘good stuff’ the technology can deliver
Content: Sam Altman of OpenAI says there is ‘a lot of daylight’ between his approach to AI safety rules and those of rival firms.Photograph: Patrick Semansky/APView image in fullscreenSam Altman of OpenAI says there is ‘a lot of daylight’ between his approach to AI safety rules and those of rival firms.Photograph: Patrick Semansky/APOpenAIAccept ‘bad things’ in return for benefits of AI, says Sam AltmanBoss of OpenAI calls for a regulatory light touch because of the ‘good stuff’ the technology can deliverRobert BoothUK technology editorMon 5 Oct 2026 09.27 EDTFirst published on Mon 5 Oct 2026 08.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSam Altman says he believes the world should accept “bad things” happening with AI in exchange for the benefits of the technology.The chief executive of OpenAI cited hacks, scams and “other bad things that will happen” in an interview that sparked an instant backlash from critics of the big AI companies. His comments came after one of his company’s safety expertsresigned, saying at the weekend that its “culture is broken”.In an interview released on Monday, Altman was asked about how OpenAI’s approach to safety differed from that of Anthropic, which has called for the industry to slow down afterone of its researchers quit, warning that AI experts believed “it could kill us all by the end of the decade”.“I think there’s a lot of daylight,” Altman said. “One of the differences between us and some of the stricter AI safety people is that we believe that the world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology and people having the agency [to use AI widely].“I do think the lighter touch regulatory stance we advocate for comes with an accepting of the fact that some bad things are going to happen as society figures out the resilience.“I wouldn’t take a trade of saying we will make sure there’s no major hacks, there’s no misuse of this technology, there’s zero scams or all the other bad things that will happen because I think that people will do tremendously – orders of magnitude – more good stuff than bad stuff.”The interview for Politico’s Decoded podcast drew a strong response from Ron DeSantis, the governor of Florida. He said he had “no dice” with the idea “a handful of tech oligarchs get to make that decision [on safety] for the rest of us”.His state last weekaskeda judge to bar OpenAI from developing new AI models without third-party approved guardrails.Gary Marcus, a prominent AI sceptic and professor emeritus at New York University, said Altman was “saying the quiet part out loud: suck it up, so you can make us rich and powerful”.Altman also reignited a feud with Elon Musk, telling Vanity Fair: “I don’t like bullies, and I think Elon’s a bully.”He had been asked if the AI industry could “grow up” and work together.“I think once in a while you got to punch a bully back in the nose,” Altman said. “And I also think Elon, like many bullies, only respects people who do. So if you want me to be able to work with him, maybe you should be happy I hit back once in a while, but I will work with Elon, of course.”Altman co-founded OpenAI with Musk in 2015 but earlier this year Muskalleged in courtthat Altman, OpenAI, and the company’s president, Greg Brockman, unjustly enriched themselves and broke a founding contract. Musk’s claim was dismissed by a judge and jury.OpenAI was hit by multiple safety crises over the summer, including when a swarm of its AI agents escaped their training “sandbox”, cheated, deceived and conspired tohackinto the Hugging Face website. Other agents accessed Australian government data. In the interview with Vanity Fair, Altman warned of “a coming tidal wave of cybersecurity problems” from rival open-source models. He suggested OpenAI could help its customers defend against the risk.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe company has scrapped the release of a cutting-edge model but Altman’s comments reflect a more bullish mood ahead of a stock market flotation.The wave of public and political concern last month about the potentially catastrophic consequences of fast-progressing AI agents that act beyond human intent had led to hopes of US-wide or even international safety agreements.However,Donald Trumpand AI bosses including Altman and Dario Amodei of Anthropic signed a far more laissez-faire pact at the White House last week. The US president said he wanted the companies to “self-police” to limit the risks from AI-enabled cyber-attacks and bioweapons.Geoffrey Irving, who worked atOpenAIand Google DeepMind and as chief scientist at the UK’s AI Safety Institute, said warnings about AI risks understated the dangers.“There’s about a 50% chance we all die because of the development of smarter-than-human AI systems,” he said, adding that actions taken over the next two to 10 years would be decisive.OpenAI’s David Robinson announced his departure at the weekend, saying “the companies building this technology aren’t being nearly careful enough” as they sprint from one product launch to the next.His view was endorsed by Miles Brundage, an AI policy researcher who worked at OpenAI for six years. He said he regretted helping “spread the idea of iterative deployment”, which may have made sense when AI was less powerful “but makes no sense at all after many deaths have been tied to AI and as we’re careening towards extinction-level risks”.Explore more on these topicsOpenAIAI (artificial intelligence)ComputingAnthropicDario AmodeiDonald TrumpSam AltmannewsShareReuse this content

title: Norway plans temporary ban on smart glasses in some public places | Norway | The Guardian
description: Camera-enabled Meta spectacles are already restricted in UK and US because of fears about unauthorised covert recording
Author: Robert Booth
Headline: Camera-enabled Meta spectacles are already restricted in UK and US because of fears about unauthorised covert recording
Content: Meta’s chief executive, Mark Zuckerberg, presents the company’s new line of smart glasses at Meta headquarters in California last month.Photograph: Carlos Barría/ReutersView image in fullscreenMeta’s chief executive, Mark Zuckerberg, presents the company’s new line of smart glasses at Meta headquarters in California last month.Photograph: Carlos Barría/ReutersNorwayNorway plans temporary ban on smart glasses in some public placesCamera-enabled Meta spectacles are already restricted in UK and US because of fears about covert recordingRobert BoothUK technology editorMon 5 Oct 2026 12.11 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNorway is planning a temporary ban on smart glasses in some public places, amid rising global concern at the spread of the AI-enabled recording devices.The Oslo government is planning a bill to prevent the use of the camera-enabled spectacles in parks, beaches, museums, shopping centres, schools, daycare centres, healthcare facilities, gyms and public events, although private use would still be allowed.There is already a growing patchwork of restrictions on the use of the glasses including in UK and US courtrooms and in pubs, cinemas and restaurants where owners have raised privacy fears.Torgeir Micaelsen, Norway’s minister of digital affairs, said he was “worried that ‌new, powerful technology is being introduced where people risk being ‌photographed, filmed or audio-recorded without knowing it”.“We do not want a society where people worry about being recorded without their knowledge, photographed or filmed in places and situations where they are accustomed to not being monitored,” he said.Norway’s Labour party, which heads a minority government, needs the support of other parties to pass the proposed ban. It said it planned to submit a bill “as soon as possible”, while tasking an expert group with drawing up permanent regulations on the issue.8:34Could Meta’s ‘pervert glasses’ be banned across the UK? - The LatestMark Zuckerberg’s Meta sells “smart” versions of Ray-Ban and Oakley glasses that allow users to film, take photos, make phone calls, play music and execute AI prompts. It hassoldat least 9m pairs of the Ray-Ban versions since the start of 2023.In the UK restaurateurs such as Jeremy King, who created the Wolseley and Delaunay restaurants, and pub chain Wetherspoons have already said they do not want customers using the devices. Cinemas said in August they had begun introducingpolicies to ban or restrict the use of smart glassesciting both privacy and film piracy concerns.Last week the governor of California, Gavin Newsom, vetoed legislation that would have penalised citizens for using smart glasses to record people without their permission in changing rooms, doctors’ offices and other spaces people generally consider private. The state already has laws governing unlawful recording.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAlbanese government considers ‘world-leading’ ban on smart glasses in public offices and buildingsRead moreIn France, the child welfare group E-enfancesaidit had this year received about 20 reports of women being filmed without their knowledge using glasses fitted with a camera, the majority of which involved Meta smart glasses. It said the incidents often followed the same pattern: a young girl or woman approached in a public place, filmed without her knowledge, with the clip then posted on social media in the form of a prank or a street interview.Meta has stressed that each pair of glasses is fitted with a tamper-proof LED light that blinks white when the user is recording or taking pictures. It advises users: “Not everyone loves being photographed. Stop recording if anyone expresses that they would rather you not.”A Meta spokesperson said: “We’re excited that our glasses continue to be very popular for listening to music, making calls, or getting live translations, so we’re continuing to expand styles and features around the world. Every pair with a camera has a bright light on the front that blinks when you take a photo or video. It can’t be turned off and the camera is disabled if someone covers or tampers with it -- something smartphones and other camera’s don’t have.”Explore more on these topicsNorwayWearable technologyMetaPrivacyEuropePrivacy & the mediaGadgetsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Sainsbury’s and Morrisons ‘held talks this year’ on multibillion-pound merger | J Sainsbury | The Guardian
description: Deal would have created a supermarket with a market share of 23.6%, still well behind Tesco’s 27.8%
Author: Lauren Almeida
Headline: Deal would have created a supermarket with a market share of 23.6%, still well behind Tesco’s 27.8%
Content: Had the two supermarkets agreed a deal it could have let to the biggest shake-up in UK supermarkets in decades.Composite: AlamyView image in fullscreenHad the two supermarkets agreed a deal it could have let to the biggest shake-up in UK supermarkets in decades.Composite: AlamyJ SainsburySainsbury’s and Morrisons ‘held talks this year’ on multibillion-pound mergerDeal would have created a supermarket with a market share of 23.6%, still well behind Tesco’s 27.8%Lauren AlmeidaMon 5 Oct 2026 11.24 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 14.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSainsbury’s held merger talks with rivalMorrisonsthis year to discuss a multibillion-pound deal that would have been the biggest shake-up for UK supermarkets in decades, according to reports.The two companies held exploratory negotiations, according to the Financial Times and Sky. It is believed they are no longer in live discussions.Morrisons, which was once one of the big four UK grocers alongside Sainsbury’s, Tesco and Asda, was bought by the US private equity firm Clayton Dubilier & Rice in 2021.The deal loaded it with more than £7bn in debt on its balance sheet, and it has since struggled to grow as fast as its rivals. The German discounter Lidlovertook it in market sharethis year.A merger between Sainsbury’s and Morrisons would have created a business with a 23.6% market share, putting it still some way behind Britain’s biggest retailer, Tesco, which has 27.8% of the market, according to analysts at Worldpanel by Numerator.The last attempt to merge two of the big four supermarkets was in 2019, when Asda and Sainsbury’s almost joined forces. That£7bn deal was blocked by the Competition and Markets Authorityon the basis that it would result in a loss of competition and higher prices for customers.The CMA would have almost certainly reviewed any merger between Sainsbury’s and Morrisons, and could have required the former to sell some of its stores to gain approval for any deal.Reducing competition in the grocery sector could also be politically sensitive, given that millions of households have grappled with persistent food inflation in recent years.Clayton Dubilier & Rice, however, is open to a tie-up between Morrisons and another major supermarket, according to Sky. It reported that Asda, which is majority owned by the private equity firm TDR Capital, could also be drawn into deal talks.Shares in Sainsbury’s, which is listed on the London Stock Exchange, were flat on Monday afternoon. The stock has fallen by 3% so far this year, compared with a 6% rise for its FTSE 100 rival Tesco.Sainsbury’s, which employs about 140,000 people, is the second biggest grocer in the UK by market share at 15.2%.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIt agreed to sell Argos for £120m in the summer to allow it to concentrate on its core food business, a decade afterbuying the retail chain for more than £1bn.News of supermarket takeover talks came as Lidl GBreported a 10% jump in its annual revenueto more than £13bn on Monday.The company said pre-tax profits at its British arm rose by 30% to £245.5m in the year that ended in February as shoppers sought out cheaper fresh meat, fruit and vegetables, as well as its Deluxe upmarket food range.Sainsbury’s and Morrisons declined to comment.Explore more on these topicsJ SainsburyMorrisonsMergers and acquisitionsRetail industrySupermarketsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Average five-year fixed mortgage rate hits 6% for first time in three years | Mortgage rates | The Guardian
description: Banks and building societies raise prices as turmoil in bond markets increases expectations of base rate rise
Author: Hilary Osborne
Headline: Banks and building societies raise prices as turmoil in bond markets increases expectations of base rate rise
Content: There has been no change in the Bank of England base rate since December last year.Photograph: ColsTravel/AlamyView image in fullscreenThere has been no change in the Bank of England base rate since December last year.Photograph: ColsTravel/AlamyMortgage ratesAverage five-year fixed mortgage rate hits 6% for first time in three yearsBanks and building societies raise prices as turmoil in bond markets increases expectations of base rate riseHilary OsborneMon 5 Oct 2026 07.39 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe average cost of a five-year fixed-rate mortgage has hit the 6% barrier for the first time in three years, as jitters in the money markets make the loans more expensive for lenders to offer.Figures from financial information provider Moneyfacts show the average is now 6.00%, its highest point since September 2023, while the average two-year fixed rate is not far behind at 5.98%, its highest since December of the same year.In recent weeks most big banks and building societies have put up prices as turmoil in global bond markets hasincreased expectations of a base rate rise.‘People are deserting it’: why are London mansions struggling to sell?Read moreMeanwhile, borrowers in Great Britain have seen their choice of fixed-rate mortgages costing below 5% shrivel to only nine options, according to Moneyfacts. That marks a 99% plunge in the market since the start of last month, when there were 1,494 deals priced below that level.There has been no change in the Bank of England base rate since December last year, but volatility in the bond markets has driven up theswap rates that affect the pricing of fixed-rate mortgages.Rachel Springall, a finance expert at Moneyfacts, said the impact on rates had been “brutal”.She said: “Average fixed mortgage rates rising back to three-year highs will be disastrous news for borrowers. Borrowers who were hoping mortgage rates would stabilise will be disappointed.”The rise in prices is bad news for borrowers finishing existing fixed-rate deals who at the start of the year may have been looking forward to falling costs, as well as those hoping to take out a mortgage to buy a property.Figures from the HomeOwners Alliance show the monthly cost of a £250,000 loan fixed at 6% for five years is £158 higher than the same-sized loan locked in at 4.94%, which was the average rate reported by Moneyfacts at the start of February.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThere are already signs that higher mortgage costs are weighing down the housing market, with Nationwide building society last weekreporting that annual price growth had halved in September.Ian Harris, the president of the estate agents’ body NAEA Propertymark, said members were “seeing first-hand how sensitive buyers are to mortgage rates”, and the rapid disappearance of sub-5% deals would add further pressure to affordability.He said: “For some buyers, even a relatively small increase in monthly repayments can mean they have to reduce their budget or step back from a purchase altogether. Equally, homeowners coming off fixed-rate deals may face significantly higher repayments, which could affect their decision to move.”Explore more on these topicsMortgage ratesMortgagesBanks and building societiesPropertyInterest ratesEconomicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Pasture lives: the rebel cheesemakers preserving an Alpine tradition | Italy | The Guardian
description: Storico ribelle is produced by a small group of mountain herders according to a traditional farming system based on seasonal and rotational grazing
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Storico ribelle is produced by a small group of mountain herders according to a traditional farming system based on seasonal and rotational grazing
Content: The Guardian picture essayItalyPasture lives: the rebel cheesemakers preserving an Alpine traditionA story of storico ribelle, produced by a small group of mountain herders according to a traditional farming system based on seasonal and rotational grazingPhotographs and text by Giuseppe NucciMon 5 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 08.57 EDTShareView image in fullscreenOreste Pedrelli, 56, a herder on Alpe Pedena for 10 yearsMy journey into the world of storico ribelle began with a shared passion for photography and the mountains. A close friend of mine lives in theOrobie Alps. He loves the mountains and the natural environment that surrounds him, and we share the same passion for photography. When I finally went to visit him, I discovered a way of experiencing the mountains that was very different from the one I knew growing up in the Apennines, where I come from.What struck me was not only the landscape, but the relationship people still have with it. Here, I discovered a world where the mountain is not simply a place to visit or explore, but a place to live and work. A world where cheese is still a tradition rather than an industrial product, and where the rhythms of the seasons, the animals and the daily work of thealpeggiatori– the mountain herders – are still deeply connected.View image in fullscreenThe horn of a cow grazing in the Trona Vaga pasture, with Pizzo Trona visible in the background, in Val GerolaThere was a poetry in this way of life that immediately inspired me. Waking before sunrise, milking, making cheese, moving with the animals and working until darkness: there was almost no separation between life and work.I felt compelled to photograph this world. I wanted to tell the story of people who continue to choose a demanding way of life in a time when agriculture is increasingly industrialised and traditional knowledge is disappearing.Portraits of Oreste Pedrelli and his trusted helper PaoloLeft: Oreste Pedrelli has been making cheese since he was eight, learning the craft from his grandparents and carrying on a tradition passed down through generations. Right: Pedrelli’s trusted helper Paolo. For 15 years, he has lent a hand every summerIn the Orobie Alps, cheese is inseparable from the landscape that gives it life. Steep pastures, stone shelters and seasonal migration have shaped a rural culture for centuries. Animals move with the seasons, milk follows them, and cheese becomes a way of preserving a way of life.Storico ribelle was born from this tradition – and from a decision to defend it. For generations, bitto cheese was made in small Alpine dairies and exchanged locally for essentials such as grain and salt. During summer, herders moved their animals progressively higher, following the pastures. Along the routes,calecc –simple stone shelters – were used for milking and transforming fresh milk into cheese. The wheels were taken to mountain cellars, orcasère, where they could mature for years.Milk containers hanging from a post, and the containers’ lidsLeft: The Alpe Cavizzola pasture. From June until the end of the season, typically September, the Alpine herders gradually move to ever higher altitudes, returning to the valley every two days to deliver the cheese. Right: Lids of thebidu, or milk containers, washed after milkingIn 1996, the introduction of the bitto DOP (protected designation of origin) brought new regulations. Some producers considered the requirements incompatible with the traditional Alpine system they wanted to preserve. They chose to continue making cheese according to their own methods, outside the DOP. Eventually, a new name emerged: storico ribelle, or historic rebel.Carlo Duca with a herd of goats, and a person milking a cowLeft: Carlo Duca, a herder and cheesemaker at Alpe Ancogno Soliva, hand-milking goats in the pasture. Right: Hand-milking a brown Alpine cow at Alpe CavizzolaThe name reflects resistance, but the deeper story is one of continuity: preserving a relationship between livestock, pasture, milk, cheese and mountain life. That relationship can still be found across Val Gerola, Valtellina and Val Brembana.At Alpe Pedena, Oreste Pedrelli, 56, has spent the last 10 years herding. He has been making cheese since he was eight, learning the craft from his grandparents. At Alpe Ancogno Soliva, Carlo Duca works with his brother Luigi. Their cheese is renowned for its extraordinary ageing potential, with some wheels maturing for up to 10 years.A cow collar, and Michele at work in the mountainsLeft: A cow collar of Alfio Sassella, a herder at Alpe Cavizzola, worn by one of his cows. Right: Michele, 15, the son of Alfio, who died away last August, at work in the pasture, following in his father’s footstepsAt about 2,000 metres, Trona Vaga is the highest storico ribelle Alpine pasture. Manuele, born in 1988, runs the pasture with his partner, Erica, who came to cheesemaking from a completely different background. She studied languages and taught herself the craft as an adult.Their stories reveal that tradition can be inherited, but it can also be chosen. This is particularly important among a younger generation. Michele Sassella, 15, continues the practice with his mother and sister in memory of his father, Alfio, who dedicated his life to protecting mountain breeds, natural farming rhythms and Alpine biodiversity.Davide Peregalli lying in bed, and Gioele Pedercini sitting for a photoLeft: Davide Peregalli, 16, a nephew of the three Curtoni brothers who run Alpe Vesenda. He has been spending his summers in the mountain pastures since he was eight, sleeping in a covered loft outside the Alpine hut. Right: Gioele Pedercini, a 17-year-old herder and agricultural student, has already spent three summer seasons working in the pastures to learn the craftDavide Peregalli, 16, has spent his summers at Alpe Vesenda since he was eight. Gioele Pedercini, 17, has already completed three summer seasons as an Alpine herder while studying agriculture. Valentina, 20, brings another perspective: with a degree in agricultural studies, she is the young cheesemaker at Alpe Orta Soliva.Valentina holding a goat, and carrying a box full of firewoodValentina, 20, holds a degree in agricultural studies and is the young cheesemaker at Alpe Orta Soliva, which was taken over by the Rabbiosi family two years agoThey represent a generation that is not simply inheriting tradition, but deciding whether it has a future.That future is fragile. Climate change is already affecting the tradition: scarce rain, increasingly violent storms, and pastures turning yellow even at high altitude. At the same time, increasingly demanding regulations make small-scale cheesemaking more expensive and labour-intensive. Yet the work continues.Smoke rising from a hut, and a copper panAculdera, a traditional bell-shaped copper cauldron, is used to heat and coagulate the milk. Placed over a wood fire, it is suspended and regulated using amàsna, a wooden swivel pulleyQuality here comes with an extraordinary human cost. It means waking before sunrise, working throughout the day and going to bed after sunset. Every hour follows the animals. Milking, often by hand, is followed by transforming fresh milk into cheese. There is little distinction between work and life.A hen on a tractor, and a closeup of a sheepdog’s faceLeft: A hen on a tractor in the Orta Soliva pasture. Right: One of the herders’ sheepdogs, an Australian shepherdStorico ribelle represents more than a product. It is the result of pasture, animals, knowledge and time – and of people willing to resist the disappearance of a world.View image in fullscreenCarlo Duca on horseback in the Ancogno Soliva pastureThe rebellion began with a choice not to follow a prescribed system. Today, its future depends on another choice: whether a new generation will continue to climb the mountain, care for the animals, make the cheese – and keep alive a way of life that exists almost nowhere else.

title: ‘Exceptionally crafted’: why Little Shop of Horrors is my feelgood movie | Musicals | The Guardian
description: The latest in our series of writers’ favorite comfort films is a tribute to the lovably quirky 80s musical
Author: Juan A Ramírez
Headline: The latest in our series of writers’ favorite comfort films is a tribute to the lovably quirky 80s musical
Content: Rick Moranis with Audrey II in Little Shop of Horrors.Photograph: Warner Bros/Sportsphoto/AllstarView image in fullscreenRick Moranis with Audrey II in Little Shop of Horrors.Photograph: Warner Bros/Sportsphoto/AllstarMy feelgood movieMusicals‘Exceptionally crafted’: why Little Shop of Horrors is my feelgood movieThe latest in our series of writers’ favorite comfort films is a tribute to the lovably quirky 80s musicalJuan A RamírezMon 5 Oct 2026 10.44 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 14.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe key to afeelgood movie, beyond the necessary rewatchability, is familiarity – the real kind that lets you look away or fall asleep without doubting your affection. Musicals are perfectly suited to this particular subgenre since the majority of them, especially the classic ones adapted for film, atrophy with second-act problems. That’s where writers suddenly remember the plot they had introduced and drop all that singing and dancing to arrive at some type of conclusion.The first act of Funny Girl? A near-flawless parade of showstoppers,Barbra Streisandas Fanny Brice having the time of her life falling in love. I’ve probably seen it 200 times. The second act … well, who ever cared about her husband’s gambling addiction?At just 94 minutes, Frank Oz’s film of Little Shop of Horrors doesn’t suffer from that sharp of a drop-off. The cult 1982 musical that translates to the screen is already a pretty perfect piece; a hilarious send-up of B-movies with glorious songs by Howard Ashman and Alan Menken, the duo whose music would soon ignite the Disney Renaissance. The whole thing is a miracle of dumpster diving: adapting an almost-forgotten1960 movieby indie legendRoger Corman, who didn’t even bother to copyright his low-budget horror comedy.But enough history. Little Shop, the movie, begins, and you’rethere: Skid Row, the derelict, richly detailed cityscape with the lovingly obvious soundstage feel that most art departments left behind sometime in the 90s in favor of realism. The son of puppeteers and the first to perform both Yoda and Miss Piggy, Oz had individuality and scene-setting in his DNA.It’s there we meet Seymour (Rick Moranis), a perennially orphaned adult who works alongside the ditzy bombshell Audrey (Ellen Greene) at a run-down flower shop owned by the miserly Mushnik (Vincent Gardenia). Their dreams of a better life arrive quickly, when a mysterious plant Seymour has been secretly nurturing grows into a national sensation.‘Should have garnered the actor an Oscar’: why Liar Liar is my feelgood movieRead moreHis trouble, of course, is that the plant – named Audrey II, due to Seymour’s simping after his co-worker – feeds exclusively on human blood. In classicMichigan J Frogfashion, the anthropomorphic Audrey II (voiced by the Four Tops’ Levi Stubbs), only voices its carnivorous needs to Seymour, who’s left alone to decide whether success (and human Audrey’s love) are worth the carnage.In the simplicity of its plot and the spectacle of Oz’s puppetry, the film is sensational. Greene, a holdover from the original stage production, gives an all-time weirdo performance that is massive, intimate and memorable, with pipes to make the celluloid rattle. And she’s surrounded by heavyweight 80s funnymen, including Steve Martin, Bill Murray andChristopher Guest.A high concept horror-comedy with an all-star cast of comedians, Little Shop is a lot likeClue, released the previous year, and which also grew a devoted cult reputation over time. And here’s where I’ll get annoying again: both are intelligent critiques of capitalism disguised as kooky popcorn fare.“Disguised” might not be the right word for Little Shop, which never hides its thematic concerns. Menken’s score is a blend of doo-wop and rock’n’roll, but mostly Motown: a genre of romance, struggle and comfort. But even before that level of analysis, you’re hit with the original plot’s fable-like message, aided by Ashman’s cheeky anti-capitalist lyrics and, on film, Oz’s remarkable visions.View image in fullscreenVincent Gardenia, Rick Moranis and Ellen Greene in Little Shop Of Horrors.Photograph: The Geffen Company/AllstarThe movie’s first real number, Skid Row (Downtown), is a masterclass in placing its character’s individual desires against the backdrop of communal conflict. Every single shot is framed to acknowledge the individual’s involvement in the class struggle, which increases with each foot-stomp and angry face inincreasing desperation. Certain frames seem lifted straight out of classic Soviet propaganda.Do you see how excited I get talking about this? How all this spews out of me with such attractive, enviable ease due to how many times I’ve witnessed it? And do you feel how that breathlessness, upon an 857th rewatch, could easily tire itself out into a daze which, soon after the iconic Suddenly, Seymour climax, leads to a satisfied doze?What should convince any skeptics that this is a feelgood classic is that (a) one of its ardent fans can’t help but sound insufferable describing its merits and, (b) it is crafted with that Muppets-era showmanship, a remnant from an age where talent and individuality ruled, but acts would get caned off the stage if they weren’t pleasing the audience.Little Shop is exceptionally designed, performed and crafted, but there’s no whiff of spotlight-seeking to detract from the greater project. Tapping into that strain of communal excellence is why Oz delivered one of the finest movie musicals of all time, building on what Ashman and Menken fertilized from Corman and screenwriter Charles B Griffith’s seed of an idea. Clearly I’m not as good an analogist as all of these men, so don’t take my word for it.
