Go feed the beast.Little Shop of Horrors is available on VOD in the US and Australia and on Now TV in the UKExplore more on these topicsMusicalsMy feelgood movieComedy filmsComedyOff-BroadwaySteve MartinBill MurrayChristopher GuestfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Pierre review – David Harewood’s twisty noir is an instant crime classic  | Television | The Guardian
description: Harewood has always had star power to burn – and he well and truly ignites this bold, sharp show about working in the police as a person of colour. What a brilliant milestone for Black British cop drama
Author: Ellen E Jones
Headline: Harewood has always had star power to burn – and he well and truly ignites this bold, sharp show about working in the police as a person of colour. What a brilliant milestone for Black British cop drama
Content: ‘It’s a cop show – but, crucially, this guy is no cop’ … David Harewood in Pierre.Photograph: Olly Courtney/Channel 4View image in fullscreen‘It’s a cop show – but, crucially, this guy is no cop’ … David Harewood in Pierre.Photograph: Olly Courtney/Channel 4TV reviewTelevisionReviewPierre review – David Harewood’s twisty noir is an instant crime classicHarewood has always had star power to burn – and he well and truly ignites this bold, sharp show about working in the police as a person of colour. What a brilliant milestone for Black British cop dramaEllen E JonesMon 5 Oct 2026 17.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 17.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSome of us are too young to have seen David Harewood playOthelloat the National Theatrein London back in ’97. It was the first time, on that stage, that Shakespeare’s Black lead was played by a Black actor – as opposed to a white one in blackface makeup. Even if you missed that groundbreaking performance, on the basis of Harewood’s star power in the London-set crime drama Pierre, you can be assured he blew the roof off.Pierre’s co-writer Roy Williams may not be the Bard, but he is another highly acclaimed playwright with an interest in how Black men fare in this country. Pierre on Channel 4 isn’t exactly Othello at the National, either, but it is another cultural milestone in the story of Black British crime drama.Williams’s show, written with John Donnelly, establishes itself with confident concision, which is largely down to Harewood’s performance. The way he enters a room and unbuttons his suit jacket, before delivering a threat or assurance. The soft Birmingham burr (Harewood’s own) that has been filed to a sharper edge by years of gritty London living.But it’s also the noirish locations, frequented by Pierre while on night shifts as a duty solicitor for a police station. And it’s the striking title graphic, comprising building-height yellow letters for the silhouetted solicitor to stride past. The plot, too, is noir with a twist: a young Black man is found dead after telling Pierre he was building a case of police harassment against an officer.View image in fullscreenBanter over a full Engllish … Harewood as Pierre with Jason Flemyng as Ronnie.Photograph: Channel 4/Olly CourtneySure, TV with vaunted cinematic ambitions is great, but have you ever been firmly taken in hand by a genre show that knows what it means to do, then does just that? “This ain’t the Premier League, my friend,” Pierre tells a potential client over the cold laminate of a custody suite table. “We’re in the lower leagues here. We don’t need the haircuts, the turns, the stepovers. We want a guaranteed 20 goals a season and someone prepared to dig their elbows in where it hurts, week in, week out.” Pierre’s shtick, like this football analogy, is clearly well rehearsed, but no less persuasive for it.It’s a cop show, then – but, crucially, this guy is no cop. Back whenIdris Elba’sLutherwas donning his detective tweeds, “positive representation” meant bucking racist stereotypes by casting Black actors as police heroes, yet otherwise steering clear of any engagement with what it mightactuallybe like to be Black in an “institutionally racist” organisation such as the Metropolitan police: the daily indignities and trade-offs; how it all reverberates in your personal life and your mental health.That changed in 2020 withRed, White and Blue, Steve McQueen’sone-off, feature-length BBC drama starring John Boyega as the real-life former Met police superintendent Leroy Logan. It changed again in 2024 withGet Millie Black, another Channel 4 series, written by the Booker prize-winning authorMarlon James, which traced British racism to its roots in the transatlantic slave trade via Kingston, Jamaica.View image in fullscreenA lot of ground to cover … Harewood as Pierre.Photograph: Channel 4/Olly CourtneyBut as entertaining as these shows were, Pierre’s specific identity as a duty solicitor – a securely middle-class Black professional who remains rooted in his community – allows him a wider jurisdiction. He can banter over a full English with his bestie, DS Ronnie Miller (Jason Flemyng) just as naturally as he comforts bereaved relatives at a vigil for a murdered teenager. He can be received at a private member’s club, the Turningham, and wryly reply, when told that the first Lord Turningham made his money “in sugar”: “There’s a surprise.”As for Pierre’s personal collection of indignities and trade-offs, these are not only explored by the drama, but also robustly challenged by his many Black peers. These include his law firm partner Charlotte (the frequent Mike Leigh collaborator Michele Austin, excellent as ever) and his wife, Celeste (Sara Powell, struggling to overcome “Skyler fromBreaking Badsyndrome” – being the underwritten, nagging wife of a dynamic antihero.)View image in fullscreenNobody does it quite like him … Harewood as Pierre with Cherrelle Skeete as Brenda.Photograph: Channel 4/Olly CourtneyPierre’s world is generously populated with colourful characters besides (bonus casting points for the inclusion of Christopher Fairbank’s delightfully Dickensian visage), which means there’s a lot of ground to cover. Pierre the show – like Pierre the man – sometimes buckles under this burden by, for instance, attempting to condense modern race and policing politics into a few lines of chatty dialogue, which lands with all the subtlety of an anvil on a pavement.But, still, his friends in places high and low agree: nobody does it quite like Pierre. So if he has been overburdened with responsibility, the only agreeable solution is to allow more time for him to work things out for everyone who depends on him. That sounds like a season two commission to me.Pierre is available on Channel 4 nowExplore more on these topicsTelevisionTV reviewDavid HarewoodTV crime dramaBlack British cultureDramaPolicereviewsShareReuse this content

title: Club Kid review – Jordan Firstman’s heartfelt comedy is irresistible | New York film festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: The actor impresses with a directorial debut about a club rat who discovers he is father to a 10-year-old boy
Author: Owen Myers
Headline: The actor impresses with a directorial debut about a club rat who discovers he is father to a 10-year-old boy
Content: Miss Benny and Jordan Firstman in Club Kid.Photograph: Courtesy of A24View image in fullscreenMiss Benny and Jordan Firstman in Club Kid.Photograph: Courtesy of A24First look reviewNew York film festival 2026ReviewClub Kid review – Jordan Firstman’s heartfelt comedy is irresistibleNew York film festival:the actor impresses with a directorial debut about a club rat who discovers he is father to a 10-year-old boyOwen MyersMon 5 Oct 2026 16.20 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 16.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn a grungy backroom of a Brooklyn warehouse, a group of glamorously dishevelled clubbers raise their voices in a secular chat. “What do we want? Drugs! When do we want them? Now!” So beginsClub Kid, an irresistible helter-skelter ride through the New York club scene from the comedian, actor and first-time director Jordan Firstman. A portrait of the importance of blood family and chosen family, it’s also one of the most bewitching debuts in recent years.A Statement review – outstanding climate change dramedy about a 1980 meetingRead morePeter (Firstman) is the life of the party and has been running his raucous Club Labor for over a decade. He always gets the drugs in, rolls up with the best-dressed crew and knows everyone. But the comedowns – bed-rot days of anime porn, takeout and self-loathing – aren’t getting any easier, and he is screwing up opportunities for the party to get to the next level. “You’re a fucking child,” spits his business partner Sophie (Cara Delevingnein her best performance yet) after he shows up to a lunch meeting with potential investors straight from the rave.Everything changes when Leonora, a British party girl who he met 10 years earlier, shows up at his door with a 10-year old named Arlo that she claims is his child. Right, Peter remembers, there was that darkroom threesome a decade ago. (“I came inside her?” he asks in disbelief. “Yeah, proper,” Leonora confirms.) Arlo’s mum recently died, and Peter finds himself responsible for the kid. After some lapses in judgment, such as when he neglects to hide his “I love Björk and bareback” T-shirt from his new charge, Peter quickly warms to Arlo and the pair settle into a sweet rhythm, bonding over a love of music, exploring the city and spending cozy nights together as Peter switches on his stove for what seems like the first time in years.After initially setting strict boundaries to his nightlife friends’ interactions with Arlo (“No talk about dicks or drugs,” he hisses), Peter finds a way to share his life with his son. He brings Arlo record shopping in the East Village staple A1, and introduces him to a DJ friend named Saffron (the luminous Saturn Risin9) who teaches the kid to use mixing decks. It’s the kind of set-up that feels too good to be true, and it is not plain sailing for father and son, with greater challenges to come.Behemoth! review - Pedro Pascal classical music drama hits all the wrong notesRead moreFirstman has held his own on-screen before, particularly in the twisted comedyRotting in the Sun, but he is magnetic here as a good-natured trainwreck that you can’t help rooting for. Queer life in New York can be messy, and Firstman lets it be. There’s an uncommon warmth that Club Kid bestows to its characters (the glow of its physical film stock renders that physical, too) that extends to its urban setting, even as you can practically smell the hot garbage outside Peter’s Lower East Side apartment. To underline the realness, Firstman cast nightlife personalities such as Alaska Riley and Miss Benny as saucy queens of the scene in addition to Diego Calva (Narcos) as a social worker and confidant and the brilliantly natural Reggie Absolom as Arlo.View image in fullscreenThe cast of Club Kid at New York film festival on 3 October 2026.Photograph: Dia Dipasupil/Getty Images for FLCThere’s a lesser, dumber version of this film that would flatten its story into a lazy redemption arc proclaiming that clubbing is a waste of time while parenthood is truly worthwhile. Unfortunately, that’s also the impression given by the film’strailer, which makes it seem like an Oscar-bait morality tale about how a cute middle-schooler teaches a wayward club rat about what really matters in life (yuck). While I found the film’s ending a little too neat, Club Kid genuinely resonates as a love letter to queer nightlifebecauseit refuses to sugar-coat its unsavory sides. Normally you have to go to the European arthouse to get this kind of grownup attitude towards partying (I thought of gems such asVictoriaandEdenmore than once). While the film is not afraid to look nightlife’s problems dead in the eye, it also captures why it can be magic: the cab rides screaming along to Rihanna, the romance of surrendering to the beat, the bodies that intertwine as sun peeks through the windows.Club Kid is a riot. I can’t think of one visual gag or scripted quip in the picture that doesn’t land. (The man sitting next to me doubled over so violently after one joke about aspiring queer philosophers that I nearly called an ambulance.) It is also a testament to how crucial it is for film-makers to tell the stories they know, and knowing that bathroom stall bumps and blurry after parties that stretch into the afternoon are worthy of 35-millimeter film stock. On stage at the film’s Lincoln Center premiere, no one looked more surprised about that than Firstman himself, but I was not surprised to see it receive a standing ovation; Club Kid is a gem that could have come from no one else.Club Kid is screening at theNew YorkFilm Festival and will be released in the US on 6 November with UK and Australia releases to followExplore more on these topicsNew York film festival 2026First look reviewComedy filmsComedyDrama filmsNew YorkClubbingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The Yellow Tie review – John Malkovich gives major hauteur as legendary record-hating maestro | Movies | The Guardian
description: This biopic of Sergiu Celibidache, the renowned Romanian conductor who refused all recordings, is a sturdy labour of love directed by his son
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: This biopic of Sergiu Celibidache, the renowned Romanian conductor who refused all recordings, is a sturdy labour of love directed by his son
Content: Querulous … John Malkovich in The Yellow TiePhotograph: Adi MarineciView image in fullscreenQuerulous … John Malkovich in The Yellow TiePhotograph: Adi MarineciMoviesReviewThe Yellow Tie review – John Malkovich gives major hauteur as legendary record-hating maestroThis biopic of Sergiu Celibidache, the renowned Romanian conductor who refused all recordings, is a sturdy labour of love directed by his sonPeter BradshawMon 5 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 06.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHere is an old-fashioned biopic from central Europe that is also a labour of love on the part of its director: a little stolid and stately, yes, but robustly made, heartfelt and high-minded, with workmanlike performances and decent visual effects work. It is the story of the Romanian conductor and composer Sergiu Celibidache, a brilliant musician who became renowned among musical connoisseurs in the years following the second world war for his unique and uncompromisingly purist belief – derived from his Zen Buddhist studies – that music should never be recorded. He believed that LPs and CDs were inert and dead, and that music had to be experienced live, in the passionately authentic present.The director is the musician’s son, Serge Ioan Celebidachi, and as an older man in his rural French retirement, he is played with unsubtly querulous hauteur byJohn Malkovich, especially in the misjudged opening scene where he yells at Japanese executives for presuming to offer him a recording deal. Ben Schnetzer is the younger Celibidache, a prodigy whose musical ambition infuriates his old-fashioned father (Sean Bean), a well-regarded functionary who assumed that his son would follow him into public office. Celebidache Sr therefore demands the return of his birthday gift, a certain type of yellow tie that had been favoured by generations of the family’s menfolk, and which here becomes a fetish of the heartbroken young Sergiu’s need to please his father but also break away from him.Celibidache studies in Berlin in the 1930s as the Nazis take power, and is menaced and bullied as a Jew, but escapes the ultimate fate; he is sensationally installed as principal conductor of the newly denazified Berlin Philharmonic in 1945, where he astonishes the authorities with his no-recording views. He is finally forced out and begins a kind of wandering musical odyssey through Europe and Latin America.It is not easy to see what point exactly has been made by Celebidache’s stand; he did not appear to accumulate many followers, and the music world was filled with musicians at least as talented and principled as him who believed the exact opposite about recorded music. But there is a kind of lonely heroism here, and who can tell if, in this digitised world where recordings are so easily available, that his views might not come into fashion? A strong, unassuming picture.The Yellow Tie is in UK and Irish cinemas from 9 October.Explore more on these topicsFilmBiopicsPeriod and historical filmsRomaniaClassical musicJohn MalkovichSean BeanreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Comédie Française review – pre-show bedlam plays theatrical chaos for laughs | Movies | The Guardian
description: French farce set in the tumultuous three hours prior to the opening night performance of Macbeth features comic-timing perfection from cast
Author: Leslie Felperin
Headline: French farce set in the tumultuous three hours prior to the opening night performance of Macbeth features comic-timing perfection from cast
Content: ‘Endearing portrait of French luvvies’ … Comédie Française.Photograph: Courtesy of Tull Stories/CharadesView image in fullscreen‘Endearing portrait of French luvvies’ … Comédie Française.Photograph: Courtesy of Tull Stories/CharadesMoviesReviewComédie Française review – pre-show bedlam plays theatrical chaos for laughsFrench farce set in the tumultuous three hours prior to the opening night performance of Macbeth features comic-timing perfection from castLeslie FelperinMon 5 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 08.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOne of Matt Groening’s Life In Hell comic strips from the 1980s,entitled How to Be a Clever Film Critic, sets out cinema’s greatest paradox: “The French are funny. Sex is funny. And comedies are funny. Yet no French sex comedies are funny.” Well, this film from Bertrand Usclat and Martin Darondeau proves that all commonly held certitudes must be disproved at some point, because here’s a French comedy, albeit one that’s not all that preoccupied with sex, that is a hoot.Set entirely inthe Parisian institution of the title, this frothy farce unfolds over the three hours before the opening night curtain goes up on a production of Macbeth, which is being directed by actor turnedmetteuren scèneNina (Pauline Clément). A series of catastrophes make it an open question as to whether the show will actually go on, starting from the moment Nina arrives at the entrance without her staff pass and has to try to get past the officious security team. Naturally, that’s just the beginning, and Nina must contend with superstitious actors, adulterous actors shagging while they rehearse (saying their lines between thrusts), a stoned grande dame (Danièle Lebrun), missing actors (Lady Macbeth is stranded in Brest while shooting a TV show on the side) and actors who understand their roles less than the usher (Sefa Yeboah), who is watching from the sidelines. Meanwhile, if there’s a technical problem, the stage manager (Christian Hecq) will tell you in tedious detail why it can’t be fixed, the wardrobe mistress (Florence Viala) discusses her colleagues’ bodily imperfections and the minister of culture is coming that evening to see the show.Not only must Nina take over the role of LadyMacbeth, her former partner also dumps their toddler on her before the show starts – prompting a whole debate about women trying to juggle careers and motherhood at the same time. This is a bit less persuasive, and some viewers may feel baffled as to why the production only seems to have six or seven actors on hand to mount what looks like a pretty traditional version of Macbeth. But try not to think about any of that too much, and just enjoy the performers’ immaculate comic timing and the endearing portrait of French luvvies ensuring the show must go on.Comédie Française is in UK and Irish cinemas from 9 OctoberExplore more on these topicsFilmComedy filmsTheatreMacbethFranceComedyEuropereviewsShareReuse this content

title: Sleeping Beauties by David Byrne review – a quirky journey through the afterlife of invention | David Byrne | The Guardian
description: The Talking Heads frontman considers dormant ideas that made a comeback – from Indian irrigation to Kafka
Author: Sukhdev Sandhu
Headline: The Talking Heads frontman considers dormant ideas that made a comeback – from Indian irrigation to Kafka
Content: David Byrne.Photograph: Jody RogacView image in fullscreenDavid Byrne.Photograph: Jody RogacBook of the dayDavid ByrneReviewSleeping Beauties by David Byrne review – a quirky journey through the afterlife of inventionThe Talking Heads frontman considers dormant ideas that made a comeback – from Indian irrigation to KafkaSukhdev SandhuMon 5 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 10.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere’s barely been a moment in  the last half-century when David Byrne hasn’t been zinging about, dancing forward, opting odd. The art-school dropout frontman ofTalking Heads, he moved sideways into ballet, dance and experimental theatre, collaborated on the proto-ambient LP My Life in the Bush of Ghosts with his fellow polymath Brian Eno, directed films, wrote musicals (on – of course – Imelda Marcos), co-founded a label (Luaka Bop) that introduced the likes of Os Mutantes and William Onyeabor to a new generation, brought out books of tree drawings, and designed bicycle racks.Byrne’s career – by most measures a remarkably successful one – has been built from code-switching, fidgety intelligence, stylistic infidelity. At first glance then, it’s surprising that Sleeping Beauties is devoted to failure – to artists who were ignored, laughed at, forgotten; to ideas deemed batty or heretical; to ways of thinking about the world – sustaining it, replenishing it – that, often for political reasons, were found wanting, and wiped from our collective memory banks. Sleeping beauties is (of course) a term he first encountered in an academic paper by Leiden University scientometrics professor Ton van Raan. That was in 2004: this book, like a lot of the ideas and energies it animates, needed time to ferment.double quotation markOf Caravaggio he asks: 'Why was he such a crazy asshole?'Some of his three-dozen case studies – Caravaggio, heliocentrism – are better known than others. Then there’s Antoni Gaudí – now celebrated as the architect of the most popular building in Spain, the still unfinished Sagrada Família – who, when he died in 1926, after being hit by a tram, was mistaken for a beggar. His career had foundered. A prominent Catalan critic called him “the Wagnerian monster of architecture” and his work “the bum-bum of the flatulence … [it] is German music in granite”. George Orwell later described his cathedral as “one of the most hideous buildings in the world”. Yet, after the second world war, Gaudí had a prominent champion in Dalí. Fashions changed: Irving Penn featured the building in a Vogue shoot. Institutional backing came in the form of Unesco making it a world heritage site. Now, after a woman who prayed to him to restore her eyesight was suddenly able to see, he is within one miracle of becoming a saint.The most revelatory chapters eschew art for environmental and infrastructural stories. In one – plainly titled Water Management in South India – Byrne recounts how rulers during the Chola dynasty that ended in AD1280 financed a complex network of pools, wells and tanks that allowed monsoon-triggered overflows to be channelled to lakes downstream. Curved stones were developed to trap silt and sludge. Water rights were managed by local people who ensured fruit trees abounded near banks, fish were plentiful in lakes, and that the area was less prone to droughts than other parts of the country. Later the East India Company brought in more clunky management systems and promoted profit above local expertise. It’s taken dogged local activists, operating in the aftermath of destructive floods, to revive the wise old waterways.Byrne’s subtitle – Why Good Ideas Go Dormant and How They Wake Up – makes it sound like a business manual in the cultural industries section of an airport bookshop. The answers he gives range from economic shifts (which have made the likes of solar energy more feasible) to the crucial role played by advocates (for example, Max Brod’s resurrection of his friend Kafka’s manuscripts). If his prose can sometimes be a bit matey (of Caravaggio he asks: “Why was he such a crazy asshole?”), he can also be sardonic (“A lesson for contemporary collectors sequestering their assets in places like the Geneva Freeport – there’s a risk the work will fall out of the conversation.”)Art that’s rediscovered can disappear again: writer Iain Sinclair has spoken of a category of authors he calls “the Reforgotten”. And rediscovered ideas, Byrne hints at too briefly, can be reactionary as well as progressive. Still, there’s an (inter)national curriculum here that schools and universities would do well to champion: engage with science and with art, be open to play and to metaphor, consider all that is counterintuitive. More? “Follow the young, the persistent, and amateurs.” Not bad advice at all.Sleeping Beauties: Why Good Ideas Go Dorrmant and How They Wake Up by David Byrne is published by Canongate (£26). To support the Guardian, order your copy atguardianbookshop.com. title: The Housekeeper by Rose Tremain review – a bloodless origin story for Du Maurier’s Rebecca | Fiction | The Guardian
description: The novelist has expanded her devastating 2014 short story about an imagined affair between Daphne du Maurier and a fictional Polish-Jewish housekeeper
Author: Clare Clark
Headline: The novelist has expanded her devastating 2014 short story about an imagined affair between Daphne du Maurier and a fictional Polish-Jewish housekeeper
Content: Lily James (front) as Mrs de Winter and Kristin Scott Thomas as Mrs Danvers in the 2020 film adaptation of Daphne du Maurier’s Rebecca.Photograph: Kerry Brown/PAView image in fullscreenLily James (front) as Mrs de Winter and Kristin Scott Thomas as Mrs Danvers in the 2020 film adaptation of Daphne du Maurier’s Rebecca.Photograph: Kerry Brown/PAFictionReviewThe Housekeeper by Rose Tremain review – a bloodless origin story for Du Maurier’s RebeccaThe novelist has expanded her devastating 2014 short story about an imagined affair between Daphne du Maurier and a fictional Polish-Jewish housekeeperClare ClarkMon 5 Oct 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe rollcall of notable novels that began life as short stories is surprisingly long and various. Two years before Clarissa Dalloway famously shopped for flowers in Virginia Woolf’s Mrs Dalloway she was shopping for gloves in Woolf’s short story Mrs Dalloway in Bond Street; Evan S Connell’s Mrs Bridge and Jeffrey Eugenides’s The Virgin Suicides began life as stories published in the Paris Review. Rachel Cusk’s story Project, which ran in the New Yorker in September 2025, serves almost word for word as the opening for her new novel, Life of M.The newest addition to that list is Rose Tremain’s 17th novel, The Housekeeper, which pays homage to Daphne du Maurier’s Rebecca by imagining the events that might have inspired it. Tremain first explored the idea in a 2014 story, also called The Housekeeper and included in her acclaimed collectionThe American Lover. Her protagonist, then and now, is Lilianne Danowski, a Polish Jew who fled the pogroms with her father as a child and who presides with reserved efficiency over a large staff at Manderville Hall near Fowey in Cornwall. When Du Maurier comes to lunch, it is Danowski, known to her employers as Danni (Danowski was “a mouthful of fishbones”), who is deputised to show her around the house, who proudly encourages Du Maurier to look through the clothes in her dead mistress’s fastidiously maintained bedroom and takes her down to the boat house. It is Danowski who, after a passionate year-long affair with Du Maurier, will be twisted into the malevolent Mrs Danvers.The married Du Maurier was violently attracted to women: her complicated, deeply closeted attitude towards her own sexuality lends Rebecca much of its darkly erotic charge. In the 2014 story, Tremain echoes that tension, offering, with her impeccable instinct for period, a masterclass in 1930s restraint. Danni is quite undone by Du Maurier, her careful armour torn away, yet bound, like the butler Stevens in Ishiguro’s The Remains of the Day, by the long habit of discretion; so she proves a tight-lipped narrator. Danni is the supplicant, the vessel; she knows she has no power. When Du Maurier, terrified of exposure, simply cuts her off, Danni scrabbles for ways to excuse her, to cling to what they shared. It is the discovery, more than a year later, that Du Maurier has immortalised her as the bitter and conniving Mrs Danvers, “ugly and diseased with jealousy”, that devastates her, smashing to pieces her passionately hoarded memories.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotiondouble quotation markTremain’s novel abounds with references to Rebecca and Du Maurier but its greater scope gives it none of Rebecca’s subversive complexityWhat moves a writer to return to a finished story after a decade, to rework it on the larger canvas of the novel? In Tremain’s case it was her story becoming a film. The Housekeeper, starring Anthony Hopkins and Helena Bonham Carter, is slated for upcoming release; Tremain wrote the screenplay.“Last night I dreamed I saw Daphne again,” Danni declares as the novel opens, recalling one of the most celebrated first lines in literature. Rebecca itself is, of course, part of a complex interplay of gothic novels, from Jane Eyre to Jean Rhys’s Wide Sargasso Sea, each book shifting the reader’s understanding of the others. Tremain’s novel abounds with references to Rebecca and Du Maurier – Daphne even confesses to Danni her fear that swooping gulls might take them for prey and attack them – but its greater scope gives it none of Rebecca’s subversive complexity. Instead, the story has fattened, its devastating reserve giving way to something softer and less substantial. Peripheral characters, evoked with discomfiting economy in Tremain’s original story, swell into caricature: Lord de Whithers, Danni’s terse, dismissive employer, becomes bumbling Lord Grenville-Whithers, kindly little boy lost, while his self-absorbed niece solidifies into a screaming harpy. Danni’s dead father is recalled in aphorisms more akin to fortune cookies than philosophy. More critically, the exquisite tension between Daphne and Danni, themselves echoes of the formidable Rebecca and the drab, shadowy second Mrs de Winter, fails to hold. With pages to play with, Tremain takes us deep inside their affair but, although this Danni tells all, the scenes remain curiously bloodless: hands and lips and tongues but no fire, no heart. Du Maurier famously called Rebecca “a study in jealousy”, but the lurching sense of malignity and darkness that gave that novel its vertiginous tension is missing here. Without it, Daphne’s final terrible betrayal of Danni feels like petty spite.“What am I to do with you, Danni? How am I to make you come alive?” Daphne demands teasingly in The Housekeeper’s opening pages. Du Maurier, of course, faced just that problem with Rebecca and pulled it off spectacularly, creating a woman of such toweringly vengeful, transgressive authority that, even in death, she rises up to dominate the book. Tremain has done the opposite. By stripping her Danni of her fierce, quiet dignity, she has robbed her of her power.The Housekeeper by Rose Tremain is published by Chatto & Windus (£20).
