title: Educating Rita review – Willy Russell’s classic still has plenty to teach us | Theatre | The Guardian
description: Director Cara Nolan keeps the play’s original 1980s setting but its message about how expectations are dictated by class and gender is anything but dated
Author: Arifa Akbar
Headline: Director Cara Nolan keeps the play’s original 1980s setting but its message about how expectations are dictated by class and gender is anything but dated
Content: Platonic ideals … Dominic Mafham and Alexandra Mardell in Educating Rita.Photograph: Jonathan PrykeView image in fullscreenPlatonic ideals … Dominic Mafham and Alexandra Mardell in Educating Rita.Photograph: Jonathan PrykeTheatreReviewEducating Rita review – Willy Russell’s classic still has plenty to teach usCurve theatre, LeicesterDirector Cara Nolan keeps the play’s original 1980s setting but its message about how expectations are dictated by class and gender is anything but datedArifa AkbarMon 5 Oct 2026 15.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSo much of the success of Willy Russell’s ivory-spired two-hander rests on the chemistry between its actors. The play traces a woman’s self-empowerment through education via her relationship with a world-weary Open University academic, but there is stiffness here between Rita (Alexandra Mardell) and Frank (Dominic Mafham) as they get acquainted.Frank learns of Rita’s desperate ambition for life beyond her job as a hairdresser and role as wife. Rita hears about his history as a published poet – and picks up on his inveterate drinking. In director Cara Nolan’s production, the dynamic between the pair does not pop in the early scenes, not through any lack of trying, especially on the part of Mardell. She makes a broad, vivacious scouser who has enrolled on to an English literature Open University course in hope to expand her intellectual horizons.The humour is sluggish and the pace is plodding, but whatever failings this production presents in the first half are redeemed in the more vibrant second. Funny lines finally zing, Frank’s quiet despair moves you – and so does Rita’s transformation. It is admirable that their dynamic never sinks into a lazy subtext of romance between them. Frank may hint at his attraction for her (he did, after all, fall in love with a former student with whom he now lives, he tells her). But what Rita and Frank have is something platonic, yet loving. He is not a Henry Higgins figure; she changes him as much as his lessons in critical thought and literature mark her.View image in fullscreenBroadening each other’s horizons … Educating Rita.Photograph: Jonathan PrykeRussell has a lovely facility for writing female subjectivity and as a play about a woman finding her voice, academic and otherwise, it holds its classic status. Rita is a compassionately drawn figure who comes into her own power and redefines her life.The play premiered in 1980 and the original setting is kept by Nolan (with an old-style trilling phone and era-specific references), yet the overarching message is still relevant, from the societal pressures on young women to have babies (exerted quite literally by Rita’s husband here) to self-determination and the endeavour to discover what freedom looks like outside of class and social expectation.AtCurve theatre, Leicester, until 17 OctoberExplore more on these topicsTheatreWilly RussellCurve theatrereviewsShareReuse this content

title: Play that funky Turbine Hall! How artist Tarek Atoui aims to take the Tate on a sonic odyssey | Tate Modern | The Guardian
description: From underwater explosions to PlayStation joysticks, the Lebanese artist makes art inspired by sound. Can this work in a space known for its chattering day-trippers, overstimulated schoolkids and echoing acoustics?
Author: Ben Eastham
Headline: From underwater explosions to PlayStation joysticks, the Lebanese artist makes art inspired by sound. Can this work in a space known for its chattering day-trippers, overstimulated schoolkids and echoing acoustics?
Content: ‘Not too worried’ … Tarek Atoui in the Turbine Hall.Photograph: Linda Nylind/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘Not too worried’ … Tarek Atoui in the Turbine Hall.Photograph: Linda Nylind/The GuardianTate ModernPlay that funky Turbine Hall! How artist Tarek Atoui aims to take the Tate on a sonic odysseyFrom underwater explosions to PlayStation joysticks, the Lebanese artist makes art inspired by sound. Can this work in a space known for its chattering day-trippers, overstimulated schoolkids and echoing acoustics?Ben EasthamMon 5 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTarek Atoui is drumming the fingers of his right hand against the table. Listen! His left hand waves a cigarette at the surrounding world. So I listen. I can hear a busker on the riverside in front ofTate Modernand the hum of people walking the promenade. The low rumble of a plane flying over London and the wash of a boat under the bridge. You can identify a city by how it sounds, the artist is telling me, as much as by how it looks. And not only that! You can play a city, just like he is playing the table, so that it sings.This is what Atoui, a musician and an impresario as much as an artist, does. He listens to the world around him, then he coaxes a tune out of it. Previous exhibitions have resembled recording studios in the midst of an especially far-out improvisation session, littered with instruments seeming to have been built out of scavenged materials on the instructions of a dream: someone might be playing a tentacular wind organ; wires might snake across the floor from a bleeping synthesiser; a glass booth may function like a walk-in flute, whistling around your body; marble boulders could emit woozy pulses, while drums beat to shifting patterns and your footsteps are picked up by microphones and fed back into the music. A world in miniature, made of sound.View image in fullscreen‘A realm in which people can listen, can play’ … the Turbine Hall undergoes a transformation for Atoui’s work.Photograph: Amer Ghazzal/ShutterstockTate Modern’s cavernousTurbine Hall– with its shifting audience of chattering day-trippers, overstimulated schoolkids and echoing acoustics – strikes me as a daunting venue for any artist working with sound. But Atoui, whose latest work is about to fill this space, is not “too worried” about these unpredictable elements, because his creations are less about the “ideal execution” of a finished piece of music than about giving a stage to the process. Transforming this enormous hall into one of his trademark “places for listening and playing” (ahead of the opening, he can’t divulge details) would mark only “the latest stage” in the movement of his work away from concert halls and “on to the street and into the market”.double quotation markI want to encourage people to play in their own livesIt’s been a winding road. Having left Lebanon to study experimental music in France, Atoui fell under the spell of experimental composers such as Iannis Xenakis and György Ligeti. But this charming and inveterately curious figure “didn’t want to work in the music industry”, stuck on the treadmill of “making albums and touring”. Instead, he wanted to travel, meet people and learn from these encounters. One model for this way of living (and making art) was provided by Fluxus, a global network of artists and musicians that in the 1960s was heavily influenced by the composer John Cage. It’s a reminder that the open field of contemporary art has long offered space to musicians whose work exceeds the auditorium.And so Atoui’s career can be charted by the places he has been and the people he has met, from revered Korean drum-makers to Palestinian children in refugee camps (for whom he developed software to compose sound through PlayStation joysticks). Perhaps the most transformative of these encounters was with students at the Amal School for the Deaf in Sharjah in the UAE through workshops that began with him using bass speakers to play frequencies so low that they are registered through the body. “I learned from working with deaf people that there is more than one way of hearing,” he says. Similarly, every space contains many worlds of sound.Think about the “mosquito alarms” that deter teenagers from loitering by emitting an irritating whine beyond the range of adults, or the silent whistle that summons a dog. These arenas of sound overlap – and the one you live in is conditioned not only by the design of your body (the density of your skull, for example) but also by your emotions (how different a song sounds when you are happy). Then there’s your attention (that electrical buzz you do not hear until your partner mentions it). Atoui is interested in all of these worlds, and how they coexist.View image in fullscreen‘More like a concert hall or educational space’ … a 2024 installation in Kunsthaus Bregenz, AustriaPhotograph: Markus TretterHis idea that we can “understand the world through sound” resonates with artists such as Lawrence Abu Hamdan. The joint winner of the 2019 Turner prize uses everything from gunshots to pirated mixtapes to reveal hidden stories. For his project Waters’ Witness, Atoui similarly records the ambient noise of the seas surrounding harbour cities from Istanbul to Sharjah. Of Athens, he says, “the waters around the Battle of Salamis are quiet now”, while Singapore’s marina is busy with “underwater explosions, military exercises, the noise of ships in the bay”. History is recorded in sounds as much as in pictures and words.Atoui’s exhibitions fulfil several functions. When no one is performing in the space, the handmade instruments are sculptures that can be appreciated for their craftsmanship. During the improvisation sessions and workshops integral to Atoui’s work, the exhibition becomes something more like a “concert hall or educational space”. What’s key is the idea that hearing cannot be separated from the other senses: what we see and feel in the space is as important as what we hear.Hi-fi society: how sound system culture took over UK art and fashionRead moreIndeed, for all that Atoui works with instrument-makers, experimental musicians and sound researchers, his most important collaborator is the audience. Visitors to his recent exhibition in Milan could stay for five minutes or an afternoon, could sit still or move through a space crowded with sounds. The artist in Atoui’s mould doesn’t spoonfeed you a song or an image, but instead provides a space to explore and some tools to be used. He makes no attempt to “anticipate” or to “determine” the visitor’s experience. You must make of it what you will.For Atoui, the process of composition is as much about bringing people together to improvise as it is about arranging harmonious patterns. He tells me that he hopes to transform the Turbine Hall into “a realm in which people can listen, can play”. Not as an escape from the everyday routine, but as something that might enliven it. “I want to encourage people to play in their own lives,” he says, because everything in Atoui’s life finds its way into his work: every place, person, conversation. “Even this one?” I ask. “Including this one!” says Atoui with a laugh, and lights another cigarette.Tarek Atoui’s Hyundai Commissionis at Tate Modern’s Turbine Hall, London, from 13 October until 11 April 2027Explore more on these topicsTate ModernSound artInstallationArtExperimental musicExhibitionsTurbine HallfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: De Profundis review – Oscar Wilde brought alive with righteous rage | Theatre | The Guardian
description: Anguished monologue based on letter to jailed playwright’s ex-lover is gripping in its illumination of a tortured artist
Author: Arifa Akbar
Headline: Anguished monologue based on letter to jailed playwright’s ex-lover is gripping in its illumination of a tortured artist
Content: Anger is an energy … Jens Harzer in De Profundis.Photograph: Joerg Brueggemann/OstkreuzView image in fullscreenAnger is an energy … Jens Harzer in De Profundis.Photograph: Joerg Brueggemann/OstkreuzTheatreReviewDe Profundis review – Oscar Wilde brought alive with righteous rageCoronet theatre, LondonAnguished monologue based on letter to jailed playwright’s ex-lover is gripping in its illumination of a tortured artistArifa AkbarMon 5 Oct 2026 08.26 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 08.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOscar Wilde’s De Profundis really does belong to the depths. Written as a letter to his ex-lover after being jailed for homosexuality, it reflects soul-crushing torments.Its adaptation into a monologue rarely gets an outing, perhaps because it is so bleak, but is staged by the Berliner Ensemble with heaps of extra angst for good measure.It is dramatised with great anguished physicality by Jens Harzer and spoken in German with English surtitles. Only his face is lit up at first and the set-up looks Beckettian in its bare, black effects: Hansjörg Hartung’s lugubrious set design accompanied by Jörg Gollasch’s variously plangent or flighty musical compositions and Steffen Heinke’s well-crafted lighting. Harzer initially looks deathly, with a luminous outline around him suggesting a man speaking from his grave.The letter opens with Wilde’s pet name for Lord Alfred Douglas – Bosie – but this production only speaks in direct, accusatory address to “you”. Bosie is decried as something of an anti-muse to the suffering artist – a grasping, sybaritic parasite whose company sucked the creative life out of Wilde.View image in fullscreenBare and Beckettian …. De Profundis.Photograph: Joerg Brueggemann/Ostkreuz.Harzer does not overplay it or tip into melodrama but blasts the part with righteous rage. He spits or shouts some lines, speaks others with numbed forbearance. In between the anger are shafts of light: remnants of love for Bosie, flashes of his past celebrated glory as a writer. He cannot let himself be filled with hate, he says, yet this monologue is irredeemably bitter.Under well-paced direction by Oliver Reese, it is remarkable that none of it feels over-wrought or leaden. It is essentially a static piece of narration but does not feel it here. Harzeris sometimes curled into himself, like Franz Kafka’s insect-like Gregor Samsa, and sometimes stretching his arms in the air in Christ-like surrender.As an interval-free production just 10 minutes short of two hours, it is an accomplishment that a piece drenched in so much darkness is also so gripping in its illumination of an artist in full-throttle throes of despair.At theCoronet theatre, London, until 7 OctoberExplore more on these topicsTheatreOscar WildereviewsShareReuse this content

title: Barkouf review – Offenbach’s lost operetta is a quirky shaggy dog story | Classical music | The Guardian
description: Opera Rara revive the 1860 work in which a dog is appointed Sultan. A fine cast, the Hallé and ENO chorus, and impeccable rhyming narration from Alistair McGowan, ensure things fizz
Author: Clive Paget
Headline: Opera Rara revive the 1860 work in which a dog is appointed Sultan. A fine cast, the Hallé and ENO chorus, and impeccable rhyming narration from Alistair McGowan, ensure things fizz
Content: Gleaming coloratura… Anne-Catherine Gillet, with Valerie Eickhoff and Alistair McGowan in Barkouf.Photograph: David Hughes / The HalleView image in fullscreenGleaming coloratura… Anne-Catherine Gillet, with Valerie Eickhoff and Alistair McGowan in Barkouf.Photograph: David Hughes / The HalleClassical musicReviewBarkouf review – Offenbach’s lost operetta is a quirky shaggy dog storyBridgewater Hall, ManchesterOpera Rara revive the 1860 work in which a dog is appointed Sultan. A fine cast, the Hallé and ENO chorus, and impeccable rhyming narration from Alistair McGowan,  ensure things fizzClive PagetMon 5 Oct 2026 07.51 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAn operetta in which a dog is appointed Sultan of Lahore and, thanks to a resourceful market trader, ushers in a more enlightened despotism – what’s not to like? Plenty, to judge by the critical mauling doled out in 1860 to Offenbach’s Barkouf. Even Berlioz – a fine one to talk – accused the composer of crimes against harmonic convention. It duly sank without trace until unpublished bits and pieces resurfaced in recent decades. It’s fallen toOpera Rarato splice it back together again, fill in the odd blank and give us a chance to judge for ourselves.Barkouf followed hot on the heels of Orpheus in the Underworld, against which it must inevitably be considered a failure. Eugène Scribe’s workaday lyrics lack the divine silliness of the composer’s finest collaborators while blunting the story’s satirical potential. Offenbach, on the other hand, was never short of an idea and his energetic score has sufficient tics and quirks to suggest he was on the trail of something a little bit different. The orchestrations are original (there’s four horns) and a string of witty ditties go off like uncorked bottles of pop. Unfortunately, at other times it runs on a lower level of inspiration.View image in fullscreenSparkling music … Paul Daniel conducts the Hallé.Photograph: David Hughes / The HalleOpera Rara, the Hallé and the English NationalOperaChorus gave it their best shot under the idiomatic baton of Paul Daniel. The music sparkled, and a fine cast of French speakers was clearly enjoying being along for the ride (a few audibility issues aside). Anne-Catherine Gillet shone as Maïma, the feisty flower seller who translates the offstage woofs and growls of their canine overlord to her own advantage. Her gleaming coloratura was a perfect match for Valerie Eickhoff’s gutsy mezzo as her market colleague Balkis.Among the men, Mathias Vidal got some of the best tunes as Maïma’s boyfriend Saëb, including a sentimental ballad with a trio of cellos and a lilting habanera. Loïc Félix worked his socks off as Bababeck, the duplicitous vizier whose treachery ends in the shaggy sultan giving his life to save the city. Pulling the strands together was the tirelessly engaging Alistair McGowan delivering an impeccably crafted rhyming narration, care of the indefatigable Jeremy Sams.Explore more on these topicsClassical musicOperaEnglish National Opera (ENO)Hallé Orchestralive music reviewsShareReuse this content

title: Forty years of the Phantom of the Opera - the show that wouldn’t die: ‘People come back to hear the impossible’ | Musicals | The Guardian
description: As Andrew Lloyd Webber’s enduring gothic melodrama celebrates its 40th birthday, producer Cameron Mackintosh and cast members from down the years recall what makes it so special
Author: Miriam Gillinson
Headline: As Andrew Lloyd Webber’s enduring gothic melodrama celebrates its 40th birthday, producer Cameron Mackintosh and cast members from down the years recall what makes it so special
Content: Spirit of the West End … Holly-Anne Hull and Jon Robyns in a 2023 production of The Phantom of the Opera.Photograph: Johan PerssonView image in fullscreenSpirit of the West End … Holly-Anne Hull and Jon Robyns in a 2023 production of The Phantom of the Opera.Photograph: Johan PerssonMusicalsForty years of the Phantom of the Opera - the show that wouldn’t die: ‘People come back to hear the impossible’As Andrew Lloyd Webber’s enduring gothic melodrama celebrates its 40th birthday, producer Cameron Mackintosh and cast members from down the years recall what makes it so specialMiriam GillinsonMon 5 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 05.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere is something about Andrew Lloyd Webber’s masterly musical The Phantom of the Opera – celebrating 40 years on the West End this month – which seems to take hold of its fans in a special way. For me, it was the show that first sparked my love of theatre and inspired me to work in the industry. Even today, Phantom is still the memory that gets my heart racing as I sit in the stalls, waiting impatiently for the curtain to come up, hoping for an experience just as intoxicating and all-consuming as that very first experience all those years ago.It’s not just the fans, either. When I talk to a cluster of key creatives, all of whom have a special working relationship with the show, each of them seems a little spellbound by Phantom. Sierra Boggess, who plays Carlotta in the 40th-anniversary production, talks tearfully about the lingering spirits of original director Hal Prince and choreographer Gillian Lynne. Jordan Donica, now starring as the Phantom in the West End, speaks passionately about the power of Lloyd Webber’s music (“It feels like heaven to me”), and John Owen-Jones, who has played the Phantom more than anyone else in the West End, talks tenderly about his long-term history with the show: “I’ve got a picture of me in full Phantom get-up holding my baby daughter. It’s an incredible thing to be part of.”Then there is producer Cameron Mackintosh who, if anything, seems even more enthusiastic about the show with each passing year. He just about stays sitting in his chair throughout our interview, yet gives the impression that he’s bouncing about the office as we discuss those early days working on Phantom: “Of all my productions, it’s the most beautiful show I’ve ever created, where every individual element contributed to its beauty.”View image in fullscreenWho scares wins … Michael Crawford and Sarah Brightman in the first run of The Phantom of the Opera in 1986.Photograph: Dennis Cooper/Rex FeaturesWhen Mackintosh and Lloyd Webber first started talking about Phantom in 1984, it was only ever meant to be a fun producing project. The two had enjoyed Ken Hill’s production at Stratford East theatre and, after rummaging around a few charity shops, tracked down a copy of Gaston Leroux’s original novel. They discovered a strange and sinister tale about a disfigured musical genius – with a face like a living corpse – lurking beneath a Parisian opera house (The Palais Garnier), seducing soprano Christine Daaé with the power of his music and causing havoc among the company performing above.As their research deepened, Mackintosh and Lloyd Webber began to unearth the unique characteristics of their new Phantom. Their new version absolutely wasn’t going to be a gothic horror story in the manner of Lon Chaney’s striking silent movie. And it definitely wasn’t going to be a Rocky Horror Show-esque pastiche. This Phantom was going to be lighter, more beautiful – and a lot more romantic.It also quickly became clear that the show was going to have to feature the music of Andrew Lloyd Webber. “The score was very much inspired by Sarah Brightman,” explains Mackintosh. “Andrew obviously had a very deep relationship with her at the time [the two were married] and it triggered something really special in her. Lots of people have attempted to do Phantom but Andrew’s music brought an emotional intensity to the show that had never been there before in any other version.”double quotation markThere’s something dangerous about the music. The vocal demand is so great and there’s a romance in thatThere was something exciting about the score from the start, but it wasn’t until late in the creative process that things came together: “The show only clicked on the first night of previews. I always describe it, up until that point, as a watch running really slowly. But on that night the audience was completely swept into another world. Maria Björnson’s incredible design, Hal Prince’s brilliant ability to shape pictures on stage; [choreographer and stager] Gillian Lynne inhabiting the real world of the opera house and giving it authentic style. It all came together and looked and sounded as one.”It is amazing to think of all the little tweaks that led to today’s production, revamped and revitalised during the Covid theatre closures, but still very much the same beast created more than 40 years ago. In the early days of rehearsals, there were big plans to include a lot more animals. Björnson was determined to have a white horse carry Phantom into the lair but perhaps unsurprisingly – despite the ingenuity of the props team – they just couldn’t make it work. At one point, Prince wanted scores of rats scampering beneath the stage, but the manufactured clump of glowing rats proved funny rather than frightening (“Those little red eyes had us in stitches!”). Prince also had his heart set on releasing white doves – played by a flock of seriously unpredictable pigeons – and having them fly up into the theatre boxes above. “It was a lovely idea,” says Mackintosh, his eyes sparkling, “except all they did was fly up to a perch and shit all over the audience.”View image in fullscreenJohn Owen-Jones as the Phantom in 2011.Photograph: Ken McKay/Rex FeaturesThe horse, the rats and the beautiful (but messy) white doves were all scrapped and the show was gradually finessed. Yet Phantom still opened to patchy reviews, with the Independent scoffing: “Starlight Express brought the form to the edge of the abyss. The Phantom of the Opera takes it back a few yards, but we’re not out of the woods yet.” Nothing about the first few weeks, months or even years working on Phantom screamed box-office gold: “We never tried to put together the most successful musical,” reflects Mackintosh. “I think if we had tried to do that it wouldn’t have succeeded. It was meant to happen the way it did.”The idea of something almost karmic behind Phantom’s success comes up throughout my conversation with Boggess, who first played Christine 20 years ago and went on to become a fan favourite. “For me, playing Christine was a dream come true,” she says. “It felt like I was supposed to be there, helping to tell this story. And now here I am playing Carlotta. It feels like it’s supposed to be.”For Boggess it’s the music, above all, that keeps the fans hooked: “There’s no other score in the world like this. People have to hear this music. It’s like it’s changing something on a cellular level.” The acute technical demands of the score are also part of the show’s appeal. “There’s something dangerous about the music,” she says. “The vocal demand is so great and there’s a romance in that. People come back to hear the impossible.”There is something about performing in Phantom’s first home, His Majesty’s theatre (formerly Her Majesty’s), that feels particularly special for Boggess: “After all the history I have with this show, I finally get to perform in the place where it all started. And there are ghosts here, too. The spirit world is all around us. I really believe that. They come and help us. It’s so much bigger than us all.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenCaught in the act … Peter Straker and Christine Collier in The Phantom of the Opera in 1991.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianOwen-Jones, who has played Phantom nearly 2,000 times, also believes that the venue itself has an important role to play in the production’s extraordinary performance history. He says the show was originally meant to run at the Palace theatre but Les Misérables – the only musical to have a longer West End run than Phantom – was refusing to close. So Phantom opened in the more intimate Her Majesty’s.“At the time, Her Majesty’s had the only functioning Victorian understage in London,” says Owen-Jones. “So the team were able to use that for things like the candelabra coming up through the floor. People hadn’t seen things like that in the West End for a long time.” Björnson’s design in this particular theatre is a huge part of Phantom’s enduring appeal: “When people watch Phantom they see this incredible set with all these old scenic elements. Flies from the top. Flies from below. Trap doors. Yet when the actors come on stage for their final bow, it’s just a black box. Maria has put all these incredible elements into the space but in the end there’s nothing to look at. It’s pure theatre.”Everyone I talk to mentions the simplicity of Phantom’s myth-like story, but also its flexibility. It’s a simple tale but a robust one too, which allows each actor – despite the powerful legacy of Michael Crawford’s haunting inaugural performance – to put his own stamp on the title role. For some that might mean imbuing the Phantom with an air of mystery, but for Owen-Jones the key was always about grounding him in reality: “In my mind the Phantom is a man. He’s not a magician. He’s not a wizard. He’s an incredibly talented engineer who can do all these magical things.”Donica, who began his stage career playing Raoul on Broadway, sees the Phantom through a very different lens: “I felt a kinship to Phantom my whole life. Being a mixed-race kid, raised by a single mum in the south and Indiana. Moving around all the time and being the new kid. The outsider. The person that’s always underestimated and made to feel unwelcome in a lot of spaces; having to show a talent that deems me worthy to be a part of society. All of these things and more, for me, very much relate to Phantom.”Andrew Lloyd Webber is ‘hot again’ – with help from new kids on musicals blockRead moreDonica describes the very first time he encountered the Phantom in the theatre, when a touring production came through Indiana. The actor had just turned nine and, in some strange way, he could literally see the power that Lloyd Webber’s music held over the audience: “We were sat in the orchestra level and you hear the Phantom before you see him. I remember hearing ‘Brava, brava, bravissima!’ and it was like a synesthetic response. I could just see the Phantom’s voice hovering over the audience and wrapping around them.”As we talk, Donica cannot help bursting into song. He talks to me about the frequencies contained in the score and, “from a hertz point of view”, the way that these frequencies connect with the audience. It’s an interesting and unusual way to think about the show; almost as if Lloyd Webber’s score is the result of some sort of physics experiment, designed to shock and move us: “The frequencies that Andrew uses in this show are what hit you to your core. You can sit there, being sceptical about the show, but when you hear those tones – ‘Da-da da-da daaaaa!’ – it automatically makes the hair on the back of your neck stand up. That’s why it works.”The Phantom of the Operais at His Majesty’s theatre, London, to 13 March 2027.Explore more on these topicsMusicalsAndrew Lloyd WebberTheatrefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Mary Beard suggests ‘tweaks’ to British Museum’s handling of queues to see Bayeux tapestry | British Museum | The Guardian
description: Classicist and museum trustee visited the line after people complained of waiting for hours, with some turned away
Author: Helena Horton
Headline: Classicist and museum trustee visited the line after people complained of waiting for hours, with some turned away
Content: The museum has announced new measures to make the viewing of the tapestry more accessible.Photograph: Amer Ghazzal/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenThe museum has announced new measures to make the viewing of the tapestry more accessible.Photograph: Amer Ghazzal/ShutterstockBritish MuseumMary Beard suggests ‘tweaks’ to British Museum’s handling of queues to see Bayeux tapestryClassicist and museum trustee visited the line after people complained of waiting for hours, with some turned awayHelena HortonMon 5 Oct 2026 07.55 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMary Beard has intervened in the row about excessively long queues for theBayeux tapestryby visiting the line and submitting a list of improvements to the British Museum.The Bayeux tapestry: a stupefying, thrilling, horrifying masterpiece that shakes the earthRead moreBeard, 71, is a trustee of the museum and inspected the queue herself after visitors to the tapestry complained that they had to wait for hours for their turn to view it, and some were turned away with no guarantee they would get another time slot.One visitor posted on social media that she had been waiting since she was seven to see the Bayeux tapestry, and had bought tickets only to be turned away after queueing.View image in fullscreenMary Beard, seen here at the announcement of the Booker prize shortlist last month, said she had some sympathies for the museum.Photograph: David Parry/ShutterstockThe museum has since announced new measures to make the viewing of the tapestry, which has returned toEnglandafter 1,000 years in France, more accessible. This includes longer opening hours to prevent queues, a new audio guide to help people move along the embroidery, and additional signage and seating.Beard, a celebrated classicist and TV presenter, told the Guardian she had visited to “chat to people in the queue”, adding: “The atmosphere was very good, with people who had come from everywhere. I thought some tweaks were necessary: more benches for old ladies like me, more guidance on wait times.”She said she had some sympathies for the museum: “We had to expect some teething troubles – this isn’t like an ordinary exhibition, everyone has come to see the same one object! The important thing is to put those teething troubles right.”Members of the public keen to see the Bayeux tapestry faced online queues of up to nine hours when tickets went on sale for the first time this summer. There were reports of 40,000 people queueing by mid-morning, with that figure ballooning to almost 80,000 by mid-afternoon. The next wave of public tickets for the tapestry will go on sale on 21 October at 10am.Adult tickets cost £33 during peak times and £27 at off-peak hours, compared with its usual €12 (£10) fee to see the tapestry in its home in Bayeux, Normandy.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFrom the Bayeux tapestry to Glastonbury: top tips and tricks to grab the hottest ticketsRead moreThe British Museum’s handling of the exhibition has come under scrutiny after the Guardian revealed that the controversial tech billionaire Peter Thiel was given a private viewing of the tapestry. The Trump-supporting businessman’s public software company, Palantir,plays a controversial role in the British state.Of the viewing, the museum’s chair, George Osborne, said: “It wasn’t like we expected anyone to know about it.” The museum’s director of development, Charlotte Appleyard, hosted Thiel at a VIP viewing of the tapestry before it opened to the public on 18 August.When asked what the museum might have received in return, Osborne said: “The short answer is [Thiel] hasn’t offered any money, and were he to offer money, the board would consider it and have to take into account the pros, you know, receiving more income, and the reputational risks.”ABritish Museumspokesperson said they were “delighted by the excitement” people had shown. They added: “We also know that some visitors have faced longer queues than we would have wanted, so we are introducing a series of measures to make the experience smoother and give more people the time they need to enjoy the tapestry.”Explore more on these topicsBritish MuseumMary BeardBayeux tapestryMuseumsLondonEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘If it’s too slick, it looks like a fashion mag’: Peter Zumthor on his £110m rammed concrete gallery | Architecture | The Guardian
description: It is one of the world’s finest collections, full of Monets, Miros and Picassos. But is the great Swiss architect’s extension for the Beyeler Foundation a worthy addition? Or is it a bit luxury boutique?
Author: Oliver Wainwright
Headline: It is one of the world’s finest collections, full of Monets, Miros and Picassos. But is the great Swiss architect’s extension for the Beyeler Foundation a worthy addition? Or is it a bit luxury boutique?
Content: ‘The stone of my youth’ … the gallery and a Louise Bourgeois spider.Photograph: Iwan Baan © The Easton Foundation / 2026, ProLitteris, ZurichView image in fullscreen‘The stone of my youth’ … the gallery and a Louise Bourgeois spider.Photograph: Iwan Baan © The Easton Foundation / 2026, ProLitteris, ZurichArchitecture‘If it’s too slick, it looks like a fashion mag’: Peter Zumthor on his £110m rammed concrete galleryIt is one of the world’s finest collections, full of Monets, Miros and Picassos. But is the great Swiss architect’s extension for the Beyeler Foundation a worthy addition? Or is it a bit luxury boutique?Oliver WainwrightMon 5 Oct 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 03.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn the early 1960s, when Peter Zumthor was a teenage apprentice in his father’s cabinet-making workshop, he designed his first cupboard. He later recalled the satisfaction of fitting the door so perfectly that it closed “with a special sucking sound”, saying his father instilled in him“the Basel pride in the well-built object”.Six decades on, with a fleet of globally celebrated projects to his name, the 83-year-old Swiss architect is back in Basel, beaming with the same local pride. He is gazing out at his latest well-built object, which is also his first project here: a monolithic new gallery that looks chiselled from the earth, its layers of pale crumbly concrete hammered into shape, its big oak and bronze doors – their handles wrapped with leather cord – closing with that same satisfyingly expensive Swiss swoosh.double quotation markThe glass lamps were blown by the only two men in Italy with the lung capacity“It was an old feeling,” Zumthor tells me, describing working in his home town to build the £110m addition to theBeyeler Foundation. “I encountered craftspeople who remembered my father, who had this special knowledge of how to make things. They weren’t surprised if something had to be custom-made.”View image in fullscreen‘Wooden womb’ … the pavilion is conceived as an open public lounge.Photograph: Mark Niedermann © 2026 Calder Foundation, New York / Artists Rights Society (ARS) New YorkIt was quite a change from his previous building site. Fresh from the recent opening of the tortuous, two-decade-long, $724maddition to the Los Angeles County Museum of Art, Zumthor is visibly relieved to be back on home turf. “The normal American architect is used to sourcing products, not looking for somebody who can make something custom-made,” he says, with a furrowed brow. “Their buildings are an assembly of products.”Not so inSwitzerland. From the pear wood handrails to the leather benches and blown glass lamps, every piece of his new gallery has been meticulously handmade. But is the sum of these bespoke parts a worthy companion to one of the country’s – if not the world’s – most beloved art museums?Designed by Italian architect Renzo Piano, the Beyeler Foundation washailedas a model of elegant restraint when it opened in October 1997 – the same month as Frank Gehry’s billowingBilbao Guggenheim– praised as a sober foil to the “iconic” tendencies of the time. Sited in Riehen, just outside Basel, in the grounds of an 18th-century villa, the museum was commissioned by Ernst Beyeler, Europe’s pre-eminent modern art dealer and co-founder of Art Basel, and his wife Hildy, to house their staggering collection of Monets and Mirós, Matisses and Picassos.A long, low, temple-like shed nestled in a garden, the foundation contains within its porphyry walls a luminous sequence of galleries, with daylight flooding through slender rooftop louvers. Piano took his hi-tech fetish and wrapped it in a luxurious stone skin, foreshadowing his bigger museums to come. But it was too small right from the day it opened. Two years later, it was extended by 12 metres and soon became the most visited art museum in the country, receiving 500,000 visitors a year. The challenge was how to extend a museum already deemed perfect by its art world patrons.View image in fullscreenPublic square of sorts … Zumthor’s Erlen Torhaus office and art-handling block, with fountain in the foreground.Photograph: Mark Niedermann“They wanted something completely different,” says Zumthor, who was selected from a shortlist of 11 architects in 2016, after 100 were approached for their ideas. “Renzo’s building is more industrial, whereas mine is almost domestic. It is the villa that this garden was missing.”The foundation acquired the Iselin-Weber park, a formerly private woodland adjacent to the museum campus, which now doubles its size, and where Zumthor’s gallery rises like a rocky outcrop. It is one of three new structures he has designed, along with a five-storey, timber-clad office and art-handling block, and an auditorium pavilion, conceived as an open public lounge – a particularly appealing space that can be accessed without a ticket. “Ninety per cent of the time,” says the foundation’s director, Sam Keller, “museum auditoriums are dead spaces. So we’ve turned it into a social space for people to come and hang out, read books, listen to podcasts or do some work, a real extension of the park.”The three buildings stand as an eclectic ensemble on either side of a lane, framing a public square of sorts, where a new drinking fountain trickles into a big stone trough, as in a traditional mountain village, welcoming art pilgrims to Zumthor-ville. Stone benches built into the museum facade greet weary wanderers. “A building is something you ought to be able to lean against every now and then,” says the architect, as Maurizio Cattelan’s unnervingsculpture of a drummer boyperches perilously on the parapet overhead, intermittently hammering his drum from the rooftop.The chance for Zumthor to finally build in Basel, a few kilometres from his birthplace, clearly brought back fond memories. In a schmaltzy new two-hour documentary by Wim Wenders called From Inside Out, the misty-eyed architect explains that this “intimate building” has “a lot to do with me growing up here”. He recounts that Jura limestone was “the stone of my youth”, describing how the village fountains and the cattle troughs “all glowed”. He wanted his own building to glow, too, so he mixed Jura stone into the concrete, and had workers tamp the dry mixture by hand, laying it at a rate of no more than 45cm a day. This is all filmed with a stirring musical backdrop. He wanted the wobbly joints between each day’s work left visible, like strata of sedimentary rock.View image in fullscreenBrighter upstairs … large picture windows framing pastoral views.Photograph: Mark Niedermann“I call it ‘farmer concrete’,” he says. “You see it everywhere in the mountains. They make it themselves, and they don’t vibrate the mixture, so it looks rough like this. You can see the building has a history, that hands have worked on it. It’s nice if you can see those traces. If it’s too slick, you just look like a fashion magazine.”Zumthor’s rugged brand of “rammed concrete” has become one of his highly published trademarks (and has indeedfeatured in fashion magazines). There is a sense of him bringing his greatest hits to the Beyeler ensemble. He used the technique for theBruder Klaus field chapelin rural Germany and aholiday house in Devonfor Alain de Botton’s Living Architecture company. The admin block, meanwhile, bears a distinct resemblance to hisatelier building in Haldenstein, also in Switzerland, its elegant oak facade (masking a concrete frame) crowned with a slender corrugated canopy.And the pavilion draws on yet another language. It’s like a warm wooden womb that’s been dug into the landscape, surrounded by walls of glass and topped with a low upholstered acoustic ceiling, full of armchairs encouraging visitors to lounge awhile. Zumthor had to wait so long for a commission in his home town, he has turned one project into three.View image in fullscreen‘It looks rough’ … the pharaonic staircase.Photograph: Oliver WainwrightThe galleries themselves are quite a departure from Piano’s top-lit white cubes. After the gleaming stone exterior, the interior feels almost cave-like, Monet’s waterlilies looking muddier than ever in the ground-floor gloom. Things get brighter upstairs, with large picture windows framing pastoral views in different directions as you ascend the three floors, looking towards the Black Forest on one side and the Jura mountains on the other. Limestone terrazzo floors, lime-washed walls and pale concrete ceilings create an all-encompassing world of beige, which somehow flattens the work on show, relieved only by dark timber-lined nooks for loos and lifts.Lozenge-shaped glass lamps (“made by the only two men in Italy who have the lung capacity to do it”, I am told) provide some ambient light, while spots highlight particular works. But you might find yourself pining for the celestial top-light of Piano’s galleries next door. Despite the architect’s protestations, it oozes the aura of a luxury boutique. As one visiting Angelino noted: “It feels like a newSkims store.”‘Starchitects go home’: what’s the truth behind Albania’s astonishing building boom?Read moreThe creamy promenade culminates in a roof terrace, with more views of pretty Swiss countryside, before visitors are shuttled down a pharaonic external stairway between the concrete walls, punched with triangular openings on one side, giving glimpses of the park and a mature ginkgo tree, around which the arms of the Y-shaped building extend. Questioned about the need for all this concrete, and its attendant carbon footprint, Zumthor is adamant. “I could not make a wooden museum,” he says. “I think it is not good for art. This kind of classical art needs more substance.”He might have questioned his own assumptions. When it first opened, the Beyeler was praised for its brave departure from the fashions of the time. Thirty years on, Zumthor, for all his talk of sensitivity to place, has created something that feels as globally ubiquitous as the Louise Bourgeois spider that crouches in the garden outside. Like the menagerie of buildings by noted architects at theVitra campusnearby, the foundation has succeeded in adding another familiar collectible to its haul of prized works.Explore more on these topicsArchitectureSwitzerlandMuseumsEuropeRenzo PianofeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Post your questions for Sofia Coppola  | Movies | The Guardian
description: A new documentary by Eleanor Coppola goes behind the scenes on her daughter’s 2006 punk classic, Marie Antoinette. To mark its release, Sofia Coppola will be taking your questions
Author: Rich Pelley
Headline: A new documentary by Eleanor Coppola goes behind the scenes on her daughter’s 2006 punk classic, Marie Antoinette. To mark its release, Sofia Coppola will be taking your questions
Content: Brought up on screen … Sofia Coppola.Photograph: Stéphane Cardinale/Corbis/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenBrought up on screen … Sofia Coppola.Photograph: Stéphane Cardinale/Corbis/Getty ImagesFilm & Music reader interviewMoviesPost your questions for Sofia CoppolaA new documentary by Eleanor Coppola goes behind the scenes on her daughter’s 2006 punk classic, Marie Antoinette. To mark its release, Sofia Coppola will be taking your questionsRich PelleyMon 5 Oct 2026 07.20 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 07.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTo say thatSofia Coppolagrew up on screen would be an understatement. The youngest child and only daughter of filmmaker Francis Ford Coppola and documentary-maker Eleanor Coppola, she appeared in all three Godfather films: as the baby being christened in 1972’s The Godfather, as a child on the steamboat in 1974’s The Godfather Part II, and, aged 19, as Mary Corleone in 1990’s The Godfather Part III.In between came small roles in several of her dad’s films, including 1983’s The Outsiders and Rumble Fish, 1984’s The Cotton Club and 1986’s Peggy Sue Got Married, in which she played Kathleen Turner’s younger sister Nancy. She also popped up all over 1990s music videos, playing a wild-eyed Joan Crawford in Sonic Youth’s 1990 Mildred Pierce, a troubled drifter in the Black Crowes’ 1992 Sometimes Salvation, one of Madonna’s clubbing friends in 1992’s Deeper and Deeper, and an injured gymnast in the Chemical Brothers’ 1997 Elektrobank, directed by her then-boyfriend Spike Jonze.Although this brings up loads of questions you may well like to ask her already – what was it like growing up in the Coppola household, with Nicolas Cage as her cousin? – it’s probably what happened when she switched to behind the camera that will intrigue you most.Did she ever thank Sonic Youth’s Thurston Moore for accidentally kickstarting her screenwriting and directing career by recommending Jeffrey Eugenides’ 1993 The Virgin Suicides to her? How terrified was she that Bill Murray would even turn up in Tokyo to film 2003’s Lost in Translation with no contract? Why is there a pair of Converse trainers in 2006’s Marie Antoinette? What was the strangest thing she found while filming 2013’s The Bling Ring inside Paris Hilton’s actual house?And now she has returned to Marie Antoinette in the documentary Making Marie Antoinette, pieced together from more than 80 hours of behind-the-scenes footage shot by Eleanor, and finished by Sofia after her death in 2024. The 20th anniversary celebrations have already started too: there’s an exhibition at the Petit Trianon in Versailles full of costumes, props and bits from the film – and New Order even turned up to play a mini concert there last month.Get your questions in by noon this Wednesday 7 October and we’ll publish her replies in the Readers Interview section. Let them eat questions!Making Marie Antoinette is in cinemas from 23 October and streams on Mubi from 6 NovemberExplore more on these topicsFilmFilm & Music reader interviewSofia CoppolaFrancis Ford  CoppolacalloutShareReuse this content

title: Alessandro Michele designs for the dancefloor at Valentino’s Paris show | Paris fashion week | The Guardian
description: Italian designer plays with ‘idea of glamour in the wrong way’ in collection of see-through gauzy fabrics and mis-buttoned blazers
Author: Chloe Mac Donnell
Headline: Italian designer plays with ‘idea of glamour in the wrong way’ in collection of see-through gauzy fabrics and mis-buttoned blazers
Content: A model walks the Valentino spring/summer 2027 show during Paris fashion week. Photo: Abdul Saboor/ReutersPhotograph: Abdul Saboor/ReutersView image in fullscreenA model walks the Valentino spring/summer 2027 show during Paris fashion week. Photo: Abdul Saboor/ReutersPhotograph: Abdul Saboor/ReutersParis fashion weekAlessandro Michele designs for the dancefloor at Valentino’s Paris showItalian designer plays with ‘idea of glamour in the wrong way’ in collection of see-through gauzy fabrics and mis-buttoned blazersChloe Mac Donnellin ParisMon 5 Oct 2026 09.57 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 17.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAlessandro Michele is the Italian designer who, during his seven year tenure as creative director at Gucci, made maximalism a meal ticket for the brand.His challenge now is to bring the same hot sauce to Valentino. He’s been in the top creative job for just30 months but time moves fast in fashion and he’s already rolled out 10 collections and four catwalk shows. AtParis fashion weekon Sunday afternoon, he ticked off show number five.A series of satin bustier tops paired with knee-length skirts opened the show. Some skirts were almost see-through in gauzy fabrics. Some came smothered in glimmering beads or trimmed with feathers or both.The show may have been held at the Sainte-Geneviève library but these were clothes made for the dancefloor. The debauched partying mood dominated menswear too, with creased trousers and silky boxers peaking out above their waistbands and mis-buttoned double-breasted blazers. Michele said he liked playing with “the idea of glamour in the wrong way”.The reaction to Michele at Valentino has been mixed. In a turbulent luxury market, its revenue declined 15% to €1.12bn in 2025. Michele’s opulent outlook has been slightly out of step with fashion’s vanilla era. However, the reign of quiet luxury is quietly coming to a close; “personality dressing” is on the rise and Michele is poised in the wings.View image in fullscreenLonger length ruffle and bow-adorned dresses had Hollywood written all over them. Photo: Abdul Saboor/ReutersPhotograph: Abdul Saboor/ReutersSpeaking after the show, Michele described “sensuality as part of the vocabulary of the brand”. This time around he had pared back his signature voluminous silhouettes, instead focusing on exposing skin.The brand’s founder Valentino Garavani famously hated the casualisation of fashion,recoiling at flip-flops and shorts, but Michele likes to toy with codes. In this case, there were deep V-cut cotton vest tops while some models wore brightly coloured baseball caps emblazoned with “Villain Teen”. Michele, who wore one in green, said he enjoyed the way it sounded a bit like “Villain-Teen-O”. But he also liked that in Italian it’s “a chic way to say you’re a little outside of the rules”, adding: “Where everything is perfect, it’s an elegant way to make something wrong.”View image in fullscreenBlazers featured heavily in the collection. Photo: Abdul Saboor/ReutersPhotograph: Abdul Saboor/ReutersValentino is controlled by Mayhoola, which owns 70% of the company, while the French luxury group Kering holds the remaining 30% and has options to increase its stake to 100% before the end of the decade.The brand’s sweet spot – and key to Michele’s turnaround strategy – is red carpet dressing. The collection’s longer length ruffle and bow-adorned dresses had Hollywood written all over them.In a world where increasingly red-carpet looks are captured in 360 degrees and quickly dissected on the internet, Michele knows a dress with a bit of extra oomph counts. A final hot pink dress featured a giant pleated train and huge black bow that bounced down the catwalk, grazing the audience’s knees.Explore more on these topicsParis fashion weekFashion weeksParisFashion industryFrancenewsShareReuse this content

title: The pet I’ll never forget: Poppy the curious, clever dog – who searches for missing people | Life and style | The Guardian
description: A beloved family pet, she is also the best employee ever, brilliant at her rescue work. If everyone could be more like Poppy, the world would be a better place
Author: Deborah Solomon
Headline: A beloved family pet, she is also the best employee ever, brilliant at her rescue work. If everyone could be more like Poppy, the world would be a better place
Content: Clever and empathetic … Steven Band’s dog, Poppy.Photograph: Courtesy of Steven BandView image in fullscreenClever and empathetic … Steven Band’s dog, Poppy.Photograph: Courtesy of Steven BandThe pet I'll never forgetLife and styleThe pet I’ll never forget: Poppy the curious, clever dog – who searches for missing peopleA beloved family pet, she is also the best employee ever, brilliant at her rescue work. If everyone could be more like Poppy, the world would be a better placeSteven Band, as told toDeborah SolomonMon 5 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen we picked up a nine-week-old black labrador from a couple just outside Callander, Scotland, I had no idea that she would soon be an employee of mine. Poppy became the family fur baby and we realised early on how clever and empathic she is. I work as a Special Operations Response Team paramedic and we decided to involve her in my search work in 2021 when she was only a year old because we knew it would play to her strengths. She took to it immediately.Poppy and our team of dogs look for missing people. My colleagues and I then provide any medical assistance needed. She is trained to search without needing to smell someone’s scent from an item such as clothing. During training, we hide our volunteers along the riverbank, in the woods, beside lochs and canals, and set the dogs off. They have to find the people and come back. Poppy’s curious nature has served her well. She loves the undergrowth, sniffing about and finding things.She has been involved in a couple of searches, including one for a missing army veteran in the Scottish Borders, which, unfortunately, turned into a body recovery. She was also tasked with going up to Inverness to help find a missing child in the woods who, thankfully, was found by the police.View image in fullscreen‘The best employee ever’ … Steven Band with Poppy.Photograph: Steven BandPoppy is the best employee. When she has her search jacket on, she knows she is going to look for people and the difference is apparent: she changes from family pet mode to working dog mode.She is also great fun – Poppy is a very active dog who has kept me fit and makes it impossible to be lazy, as she will want to go for a walk regardless of the weather. She also loves getting involved in family outings and activities, such as paddleboarding. She has her own lifejacket and will happily swim alongside us when we paddleboard on one of the lochs, which the kids absolutely love. They all spoil her rotten.She can seem intimidating at first, as she’s a big dog, but she gets on with everyone. There is nothing she loves more than being with people and she is the first to notice if someone is upset. She’ll put her head in your lap as if to say: it’ll be all right, tell me all about it.Poppy is a role model for us all. The way she interacts with other people is how you want to interact with people. She’s not judgmental and she’s happy to go up to anyone with a lovely attitude. She’s not got a vicious or snarly bone in her body. If we strive to be more like Poppy, I think we can make the world a better place.Explore more on these topicsLife and styleThe pet I'll never forgetPetsDogsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Georgina Hayden’s quick and easy recipe for corn gado gado | Food | The Guardian
description: A great way to pack in your vegetables, while adding pops of colour to your rotation of meals
Author: Georgina Hayden
Headline: A great way to pack in your vegetables, while adding pops of colour to your rotation of meals
Content: Georgina Hayden’s charred corn gado gado.Photograph: Louise Hagger/The Guardian. Food styling: Emily Kydd. Prop styling: Jennifer Kay. Food styling assistant: Laura Lawrence.View image in fullscreenGeorgina Hayden’s charred corn gado gado.Photograph: Louise Hagger/The Guardian. Food styling: Emily Kydd. Prop styling: Jennifer Kay. Food styling assistant: Laura Lawrence.FoodGeorgina Hayden’s quick and easy recipe for corn gado gadoA great way to pack in your vegetables, while adding pops of colour to your rotation of mealsGeorgina HaydenMon 5 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIam still making large, nourishing and vibrant salads, with gado gado being one of my favourites. It is a well-loved Indonesian salad, and something I devoured almost daily when we travelled around the islands many moons ago. It is also an excellent way of eating an abundance of veg, and can be made to suit your taste. If I was going all out, I’d add tofu or tempeh, some prawn crackers and beansprouts, but feel free to make the bowl as you wish, with whatever you have to hand – have a play.Charred corn gado gadoFor those who have a peanut allergy, this dressing works well with good-quality almond butter, too.Prep10 minCook30 minServes42 tbsp vegetable or groundnut oil1 tbsp red Thai curry paste80g pure peanut butter, crunchy or smooth2 tbsp soy sauce1 tbsp light soft brown sugar200ml coconut milkSea salt andwhite pepperJuice of 1 lime,plus 1 lime, quartered, to serve300gbaby potatoes4 large eggs150g green beans, trimmed2 ears of corn100g baby spinach, washed½ bunchcoriander, leaves picked and choppedStart by making the dressing. Pour the oil into a small saucepan, add the curry paste and fry, stirring, for a few minutes. Stir in the peanut butter, soy sauce, sugar and 175ml of the coconut milk, then season with salt and white pepper, and bring to a gentle boil.Add the lime juice and simmer for five minutes, until thick, rich and creamy. Add the remaining 25ml coconut milk, simmer for a further minute, then take off the heat and leave to cool.Meanwhile, get the rest of the salad ready. Put the potatoes in a pan of salted cold water, bring to a boil and cook for about 15 minutes, until tender. Boil the eggs for seven minutes for just-set yolks, give the beans six minutes and the corn five minutes.Drain everything, leave to cool, then stand the corn ears upright and carefully cut off the kernels. Assemble the bowls with all the different components in sections: a quarter of the potatoes, the green beans, the shaved corn, a handful of spinach leaves and a boiled egg cut into quarters. Drizzle over the cooled sauce, and serve topped with a scattering of coriander and with a wedge of lime for squeezing over.Explore more on these topicsFoodAutumn food and drinkVegetablesIndonesian food and drinkPotatoesNuts and seedsEggsrecipesShareReuse this content

title: Nik Sharma’s recipes for spiced French onion soup and Indian-style Turkish eggs | Food | The Guardian
description: A spice-rich twist on a classic soup, and poached eggs with garlic yoghurt and green chutney
Author: Nik Sharma
Headline: A spice-rich twist on a classic soup, and poached eggs with garlic yoghurt and green chutney
Content: Nik Sharma's poached eggs with green chutney and yoghurt.Photograph: Ola O Smit/The Guardian. Food and prop styling: Lucy Turnbull. Food styling assistant: Lilli Gavin.View image in fullscreenNik Sharma's poached eggs with green chutney and yoghurt.Photograph: Ola O Smit/The Guardian. Food and prop styling: Lucy Turnbull. Food styling assistant: Lilli Gavin.FoodNik Sharma’s recipes for spiced French onion soup and Indian-style Turkish eggsA spice-rich twist on a classic soup, and poached eggs with garlic yoghurt and green chutneyNik SharmaMon 5 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhile purists might scoff and find the combination of spices in my French onion soup a little blasphemous, do give it a shot. Nigella seeds are the best flavour-enhancer for onions, while using ghee instead of butter adds a warm, nutty, caramel flavour. Then, my Indian-inspired twist on çılbır, the classic Turkish breakfast of poached eggs with yoghurt. It features my go-to poached egg method, which I learned fromNigella Lawson.Poached eggs with green chutney and yoghurt (pictured top)Stirring the barely simmering water right before adding the egg creates a vortex, forcing the egg white to wrap around the yolk, cradling it and keeping it intact and compact.Prep10 minCook35 minServes2For the green chutney2tbsp pumpkin seeds1 tsp cumin seeds200gcoriander, tender leaves and stems, plus a few sprigs to garnish1 green chilli, such as bird’s eye, serrano or jalapeño60mlice-cold water2-3tbsplime or lemon juice1tbsp grated fresh ginger1 garlic clove, peeled and chopped1 tsp sugar, or honey or maple syrup, plus more as neededFine sea saltFor the yoghurt480gplain full-fat Greek yoghurt1-2 garlic cloves, peeled and gratedFine sea saltFor the poached eggs4 large eggs4 tsp lemon juiceToastedsourdough, preferably buttered or drizzled with olive oil, to serveTo make the chutney, toast the pumpkin seeds in a small, dry saucepan over medium heat, stirring often. After a minute, add the cumin seeds and continue toasting for a minute and a half to two minutes, until they turn fragrant and light brown (if they burn, discard them and start again). Put the pumpkin, cumin seeds, coriander, chilli, ice-cold water, lime juice, ginger, garlic and sugar in a blender, and blitz smooth; if need be, add a few more tablespoons of ice-cold water, one at a time, to loosen – the chutney should not be very runny. Taste and season with salt and more sugar as needed. The chutney can now be stored in an airtight container in the fridge for up to three days.Fill a medium saucepan with enough water to submerge a whole egg, bring it to a boil on a medium-high heat, then turn down the heat to a simmer. Put 2½cm water in a second medium saucepan and bring it to a low simmer.To make the yoghurt, in a medium metal bowl, mix the yoghurt and garlic, then season with salt. Set the bowl over the second saucepan, and whisk for two or three minutes, until smooth and creamy. Spoon the yoghurt into two serving bowls.For the poached eggs, crack one egg into a fine-mesh strainer set over a small bowl, and let the loose, liquid portion of the egg white drain for about 10 seconds. Gently transfer the remaining egg to a small bowl and add a teaspoon of lemon juice. Stir the simmering water in the first saucepan with a spoon – the water should barely be bubbling – then carefully slide in the egg. Repeat with the second egg. Leave the two eggs to poach undisturbed for three or four minutes, until the whites turn opaque, then, using a slotted spoon, lift out the eggs, allow any excess water to drain off, then place them on top of the yoghurt in the serving bowls. Repeat with the remaining two eggs.Top the eggs with generous spoonfuls of chutney, garnish with sprigs of coriander., and serve with toasted sourdough.Nigella-scented French onion soupView image in fullscreenNik Sharma’s nigella-scented French onion soup.Photograph: Ola O Smit/The Guardian. Food and prop styling: Lucy Turnbull. Food styling assistant: Lilli Gavin.Prep15 minCook2 hrMakes455gghee, or unsalted butter1.6kgyellow onions(about 4 large ones), peeled and halved through the root, then thinly sliced2 garlic cloves, peeled and grated2 tsp nigella seedsFine sea salt4 sprigs fresh thyme2 tsp black peppercorns1 bay leaf945mllow-sodium vegetable stock2tbsp white or yellow miso2tbspplain flour2tbsp dry sherry, or apple cider vinegarFor the croutons8 slicessourdough baguette(about 13mm-thick)115ggratedgruyere2 tsp nigella seeds2 tsp thyme leavesIn a Dutch oven or large, heavy-based saucepan, melt the ghee over a medium heat. Add the onions, garlic, nigella seeds and a tiny pinch of salt, toss to coat the onions, then cover and leave to cook, stirring occasionally to prevent scorching, for about 30 minutes, until the onions turn soft and translucent.Take off the lid, turn the heat to low and cook for about another hour (they might take longer), until the onions turn golden brown; if at any point the onions start to stick and burn, add a few tablespoons of water.Meanwhile, wrap the thyme, peppercorns and bay leaf in cheesecloth and tie with kitchen twine. Put the bag in a medium saucepan, add the stock and 240ml water, then whisk in the miso. Bring to a boil, then turn down to a simmer, cover and leave to steep at a low simmer for 30 minutes. Remove and discard the spice bag.Stir the flour into the onions and cook on a medium-high heat, stirring, for about two minutes, to cook away the raw flour flavour. Turn the heat to low, add the sherry, then stir in 240ml of the hot stock to ensure there are no flour lumps. Scrape the bottom of the pot to release any stuck-on browned bits, then gradually stir in the remaining stock. Bring to a boil, then turn down the heat to low and simmer for six to eight minutes, until slightly thickened. Taste and season, if need be.Heat the oven to 200C (180C fan)/400F/gas 6. To make the croutons, put the baguette slices on a baking sheet and bake for 12-15 minutes, until golden brown, flipping once halfway. These can be made up to a day ahead and stored in an airtight container at room temperature.Heat the grill to high and put an oven rack 15cm from the grill. Put four 600ml ovenproofcrockson a baking sheet and divide the soup evenly between them, filling them to at least 6mm from the top. Top each bowl with two slices of the toast, sprinkle with the gruyere and nigella seeds, then grill for about a minute, until the cheese bubbles and melts. Garnish with the thyme leaves and serve hot.These recipes are edited extracts from Fundamentals of Flavor: 100 Recipes for the Science of Better Cooking by Nik Sharma, published by Chronicle Books at £35.
