title: Holiday cottage company insisted on a death certificate to amend our break | Money | The Guardian
description: Sykes Holiday Cottages showed no empathy and insisted on paperwork we didn’t have so soon after my husband’s death
Author: Anna Tims
Headline: Sykes Holiday Cottages showed no empathy and insisted on paperwork we didn’t have so soon after my husband’s death
Content: A death in the family meant our planned holiday in Cumbria had to change.Photograph: John Morrison/AlamyView image in fullscreenA death in the family meant our planned holiday in Cumbria had to change.Photograph: John Morrison/AlamyConsumer championsMoneyHoliday cottage company insisted on a death certificate to amend our breakSykes Holiday Cottages showed no empathy and insisted on paperwork we didn’t have so soon after my husband’s deathAnna TimsMon 5 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 14.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWe booked a break with Sykes Holiday Cottages for 11 of us to celebrate my mum’s 80th birthday last February. The cost was £2,400, paid for by my 87-year-old dad, but it was my husband who made the booking.In January, my husband was diagnosed with aggressive lymphoma, and he died 10 days before the trip. My parents and some other members of the party still planned to take the holiday, and my dad informed Sykes of the death, since my husband was their point of contact.Sykes declared that the booking could not be honoured in my late husband’s name and that they would need a copy of his death certificate to move it into my name. We did not have one since an inquest into the death had been ordered.Sykes said a copy of my marriage certificate would suffice. I submitted this, only to be told that “an official document recognised by the state that confirms the passing of the deceased” was required.We provided a screenshot of the inquest listing from the coroner’s court website but were advised that this was not sufficient evidence.My GP wrote a letter confirming the death, but Sykes did not reply, and by then we were all too distressed to continue.Later, Sykes sent numerous emails to my late husband’s email address asking whether he had enjoyed the stay. We never received a refund, and I have not felt emotionally strong enough to do anything further before now.TB,Huddersfield, West YorkshireMy wife died but Virgin Media seems unable to transfer account to my nameRead moreI could hardly believe what I was reading as I trawled through Sykes’s correspondence. Its response, on being informed of your husband’s untimely death, was to send him an email asking for information.When Sykes received the requested marriage certificate, the company simultaneously stated in an email that this provided sufficient proof for the booking to be transferred to your name, and that the booking could not be transferred without an official confirmation of death.The GP letter confirming the death merely elicited an email saying Sykes would be in touch. By then, the trip was two days away. Sykes still did not amend the booking name, nor did it acknowledge the link to the coroner’s inquest listing.The next you heard from them was the first of several emails addressed to your late husband hoping that he had enjoyed the holiday. When you asked them to stop using his email address, Sykes apologised for the “inconvenience”.Four days later, when you had to complain about another such email to him, you were told unapologetically that feedback forms are sent automatically. By then, Sykes had been informed multiple times over a fortnight that your husband had died.Sykes, I discover, does not have an official bereavement policy which, given the size of the business, is poor enough. But empathy does not require an official mandate and you received none.Its onerous name change requirements are more suitable for a visa application than checking into a Cumbrian cottage. It refunded the £2,400 pronto when I got in touch and added £150 in “goodwill”. I think that’s a paltry sum for the distress it caused, but you have accepted it so you can put the ordeal behind you.A spokesperson said: “We have contacted the family directly to apologise and resolve the matter, and are reviewing our processes to ensure situations like this are always handled with the care and sensitivity they deserve.”Hats off to first-class customer serviceOur spirits need some good news, so here are some tales of how customer service ought to be.“We bought a secondhand Scandibørn bed from a third-party seller and found four screws were missing,” writesCC. “They were so specialist that no shop even knew what they were called. We contacted Scandibørn with low expectations of help, but they immediately offered to send us the missing screws for free. Exemplary customer service, which has earned a customer for life.”MS, meanwhile, raises his revamped hat to Tilley. “Thirty years ago I bought a Tilley hat, which became a constant companion on walks and holidays. It was beginning to show its age and, since the label promised a lifetime guarantee, I contacted Tilley. I was asked to submit photographs and was promptly invited to choose from three designs. The replacement was dispatched within days, with a handling charge of £20. Sadly, this one will outlast me.”We welcome letters but cannot answer individually. Email us atconsumer.champions@theguardian.comor write to Consumer Champions, Money, the Guardian, 90 York Way, London N1 9GU. Please include a daytime phone number. Submission and publication of all letters is subject toour terms and conditions.Explore more on these topicsMoneyConsumer championsConsumer affairsConsumer rightsTravel & leisureBereavementDeath and dyingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: My search for the perfect Italian aperitivo in Verona | Verona holidays | The Guardian
description: The classic pre-dinner drink and snack combo varies depending where you are in Italy. In this fair city, it’s an institution that can even be enjoyed first thing
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The classic pre-dinner drink and snack combo varies depending where you are in Italy. In this fair city, it’s an institution that can even be enjoyed first thing
Content: In Verona, the osteria is an institution at the heart of the city’s drinking culture.Photograph: Olena_Z/Getty Images/iStockphotoView image in fullscreenIn Verona, the osteria is an institution at the heart of the city’s drinking culture.Photograph: Olena_Z/Getty Images/iStockphotoVerona holidaysMy search for the perfect Italian aperitivo in VeronaThe classic pre-dinner drink and snack combo varies depending where you are in Italy. In this fair city, it’s an institution that can even be enjoyed first thingGabriele PascaMon 5 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 03.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleI arrived in Verona, I admit, without a particularly clear idea of whataperitivomeant. In Italy, the ritual – broadly, a drink and something small to eat before a meal – speaks a different dialect in every city.Milan has turned it into a polished after-work institution. In Venice, it is more itinerant: anombra(a small glass of wine) along with acicchetto(a bite-size snack) and then on to the nextbacaro(one of the city’s traditional wine bars). Verona follows another logic.Veronese wine writer Angelo Peretti has described theosteria(the traditional tavern at the heart of the city’s drinking culture) as a Verona institution: somewhere its social life takes shape over agòto(the local word for a glass of wine), usually with something small to eat at the counter, often while standing.double quotation markAt about 9.30am, while drinking coffee opposite the Teatro Filarmonico, I noticed that aperitivo had already begunI thought I understood. Then, at about 9.30am one morning, while drinking coffee opposite theTeatro Filarmonico, I noticed that aperitivo had already begun without me. A woman ordered abianchetto, a small glass of white wine. A couple, already defeated by the heat, asked for two spritzes. Two friends shared a bottle of sparkling wine.Nobody had announced that it was “aperitivo time”. More strikingly, nobody seemed to find any of this unusual.That was when my search really began. I decided not to look for one type of bar, or even one type of drink. What mattered was whether I would actually stop there for an aperitivo – alone, with friends or simply while waiting for dinner.Caffè Monte BaldoView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Gabriele PascaAt Monte Baldo, which opened in 1909, the counter was still being set up, with a man I took to be the owner assembling the day’startine(small open sandwiches with various toppings). A very young waitress offered to help me choose a wine. There were more than 30 wines by the glass, mostly priced between €5.50 and €11. I chose analtalanga, a traditional-method sparkling wine from Piedmont, partly because the bottle was still unopened. They opened it without hesitation.With lunch ahead, I ordered two tartine:baccalà mantecato(Veneto’s creamy stockfish spread whipped with olive oil) and boiled egg with anchovy. Both were excellent: fresh bread, generous toppings, clearly just made. The tartine cost €4.60; the wine €7.As I was leaving, a man walked in carrying a motorcycle helmet. Before he had time to order came the question: “Your usual?” However many tourists pass through Verona, somebody still has a usual.8.5/10Antica Bottega del VinoView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Gabriele PascaThis is one of Verona’s great wine institutions. I arrived before 7pm, as the tartine counter was being filled. The mood was formal: staff in crisp uniforms and a queue of slightly bewildered tourists. With one person serving, it moved slowly as he explained the wines, €3 tartine and where to eat them – at the bar, at small indoor tables, or outside.I chose an €8 glass of franciacorta, Lombardy’s traditional-method sparkling wine, with two tartine:pancetta coppata(cured pork neck wrapped in pancetta) and gorgonzola cream. Both were generously topped, though the bread, while perfectly decent, wasn’t anything to write home about. Total: €14.As I drank, nearby tables were laid for dinner and reserved signs appeared. I asked whether I should move. “Absolutely not.” Those few aperitivo tables, I was told, stay for drinkers unless the place is exceptionally busy.6.5/10Tor-TorView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Gabriele PascaA sommelier I trust at one of Verona’s grander restaurants sent me to Tor-Tor, perhaps revealing more interest in wine than in the finer points of aperitivo. Still, it seemed worth a punt. Tucked down a side street behind theArena, every outdoor table was taken; inside, a regular occupied the counter, deep in wine talk with the owners.The blackboard and a small wooden menu board revealed a serious selection of natural wines, with plenty from Veneto. I went for a €7 orange wine – white grapes fermented in their skins – which came with popcorn, then added two €2polpette(small savoury balls, one meat, one aubergine) plus €1.50 olives dressed with oil and chilli.Thepolpettedid the job nicely; the wine was excellent and expertly recommended. The crowd was overwhelmingly local, and the regular at the counter was still talking wine when I left.8/10skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice a weekSign up toThe TravellerGet travel inspiration, featured trips and local tips for your next break, as well as the latest deals from Guardian HolidaysEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionOsteria Ai PretiView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Gabriele PascaJust across the Adige river in Veronetta, on the edge of Verona’s main tourist circuit, Ai Preti feels like a neighbourhood local. It is large, with dark wood throughout, and has the sort of retro look that comes from never having tried to look retro.Two counters divide the food between cold tartine and hot snacks. I chose one withbaccalà mantecato, another with caramelised onions, and a horse meat polpetta. Tartine cost €2, the polpetta slightly less; with a €4 glass of wine, the whole aperitivo came in under €10.By 7.45pm, both displays were almost bare, although my polpetta seemed freshly cooked. The crowd looked entirely local, paying far more attention to one another than to the labels. Magazines lay around for anyone drinking alone. Here, aperitivo felt like the working day quietly unwinding.7/10VelvetView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Gabriele PascaI was early for dinner. The restaurant next door was still closed and I had half an hour to kill. Filling the gap before dinner is, after all, the primary function of the aperitivo.Velvet occupies part of a 15th-century palazzo. There is a handsome counter with stools, though I chose a small table. Three nearby tables were already occupied by a more dressed-up crowd than I had encountered in Veronetta, drinking and talking without much hurry.There was plenty of wine on the list, but I went for a €12 negroni. It arrived with fried plantain crisps, cashews and little savoury pastries with tomato – at no extra cost. A separate food menu offers more substantial bites, including edamame falafel and chicken wings.By the time I’d finished my drink, the restaurant next door was open. Half an hour neatly accounted for.8/10Osteria da MorandinView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Gabriele PascaMorandin was the only place I visited twice. My first visit was almost accidental – a glass of wine became dinner – so I returned a week later, just before 9pm, to make sure I hadn’t simply got lucky. On paper, its long afternoon closure, from 2.30 to 7pm, had been my only doubt.It was another punishingly hot evening in Veronetta. Every outside table was taken and the fans inside did little more than move the heat around. I was wearing absurd red-and-blue striped trousers. A man I took to be one of the owners, there as a customer, noticed our near-matching trousers and came over for a high five. “They say we look like we’re in pyjamas. They don’t understand fashion.”Wines run from €2.50 to €6 and, even at that relatively late hour, the cicchetti display was the fullest I had seen: battered vegetables, frittata, prawn skewers, €1.30 meatballs withtastasal(seasoned pork mince) and €1.80 tartine. I chose a durello, the crisp local sparkling wine from the Lessini hills, a meatball and a tuna-and-egg tartina.The waiters were run off their feet; regulars greeted one another and foreign voices were scarce. Fifteen minutes later, I asked about dinner. “Full.” Ten minutes on, a table appeared. Aperitivo had not replaced dinner; it had made staying for it irresistible.10/10Explore more on these topicsVerona holidaysFood and drinkEurope holidaysItaly holidaysBars, pubs and clubsCity breaksShort breaksShareReuse this content

title: A new start after 60: Menopausal and out of work, I sat crying in my car. Now, I’m a standup comedian | Comedy | The Guardian
description: When Barbara Scully tried to get a job after years as a stay-at-home mum, no one would hire her. So she made her own work as a writer and broadcaster – and soon found herself on TV and stage
Author: Paula Cocozza
Headline: When Barbara Scully tried to get a job after years as a stay-at-home mum, no one would hire her. So she made her own work as a writer and broadcaster – and soon found herself on TV and stage
Content: Barbara Scully at a Funny Women show at Whelan’s, Dublin, in February.Photograph: Paul SherwoodView image in fullscreenBarbara Scully at a Funny Women show at Whelan’s, Dublin, in February.Photograph: Paul SherwoodA new start after 60ComedyA new start after 60: Menopausal and out of work, I sat crying in my car. Now, I’m a standup comedianWhen Barbara Scully tried to get a job after years as a stay-at-home mum, no one would hire her. So she made her own work as a writer and broadcaster – and soon found herself on TV and stagePaula CocozzaMon 5 Oct 2026 01.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIf anyone had toldBarbara Scullyfive years ago that she would soon be enjoying her “sixth career” – this time as a standup comedian, or comic storyteller – she would have laughed in their face. “But once you get to 60, you realise that failure isn’t a big deal,” she says. “As long as nobody’s going to die, that’s grand.”Scully, who lives in Dublin, is now performing her one-woman showBecause I’m Worth Itaround Ireland to capacity audiences of up to 200 people. “I’m on a mission to try to tell women in particular not to fear getting older, to embrace it, to push back against all the bullshit about how you should be fighting ageing,” she says. “The more women like me who are willing to stand up and say: ‘This is me and I am 64 and I’m not really bothered about spending my time and money and energy on trying to look younger …’” She trails off. “I’m actually spending my time and money and energy doing stuff that makes me happy.”Her previous five careers comprise travel agent, word-processing tutor, fundraiser, stay-at-home parent and author-broadcaster. She embarked on No 5 after a personal crisis. “I couldn’t get a job, even though I had a chunky enough CV. I presume it was the fact that I was 50 and had a 10-year gap where my career used to live [while she was raising children],” she says.View image in fullscreen‘After two or three minutes, I felt laughter coming back at me. It was like rocket fuel.’Photograph: Paul Sherwood“The day I realised I couldn’t even get social welfare, I sat in the car on the driveway in tears, thinking: that’s it, I’m washed up, I’m done. Once I pulled myself together, I thought: OK, if this were one of my kids, what would I tell them? You’re going to have to make your own work. Look at what it is you enjoy doing and try to make that work for you.”Scully had always loved writing and talking – she had done a fair amount of both as a charity fundraiser. Over the next decade, she built up a freelance portfolio: she wrote opinion pieces for newspapers and a book called Wise Up: Power, Wisdom and the Older Woman; she appeared as a panellist on the chatshows Midday and Elaine on the free-to-air channel Virgin Media One. She continues to co-host a regular agony aunt slot onSeán Moncrieff’s showon the national radio station Newstalk.When her book was published in 2022, Scully was contacted by two women who were setting up an Irish chapter ofFunny Women, a community of women in comedy. They asked her to help with a show – to publicise it, she thought. “No. We’d like you to be in it,” they said.She agreed to read out part of her book between comedy slots, but when the day came, she realised that a reading would “kill the energy”, so she rewrote a chapter onsmear testsas a sketch.double quotation markI’m spending my time and money and energy doing stuff that makes me happy“I went on stage and after two or three minutes felt laughter coming back at me. It was like rocket fuel. It was something I’d never experienced before. It was huge. Really energising … I came off stage and I went: ‘Oh my God, I loved that.’”A year later, in December 2024, Scully was approached by a hotel to do an event about her book. She performed a one-woman show instead. “The following year, I toured that show around modest venues, small rooms, capacities probably 70 to 100. I was starting to realise that life was not what I was expecting it to be. Actually, it was much better. There’s so much negative talk about menopause … But menopause is only a portal. Once you’re through it, you’ve got this tremendous period of life.”Scully grew up in Dublin, “in a male-dominated house” she shared with her parents, three brothers and sometimes a grandfather and an uncle. By 16, she was 6ft (183cm) tall. Her brothers nicknamed her “H”, for heifer. “I was never going to fit into society’s idea of how a girl should be – petite and not taking up space,” she says. “I learned to use my voice pretty early on.”Increasingly, she senses “a huge connection between who I am at 64 and who I was at 18 or 19. There’s that same feeling. The world’s my oyster. I can do whatever I want to do.”Tell us: has your life taken a new direction after the age of 60?Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick hereExplore more on these topicsComedyA new start after 60IrelandEuropeWomenMenopauseMiddle ageOlder peoplefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Apple iPhone 18 Pro review: big changes for small differences | iPhone | The Guardian
description: Longer battery life, better screen, upgraded Siri and new variable aperture camera in refreshed design from last year’s model
Author: Samuel Gibbs
Headline: Longer battery life, better screen, upgraded Siri and new variable aperture camera in refreshed design from last year’s model
Content: The iPhone 18 Pro packs all of Apple’s best technology into a pocketable package.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe iPhone 18 Pro packs all of Apple’s best technology into a pocketable package.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.iPhoneReviewApple iPhone 18 Pro review: big changes for small differencesLonger battery life, better screen, upgraded Siri and new variable aperture camera in refreshed design from last year’s modelSamuel GibbsConsumer technology editorMon 5 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 07.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleApple’s smaller ProiPhonegets the best kind of spec bump for 2026: longer battery life, faster chips and a fancy new variable aperture for the main camera.The iPhone 18 Pro is one of a pair of slab phones launched alongsideApple’s first folding phone, the iPhone Duo, and is the cheapest of the new phones, with a regular iPhone 18 yet to be announced.It isn’t exactly low cost, priced from £1,199 (€1,449/$1,199/A$2,099), with a £100 or equivalent rise over previous modelscourtesy of RAMageddon.Having fully revamped the design of the body for theiPhone 17 Pro, the new model is a modest refinement. It is 7g heavier and the back glass now matches the colour of the aluminium body, which is available in a handful of new shades.View image in fullscreenThe dynamic island at the top of the screen can now show three live activities at once, such as music playback, a timer and maps navigation.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianApple has shrunk the amount of the screen taken up by the Face ID camera, allowing the dynamic island to show three continuing tasks, up from two on previous devices. It also now shows the 3/4/5G indicator next to the signal level when playing music, which is a most appreciated feature for public transport commuters sorely missed on previous models.Otherwise, the 6.3in screen is one of the very best on a phone: super bright, crisp and smooth, while being big enough without making the phone enormous. An anti-glare coating makes it much easier to see outside, too.SpecificationsScreen:6.3in Super Retina XDR (120Hz OLED) (460ppi)Processor:Apple A20 ProRAM:12GBStorage:256GB, 512GB or 1TBOperating system:iOS 27Camera:48MP + 48MP UW + 48MP 4x, 18MP front-facingConnectivity:5G, wifi 7, NFC, Bluetooth 6, Thread, USB-C, Satellite, UWB and GNSSWater resistance:IP68 (6 metres for 30 mins)Dimensions:150 x 71.9 x 8.75mmWeight:211gFaster chip and longer battery lifeView image in fullscreenA full charge takes 59 minutes, hitting 80% in 33 minutes, using a 60W or greater USB-C adaptor.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianThe 18 Pro has Apple’s new A20 Pro chip, which is about 27% faster than the A19 Pro in last year’s model, with about 45% faster graphics performance. Since the A19 Pro was no slouch, that’s quite the leap and puts it miles ahead of the competition, ready to handle anything.The phone has a redesigned cooling system for longer peak performance, too, which is especially useful for running games on top settings.The battery lasts a solid six hours longer than the iPhone 17 Pro, managing to stretch to about two days between charges with more than six hours of active screen use across apps, browsing, messaging and photos. Even with the heaviest of use while out and about, the 18 Pro managed to end the day with 40% left in the tank. Most people will only need to charge it every other day.iOS 27 with new SiriView image in fullscreenThe new iOS 27 is familiar but faster and debuts Apple’s attempt to catch up to the competition on AI.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianThe 18 Pro ships runningiOS 27, which was released for the rest of the iPhone line on 14 September. It refines the relatively controversialLiquid Glass redesignfrom last year and speeds up the system, including app launches. But the big new addition is Apple’s revamped Siri, backed by Google’s AI technologies.Siri AI, as thenew system is called, is significantly more capable of understanding and answering questions than previous iterations. It is a chatbot like most other AI assistants, but it is less chatty and sycophantic than others, being more likely to just get the job done. As well as a choice of voices, there are sliders to control how fast it talks and how expressive its responses are. It has its own app where you can review previous interactions, but it is accessible anywhere on the phone via the side button, is built into Spotlight search and can see what’s on your screen, including when using the camera.It can also offer suggestions, such as adding an event to your calendar from the messages or mail apps, and attempts to display relevant information from your emails in the phone app when you call a business. But Siri can only do so if you use Apple’s apps, so if you use WhatsApp for texting and Gmail for your email, none of it works.SustainabilityThe battery will lastmore than 1,000 full-charge cycleswith at least 80% of its original capacity and can bereplaced for £119. Out-of-warrantyscreen repairs cost £349. The specialists iFixit awarded the phone aseven out of 10for repairability.It contains more than 40% recycled material. The company breaks down thephone’s environmental impactin its report. Apple offers trade-in and free recycling schemes, including for non-Apple products.CameraView image in fullscreenThe camera app has new customisable shortcuts to your most used tools and settings, as well as aperture, shutter speed and exposure controls.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianThe 18 Pro has a similar camera system to last year’s 17 Pro with one big addition, a variable aperture for the main camera.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThat means it has a very good 18MP centre stage selfie camera on the front and three 48MP cameras on the rear: main, 0.5x ultrawide and 4x telephoto.The ultrawide is one of the best on a phone, handy for landscapes and group shots. The 4x telephoto is very good too, full of detail and manages lower light settings well. It shoots excellent photos with a crop zoom to reach 8x before digital zoom is required, which is a little behind rivals with 5x/10x telephoto zooms.The variable aperture on the main camera can be left on automatic or controlled manually. It allows the camera to open wider than previous models for better low light performance, speeding up night mode shots and reducing unwanted motion blur.But it also enables a number of creative uses, such asmaking starburstsby narrowing the aperture when shooting lights, which is very fun, or controlling the depth of field in your photo. However, because the iPhone’s camera is tiny compared with anAPS-Corfull-framecamera, the difference in depth of field – where the foreground and background of the image are either in focus or blown out for a nicebokeheffect – is pretty minor. When shooting something up close, manually closing the aperture to f/4.0 can bring things in the foreground or background into focus, but otherwise the difference for most shots is small.View image in fullscreenYou can see the six aperture blades open and close on the bottom left camera lens using a torch.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianThe 18 Pro’s camera has a number of other useful upgrades. My favourite is AI-powered focus tracking that keeps a subject in focus as it moves about or into and out of the frame, which has been one of the best features of a Pixel camera for years and is extremely handy for fast-moving children or pets.Apple has also added texture and grain control to itsPhotographic Stylesfeature to customise how the camera shoots photos beyond what was introduced with theiPhone 16 Pro, including film simulation. Finally, the newApple Reference Imagefeature can sign an image for authenticity, on a per pixel level directly on the sensor, to help later prove a shot is not AI-generated, similar to a digital negative.The camera shoots some of the very best video on a phone, too. New for this year is the ability to convert a regular videoto a cinematic one after the fact, a bit like the excellent automatic portrait mode for photos.PriceThe iPhone 18 Pro costs from£1,199(€1,449/$1,199/A$2,099).For comparison, theiPhone 17costs£899, theiPhone Aircosts£1,099, the iPhone 18 Pro Max costs£1,299, theGoogle Pixel 11 Procosts£1,079and theSamsung Galaxy S26 Ultracosts£1,359.VerdictThe iPhone 18 Pro is an iterative upgrade on an already great device from last year. Inside, it has some quite big changes, but their impact is fairly minor on the whole experience.The new A20 Pro chip is super fast, but you can’t really notice the difference day to day, as previous iPhone chips have already been very quick. The extended battery life is great, but most people will still have to charge it every other day. The smaller camera cutout in the dynamic island now shows three continuing activities instead of two. Even the variable aperture in the main camera makes only a small difference to image quality unless you’re really trying to get creative.The screen is fantastic and big enough. The aluminium body feels great to hold. The cameras are some of the best on a phone and even Siri is better now.All of these things add up. The 18 Pro is without doubt the best iPhone ever made and at this size is one of the very best smaller phones available. It’s just not a transformative change unless you’re upgrading from a much older model and it now costs even more thanks to RAMageddon.Pros:relatively compact, great screen, better dynamic island, longer battery life, great cameras, variable aperture, USB-C, top performance, long software support, Face ID, better AI.Cons:small upgrade on last year, expensive, heavier than previous model, AI tools still lag behind top competitors.Explore more on these topicsiPhoneAppleMobile phonesSmartphonesComputingPhotographyGadgetsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Is it true that … houseplants freshen the air in our homes and offices? | Life and style | The Guardian
description: If you want to seriously oxygenate your rooms with greenery, you’re going to need a lot of space
Author: Kate Lloyd
Headline: If you want to seriously oxygenate your rooms with greenery, you’re going to need a lot of space
Content: Illustration: Edith Pritchett/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Edith Pritchett/The GuardianIs it true that …Life and styleIs it true that … houseplants freshen the air in our homes and offices?If you want to seriously oxygenate your rooms with greenery, you’re going to need a lot of spaceKate LloydMon 5 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘Plants take in carbon dioxide and release oxygen when they photosynthesise,” says John Tregoning, a professor at Imperial College London and author ofLive Forever? A Curious Scientist’s Guide to Wellness, Ageing and Death. “If you’ve got enough of them, they should produce more oxygen than there was initially.”It’s tempting to think of plants as a kind of natural air filter, cleaning the air in stuffy, poorly ventilated spaces. But the reality is different.The average plant produces just a few litres of oxygen a day. A person, by comparison, consumes about 500 litres. So, to produce enough oxygen for one person, you’d need hundreds of plants. “Quite a mad number of plants to have in a room,” says Tregoning. You would also need plenty of light for photosynthesis to take place.Tregoning points out that we shouldn’t look to keep increasing the oxygen level indoors infinitely: “It’s quite poisonous at high levels.”double quotation markFor cleaner, fresher air, the most important thing is to keep the windows openHe says people are right to think about air quality in their homes and offices. “Higher levels of carbon dioxide are going to make you feel a bit groggy. If you’re working with lots of other people, poor ventilation is also going to lead to faster transmission of colds and illnesses.”Is it true that … having a hot drink will cool you down?Read moreBut plants aren’t a substitute for good ventilation. If you want cleaner, fresher air in an office or home, the most important thing is to make sure the air is regularly replaced by keeping windows open, for example.Still, he says, trees and plants can have a beneficial effect on our health. He pointsto a studyfrom the 1980s that looked at patients recovering from surgery. One hospital ward had windows overlooking trees, while another faced a brick wall. Patients in the tree-facing ward self-administered less pain medication and recovered faster than those facing the wall.Explore more on these topicsLife and styleIs it true that …HouseplantsfeaturesShareReuse this content
