title: Guardian readers fund life-changing surgery for Somali boy injured in US airstrike | Global development | The Guardian
description: After Guardian investigation uncovered drone strike that killed 12 civilians and injured many more, seven-year-old Abdiqadir Salah underwent vital operation in Mogadishu
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: After Guardian investigation uncovered drone strike that killed 12 civilians and injured many more, seven-year-old Abdiqadir Salah underwent vital operation in Mogadishu
Content: Abdiqadir Salah and his mother, Marian Haji Abdi Guled. ‘I didn’t know people like this existed,’ she says of the people who raised the money for her son’s surgery.Photograph: Mohamed GabobeView image in fullscreenAbdiqadir Salah and his mother, Marian Haji Abdi Guled. ‘I didn’t know people like this existed,’ she says of the people who raised the money for her son’s surgery.Photograph: Mohamed GabobeRights and freedomGlobal developmentGuardian readers fund life-changing surgery for Somali boy injured in US airstrikeAfter Guardian investigation uncovered drone strike that killed 12 civilians and injured many more, seven-year-old Abdiqadir Salah underwent vital operation in MogadishuSupported byAbout this contentMohamed Gabobe in MogadishuMon 5 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 09.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn the rickshaw ride to the hospital, Marian Haji Abdi Guled felt a mixture of joy and apprehension: the day they had been waiting for had finally arrived.Almost a year earlier, her then seven-year-old son, Abdiqadir Salah, had been seriously injured, alongside his two siblings, in what aGuardian investigationfound was a US drone strike on the village of Jamaame in Somalia that killed at least 12 civilians, including eight children.Abdiqadir’s small body had been impaled by shrapnel in the attack, and several chunks remained embedded in his back.Doctors feared that without an operation to remove them, the boy would lose his ability to walk, but Guled hadno money for an operation. For 10 months, the family had languished in Mogadishu with growing expenses and no income – unable to afford surgery, but unwilling to let the boy return to the village without it.After the investigation, which told the story of Guled and other civilians affected by the attack, a group of Guardian readers from across the globe fundraised for Abdiqadir’s surgery and recovery.Within a few hours, enough money was raised to cover his treatment and rehabilitation, as well as any medical expenses and treatment for her other two children, who sustained less extensive injuries.“I was so happy when I found out that Guardian readers raised the money needed for my son’s surgery. I didn’t know people like this existed,” Guled said.“The people who contributed to the surgery – I really appreciate their support and how they stood by our family when we needed it the most.”On a Saturday morning in September, Guled waited anxiously as Abdiqadir was finally taken for surgery at Kaafi hospital in Mogadishu.“Other patients were taken into surgery after him and came out before him – so I worried maybe something went wrong,” she said. “I got to a point where I knocked on the operating room door asking if my son was still alive, then was held back by other patients.”Finally, her son emerged. Doctors told Guled the surgery had been successful, but complex. While the first two pieces of shrapnel from the missile had been successfully removed, taking out the final piece was considered too risky, possibly resulting in paralysis, so they concluded that it was safer to leave it and monitor his condition.When the Guardian visited Abdiqadir a few weeks later, he appeared bright, energised and visibly happy. “I have one piece of metal still in me, and if they touch it, I might become paralysed,” the seven-year-old said. “[But] I don’t have any problem with the last piece of metal in my body, because I’m no longer in pain.”View image in fullscreenDoctors took out two pieces of shrapnel from Abdiqadir Salah’s back but could not remove a third.Photograph: Mohamed GabobeTheGuardian investigationinto the US airstrikes that injured Abduqadir raised myriad questions about US military intelligence, such as how the targets were selected and why children were hit while they were clearly visible and out in the open. The US has not responded to any questions about the Jamaame attack.In the months since then, US attacks on the area have continued: from December 2025 to July 2026, it carried out at least three airstrikes around Jamaame, according toresearch by New America, a security thinktank that documents US military operations abroad. Residents say drones continue to fly above the town.“We cannot return to Jamaame because what caused my children to be hurt is still there,” Guled said. “I fled Jamaame with my wounded children because of the drones, and the drones are still [flying].”With the remaining financial support she received from Guardian readers, Guled plans to relocate with her children to the government-controlled port city of Kismayo, which has not been the target of drone strikes, and where Abdiqadir can receive further surgery if needed.She still wants answers from the US government, nearly a year after they were bombed. “My son has been left scarred for life,” she said.“I want the US government be held accountable for what they did to my family and for the US to stop bombing our community.”Explore more on these topicsGlobal developmentRights and freedomSomaliaDrones (military)US foreign policyAfricaMiddle East and north AfricaPhilanthropynewsShareReuse this content

title: Skull fractures suggest servants of Egypt’s ancient kings were sacrificed  | Archaeology | The Guardian
description: Study of remains taken from royal cemetery at Umm el-Qa’ab appears to confirm early Egyptologist’s theory
Author: Nicola Davis
Headline: Study of remains taken from royal cemetery at Umm el-Qa’ab appears to confirm early Egyptologist’s theory
Content: A fresco depicting a funeral procession in ancient Egypt.Photograph: DEA/F Guenet/De Agostini/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA fresco depicting a funeral procession in ancient Egypt.Photograph: DEA/F Guenet/De Agostini/Getty ImagesArchaeologySkull fractures suggest servants of Egypt’s ancient kings were sacrificedStudy of remains taken from royal cemetery at Umm el-Qa’ab appears to confirm early Egyptologist’s theoryNicola DavisScience correspondentMon 5 Oct 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 00.23 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCourt officials and craftspeople serving early Egyptian kings may have been sacrificed when their ruler died, according to research that found fractures in several ancient skulls.The royal cemetery of Umm el-Qa’ab near Abydos features the tombs and enclosures of the First Dynasty rulers of Egypt, and dates as far back as 3,000BC.Not only royalty were buried at the site: surrounding these structures are graves thought to belong to people associated with the royal households – including ladies, seal-bearers, inspectors and artisans.Writing in the journalFrontiers in Environmental Archaeology, Dr Roselyn Campbell, author of the study from Purdue University in the US, notes: “While Aha, the first ruler of the First Dynasty, seems to have only had a few subsidiary burials, his successors included hundreds of subsidiary graves around their tombs and enclosures.”The graves of the retainers were excavated in the 1920s by the English Egyptologist Flinders Petrie, who believed them to be an example of human sacrifice – a view some later experts agreed with.View image in fullscreenEgyptologist Flinders Petrie examining pottery, 1932.Photograph: Fox Photos/Getty ImagesBut there was a snag: Petrie did not find any evidence of trauma on the remains. While he suggested the individuals may have been buried alive, others suggested the retainers died naturally and were later reburied at Abydos when their ruler died.Campbell re-examined the skulls of 46 retainers excavated from graves surrounding the funerary enclosures of three different royals – King Djer, King Djet, and Queen Merneith – from the Duckworth Collections at the University of Cambridge.View image in fullscreenThe tomb of King Djer of Egypt, in Abydos.Photograph: Mike P Shepherd/Alamy“This question of whether or not retainer sacrifice was practised in Egypt has been debated for over a century, but this is the first study to examine the human remains from the tombs themselves,” Campbell told the Guardian.Campbell reports that 18 of the skulls showed signs of potentially lethal trauma such as fractures and – in one case – a chopping injury to the eye.Campbell believs Petrie may have seen the skull fractures but did not realise they were injuries that occurred around the time of death, rather than arising as a result of later damage.The fractures, she adds, are unlikely to have been caused by a mace – a weapon often depicted in ancient Egyptian art as being used by a victorious king to smite his enemies. Instead they are more likely to have been caused by flat, wide objects made of wood or antler.“For the crania without trauma, we cannot be certain they were sacrificed. It’s quite possible that some of the retainers were sacrificed, while others were not,” she said. “With such a small sample size of the original burial population, we simply can’t see the full extent of these funerary rituals, nor can we be sure that this sample is truly representative of all the retainers.”Campbell noted the number of subsidiary graves tapered off quickly and seems to have disappeared with the beginning of the Second Dynasty.Salima Ikram, a professor at the American University in Cairo, said while the idea of retainer sacrifice was not totally new, “this paper is one of the few times that rigorous current methodologies are being used to evaluate these remains”.She added: “The practice was short-lived, with people being replaced by statuettes. Possibly some or all retainers felt that this was a boon and that they would enjoy an eternal life in the service of the god-king, though they might also have resented it, been terrified, and tried to escape this fate.”Dr Dawn McCormack, an Egyptologist at Samford University, Alabama, said similar sacrifices had occurred across different cultures and times, adding that not everyone at the Egyptian site may have been compliant.“If you really think about what those scenes would have looked like, it would have been very gruesome,” she said. While noting that the study only involved a small number of skulls from the burial site, “the idea that some of the people may have been violently killed, I think, is something that in reality we might expect”, she said.Explore more on these topicsArchaeologyEgyptMiddle East and north AfricaAfricaForensic sciencenewsShareReuse this content

title: Flávio Bolsonaro poised to win Brazilian presidency after shock first-round victory | Flávio Bolsonaro | The Guardian
description: Progressive voters and supporters of incumbent president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva left reeling after far-right surge
Author: Tom Phillips
Headline: Progressive voters and supporters of incumbent president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva left reeling after far-right surge
Content: Flávio Bolsonaro received 47% of the vote – 56.1m votes – compared with Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s 45% (53.8m).Photograph: Diego Herculano/ReutersView image in fullscreenFlávio Bolsonaro received 47% of the vote – 56.1m votes – compared with Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s 45% (53.8m).Photograph: Diego Herculano/ReutersFlávio BolsonaroFlávio Bolsonaro poised to win Brazilian presidency after shock first-round victoryProgressive voters and supporters of incumbent president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva left reeling after far-right surgeTom PhillipsandTiago Rogeroin Rio de JaneiroMon 5 Oct 2026 16.06 EDTFirst published on Mon 5 Oct 2026 12.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFlávio Bolsonaro is in pole position to win Brazil’s presidential election, after a far-right tsunami propelled him to a shock first-round victory over the incumbent,Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, leaving progressive voters reeling.The 45-year-old rightwing candidate received 56.1m votes to Lula’s 53.8m – 47.03% to 45.16% – meaning the 80-year-old leftwinger has a mountain to climb if he is to bounce back in the second round on 25 October. Never, since the return of democracy toBrazilin 1985, has the first-round runner-up managed to turn the game around and win the second ballot.“Miracles are possible in politics. But I don’t see that happening,” the political scientist Miguel Lago said of Lula’s chances of snapping back. “I don’t see Flávio losing this election now.”Speaking outside the White House on Monday, Donald Trump told reporters: “Well, it’s a big victory: close but a very, very big victory. Amazing, actually.”Trump, who is a longtime ally of the Bolsonaro family, predicted the runoff would be “a very close election”.The far-right surge was a triumph – albeit an incomplete one – for the Bolsonaro clan and its 71-year-old patriarch,Jair Bolsonaro.View image in fullscreenSupporters of Flávio Bolsonaro celebrate the first-round results in Porto Alegre on Sunday.Photograph: Sílvio Ávila/AFP/Getty ImagesThe disgraced ex-president, who is serving a 27-year sentence for plotting a coup after losing the 2022 election to Lula, saw four relatives elected to congress. His 44-year-old wife, Michelle Bolsonaro, won a seat in the senate, as did his second son, Carlos Bolsonaro, who is 43. Bolsonaro’s youngest son, 28-year-old Jair Renan Bolsonaro, and the ex-president’s 62-year-old brother, Renato Bolsonaro, both won seats in the lower house of congress.Across Latin America’s biggest democracy, key congressional and gubernatorial races were also won by staunchBolsonaristasincluding Tarcísio de Freitas, who was re-elected as the governor of São Paulo state, and Sérgio Moro, who was elected governor of the southern state of Paraná. Both men were ministers during Bolsonaro’s 2018-22 government.Bolsonaro’s Liberal party (PL) will now boast the largest caucus in the senate with 28 of its 81 seats. Combined with the seats of other hard-right parties, that number rises to 43, giving the movement an upper house majority.A map graphic breaking down the results by municipalityMeanwhile, pro-Lula senate candidates, including the former environment minister Marina Silva, the leftwing veteran Benedita da Silva, and the centrist former planning minister Simone Tebet, suffered bitter defeats.Nikolas Ferreira and Lucas Pavanato, two youngBolsonaristasocial media warriors, became the best-voted congresspeople in Brazilian history, securing more than 3m votes.“We are experiencing a revolution …The far rightis growing in a very consistent way, election after election,” said Lago, calling the election the worst for progressive and moderate centrist parties since the late 80s.View image in fullscreenNikolas Ferreira, a 30-year-old congressman from Minas Gerais, is seen as one of the most influential members of the Bolsonarista right; he has more than 5 million followers on Instagram.Photograph: Alan Lima/The GuardianLago believed Lula had managed to interrupt the advance of Bolsonaro’s populist movement in 2022, thanks to positive voter memories of his first two terms, from 2002 to 2010. Back then, a global commodities boom allowed Brazil’s first working-class president to fund major social welfare programmes that helped millions escape poverty. “Butit was just an interregnum,” Lago said.Control of the senate should allow pro-Bolsonaro politicians to approve an amnesty for their movement’s charismatic leader, allowing the former president to emerge from the Brasília mansion where he is living under house arrest and reassert his leadership of the far right.A bar graph showing the proportion of votes won by candidate“I think he will be freed and I think he will be very important during Flávio Bolsonaro’s [presidency],” said Lago. “Flávio will be running the country and [Jair] Bolsonaro will be doing what he has always done: leading the revolution.”The senate majority may also help Bolsonaro’s third son, Eduardo Bolsonaro, return from self-imposed exile in the US. The 42-year-old, who has close ties to Donald Trump’s Maga movement, was sentenced in absentia to four years in prison earlier this year for coercion – the result of his lobbying the Trump administration to interfere in his father’s coup trial. Eduardo Bolsonaro reportedly hopes to become foreign minister if his brother wins the presidency.The result is good news for Trump, who has been accused of trying to sway the election in Bolsonaro’s favour, and his attempt to expand the conservative “orange wave” sweeping Latin America to its biggest democracy and economy. Recent years have seen a succession of pro-Trump presidents win power in the region, from Costa Rica, Honduras and El Salvador to Chile and Colombia.View image in fullscreenEduardo Bolsonaro, seen here at the Conservative Political Action Conference (Cpac) in Buenos Aires in 2024, reportedly hopes to become foreign minister if his brother wins the presidency.Photograph: Juan Mabromata/AFP/Getty ImagesOne of Trump’s most enthusiastic regional cheerleaders, the Argentinian president, Javier Milei, celebrated Bolsonaro’s “historic” victory against “the communist Lula”. “The American continent belongs to citizens who want to live in freedom,” Milei wrote on X.The prime minister of Israel, Benjamin Netanyahu, wished Bolsonaro “good luck in the final” and celebrated his “great victory”. He wrote on X: “I look forward to restoring the extraordinary friendship between Israel and Brazil.”Speaking after Sunday’s result was confirmed, Lula put a brave face on what analysts called a catastrophic night for the left. “From tomorrow we will launch a new campaign: [and in] a campaign with only two candidates we will be able to show the difference between our proposals for Brazil,” he said, vowing to expose his rival’s “dark past”, which involves well-documented ties to members of Rio’s underworld and corruption allegations, which Bolsonaro has denied.View image in fullscreenLuiz Inácio Lula da Silva said his Workers’ party ‘will launch a new campaign’.Photograph: Xinhua/ShutterstockBut the mood at Lula’s post-election event wasreportedly funerealand Bolsonaro goes into the second round as the firm favourite. He is likely to be boosted by the migration of votes from the election’s other rightwing candidates – Ronaldo Caiado, Renan Santos and Romeu Zema – who, between them, won more than 5.5m votes.Santos quickly announced he would endorse neither candidate, considering both Lula and Bolsonaro to be “crooks”. Zema has vowed to vote against Lula’s Worker’s party (PT) in the runoff, while Caiado has yet to declare his intentions.Lula’s best hope may be convincing some of the record 33 million Brazilians who did not vote to turn out next time. “He will need to mobilise these apathetic voters who, in a sense, have already abandoned politics, which will be an extremely difficult task,” said Camila Rocha, a political scientist who studies Brazil’s new right.Rocha has spent recent months interviewing undecided voters and identified “a great deal of voter apathy, especially among those who are not aligned withBolsonarismo, and who could potentially vote for Lula”.Although Flávio Bolsonaro has held political office for more than 20 years, “for undecided voters, his main positive characteristic is this idea of ‘renewal’, despite his possible involvementin corruptionand withparamilitary groups,” Rocha added.Lago believed only a dramatic shift from Lula’s campaign – such as changing the candidate, or a severe scandal involving Bolsonaro – could change the election’s outcome. But he was doubtful that would occur.Explore more on these topicsFlávio BolsonaroLuiz Inácio Lula da SilvaBrazilThe far rightJair BolsonaroAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: Far right on the march and Lula’s failures: key drivers of Flávio Bolsonaro’s Brazil surge | Brazil | The Guardian
description: Experts say strength of evangelical church and stubbornness of Lula, 80, also helped propel Jair Bolsonaro’s son to first-round election win
Author: Tom Phillips
Headline: Experts say strength of evangelical church and stubbornness of Lula, 80, also helped propel Jair Bolsonaro’s son to first-round election win
Content: Flavio Bolsonaro celebrates after winning the most votes in Brazil’s presidential election. He will go to a runoff against Lula on 25 October.Photograph: Adriano Machado/ReutersView image in fullscreenFlavio Bolsonaro celebrates after winning the most votes in Brazil’s presidential election. He will go to a runoff against Lula on 25 October.Photograph: Adriano Machado/ReutersBrazilFar right on the march and Lula’s failures: key drivers of Flávio Bolsonaro’s Brazil surgeExperts say strength of evangelical church and stubbornness of Lula, 80, also helped propel Jair Bolsonaro’s son to first-round election winTom Phillipsin Rio de JaneiroMon 5 Oct 2026 14.42 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn Sunday night, as the scale of the far-right triumph inBrazilsank in, an adapted football chant rang out in one of Rio’s most leftwing areas.“Let’s turn this around, Lu-laaaaa! Let’s turn this around, Lu-laaaaa! Let’s turn this around, Lu-laaaaa!” crestfallen progressives bellowed while drowning their sorrows after witnessing an excruciating election setback for their leader,Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.But the scale of the challenge facing the veteran leftist looks immense afterFlávio Bolsonaro’s shock first-round win, which analysts attribute to a complex lattice of social, political and religious phenomena.“Flávio Bolsonaro’s result shows that Bolsonarismo is a far-right movement … that has put down deep roots in Brazilian society,” said Bernardo Mello Franco, a political columnist for the Rio broadsheet O Globo. “His father [Jair Bolsonaro] was convicted and jailed for attempting a coup d’état [in 2022-23] yet despite this, his allies won elections across the country, and his son is the frontrunner in the second round of the presidential election.”Among the main drivers behind Bolsonaro’s strong showing:1.The evangelical churchBrazil’s evangelical church has expanded dramatically since the 1980s, with evangelical Christians now making up nearly a third of the population.Many evangelical voters – often influenced by church leaders – have thrown their weight behind the radical populist movement built by Jair Bolsonaro, and now spearheaded by his evangelical eldest son. As president from 2018 to 2022, Bolsonaro’s ultra-conservative policies helped him cement a lasting alliance with powerful megachurch leaders such as the televangelist Silas Malafaia.“This religious machine …was put at the service of Bolsonarismo: starting with these pastors who have millions of followers on social media, who buy airtime on TV, who lead churches with millions of members, and who turned themselves into canvassers for the Bolsonaro family,” said Mello Franco.2.Urban violenceMello Franco believed urban violence was another factor that had turbocharged the “far-right windstorm” sweeping Brazil.Rightwing populists such as the pro-gun Bolsonaros were offering voters “misguided but easy-to-understand solutions” to high crime rates, such as increased police violence, mass incarceration and lowering the age of criminal responsibility. “This appeals to an electorate that is scared of violence and crime,” Mello Franco said.The leading light of such“security populism”in Latin America is El Salvador’s authoritarian president, Nayib Bukele, who has jailed thousands of people, often without due process, in his successful bid to cut murder rates. Mello Franco said El Salvador’s “proto-dictator” and his supposedly “magic solutions” had been held up as an inspiration by Bolsonarista politicians during the 2026 campaign.Such hardline proposals have also been boosted by Donald Trump’s decision to designate Brazil’s two biggest crime groups, Rio’s Red Command and São Paulo’s PCC, as foreign terrorist organizations. On the campaign trail, Bolsonaro and his allies have vowed to “neutralize narco-terrorists” and chemically castrate rapists – promises that appear to have won over many violence-weary voters.3.Lula’s campaignAnalysts say Lula’s failure to focus on day-to-day issues such as crime may have hurt his prospects.The leftwing veteran spent much of the campaign vowing to defend Brazil’s sovereignty from Donald Trump’s “colonial” designs and protect its rare earth reserves. “Meanwhile, what voters wanted were solutions to more immediate problems such asbank debts, the cost of food, and insecurity,” Mello Franco said.During one recent rally in suburban Rio, some Lula supporters visibly zoned out as the president waxed lyrical about critical minerals and artificial intelligence.Political analyst Thomas Traumann, who was spokesperson for the former leftwing president Dilma Rousseff, believed Lula’s third administration had ignored a large chunk of society that was unsatisfied over economic issues or because of controversies involving the supreme court.“The government treated any kind of criticism … as a display of fascism – which undoubtedly exists in Brazil – and elitism, which also exists,” he said. “But what also exists is a group of voters who expected more from the government and who are neither fascists, nor elitists. They are simply people who didn’t like the government and decided to punish it.”4.A Brazilian Biden?Some critics have also pointed to Lula’s age as his achilles heel and blame him for failing to produce an obvious successor. He will turn 81 two days after the election’s 25 October second round. One recent story in the Economist called Lula “a doddering leftie” and compared him to the “geriatric leader” Joe Biden, who was forcedto abandon his 2024 re-election campaignafter a disastrous debate performance against Trump.Traumann called questions over Lula’s physical or mental state “ridiculous”. “When you see him speak, you can tell it’s not about this,” he said ofthe gym-going octogenarian.Mello Franco agreed: “Unlike Biden, Lula has at no point shown any kind of physical frailty or cognitive impairment. I don’t think this was an issue.”But Traumann did see one parallel with the former US president: like Biden, Lula was stubborn, had not listened enough to others, and appeared to have thought decent economic indicators were enough to ensure re-election. “This disconnection from reality reminds me of Biden,” he said, attributing it to “the stubbornness of age”.From the start of the campaign, Lula seemed to believe “the election was in the bag”.“And it wasn’t,” Traumann said.5.The global far rightMany observers saw Sunday’s rightwing victory as another chapter in the global advance of the social media-savvy far right.“We’re seeing this revolution in many other parts of the world. We’re seeing this in the US, we’re seeing it in parts of Latin America, we’re see this in a different way in Europe,” said Miguel Lagos, a political scientist.Lagos believed that in Brazil, the movement was driven by a deep “rage against the classical political elites” including journalists, traditional politicians and intellectuals.Jair Bolsonaro and his son Flávio are career politicians. Between them, they have spent half a century working in Rio’s state legislature or the Brazilian congress. Even so, father and son have managed to portray themselves as Trump-style anti-establishment outsiders who have come to drain a swamp of which they, too, are part.Mello Franco believed Bolsonaro was now the favourite to become president. “But I don’t think the contest is over,” he cautioned. “Brazil is always showing us that plot twists aren’t just possible – they’re practically part of the landscape.”Explore more on these topicsBrazilJair BolsonaroLuiz Inácio Lula da SilvaAmericasfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Quebec poised to elect separatists to power for first time in more than a decade | Quebec | The Guardian
description: Parti Québécois promises to hold an independence referendum in Canada’s French-speaking region by 2028
Author: Martin Patriquin
Headline: Parti Québécois promises to hold an independence referendum in Canada’s French-speaking region by 2028
Content: Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, leader of the Parti Québécois.Photograph: Canadian Press/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenPaul St-Pierre Plamondon, leader of the Parti Québécois.Photograph: Canadian Press/ShutterstockQuebecQuebec poised to elect separatists to power for first time in more than a decadeParti Québécois promises to hold independence referendum in Canada’s French-speaking region by 2028Martin Patriquinin MontrealMon 5 Oct 2026 05.30 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 11.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleVoters in Quebec are going to the polls in provincial elections which will probably result in victory for a party that has promised to hold a referendum on independence fromCanadawithin the next two years.If polls are correct, the Parti Québécois (PQ) will form the government of the province of roughly nine million, the first time that the separatist movement will have gained power in the French-speaking region for more than a decade.A PQ victory in Monday’s election would also be likely to trigger a return topitched battles over questions of language and identitybetween Quebec and the federal government.Long considereda declining force in Quebec politics, the PQ owes its resurgence to party leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon. The 49-year-old Oxford-educated lawyer and polyglot has positionedhimself as a TikToking gen-X rebuttalto François Legault, Quebec’s long-serving Premier until he resigned early this year.View image in fullscreenPaul St-Pierre Plamondon is greeted by his children and partner ahead of a leaders debate in Montreal in September.Photograph: Canadian Press/ShutterstockAnalysts say that St-Pierre Plamondon’s electoral success is not because he is a separatist – the majority of voters do not support an independentQuebec– but because of his rightwing take on red-meat identity issues.He hasblamedimmigrants for Quebec’s overflowing schools, increased crime and skyrocketing housing prices, while promising to slash immigration levels and ban “conspicuous” religious symbols from the bodies of teachers and their students. He has derided his critics from the leftist Quebec Solidaire party as “woke”, and has taken to repeating the talking points of hard-right columnists.Many in the province agree with St-Pierre Plamondon’s rhetoric, even though it strays from PQ’s social democratic roots, according to radio host Patrick Lagacé. “Most Quebecers traditionally see themselves as being on the left. Increasingly, though, they are on the right when it comes to social issues like systemic racism and accommodation of religious behaviour. They’ve hardened on these issues, and don’t see themselves in the left’s recent fixation on identity issues,” Lagacé said.How Trump’s Canada threats dampened Quebec separatist movement – for nowRead moreThe biggest drag on St-Pierre Plamondon’s popularity has been his oft-repeated promise to hold a referendum during the first mandate of a PQ government. An overwhelming majority of Quebecersdon’t want such a thing any time soon– particularly with Canada locked in a trade war with the US. The province mostly voted for Liberal leader Mark Carney over the separatist Bloc Québécois in last year’s federal election, expressly because of Carney’s “elbows up” posturing against the Trump administration.But for the PQ,Donald Trump was at first a curse, then a gift. Early in the campaign, St-Pierre Plamondon said he wouldn’t hold a referendum as long as Trump was in power, defusing the issue and allowing St-Pierre Plamondon to concentrate on attacking immigration and immigrants.The party has also benefited from a four-way race for the right-leaning nationalist vote beyond the reliably Liberal fiefdom of Montreal – particularly around Quebec city, where the upstart Parti Conservateur du Québec has made significant inroads. “The Parti Québécois is benefiting from a massive vote split because those who don’t like the PQ don’t agree on who to vote for,” said poll analyst Philippe Fournier.Though the PQ will probably form the next provincial government, it remains unclear what sort of mandate it will have. Polls have the party hovering at roughly 30%, somewhat below the likely threshold for a majority government.In any case, St-Pierre Plamondon is laying the groundwork for confrontation with the federal government. He has mused about defunding the office of Quebec’s lieutenant-governor (the British Crown’s representative in the province) and promised to introduce a law to abolish the province’s ties with the monarchy, which separatists see as the ultimate symbol of oppression of Canada’s French minority.St-Pierre Plamondon also tore into Carney, after the prime ministersaidthe government will probably increase immigration rates in the country. Doing so, St-Pierre Plamondon said, was an “abuse of power” that would have further nefarious effects on French-language services in Quebec.For a man who trades on his relative youthfulness, St-Pierre Plamondon’s attacks on the monarchy have the whiff of anachronism – the kind of thing the PQ did in its 1970-era heyday.Attacking the federal government is similarly outdated, and potentially risky for St-Pierre Plamondon. Carney remains popular in Quebec, and is likely to remain so, at least until the existential threat of Trump recedes.Explore more on these topicsQuebecCanadaAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: Sass Jordan, Canadian rock singer-songwriter, dies aged 65 | Pop and rock | The Guardian
description: Musician who had hit albums with Racine and Rats later became a judge on six seasons of Canadian Idol
Author: Ben Beaumont-Thomas
Headline: Musician who had hit albums with Racine and Rats later became a judge on six seasons of Canadian Idol
Content: Sass Jordan performing in Toronto, 2009.Photograph: ZUMA Press, Inc./Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News.View image in fullscreenSass Jordan performing in Toronto, 2009.Photograph: ZUMA Press, Inc./Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News.Pop and rockSass Jordan, Canadian rock singer-songwriter, dies aged 65Musician who had hit albums with Racine and Rats later became a judge on six seasons of Canadian IdolBen Beaumont-ThomasMon 5 Oct 2026 05.22 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 05.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSass Jordan, the singer-songwriter who became a significant success in Canada’s rock scene in the 1990s before starring as a judge on Canadian Idol, has died aged 65.No cause of death has been given. A statement on social media said she died on 2 October “surrounded by her loving family … She remains in our hearts, an inimitable force of nature. An irreplaceable being of light and joy!”Born in Birmingham, England, in 1960, Jordan moved to Montreal as a child when her French academic father took a position at the city’s Concordia University. She began performing in her teens, and by her 20s was recording with a range of Montreal acts: she wrote a song for singer Michael Breen that became a Canadian Top 40 hit.By 1988 she was signed to Atlantic Records, who released her debut album Tell Somebody, with two singles – the title track and Double Trouble – charting just outside the Canadian Top 10. The following year she won a Juno (the Canadian equivalent of the Grammys) for most promising female vocalist.Her 1992 album Racine contained four Canadian Top 20 hits and, coupled with a move to Los Angeles, a new label in RCA, and an appearance on the bestselling soundtrack to The Bodyguard broke Jordan into a wider US market. Sun’s Gonna Rise, from 1994 album Rats, became her only US Hot 100 hit, and her biggest hit in Canada, reaching No 7. Taylor Hawkins, later the drummer for Foo Fighters, was her live drummer during this period.Her RCA deal ended and Jordan later voiced disappointment in the glossy sound of her next couple of albums, but her career received a boost from being a judge on the six seasons of TV talent show Canadian Idol, and she returned to recording with 2006’s You Get What You Give. In 2001 she also performed as Janis Joplin in the off-Broadway musical Love, Janis.She later embraced a bluesier sound, with 2020 album Rebel Moon Blues reaching the top five of the US blues chart, followed by her most recent studio recording, 2022’s Bitches Blues.In September, Jordan cancelled tour dates, citing “a serious medical condition”.Explore more on these topicsPop and rockCanadaAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: Brazil presidential election 2026: first-round live results | Brazil | The Guardian
description: Incumbent leftwing president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva is standing against Flávio Bolsonaro. Follow the latest results live
Author: Seán Clarke
Headline: Incumbent leftwing president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva is standing against Flávio Bolsonaro. Follow the latest results live
Content: BrazilBrazil presidential election 2026: first-round live resultsLuiz Inácio Lula da Silva is standing against Flávio Bolsonaro in the first round of the presidential raceSeán ClarkeandTom PhillipsSun 4 Oct 2026 20.24 EDTFirst published on Sun 4 Oct 2026 15.01 EDTShareLive first round results...Guardian graphic. Source: TSEResults by stateHow the election worksBrazil’s president is directly elected: each voter’s ballot counts equally and there is no electoral college. If no candidate wins more than 50% of the valid votes cast in the first round, a second runoff election will be held three weeks later between the two candidates who polled highest.According to opinion polls, there are two leading candidates. The first is the incumbent president, Lula, 80, a veteran of the Brazilian left who has served three terms. During his first two terms, between 2003 and 2011, he was credited with overseeing a historic period of commodity-fuelled growth and poverty reduction.Brazilian presidents are limited to two consecutive terms, so if he wins this time he will not be able to stand in 2030. In 2018 Lula was jailed on corruption charges, althoughhis conviction was quashedafter 580 days behind bars.Lula’s principal opponent is the far-right candidate Flávio Bolsonaro,son ofJair Bolsonaro, who is in prison. Flávio is a 45-year-old lawyer and a former senator from Rio de Janeiro. Bolsonaro senior is serving a 27-year sentence for masterminding a failed coup after losing the 2022 election but has endorsed his son’s campaign and hopes to regain his freedom if he wins.Opinion polls suggest no other candidate will come close to the two frontrunners, but neither is there a clear leader in polling for the 25 October runoff. The new leader will take power on 5 January 2027.One of the most important states to watch is Minas Gerais, a mountainous mining and agricultural region that is larger than France and has 21 million inhabitants, and is Brazil’s bellwether state. Since democracy returned in the 1980s, no candidate has won the presidency without triumphing in Minas. In 2018,Jair Bolsonarobeat Lula’s candidate there by more than 1.7m votes and was elected president.Four years later, Lula reclaimed the state by fewer than 50,000 and also won the nationwide race. History suggests that whoever wins Minas, will win the election.

title: Fuel from South Korea being shipped to Russia as Ukraine war grinds on | South Korea | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Guardian analysis finds more than 150,000 tonnes of fuel was shipped to Russian ports in July and August, some using sanctioned tankers
Author: Raphael Rashid
Headline: Exclusive: Guardian analysis finds more than 150,000 tonnes of fuel was shipped to Russian ports in July and August, some using sanctioned tankers
Content: Drone Aerial View of an Oil Tanker Ship Sailing under a bridge in Busan, South Korea.Composite: Guardian DesignView image in fullscreenDrone Aerial View of an Oil Tanker Ship Sailing under a bridge in Busan, South Korea.Composite: Guardian DesignSouth KoreaFuel from South Korea being shipped to Russia as Ukraine war grinds onExclusive: Guardian analysis finds more than 150,000 tonnes of fuel was shipped to Russian ports in July and August, some using sanctioned tankersRaphael Rashidin SeoulMon 5 Oct 2026 19.50 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 21.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFuel is being shipped fromSouth Koreato Russia via sanctioned tankers as Moscow scrambles for supplies amid the war in Ukraine, a move one expert said “undermines” Seoul’s public backing for Kyiv.Guardian analysis of port records and ship-tracking data found that in July and August over 176,000 tonnes of fuel, mostly diesel, was loaded at several South Korean ports on to seven tankers that made 14 voyages to Russia’s far east.Three of the vessels were under sanctions by the UK and EU, and one took on its cargo through aship-to-ship transferin South Korean waters – a method that can obscure where a cargo came from and lets ships avoid calling at port terminals.“It is shocking that EU-sanctioned tankers loaded fuel at South Korean ports and carried it to Russia”, said Isaac Levi, an analyst at the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA), a Finnish thinktank. “This undermines the sanctions regime and South Korea’s support forUkraine.”British armed forces intercept Russian shadow fleet oil tanker in ChannelRead moreSeoul has sent Ukraine humanitarian aid and non-lethal military supplies such as helmets, body armour and demining vehicles, and in 2023 pledged $2.3bn in support, most of it in loans.ButSouth Korea has long sought to balance its support for Ukraine with its desire to improve ties with Russia. Throughout the war, Seoul has ruled out sending weapons directly to Ukraine, in line with its practice of not supplying lethal arms to countries at war. Moscow has signalled an interest in restoring relations with South Korea, including trade ties.While the fuel trade involves vessels sanctioned by some of Seoul’s western partners, it does not appear to breach South Korean law. South Korea’s own measures against Russia rely mainly on export controls on goods such as industrial machinery, electronics and vehicles.The shipments, however, risk making Seoul look like a weak link in western efforts to pressure Russia, as relations with Kyivcome under strainover the transfer of two North Korean prisoners of war to South Korea, which Seoul says was meant to remain secret.It is unclear who owned or sold the fuel, which South Korean port records do not show.The largest carrier, the sanctionedLayla, made two voyages from the south-eastern port of Ulsan to Vladivostok leaving on 19 July and 10 August and carrying 57,000 tonnes of diesel in total. On the first trip, it told South Korean authorities its destination was Vladivostok, but on the second it said it was bound for Niigata in Japan.Korea-Russia mapAnother sanctioned tanker, the Russian-flaggedAstoria, which is also under Australian sanctions, loaded nearly 11,000 tonnes of fuel at Ulsan on 1 August, declaring Japan as its destination, before sailing to Vladivostok.Russia and North Korea open first road bridge across their shared borderRead moreThe third sanctioned tanker, theChongchon, never berthed. It took on about 26,000 tonnes of fuel from an unsanctioned tanker, the Celeste I,at an anchorage off the southern South Korean port of Yeosu in early August, then headed to Vladivostok after declaring Singapore as its destination.The owners and managers of the four tankers did not respond to requests for comment.Russia’s capacity to refine oil has beenseverely disruptedby Ukrainian drone strikes. Its refinery throughput fell in June to its lowest level in more than 20 years, and diesel output is down nearly 30% on last year, according to the International Energy Agency.Ukraine’s military intelligence agency, the HUR, says Moscow has been forced to import fuel products to feed the “Russian war machine”.According to data from the maritime analytics firm Kpler, the buyers included Rosneft, Russia’s state-controlled oil company, which is underUK, US, EU and Australian sanctions, and NNK, a Russian oil group whose owner,Eduard Khudainatov, and one of its companies, NNK-Oil, are under UK sanctions.In August, Russia imported 368,000 tonnes of oil products by sea, more than seven times the previous month and the highest monthly total since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, according to Kpler data analysed by CREA. South Korea accounted for 112,000 tonnes, or 31%, of that amount, second only to India.Loadings at South Korean ports began to surge in July, just as the country’s president, Lee Jae Myung, pledged $100m for Ukraine’s reconstruction at aNato summitin Turkey.A 2025 trade association survey found that nearly 80% of South Korean firms that had stopped exporting to Russia since the war began were open to resuming trade.In March, as thewar with Iranshut the strait of Hormuz, South Korea capped exports of certain fuels and imported Russian naphtha under a US sanctions waiver.On 1 October, the UK temporarily exempted South Korea’s existing gas contracts from a ban on maritime services for Russian LNG that takes effect in January 2027.When contacted, South Korea’s foreign ministry did not address the shipments or the sanctioned tankers. In a statement, it said that as “a responsible member of the international community, the government supports, and is actively taking part in, international efforts to help end the war in Ukraine and bring about a peaceful recovery.”It said ithad expanded its export controlson Russia under the Foreign Trade Act “beyond strategic items to 1,402 non-strategic items with a high potential for diversion to military use” and was “strictly enforcing” them.The government “continues to monitor the implementation of its export controls on Russia and, where necessary, takes action in accordance with the relevant laws and regulations,” the ministry said.The UK Foreign Office did not answer questions about the UK-sanctioned tankers using South Korean ports, or say whether the shipments had been raised with Seoul.A spokesperson said: “The UK remains firmly committed to the effective monitoring of our sanctions and to working with international partners to increase economic pressure on Russia and reduce the revenues funding its illegal war against Ukraine.”Explore more on these topicsSouth KoreaRussiaUkraineAsia PacificOilCommoditiesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Extreme heat warnings issued for parts of southern California | California | The Guardian
description: Temperatures in US state forecast to hit high 30s this week, while parts of Indonesia grapple with wildfires
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Temperatures in US state forecast to hit high 30s this week, while parts of Indonesia grapple with wildfires
Content: A vendor walks with a cooler of waters during high temperatures at Venice Beach in Los Angeles, California.Photograph: Caroline Brehman/ReutersView image in fullscreenA vendor walks with a cooler of waters during high temperatures at Venice Beach in Los Angeles, California.Photograph: Caroline Brehman/ReutersWeather trackerCaliforniaExtreme heat warnings issued for parts of southern CaliforniaTemperatures in US state forecast to hit high 30s celsius this week, while regions in Indonesia grapple with wildfiresJames Michelin for MetDeskMon 5 Oct 2026 04.20 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 13.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe National Weather Service in the US has issued extreme heat warnings for parts of southernCalifornia, including Los Angeles, until Thursday, as temperatures are expected to hit the high 30s celsius. Burbank, a suburb north of Los Angeles, recorded 39C on Saturday, a few degrees shy of the October record for the region set in 1987. A persistent area of high pressure will remain in place this week, leading to further hazardous hot weather and increased fire risk.Parts of Indonesia are in the midst of an extreme wildfire season, which has peaked over the past month. Western Kalimantan (Borneo) and southern Sumatra have been particularly badly affected. The lack of rainfall has dried the usually water-logged tropical soils, meaning that fires have been able to spread quickly, above and below the surface. Indonesia’s soils are also extremely rich in peat, meaning that the smoke produced from the fires contain higher levels of toxic gases such as sulphur dioxide and carbon monoxide. Cities in surrounding areas and as far as Malaysia and Singapore have experiencedreduced air qualityin recent weeks as a result. Drought and wildfires are more common in this part of the world duringEl Niñoevents owing to suppressed thunderstorm activity.View image in fullscreenIndonesian firefighters work to extinguish wildfires near a residential area in Palembang, south Sumatra.Photograph: Muhammad Fajri/NurPhoto/ShutterstockOn the flip side, El Niño is contributing to an extremely active period for tropical cyclones in the Pacific Ocean. After recent hurricanes in the eastern half of the basin, Super Typhoon Choi-Wan is now active and a category 4 typhoon to the south-east ofJapan, while on a strengthening trend. After developing on 30 September, Choi-Wan moved through the Northern Mariana Islands as a tropical storm, causing power outages on the island of Tinian, forcing the closure of schools and government offices. Choi-Wan underwent rapid intensification after clearing the islands on Sunday, and as of Sunday night has sustained winds of 150mph, and gusts of up to 180mph. The system is expected to curve away from mainland Japan and areas affected by Typhoon Dujuan last month, while steadily weakening over the coming week.Explore more on these topicsCaliforniaWeather trackerExtreme heatWest CoastIndonesiaAsia PacificEl Niño southern oscillationExtreme weathernewsShareReuse this content

title: Max Chandler-Mather pitches Mamdani-style $25bn plan to nationalise 200 Coles and Woolworths supermarkets | Australian Greens | The Guardian
description: Former MP and Green Institute head says proposal for publicly owned supermarket chain will ease grocery prices
Author: Tom McIlroy
Headline: Former MP and Green Institute head says proposal for publicly owned supermarket chain will ease grocery prices
Content: Max Chandler-Mather says consumers would save up to 22% on the average shop under a Greens thinktank plan to nationalise Coles and Woolworths supermarkets.Photograph: Mick Tsikas/AAPView image in fullscreenMax Chandler-Mather says consumers would save up to 22% on the average shop under a Greens thinktank plan to nationalise Coles and Woolworths supermarkets.Photograph: Mick Tsikas/AAPAustralian GreensMax Chandler-Mather pitches Mamdani-style $25bn plan to nationalise 200 Coles and Woolworths supermarketsFormer MP and Green Institute head says proposal for publicly owned supermarket chain will ease grocery pricesGet ournew political email,free appordaily news podcastTom McIlroyPolitical editorMon 5 Oct 2026 15.55 EDTFirst published on Mon 5 Oct 2026 09.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMore than 200 Coles andWoolworthssupermarkets would be nationalised, and hundreds of government grocery stores opened, under a $25bn plan being put forward by former Greens MP Max Chandler-Mather.Channelling New York mayorZohran Mamdani’s planfor publicly owned grocery stores, Chandler-Mather, the head of the party’s thinktank, the Green Institute, wants to use new forced divestiture laws to take over major supermarket sites and three distribution centres.The Green Institute - the research arm of the party - was established to drive policy ideas, train volunteers and build its movement.The government would fund another 424 new supermarkets and 10 distribution centres, taking about 20% of the market share of commercial operators for the new non-profit network.Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter hereChandler-Mather says the new stores – dubbed Fair Go Grocers – would save consumers as much as 22% on the average shop, or $60 a week for a four-person household. Heavy discounts would be put in place for essentials including fruit and vegetables, bread, milk and meat.Groceries rise by 7% across Coles, Woolworths, IGA and Aldi, Choice findsRead moreA statutory authority would be established to set prices each month, as well as minimum wholesale rates for suppliers. Its members would include experts in supermarket operations, nutrition and food science, and farming.The federal government would pay for capital costs including land, construction, and acquisition, and stores would be located in areas of the highest need.After an initial $25.1bn price tag over five years, Chandler-Mather says the stores would be self-funded and not require additional taxpayer cash.By comparison, the federal government currently spends about $24bn each year on the Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme.“Kids are going to school hungry, families are skipping meals, people are cutting back on essentials, all because Labor has allowedColesand Woolworths to jack up prices for extra profit, regardless of the human consequences,” Chandler-Mather said.“Just like healthcare and education, food is essential to life. And just like Medicare and public schools, it’s time we had a public option for food.”The proposal is similar to Mamdani’s plan for five city-owned and subsidised grocery stores, one in each of New York City’s boroughs, opening by 2029. Last month a local business groupsued the Democratic Socialist mayor, arguing existing small grocery stores would be unable to compete.The New Zealand Greens have a plan to nationalise 120 supermarkets and establish a new publicly owned chaincalled KiwiMark.The Green Institute commissioned pollsters YouGov to test public support for the proposal last month, with background on Mamdani’s plan for government-owned stores that cut out profits made by private corporations.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toPolitics, reallyOur political team brings you up to speed on the stories that really matter and what they mean for youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion30:30Greens’ David Shoebridge on his plan to beat One Nation and replace Labor – videoVoters were asked: “Would you support or oppose publicly owned supermarkets being tried in Australia?” A total of 84% said they strongly supported or somewhat supported the idea, while 16% somewhat or strongly opposed the idea.Support was strongest among voters aged 25-34 (88%), among Greens voters (96%) and women (88%).The newly elected Greens leader,David Shoebridge, under pressure to spur enthusiasm and attention for the party, has welcomed the proposal, saying the Greens should be focused on improving the material conditions of individuals, the environment and community.“A publicly owned supermarket with cheaper food is wildly popular, because it makes people’s lives better,” he told Guardian Australia.“Of course this is the sort of policy that we should be discussing right now.”Shoebridge said Mamdani’s message about the government needing to address the needs of citizens was working.“When I talk to people, I hear about the dread they feel heading down the supermarket aisle – the shopping trolley feels like pushing a boulder up to the checkout,” he said.“While 99% of us are paying more for food, and many are making decisions about enough food or some other essentials, the 1% who own Coles and Woolies are laughing.”The competition watchdog has brought cases against both Coles and Woolworthsover false or misleading representations about in-store discounts, and a report released last year found they wereamong the most profitable grocers in the world.The Greens allege Labor’s new laws banning supermarkets from excessive pricing are ineffective and have not resulted in lower prices for consumers.Explore more on these topicsAustralian GreensSupermarketsCost-of-living crisisNationalisationDavid ShoebridgeAustralian politicsRetail
