title: Hundreds of Australians, including war veterans, are being buried in unmarked communal graves | New South Wales | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Guardian Australia investigation reveals state governments use shared graves to bury those deemed too poor to pay for funerals. ‘It’s unspeakable,’ one relative says
Author: Christopher Knaus
Headline: Exclusive: Guardian Australia investigation reveals state governments use shared graves to bury those deemed too poor to pay for funerals. ‘It’s unspeakable,’ one relative says
Content: Christine Halpin was buried in an unmarked pauper's grave in Sydney’s Rookwood cemetery in 1989.Composite: David Maurice Smith/Guardian designView image in fullscreenChristine Halpin was buried in an unmarked pauper's grave in Sydney’s Rookwood cemetery in 1989.Composite: David Maurice Smith/Guardian designUnmarked gravesNew South WalesHundreds of Australians, including war veterans, are being buried in unmarked communal gravesExclusive:Guardian Australia investigation reveals state governments use shared graves to bury those deemed too poor to pay for funerals. ‘It’s unspeakable,’ one relative saysFind more from theUnmarked graves investigationhereGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastChristopher KnausandAriel BogleMon 5 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 15.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleVietnam veterans, rough sleepers and other impoverished Australians are being buried in unmarked communal graves often holding four or more people, a practice relatives have described as “unspeakable” and “a disgrace”.A Guardian Australia investigation has identified more than 100 unmarked graves acrossNew South Wales, and some in Queensland, that are being used by state governments to bury those deemed too poor to afford their own funerals.Using evidence from family, friends and the homelessness sector, together with analysis of cemetery registries and aerial imagery, the Guardian has established that the NSW government is using bare stretches of earth between dirt walkways and old headstones at Rookwood cemetery inSydneyto bury the remains of four to six strangers together in communal graves.Among those being buried together are war veterans, cancer sufferers, people with gambling addictions and severe mental illness, and migrants from developing countries whose families cannot afford exorbitant repatriation costs.Peter and Maria were mourned by people who loved them. So how did they end up in unmarked communal graves?Read moreIn at least six cases, the Guardian has identified failures by authorities that meant friends, family or support workers were either not contacted or not told of the use of unmarked and common graves. The failures are likely breaches of a NSW policy designed to “avoid causing unnecessary distress to people who may have wished to make other funeral arrangements”.Shocked family and friends say they have been left feeling robbed.View image in fullscreenRoger Davies was buried in an unmarked communal grave at Rookwood cemetery“It’s unspeakable,” said Chantel Dubsky, whose brother Roger Davies, a rough sleeper, was buried in an unmarked grave with four strangers at Rookwood without her knowledge. “He should have had the opportunity to be laid to rest with his mother, his grandparents and the people he loved, at his home in Adelaide.“He wasn’t just someone off the street – he was someone’s son, he was someone’s brother. He was my brother.”By crosschecking names with homelessness services in Sydney, Guardian Australia has also identified a further 18 individuals in the communal graves who had experienced homelessness.The homelessness sector is outraged by the revelations.Two leaders in Sydney’s homelessness sector say they were never made aware of the practice of using unmarked communal graves and are not being given the chance to intervene on behalf of their clients to fund a proper burial.A third service, the Rev Bill Crews Foundation, an inner-city Sydney homelessness charity, says it has repeatedly raised concerns with the state government about the possible use of unmarked and communal graves but has been ignored.The Rev Bill Crews, who runs the foundation, identified three of his clients as being among those in the communal graves but said he had not been told about their deaths and impending burials.“It’s outrageous,” Crews said. “We did not know – they would all have had a dignified funeral and a proper cremation, and their ashes would have been scattered in the sea.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailThe foundation regularly uses its own funds to conduct funeral services for rough sleepers when it becomes aware they have died. It was given no notification in the three cases.“For us, it’s frustrating. Incredibly frustrating.”Guardian Australia has also established that two veterans of the Vietnam war, who both served in the Royal Australian Navy, were buried in unmarked communal graves in 2024 and 2025.The pair were buried despite the availability of a federal funding program run by the Department of Veterans’ Affairs to help pay for the funerals of impoverished veterans. NSW policy recommends state health authorities approach DVA in such cases.DVA was never asked for funding for the 2024 and 2025 burials. A spokesperson said it has “not been approached to help fund the burials of destitute persons since 2020”.Aerial imagery shows new graves appearing at Rookwood cemetery between 2025 and 2026 - NearmapThe Guardian’s investigation has prompted an apology from NSW Health, which has flagged changes to improve the process, and criticism from the health minister, Ryan Park, who described the failings as “unacceptable”.In the first half of this year alone, a 17-metre stretch of earth adjacent to a dirt pathway at Rookwood has been dug up and used to bury the remains of more than 40 people in unmarked communal graves, including a rough sleeper who was well-known to most major homelessness services.Nothing has been left to mark the 17-metre stretch of graves. Inspections of the sites of hundreds of other burials at Rookwood since 2010 show only about a dozen are marked by crosses or plaques.The vast majority have no crosses, plaques or headstones to name the groups of deceased in each plot. There are also no signs to indicate the presence of graves.Older sites, where the earth has settled, appear simply as long stretches of grass.Markings are generally not used inQueenslandfor the smaller number of people buried under its scheme. The use of communal graves is much rarer in that state.The situation contrasts sharply with the process embraced byVictoria, where each individual is given their own grave and a simple marking, identifying who is interred below.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe NSW government has previously pledged to stop the use of unmarked graves for destitute burials.View image in fullscreenThe site where Roger Davies was buried in 2015. The unmarked graves are beneath the grassed area to the right, between the walkway and the old headstones.Photograph: Christopher  Knaus/The GuardianThat came after lobbying by Barbara Davis, who was never told that her foster daughter Christine Halpin had been buried in Rookwood in 1989.Davis and Christine’s biological daughter Jayne say they weretold by the NSW government in 2013that the use of unmarked graves would cease. The cemetery erected a “path of remembrance” that allows people to pay more than $800 to put a plaque on a rock, about 1km from some of the gravesites, but this has been used in a few dozen cases since 2020.Christine’s gravesite remains unmarked. Davis and Jayne are both furious.“It is a disgrace,” Davis said. “Whether you’re a prince or a pauper, you deserve a decent burial site, even just with a wooden cross with your name on it.”In another case, a young Fijian who came to Australia to play rugby in Leeton, in NSW’s Riverina region, was buried in a communal unmarked grave after dying of cancer in 2022.After eight months, the body of Bikram Lama – Sydney’s ‘birdman’ – is finally going homeRead moreA former Leeton mayor, Paul Maytom, now president of the Leeton Multicultural Support Group, said he had previously helped raise funds from local Solomon Islander and Vietnamese communities to provide repatriation or proper burials.He was not informed about the Fijian’s death.“There should be a point of contact when this type of thing happens,” Maytom said. “And you should never have a situation where someone ends up in an unmarked grave, particularly when there are community members who are willing to help pay.”A NSW Health Pathology spokesperson apologised for the failings, acknowledging they meant the dead and families and friends were not always treated with dignity and respect.“Families and friends who have lost a loved one face many challenges managing arrangements during a time of grief, and all deceased persons should be treated with dignity and respect, regardless of their financial circumstances,” a spokesperson said.“It is clear this has not always occurred with respect to the burials or cremations for deceased people without the financial means to pay for a funeral, and NSW Health apologises for the distress this has caused to those who have lost someone they love.”NSW Health said it had made changes to the process in 2025 and in recent months to improve the way the funerals were handled. That includes giving NSW Health greater control, in place of police, and creating a dedicated six-person team within NSW Health Pathology to provide “alternative funeral arrangements and alternate sources of support for families and friends that may be willing to assist”.It also flagged improving its relationships with “religious, cultural, charitable, community, and government organisations” to find funding for funerals after deaths.Two NSW ministers, Park and the homelessness minister, Rose Jackson, said the dead and their families should be treated with respect, regardless of their financial circumstances.“Previous arrangements have meant that this has not always been the case, and that is unacceptable,” Park said.“Since early 2025, NSW Health has made significant changes to establish a more comprehensive and person-centred approach to ensure all deceased persons are treated with the respect and compassion they deserve.”A spokesperson for Metropolitan Memorial Parks, which operates Rookwood general cemetery, said the NSW government did not fund it to provide grave markings for persons without means.MMP said destitute burials were not the only burial type that used multiple interments in a single plot, and rejected any suggestion that those buried through the process were being placed between individual headstones, under walkways or in trenches.It also said it had identified no legislation or regulation that had given effect to the government’s 2013 promise to mark graves.Explore more on these topicsNew South WalesUnmarked gravesQueenslandVictoriaHomelessnessPovertySocial exclusionSydneynewsShareReuse this content

title: Green party of England and Wales facing international ostracism over ‘Zionism is racism’ vote | Green party | The Guardian
description: European Green party says motion goes against its policy, with German Green co-leader calling it ‘intolerable and unacceptable’
Author: Aletha Adu
Headline: European Green party says motion goes against its policy, with German Green co-leader calling it ‘intolerable and unacceptable’
Content: Zack Polanski speaking at the Green party conference in Brighton.Photograph: Phil Lewis/SOPA Images/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenZack Polanski speaking at the Green party conference in Brighton.Photograph: Phil Lewis/SOPA Images/ShutterstockGreen partyGreen party of England and Wales facing international ostracism over ‘Zionism is racism’ voteEuropean Green party says motion goes against its policy, with German Green co-leader calling it ‘intolerable and unacceptable’Zack Polanski may rue lack of leadership when Greens needed him to actAletha Adu,Peter WalkerandDeborah ColeMon 5 Oct 2026 15.10 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe English and Welsh Greens are facing international ostracism after adopting a policy declaring Zionism as a form of racism, which has drawn dismay from the group representing European Greens.Head of Jewish Greens says she may leave party over ‘Zionism is racism’ voteRead moreThe co-leader of the German Greens separately said the policy was “intolerable and unacceptable”, running contrary to its belief in the right ofIsraelto exist.The binding policy motionpassed in a vote at the Greens’ conferencein Brighton on Sunday. Four of the party’s five MPs opposed it.The policy saysZionism, the movement for a Jewish state, should be “treated as any other form of racism”, and backs a single democratic Palestinian state across historic Palestine “with equal rights for all”.The EuropeanGreen party, which represents 47 parties, including the Green party of England and Wales (GPEW), said it supported a two-state solution for Israel and Palestine, and the new motion went against this.The alliance “will immediately demand clarity from the leadership and parliamentary group of GPEW, to understand the official party policy of GPEW, how they position themselves towards the self-determination of Israelis and Jews as well as the protection of Jewish people and members in the party”, it said in a statement.View image in fullscreenFelix Banaszak, the co-leader of the German Greens, said the policy ‘runs counter to what the European Green party stands for’.Photograph: snapshot/Future Image/M Behrens/ShutterstockFelix Banaszak, the leader of the German Greens, known formally as Alliance 90/the Greens, told a press conference the motion was “intolerable and unacceptable”.“It runs counter to everything that Alliance 90/the Greens stands for inGermany, and it also runs counter to what the European Green party stands for,” he added.Banaszak said: “There is a widely held view within the European Green party that Israel has a right to exist and that this right must not be undermined.” His party would “approach our partner parties in Europe to clarify how to deal with this”.Sandy Ruthven, the chair of Amnesty International UK’s charitable trust and a longstanding Green member, resigned over the motion and accused the party of failing to confront antisemitism.The fallout from Sunday’s vote has also intensified a debate over whether the Greens’ highly decentralised policymaking structures remain suitable for a party whose membership has expanded rapidly.View image in fullscreenEllie Chowns, who opposed the motion, said the party’s policymaking ‘urgently needs to be modernised’.Photograph: Ellie & Adrian 2025/PAPolicy is made at the party’s two annual conferences, which generally involve a small proportion of members. The Zionism motion won just over 1,000 votes, approximately 0.4% of the total membership.Ellie Chowns, a former co-leader, said the party’s governance and policymaking “urgently need to be modernised”.“As a party we pride ourselves on our democratic member-led policymaking process, but I do think we need to ask ourselves some searching questions when less than 1% of our members actually participate,” Chowns, the Green MP for North Herefordshire, told the Guardian. “This is long overdue and has become even more urgent with the huge expansion of our membership.”Chowns said she understood the concerns of European Greens, which she shared, but stressed: “There is still much more that unites us than divides us.”One source in the party said the criticism from European Greens, especially those in Germany, was understandable given their differing stances on Gaza and Israel.They said: “The German Greens support arming Israel, opposed a ceasefire to Israel’s onslaught on Gaza, backed the suspension of funding to Unrwa and co-sponsored a Bundestag resolution describing the arguments and methods of the peaceful, Palestinian-led BDS campaign as antisemitic.”Any change to internal party structures would be hard to implement. One Green insider said that to give MPs greater authority over members would undermine the party’s commitment to grassroots democracy. However, they said the existing model could produce a lack of coherence and strategic direction, while giving a disproportionate influence to members with the most time to participate in policymaking.They suggested members could determine broad strategic priorities, with smaller bodies developing detailed policy while remaining accountable to the membership.View image in fullscreenThe Green party leader, Zack Polanski,who missed the vote himself, earlier addressed the conference alongside the MPs Hannah Spencer, left, and Siân Berry, right. Berry opposed the motion.Photograph: Sean Smith/The GuardianAnother senior Green defended the party’s model of direct democracy, arguing that allowing members to determine policy was fundamental to the party’s character.What is Zionism and why do some critics describe it as racist?Read moreDaniel Schuster, the regional director of the Simon Wiesenthal Center’s European office, said: “The British Green party’s decision to formally classify Zionism as a form of racism is absurd, not based on any logical basis and is itself racist. And timing, just days before the third anniversary of the 7 October terrorist Hamas attacks, is designed to inflict pain on a deeply solemn occasion.“Branding Zionism itself as racism crosses a profoundly consequential line. It takes a movement for Jewish national self-determination and transforms it into something for which Jews are expected to apologise. We will not.”In a statement, the Green party leader in England and Wales, Zack Polanski, said: “Antisemitism and criticism of the Israeli state are, and must always be, completely distinct – blurring the line between the two is not only wrong but antisemitic, and makes Jewish people less safe. It’s our role as a movement for justice to protect both the rights of Palestinians and our Jewish communities here in the UK. As leader I will not accept any exclusion, or refusal to engage with anyone, because of the religious or communal body they are part of.”He added: “Through the Green party’s unified stance and dedicated pressure, we have begun to shift this government away from its complicity with the Israeli government’s atrocities in Gaza, with the foreign secretary now taking the long overdue step of ending trade with illegal settlements.”Explore more on these topicsGreen partyRaceAntisemitismGermanyEuropeIsraelJudaismnewsShareReuse this content

title: Norway plans temporary ban on smart glasses in some public places | Norway | The Guardian
description: Camera-enabled Meta spectacles are already restricted in UK and US because of fears about unauthorised covert recording
Author: Robert Booth
Headline: Camera-enabled Meta spectacles are already restricted in UK and US because of fears about unauthorised covert recording
Content: Meta’s chief executive, Mark Zuckerberg, presents the company’s new line of smart glasses at Meta headquarters in California last month.Photograph: Carlos Barría/ReutersView image in fullscreenMeta’s chief executive, Mark Zuckerberg, presents the company’s new line of smart glasses at Meta headquarters in California last month.Photograph: Carlos Barría/ReutersNorwayNorway plans temporary ban on smart glasses in some public placesCamera-enabled Meta spectacles are already restricted in UK and US because of fears about covert recordingRobert BoothUK technology editorMon 5 Oct 2026 12.11 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNorway is planning a temporary ban on smart glasses in some public places, amid rising global concern at the spread of the AI-enabled recording devices.The Oslo government is planning a bill to prevent the use of the camera-enabled spectacles in parks, beaches, museums, shopping centres, schools, daycare centres, healthcare facilities, gyms and public events, although private use would still be allowed.There is already a growing patchwork of restrictions on the use of the glasses including in UK and US courtrooms and in pubs, cinemas and restaurants where owners have raised privacy fears.Torgeir Micaelsen, Norway’s minister of digital affairs, said he was “worried that ‌new, powerful technology is being introduced where people risk being ‌photographed, filmed or audio-recorded without knowing it”.“We do not want a society where people worry about being recorded without their knowledge, photographed or filmed in places and situations where they are accustomed to not being monitored,” he said.Norway’s Labour party, which heads a minority government, needs the support of other parties to pass the proposed ban. It said it planned to submit a bill “as soon as possible”, while tasking an expert group with drawing up permanent regulations on the issue.8:34Could Meta’s ‘pervert glasses’ be banned across the UK? - The LatestMark Zuckerberg’s Meta sells “smart” versions of Ray-Ban and Oakley glasses that allow users to film, take photos, make phone calls, play music and execute AI prompts. It hassoldat least 9m pairs of the Ray-Ban versions since the start of 2023.In the UK restaurateurs such as Jeremy King, who created the Wolseley and Delaunay restaurants, and pub chain Wetherspoons have already said they do not want customers using the devices. Cinemas said in August they had begun introducingpolicies to ban or restrict the use of smart glassesciting both privacy and film piracy concerns.Last week the governor of California, Gavin Newsom, vetoed legislation that would have penalised citizens for using smart glasses to record people without their permission in changing rooms, doctors’ offices and other spaces people generally consider private. The state already has laws governing unlawful recording.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAlbanese government considers ‘world-leading’ ban on smart glasses in public offices and buildingsRead moreIn France, the child welfare group E-enfancesaidit had this year received about 20 reports of women being filmed without their knowledge using glasses fitted with a camera, the majority of which involved Meta smart glasses. It said the incidents often followed the same pattern: a young girl or woman approached in a public place, filmed without her knowledge, with the clip then posted on social media in the form of a prank or a street interview.Meta has stressed that each pair of glasses is fitted with a tamper-proof LED light that blinks white when the user is recording or taking pictures. It advises users: “Not everyone loves being photographed. Stop recording if anyone expresses that they would rather you not.”A Meta spokesperson said: “We’re excited that our glasses continue to be very popular for listening to music, making calls, or getting live translations, so we’re continuing to expand styles and features around the world. Every pair with a camera has a bright light on the front that blinks when you take a photo or video. It can’t be turned off and the camera is disabled if someone covers or tampers with it -- something smartphones and other camera’s don’t have.”Explore more on these topicsNorwayWearable technologyMetaPrivacyEuropePrivacy & the mediaGadgetsnewsShareReuse this content

title: France braces for national day of school protests as boy loses hand | France | The Guardian
description: Thousands expected to join marches of support on Tuesday across the country as concerns grow over police response
Author: Angelique Chrisafis
Headline: Thousands expected to join marches of support on Tuesday across the country as concerns grow over police response
Content: Police officers face a protesting student from the Gustave Eiffel secondary school in Bordeaux on Monday.Photograph: Ugo Amez/SIPA/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenPolice officers face a protesting student from the Gustave Eiffel secondary school in Bordeaux on Monday.Photograph: Ugo Amez/SIPA/ShutterstockFranceFrance braces for national day of school protests as boy loses handThousands expected to join marches of support on Tuesday across the country amid growing concerns over police responseAngelique Chrisafisin ParisMon 5 Oct 2026 11.50 EDTFirst published on Mon 5 Oct 2026 08.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFrance is bracing for a national day of protests and high-school blockades as a youth protest movement gathers pace amid a growing debate over the scale of the police response.In one incident, a 15-year-old protesting against what demonstrators said were France’s dilapidated ⁠and understaffed ​schools ‌had his hand ‌blown off outside a high schoolin the northern town of Lens, said François-Xavier Lauch, the prefect of Pas-de-Calais.Lauch declined to comment on the exact circumstances, but said between 150 and 200 protesters had been hurling a series of objects at police when riot officers intervened. It was uncertain if the incident had involved a police stun grenade or how the injury happened. Lauch said ​an investigation had ​been opened.The family of a 16-year-old school pupil in Tours also filed a complaint about police violence after he lost sight in his right eye last week.The state prosecutor said the boy’s injuries were in line with the impact from a police rubber bullet. A police investigation is under way.The French prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, had earlier attempted to calm the protests by accepting schoolchildren’s grievances as “legitimate” and saying the government must listen.View image in fullscreenClashes between student protesters and police in the 12th arrondissement of Paris on Monday.Photograph: Raphaël Lafargue/ABACA/ShutterstockLecornu ordered ministers to tackle the students’ five major demands. These include organising the replacement of absent teachers, in recognition that pupils in some areas miss months of teaching because of staff absences – even in key exam years. Lecornu also called for a review of France’s lengthy school days, which are among the longest inEurope.The government will also look at repairs to dilapidated school buildings. Children on blockades across France have described water leaking into classrooms during class, cockroaches, collapsing ceilings andunbearable heat in summer. Lecornu said ministers must come up with proposals by the end of the month.Sophie Binet, the head of the leftwing CGT trade union, said the government had been late in offering to tackle the schoolchildren’s demands. She said the number of absent teachers who were not replaced had doubled in 10 years and class sizes were at a record high.“Amid such anger, a few measures just for show aren’t going to satisfy demands,” Binet said. She called for the government to instead stop all budget cuts as well as cuts to teachers’ positions.Student unions have called for a national day of protest on Tuesday with more schools expected to be barricaded. Thousands of trade unionists, teachers, public sector workers and parents’ groups are expected to join marches of support in cities and towns across France.View image in fullscreenProtesting students blockade the Turgot secondary school in Paris.Photograph: Raphaël Lafargue/ABACA/ShutterstockBinet said trade unionists would march to ensure there was no violence on the edge of any protests on Tuesday, as she criticised heavy policing. “We’ve been appalled by what we have seen over the past 10 days and by the unprecedented crackdown that the government has organised against the protests by high school students,” she said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionUniversity students continued to support the school protests on Monday, with up to 40 university buildings blockaded across France. Philippe Baptiste, the minister for higher education, told French radio he felt student and high school protests could intensify with the national protests due to take place on Tuesday.Between 400 and 500 high schools are expected to remain completely or partly closed on ⁠Monday out of a total of 3,700, the minister said.A government spokesperson, Maud Bregeon, told CNews television on Monday: “Our priority is to restore order.”The protests began in late September ‌at a high school ‌in a Paris suburb over teacher shortages. The government was taken by surprise as protests then spread nationwide, amid anger at social inequality and a lack of investment in the education system.Since last Monday, about 5,000 people, mostly ‌teenagers, have been arrested across France and dozens injured.Teachers have also been injured. Damage to property is estimated in the tens ​of millions of euros.Explore more on these topicsFranceEuropeProtestYoung peoplenewsShareReuse this content

title: US closely monitoring case of lab worker who ‘possibly’ died of plague in Siberia, says Rubio | Russia | The Guardian
description: Quarantine measures in place in several hospitals in eastern Russia amid uncertainty over death of Darya Shipilova
Author: Pjotr Sauer
Headline: Quarantine measures in place in several hospitals in eastern Russia amid uncertainty over death of Darya Shipilova
Content: Darya Shipilova, who worked at a plague research institute in Siberia, died on the night of 2 October at a regional hospital in Shelekhov, Russia.Photograph: Social MediaView image in fullscreenDarya Shipilova, who worked at a plague research institute in Siberia, died on the night of 2 October at a regional hospital in Shelekhov, Russia.Photograph: Social MediaRussiaUS closely monitoring case of lab worker who ‘possibly’ died of plague in Siberia, says RubioQuarantine measures in place in several hospitals in eastern Russia amid uncertainty over death of Darya ShipilovaPjotr SauerandLuke HardingMon 5 Oct 2026 11.36 EDTFirst published on Mon 5 Oct 2026 06.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, has said the US is closely monitoring the case of a Russian laboratory worker who died last week after a reported accident at a plague research institute in Siberia.“We’re watching and monitoring it closely,” Rubio said on Monday before leaving for a trip toEurope. “I ⁠don’t think it’s cause for alarm, but it is cause for focus and a cause just to keep an ⁠eye on it.”Darya Shipilova, a 28-year-old employee at the anti-plague institute in the city of Irkutsk, became ill at work. She died two days later on the night of 2 October at a regional hospital in the nearby town of Shelekhov.It remains unclear how she became unwell. Unconfirmed reports in Russian media have suggested Shipilova may have been infected after a mishap at the laboratory. Officials have not publicly confirmed that account.Local media have reported that the institute has subsequently been locked down, with staff forced to sleep on the floor and on chairs. “They’ve been isolating everybody since Friday – more than 60 people,” one relative, Roman,told the news portal Siberia.Realities.He said family members were allowed to drop off food at a checkpoint while tests were carried out inside the building. Similar quarantine restrictions have been placed on several other hospitals in and around the city.Rubio, citing what ‌Russians have released about the death, said it seemed a worker in the lab became ​infected and there was concern the disease may have spread internally.“There’s very limited travel between the US and Russia, obviously,” he said. “But like anything else, something like that gets out, it just quickly spreads.”Senior Russian officials have added to public disquiet by sending conflicting messages. Alexey Tsydenov, the head of the Buryatia region, which neighbours Irkutsk, initially wrote that Shipilova had died of plague, before editing his post to say she had “possibly” died of the disease.Rospotrebnadzor, Russia’s health watchdog, said Shipilovadied from “pneumonia of unknown aetiology”. It insisted that tests found no micro-organisms linked to her professional work anddescribedthe “sanitary and epidemiological” situation in the area as stable.Authorities in the nearby city of Baikalsk briefly urged residents to avoid travelling to Shelekhov and surrounding settlements after what they said was unofficial information about a possible plague infection. They later deleted the post from social media.“There are no obvious changes to daily life on the streets, but people are worried and anxious. Locals are angry that they are not being told anything,” said Elena Trifonova, a journalist withPeople of Baikal, an exiled Russian media outlet specialising in Siberia.Despite the lack of a confirmed diagnosis, precautionary measures appear to have been introduced across the region. The US-funded Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty reported on Monday that several hospitals in Irkutsk had been placed under quarantine.The outlet confirmed that staff from Shipilova’s workplace, the Irkutsk Anti-plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East, had been kept inside the institute since 2 October.Patients at Irkutsk city clinical hospital No 1 and the Ivano-Matreninskaya children’s hospital said relatives were not being allowed to visit and people inside were not permitted to leave.On social media, local residents described some of the precautions being introduced.Ulyana Gavryunina, who went on Monday to one of Irkutsk’s main maternity hospitals for a routine check-up on Monday, said doctors refused to allow her mother in, citing a quarantine imposed over the suspected plague case. Gavryunina said staff member checked her for flu-like symptoms and asked her to fill out a screening form for infections, on which “plague” was listed. She posted a photograph of theformon Instagram.Elsewhere, a mask requirement was introduced at the Irkutsk aluminium smelter in Shelekhov. The plant’s director, Artyom Fominykh,called it a preventive measure, saying: “Better safe than sorry.” Over the weekend several public events in Irkutsk were cancelled.Shipolova’s death has prompted intervention from senior federal health officials. Anna Popova, the head of Rospotrebnadzor and the country’s chief sanitary doctor, travelled to Irkutsk on Friday.She attended an emergency meeting of the regional sanitary and anti-epidemic commission over what officials called a suspected case of a “particularly dangerous infection”.Igor Kobzev, the governor of the Irkutsk region, urged residents to remain calm after meeting Popova to coordinate the response. “All identified contacts have been placed under medical observation. As of today, none is showing signs of illness and laboratory tests have returned negative results,” he wrote on Telegram.Kobzev made no reference to reports that a laboratory worker had died.US politicians have raised concerns about the incident, which follows longstanding and unfounded allegations by the Kremlin that Ukraine has secretly carried out biological weapons research with the support of Washington.A Republican representative, Don Bacon, a senior member of the House armed services committee, wrote on social media: “I remember hearing from anti-Ukraine voices about their so-called bio labs. It was Russian disinformation ops at their best. But in reality it is Russia with the bio labs.”Plague remains endemic in parts of Siberia and the Russian far east, where the bacterium persists naturally among wild rodents and their fleas.But human cases in Russia are rare. Before the suspected Irkutsk case, the country’s last recorded human infection was in 2016, when a 10-year-old boy in Siberia’s Altai Republic contracted plague after helping butcher a marmot.“This case here seems like a rare lab accident and is unlikely to go much further,” Prof Ian Jones, a professor of virology at the University of Reading, in the UK, said. “Although it is true that pneumonic plague is directly transmissible, the contacts of the primary case are known and can be treated if they show any sign of infection.”He added: “Plague carries a huge history and is still present in many parts of the world, including Russia, but the living conditions associated with previously spread plague are no longer generally true, antibiotics are available and its potential is therefore limited.”Explore more on these topicsRussiaEuropeBubonic plaguenewsShareReuse this content

title: Saudi-backed forces recapture key areas around strait from Houthis in Yemen | Yemen | The Guardian
description: Government offensive launched under air cover by Saudi military coalition aims to retake all Houthi-held territory
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Government offensive launched under air cover by Saudi military coalition aims to retake all Houthi-held territory
Content: A commercial vessel is anchored off Yemen's coast at Bab al-Mandab on 12 September 2026.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA commercial vessel is anchored off Yemen's coast at Bab al-Mandab on 12 September 2026.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesYemenSaudi-backed forces recapture key areas around strait from Houthis in YemenGovernment offensive launched under air cover by Saudi military coalition aims to retake all Houthi-held territoryGuardian staff and agenciesMon 5 Oct 2026 15.44 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 16.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleForces of the Saudi-led coalition fighting inYemenhave recaptured several key areas around Bab al-Mandab strait from Iran-backed Houthi rebels, Yemeni officials said on Monday.Yemen’s Saudi-backed government launches military drive to retake all Houthi-held territoryRead moreThe officials said forces allied with the internationally recognized government have retaken the crucial town of Dhubab just north of the strait. They also captured the towns of Bab and Hadeid, said the officials, who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak to reporters. Witnesses said they saw government tanks and forces entering the towns.The government push came as part of a major offensive launched early Monday under an air cover by a Saudi military coalition, aiming to retake all territory held by theHouthis.However, the offensive came just after the rebels said they had captured more territory in the south-western part of Yemen, taking the key town of Turbah in a blow to the Saudi-backed forces as they advanced toward the strategic provincial capital of Taiz, Yemen’s third-largest city.The Saudi-led coalition spokesperson, Maj Gen Turki al-Malki, said 100 fighter jets were providing support to the forces of Yemen’s internationally recognized government fighting against the Houthis. He said the coalition had secured “air protection” of the strategic Bab al-Mandab strait and destroyed hundreds of Houthi targets as part of the ongoing campaign.Marco Rubio told reporters that it was expected that the Saudi-backed government in Yemen would hit back at the rebels to reclaim territory. Asked if the Saudi-led coalition coordinated the action with the United States, the US secretary of state said thatSaudi Arabiaand the US had a defense agreement but would not offer more details.He said the Yemeni government was ousted from some of its territory by a Houthi campaign and the Saudis had come under attack, and “they have a right to defend themselves”.The new push sets an ambitious goal for the embattled government, which recently lost swathes of the country’s Red Sea coastline and areas around the Bab al-Mandab strait – a chokepoint for international shipping – after alightning offensiveby the Iran-backed Houthis.Yemen’s internationally recognised government has struggled to roll back the surge, even with the military support of Saudi Arabia. The Houthis have increasingly targeted Saudi Arabia in recent weeks, and on Sunday said they had attacked oil infrastructure in the capital again.Saudi Arabia urged to reconcile with UAE to drive back Houthi separatists in YemenRead moreThe statement came just hours after the Houthis cut a vital supply route linking thebesieged city of Taizwith the government’s interim capital, Aden, according to four security sources.The Houthi advance followed days of heavy fighting in and around the city.“We were informed that the Houthis had taken control of the al-Safiya area, where they cut the main road and took control of the police station,” a police source in the area said.Three sources with the Yemeni military also confirmed Houthi control over the area and the supply route, with traffic along the road halted and the group now surrounding Taiz city. Fighting in the area was ongoing, they added.Sources from both sides told AFP on Sunday that fighting in and around the western province of Taiz had killed more than 70 people over the past day.Sources from the internationally recognised government reported that 34 government troops were killed – 20 on the edge of Taiz province in neighbouring Lahj – while Houthi military sources said 39 of their fighters were killed in fighting across Taiz and in border areas with Lahj.Children forced to give up school for work as fighting upends daily life in YemenRead moreTaiz city itself remains under the control of government forces but has long been besieged from the north, east and west by Houthi fighters and remains one of the main fronts in Yemen’s long-running civil war.A Houthi military spokesperson, Yahya Saree, said on Sunday the group launched ballistic missiles and drones at the Saudi energy company Aramco’s sites in Riyadh and in the Khurais area in the east, causing large fires.The attacks were in response to what the Houthis claimed were 50 Saudi-led ‌air and missile strikes in Yemen in the past 12 hours.There was no immediate confirmation from Saudi Arabia.Saudi oil exportswere already under pressure due to Iran’s blockade of the strait of Hormuz in the Gulf.The Houthi’s Al-Masirah TV channel reported Saudi strikes on Sunday in the northern governorates of al-Jawf and Saada, saying at least two people had been wounded.With Reuters and Agence France-PresseExplore more on these topicsYemenHouthisMiddle East and north AfricaSaudi ArabianewsShareReuse this content

title: Flydubai co-pilot originally planned attack for July, investigators believe | Flydubai plane incident | The Guardian
description: Police and security agencies in multiple countries scramble to piece together background and intentions of Hamam al-Hammami
Author: Jason Burke
Headline: Police and security agencies in multiple countries scramble to piece together background and intentions of Hamam al-Hammami
Content: Israeli media have reported that the flydubai co-pilot Hamam al-Hammami planned to crash into Ben Gurion airport, near Tel Aviv.Photograph: Ammar Awad/ReutersView image in fullscreenIsraeli media have reported that the flydubai co-pilot Hamam al-Hammami planned to crash into Ben Gurion airport, near Tel Aviv.Photograph: Ammar Awad/ReutersFlydubai plane incidentFlydubai co-pilot originally planned attack for July, investigators believePolice and security agencies in multiple countries scramble to piece together background and intentions of Hamam al-HammamiJason Burkein London andStephanie Kirchgaessnerin WashingtonMon 5 Oct 2026 14.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 14.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleInvestigators believe the co-pilot who tried to take control of a plane from Dubai to Tel Aviv last week originally planned his attack for July but postponed the hijacking, possibly because a friend was among the crew, regional and Israeli officials have said.The evidence of prior planning suggests that Hamam al-Hammami, 29, may have specifically sought employment with an airline that flew to Israel in order to carry out the attack on last Wednesday’s flydubai ‌flight FZ1073, experts believe.Police and security agencies in at least six countriesare scrambling to piece togetherthe background of Hammami, an Omani national, and his intentions, as well as to establish if he acted entirely alone.Hammami allegedlyused an emergency crash axekept in the cockpit to launch a surprise attack on the pilot approximately two hours and 20 minutes after takeoff. The plane was carrying more than 180 passengers – almost all Israeli – and crew on a routine flight.3:28How the stabbing incident unfolded on Israel-bound flydubai plane | DeconstructedIsraeli media havequoted from Hammami’s statements to interrogators since being transferred to United Arab Emirates custody on Thursday to report that he planned to crash into Ben Gurion airport near ⁠Tel Aviv, or possibly another high-profile target nearby.The flight’s captain, Smit Machchhar, said on Saturday that shortly after Hammami had left his seat to pray, he felt a “big blow” to the back of his head.In a phone call with Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, on Saturday, Machchhar said: “The blows kept coming … That’s when I realised that it’s not the aircraft, it’s the other guy who was in the cockpit with me.”Despite his injuries Machchhar was able to unlock the cockpit’s security door to allow passengers to overpower Hammami. A reserve flydubai pilot travelling on the flight took control of the aircraft and landed it at a regional airport in north-westernSaudi Arabia, where the co-pilot was detained by Saudi authorities.View image in fullscreenCapt Smit Machchhar was visited on Sunday in hospital in the UAE by Hamdan bin Mohammed Al Maktoum, the crown prince of Dubai.Photograph: Hamdan bin Mohammed/X/ReutersThe investigation into Hammami has now spread to more than eight countries. Authorities in New Zealand and Australia are examining reports thatthe co-pilot studied in bothnations about 10 years ago.Hammami, who has an Omani father and a Syrian mother, is thought to have been employed by Oman Air from 2018 to June 2025, butleft the airlineafter being moved to a desk job out of concerns that he had developed extremist views. He was then hired by Royal Air Maroc, the Moroccan national flag carrier, but did not obtain permission to fly and gave up his job there.Shortly afterward, Hammami was hired at the state-owned flydubai, which has needed pilots as it expands rapidly. The airline conducted checks for a criminal record but not for evidence of radicalisation, officials have said.A key question for investigators is when Hammami began to formulate his plan to attack a plane full of Israelis or target Israel.Netanyahu has claimedHammami had undergone “radical Islamist indoctrination” and was clearly suicidal, without giving details.View image in fullscreenFlyDubai conducted checks on Hammami for a criminal record but not for evidence of radicalisation, officials have said.Photograph: Fadel Senna/AFP/Getty ImagesNine hours after the attack, a post was made to an online social media account in Hammami’s name praising Ayman al-Zawahiri, a former al-Qaida leader, as well as a militant responsible for a lethal suicide attack on US troops in Afghanistan in 2009. A second post contained religious imagery.An analysis of Hammami’s X account by a company that uses AI to measure the toxicity of individuals’ social media accounts found dozens of misogynistic posts, including public threats against women. The analysis by Accountability! – which recovered Hammami’s deleted account by scraping internet archives, and reviewed almost 3,000 posts and responses – found repeated use of slurs against women, and a “consistent pattern” of use of terms meaning “whores”, and “filthy feminist”. The researchers also found homophobic slurs directed at men.“Beyond offensive language, the analysis surfaced explicit conditional threats of physical violence … including repeated imagery of stomping on a woman’s head and making her ‘a lesson for others’,” the analysis found.“Online toxicity isn’t just corrosive, it’s a warning sign. This pilot was telling the world who he was in his posts. Had anyone in charge been listening, nearly 200 people might never have been put in danger,” said Gur Megiddo, a co-founder and chief executive of Accountability!.Regional officials said Emirati authorities had shared information about the passengers and crew, including their nationalities, with Israel.The Shin Bet, Israel’s domestic security agency, said the transportation ministry was responsible for vetting passenger lists from foreign flights but the transportation minister, Miri Regev, said on X that the security agencies handled flight security.Israeli newspapers reported that a key database of foreign pilots had not been checked despite concerns raised by official reports.The attack occurred at a sensitive time for Israel, a week before the anniversary of the Hamas-led attack on 7 October 2023 which triggered the war in Gaza, and weeks before a fiercely contested general election in which security – and responsibility for failures to keep Israelis safe – has been a central issue.Opposition politicians have seized on the apparent lapses to attack Netanyahu, who has boasted of his ability to keep Israelis safe.“This is exactly what system collapse looks like,” Yair Golan, the head of the opposition Democrats party, wrote on X. “A transportation minister who completely abandons our skies, and a prime minister who abandons national security.”Explore more on these topicsFlydubai plane incidentAir transportMiddle East and north AfricaIsraelDubaiSaudi ArabiaUnited Arab EmiratesnewsShareReuse this content

title: UK threatens to expel Israeli diplomats over planned East Jerusalem consulate closure | Israel | The Guardian
description: Tit-for-tat expulsions expected after relations deteriorate as a result of UK ban on goods from illegal settlements
Author: Patrick Wintour
Headline: Tit-for-tat expulsions expected after relations deteriorate as a result of UK ban on goods from illegal settlements
Content: Israel is expected to close British consulate in East Jerusalem this week.Photograph: Ahmad Gharabli/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenIsrael is expected to close British consulate in East Jerusalem this week.Photograph: Ahmad Gharabli/AFP/Getty ImagesIsraelUK threatens to expel Israeli diplomats over planned East Jerusalem consulate closureTit-for-tat expulsions expected after relations deteriorate as a result of UK ban on goods from illegal settlementsPatrick WintourDiplomatic editorMon 5 Oct 2026 13.53 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe UK has threatened to expel one Israeli diplomat for every British diplomat forced to leave Israel as a result of Israel’s decision toclose the UK consulatein East Jerusalem later this week.This could mean as many as 27 Israeli diplomats being expelled from the UK, a step that would arguably mark the lowest point in British-Israeli diplomatic relations since the formation of the state ofIsrael.The mass expulsion threat – more reminiscent of British-Russian diplomatic relations – was first reported by the Israeli newspaper Ynet, citing a message sent to Israeli officials. The UK Foreign Office said it would not comment on speculation, rather than denying the report outright.Israel has threatened to close the UK consulate in East Jerusalem in protest at the UK decision toban trade in goods from illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bankand to impose sanctions on British firms that aid, support or facilitate the construction of further illegal settlements.Israeli forces overwhelmed by violent settlers in ‘terrorist attack’ on Palestinian familyRead moreThe Foreign Office has been advised informally by the former UK attorney general Dominic Grieve that Israel is acting unlawfully if it closes the consulate on the basis it is sited in East Jerusalem, which is recognised by the United Nations and most of its members, including the UK, as being occupied Palestinian territory.Israel’s foreign minister, Gideon Sa’ar, has said that Britain’s ‌decision to impose sanctions was “morally distorted” and accused Britain’s ruling Labour party of being hostile towards the country.The consulate, which Israel’s foreign ministry has said will close on Thursday, is separate from the UK embassy based in Tel Aviv and has a distinct diplomatic role, covering East Jerusalem, the rest of theWest Bankand Gaza. It is located in the Sheikh Jarrah neighbourhood of East ​Jerusalem.An Israeli diplomatic source said: “There is no reason for us to respond to speculation about decisions that other countries may or may not take in the future.“We have already demonstrated that any step taken against Israel will be met with an appropriate response, and that will continue to be the case.”The UK national security adviser, Jonathan Powell, travelled to Jerusalem last week in an effort to persuade the Israeli government to rescind or defer the closure of the consulate but the talks failed.It has been reported that Powell opposed the decision of theUK foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, to press ahead with the settlement trade ban decision, fearing that it might play to the advantage of the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, in the national election on 27 October as he seeks to bolster his case that only his brand of leadership can bring Israel security. There is no evidence yet that the UK decision has featured in the campaign, but tit-for-tat expulsions of diplomats may raise its profile.The ‌incident highlighted growing frustration among Israel’s longtime allies over its settlements in the occupied West Bank, viewed by much of the world as illegal under international law. In his statement to the UK parliament, Miliband said settler terrorists, supported by Netanyahu’s government, arecommitting ethnic cleansingin the West Bank. Israel disputes this.Diplomats from other western countries have been very worried about the closure setting a precedent, and suggest that Britain had to respond strongly to the Israeli move because it has implications beyond the immediate dispute.Shutting down the consulate involves Israel claiming authority in Jerusalem that it does not have under international law, so it is effectively a challenge to the status quo.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“We are all concerned because if this (closure of the consulate) goes ahead it would be an incredibly damaging precedent for the status of missions in Jerusalem, which are monitoring the status quo,” said one western diplomat, speaking on condition of anonymity.“It would be inconceivable for the British government to accept (the closure) because they don’t recognise the authority of the Israeli government over Jerusalem under international law. Particularly as Israel is taking this step over British measures which are simply applying international law.”Israel has also said it is to revoke the credentials of Dutch diplomats from the country’s mission toPalestine, in response to the Netherlands’ ban on imports from illegal Israeli settlements. Israel’s military occupation of the West Bank, East Jerusalem and Gaza means diplomats need Israeli accreditation to operate in Palestine. The decision also in effect bars them from Israel-controlled East Jerusalem.France and Canada, which also joined the UK in the settlement trade ban, have not had action taken against them.Miliband received a very warm reception at the UK Labour party conference last week during a speech in which he highlighted his decision to get tough with Israel over illegal settlements.UK-Israeli relations have deteriorated steadily during the war in Gaza begun by Hamas’s 7 October 2023 massacre of Israelis as the UK became increasingly critical of the way in which Netanyahu seemed prepared to tolerate the death of thousands of Palestinians in a bid to render Hamas inoperative, a task both the Conservative and Labour governments thought was unachievable through his methods.The UK has rescinded a large number of arms export licences to Israel as a result and Miliband has spoken of evidence of war crimes in Gaza. He has declined to accuse Israel of genocide on the grounds that he believes this is a matter for international courts alone to determine.Explore more on these topicsIsraelWest BankForeign policyBenjamin NetanyahuMiddle East and north AfricaEd MilibandnewsShareReuse this content
