title: Air campaign against Houthis under way in Yemen, says Saudi-led coalition | Yemen | The Guardian
description: Operation supported by 100 fighter jets said to have secured ‘air protection’ of Bab al-Mandab strait and destroyed hundreds of targets
Author: Patrick Wintour
Headline: Operation supported by 100 fighter jets said to have secured ‘air protection’ of Bab al-Mandab strait and destroyed hundreds of targets
Content: Yemeni military reinforcements travel along the coastal road between Aden and Mocha, Yemen, on Monday.Photograph: Abdulnasser Alseddik/APView image in fullscreenYemeni military reinforcements travel along the coastal road between Aden and Mocha, Yemen, on Monday.Photograph: Abdulnasser Alseddik/APYemenAir campaign against Houthis under way in Yemen, says Saudi-led coalitionOperation supported by 100 fighter jets said to have secured ‘air protection’ of Bab al-Mandab strait and destroyed hundreds of targetsPatrick WintourDiplomatic editorMon 5 Oct 2026 11.21 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLeaders of a Saudi-led coalition inYemenclaimed a broad air campaign involving 100 jet aircraft was under way on Monday against the Iran-backed Houthi rebels along the Red Sea coastline and farther north in the capital, Sana’a.The Saudi coalition spokesperson, Maj Gen Turki al-Maliki, said the 100 fighter jets participating in Operation Dawn of Yemen were providing support to forces of Yemen’s internationally recognised government.He said the coalition had secured “air protection” of the strategic Bab al-Mandab strait and destroyed hundreds of Houthi targets. He claimed hundreds of Houthi fighters had been besieged in the Dhubab district, including the airport, close to the Bab al-Mandab strait, with some Houthi fighters fleeing across the Red Sea in boats.View image in fullscreenA man inspects the damage at a factory in Sana’a that was hit by an airstrike on Sunday.Photograph: ReutersSouthern Yemeni forces known as the Giants Brigades, who are allied with the government, earlier on Mondaylaunched a ground offensiveagainst the rebels on the eastern flank of the coastal areas that the Houthis seized in their latest advances. The government forces also claimto have cut the roadbetween Mocha and Dhubab, and that Houthi forces were deserting therecently captured city of Mochaas residents stayed behind closed doors.Previous Saudi-led statements about territorial gains in recent weeks have often proved partial, but footage appeared to back up the Saudi claims ofHouthisretreating by the seashore.The president of the Saudi-backed government, Rashad al-Alimi, had promised a new offensive on Sunday, saying patience with the Houthis had run out. “Today we are embarking on a decisive phase in the history of our nation,” he said.View image in fullscreenSmoke rises from the site of an airstrike in Sana’a on Sunday.Photograph: ReutersAirstrikes were also reported on Monday in Sana’a and the Houthi stronghold of Saada in the north of Yemen. Command and control centres, camps and weapons depots were targeted.The Houthis, who captured Sana’a in 2014, have in recent weeks made lightning advances down the west coast of Yemen, reaching the Bab al-Mandab and seizing strategic islands on the strait.On Monday Houthi sources denied reports of a retreat, and pointed to the explosions at a Saudi Aramco plant in Riyadh as a sign of the damage the group could still inflict on exposed Saudi oil installations, and by extension the world economy.View image in fullscreenFlames burn on Saturday at an oil facility south of Riyadh belonging to Saudi Aramco.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesIt appears a political agreement reached between the two main external Arab actors in Yemen – Saudi Arabia and theUnited Arab Emirates– permitted the UAE-backed Southern Giants to coordinate with the Saudi air force in the attack towards the coast.It is being stressed by the Giants Brigades that no other ground forces supporting the Saudi-backed government are involved in the offensive. The brigades, who are linked with the Southern Transitional Council, a political group outlawed in Yemen fortrying to set up a secessionist state, are certain to have sought political commitments about the future status of Yemen in order to have thrown their military weight behind it.It is not clear how the Saudis propose to address the age-old southern question. Concessions to the Southern Transitional Council (STC) about the future governance of the south are certain to have been demanded, even if the UAE itself does not return to Yemen.But the cooperation between the Saudi air force and the Giants Brigades is a remarkable turnaround, since as recently as January the Saudi air force was bombing UAE shipments of arms arriving in southern Yemen for STC-backed forces.The Saudi bombing triggered the UAE pullout from Yemen in January, the sudden dissolution of the STC, andthe exile of its leader, Aidarous al-Zubaidi.At the weekend his supporters vowed to hold demonstrations later this month in support of the return to a separate southern state.Houthi government officials claimed British fighter jets were supporting the Saudi air force with refuelling, somethingthe UK Ministry of Defence has already announced.The fighting was under way as senior ministers from Pakistan, Turkey andSaudi Arabiamet in Riyadh to discuss the support Saudi Arabia might need to protect itself from the Houthis. They have formed a joint defence pact but it is not known how it will operate.Explore more on these topicsYemenHouthisSaudi ArabiaUnited Arab EmiratesMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Supporters of Imran Khan start march on locked-down Islamabad | Imran Khan | The Guardian
description: Pakistani authorities insist marchers calling for former PM to be released from jail will not reach the capital
Author: Hannah Ellis-Petersen
Headline: Pakistani authorities insist marchers calling for former PM to be released from jail will not reach the capital
Content: The march calling for the release of Imran Khan began in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, a stronghold of his Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf party.Photograph: Marwat Akbar/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe march calling for the release of Imran Khan began in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, a stronghold of his Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf party.Photograph: Marwat Akbar/AFP/Getty ImagesImran KhanSupporters of Imran Khan start march on locked-down IslamabadPakistani authorities insist marchers calling for former PM to be released from jail will not reach the capitalHannah Ellis-Petersenin DelhiMon 5 Oct 2026 11.19 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 12.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleImran Khan’s supporters have begun a march to Islamabad to demand his release from jail after efforts by the government to halt the protest failed.The march began in the former prime minister’s stronghold province of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa in north-westPakistanon Sunday, according to leaders of his Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party.Concerns have grown over the health of the 74-year-old former Pakistan cricket captain who has been in prison since 2023. Party colleagues and family claim he is being held in solitary confinement and has been denied visits by his doctor or relatives despite having a serious eye condition and high blood pressure.The government had gone to extreme lengths to try to stop PTI holding the long march, including shutting down Islamabad and barricading the capital’s entrances with shipping containers and sandbags. Khan’s three sisters were amongthose detainedlast week on grounds of national security.Two rounds of negotiations between the government and PTI leaders took place over the weekend but broke down when Khan’s allies insisted that he be part of political talks.View image in fullscreenSecurity officials at a checkpoint in Peshawar, the first major stop on the march by Imran Khan’s supporters.Photograph: Arshad Arbab/EPAAttaullah Tarar, the information minister, accused the PTI of “double standards and hypocrisy”.Thousands of supporters had joined the protest by Monday afternoon and the crowds are expected to grow on the way to Peshawar, the main city in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, which the marchers should reach by Wednesday.The march is being led by the province’s chief minister, Sohail Afridi, who described those taking part as “Imran Khan’s soldiers”.Pakistan locks down Islamabad as Imran Khan’s party vows to march on capitalRead more“I call upon you all to come out, the youngsters to come out for the sake ​of your leader who is sitting in jail,” he said.Khan was prime minister from 2018 to 2022, when he was toppled by a parliamentary vote of no confidence. Since then, he and the PTI have faced mounting government pressure, which culminated in his arrest in 2023. The harassment and detention of other PTI leaders continues.View image in fullscreenMarchers with a banner of Imran Khan, who was toppled in 2022 and is said to be held in solitary confinement.Photograph: Saood Rehman/EPAKhan is widely considered the country’s most popular politician, while the ruling coalition government, which is backed by the military, is facing discontent over an economic crisis and a surge in terrorism.Ministers say the march is illegal and all measures will be taken to ensure it does not break through the capital’s boundaries.Tens of thousands of police and paramilitary personnel were deployed to Islamabad and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa last week, raising fears that Khan’s supporters will be met with state violence. Government politicians falsely claimed that the PTI was allowing militants from the Pakistan Taliban to take part in the march.Opposition leaders fear the prime minister will impose emergency rule on Khyber Pakhtunkhwa to stop the march.Explore more on these topicsImran KhanPakistanSouth and central AsianewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘A God-almighty punch-up’: rare footage shows Battle of Hastings (the 1966 one) | English Heritage | The Guardian
description: English Heritage acquires film of first re-enactment, ‘a lot of pushing and shoving’ between Kent and Sussex students
Author: Esther Addley
Headline: English Heritage acquires film of first re-enactment, ‘a lot of pushing and shoving’ between Kent and Sussex students
Content: 1:05Unseen footage of the first Battle of Hastings re-enactment in 1966 – videoEnglish Heritage‘A God-almighty punch-up’: rare footage shows Battle of Hastings (the 1966 one)English Heritage acquires film of first re-enactment, ‘a lot of pushing and shoving’ between Kent and Sussex studentsEsther AddleyMon 5 Oct 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt the top of a hill in a field near Hastings, a group of defiant English combatants awaited the invading army of William the Conqueror, brandishing their spears and shouting “Harold! Harold!”.Unfortunately, the Norman army had been held up in traffic on the A27 from Brighton, meaning the most significant battle in English history had to be delayed by 20 minutes while the French got into their costumes.On 14 October 1966, when a group of 500 students from Kent and Sussex universities met to re-enact the Battle of Hastings to mark its 900th anniversary, not every aspect was strictly historically accurate. Yes, the event was being staged on the same fields outside Battle in East Sussex where the original clash happened, but the English were wearing belted sacks and their swords and axes were made of wood and hardboard that had been painted silver.View image in fullscreen‘A pleasingly Monty Pythonesque record’: university students in combat at the first Battle of Hastings re-enactment in October 1966.Photograph: Keystone Press/AlamyThe rivalry between Kent and Sussex universities was real enough, however, according to Peter Sampson, a Sussex fresher who had been persuaded to sign up by the prospect of “a grand day out” and the promise of free beer. Once the two sides met, he says, it turned into “a God-almighty punch-up”.“There was actually a lot of real pushing and shoving, a lot of fighting going on in there … My friend John got a big whack around the head with the end of a [fake] spear, which hurt his face quite a lot.”Sixty years after that first re-enactment spawnedan annual eventwhich still attracts thousands of visitors each year, English Heritage has acquired rare colour footage of the inaugural event, at which a bemused French foreign minister attended, Queen Matilda was played by Miss World and health and safety was a far-off dream.View image in fullscreenChaps in fake chainmail bonking each other on the heads with fake weapons: Battle of Hastings re-enactors in 1966.Photograph: Keystone Press/AlamyIt was filmed by Alan Wootton, aninnovative manufacturer of electronicswho lived in Hastings and had been invited to capture a film record of the celebrations by Hastings town council. The film came to light when Alan’s son Cliff, who had helped out on the day as a 12-year-old, recently visitedBattle Abbey, the medieval foundation that was built on the site of the skirmish and is today overseen by English Heritage. He mentioned to a volunteer that he had 300 reels of film of the event, and would the charity be interested in seeing them?The result – condensed into a 12-minute film – is a pleasinglyMonty Pythonesquerecord of chaps in fake chainmail bonking each other on the heads with fake weapons while others ride around a bit on horses and 30,000 highly partisan (ie anti-French) spectators look on. (Though the era-defining British comedy, pedants will note, did not air untilthree years later.)“When Cliff showed me the footage, I was blown away by it, it was really, really impressive,” says James Witcombe, the site manager of Battle Abbey.View image in fullscreenRe-enactors marking the 950th anniversary of the Battle of Hastings in October 2016.Photograph: Jack Taylor/Getty ImagesThe film is, he says, very much of its time – and very different from the event which the charity has continued to stage every year since. “Looking at it from a modern perspective – yeah, it is a little bit of an interesting watch. I think the thing that’s very obvious is that it’s a load of amateurs getting together and really having fun … From our point of view, that’s the atmosphere that we want to preserve, just making sure we’ve got a few more sort of boundaries in place and nobody actually gets hurt.”Present-day crowds still tend to back “the home side”, he says, though “it’s a bit less partisan than it used to be”. This year’s event will be staged on 10 and 11 October, with a full battle run-through each day (though the result, sadly for England fans, does not change).View image in fullscreen‘It’s a bit less partisan than it used to be: thousands of visitors now attend the annual event (October 2018 pictured).Photograph: Jonny Weeks/The GuardianToday’s re-enactors– 1,000 combatants are expected this year – pay rather more attention to historical details, says Witcombe. “Whereas in 1966, there were knitted outfits and all that sort of stuff, the re-enactors today take it very seriously. It’s all about authenticity and, actually, experimental archaeology – [the idea that] living the experience gives you a much greater insight.” Withthe Bayeux tapestry’s presence in Londonhaving driven up interest in all things Norman, English Heritage is expecting bumper crowds – and is inviting any of those involved in the original 1966 event to come along.As Sampson recalls, while the battlefield itself was certainly “edgy”, once hostilities ended after 25 minutes of fisticuffs, things became much more convivial. After the promised free beer did not materialise, “we took matters somewhat into our own hands and, shall we say,liberateda couple of beer kegs from the back of the refreshment tent.“We cracked them open and then sat down with the Kent lads and lasses, and in the warm afternoon sunshine, just discussed the events of the day. So it became very friendly at the end of the day.”Explore more on these topicsEnglish HeritageHeritageBayeux tapestryWest SussexnewsShareReuse this content

title: Jeffrey Archer, former Conservative politician and novelist, dies aged 86 | Jeffrey Archer | The Guardian
description: Publisher says author died peacefully at home ‘between writing sessions’
Author: Harry Cockburn
Headline: Publisher says author died peacefully at home ‘between writing sessions’
Content: Jeffrey Archer in his penthouse suite on the Albert Embankment, London in September 2018.Photograph: Geoff Pugh/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenJeffrey Archer in his penthouse suite on the Albert Embankment, London in September 2018.Photograph: Geoff Pugh/ShutterstockJeffrey ArcherJeffrey Archer, former Conservative politician and novelist, dies aged 86Publisher says author died peacefully at home ‘between writing sessions’Harry CockburnMon 5 Oct 2026 18.31 EDTFirst published on Mon 5 Oct 2026 16.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJeffrey Archer, the bestselling author and former MP whose political career ended in disgrace when he was imprisoned for perjury, has died at the age of 86.Archer, who was a Conservative MP for five years before serving as the party’s deputy chair, died “suddenly and peacefully” at his home “between writing sessions” on Monday, his publisher HarperCollins said.He had a successful career as an author and was made a life peer in 1992.During a run to become mayor of London for theConservativesin 1999, his political career was in effect ended when it emerged he had lied in court over a decade earlier when a newspaper accused him of paying money to a sex worker. He was convicted of perjury and perverting the course of justice and imprisoned for four years.An Old Bailey jury found that he had lied in a libel action he had brought against the Star newspaper in 1987 in which he had been awarded £500,000 in damages.View image in fullscreenJeffrey Archer with his wife, Mary, arriving at the high court for the eighth day of his libel action against the Star newspaper and its editor, Lloyd Turner.Photograph: PAHe was released early in 2003 and returned to the House of Lords until he retired in 2024.Kate Elton, HarperCollins UK’s chief executive and Archer’s editor, said: “It has been one of the great privileges of my publishing life to have been Jeffrey Archer’s editor.“He was the master storyteller and an editor’s dream – phenomenally hard-working, utterly committed to completing draft after draft to get every word as perfect as possible, and a true champion of the team nature of great publishing.”Archer’s death came just one day before the publication of his new novel, Adam and Eve, on Tuesday 6 October.His first novel, Not a Penny More, Not a Penny Less, was published in 1976, two years after bankruptcy marked the end of his time as a sitting MP. This marked the beginning of an enviable writing career. Archer spent a total of 14 years and five months on the Sunday Times bestseller lists and over five years on the New York Times bestseller lists, selling 300 million books in 119 countries in 49 languages. His 1979 novel Kane and Abel remains among the best-selling books in the world, having sold more than 30 million copies to date.View image in fullscreenJeffrey Archer arrives for the funeral of Katharine, Duchess of Kent at Westminster Cathedral, London on 16 September 2025.Photograph: Karwai Tang/WireImageHis death came less than 24 hours after Archer had met and signed books for hundreds of fans at a sold-out event with broadcaster Gyles Brandreth at the Leicester Square Theatre in central London on Sunday, HarperCollins said.Writing on X, Brandreth said: “Just yesterday I did a show with Jeffrey Archer to celebrate his new novel –he said it was to be his last.“He was in the most wonderful, ebullient form and had such a great reception from a packed house. He was funny, engaging and self-deprecating – a great storyteller to the last.”Archer was first elected an MP in a 1969 byelection for the constituency of Louth in Lincolnshire when he was 29 years old, having already worked as a Conservative councillor for Havering in north-east London, a period during which he also ran a Mayfair art gallery.Archer cast himself as a centrist in parliament, frequently rebelling against the right wing of the Conservative party, but his political career stalled when he became the victim of a fraudulent investment scheme, which left him almost half a million pounds in debt. He said he would therefore not stand in the 1974 election “due to financial difficulties”.His first novel was a direct effort to regain financial control – a move that paid off, and Not a Penny More, Not a Penny Less was adapted for radio, and later, for TV. By the mid-1980s Archer had written several successful novels as well as short stories, plays and children’s books.As his literary career bore fruit, Archer returned to politics, becoming a popular speaker at grassroots events, leading Margaret Thatcher to appoint him deputy chairman of the Conservative party in 1985.But in October 1986 he became embroiled in scandal when the News of the World claimed he’d spent £2,000 to pay off a “vice girl”, a story immediately followed by a more detailed story in the Star alleging Archer had paid a woman named Monica Coghlan for sex. Archer sued the Star, and the case came to court the following year, winning £500,000 in damages but sowing the seeds for his downfall over a decade later.When the allegations broke, the leader of the Conservative party at the time, William Hague, expelled Archer from the party saying: “This is the end of politics for Jeffrey Archer. I will not tolerate such behaviour in my party.”At the time he was charged in 2000, he was also making headlines by starring in his own West End play The Accused, which ran at the Theatre Royal Haymarket in London, and in which Archer’s character played an alleged murderer on trial and in which the audience voted on whether they believed Archer’s character was guilty or innocent at the end of each performance.Archer’s perjury trial began on 30 May 2001, a month after Monica Coghlan was killed in a road traffic accident.Following sentencing he was imprisoned at Belmarsh, a category A prison in London but later moved to four other prisons before his release in 2003, having served half of his sentence.Despite retaining his seat in the House of Lords, Archer did not take an active role in the upper chamber of parliament and gave up his seat in 2024.The former Tory minister, Nadhim Zahawi, paid tribute to Archer, writing on X: “Jeffrey Archer was a dear friend and an extraordinary human being. His gift for storytelling was matched by his wit, warmth and boundless energy. Life was never dull in Jeffrey’s company.”Archer had been due to be at the Cheltenham festival later in the month to discuss his forthcoming novel.Archer is survived by his wife, Mary, and their sons, William and James.Explore more on these topicsJeffrey ArcherConservativesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Conservatives propose £10bn ‘Britannia Shield’ inspired by Israel’s Iron Dome | Conservatives | The Guardian
description: Party to unveil plans for one of UK’s ‘most significant military programmes since the cold war’
Author: Jessica Elgot
Headline: Party to unveil plans for one of UK’s ‘most significant military programmes since the cold war’
Content: Rocket trails from an interception by Israel's Iron Dome missile defence system are pictured over Jerusalem earlier this year.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenRocket trails from an interception by Israel's Iron Dome missile defence system are pictured over Jerusalem earlier this year.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesConservativesConservatives propose £10bn ‘Britannia Shield’ inspired by Israel’s Iron DomeParty to unveil plans for one of UK’s ‘most significant military programmes since the cold war’Jessica ElgotandDan SabbaghMon 5 Oct 2026 17.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheConservativeswill announce plans to build a £10bn British “Iron Dome” similar to Israel’s air and missile defence system, which the party will christen “Britannia Shield” in an announcement at conference on Tuesday.The shadow defence secretary, James Cartlidge, will say Britain needs to be ready to defend itself from potential aerial attacks and that new investment was needed in advanced radar and interceptor missiles.Claiming it was “one of Britain’s most significant military programmes since the cold war”, he will say it is one that was “totally necessary because of the threats we face”.Britain’s military has traditionally believed it does not need to purchase Iron Dome-style air defence systems given other spending priorities and the fact that the UK has not faceddrone and missile strikesas has Israel or Ukraine.Military officials argue that the UK’s strategy is based around deterring any attack or a full-blown war with nuclear weapons and that any conflict that involved a direct threat to the British homeland would almost certainly involveNato alliesassisting.The UK does not own any Patriot air defence systems, and in an acute crisis would have to rely on Royal Navy Type 45 destroyers to protect coastal areas, but the circumstances in which expensive air defence would be needed in the UK are very remote.The Conservatives will say the new system would be funded out of the defence uplift from their commitment last month to increase defence spending by more than £10bn a year to reach 3% of GDP by 2030.Cartlidge will say in his speech that the aim would be to deliver a minimum deployable capability within the first five years, with further improvements, expanded capability and missile stockpiles delivered over the following five years.The party will argue that the UK is being left behind in Europe when it comes to investment in air defences, which was criticised in a report from the defence select committee last November. The government has currently committed about £790m for integrated air and missile defence (IAMD) in the Defence Investment Plan.Cartlidge will say that the British version of the Iron Dome will have new advanced radar systems to detect threats, a new command and control system and a new stockpile of missiles and counter-drone capabilities.That would in practice be a fundamentally different model to the Israeli Iron Dome system, which protects a country a twelfth of the size of Great Britain and is primarily designed to counter short-range threats like rockets and artillery, with other defence systems that counter longer-range missiles.Other European countries, including Germany, Greece, Cyprus and Poland, are investing significantly in air defence systems, though the UK is under limited direct threat from ongoing conflicts, unlike some of those nations.The Conservative leader, Kemi Badenoch, said that Labour were “failing that basic test” of keeping the country safe. The chancellor, John Healey – who previously quit as Keir Starmer’s defence secretary over the limitations of his defence settlement – is now unlikely to set out when the UK will meet the target ofspending 3% of GDP on defenceuntil next year’s spending review.“The world will not wait for Britain to get ready. War has returned to Europe. Missiles and drones are transforming warfare in the Middle East. Cheap weapons can now threaten cities, military bases and critical infrastructure in ways that would have sounded like science fiction a generation ago,” Badenoch said, announcing the air defence investment.“If a missile or drone is launched at Britain, we do not get a second chance to wish we had prepared. Families can make their own choices. Businesses can build and innovate. But only government can defend the country.”Explore more on these topicsConservativesKemi BadenochDefence policyNatoMilitaryConservative conference 2026IsraelnewsShareReuse this content

title: London to Chicago BA flight declares emergency after dropping 28,000 feet | British Airways | The Guardian
description: British Airways Boeing abruptly lost altitude over Ireland due to ‘technical issue’ and returned to Heathrow
Author: Harry Cockburn
Headline: British Airways Boeing abruptly lost altitude over Ireland due to ‘technical issue’ and returned to Heathrow
Content: One of British Airways’ fleet of Boeing 777-200ER aircraft. In the incident on Monday the passenger jet deployed oxygen masks.Photograph: Bayne Stanley/Zuma Press Wire/Rex/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenOne of British Airways’ fleet of Boeing 777-200ER aircraft. In the incident on Monday the passenger jet deployed oxygen masks.Photograph: Bayne Stanley/Zuma Press Wire/Rex/ShutterstockBritish AirwaysLondon to Chicago BA flight declares emergency after dropping 28,000 feetBritish Airways Boeing abruptly lost altitude over Ireland due to ‘technical issue’ and returned to HeathrowHarry CockburnMon 5 Oct 2026 16.33 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 17.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA flight from London to Chicago declared an emergency after a sudden and steep descent of 28,000 feet over Ireland and was forced to turn back to Britain.British Airways flight BA295 was bound for Chicago’s O’Hare airport but after a “technical issue” during which oxygen masks were deployed from the ceiling, the plane landed safely back at London Heathrow.The aircraft, a Boeing 777-200ER, had departed Heathrow at 12.14pm on Monday for its scheduled transatlantic flight, and an hour into the journey had ascended to its cruising altitude of 37,000 feet.According to passengers, the plane then encountered turbulence moments before the masks dropped, prompting “uncertainty” among those on board.Pilots descended to below 10,000 feet and issued a 7700 emergency squawk to air traffic control – the international general emergency code – and made a U-turn to head back towards England.Flight-tracking services showed the aircraft flying in a looping holding pattern over the Bristol Channel between Pembrokeshire and North Devon as the plane burnt off fuel in order to lower its weight, allowing the pilots to make a normal landing just after 5pm.Passenger Tom Nichollssaid there was a “sudden bit of turbulence”before the emergency was declared and that the quick descent to 9,000ft hadn’t been too uncomfortable.He said: “The plane adjusted but it didn’t feel like it was descending rapidly. I’d say the pilots did a very good job.“The oxygen masks popped out soon after and there was a bit of uncertainty onboard. The couple in front couldn’t get to theirs but by the time they’d found a spare seat with a mask, the captain announced we were below 10,000ft so they were not needed.”A spokesperson for BA said: “The safety of our customers and crew is always our top priority, and the aircraft landed safely after our highly trained pilots returned to Heathrow following a technical issue.“Customers disembarked the aircraft normally and our teams are working to get their travel plans back on track as quickly as possible.”Photographs taken by passengers and shared on social media showed oxygen masks dangling from the ceiling as the plane made the return journey.A rapid descent to below 10,000 feet and a 7700 emergency squawk are routinely associated with aircraft experiencing cabin depressurisation but the official cause of the emergency has yet to be confirmed by BA.The Boeing 777-200ER is one of BA’s oldest planes in service, having been delivered to the carrier almost 30 years ago – in July 1997. Live streams showed the aircraft making its descent and safe landing back at Heathrow.Many passengers have been booked on to new flights departing on Tuesday.Explore more on these topicsBritish AirwaysHeathrow airportAir transportAirline industryTransportnewsShareReuse this content

title: Tories are united behind Badenoch, but MPs want focus on economy over culture wars to win back voters | Conservatives | The Guardian
description: Party has common enemy in defectors, while Nigel Farage’s woes have given some insiders reason to hope
Author: Pippa Crerar
Headline: Party has common enemy in defectors, while Nigel Farage’s woes have given some insiders reason to hope
Content: This time last year, mutinous Tory MPs were privately predicting Badenoch’s demise. Now, she is the longest serving leader since Boris Johnson.Photograph: Ian Forsyth/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThis time last year, mutinous Tory MPs were privately predicting Badenoch’s demise. Now, she is the longest serving leader since Boris Johnson.Photograph: Ian Forsyth/Getty ImagesConservativesAnalysisTories are united behind Badenoch, but MPs want focus on economy over culture wars to win back votersPippa CrerarPolitical editorParty has common enemy in defectors, while Nigel Farage’s woes have given some insiders reason to hopeMon 5 Oct 2026 14.57 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 21.31 EDTShareDuring a quick-fire Q&A at the Conservative party conference this weekend,Kemi Badenochwas asked who she would pick between Robert Jenrick or Suella Braverman.“Why do you keep offering me these? It’s like asking if I’d rather be shot or drowned,” the Tory leader responded with her trademark directness.The Tories appear more united than they have done in years. Part of that is because they have a common enemy to unite against: Tory defectors.It is not lost on Badenoch’s team that this time last year, it was a matter of when, not if, Jenrick, her erstwhile leadership rival, would try to oust her.View image in fullscreenA year ago it seemed a matter of when, not if, Robert Jenrick would try to oust Badenoch. He was kicked out the party weeks later.Photograph: Guy Bell/ShutterstockMutinous Tory MPs were privately predicting her demise. But after a successful conference, Badenoch limped on – and Jenrick emerged a diminished figure who weeks later would be kicked out of the party.His presence, however, lives on, with shadow ministers openly sharing their relief that he is no longer among their number.“Nobody knew how much we hated Robert until he left,” said one shadow cabinet member. Others were less polite. “Rob going was like pulling out a splinter,” one said. “I miss him like I miss an abscess in my molar,” another added.But while the unity comes, in part, from a mutual dislike, there are of course other factors: Badenoch’s strength as a leader; the country’s yearning for stability; the constant threat ofReform UKto the party’s right.Badenoch has been running the show for almost two years – the longest serving Tory leader since Boris Johnson – and has begun to set out her principles, writing a 30,000 word pamphlet titled The Right Way before the conference.Tory MPs also seem to have finally realised that voters take a dim view of the party cycling through leaders at such breakneck speed, with five in the past eight years.Nigel Farage’s woes have also given them reason for hope: while the Reform leader believes his party will recover from a difficult summer, some Tory MPs are confident that his party has peaked.View image in fullscreenKemi Badenoch believes she can beat Labour and Reform on the issue of the economy, insiders say.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianOther party insiders – possibly more plugged into what is going on in their constituencies – concede that Farage still represents a huge threat. They are among those concerned about Badenoch pitching to the right.Instead, they say that she needs to do more to win over centrist voters for the party to stand a chance of winning another election. Part of that is by focusing more on the economy and less on culture wars.“There’s no point telling Kemi not to do anything. But we do have to be careful with our language,” one MP said. Another added: “That’s not Kemi’s instinct. But she does finally seem to understand it all has to be about the economy. That’s where we win.”Badenoch believes she can “shrug off” the Liz Truss anchor and beat Reform and Labour on the economy, MPs say. Andrew Griffith, her shadow chancellor who has previously worked in business, helps the party’s credibility, they add, and Badenoch will speak more about the topic this week.The Tory leader also polls ahead of her party, which insulates her from much internal criticism. One adviser said the Tories do better when their leader is in that position – citing David Cameron and Boris Johnson – but worse when they’re behind, as Rishi Sunak was.Badenoch has told her top team that they have to work “day by day” to restore the party’s fortunes. Yet there is no escaping that almost two years after she was elected as leader, the Tories are still polling lower than they did in 2024 with their catastrophic general election defeat.“You won’t hear much from us on that,” one senior aide said. “The qualitative stuff is good but it’s not backed up yet by the numbers. We need to put on three or four points in the polls. If we do that and gain momentum we’re back.”Others are hopeful that the exposure of their conference week can give them enough of a lift in the polls to help them maintain the narrative that they’re on the march.The spectre hanging over the whole affair, however, is the prospect of a snap general election. Andy Burnham’s political away day at Chequers on Monday has got many Tories spooked, even though the prime minister has ruled out calling an early election.Perhaps more in hope than expectation, shadow cabinet ministers said they did not believe Burnham would call an election. “He said it would be irresponsible and it’s hard to walk that back,” said one.However, Badenoch told a bash for Tory MPs on Sunday night the party was getting ready for an election regardless. But while she sounded bullish, her closest lieutenants are anything but. “If there is one, we’re all fucked,” they said.Explore more on these topicsConservativesKemi BadenochReform UKConservative conference 2026Conservative conferenceEconomic policyConservative leadershipanalysisShareReuse this content
