title: US supreme court hears big oil’s bid to block climate damage lawsuits | US supreme court | The Guardian
description: How the court will lean is unclear amid Suncor Energy and ExxonMobil’s attempt to stop lawsuits at state level
Author: Hilary Beaumont
Headline: How the court will lean is unclear amid Suncor Energy and ExxonMobil’s attempt to stop lawsuits at state level
Content: Suncor Refinery in Commerce City, Colorado, on 26 July 2023.Photograph: Hyoung Chang/Denver Post/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSuncor Refinery in Commerce City, Colorado, on 26 July 2023.Photograph: Hyoung Chang/Denver Post/Getty ImagesDemocracy, climate and justiceUS supreme courtUS supreme court hears big oil’s bid to block climate damage lawsuitsHow the court will lean is unclear amid Suncor Energy and ExxonMobil’s attempt to stop lawsuits at state levelDemocracy, climate and justice is supported byAbout this contentHilary BeaumontMon 5 Oct 2026 15.57 EDTFirst published on Mon 5 Oct 2026 09.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheUS supreme courtbegan its new nine-month term hearing arguments on Monday in a majorcasein which big oil companies attempted to strike a fatal blow against lawsuits that seek to hold them accountable for theclimate crisis.After the almost two-hour hearing, while it was not yet clear which way the justices were leaning, experts said the court may find it challenging to write a majority decision siding with industry.InSuncor Energy Inc v County Commissioners of Boulder County, local officials in Boulder are suing Suncor Energy and ExxonMobil in state court to force the companies to share a portion of the costs that the climate crisis has imposed on local taxpayers. However, Exxon and Canada-based Suncor are arguing that federal law prevents state courts from hearing Boulder’s climate change lawsuit.If the supreme court justices side with Boulder or decide that the case is not in their jurisdiction, then it would continue in state court. But if the fossil fuel industry convinces the justices, the decision could apply not only to the Boulder case, but also to dozens of other climate cases brought by state and local governments around the US.As a result of Justice Samuel Alito’srecusalfrom the case, there are only five conservative justices weighing in, so Boulder county must only convince one conservative justice to win, assuming the three liberal justices back Boulder. Some noted that the justices focused their questions primarily on the merits of the case rather than askingif the court had jurisdiction to hear it, suggesting they will make a decision on the question of whether federal law pre-empts Boulder’s state climate case.Kannon Shanmugam, a lawyer for the fossil fuel companies, told the justices that climate change was a pressing issue, but state cases such as the one filed by Boulder were the wrong way to resolve it, and the issue should be left to lawmakers. He argued that if the cases were heard in state courts, it would allow a high number of lawsuits to be filed. “The breadth of Boulder’s argument is astonishing,” he said.Samuel Alito steps aside in a major climate case amid scrutiny over oil stock holdingsRead moreShanmugam argued that climate change is different from other interstate pollution cases “because the claim runs through global climate change” and involves anyone who uses fossil fuels worldwide.Kirti Datla, the director of Earthjustice’s strategic legal advocacy program, said the industry lawyer needed five justices to agree with him. “Some of the justices seemed to be persuaded by the idea that climate change is different, or the sheer number of these suits creates a problem of a different kind,” Datla said. But she added that the justices were struggling to come up with reasons based in law that would support the industry arguments. “It’s always been Suncor’s task to provide them with clear answers to those questions, and I didn’t hear clear answers to those questions in argument.”Dennis Fan, the founder and director of the Appellate Litigation Clinic at Columbia Law School who wrote an amicus brief in the case, said it was too close to call, but he was concerned for the future of the climate cases. “They focused more on the merits,” he said. “That had me much more worried for Boulder.”Fan said the industry hopes this case is going to be the “death blow” to this type of lawsuit.“The industry is going for the home run … They’re thinking, ‘If we win this argument, there will never, ever be climate change litigation again.’”Boulder officials filed a lawsuit inColoradocourt in 2018 arguing that Exxon and Suncor concealed and misrepresented to the public what they knew about the damage that burning fossil fuels would do to the climate, and that they should pay for the resulting costs of disasters. Initially, the firms sought to have the case moved to federal court. Then when the Colorado supreme court allowed Boulder’s case to make its way toward trial in state court, Exxon and Suncor appealed that ruling up to the supreme court, arguing it should be dismissed on grounds of federal pre-emption.Typically, cases must be decided by lower courts before reaching the supreme court, but the justices agreed to hear this case while the state case is ongoing. “That’s an incredibly weird thing to have happen,” Fan said.The supreme court considered whether it had proper jurisdiction to hear Boulder’s case right now, and whether federal law pre-empted Boulder’s case from being heard in state court.Congress has the power to pass federal laws that invalidate state laws, but the question is whether there are any federal laws that invalidate state climate cases. “They’ve had a little bit of difficulty identifying exactly what that source of federal law is,” Fan said. For instance, the fossil fuel companies claim that the federal Clean Air Act pre-empts Boulder’s case from state court, even though the law specifies that “air pollution control at its source is the primary responsibility of states and local governments”.So the fossil fuel companies in their brief claimed that supreme court decisions from a century ago suggested that federal courts have power to hear environmental cases, even without federal laws on the books, and that these decisions created a “federal common law” governing environmental lawsuits across state lines. They asserted that this federal common law was still in effect and existed in the “structure of the Constitution” even though the federal Clean Air Act has since declared states have primary jurisdiction over local air pollution.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionShanmugam presented the constitutional theory to the justices on Monday, but Kevin Russell, Boulder’s attorney, repeatedly drew their attention back to the constitution. Russell argued that the industry attorney was asking them to “jump through a number of hoops” to answer a complicated question. “Instead, I would suggest that the court can and should directly answer the question: what in the constitution implicitly prohibitsColoradoor any other state’s law from applying to these claims?”Datla of Earthjustice said some conservative justices appeared to agree with Boulder on this point. “Chief Justice [John Roberts] and Justice [Neil] Gorsuch seemed to ask questions that indicated that they thought that broad constitutional rule was complicated at a minimum,” she said.Datla said the reaction of the conservative justices suggested they would find it difficult to write a decision supporting Suncor. “The fact that there wasn’t a clear position that the conservative justices seem to coalesce around as to which one of Suncor’s arguments was right is, I think, telling that maybe they don’t all think this is a foregone conclusion.”The supreme court has not historically agreed with the argument the oil companies are making, Fan said. He pointed to the tobacco and opioid companies that previously faced state public nuisance cases. “For decades, the tobacco industry tried to get the supreme court and other courts to stop state court litigation from happening against the tobacco industry, and they failed every single time,” he said.US states and cities sue over Trump EPA’s repeal of emissions rulesRead moreClimate advocates and wildfire survivors rallied on Monday morning outside the supreme court in Washington DC.Daryl McCool, an artist wholost her homewhen the 2021Marshall firedestroyed her neighborhood in Boulder county, Colorado, is not involved in the case but planned to attend the rally. The fire caused damage estimated atmore than $2bn, and a recent report estimated that the climate crisis could cost Colorado up to$37bnby 2050. “The case itself is meaningful because it affects every single human, every single creature, it affects everyone that is on this earth,” McCool said.TheTrump administrationhas sided with the oil companies and has carried out a series of pollution regulations, includingrevokingthe 2009 bedrock scientific determination that gives the government the ability to regulate climate-heating pollution.A ruling is expected next summer.Explore more on these topicsUS supreme courtDemocracy, climate and justiceClimate crisisLaw (US)Samuel AlitoOil and gas companiesOilGasnewsShareReuse this content

title: Mark Thompson will remain chief executive at CNN after Paramount sale | CNN | The Guardian
description: Decision by Paramount Skydance executive David Ellison was relief to employees who feared overhaul – and possibility of Bari Weiss taking over
Author: Jeremy Barr
Headline: Decision by Paramount Skydance executive David Ellison was relief to employees who feared overhaul – and possibility of Bari Weiss taking over
Content: Mark Thompson on 15 May 2024 in New York City.Photograph: Dimitrios Kambouris/Getty Images for Warner Bros DiscoveryView image in fullscreenMark Thompson on 15 May 2024 in New York City.Photograph: Dimitrios Kambouris/Getty Images for Warner Bros DiscoveryCNNMark Thompson will remain chief executive at CNN after Paramount saleDecision by Paramount Skydance executive David Ellison was relief to employees who feared overhaul – and possibility of Bari Weiss taking overJeremy BarrMon 5 Oct 2026 10.14 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 10.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMark Thompson, who since 2023 has served as chair and chief executive of CNN after a storied career in British and American media, will retain his role even after Paramount Skydance takes control of the company, he announced in a memo to network staffers on Monday morning.While Thompson wrote that the “specifics of howCNNwill plug into and operate in the new company have yet to be finalized”, he offered some pledges about his role at the combined company, which will be led by David Ellison, the Paramount Skydance chief executive, after the company merges with CNN parent company Warner Bros Discovery. The deal is expected to formally close on Tuesday.“First, I’m convinced that from David Ellison on down, Paramount Skydance leadership really does believe in news alongside entertainment as a top strategic opportunity for our new company,” Thompson wrote. “They’ve seen our digital strategy and are as excited about it as we are.“And second, having now spoken to them at length on the topic, I have real confidence that they both understand and will fully support the principle and practice of the kind of independent news that CNN has always stood for. That’s why I will be leading CNN into this new chapter as it becomes one of Skydance’s suite of major media assets and global brands, and leading it as an independent editor-in-chief with the same responsibilities and prerogatives that I have now.”The decision by Paramount Skydance leadership will bring relief to many CNN employees who feared a complete overhaul of the network. Some employees had also shared concerns that Ellison could install Bari Weiss, editor in chief of CBS News, atop the cable news network. (The Wall Street Journalfirst reportedthat Ellison had asked Thompson to stay on.)“That sound you hear is a giant sigh of relief from halls of Techwood,” said a CNN producer, who was not authorized to comment, referring to the company’s Atlanta headquarters. That sentiment was shared by other CNN employees who spoke with the Guardian.According toan announcementof the combined company’s leadership team, Weiss will also remain in her role as editor in chief of CBS News,despite some speculationabout a potential change in her purview.Thompson, 69, was brought on to take charge of CNN in 2023 after the tumultuous leadership of chief executive Chris Licht, who lacked network management experience and lasted just over a year. Thompson had previously served as director-general of the BBC from 2004 to 2012 and then as president and CEO of the New York Times from 2012 to 2020.At CNN, Thompson has prioritized the network’s digital and streaming operations, as well as the creation of a new direct-to-consumer product called CNN All Access in October 2025. The CNN producer credited Thompson with “stabilizing” the business and helping to build its post-linear television future.Thompson has also had his hands full with Donald Trump’s White House, which last month barred CNN – along with MS Now and Politico – from the building before a judge temporarily restored access.A former longtime CNN producer said that Thompson’s presence would be reassuring because he is a known entity. “They know what he brings,” the person said.When Paramount Skydance’s acquisition of CNN parent company Warner Bros Discovery closes on Tuesday, after the settlement of lawsuits aimed at blocking the deal, the company will begin the process of integrating the various media assets it has acquired.It is unclear if, when or how CNN and CBS News will be merged, though they will share a parent company. The two networks have different corporate structures and serve different audiences. At an industry conference on 30 September, Paramount’s chief legal officer, Makan Delrahim, noted those distinctions. “CBS News is a handful of hours of programming,”he reportedly said. “CNN is 24-7. Just completely different markets.”While both CBS News and CNN have large American audiences, CNN has a much larger international footprint, and there has been speculation that its foreign team could take precedence if the companies are merged. There is also the expectation of widespread layoffs across the entire company, including at CBS News and CNN, as part of an effort to slash costs.And there have been concerns about whether the Ellison family, which controls a large chunk of American media and entertainment assets, could move CNN in a more conservative direction, a fear that Ellison himself has dismissed.As part of a settlement reached between Paramount and a coalition of 12 state attorneys general last month who sued to block the deal, the company has agreed to create a five-personnews editorial independence boardwithin 180 days of closing the deal. The board will “establish guiding editorial and journalism principles for the combined entity’s news channels” and will ensure those principles are adhered to. But some employees at CNN and CBS News have dismissed the planned board, fearing it will lack teeth.Thompson hinted at the uncertainty surrounding the merger in his memo. “I know many of you have had trepidations about this moment. That’s understandable – indeed, as I’ve hinted before, I’ve had the odd moment or two myself!” he said. “But I want to say that on the eve of the acquisition of CNN by Paramount Skydance, I find myself in a very positive frame of mind. I really do believe we’ll be working alongside a team who don’t just have real vision and real energy, but real values as well.”Thompson told CNN employees that he would have more details to share on Tuesday.Explore more on these topicsCNNMark ThompsonUS press and publishingUS televisionMedia businessnewsShareReuse this content

title: Trump’s recent statements on the economy are even more bonkers than usual | Steven Greenhouse | The Guardian
description: Our ‘genius’ president is revealing his ignorance of economics, fueling concerns about the threat he poses to the world
Author: Steven Greenhouse
Headline: Our ‘genius’ president is revealing his ignorance of economics, fueling concerns about the threat he poses to the world
Content: ‘Economists and corporate executives were especially alarmed by two Trump statements.’Photograph: Aaron Schwartz/Pool/Aaron Schwartz - Pool/CNP/ShutterstockView image in fullscreen‘Economists and corporate executives were especially alarmed by two Trump statements.’Photograph: Aaron Schwartz/Pool/Aaron Schwartz - Pool/CNP/ShutterstockOpinionDonald TrumpTrump’s recent statements on the economy are even more bonkers than usualSteven GreenhouseOur ‘genius’ president is revealing his ignorance of economics, fueling concerns about the threat he poses to the worldMon 5 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 11.47 EDTShareDonald Trump recently made a bold claim about his abilities,writing on Truth Social: “The only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!”But in the days before and after that post, Trump made one mind-boggling statement after another, including one thatraised the possibility of cutting off all tradewith dozens of the US’s trading partners. The president’s statements had many experts questioning not just his intelligence, but also whether he – and the outlandish policies he was proposing – were a clear and present danger to both the US economy and the world economy. Public respect for Trump’s economic sense has fallen so low that just 7% of Americans think he should take the lead in regulating AI, according toa recent WSJ poll.Responding to Trump’s reckless statements, one prominent advocacy group, Republicans Against Trump,derided him as “Dumbest. President. Ever.”Economists and corporate executives were especially alarmed by two Trump statements. First, he wrote on Truth Social: “I’ll stop trading with countrieswith which we have a deficit” if the Federal Reserve doesn’t cut interest rates.The second disconcerting statement was: “If we stopped Trading with every countrythat we have a Deficit with, which is most of them, we would make, at least, 1.5 Trillion Dollars a year.”Trump’s $5,000 pledge to voters is a shameless bribe | Steven GreenhouseRead moreNot only is Trump’s arithmetic childishly silly here, but any college student who took Econ 101 knows that if a trade-dependent nation like the US suddenly ended all trade with dozens of countries, that would lead to economic disaster. What’s more, it was worrisome that Trump views himself as almighty emperor with the power to singlehandedly halt hundreds of billions of dollars in trade.If Trump ordered the US to terminate all trade with every place with which it has a trade deficit – that includes China, Mexico, Taiwan and the European Union – many US manufacturers would quickly find themselves in desperate straits, unable to obtain critically needed computer chips, rare earths, auto parts, aluminum and much more. As a result, many factories would be forced to close. Not only that, many farmers would be crippled because they couldn’t import the fertilizer they need, while many homebuilders would have to stop work because they couldn’t import needed lumber.Those were by no means Trump’s only recent mind-boggling statements.Two days before the Federal Reserve raised its short-term interest rates to 3.75% to 4% to combat inflation, Trump was on a tear, badgering and bullying the Fed, telling it not only not to raise interest rates, but to cut rates sharply. “We should be at 1%or half a percent,” Trump said. Again, anyone who took Econ 101 knows that cutting rates so sharply and so low will push prices skyward at a time when the Fed and consumers already think inflation is too high. And let’s not forget that Trump was the guy who promised toreduce prices on day oneas president.With that statement, the self-described “stable genius” president showed his utter failure to understand one of the most basic teachings of Econ 101 – when interest rates are extremely low, like 1%, that heats up the economy and that revved-up economic activity fuels inflation. The University of Michigan economist Justin Wolfers called Trump’s demand for a 1% interest rate “the dumbest thing ever saidby a president”.Then there was this whopper. Trump said that if the Fed bowed to his demands and slashed interest rates, “we could have a GDP [growth] of 14, 15, 16 and 20.”Those numbers are absurd, fantastical. Considering that the US economygrew at a moderate 2.2% rate in this year’s second quarterand rarely grows faster than 5%, talk of 20% growth is delusional. Since the second world war, the US economy has grown at arate at 20% or higher just once. That happened in the third quarter of 2020 due to extraordinary circumstances – in that quarter, myriad businesses rushed to reopen after the worst pandemic in a century caused many to suddenly shut down during the previous quarter. (GDP plunged at a 28% rate that quarter.)Then there was this colossally wrong-headed statement about trade: “The word ‘Deficit’ is nothing more thana fancy word for LOSS.” Trump coupled that assertion with his misbegotten statement that the US would magicallybe $1.5tn richerif it terminated all trade with every nation with which it has a deficit.This shows an infantile understanding of trade – and a stunning blindness to its mutual benefits.To explain how inane Trump is being here, let’s hypothesize for a second that in the US-France trade relationship, the only goods traded are wine and bourbon. Under Trump’s ludicrous logic, if the US buys $2bn of wine from France, and the French import $1bn worth of Kentucky bourbon, the resulting $1bn trade deficit means the US is simply giving away $1bn to France.US ban on Canadian imports likely to weaken already fragile relationshipRead moreTrump bafflingly sees that as an outright $1bn loss. Blinded by ignorance, ideology or anidée fixe, Trump fails to see that that’s not a harmful $1bn “loss” – rather, Americans are getting $1bn worth of fine wine to enjoy. No doubt wine lovers across the US see that as a gain and certainly not as a $1bn loss.Bottom line, Trump’s delusional statements on the economy show that he is becoming more detached from reality and from rational understanding of how the world works. One can’t help but wonder why his economic advisers don’t stop him from making such ridiculous and at times dangerous statements. If Trump turns his absurd economic notions into reality, as he has done in his ugly, unnecessary trade war with Canada, that will be more bad news for Americans.Voters should realize that Trump, with his failure to grasp basic economics, is a danger to the economy. He has brought us higher prices, slower GDP growth, and constant economic chaos and uncertainty. His tariffs and disastrous war against Iran have hit the great majority of Americans in their wallets and pocketbooks.Tragically, Trump’s Republican supporters in Congress either cheer him on or remain dismayingly silent while Trump does serious damage to the economy and to the finances of millions of struggling families. Americans shouldn’t forget this when they vote in November’s midterm elections.Steven Greenhouse is a journalist and author, focusing on labor and the workplace, as well as economic and legal issuesExplore more on these topicsDonald TrumpOpinionTrump administrationUS economyEconomicsUS politicscommentShareReuse this content

title: Euro falls to 17-month low against dollar amid French debt fears | Euro | The Guardian
description: France’s Cac 40 index slides as announcement of snap election in Spain also helps fuel eurozone uncertainty
Author: Richard Partington
Headline: France’s Cac 40 index slides as announcement of snap election in Spain also helps fuel eurozone uncertainty
Content: The euro fell to below $1.12 against the dollar on Monday, before recovering slightly.Photograph: Dado Ruvić/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe euro fell to below $1.12 against the dollar on Monday, before recovering slightly.Photograph: Dado Ruvić/ReutersEuroEuro falls to 17-month low against dollar amid French debt fearsFrance’s Cac 40 index slides as announcement of snap election in Spain also helps fuel eurozone uncertaintyBusiness live – latest updatesRichard PartingtonSenior economics correspondentMon 5 Oct 2026 07.18 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 14.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe euro has slumped to the lowest level against the dollar in 17 months amid growing concern France’s debt position could threaten the stability of the wider single currency bloc.The single currency fell as much as 0.8% against the dollar in early trading on Monday to below $1.12, its lowest level since May 2025. It has slumped by about 1.2% this month, accelerating a drop of about eight cents against the greenback from a peak of $1.20 in January.Investors said the sell-off in the euro was fuelled by concerns over France’s rising debt costs as the government battles to control its stretched public finances in the run-up to next year’s presidential election.Global oil stockpiles ‘scarily thin,’ says Saudi Aramco chief; euro hits 17-month low on France debt fears – business liveRead moreFrance’s blue-chip Cac 40 index of leading company shares fell by 1% on Monday, as markets elsewhere acrossEuroperallied. The FTSE 100 was up 0.2%, while Germany’s Dax was little changed.Monday’sannouncement of a snap election in Spainby the socialist prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, after rightwing parties torpedoed emergency housing legislation last week has also fuelled eurozone uncertainty. Madrid’s benchmark Ibex 35 index rose by 0.5%.“Europe is taking the spotlight at the start of the week, as fiscal and political concerns hit the bloc,” said Kathleen Brooks, the research director at XTB. “France is the epicentre of the concerns; however, Spain is also set to get ready for an early election, which is adding to investor worries.”Amid a global sell-off in sovereign debt as the Iran war rattles markets, the yield – in effect the interest rate – on French 10-year government bonds last week hit the highest level since 2002, before dipping back on Friday.This pushed the gap between France and Germany’s borrowing costs, an important measure of investor concern, to its widest level since 2012 at the height of theeurozone sovereign debt crisis.Investors are focused on Paris’s fiscal position and concerns that the presidential election and a hung parliament – with Marine Le Pen’s far-right National Rally partygaining ground– could make it tougher for the government to curtail a yawning budget deficit.The minority government of the French prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, announced plans last month for a €54bn (£45.8bn) savings drive to curb borrowing levels, setting the stage for a fierce political battle.With President Emmanuel Macron’s centrist administration under pressure amidstrikes and protests across the country, the budget measures involve cutting pensions spending and funding for government departments, excluding defence.Lecornu said the savings would result in limiting a budget deficit of 5.5% of GDP this year to 5% next year. He warned that without action the shortfall between public spending and revenue could reach 6.5%.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHowever, investors fear political pressures could derail fiscal consolidation, threatening to push up borrowing and adding to France’s debt pile at a time of soaring government borrowing costs.Analysts warned the stresses in the French bond market could spread to other countries in the euro area, stoking fears over a return to the dynamics of the 2010s sovereign debt crisis.It comes amid concerns over the test facing the European Central Bank from mounting inflationary pressures from the war in the Middle East and the risk France’s debt problem spreads throughout the euro area.Roberto Mialich, a currency strategist at the Italian bank UniCredit, said: “Investors still do not rule out riding a further decline of the euro, making a retest of $1.10 possible in the near term.“This is also because growing political tensions across the eurozone (primarily in France and Spain) and fears of contagion across the European sovereign debt market are putting pressure on the euro.”Explore more on these topicsEuroCurrenciesEconomicsEuropean UnionFranceEuropeDollarnewsShareReuse this content

title: NFL suspends line judge for swearing at Cardinals’ Trey McBride during game | Arizona Cardinals | The Guardian
description: The NFL has suspended a line judge two games for swearing at Arizona tight end Trey McBride
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The NFL has suspended a line judge two games for swearing at Arizona tight end Trey McBride
Content: Trey McBride played in Arizona’s loss to the New York Giants.Photograph: Seth Wenig/APView image in fullscreenTrey McBride played in Arizona’s loss to the New York Giants.Photograph: Seth Wenig/APArizona CardinalsNFL suspends line judge for swearing at Cardinals’ Trey McBride during gameIncident came after tight end appealed non-callSecond official suspended for actions in Minnesota gameAgenciesMon 5 Oct 2026 17.04 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 17.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheNFLhas suspended a line judge two games for swearing at Arizona tight end Trey McBride.Line judge Jeff Seeman wascaught on camera cursing at McBrideduring the Cardinals’ loss at the New York Giants on Sunday. The incident drew the ire of union leader JC Tretter.“This kind of behavior from an official towards a player is unacceptable,” Tretter, the NFL Players Association’s executive director, said on social media along with a video clip of the incident. “Players are consistently held accountable when the roles are reversed. We expect the NFL to hold officials to the same standard.”Allow content provided by a third party?This article includes content hosted onembed.bsky.app. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as the provider may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content,click 'Allow and continue'.Allow and continueThe incident took place with just under five minutes left after officials did not call a penalty on New York’s Dru Phillips on a crucial third down, which the Cardinals did not convert. McBride questioned the call and Seeman appeared to respond to his appeal by saying “fuck you”. Arizona punted and the Giants went on to win the game 36-24. McBride did not address the incident in his postgame comments.Referee Adrian Hill was also suspended Monday for unprofessional conduct in the Miami-Minnesota game. Hill yelled at Eric Wilson and pointed for him to get away after the Vikings linebacker tried to help him to his feet after a collision knocked him over.The terrifying, unbeaten Chiefs would like you to know your predictions were wrongRead more“I just think it’s one of those situations in kind of a high-energy moment there,” Minnesota coach Kevin O’Connell said Monday. “I think stuff like that can happen sometimes, but I don’t have any major concerns, and I think Adrian’s a really good official and does a really good job. I think that was just kind of fast moment that happened, and we can put it behind us, hopefully.”Wilson said he had no issues with Hill’s conduct. “That was funny, honestly,” Wilson told reporters after the game. “I ended up apologizing to him and explained the situation. He was cool about it. He understood what was going on.”The league’s vice-president of officiating, Ramon George, issued the suspensions.This isn’t the first time an official has been punished for his interactions with a player on the field.Umpire Roy Ellison was punished twice for his behavior. In 2018, he was fined $9,300 and placed on administrative leave for one game after he was accused of calling Buffalo defensive end Jerry Hughes a derogatory term. Ellison was also suspended for one game in 2013 for making “a profane and derogatory statement” to Washington left tackle Trent Williams.Explore more on these topicsArizona CardinalsNFLUS sportsnewsShareReuse this content

title: The terrifying, unbeaten Chiefs would like you to know your predictions were wrong | NFL | The Guardian
description: Kansas City beat the surprisingly feisty Las Vegas Raiders on Sunday. They already look like a very real contender after a lost season in 2025
Author: Doug Farrar
Headline: Kansas City beat the surprisingly feisty Las Vegas Raiders on Sunday. They already look like a very real contender after a lost season in 2025
Content: Patrick Mahomes warms up before the Chiefs’ win over the Raiders on Sunday.Photograph: Rick Scuteri/APView image in fullscreenPatrick Mahomes warms up before the Chiefs’ win over the Raiders on Sunday.Photograph: Rick Scuteri/APNFLThe terrifying, unbeaten Chiefs would like you to know your predictions were wrongKansas City beat the surprisingly feisty Las Vegas Raiders on Sunday. They already look like a very real contender after a lost season in 2025Doug FarrarMon 5 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 13.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe rivalry between theKansas City Chiefsand the Las Vegas Raiders goes back to the formation of the American Football League in 1960, when the Chiefs were the Dallas Texans, and the Raiders resided in Oakland. At no time in that rivalry had both teams faced each other with a record of 3-0 or better until Sunday’s game at Las Vegas’s Allegiant Stadium. An unbeaten record wasn’t entirely surprising for the Chiefs with Patrick Mahomes, but the Raiders? The team won only three games in the whole of last season, but this new Raiders team under Klint Kubiak presents all kinds of challenges for opponents.At first, it appeared that the Raiders might go on to their first 4-0 start to a season since 2002, when they made it all the way to the Super Bowl, where they were vivisected by the Tampa Bay Buccaneers and their former head coach, Jon Gruden. Kubiak’s team held a 13-10 halftime lead on Sunday, and Kubiak told CBS’s Tracy Wolfson at the halfthat his team was going to win the game.Things looked promising the Raiders until running back Kenneth Walker’s two fourth-quarter touchdowns put the score at 30-19 in Kansas City’s favor, and as game as the Raiders were to stage a comeback, it didn’t quite happen. Kirk Cousins’ amazing 20-yard touchdown pass to tight end Brock Bowers with 1:46 left in the game, and Cousins’ successful two-point conversion to receiver Cody White, put the score at 30-27, and the Chiefs went three-and-out on their subsequent drive after an unsuccessful onside kick by the Raiders. But Chiefs punter Matt Araiza placed the ball perfectly at the Las Vegas one-yard line, and Chiefs safety Xavier Nwankpa’s interception of a Cousins pass with 10 seconds sealed the game.The Raiders may not have won the game, but they continue to win respect they haven’t earned in years. Kubiak brought all the smarts he showed as the Seattle Seahawks’ offensive coordinator last season, and defensive coordinator Rob Leonard has a bunch of lesser-known players (as well as edge demon Maxx Crosby) playing above their projected stations. And it doesn’t hurt that Cousins, at the age of 38, is playing some of the best football of his career.As for the 4-0 Chiefs, they are officially back to the top of the NFL after a disastrous 6-11 2025 season. Everybody who picked other teams to make the Super Bowl (and that includesjust about everybody) may want to check those opinions at the door. Mahomes isn’t the force who blew away opponents at his peak, but he has been careful with the ball this season. He only has two interceptions to go alongside his seven touchdown passes, and is still unflappable on third downs. Two of his main targets were injured in Sunday’s game – Rashee Rice left with a hamstring issue and Tyquan Thornton was carted off after sufferinga dislocated ankle– but the offense has been boosted by the arrival of Walker, who has rushed for 173 yards, 117 yards, 70 yards and 177 yards in his first four games since arriving in Kansas City from the Seattle Seahawks. And that’s before we get to the now routine brilliance of Steve Spagnuolo’s defensive schemes.The Week 18 rematch between these two teams may be for a lot more than just AFC West bragging rights.MVP of the weekCeeDee Lamb, WR, Dallas Cowboys.Lamb’s work against the Houston Texans in Dallas’s 34-30 win may have been his single-game masterpiece. Lamb saw 21 targets, catching 17 passes for 189 yards and the game-winning touchdown with 40 seconds left. The 21 targets in a gameis tied for fifth-most since records began, and the 17 catches is tied for fourth all-time.View image in fullscreenCeeDee Lamb leaves the field after a brilliant performance.Photograph: Erik Williams/Zuma Press Wire/ShutterstockMoreover, had Dak Prescott seen Lamb wide open on a play where he didn’t get the ball (much to Lamb’s extreme frustration), the receiver’s final numbers could have been even better. One week after the Cowboys’ coaching staff failed the players in all three phases, Lamb apparently decided to take care of business by himself – though he did have a little help from running back Javonte Williams and his three touchdowns.As for the 0-4 Texans, we’re sure they already know that the only team ever to make the postseason with that kind of opening deficitare the 1992 San Diego Chargers.Video of the weekThrough the first three weeks of the season, the regression of Drake Maye was one of the league’s most disconcerting stories. The 2025 MVP runner-up hadn’t resembled that player all season long, but Maye looked good in a crucial 29-26 win over the Buffalo Bills on Sunday. Maye completed 22 of 37 passes for 269 yards, three touchdowns, one interception, and a passer rating of 97.7, and his game-winning touchdown to Efton Chism with 1:50 left was certainly a highlight for the second-year undrafted free agent from Eastern Washington, who had caught two passes on three targets for minus one-yard this season before his 23-yarder here.Allow content provided by a third party?This article includes content hosted onembed.bsky.app. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as the provider may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content,click 'Allow and continue'.Allow and continueStat of the weekIt had been one of the weirdest streaks in football history. The New York Jets failed to record an interception last season, and the drought continued through the first three games of the 2026 campaign.It appeared that relief had finally come in the first quarter of the Jets’ Sunday game against the Chicago Bears when defensive tackle T’Vondre Sweat came up with a Tyson Bagent pass,but the interception was called backdue to an illegal use of hands penalty on cornerback Azareye’h Thomas.The Jets’ long nightmare would end later in the half, though, when Minkah Fitzpatricknabbed a deep Bagent pass to Colston Loveland.It was the Jets’ first interception in 637 days, 636 opponent pass attempts, and 20 games.View image in fullscreenThe Jets celebrate the end of some unwelcome history.Photograph: David Banks/APWe’re guessing that no team will come anywhere close to that “record” for a very long time. Aaron Glenn’s team lost the game 23-12, and the Bears had more first downs (34) than the Jets had offensive plays (32), but you take the wins wherever you can.Elsewhere around the leaguePhiladelphia Eagles fans are not generally patient with their team, and they have reasons for angst after Sunday. With 7:31 left in the game, and the Eagles up 20-10, Philly had fourth-and-goal at the Los Angeles two-yard line. At this point, the Rams had a win probability of 3.2%. Jalen Hurts threw an incompletion to Darius Cooper (who had already caught two touchdown passes in the game), and the Rams – who were fighting to avoid a 1-3 start to their season – started their own drive 98 yards from the end zone.Sean McVay’s team traveled that entire distance in a 10-play drive that included four Eagles penalties, and ended with Kyren Williams’s one-yard touchdown run. The Eagles went three-and-out on their next drive. Then the Rams went 79 yards on 10 plays and ended that drive with a Williams run that put the Rams up 24-20.It was up to the Eagles to respond, and they didn’t. On their final drive of the game Hurts was sacked twice, and threw two incompletions. Overall, the Eagles went 0-12 on third down, their 172 yards of total offensewas their lowest in a game in 12 years, and their 68 net passing yards was the lowest total for the team in 23 years.View image in fullscreenThe Eagles let a big lead slip on Sunday.Photograph: Chris Szagola/APYes, the Eagles were missing key players, including right tackle Lane Johnson, receiver DeVonta Smith, and running back Saquon Barkley, but this is going to be a tough one to swallow for the entire city of Philadelphia.It used to be that the field goal of 60 or more yards was pro football’s ultimate rarity. Just four such field goals were made in the entire 20th century. That has certainly changed over the last few seasons, as better kicking balls and better kickers have invaded the NFL.Kickers made 12 of 22 attempts of 60-plus yards last season, and it’s become even more commonplace in 2026.In Week 4’s early slate alone, three kickers attempted kicks of 60 or more yards near the end of the first half, and two successfully converted them.Brandon Aubrey of the Dallas Cowboys,who has made at least one such field goal in each of his four NFL seasons, was the guy who missed. But Chad Ryland of the Arizona Cardinals nailed a 60-yarder with two seconds left in the first half – sadly, that wasn’t enough to beat the New York Giants, who triumphed 36-24. And in his team’s 24-18 win over the Tennessee Titans, Baltimore Ravens kicker Tyler Loop hit a 64-yarder.Drake Maye has returned to form (at least for the moment), which means that the travails of Los Angeles Chargers quarterback Justin Herbert remain the most baffling story of the season. Herbert was supposed to match his rare physical gifts to new offensive coordinator Mike McDaniel’s schematic genius, but that has not happened in any way. Against the Seattle Seahawks, Herbert threw an interception on the first play of the game. On the very next play, Seahawks quarterback Sam Darnold threw it right back to the Chargers, via edge-rusher Tuli Tuipulotu.This marked the first time in pro football historythat quarterbacks traded interceptions on the first two plays of a game. From there, though, the Seahawks took care of business. And now the Chargers sport an 0-4 record, which very few people expected when the season began.Some well-deserved praise for Brian Flores, the Minnesota Vikings’ defensive coordinator. Flores’s crewhas already been one of our pleasant surprises of the season, and in their 15-10 win over the Miami Dolphins, the Vikings didn’t score a touchdown. They also didn’t score a touchdown in their 9-3 Week 2 win over the Chicago Bears. Why is this relevant? Because it hasn’t happened since the earliest days of pro football. The last teams to start 4-0 while failing to score touchdowns in two of those games were (in order)the 1922 Chicago Cardinals, the 1923 Chicago Cardinals, and the 1934 Detroit Lions.Don’t worry Bryce Young, we see youturning into a competent NFL quarterback(with some help from Tetairoa McMillan).Finally,if you’re going to swearplease remember that the cameras are everywhere on an NFL field.Explore more on these topicsNFLKansas City ChiefsLas Vegas RaidersUS sportsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Daniil Medvedev disqualified from China Open semi after hitting fan with ball | Tennis | The Guardian
description: Daniil Medvedev was disqualified from his China Open semi-final with Novak Djokovic ⁠after hitting a rebounding ball into the crowd
Author: John Brewin
Headline: Daniil Medvedev was disqualified from his China Open semi-final with Novak Djokovic ⁠after hitting a rebounding ball into the crowd
Content: A spectator is injured after Daniil Medvedev hit a ball into the crowd during his semi-final match against  Novak Djokovic at the China Open.Photograph: Tingshu Wang/ReutersView image in fullscreenA spectator is injured after Daniil Medvedev hit a ball into the crowd during his semi-final match against  Novak Djokovic at the China Open.Photograph: Tingshu Wang/ReutersTennisDaniil Medvedev disqualified from China Open semi after hitting fan with ballPlayer struck rebounding ball into Beijing crowdDjokovic advances to final against De MinaurJohn BrewinMon 5 Oct 2026 10.35 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 15.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDaniil Medvedev was disqualified from his China Open semi-final with Novak Djokovic on Monday after hitting a rebounding ball into the crowd that struck a ​spectator in the eye.The Russian world ‌No 5 was ‌trailing 7-5, 5-3 and had lost a point ‌when, in frustration, he struck a ball that had come off the back wall. The spectator, sitting in the first row, clutched his left eye and appeared in pain as he left the gallery, assisted by the stadium’s ‌staff.“Terribly sorry to the spectator, first of all,” Medvedev said, adding it was “100% an accident” and that he wished to apologise in person. “The ball was bouncing back so I tried to just hit it anywhere so it doesn’t go out from the court. When I saw the result I felt horrible.”View image in fullscreenDaniil Medvedev is disqualified from the match.Photograph: Jessica Lee/EPAThe incident added further to a fiery reputation for the 2021 US Open champion, three times a losing finalist at the Australian Open, born of a series of incidents where Medvedev’s temper has flared. In April, at the Monte Carlo Open,he smashed his racket several timesand placed the remnants in a courtside dustbin during his 6-0, 6-0 loss to Matteo Berrettini.At the 2025 US Open,he received a $42,500 fineafter losing his temper when a photographer interrupted Benjamin Bonzi’s serve for match point. Play was held up for more than six minutes as Medvedev riled up the crowd and insulted the umpire. “What I say and what I do, in my head, I want to do worse and I cannot because there are rules, because we’re on a tennis court,” he said.View image in fullscreenDaniil Medvedev speaks to the media after being disqualified.Photograph: Andy Wong/APAt the 2025 Australian Open,he was fined £54,000, one of biggest sums in grand slam history, after breaking a net camera by repeatedly smashing it with his racket. He also had to pay for the camera.“I was shocked. I hope that person is not badly injured,” said ​Djokovic, who wasdisqualified from the US Open in 2020under similar circumstances. “On the other hand, I also feel sorry for Daniil because I know exactly how it feels to be disqualified in a big match. I’m sure Daniil didn’t ​want to do this intentionally.”Both ​semi-finals in Beijing ended prematurely as Hubert ​Hurkacz retired with ‌an adductor ​injury. Australia’s Alex de Minaur was leading 6-4, 3-2 when his opponent, who had struggled with movement throughout the match, retired.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |FortnightlySign up toThe HotspotA new fortnightly newsletter covering the intersection of sport and the climate crisisEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionQuick GuideHow do I sign up for sport breaking news alerts?ShowIn the Guardian app, tap the Profile settings button at the top right, then select Notifications. Turn on sport notifications.If you already have the Guardian app, make sure you’re on the most recent version.If you don't have the Guardian app, download it from theiOS App Storeon iPhone or theGoogle Play storeon Android by searching for 'The Guardian'.Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Elsewhere, the defending champion, Carlos Alcaraz, overcame early wobbles on his serve to outclass fellow Spaniard Jaume Munar 5-7, 6-3, 6-1 and reach the Japan Open final, taking a step towards his first singles title after ​his comeback from a wrist injury. He will face Jiri Lehecka in Tuesday’s final.The ​23-year-old, who moved through the gears ‌duringTeam Europe’s triumphant ‌Laver Cup campaign last month, looked comfortable against the qualifier in Tokyo at ‌5-4 before gifting him the opening set with two shaky service games.“I don’t know what happened,” said Alcaraz, who dropped 16 consecutive points at the end of the first set. “I started the match well, got a break and was serving for the set.“It seems like I’m struggling every first set. But the way I come back every time, ​I’m really happy about it. Jaume’s a pretty tough player and these conditions suit him pretty well. I just tried to stay there as much as I could.”Explore more on these topicsTennisDaniil MedvedevNovak DjokovicnewsShareReuse this content

title: Ronaldo’s break with Portugal is sad, fitting, and long overdue | Cristiano Ronaldo | The Guardian
description: The star’s rift with Jorge Jesus is an unfortunate affair. But the forward has been holding his national team back for years
Author: Jonathan Wilson
Headline: The star’s rift with Jorge Jesus is an unfortunate affair. But the forward has been holding his national team back for years
Content: Cristiano Ronaldo and Portugal coach Jorge Jesus were at odds during this international window.Composite: Getty, ShutterstockView image in fullscreenCristiano Ronaldo and Portugal coach Jorge Jesus were at odds during this international window.Composite: Getty, ShutterstockSoccer with Jonathan WilsonCristiano RonaldoRonaldo’s break with Portugal is sad, fitting, and long overdueThe star’s rift with Jorge Jesus is an unfortunate affair. But the forward has been holding his national team back for yearsSign up for our free newsletter hereJonathan WilsonMon 5 Oct 2026 11.30 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 11.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIf this is to be the end forCristiano Ronaldoat international level, at least it can be said that he left the stage as he bestrode it: with monumental self-regard. Ronaldo has always been a preening, self-absorbed player, but for a time, when he was one of the best in the world, it could be tolerated. For the past four years, though, he has actively and obviously held Portugal back. There is a great generation of technical talent here weighed down by the monstrous albatross of his ego.To recap the basic details of the past couple of weeks. Ronaldo played 67 minutes ofPortugal’s scratchy 1-0 win over Wales. Portugal coach Jorge Jesus, who replaced Roberto Martínez after the World Cup, said he had a verbal agreement with Ronaldo that he would not start the following game against Norway but would perhaps come off the bench. Early in the second half, Ronaldo went to warm up – although whether that was on his own initiative or because Jesus had told him to is unclear. The game was tight, Portugal ultimately winning 2-1, and Jesus did not bring Ronaldo on.Cristiano Ronaldo’s Portugal walkout divides a nation as Jorge Jesus asserts controlRead moreTo Ronaldo and his army of apologists, Jesus was guilty of an unacceptable provocation. Jesus’s view was that winning the game took priority over the extremely delicate feelings of a 41-year-old forward.Ronaldo walked out on the squad, and perhaps on his international career, although only three days later, seemingly after Jesus had refused to pay penance for his blasphemy. Which is sad, although perhaps not quite in the way Ronaldo thinks it is.It’s possible Jesus, who also coached Ronaldo at Al Nassr, could have handled the situation differently. He is not, it’s fair to say, a diplomat. After Martínez’s soft-pedalling, that is, though, perhaps exactly what was needed. Jesus is 72. His vision of management is old-school, which is to say that he is a dictator and he takes orders only from the club president, and then only if he feels like it. His career has been characterized by rifts with players who have resisted him. In a sense the only surprise is that his falling out with Ronaldo took until the second game of his reign.View image in fullscreenCristiano Ronaldo was left on the sidelines against Norway.Photograph: Grzegorz Wajda/SOPA Images/ShutterstockOthers might have been cowed in the face of Ronaldo’s sulk, the online backlash and criticism from some of the Portuguese press, certain elements of which Ronaldo owns, but not Jesus. He is a man of great eloquence and is always quotable but, even by his standards, his response to the furore has been remarkable as he has insisted on the primacy of the team over any individual. “I can say to any player that you’re starting on the bench: if I need you for 30 minutes you’re going to play, if I don’t need you, you’re not going to play,” he said. “The way I was reading the game he didn’t come on. Because it’s not Cristiano, just like it will never be any player that will change my ideas as the coach. Never! Not him, not anyone in football. Not him, not anyone, not any president. Never! Zero!”His hardline approach might have backfired had Portugal then lost to Denmark, but they won 4-2, playing superbly. Gonçalo Ramos, who might have thought he had already settled this argument by replacing Ronaldo at the 2022 World Cup for the last-16 game against Switzerland andscoring a hat-trick in a 6-1 win, set up the first and scored another against the Danes, having already scored the winner against Norway. “The new manager is a great help,” Ramos said. “We have clearer ideas; we know exactly where each teammate is, both in defense and attack. We’re improving day by day, and it’s all part of a process. We’re very happy with the win, once again against a good team.” Ramos was on target Sunday as Portugal came from behind to beat Norway at home, making it four wins out of four in this window.The tendency until now has been for the otherPortugalplayers to back Ronaldo, to insist he was an icon and that they didn’t mind his superannuated lumbering. Bruno Fernandes has been notably diplomatic, but others are starting to break cover. Ramos’s former Paris Saint-Germain teammate Vitinha, for instance, who has seen at club level how beneficial a purge of egos can be, observed that Portugal’s improvement has been “the work of the coach … I think beyond the win, the content of our game was great.”Jesus has offered Ronaldo another meeting to try to resolve the situation, but the Portuguese football federation seems already to have accepted how the affair will end, beginning plans for a farewell game for the country’s record scorer. Both Jesus and Ronaldo have indicated they will say more this week.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice weeklySign up toSoccer DeskJonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBut the truth is that this is a break that should have happened long ago. For three tournaments, Ronaldo has undermined an extremely talented Portugal. This is a sad story. It is sad Ronaldo’s career should have ended this way. But the saddest element is that a great player could be so deluded about his own fading ability that a national team’s hopes and dreams should have been sacrificed to his quest to break goalscoring records.This is an extract from Soccer Desk, a newsletter from the Guardian US.Subscribe for free here.Explore more on these topicsCristiano RonaldoSoccer with Jonathan WilsonPortugalUefafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: F1 looks amateurish and incompetent after farcical scenes in Sepang | Formula One 2026 | The Guardian
description: Review is under way, but there will be no quick fix for misconceived regulations that resulted in cars being unable to run in the rain
Author: Giles Richards
Headline: Review is under way, but there will be no quick fix for misconceived regulations that resulted in cars being unable to run in the rain
Content: Heavy rain delayed the race in Sepang and led to chaos as software in the cars was unable to cope with the conditions.Photograph: I-Hwa Cheng/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenHeavy rain delayed the race in Sepang and led to chaos as software in the cars was unable to cope with the conditions.Photograph: I-Hwa Cheng/AFP/Getty ImagesFormula One 2026AnalysisF1 looks amateurish and incompetent after farcical scenes in SepangGiles RichardsReview is under way, but there will be no quick fix for misconceived regulations that resulted in cars being unable to run in the rainMon 5 Oct 2026 11.13 EDTFirst published on Mon 5 Oct 2026 08.12 EDTShareFormula One has gone to no little pains this season in insisting the new format is more popular than ever, despiteoverwhelming disapproval from the driversregarding engine regulations. In short, there is nothing to see here.But the farcical scenes that accompaniedthe opening to the Bahrain Grand Prixin Malaysia on Sunday were all too visible and left some drivers expressing open mockery.‘Insane’: F1 drivers unite over engine regulations after chaotic Bahrain GPRead moreMax Verstappen won the race, held at Sepang to replace thecancelled Bahrain GP. It was a dominant drive for his first win of the season, but overshadowed by the sport – that styles itself as the pinnacle of motor racing – looking at best amateurish and at worst incompetent.The race was delayed because of heavy rain and the track was still very wet as the field lined up for the first time this season in such conditions. They ran behind the safety car to conduct two formation laps before the proposed start.As they toured round at low speed in low-grip conditions, the engines’ software, now an integral part of the application of power in engines using an almost equal split of electrical and combustion energy, found itself in a scenario beyond its parameters. Chaos ensued. First, Verstappen announced he could no longer accelerate, thenLewis Hamiltonslowed and came to a stop before having to do a forced reboot of his car to get moving again. A number of drivers reported the same problem as they crawled around and one Haas and one Cadillac ground to a halt. The field was in disarray and the start had to be suspended.The problem was caused by a combination of low engine speeds, low grip and the circuit layout coming up against the wet-weather management of the power-delivery software. An unanticipated bug, as the governing body, the FIA, described it. There was a 53-minute delay while the FIA wrote and applied a software update. Verstappen and Hamilton mockingly compared it to the time they had driven in Lego cars as part of the pre-race entertainment at Silverstone in July.“These engines are so complicated and a lot of software is implemented,” said Verstappen. “When there is some kind of error or glitch, that’s the problem. I triggered it first, then I look in my mirror and I just see everyone … I was, like, wait, are they waiting for me?”“It was like the Lego race,” said Hamilton. “Yeah, we had the same speed,” said Verstappen. Both drivers were, by now, laughing at the absurdity of the situation.The FIA said it will conduct a review with the teams and the power-unit manufacturers, but the damage has been done, once more highlighting the foibles of these engines and how much has been taken out of drivers’ control.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |FortnightlySign up toThe HotspotA new fortnightly newsletter covering the intersection of sport and the climate crisisEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionQatar and Abu Dhabi grands prix to go ahead despite Middle East conflict, says F1 chiefRead moreThe debate on the engines has raged all season. Addressing questions about why, for example, battery-usage data was not part of F1’s broadcasts, amid accusations it would demonstrate how hamstrung drivers were by battery management, F1’s chief executive Stefano Domenicali cited a conversation about the sport’s accessibility with the Star Wars creator George Lucas, himself a noted car enthusiast.“He gave us an incredible chance to see how we can really simplify things because the new fans are not understanding … what is behind the scenes. They are fascinated on the fact there is a lot of action.”F1 clearly believes the force is strong with its product the way it is and will doubtless point to the fact that when the race did eventually get under way it was an entertaining affair.Hamilton came back from dropping to 17th to third place, Verstappen was at his imperious best out front, while George Russell’s dramatic late retirement all but put paid to his title hopes.Yet even the new fans cannot fail to have observed the reality that was laid bare in Sepang: drivers reduced to furiously pushing buttons on a steering wheel, hostages to software over which they have no control, then deriding and condemning the situation afterwards.Moreover, F1 might also consider it dodged a bullet. Had the race started in the dry and then a downpour arrived, the failure would have happened as the cars circulated mid-race behind the safety car.The finger should not be simply pointed at the FIA. These rules were agreed with full input from F1, the teams and the power unit manufacturers.As Carlos Sainz perceptively asked: “My only question is who, five years ago, decided this was the direction to go?”No quick fix is coming, but what happened in Sepang emphasised how misconceived these regulations were, regardless of how they are perceived by fans of every persuasion.View image in fullscreenMax Verstappen won the race, but mocked the situation that unfolded before the start.Photograph: Eric Alonso/DPPI/ShutterstockExplore more on these topicsFormula One 2026Formula OneMotor sportMax VerstappenLewis HamiltonanalysisShareReuse this content

title: NHL’s all-time leading goalscorer Alex Ovechkin to retire at end of season | Washington Capitals | The Guardian
description: Alex Ovechkin said on Monday that his 22nd season in the NHL will be his last, beginning the farewell tour for the longtime Washington Capitals captain
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Alex Ovechkin said on Monday that his 22nd season in the NHL will be his last, beginning the farewell tour for the longtime Washington Capitals captain
Content: Alex Ovechkin will retire as one of the NHL’s greatest ever players.Photograph: Adam Hunger/APView image in fullscreenAlex Ovechkin will retire as one of the NHL’s greatest ever players.Photograph: Adam Hunger/APWashington CapitalsNHL’s all-time leading goalscorer Alex Ovechkin to retire at end of seasonRussian led Capitals to their first-ever Stanley Cup winOvechkin turned 41 in SeptemberAssociated PressMon 5 Oct 2026 12.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAlex Ovechkin said on Monday that his 22nd season in the NHL will be his last, beginning the farewell tour for the longtime Washington Capitals captainwho holdsthe league’s career goalscoring record.Ovechkin told his teammates of his decision before the Capitals posted a message from the Russian star on social media.Alex Ovechkin claims he’s ‘not in politics’. His pro-Putin video says the oppositeRead more“It’s sad, but it is what it is,” Ovechkin said in his locker room address. “It’s hard, but let’s enjoy it and let’s do some special things this year.”Ovechkin signed a one-year contract this past summer and turned 41 in September. All signs pointed to this being the end of his career, and he said he and his family decided as much in recent months.“I love this game so much, but I know in my heart it’s the right decision,” he said in Monday’s statement. The Capitals’ home opener is on Wednesday night.Ovechkin broke Wayne Gretzky’s goals record in April 2025 and entered this season at 929. The front office acquired Jordan Kyrou and Alex Tuch in trades and signed fellow forward Boone Jenner and defenseman Vincent Desharnais in free agency to add around a young core in the hopes of making another long playoff run and contending for the Stanley Cup.“We have an unbelievable team this year,” Ovechkin said. “Let’s make the playoffs, let’s have fun and enjoy the moment because times fly.”Ovechkin has spent his entire career with Washington, winning the Calder Trophy as rookie of the year in 2005-06, the Hart Trophy as MVP three times and leading the NHL in scoring nine times. He was playoff MVP in 2018 when he led the Caps to thefirst Stanley Cup championship in franchise history.There’s been speculation Ovechkin could receive an unfriendly reception on the roadafter he appeared in an adfor a party aligned with Vladimir Putin during the offseason. But there wasn’t much sign of that during the first two games of the season – at Carolina and at Tampa Bay.When he addressed the fallout from that the Putin advert, Ovechkin confirmed he’d be going back to live in Russia when he retired from theNHL.In Washington’s season-opening win over the Hurricanes, Ovechkin had just under 13 minutes of ice time, the lowest of his career in a game when he wasn’t injured or ejected.The Capitals missed the playoffs in 2025-26, but Ovechkin played all 82 games and scored 32 goals. He’s reached 30 in every season of his career except 2020-21, when he played only 45 games.Long before he broke through during the Capitals’ Stanley Cup run, Ovechkin had rejuvenated hockey in Washington, and he’ll retire as one of the city’s most accomplished athletes in any sport. The Capitals drafted him No 1 overall in 2004, and he and Pittsburgh’s Sidney Crosby became stars almost immediately in 2005 when the league emerged from missing a season because of a lockout.Ovechkin’s combination of goalscoring skill, physicality and boundless energy made him an instant hit, and he scored a career-high 65 goals in his third season, which earned him the first of his Hart Trophies.Washington’s penchant for postseason heartache, which existed long before Ovechkin showed up, followed him for a while as well. The Capitals won the Presidents’ Trophy three times with the league’s best regular-season record, falling short in the playoffs each time before a Washington team that merely won its division finally went all the way in the playoffs.In four postseason meetings between Crosby and Ovechkin – in 2009, 2016, 2017, 2018 – the winner won the Stanley Cup each time.Explore more on these topicsWashington CapitalsNHLIce hockeyUS sportsnewsShareReuse this content

title: The USMNT’s kids are thriving, and ‘they have a bit of swag to them’ | USA | The Guardian
description: The post-World Cup youth movement has paid off with historic plays that, for the moment, feel natural, sustainable, and needed
Author: Jeff Rueter
Headline: The post-World Cup youth movement has paid off with historic plays that, for the moment, feel natural, sustainable, and needed
Content: Cavan Sullivan’s first international goal was one to remember.Photograph: Kevin Abele/Icon Sportswire/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenCavan Sullivan’s first international goal was one to remember.Photograph: Kevin Abele/Icon Sportswire/Getty ImagesUSAThe USMNT’s kids are thriving, and ‘they have a bit of swag to them’The post-World Cup youth movement has paid off with historic plays that, for the moment, feel natural, sustainable and neededJeff Rueterin St Paul, MinnesotaMon 5 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 13.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFrom the outside, a moment like the one Cavan Sullivanproduced Saturdayseemed to be pulled directly from dreamland. Turns out, it pretty much was.“I was amazed. I was excited,” the 17-year-old said of learning he’d start for the US men’s national team against Mexico, in what would become a 3-0 win. “I texted my family right after, and after lunch, I took a nap. Before I go to sleep, I visualize and try to manifest good things for the night. Some things come to fruition, some don’t.”Sullivan visualized scoring, and celebrating with a knee slide towards the corner. Hours later, he was doing exactly that, picking off a poor pass from goalkeeper Raúl Rangel and chipping him from 35 yards out to become the USMNT’s youngest-ever goal scorer, sliding toward the corner flag after a full sprint with his teammates in hot pursuit.“That wasn’t the way I pictured scoring a goal, but the celebration was,” Sullivan said.The more incredible thing about Sullivan’s moment, aside from its historic nature and its semi-dreamy origins, is how normal it is for this window for the US. All but one of the 13 potential debutants called in byMauricio Pochettinohave seen time on the field, most of them impressing. Julian Hall, 18, has scored in all three of his appearances. Mathis Albert broke Christian Pulisic’s decade-old benchmark to become the program’s youngest goalscorer and held the record for a whole four days before Sullivan’s chip.View image in fullscreenMathis Albert was briefly the youngest goal scorer in USMNT history.Photograph: Taylor Banner/USSF/Getty ImagesGiven the opponents so far, it’s fair to say these players aren’t inching into the shallow end of the pool. They’ve been thrown in at the deep end, and they are swimming.Peru and Chile missed this summer’s World Cup, but they are far from pushovers. While the US struggled to keep them off the scoreboard, the Americans made up for defensive miscues with a commitment to attacking, scoring four goals in each friendly.Cavan Sullivan’s stunner makes him youngest-ever USMNT scorer in romp over MexicoRead moreThe back half of this long-winded window was primed to be even more enlightening, with Saturday’s win over Mexico and Tuesday’s date with Canada still to come. Newly appointed captain Tyler Adams has said that these games will help determine the region’s top dog. Their final opponent of the quartet will hardly give them an inch, with Canada raring to take another step inJesse Marsch’ssecond cycle at the helm.On Saturday, the US showed they can weather a storm. Pochettino’s young side were unable to get anything going in the attacking half for most of the first 45 minutes. Mexico stymied the hosts with a man-marking scheme that was appreciated by the El Tri faithful, whose numbers in the stadium dwarfed those of the US. And yet, as Pochettino put it, a lineup with an average age of 23 years and 25 days “suffered together” without conceding before a shock US opener flipped the script.Young? Bet, as they’d say.“It’s really important to play this type of game,” Pochettino said. “To build our experience, to know what [is needed] to play this type of game, and the adversity. I think it will help when we start the qualification for the World Cup. I think that experience will help the team to manage the pressure and stress in a different way. You need to feel that.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice weeklySign up toSoccer DeskJonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionJesse Marsch: ‘We Americans have been inundated with propaganda since we were young’Read moreImportantly, this added experience comes to several new players who offer reinforcement in crucial areas of need.Diego Kochen has been the standout of the four selected goalkeepers, more confident commanding his area than Chris Brady and more natural in possession than Matt Freese. Sullivan has quickly found ways to affect the game at right wing, a role Pochettino largely entrusted to Sergiño Dest throughout the World Cup summer. Hall’s exceptional off-ball movement makes him another capable goalscorer as an alternative to Folarin Balogun (and even more competition for Ricardo Pepi).Others also look like safe bets to stick around. Albert and Justin Ellis are dynamic options for the team in transition. Neil Pierre and Adri Mehmeti could be useful additions in central defense and midfield, respectively. There’s little room for complacency among Pochettino’s core.“They’re battling for it, and I love to see it,” center-back Chris Richards said Saturday. “I mean, the young guys, they’re hungry. They have a bit of swag to them, and that’s something that I’ve been very impressed with.”View image in fullscreenAdri Mehmeti and Julian Hall have each impressed in their first international camp.Photograph: Bill Barrett/ISI Photos/Getty ImagesThis mass debut event differs considerably from the last one, which immediately followed the US’s failure to qualify for the 2018 World Cup. That period saw the emergence of Adams, Weston McKennie, Antonee Robinson and Tim Weah, giving the fanbase sorely needed fresh faces. They joined a team with few, if any, senior figures around for the rebuild.This time around, the young guys can get their sea legs without the additional pressure.“I think the balance that we’ve been able to have in lineups, surrounding them with guys that have experience, they can go under the radar for some parts of the game,” Adams said. “They don’t have to put in crazy, crazy performances. We just want to get them in the good spots where they’re comfortable to score goals, to go 1v1, to show the qualities that they have, and we were able to do that.”The trick, then, will be to keep the good vibes of this camp from being an aberration – to avoid the wild fluctuations that have defined much of Pochettino’s USMNT tenure so far.“We need to protect them. We need to support them,” Pochettino said. “Our responsibility now is [ensuring] that this group of talented players [will] grow in the right direction. Today, they were so excited to play. Again in St Louis, against Chile, they were so excited, and they were so excited in playing against Peru in Orlando.“We need to continue with that idea, keep that feeling. Every time that they can be part of this national team is the most important. OK, maybe it’s tough to say that, but I think that is what we expect [as] a coaching staff. It’s not ‘play well or not’. It’s that commitment and the desire to play, that today is the best and the most important game in your life. That is what we try to translate. We need to come to the national team for business, not for fun, and that is what is most important.”Explore more on these topicsUSAUS sportsMauricio PochettinofeaturesShareReuse this content
