title: How did some City fans become aggressive defenders of a nation state’s regime? | Manchester City | The Guardian
description: The Manchester City case is one example of how fandom has warped beyond previous boundaries in online spaces
Author: Sean Ingle
Headline: The Manchester City case is one example of how fandom has warped beyond previous boundaries in online spaces
Content: The Etihad Stadium has not hosted a men’s match since the Premier League’s verdict was announced.Photograph: Adam Vaughan/EPAView image in fullscreenThe Etihad Stadium has not hosted a men’s match since the Premier League’s verdict was announced.Photograph: Adam Vaughan/EPAManchester CityHow did some City fans become aggressive defenders of a nation state’s regime?Sean IngleThe Manchester City case is one example of how fandom has warped beyond previous boundaries in online spacesMon 5 Oct 2026 17.29 EDTFirst published on Mon 5 Oct 2026 16.08 EDTShareAvideo of Liam Gallagher playing in a 1996 charity football match resurfaced on social media recently. Dressed in Manchester City blue and a bucket hat, in truth he appears to be in a fug of cigarettes and alcohol. But then, out of nowhere, he hitsa shot into the top corner. Since last week, though, the Oasis singer has preferred to defend the honour of his club with his studs up.As the fallout from thebiggest scandal in British football historyheaded into a second week, Gallagher was asked what he made of rival fans wanting City tolose all their trophiesafter being found guilty of all the serious charges against them. “There all NEUROTIC little GIMPS,” came the reply on social media. It was one of dozens of sweary, punchy, and often amusing responses, all built on a solitary article of faith: that City will somehow find a way to wriggle free.Let there be blanks instead of Manchester City’s name on trophies: there was no honour there | Jonathan WilsonRead moreBut Gallagher is hardly standing alone. Over at Bluemoon, the biggest City forum, the tone has been just as defiant – albeit with a sprinkle of gallows humour. “Have we been blamed for the Titanic hitting the iceberg yet?” asked one user. “Manchester City shot JFK,” wrote another. “This isn’t just a fight between the PL & City. It’s a fight for the heart, soul & future of football,” reckoned a third.Staggeringly, the forum now has over 192,000 posts since the initial charges against City, dating back to 2023. Naturally the Premier League, jealous rivals and the media all come under heavy fire. Yet there remains a curious reluctance among fans to accept wrongdoing – or to criticise the club’s owners.How might we explain that? I am not sure it is down to pure tribalism, or a determination among City fans to wait for the club’s appeal to play out. It’s more complicated, and more interesting, than that.Let us try to get into the head of the most vociferous City fan since last Tuesday. For decades they were in United’s shadow, then everything changed. Their city did too, given how much Abu Dhabi United Group pumped into it. You can forgive them, then, for not wanting to believe that it was all built on sand during the legal process.But now? Now there is no excuse. So what might explain the reluctance to accept what the independent commission report lays out in great detail? According to the Irish academic Colm Kearns, one reason is because the United Arab Emirates has not only brought unprecedented success and forged emotional bonds with City fans “but have also co-opted elements of the club’s fanbase as aggressive defenders of their regime”.In 2023 Kearns and his colleaguesanalysed huge numbers of postsfrom City fans, going back years, and found that some of them would not only “overlook ethical violations by the Group, but decry and – in some cases – attack the Group’s critics.”In other words the club’s owners had successfully leveraged the tribal loyalty of City fans into being Manchurian Candidates – or, rather, Manchesterism Candidates.Kearns tells me that some sports journalists had even self-censored because of the impact of online abuse from City fans. “We had people talking about how fans would go online and try to find their troll through their personal social feeds, and it sent that on to their editor to get them in trouble,” he says.There is another massive factor here: social media, and the way we now consume sport and communicate with other fans. Thirty years ago, most City fans would live near Manchester and see fans from other clubs at work and in the pub. Nowadays, they can dwell in an online space made up entirely of people who support their own club.View image in fullscreenSocial media has created tribal online spaces for sports fans.Photograph: Lee Smith/Action Images/Reuters“I think it makes fans perhaps more tribally myopic than they would have been before and less likely to look outside of their own club’s perspective,” says Kearns.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAcademics also talk of “sports fandom circles”, in which supporters across the globe increasingly mobilise and fiercely defend athletes or their teams. That phenomenon, which came out of east Asia with popular culture and music, leads supporters to be laser-focused on their own tribe. But it hardly encourages lighthearted banter, common ground, or compromise.In City’s case, Kearns suspects that some fans are putting the club above the wider game, citing a Reddit post that said: “I am a City fan first and a football fan second.” Although, as he concedes, it is impossible to know how many online posters do not live in Manchester, or go to games, and therefore feel the need to prove their bona fide credentials by sticking up for the club at all costs.Either way, where we could go next is interesting. If you were a far-right tech billionaire, why wouldn’t you want to buy a successful sports team – especially if you knew there was an army of potential defenders of your reputation among your new fanbase?Over the weekend I went through the fan forums of other clubs to see what their supporters made of the guilty verdict against City. The overwhelming majority welcomed it, of course, even if some questioned whether City would really get properly punished for their crimes, given the relationship with Abu Dhabi and the British government.“Once you lose faith that the rules apply equally, football becomes something else,” one wrote. “Every title, every match, carries a question mark. I feel cheated. I’m one of the victims. And for that, I hate Manchester City.”Some will agree with that sentiment. Others will raise their eyebrows. I do wonder, though, would that poster feel the same way if the boot was on the other foot, and their club was in the line of fire?Explore more on these topicsManchester CitycommentShareReuse this content

title: Nations League roundup: Olise leads late charge as France bowl over Belgium | Nations League | The Guardian
description: France scored four goals in 14 minutes to triumph against their rivals, two coming from Michael Olise, while Italy saw off Turkey and Hungary edged out Ukraine
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: France scored four goals in 14 minutes to triumph against their rivals, two coming from Michael Olise, while Italy saw off Turkey and Hungary edged out Ukraine
Content: Michael Olise embraces Désiré Doué after scoring France’s third goal of the game.Photograph: Benoît Tessier/ReutersView image in fullscreenMichael Olise embraces Désiré Doué after scoring France’s third goal of the game.Photograph: Benoît Tessier/ReutersNations LeagueNations League roundup: Olise leads late charge as France bowl over BelgiumFrance score four goals in 14 minutes to triumphItaly see off Turkey, Hungary edge out UkraineAgenciesMon 5 Oct 2026 17.31 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 18.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMichael Olise came off the bench to inspire France toa 4-1 win over Belgiumin the Nations League, handing Zinedine Zidane his first home victory since taking charge.Dodi Lukébakio putBelgiumon course for their first competitive win overLes Bleusin 45 years when he fired the visitors in front in the first half at the Stade de France. But the hosts turned the match on its head in a blistering finish, scoring four times in 14 minutes to preserve Zidane’s unbeaten start and move closer to the quarter-finals.Mamardashvili saves penalty as Georgia hold Northern Ireland in Nations LeagueRead moreDésiré Doué hauledFrancelevel in the 77th minute with a low drive from the edge of the area before Olise teed up Rayan Cherki to fire them ahead four minutes later. Olise then put the result beyond doubt with a third goal before adding another in stoppage time to cap a stunning French comeback.France, who also beat Belgium 1-0 in Brussels last week thanks to a late goal from Olise, moved three points clear of Italy at the top of Group A1, with Belgium another point back.ItalybeatTurkey3-1 in Bologna to condemn their opponents to a fourth straight loss, goals from Gianluca Scamacca, Riccardo Calafiori and Pio Esposito doing the business.Zidane heavily rotated his team for the last match of this three-week long international window, with only Ousmane Dembélé keeping his place among the 10 changes. The Manchester United defender Leny Yoro and the Toulouse goalkeeper Guillaume Restes made their debuts, with Dembélé again captaining the side in the absence of the injured Kylian Mbappé.Belgium were without the suspended duo of Kevin De Bruyne and Youri Tielemans but caught France cold when Roméo Lavia’s superb ball split open the home defence, allowing Lukebakio to race clear and produce a clinical finish. Maarten Vandevoordt, making his debut in goal for Belgium, kept out efforts from Esteban Lepaul and Cherki as France pressed for an equaliser, but the dam eventually burst.Doué gathered the ball and shot on the turn, beyond the reach of Vandevoordt, to haul France level. Cherki then turned home a cutback from Olise to give the hosts the lead as the Bayern Munich winger stole the show late on.Olise scrambled in a third in the 88th minute and rolled in a fourth after skilful work from Doué to complete a remarkable turnaround.“That’s football, that’s what we love. There were ⁠difficulties, but that’s part of the game, part of the kinds of matches you can have,” Zidane told TF1.“It’s good to put things right, and ​that’s what we did with an extraordinary second half. We were ‌just missing that final few metres in ‌the first half, but then we turned the match around, it was good.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenMark Csinger punches the air after scoring Hungary’s winner against Ukraine.Photograph: Tibor Illyes/MTI/APIn Group B2, Mark Csinger’s late goal earned second-placedHungarya 2-1 win againstUkrainein Trnava.Viktor Gyökeres scored in his seventh consecutiveNations Leaguegame asSwedenearned a 1-0 win againstRomaniain Group B4, while Ivan Basic’s late penalty gaveBosnia and Herzegovinaa 1-0 victory overPoland. The Burnley striker Marcus Edwards scored a stoppage-time winner asCyprushit back from behind to beatLatvia2-1 in Group C2.Explore more on these topicsNations LeagueFranceBelgiumItalyTurkeynewsShareReuse this content

title: Mamardashvili saves penalty as Georgia hold Northern Ireland in Nations League | Nations League | The Guardian
description: Isaac Price saw his second-half penalty saved as Northern Ireland failed to convert their chances in a goalless draw with Georgia in Belfast
Author: Ewan Murray
Headline: Isaac Price saw his second-half penalty saved as Northern Ireland failed to convert their chances in a goalless draw with Georgia in Belfast
Content: Isaac Price covers his face after failing to convert his second-half penalty.Photograph: Liam McBurney/PAView image in fullscreenIsaac Price covers his face after failing to convert his second-half penalty.Photograph: Liam McBurney/PANations LeagueMamardashvili saves penalty as Georgia hold Northern Ireland in Nations LeagueEwan Murrayat Windsor ParkMon 5 Oct 2026 17.08 EDTFirst published on Mon 5 Oct 2026 17.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis game concluded with mutual irritation and a touch of chaos. It is an indicator of Northern Ireland’s progress that scoreless parity led to wincing from players, management and fans alike. Isaac Price’s 84th-minute missed opportunity from the penalty spot added to the sense of annoyance.Michael O’Neill’s team are atop B2 after a window which, going by the players’s physical condition in the dying stages, has been exhausting. Northern Ireland and their youthful setup are a fascinating international story. They are a team on an upward curve, with standards elevated accordingly. O’Neill bemoaned “immaturity” in the second half, saying: “The disappointing thing is we have eight points instead of 10.”Nations League roundup: Olise leads late charge as France bowl over BelgiumRead moreGeorgia were reduced to fury with seconds of the five minutes of stoppage time remaining. The visitors were adamant they should have been awarded a spot-kick of their own as Saba Sazonov toppled under a challenge from Callum Marshall. Ramaz Svanadze, theGeorgiacoach, diplomatically said he would have to view the incident again.The difficulty for Northern Ireland related to a rising expectation. The superb performance duringFriday’s 3-0 win over Ukrainebacked upvictory away to Georgiaanda draw with Hungary. O’Neill’s men were yet to concede a goal in this section. A team quietly tipped to peak around qualification for Euro 2028 was blossoming earlier than anticipated, and this without the long-term absentee Conor Bradley. Northern Ireland’s oldest starter for Georgia’s visit was the 28-year-old Ciaron Brown.Georgia are a curious case, outside the top 70 in the world yet containing one of its finest players. Clearly Khvicha Kvaratskhelia cannotcarry a nation on his own. Indeed, the superstar’s first act was to pass the ball straight to Ethan Galbraith in the Northern Ireland midfield. During the nondescript early exchanges, Kvaratskhelia also gifted possession to Jamie Donley.What football existed in the first half came from the hosts. Ruairi McConville came closest to opening the scoring with a header from Justin Devenny’s cross, Giorgi Mamardashvili not at all convincing in denying him. Georgia responded, an excellent save from Pierce Charles necessary to deny Zuriko Davitashvili. The let-off triggered a sweeping Northern Ireland move which culminated in Devenny overhitting a low cross.View image in fullscreenKhvicha Kvaratskhelia was kept relatively quiet, but even so came close to scoring a fantastic goal.Photograph: Cathal McNaughton/ReutersNorthern Ireland were frustrated by the wasting of umpteen set plays during that first period. That Davitashvili moment aside, Georgia offered nothing in an attacking sense. Northern Ireland should have edged ahead four minutes before the interval, Patrick Kelly instead fluffing his lines having evaded the Georgia defence from Trai Hume’s through ball. Kelly appeared in two minds over whether to shoot or play in a teammate, with the visitors seizing upon his indecision. The half ended with Price curling a free-kick into the wrong side of the side-netting.Price, born in Yorkshire, exemplifies Northern Ireland’s diligence in sourcing players through bloodline eligibility. The Manchester-born Charles brothers – Shea, the captain, was once again classy in midfield as Pierce kept goal – do likewise. This is, however, no team pulled together from afar; Galbraith was a boy wonder in Belfast before being coaxed to Manchester United as a teenager. His imaginative playmaking will surely one day be worthy of a grander stage than Stoke and the ChampionshipThis big-picture stuff was irrelevant as Georgia stood firm. This was a game of intrigue, where Northern Ireland were superior while lacking a ruthless touch. Georgia’s threat was understated but real.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionGalbraith limped off with 25 minutes to play, in what constituted a blow to O’Neill. The game by now was tense and scrappy. While against better opponents that may have suited Northern Ireland, that was patently not the case this time. Georgia were managing to sap energy from the home support.With fatigue apparent across the pitch, O’Neill turned to a 36-year-old who plies his club trade at Stevenage to beef up the attack. Josh Magennis edges ever close to 100 caps, this was No 93.Kvaratskhelia had been strangely subdued for 79 minutes, but striding forward from midfield, the Paris Saint-Germain forward cracked a 20-yard drive just over the bar. What an outstanding goal it would have been.Magennis was handed a golden chance but Mamardashvili saved. A melee from the subsequent corner led to the crossbar being struck but, more significantly, the video assistant referee’s attention drawn towards a kick in the face of McConville by Budu Zivzivadze. A spot-kick was correctly awarded. Up stepped Price, whose penalty was saved, low to his right, by the Liverpool goalkeeper. Northern Ireland had passed up their moment. Georgia believed they should have been given scope to rub salt into wounds.Explore more on these topicsNations LeagueNorthern IrelandGeorgiamatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Jude awakening: how a more fluid England are ‘unlocking’ Bellingham’s full potential | Jude Bellingham | The Guardian
description: Assistant coach Anthony Barry says new structure means their key attackers are not ‘caged in’ after 7-0 rout of Croatia
Author: David Hytner
Headline: Assistant coach Anthony Barry says new structure means their key attackers are not ‘caged in’ after 7-0 rout of Croatia
Content: Jude Bellingham is enjoying a greater licence to drift in his No 10 position under Thomas Tuchel.Photograph: Marko Perkov/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenJude Bellingham is enjoying a greater licence to drift in his No 10 position under Thomas Tuchel.Photograph: Marko Perkov/AFP/Getty ImagesJude BellinghamJude awakening: how a more fluid England are ‘unlocking’ Bellingham’s full potentialAssistant coach Anthony Barry says new structure means their key attackers are not ‘caged in’ after 7-0 rout of CroatiaDavid HytnerMon 5 Oct 2026 14.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAnthony Barry knows the hunt is on. The England assistant coach has been through the debriefs. He has mulled over the minutiae with Thomas Tuchel to such an extent he is allowed to make a joke at the boss’s expense. “He’s doing my head in,” Barry says with a smile. What is the missing piece of the puzzle? After all the emotion ofEngland’s semi-final finishat the World Cup, how can they take the decisive step to glory?It is early days in the Nations League campaign, which everybody at the Football Association wants to use asa slingshot into Euro 2028when England will co-host, but Barry can see the genesis of an answer. It comes down to liberation, enabling England’s top players to fully express themselves, and there is a reason why he finds himself talking about Jude Bellingham.Bournemouth unhappy over Scott injury but Tuchel says England took ‘zero risk’Read moreThe Real Madrid player was sensational in Saturday’s7-0 win over Croatiain Rijeka, just as he was in the3-2 defeat against Spainat Wembley on the Saturday before that. Playing in the No 10 role but with greater licence to drift, to overload on either side, there were times when Bellingham seemed to be playing with his own ball.The story about why he wore the No 22 shirt at his first club, Birmingham, is well told. Because he was a No 4, a No 8 and a No 10 rolled into one. Tuchel appears to have reached a conclusion, the basis of which was formed at the World Cup when Bellingham excelled: when a talent like him can play in so many positions, perhaps it is better not to give him one at all.“The structure [now in the Nations League] allows Jude to play more from his intuition,” Barry says, “and less from being locked down or caged in a certain position. It allows him to roam and operate in spaces in which he thinks he can be dangerous and so far it’s brought out the best in him.“It is a challenge because Jude can play in any of those positions comfortably and on a high level. So the challenge is to give him a space where he can do it all at once inside of one game. Right now, in a short sample, it seems like we found a solution to unlock all of the potential that Jude has. But we have to continue.”The point is that it is not just about Bellingham, even if he has drawn the eye almost inexorably so far this season. The blueprint was there for all to see against Croatia and it is one in which plenty of players were encouraged to push into new zones away from those traditionally dictated by their positions. Hence Tuchel had the full-backs extremely high, the wingers making zipping runs off the sides.It is about the combinations, the slicker the better, but also about players dropping into unusual areas to provide cover and using their footballing intelligence to ensure the overall structure retains its shape. Hence there was the sight of Harry Kane dropping into defensive spaces out of possession, the kind where most No 9s would never tread.View image in fullscreenJude Bellingham takes on Luka Modric during England’s thrashing of Croatia.Photograph: Raddad Jebarah/ShutterstockIt was impossible to ignore the ferocity of England’s counterpress; how if one player lost the ball, he and his teammates sought to regain it within two or three seconds. Croatia were overwhelmed, especially in the first half, which ended with England four goals up. The intensity has to endure. But it is the proactive add-ons that the management hope will drive the new tournament cycle,continuing against Czechiain the Nations League at Wembley on Tuesday night. It is no longer a positional style. The idea is that it is freer. Is it a reaction to the inhibitions England came to feel in the World Cup semi-final defeat against Argentina?“We have moved to a more principle-driven approach, which allows for more flexibility and fluidity,” Barry says. “But fluidity only looks good if it’s anchored by real principles. There is always a danger in international football with such a lack of time to prepare that if you go for this fluid model it can look quite messy. With the IQ of the players we have, it’s been quite natural for them to work together, operate in different spaces.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“It’s not about starting new, it’s about continuation and adding stuff on top. It’s less prescribed, less fixed in the idea of: ‘You play here, you play there.’ It’s more interchanges of position. We feel it suits this group of players and is the best way to break down opposing blocks.“When you have players like Harry and Jude on the frontline that are really better at moving, that have this deep intuition and IQ for the game … [it is] to trust them, open up spaces for them to operate. It’s also part of the model that we’re moving forward with. We have elite penetration on the last line, whether that comes from our wingers or our full-backs. And we have fluid midfielders with Elliot [Anderson], Alex [Scott] and Declan [Rice], who are happy to move for miles.”Kane is primed to win his 125th cap on Tuesday night and equal Peter Shilton’sEnglandmen’s record. It is a time for tributes and Barry was effusive in his praise of Kane’s professionalism and leadership, his selflessness, his lack of ego; how he is happy to “track back and do the dirty work”.Barry had a better line. “He’s the best ball-striker I have ever worked with,” he said. It is worth noting Barry worked with Cristiano Ronaldo during his time with Portugal as the assistant manager to Roberto Martínez. It is one key reason for Barry’s sense of optimism. There are many others.Explore more on these topicsJude BellinghamEnglandNations LeaguefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Police occupy Djibouti FA headquarters amid attempt to oust Fifa council member | Soccer | The Guardian
description: Attempts to oust Souleiman Waberi as the president of the Djibouti football federation reached a dramatic climax on Monday
Author: Romain Molina
Headline: Attempts to oust Souleiman Waberi as the president of the Djibouti football federation reached a dramatic climax on Monday
Content: Souleiman Waberi (centre) pictured at a Fifa council meeting last October.Photograph: Marcio Machado/Fifa/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSouleiman Waberi (centre) pictured at a Fifa council meeting last October.Photograph: Marcio Machado/Fifa/Getty ImagesSoccerPolice occupy Djibouti FA headquarters amid attempt to oust Fifa council memberGroup of clubs wants FA president Souleiman Waberi outWaberi has faced mounting opposition for weeksEd AaronsandRomain MolinaMon 5 Oct 2026 13.36 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 17.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAttempts to oust Souleiman Waberi as the president of the Djibouti football federation (FDF) reached a dramatic climax on Monday as police occupied the federation’s headquarters after a group of club presidents called an extraordinary general assembly aimed at removing theFifacouncil member and his executive committee.The FDF said police first occupied its national technical centre at about 5.30pm on Sunday, without presenting an administrative document or court order. According to the federation, on Monday a much larger police contingent ordered Waberi, members of the executive committee, staff and other federation members to leave the premises.Nations League roundup: Olise leads late charge as France bowl over BelgiumRead moreThe FDF said 16 club presidents then entered the building under police escort and proceeded to hold what it described as a “purported” EGM. The federation rejected the meeting as illegitimate, saying it had not been properly convened and that the notice periods and procedures required under its statutes and electoral code had not been respected. It declared any decisions taken “null and void”. But sources in Djibouti have insisted the number of delegates required by the statutes was present. They unanimously voted to remove Waberi and the executive committee before establishing an interim committee to oversee the federation.Quick GuideHow do I sign up for sport breaking news alerts?ShowIn the Guardian app, tap the Profile settings button at the top right, then select Notifications. Turn on sport notifications.If you already have the Guardian app, make sure you’re on the most recent version.If you don't have the Guardian app, download it from theiOS App Storeon iPhone or theGoogle Play storeon Android by searching for 'The Guardian'.Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.The confrontation follows weeks of mounting opposition to Waberi, a member of the Confederation of African Football (Caf) executive committee as well as Fifa’s council and a close ally of Gianni Infantino. At the start of September, a coalition of 27 clubs announced its intention to vote on the removal of the executive committee and insisted it had secured the two-thirds support required under the federation’s statutes.The FDF disputed that calculation, saying it has 67 members and that 45 – not 27 – would be required to trigger an extraordinary assembly. The dispute escalated as additional clubs and delegates joined the campaign against the executive committee. The government then intervened, with the secretary of state for sport, Fatouma Ali Abdallah, ordering the FDF to convene an extraordinary general assembly within 72 hours.The FDF has appealed to Fifa and Caf, arguing that the use of state security forces to remove elected officials could constitute interference in the affairs of a national football association. It warned that the consequences could include suspension, exclusion of Djiboutian clubs and national teams from international competitions, and a freeze on development programmes and funding. The Guardian has requested a comment from Fifa.It is understood Waberi and several other officials could be facing charges this week after a police investigation of the FDF related to suspected embezzlement and money laundering was completed. They were arrested in September 2024 after a government inspection of the FDF identified financial and administrative irregularities, including weaknesses in procurement, cash management and financial controls. The government’s investigation also raised concerns about anomalies in payments to third parties, failure to pay tax on salaries and wages and “misuse of cash payments” totalling almost £500,000. The police then carried out its investigation.Waberi has denied wrongdoing. He said in August after the FDF was accused by a club official of misusing funds that Fifa’s “monitoring mechanisms have revealed no indication of wrongdoing regarding the funds it disbursed”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSport in FocusOur picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown inEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFifa, which along with Caf contributes more than $1m (£760,000) a year to the FDF through its forward development programme, has financed football infrastructure and youth-development programmes in Djibouti, including the Douda academy and artificial-pitch projects in Arta and Dikhil. But it is understood that various tenders are under investigation because they did not comply with standard procedures.Several foreign workers who were not in compliance with immigration regulations were sent back to their home countries, meaning construction was halted. According to several Caf and Fifa employees and contractors, the projects in Djibouti are “a complete farce”. “We pass on the information but nothing happens,” said one contractor. “The money has gone missing, the projects are never finished – or if they are, it’s just a bare-bones version – and nobody says a word. It breaks my heart for the young people who just want to play football.”Explore more on these topicsFootballFifaFootball politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: WSL talking points: heat cranks up on Arsenal and Putellas and Diani shine | Women's Super League | The Guardian
description: Pressure continues to build on the Gunners’ head coach, while powerful London City Lionesses demolished Spurs
Author: Tom Garry
Headline: Pressure continues to build on the Gunners’ head coach, while powerful London City Lionesses demolished Spurs
Content: From left: Kadidiatou Diani of London City Lionesses, Arsenal’s Renée Slegers and Chelsea’s Keira Walsh.Composite: Getty, ShutterstockView image in fullscreenFrom left: Kadidiatou Diani of London City Lionesses, Arsenal’s Renée Slegers and Chelsea’s Keira Walsh.Composite: Getty, ShutterstockWomen's Super LeagueWSL talking points: heat cranks up on Arsenal and Putellas and Diani shinePressure continues to build on the Gunners’ head coach, while powerful London City Lionesses demolished SpursTom Garry,Suzanne Wrack,Sophie Downey,Renuka OdedraandRéshma RaoMon 5 Oct 2026 07.22 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 13.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google1Fans stay connected to SlegersTravelling Arsenal fans showed no animosity towards the head coach, Renée Slegers, despite their side’s run of one win in six games in all competitions and slipping 10 points behind Manchester City. Slegers walked over to applaud the 2,000 away fans afterthe 4-2 defeat at Etihad Stadium, on Sunday and they applauded her back. Slegers said: “I mostly went there to thank them, connect with them and show them I care for them and appreciate them coming to Manchester. And also to show them that I feel – not sorry for them because I’m a big part of it and things are within my control – but they’re coming here and they’re not getting the rewards, just like the team. I wanted to connect with them instead of walking away and hiding.”Tom GarryMatch report: Manchester City 4-2 ArsenalView image in fullscreenLauren Hemp celebrates scoring Manchester City’s third goal.Photograph: Martin Rickett/PA2Forward-thinking Walsh lifts ChelseaChelsea’s midfield came to the fore again in their 3-0 win over West Ham. Keira Walsh was the heartbeat of the team, collecting her third straight player of the match award with the 29-year-old enjoying a more attacking role this season. With the introduction of Lexi Potter at half-time, Walsh was able to push forward fruitfully again. She scored her second WSL goal of 2026-27 – the same as she managed last season – and took more shots (five) and completed more dribbles (three) than anyone else. “It helps us a lot in terms of creating opportunities,” said her coach, Sonia Bompastor. “We know how good she is at the edge of the box … It’s good to have a player who is confident and brings us the solution to scoring goals.”Sophie Downey3Lionesses flex their musclesLondon City showed their Champions League qualification credentials with a 6-1 rout of Tottenham to move above them into third. They were at their fluid and clinical best against a team many believe will rival them as challengers to the traditional top three, with 47.6% of shots on target compared with Tottenham’s 11%. Superstar signings Alexia Putellas and Kadidiatou Diani both scored twice, but most impressive was the muscle the squad showed. They looked more robust and hungrier than Tottenham, their physical presence combined with an aggressive press making the home team look pedestrian and lightweight despite an unbeaten start to the season. With lots of summer changes it can take time for players to gel and that physical presence can make a difference when things aren’t clicking. When things are clicking, though, it appears anything is possible.Suzanne Wrack4Pointless Charlton neglect basicsThe Charlton manager, Karen Hills, did not mince her words after her side conceded five despite taking the lead at Brighton. “It’s unacceptable if we can’t deal with one v ones,” she said. “The game is about one v one duels, about tackling, doing the basics and doing them really well. Unfortunately, we didn’t do that today. We found ourselves on the end of the scoreline which isn’t very flattering for us. We need to be more accountable for some individual stuff, but at the same time I take full responsibility because that’s my team out there.” The international break comes at a critical time for the team, who are yet to pick up a point. Even with some time to work on their unacceptable handling of the basics, it is hard to where Charlton’s first point is coming from.SW5Liverpool unsuccessfully copy UnitedGareth Taylor admitted surprise at Manchester United’s directness after his Liverpool team succumbedto a 1-0 defeatat Leigh Sports Village. Possession was split almost evenly, with 51% for Liverpool, and the hosts created more goalmouth opportunities, but could not convert them. Taylor told the BBC: “We ended up becoming what they are, very direct. We have got to be braver – and do what we do.”TGskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMoving the GoalpostsNo topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMatch report: Manchester United 1-0 LiverpoolView image in fullscreenJulia Zigiotti Olme of Manchester United (left) celebrates after her goal settled the match against Liverpool.Photograph: Craig Brough/Action Images/Reuters6Familiar problems for Sørensen at VillaBrian Sørensen’s first WSL game as Aston Villa’s interim manager ended in a 1-1 draw with Crystal Palace. The Dane took over on Tuesdayafter Natalia Arroyo’s dismissal, with Villa having won two points from their opening four league matches. Villa took the lead through Noelle Maritz in the 55th minute, but Abbie Larkin’s equaliser 19 minutes later ensured Villa remain without a league win. Villa were fortunate not to concede again as Palace’s confidence grew and created several chances late on, and the draw leaves them 12th. Villa and Sørensen have work to do, whether his appointment remains temporary or becomes permanent.Réshma Rao7Mace ends Everton’s goal waitIt was quite a feat for Everton to be in the top five without registering anything other than an own goal and their luck continues. They finally scored goals of their own in a 2-1 victory against Birmingham. It was all thanks to Ruby Mace, who scored them both. Her most recent WSL goal came playing for the visitors in 2021. The first was a stunning left-foot strike into the far corner; the second a deflected shot from the edge of the area. “I’m really happy. title: Celtic celebrate heated win over Rangers in final of revived Tennent’s Sixes | Soccer | The Guardian
description: The intensity of the football rivalry in Glasgow was evident on Sunday night as Celtic turned the tables on Rangers to win the Tennent’s Sixes
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The intensity of the football rivalry in Glasgow was evident on Sunday night as Celtic turned the tables on Rangers to win the Tennent’s Sixes
Content: Rangers’ Kirk Broadfoot and Celtic player Efe Ambrose during the Tennent's Sixes final in Glasgow.Photograph: Craig Foy/SNS GroupView image in fullscreenRangers’ Kirk Broadfoot and Celtic player Efe Ambrose during the Tennent's Sixes final in Glasgow.Photograph: Craig Foy/SNS GroupSoccerCeltic celebrate heated win over Rangers in final of revived Tennent’s SixesCharlie Mulgrew admits getting carried away after gameAngry scenes in Rangers dressing room emerge in videoPress AssociationMon 5 Oct 2026 09.21 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 15.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe intensity of the football rivalry in Glasgow was evident on Sunday night as Celtic turned the tables onRangersto win the Tennent’s Sixes. Celtic beat their rivals 5-4 in the final at Braehead Arena after being on the end of a 7-1 defeat by Rangers in the group stage on Saturday.The tournament was for retired players from all 12 Premiership teams as the SPFL revived a tournament that took place between first teams from 1984 to 1993. But the reactions were similar to any major trophy final.When Soccer Six was the perfect Christmas present for football fansRead moreCeltic’s Charlie Mulgrew admitted he got carried away in his celebrations after he ignored handshake attempts from the Rangers captain, Andy Halliday, in order to salute the crowd, and exchanged words with the Rangers manager, Barry Ferguson.There was a heated post-match analysis in the Rangers dressing room. In a video leaked on social media, Kirk Broadfoot appears to be heavily criticising the goalkeeper Lee Robinson.Mulgrew had calmed only slightly when he spoke to Premier Sports. “A lot of adrenaline was flowing, a few nasty tackles,” the 40-year-old said. “I mean, I know it was the Tennent’s Sixes, but you get caught up in the moment.“You don’t like to get beat from Rangers, our closest rivals, 7-1, so that hurt. We had a few beers, a wee chat, a wee night out, so we managed to turn it around. We got a few things ironed out, although I was a wee bit rough in the morning.“It feels like I’ve won an actual, real cup. It’s mental. I got a bit carried away at the end there but it builds up. There was a lot of emotion in that. Sometimes that’s what happens, it spills over.“Football’s like that. I got nutmegged a couple of times by [Martyn] Waghorn, and exchanged words with him, then that was me. I was just fired up and fired into a few tackles. In the end, because we had that spirit, we won.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionCeltic’s manager, Tom Boyd, said he was “pretty angry” with his players on Saturday night and that it “feels like winning the league”.His assistant, Simon Donnelly, admitted they were all “embarrassed” by Saturday’s heavy defeat and told Celtic Player after the final: “It’s against Rangers, so it’s as if it’s a Scottish Cup final there. That’s the feeling. You could play Rangers at tiddlywinks and you’d still want to win.”Press AssociationExplore more on these topicsFootballCelticRangersnewsShareReuse this content

title: Jake Connor is shock omission from England squad for Rugby League World Cup | Rugby League World Cup 2026 | The Guardian
description: Brian McDermott said he wants players who ‘can best stick to the gameplan’ after leaving Leeds Rhinos’ Jake Connor out of Rugby League World Cup squad
Author: Aaron Bower
Headline: Brian McDermott said he wants players who ‘can best stick to the gameplan’ after leaving Leeds Rhinos’ Jake Connor out of Rugby League World Cup squad
Content: Jake Connor will not be involved when England start the tournament in Australia on 17 October.Photograph: Jess Hornby/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenJake Connor will not be involved when England start the tournament in Australia on 17 October.Photograph: Jess Hornby/Getty ImagesRugby League World Cup 2026Jake Connor is shock omission from England squad for Rugby League World CupMcDermott wants those who ‘can best stick to gameplan’Hull KR’s Lewis in but no Wakefield players includedAaron BowerMon 5 Oct 2026 09.41 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBrian McDermott, the England head coach, has justified his surprise decision to omit Jake Connor from England’sRugby League World Cupsquad by insisting the players selected are better suited to his plans to defeat the world’s best.For the second consecutive year, Leeds Rhinos half-back Connor is the major talking point in a squad that has no players from thenew Super League champions, Wakefield. He was left out by Shaun Wane for last autumn’s Ashes despite winning Super League’s Man of Steel award. England lost that series 3-0 after a string of limited attacking displays.Sam Walker tops off NRL glory with Kangaroos call-up for Rugby League World CupRead moreConnor has been in impressive form this year for Leeds, but once again he has been overlooked. McDermott has made no secret of his desire to introduce a more off-the-cuff and exciting brand of rugby rather than attempting to go toe-to-toe with Australia and New Zealand, and has selected Hull KR’s Mikey Lewis rather than Connor.He did not shy away from explaining why Connor did not fit his philosophy. “We can’t do the usual things,” he said. “We’ve got to play with a point of difference. I’ve got a squad of players of how I want England to play. Jake Connor missed out on selection by a small margin, it came down to who I think can best stick to the gameplan.”Lewis has been one of Super League’s best players in recent seasons, but he had a disappointing year for Hull KR in 2026, punctured by off-colour performances and disciplinary problems. But McDermott appeared to suggest he can get the best out of the half-back.“Mikey still won a World Club Challenge with Hull KR and guided them to a cup final this year,” he said. “I get he wasn’t in the best of shape in the back of the year and incurred a couple of bans, but I’ll point everyone to the attack plan and the game model I think England needs to have to compete with the bigger nations.”Quick GuideEngland's Rugby League World Cup squadShowMatty Ashton, AJ Brimson, Ben Currie, Zach Eckersley, Herbie Farnworth, Ethan Havard, Max King, Morgan Knowles, Mikey Lewis, Jez Litten, Junior Nsemba, Brad O’Neill, Kai Pearce-Paul, Victor Radley, Hugo Savala, Harry Smith, Morgan Smithies, Luke Thompson, Sam Walters, Ben Talty, Jack Welsby, George Williams, Dom YoungWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.McDermott has been hindered by a number of withdrawals, not least from Wakefield. It is understood they would have had four members of their squad on the plane to Australia this week: winger Tom Johnstone, half-back Jake Trueman and forwards Mike McMeeken and Caleb Hamlin-Uele, but they have opted to undergo post-season surgeries. “I’m really disappointed, it’s a real shame the Wakefield boys aren’t available,” he said.There are further significant absences across the backline in Rhinos’ Ash Handley and Wigan’s Jake Wardle. That has led to surprising call-ups for Australian-born players including Brisbane Broncos forward Ben Talty and Sydney Roosters’ utility Hugo Savala, who will now probably start at centre against Tonga in England’s first game of the tournament in Perth on 17 October.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThere is a heavy NRL influence, with 10 players based in Australia selected. That includes the debutant Max King, who was born in Huddersfield but has excelled for Canterbury Bulldogs. Herbie Farnworth, arguably the best centre in the world, is also included and will be critical to England’s chances of qualifying from their group.After facing Tonga, England play France the following week before a showdown with Papua New Guinea in Wollongong that could well decide whether they make the semi-finals or face an early exit.Explore more on these topicsRugby League World Cup 2026England rugby league teamRugby League World CupRugby leaguenewsShareReuse this content

title: Bournemouth unhappy over Scott injury but Tuchel says England took ‘zero risk’ | England | The Guardian
description: Alex Scott has withdrawn from the England squad after a thigh problem worsened during his impressive performance in Croatia
Author: Jacob Steinberg
Headline: Alex Scott has withdrawn from the England squad after a thigh problem worsened during his impressive performance in Croatia
Content: Alex Scott made his full debut for England against Croatia on Saturday.Photograph: Carl Recine/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAlex Scott made his full debut for England against Croatia on Saturday.Photograph: Carl Recine/Getty ImagesEnglandBournemouth unhappy over Scott injury but Tuchel says England took ‘zero risk’Midfielder may be out for two months with thigh injuryScott played in pain but Tuchel says he got ‘green light’Jacob SteinbergMon 5 Oct 2026 09.08 EDTFirst published on Mon 5 Oct 2026 04.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThomas Tuchel has insisted England took zero risk with Alex Scott after the midfielder’s withdrawal with a thigh injury left Bournemouth unhappy over his treatment.Scott excelled during Saturday’s7-0 win over Croatiain the Nations League, but will play no further part in this international break and could be out for two months after exacerbating a muscle issue during his full debut for the national team.Tuchel says Alex Scott’s emergence gives England – and Rice – ‘high level’ competitionRead moreThe frustration forBournemouthis that the 23-year-old played through the pain after feeling discomfort before facing Croatia. Scott, who was in line to start again when England host Czechia in their fourth and final game of this camp on Tuesday, made way for James Garner after 70 minutes in Rijeka and underwent tests on the problem on Sunday.Bournemouth face being without one of their most important ­players as they enter a busy part of the season. They are seeking their first win in the Premier League and are in the Europa League. But Tuchel is ­adamant ­England, who have also lost the ­Arsenal defender Ezri Konsa to a quad injury, followed the proper medical procedure with Scott.“It’s a strange one,” the head coach said. “I’m very sad about it. He trained in full before Croatia, did extra work after the training sessions. We knew he was in treatment, but there were only green lights from him and the medics.“When we were aware there was slight discomfort during the match and asked if he wanted to come off he said no. After the match, he said he could have played 90 minutes and didn’t feel an injury. Even before the scan he didn’t feel injured.“There was zero risk taken from our side. On a human level, I feel bad that he has not the next cap tomorrow.”Asked if he had a clear conscience, Tuchel said: “100%. I would not have taken any risk.”Scott’s determination to represent his country was underlined by his decision to stay with the squad after the recent death of his grandfather. The former Bristol City midfielder, who remains a key target for Chelsea, made his debut when he came on during last week’swin over Czechiain Prague. He earned a starting place against Croatia and reprised his excellent partnership with Elliot Anderson from last year’s Under-21 European Championship.View image in fullscreenThomas Tuchel praised Harry Kane, who is poised to win a record-equalling 125th England cap on Tuesday.Photograph: John Walton/PAScott is unlikely to be available when England face ­Croatia and Spain in their final two games in Nations League Group A3 next month. He has emerged as ­competition for Declan Rice during the past fortnight.Tuchel maintained England had not let Bournemouth down. “The medical and physical department is in constant contact,” he said. “We are sharing information and this is a totally open process. We are not on the phone to clubs asking for advice because then it would be an empty camp.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTuchel has questioned Fifa’s ­decision to extend this international window, saying the format is testing from a physical perspective because of the amount of travel and training time after the 48-team World Cup. England last week lost the ­Manchester City left-back Nico O’Reilly, whose place has been taken by Rico Lewis.Rice and Kobbie Mainoo withdrew at the start of this camp, leaving Tuchel with Anderson, Garner and Myles Lewis-Skelly as his midfield options against Czechia. England are second in their group, well placed to make March’s two-leg quarter-finals. A major talking point will be Harry Kane equalling Peter Shilton’s record of 125 England men’s appearances.“I’m not sure I have any more words,” Tuchel said of the England captain. “He’s on the shortlist for the Ballon d’Or. We’ve spoken so often about him and I try to find new words which then make no sense.“Everything he does, he does it on the highest level. Since he took this major role for Bayern Munich, he found a new level. It’s the highest level, on and off the pitch.”Trevoh Chalobah is likely to replace Konsa and Tuchel has not decided how heavily to rotate. He said Trent Alexander-Arnold had a chance to replace Jarell Quansah at right-back.Explore more on these topicsEnglandBournemouthNations LeagueThomas TuchelnewsShareReuse this content

title: ICC delays plans for World Club Championship after ‘Big Three’ object | International Cricket Council | The Guardian
description: The ICC will not introduce a World Club Championship or more international multilateral tournaments until 2031 at the earliest after resistance from England, Australia and India
Author: Matt Hughes
Headline: The ICC will not introduce a World Club Championship or more international multilateral tournaments until 2031 at the earliest after resistance from England, Australia and India
Content: India fans at the 2023 World Cup final against Australia in Ahmedabad. England, Australia and India have resisted adding more tournaments to the calendar.Photograph: Saurabh Sirohiya/Zuma Press/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenIndia fans at the 2023 World Cup final against Australia in Ahmedabad. England, Australia and India have resisted adding more tournaments to the calendar.Photograph: Saurabh Sirohiya/Zuma Press/ShutterstockInternational Cricket CouncilICC delays plans for World Club Championship after ‘Big Three’ objectEngland, Australia and India say no space for extra eventsNo new international tournaments until 2031 at earliestExclusive byMatt HughesMon 5 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheInternational Cricket Council(ICC) will not introduce a World Club Championship or more international multilateral tournaments until 2031 at the earliest because of resistance from England, Australia and India.After informal discussions between the ICC and member boards over several months, a cricket ­operations workshop in Dubai last week concluded without any ­additional events being proposed. This means the next Future Tours Programme (FTP), covering 2027 to 2031, will ­mirror that of the current cycle.Sandpaper made Australia the story in 2018 while South Africa’s achievement faded into irrelevanceRead moreThe one possible change is the expansion of the World Test Championship to 12 teams from next year, with the addition of Afghanistan, Ireland and Zimbabwe. The ICC has yet to issue finalised plans to its members.The ICC remains eager to explore new competitions as it seeks to grow the sport and its own revenues, which is likely to lead to tension with the so-called Big Three, although in reality India are out on their own as they ­generate about 70% of cricket’s global revenue.The ICC suggested a number of new concepts for discussion, ­including a World Club Championship and a series of four-team T20 competitions for international sides to take place during additional windows.The triangular format has declined in popularity in recent years, although England will travel to Pakistan for a series this month that also features Sri Lanka. The ICC is eager to explore the possibility of staging quadrangular tournaments.England, Australia and India are adamant there is no space in the ­calendar for additional events unless the ICC removes existing tournaments such as World Cups and the Champions Trophy, which has not been discussed.One source involved in the ­discussions said there is no appetite among the Big Three for additional multilateral events, although conceded there was interest from smaller nations. Another described the concepts as an ICC landgrab.Many of the ideas for new competitions stem from a strategic review conducted by the US consultants McKinsey, whose full report will be presented to the ICC members at the next quarterly meeting in Bali next month.The strategic review was commissioned because of ICC concern at the probability that the value of media rights will fall significantly from next year. Its Indian rights deal is viewed as ­unsustainable, which has led to a desire to schedule additional events.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe SpinSubscribe to our cricket newsletter for our writers' thoughts on the biggest stories and a review of the week’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAustralia’s Marnus Labuschagne set for South Africa Test after first ton in 11 monthsRead moreDisney Star paid $3.1bn for the ICC’s rights in India between 2024 and 2027, but it has since merged with Viacom 18 to create JioStar, removing competition from the market.While the ICC sells its rights on a regional basis to 11 ­different ­territories, the Indian deal ­contributes the vast majority of its $3.5bn (£2.64bn) global broadcast revenues and cannot be replaced from elsewhere.While the FTP will not be finalised until next month’s meeting in Bali, England, Australia and India have already agreed schedules ­involving each other until 2031. The Ashes takes place in England next summer in the first series of the next World Test Championship followed by a tour of Australia in 2029-30.England have agreed to travel to India for a five-Test series in early 2028 before hosting them in 2029.The FTP operates on a slightly different cycle to the ICC’s TV rights sales, with its next auction covering the period from 2028 to 2032. That will feature two T20 World Cups, the 2029 Champions Trophy and the 2031 50-over World Cup.The ICC declined to comment.Explore more on these topicsInternational Cricket CouncilCricketEngland cricket teamAustralia cricket teamIndia cricket teamnewsShareReuse this content

Kangaroos call-up for Rugby League World CupRoosters’ halfback among six debutants in Walters’ Australia squadJillaroos veteran Ali Brigginshaw left out of women’s teamAustralian Associated PressSun 4 Oct 2026 22.06 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 05.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIsaah Yeo will delay pectoral surgery to captain Australia’s men’sRugby League World Cupcampaign, after Roosters.Roosters skipper, Isabelle Kelly, will captain Australia with Easts halves, Tarryn Aiken and Jocelyn Kelleher named ahead of Brigginshaw.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every title: Accept ‘bad things’ in return for benefits of AI, says Sam Altman | OpenAI | The Guardian
description: Boss of OpenAI calls for a regulatory light touch because of the ‘good stuff’ the technology can deliver
Author: Robert Booth
Headline: Boss of OpenAI calls for a regulatory light touch because of the ‘good stuff’ the technology can deliver
Content: Sam Altman of OpenAI says there is ‘a lot of daylight’ between his approach to AI safety rules and those of rival firms.Photograph: Patrick Semansky/APView image in fullscreenSam Altman of OpenAI says there is ‘a lot of daylight’ between his approach to AI safety rules and those of rival firms.Photograph: Patrick Semansky/APOpenAIAccept ‘bad things’ in return for benefits of AI, says Sam AltmanBoss of OpenAI calls for a regulatory light touch because of the ‘good stuff’ the technology can deliverRobert BoothUK technology editorMon 5 Oct 2026 09.27 EDTFirst published on Mon 5 Oct 2026 08.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSam Altman says he believes the world should accept “bad things” happening with AI in exchange for the benefits of the technology.The chief executive of OpenAI cited hacks, scams and “other bad things that will happen” in an interview that sparked an instant backlash from critics of the big AI companies. His comments came after one of his company’s safety expertsresigned, saying at the weekend that its “culture is broken”.In an interview released on Monday, Altman was asked about how OpenAI’s approach to safety differed from that of Anthropic, which has called for the industry to slow down afterone of its researchers quit, warning that AI experts believed “it could kill us all by the end of the decade”.“I think there’s a lot of daylight,” Altman said. “One of the differences between us and some of the stricter AI safety people is that we believe that the world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology and people having the agency [to use AI widely].“I do think the lighter touch regulatory stance we advocate for comes with an accepting of the fact that some bad things are going to happen as society figures out the resilience.“I wouldn’t take a trade of saying we will make sure there’s no major hacks, there’s no misuse of this technology, there’s zero scams or all the other bad things that will happen because I think that people will do tremendously – orders of magnitude – more good stuff than bad stuff.”The interview for Politico’s Decoded podcast drew a strong response from Ron DeSantis, the governor of Florida. He said he had “no dice” with the idea “a handful of tech oligarchs get to make that decision [on safety] for the rest of us”.His state last weekaskeda judge to bar OpenAI from developing new AI models without third-party approved guardrails.Gary Marcus, a prominent AI sceptic and professor emeritus at New York University, said Altman was “saying the quiet part out loud: suck it up, so you can make us rich and powerful”.Altman also reignited a feud with Elon Musk, telling Vanity Fair: “I don’t like bullies, and I think Elon’s a bully.”He had been asked if the AI industry could “grow up” and work together.“I think once in a while you got to punch a bully back in the nose,” Altman said. “And I also think Elon, like many bullies, only respects people who do. So if you want me to be able to work with him, maybe you should be happy I hit back once in a while, but I will work with Elon, of course.”Altman co-founded OpenAI with Musk in 2015 but earlier this year Muskalleged in courtthat Altman, OpenAI, and the company’s president, Greg Brockman, unjustly enriched themselves and broke a founding contract. Musk’s claim was dismissed by a judge and jury.OpenAI was hit by multiple safety crises over the summer, including when a swarm of its AI agents escaped their training “sandbox”, cheated, deceived and conspired tohackinto the Hugging Face website. Other agents accessed Australian government data. In the interview with Vanity Fair, Altman warned of “a coming tidal wave of cybersecurity problems” from rival open-source models. He suggested OpenAI could help its customers defend against the risk.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe company has scrapped the release of a cutting-edge model but Altman’s comments reflect a more bullish mood ahead of a stock market flotation.The wave of public and political concern last month about the potentially catastrophic consequences of fast-progressing AI agents that act beyond human intent had led to hopes of US-wide or even international safety agreements.However,Donald Trumpand AI bosses including Altman and Dario Amodei of Anthropic signed a far more laissez-faire pact at the White House last week. The US president said he wanted the companies to “self-police” to limit the risks from AI-enabled cyber-attacks and bioweapons.Geoffrey Irving, who worked atOpenAIand Google DeepMind and as chief scientist at the UK’s AI Safety Institute, said warnings about AI risks understated the dangers.“There’s about a 50% chance we all die because of the development of smarter-than-human AI systems,” he said, adding that actions taken over the next two to 10 years would be decisive.OpenAI’s David Robinson announced his departure at the weekend, saying “the companies building this technology aren’t being nearly careful enough” as they sprint from one product launch to the next.His view was endorsed by Miles Brundage, an AI policy researcher who worked at OpenAI for six years. He said he regretted helping “spread the idea of iterative deployment”, which may have made sense when AI was less powerful “but makes no sense at all after many deaths have been tied to AI and as we’re careening towards extinction-level risks”.Explore more on these topicsOpenAIAI (artificial intelligence)ComputingAnthropicDario AmodeiDonald TrumpSam AltmannewsShareReuse this content
