Author: Samuel Gibbs
Headline: Longer battery life, better screen, upgraded Siri and new variable aperture camera in refreshed design from last year’s model
Content: The iPhone 18 Pro packs all of Apple’s best technology into a pocketable package.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe iPhone 18 Pro packs all of Apple’s best technology into a pocketable package.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.iPhoneReviewApple iPhone 18 Pro review: big changes for small differencesLonger battery life, better screen, upgraded Siri and new variable aperture camera in refreshed design from last year’s modelSamuel GibbsConsumer technology editorMon 5 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 07.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleApple’s smaller ProiPhonegets the best kind of spec bump for 2026: longer battery life, faster chips and a fancy new variable aperture for the main camera.The iPhone 18 Pro is one of a pair of slab phones launched alongsideApple’s first folding phone, the iPhone Duo, and is the cheapest of the new phones, with a regular iPhone 18 yet to be announced.It isn’t exactly low cost, priced from £1,199 (€1,449/$1,199/A$2,099), with a £100 or equivalent rise over previous modelscourtesy of RAMageddon.Having fully revamped the design of the body for theiPhone 17 Pro, the new model is a modest refinement. It is 7g heavier and the back glass now matches the colour of the aluminium body, which is available in a handful of new shades.View image in fullscreenThe dynamic island at the top of the screen can now show three live activities at once, such as music playback, a timer and maps navigation.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianApple has shrunk the amount of the screen taken up by the Face ID camera, allowing the dynamic island to show three continuing tasks, up from two on previous devices. It also now shows the 3/4/5G indicator next to the signal level when playing music, which is a most appreciated feature for public transport commuters sorely missed on previous models.Otherwise, the 6.3in screen is one of the very best on a phone: super bright, crisp and smooth, while being big enough without making the phone enormous. An anti-glare coating makes it much easier to see outside, too.SpecificationsScreen:6.3in Super Retina XDR (120Hz OLED) (460ppi)Processor:Apple A20 ProRAM:12GBStorage:256GB, 512GB or 1TBOperating system:iOS 27Camera:48MP + 48MP UW + 48MP 4x, 18MP front-facingConnectivity:5G, wifi 7, NFC, Bluetooth 6, Thread, USB-C, Satellite, UWB and GNSSWater resistance:IP68 (6 metres for 30 mins)Dimensions:150 x 71.9 x 8.75mmWeight:211gFaster chip and longer battery lifeView image in fullscreenA full charge takes 59 minutes, hitting 80% in 33 minutes, using a 60W or greater USB-C adaptor.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianThe 18 Pro has Apple’s new A20 Pro chip, which is about 27% faster than the A19 Pro in last year’s model, with about 45% faster graphics performance. Since the A19 Pro was no slouch, that’s quite the leap and puts it miles ahead of the competition, ready to handle anything.The phone has a redesigned cooling system for longer peak performance, too, which is especially useful for running games on top settings.The battery lasts a solid six hours longer than the iPhone 17 Pro, managing to stretch to about two days between charges with more than six hours of active screen use across apps, browsing, messaging and photos. Even with the heaviest of use while out and about, the 18 Pro managed to end the day with 40% left in the tank. Most people will only need to charge it every other day.iOS 27 with new SiriView image in fullscreenThe new iOS 27 is familiar but faster and debuts Apple’s attempt to catch up to the competition on AI.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianThe 18 Pro ships runningiOS 27, which was released for the rest of the iPhone line on 14 September. It refines the relatively controversialLiquid Glass redesignfrom last year and speeds up the system, including app launches. But the big new addition is Apple’s revamped Siri, backed by Google’s AI technologies.Siri AI, as thenew system is called, is significantly more capable of understanding and answering questions than previous iterations. It is a chatbot like most other AI assistants, but it is less chatty and sycophantic than others, being more likely to just get the job done. As well as a choice of voices, there are sliders to control how fast it talks and how expressive its responses are. It has its own app where you can review previous interactions, but it is accessible anywhere on the phone via the side button, is built into Spotlight search and can see what’s on your screen, including when using the camera.It can also offer suggestions, such as adding an event to your calendar from the messages or mail apps, and attempts to display relevant information from your emails in the phone app when you call a business. But Siri can only do so if you use Apple’s apps, so if you use WhatsApp for texting and Gmail for your email, none of it works.SustainabilityThe battery will lastmore than 1,000 full-charge cycleswith at least 80% of its original capacity and can bereplaced for £119. Out-of-warrantyscreen repairs cost £349. The specialists iFixit awarded the phone aseven out of 10for repairability.It contains more than 40% recycled material. The company breaks down thephone’s environmental impactin its report. Apple offers trade-in and free recycling schemes, including for non-Apple products.CameraView image in fullscreenThe camera app has new customisable shortcuts to your most used tools and settings, as well as aperture, shutter speed and exposure controls.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianThe 18 Pro has a similar camera system to last year’s 17 Pro with one big addition, a variable aperture for the main camera.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThat means it has a very good 18MP centre stage selfie camera on the front and three 48MP cameras on the rear: main, 0.5x ultrawide and 4x telephoto.The ultrawide is one of the best on a phone, handy for landscapes and group shots. The 4x telephoto is very good too, full of detail and manages lower light settings well. It shoots excellent photos with a crop zoom to reach 8x before digital zoom is required, which is a little behind rivals with 5x/10x telephoto zooms.The variable aperture on the main camera can be left on automatic or controlled manually. It allows the camera to open wider than previous models for better low light performance, speeding up night mode shots and reducing unwanted motion blur.But it also enables a number of creative uses, such asmaking starburstsby narrowing the aperture when shooting lights, which is very fun, or controlling the depth of field in your photo. However, because the iPhone’s camera is tiny compared with anAPS-Corfull-framecamera, the difference in depth of field – where the foreground and background of the image are either in focus or blown out for a nicebokeheffect – is pretty minor. When shooting something up close, manually closing the aperture to f/4.0 can bring things in the foreground or background into focus, but otherwise the difference for most shots is small.View image in fullscreenYou can see the six aperture blades open and close on the bottom left camera lens using a torch.Photograph: Samuel Gibbs/The GuardianThe 18 Pro’s camera has a number of other useful upgrades. My favourite is AI-powered focus tracking that keeps a subject in focus as it moves about or into and out of the frame, which has been one of the best features of a Pixel camera for years and is extremely handy for fast-moving children or pets.Apple has also added texture and grain control to itsPhotographic Stylesfeature to customise how the camera shoots photos beyond what was introduced with theiPhone 16 Pro, including film simulation. Finally, the newApple Reference Imagefeature can sign an image for authenticity, on a per pixel level directly on the sensor, to help later prove a shot is not AI-generated, similar to a digital negative.The camera shoots some of the very best video on a phone, too. New for this year is the ability to convert a regular videoto a cinematic one after the fact, a bit like the excellent automatic portrait mode for photos.PriceThe iPhone 18 Pro costs from£1,199(€1,449/$1,199/A$2,099).For comparison, theiPhone 17costs£899, theiPhone Aircosts£1,099, the iPhone 18 Pro Max costs£1,299, theGoogle Pixel 11 Procosts£1,079and theSamsung Galaxy S26 Ultracosts£1,359.VerdictThe iPhone 18 Pro is an iterative upgrade on an already great device from last year. Inside, it has some quite big changes, but their impact is fairly minor on the whole experience.The new A20 Pro chip is super fast, but you can’t really notice the difference day to day, as previous iPhone chips have already been very quick. The extended battery life is great, but most people will still have to charge it every other day. The smaller camera cutout in the dynamic island now shows three continuing activities instead of two. Even the variable aperture in the main camera makes only a small difference to image quality unless you’re really trying to get creative.The screen is fantastic and big enough. The aluminium body feels great to hold. The cameras are some of the best on a phone and even Siri is better now.All of these things add up. The 18 Pro is without doubt the best iPhone ever made and at this size is one of the very best smaller phones available. It’s just not a transformative change unless you’re upgrading from a much older model and it now costs even more thanks to RAMageddon.Pros:relatively compact, great screen, better dynamic island, longer battery life, great cameras, variable aperture, USB-C, top performance, long software support, Face ID, better AI.Cons:small upgrade on last year, expensive, heavier than previous model, AI tools still lag behind top competitors.Explore more on these topicsiPhoneAppleMobile phonesSmartphonesComputingPhotographyGadgetsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Internet Watch Foundation reports huge rise in AI child sexual abuse material | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: Abuse material monitor says number of AI images assessed this year is already 40% higher than last year’s total
Author: Dan Milmo
Headline: Abuse material monitor says number of AI images assessed this year is already 40% higher than last year’s total
Content: The UK-based IWF has assessed 6,310 AI images that met legal definition of child sexual abuse this year, compared with about 4,500 in all of 2025.Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe UK-based IWF has assessed 6,310 AI images that met legal definition of child sexual abuse this year, compared with about 4,500 in all of 2025.Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The GuardianAI (artificial intelligence)Internet Watch Foundation reports huge rise in AI child sexual abuse materialAbuse material monitor says number of AI images assessed this year is already 40% higher than last year’s totalDan MilmoGlobal technology editorMon 5 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 01.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAI-generated child sexual abuse material is proliferating online, with the amount of illegal material investigated this year already exceeding the total for 2025.Analysts at the Internet Watch Foundation have found more photorealistic child sexual abuse material in the first half of 2026 than for the whole of the prior year. The UK-based IWF, which monitors abuse material globally, said it had assessed 6,310 AI images that met the legal definition of child sexual abuse, 40% higher than last year’s total of more than 4,500.Instances of AI-made child sexual abuse material have been rising for several years,with a huge surge in videos in particular, although the latest IWF figures refer to still images only. The majority of the images seen by analysts were of girls, and of children aged seven to 13.The IWF said the figures underlined the need for new statutory regulation on AI.Andy Burnham’s government has not signalled that a new bill focused on the technology is imminent. Kanishka Narayan, the UK’s AI minister, has said “nothing is off the table” in terms of fresh regulation, but that the test for any legislative proposal will be: “Will it make the British people safer?”Hannah Swirsky, the head of policy at the IWF, said she backed calls from parliamentarians for “binding legislation on AI” to compel companies to build safer models. “It is incumbent on tech companies to build tools which cannot be abused this way,” she said. This problem has been created by technology, and if companies won’t build tools which are safe by design.”AI-generated child sexual abuse material is illegal in the UK and the government has also made it illegal to adapt an AI model to create abuse material or to distribute such models to others. Developing a model designed to produce hyper-realistic child sexual abuse material carries a criminal sentence of up to five years.A government spokesperson said: “UK law is clear that child sexual abuse material is illegal, regardless of whether it is AI-generated or not. We are going further by banning AI models that are used to create this type of abuse material and produce sickening, hyper-realistic imagery that often contains the likeness of real children.”AI has also enabled online predators to create explicit images of children. The Report Remove service, which blocks intimate images from appearing online,has received 420 reportsfrom children concerning images of themselves that they believed had been faked or manipulated to appear explicit. The number has already exceeded its 2025 total of 397.The use of AI tools to create abuse tools has led to the National Crime Agency and IWFencouraging parents and guardiansto keep pictures of their children off social media. The guidance suggests making social media accounts private or sharing pictures of children through a “close friends” group only.Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)Internet safetyOnline abuseChildrenAidnewsShareReuse this content

title: OpenAI executive Jason Kwon to face grilling at parliament about AI hacking Australians’ private data | Australian politics | The Guardian
description: Unions, employer groups, banks and industry experts will also appear at the four-day Joint Select Committee on Artificial Intelligence hearings
Author: Josh Butler
Headline: Unions, employer groups, banks and industry experts will also appear at the four-day Joint Select Committee on Artificial Intelligence hearings
Content: OpenAI’s chief strategy officer, Jason Kwon, will front the hearing alongside Adam Cohen, the company’s head of economic policy, and Asia-Pacific national security lead, Peter Anstee.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenOpenAI’s chief strategy officer, Jason Kwon, will front the hearing alongside Adam Cohen, the company’s head of economic policy, and Asia-Pacific national security lead, Peter Anstee.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesAustralian politicsOpenAI executive Jason Kwon to face grilling at parliament about AI hacking Australians’ private dataUnions, employer groups, banks and industry experts will appear at the four-day hearings along with OpenAI, Anthropic, Microsoft and GoogleGet ournew political email,free appordaily news podcastJosh ButlerMon 5 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 16.27 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOpenAI must explain how they will stop their models from inappropriately accessing Australian data, the Labor chair of the parliament’s committee on artificial intelligence has warned, ahead of federal inquiry hearings which will grill the tech company alongside Anthropic, Microsoft and Google.Independent senator David Pocock is also demanding answers, saying OpenAI “still have a lot they need to answer” about their AI agentaccessing Services Australia data on Medicareand the company’s “appalling”tardiness in notifying the federal governmentabout the incident.The Joint Select Committee on Artificial Intelligence will hold four days of hearings this week, hearing from tech companies as well as unions, employer groups, banks and industry experts. Tuesday’s hearing will include representatives from copyright and artists’ groups, to probe issues around access to data to train AI models, as well as the Australian Broadcasting Corportation, whichwarned in its submission of a “cannibalisation” of journalismand demanded AI companies be subject to the same copyright, defamation and privacy rules as news outlets.Follow our Australia politics live blog for latest updatesOpenAI’s chief strategy officer, Jason Kwon, will front the hearing alongside Adam Cohen, the company’s head of economic policy, and the company’s Asia-Pacific national security lead, Peter Anstee. OpenAIlast week apologised for the Services Australia incidentand the manner in which it informed the government, saying it was “working to do better”.But the Labor MP chairing the committee, Jo Briskey, said the company still had questions to answer.“We have heard what happened, we understand what has occurred, and there’s some pretty problematic issues around not only the fact that these AI agents did access non-public data, but the reality was also that they took far too long to to notify us,” she said.“We’ve seen OpenAI make its public apology to Australians. That’s important … my focus is on what do they do next? How do they assure Australians that they that this won’t happen again? And that’s a difficult question.”Briskey said her starting point would be to interrogate how to balance the potential risks and rewards of AI, such as economic benefits as well as cyber security and defence applications. She said she would also raise concerns about online safety, scams, and how any benefits would be spread among all Australians.“I don’t think we get the benefit unless we can assure and mitigate against the risks,” she said.Pocock, who is also on the committee, also plans to seek more answers from OpenAI about the Services Australia incident.“You’ve got a bunch of companies that areessentially self-regulating with Donald Trump. I don’t think many people would trust Sam Altman and OpenAI … This is supposedly a company the Australian government wants to welcome with open arms and do deals with,” he said.“The Medicare hack stuff will be pretty well looked at through the committee process. It’s been a fairly appalling response from them.”Altman, inan interview with Politicopublished on Monday, said OpenAI “believe that the world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology and people having the agency.”Pocock has raised alarm about the potential impacts on artists, creatives and copyrighted material and said he was still to be convinced about the technology.“There’s still big questions over the long-term benefit of all this for Australia … Nobody has been able to answer that,” he said.“[The government] is chasing this GDP sugar hit, but we haven’t hit the big part of the datacentre buildout yet, and we’re already [seeing] inflation going up. They want to raise GDP, but after the buildout phase, how do we get a return? Looking at how much tax big tech companies pay, it’s not much, and I don’t see how it’ll change.”Pocock is keen to interrogate the government plans to address copyright issues. Anthropic, in its submission, suggested a form of “opt-out” model where rightsholders could request their data not be scraped; an idea SBS, in its submission, claimed was “routinely ignored or bypassed”.Pocock said it was “hard to cop this industry saying it’s too hard to deal with rightsholders when they’re heading for multi-trillion-dollar valuations”, and said the government should “force them [AI companies] to negotiate deals.”Explore more on these topicsAustralian politicsOpenAIAI (artificial intelligence)David PococknewsShareReuse this content

title: Hegseth is obsessed with increasing testosterone. If anything, the US could use less | Dave Schilling | The Guardian
description: Maybe the key to life is being able to bench press 300lb at 75. But do we need more muscle-bound, angry guys around?
Author: Dave Schilling
Headline: Maybe the key to life is being able to bench press 300lb at 75. But do we need more muscle-bound, angry guys around?
Content: ‘Will testosterone regrow my hair? I’d at least consider it if it did, but apparently, it makes hair lossworse.’Illustration: Fortunate Joaquin/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘Will testosterone regrow my hair? I’d at least consider it if it did, but apparently, it makes hair lossworse.’Illustration: Fortunate Joaquin/The GuardianOpinionPete HegsethHegseth is obsessed with increasing testosterone. If anything, the US could use lessDave SchillingMaybe the key to life is being able to bench press 300lb at 75. But do we need more muscle-bound, angry guys around?Mon 5 Oct 2026 11.44 EDTFirst published on Sun 4 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTShareI loathe going to the doctor.Not a controversial opinion, compared with some of the other ones in this section of the Guardian. I’m not exactly arguing for universal basic income or for Manchester City to be relegated to the Saudi Pro League here. No one looks forward to a doctor visit, with its recriminations for bad habits or various intrusive blood tests. People don’t have cocktail parties to celebrate their yearly check-up, and yet, it seems like every day, there’s a new reason to go get prodded by a stranger in a lab coat.Our collective fascination with testosterone levels is just another instance of me (specifically me) being shamed into more medical tests.The defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, and others in the Trump administrationhave been prattling onabout testosterone for years now, claiming it’s the key to maintaining what’s left of our civilization. Hegseth wants to test soldiers for T levels, and offer testosterone replacement therapy (TRT) to those who don’t have sufficient medically verifiable machismo. He sees this as “restoring and optimizing your natural capabilities, protecting your longevity, and ensuring you have the biological foundation required to sustain the fight”.Pete Hegseth wants testosterone for his soldiers. Finally, some gender-affirming care | Arwa MahdawiRead moreThe health secretary,Robert F Kennedy Jr, removed limits on TRT in June of this year, so that more men could be legally prescribed testosterone rather than, say, buying it at a gas station or from the back of a 2007 Dodge Caravan in the parking lot of an Arby’s.The science behind the perceived benefits of testosterone replacement therapy for cisgender men are hotly debated – a debate I’m simply too stupid to wade into. I have a hard time doing long division. How am I going to understand what injecting hormones into my body is going to do? Maybe testosterone will make me smarter. Probably not. I think that’s probably the one thing we can agree it doesn’t do.It’s bad enough that I have to be tested for blood pressure, cholesterol, A1C and eyesight. Why throw another thing on the pile of stuff I have to worry about? And is this actually worth my concern?Testosterone allegedly makes you more athletic, more virile, and more sexually active. First of all, I’m not a professional athlete. I don’t need to dunk a basketball or dominate my gym’s racquetball league. I’m a writer. My fingers work just fine.Do I need to function better sexually? If anything, I wouldn’t mind my libido toning down a bit. Will testosterone regrow my hair? I’d at least consider it if it did, but apparently, itmakes hair lossworse. What good will a bit more muscle mass be if I end up looking like Steve Harvey without the millions of dollars that make Steve Harvey attractive? If you give me a million dollars, I’ll take testosterone. There, the offer is in writing.While fightinghormone therapy for trans troops, the Trump administration is simultaneously suggesting to cis men like me that I should be taking it instead, even if I don’t actually want it. Or need it. Considering my high interest in sex, perfectly acceptable athletic ability and generally sedentary lifestyle, if anything, maybe I have too much testosterone.I’m perpetually angry – about someone cutting me off in traffic, the escalator at the AMC Burbank 16 that never works, and the Lakers’ starting lineup. Would I be a more valuable member of society if I got out of my car and walloped the guy who swerved in front of me? Should I be bashing the escalator at the AMC with an aluminum baseball bat until the police arrive?Hegseth confirms plan to cut 20% of US top military brass and rails at ‘beardos, weirdos and wimps’Read moreLike any normal person my age, I take my aggression out in video games. Whenever I get too apoplectic to function, I turn on my Playstation 5 and queue upRoboCop: Rogue City, a game where you play as the titular cybernetic lawman of the future – blasting criminals with a high-powered, rapid-fire pistol. The only thing more satisfying than a robot eviscerating drug-addled gutter punks inside a game is when you get to issue parking citations and arrest people for public urination. Yes, you can do that in the game. It never gets old.I’m sure this is not whatPete Hegsethmeans when he talks about “lethality”, but this is as close as I’m going to get – wiping out a street gang with a rocket launcher. I assure you I don’t need more testosterone for that.Underneath much of this tedious discourse and my own dread of seeing a doctor, though, is the fundamental premise that there’s something wrong with the natural progression of the human body. That, for some reason, we need to fix people who aren’t sick – as though we’re in some Jean-Claude Van Damme movie and need to be turned into a biologically enhanced weapon so we can swim more laps or something.Is the key to life being able to bench-press 300lb at the age of 75? For some, sure. I salute them. And yet, we are destined to age, to be rendered irrelevant, and to die. No matter what you inject or swallow from the pharmacist, it’s going to happen. That’s as normal as a stiff breeze. There’s no conquering reality. Just ask your doctor.Dave Schilling is a Los Angeles-based writer and humoristExplore more on these topicsPete HegsethOpinionHealthTrump administrationUS militaryMenRobert F Kennedy JrcommentShareReuse this content

title: Vance wants voters to ‘give us another chance’. But he is cornered | Sidney Blumenthal | The Guardian
description: The vice-president’s recent remarks seek to maintain a posture of strength while they inadvertently expose political realities
Author: Sidney Blumenthal
Headline: The vice-president’s recent remarks seek to maintain a posture of strength while they inadvertently expose political realities
Content: ‘The Republicans without a cause are seeking “another chance” without being able to articulate a difference from the past.’Photograph: Kevin Lamarque/Pool Reuters/APView image in fullscreen‘The Republicans without a cause are seeking “another chance” without being able to articulate a difference from the past.’Photograph: Kevin Lamarque/Pool Reuters/APOpinionJD VanceVance wants voters to ‘give us another chance’. But he is corneredSidney BlumenthalThe vice-president’s recent remarks seek to maintain a posture of strength while they inadvertently expose political realitiesMon 5 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 13.56 EDTShareJD Vance has parachuted into the midterm election campaign on a rescue mission in a new guise: a risk management consultant. Speaking in the flat language of the expert hired to identify threats, weaknesses and losses affecting a business’s reputation, he has presented his executive summary for limiting vulnerabilities and a scenario for averting disaster.“There’s a lot of good that’s been done, but there’s a lot of work left to do,” heinformedhis clients on 15 September about the words to use. “Give us another chance, or give us another couple of years, to continue to work on the amazing things that we’ve been doing for the past two years.” He turned the focus to harm reduction rather than total agreement and then shifted the equation to a negative binary choice. “Even if you don’t agree with us on every issue, the other party is consumed by craziness.”His proposal for a “another chance”, however, did not acknowledge harm, express remorse or offer any pledge to change. Skipping the apology avoided admitting error, wrongdoing or enlightenment. The lack of an apology allowed Vance – andDonald Trump– to maintain a posture of unwavering strength, to demand continued fealty and to maintain their pretenses.Vance’s strategy does double duty by firmly establishing his stake to become the prospective successor to Trump as the Republican presidential candidate in 2028. He himself embodies “another chance”. But his implicit self-characterization creates an indelible political identity that the man of many identities must carry forward through this campaign and the next.Every vice-president seeking to become president is inevitably “another chance”. Vance carries the burden of one of themost unpopular presidentsof modern times. His gameplan depends upon more than calculated forgetfulness. Abject failure should be seen as “amazing” success. Explaining away Trump means never having to say you’re sorry.Vance’s plea for “another chance”, however, has not produced the desired effect. Instead of Maga minions aroused to march in a phalanx through Trump’s Arch of Triumph, Vance’s defensive positioning has dampened fervor while opening the door to criticism within his party. Beleaguered Republican Senate candidates who had been in lockstep with Trump have suddenly started to flake off. Yet even as they edge away, they still take timid steps.Mike Rogers in Michigan had previously argued that congressional efforts to limit Trump’s authority in the Iran war would “not be good for America” and dismissed concerns about rising fuel costs. “We’re going to be fine, we got plenty of oil,” hesaid. Senator Ashley Hinson in Iowainsistedthat the US needed to “finish the job”, voting numerous times against invoking the War Powers Resolution to force an end to US involvement or curb executive authority without congressional approval.Then Rogersreversedhimself, “I think the best option now is to wind it down … The time is now.” Hinson followed suit, pleading that “the war needs to be brought to a successful and immediate end.”The panicked Republicans are not really defectors. None of them has offered a single reason why any Trump policy has been flawed, damaging or counterproductive. But now they want out, somehow to reduce their vulnerabilities. They demand an export ban on diesel as a panacea, which the Financial Timesreports“wouldn’t be workable” and would have unintended consequences that would lead eventually to fuel price spikes.TheRepublicanswithout a cause are seeking “another chance” without being able to articulate a difference from the past. They are pivoting into a void.Having supported Trump down the line they would prefer not to be held responsible for the consequences. But their fracturing underscores that the president and the policies they supported are the source of their quandary.The Republican freak-out validates voters’ anxieties that continuing the Trump status quo carries unacceptable risk. Rogers, Hinson and others cannot be dismissed as Democratic complainers. Their attempt to distance themselves grounds the Democratic criticism in more than partisanship and undermines the simple choice of rejecting the Democrats as the radicals. Intra-party disintegration makes theTrump administration, not the opposition, appear more unpredictable and untrustworthy.The uneasy Republicans’ bid for “another chance” subverts Vance’s framing of the midterms as a judgment about who flew over the cuckoo’s nest. “So, to the American people, I’d say, send these people packing, put them in the mental hospital, do not put them in Congress, because even if you don’t agree with us on every policy issue, at least we’re motivated by common sense and American interest.”Vance’s pitch relies on vapid “common sense”, but when Republicans turn tail the illusion of irresistible power is shattered and the dogma loses its magnetism. It is the Republicans above all who are neutralizing Vance’s damage control. His request for “another chance” to manage voter dissatisfaction through relative comparison places a marker against which the uncertainty, doubt and fear of Republicans is gauged.At a pep talk to House Republicans, Vance suggested what he thought was a clever pointer about how to demonize Democrats. “And if you are one of the few Republicans who’s running against a Democrat who’s not that crazy, then just talk about Abdul El-Sayed,” hesaid.But Vance’s advice overstretched his less-than-crazy defense, not least with El-Sayed polling ahead of Rogers. Vance disclosed the hollowness and falsity of his strategy by acknowledging that Democrats are “not that crazy” and that the insinuation must be contrived, a trick he has done before.Vance’s insistence on making the election into a contest of who is crazier is his most self-defeating idea. In that competition, Trump will always be the winner. The Economist/YouGovpoll, taken at the same moment Vance delivered his advice, showed that 51% of registered voters selected the word “dangerous” to describe Trump, alongside 53% choosing “corrupt” and 47% “out-of-touch”. Only 18% called him “steady”.Vance’s simplification discards the cult of personality in which the leader can do no wrong and ideology brooks no debate. The leader must always be uniquely capable, his words unassailable and the movement always winning, so much you’ll get tired of it.Vance’s imploring introduces an element of skepticism. He shifts the basis for support from zealotry to a cold calculation. Ideology is unmasked, vision lost, the leader becomes fallible. Without unquestioning belief, the cult of personality no longer is attributed magic but depends on risk management.When Vance confesses that it is the Trump administration that is the incumbent regime that must be defended and Republicans are banging to get out of Trump’s Iran war, resentment cannot be easily mobilized against “the deep state”, “the establishment” or “globalist elites”. When Trump rolled out the red carpet for the Chinese communist leader, Xi Jinping, he rolled it over the trope against Democrats as “communists”.Once again, “another chance” Vance has inverted his personal identity, contradicting the character he projected in Hillbilly Elegy, his foundation myth. Scourged by his dysfunctional upbringing he rejected the endless excuses of his alcoholic and drug-addicted mother and accepted the raw honesty and moral clarity of his “Mamaw” and “Papaw”, and found the road to redemption.Vance wrote urgently about the danger of false messiahs blaming scapegoats such as immigrants instead of offering hard truths of responsibility to working-class people. He depicted himself as a “cultural emigrant”, bearing authentic Appalachian values among the “elite” toward whom he had an “almost primal scorn”.In 2016, Vancereferred to Trumpas “reprehensible”, “an idiot”, and wondered to a friend if he was “America’s Hitler”. Vance wrote inthe Atlanticthat Trump was like “cultural heroin” and offered private advice to Hillary Clinton’s campaign, according to Chris Whipple’sprofileof him in Vanity Fair.Vance was recruited to Silicon Valley as a venture capitalist set up by Peter Thiel of the Paypal mafia and co-founder of Palantir, whohad notoriously stated: “I no longer believe that freedom and democracy are compatible.” When Vance ran for the US Senate from Ohio in 2022, Thiel bankrolled his campaignto the tune of $15m. Vance transformed himself into the stalwart Trump supporter. “I regret being wrong about the guy,”he said. But he didn’t explain the inner process of his Damascene conversion.After barely serving in the Senate, his new best friends, Tucker Carlson and Donald Trump Jr,promoted himto Trump into the vice-presidency. During the 2024 campaign, Vance cemented his latest new identity by scapegoating Haitian immigrants for supposedly eating pets. He confessed he made it up. “If I have to create stories so that the American media actually pays attention to the suffering of the American people, then that’s what I’m going to do,” headmitted.Vance announced he had converted from evangelical Protestantism to Catholicism, and he has clashed with Pope Leo. “I think it’s very, very important for the pope to be careful when he talks about matters of theology,” Vance said in April about Leo, channeling Trump’s spirit of retribution. Leorepliedthat he had “no fear” of the Trump administration for “speaking out loudly of the message of the Gospel, which is what I believe I am here to do”.In June, Vance published another memoir, Communion: Finding My Way Back to Faith, in which he credits Thiel – “possibly the smartest person I ever met” – for his conversion, but mentions Leo only in passing, avoiding reference to his feud. Vanceidentifies himself with a narrow “postliberal” rightwing movement. The Catholic theological historians James M Patterson and Thomas D Howes, in their new book,Why Postliberalism Failed, explicitly describe Vance’s newfound faith as “an ideology that failed”.Vance’s ritualistic non-apology, “another chance”, is a sheer power play that repudiates his original transformation as described in Hillbilly Elegy in which he achieves mature reflection by the grace of accepting personal responsibility.More dangerously to him, his opportunism may have closed off his opportunity. Vance has cornered himself into perhaps not simply his latest but his last political identity – the unapologetic apologist – from which he cannot escape through the election of 2028. In calling for “another chance”, Vance may have run himself out of identities.Sidney Blumenthal, former senior adviser to President Bill Clinton and Hillary Clinton, has published three books of a projected five-volume political life of Abraham Lincoln:A Self-Made Man,Wrestling With His AngelandAll the Powers of Earth. He is a Guardian US columnist and co-host of theCourt of History podcastExplore more on these topicsJD VanceOpinionUS midterm elections 2026RepublicansUS politicsTrump administrationDonald TrumpcommentShareReuse this content

title: Trump’s recent statements on the economy are even more bonkers than usual | Steven Greenhouse | The Guardian
description: Our ‘genius’ president is revealing his ignorance of economics, fueling concerns about the threat he poses to the world
Author: Steven Greenhouse
Headline: Our ‘genius’ president is revealing his ignorance of economics, fueling concerns about the threat he poses to the world
Content: ‘Economists and corporate executives were especially alarmed by two Trump statements.’Photograph: Aaron Schwartz/Pool/Aaron Schwartz - Pool/CNP/ShutterstockView image in fullscreen‘Economists and corporate executives were especially alarmed by two Trump statements.’Photograph: Aaron Schwartz/Pool/Aaron Schwartz - Pool/CNP/ShutterstockOpinionDonald TrumpTrump’s recent statements on the economy are even more bonkers than usualSteven GreenhouseOur ‘genius’ president is revealing his ignorance of economics, fueling concerns about the threat he poses to the worldMon 5 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 11.47 EDTShareDonald Trump recently made a bold claim about his abilities,writing on Truth Social: “The only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!”But in the days before and after that post, Trump made one mind-boggling statement after another, including one thatraised the possibility of cutting off all tradewith dozens of the US’s trading partners. The president’s statements had many experts questioning not just his intelligence, but also whether he – and the outlandish policies he was proposing – were a clear and present danger to both the US economy and the world economy. Public respect for Trump’s economic sense has fallen so low that just 7% of Americans think he should take the lead in regulating AI, according toa recent WSJ poll.Responding to Trump’s reckless statements, one prominent advocacy group, Republicans Against Trump,derided him as “Dumbest. President. Ever.”Economists and corporate executives were especially alarmed by two Trump statements. First, he wrote on Truth Social: “I’ll stop trading with countrieswith which we have a deficit” if the Federal Reserve doesn’t cut interest rates.The second disconcerting statement was: “If we stopped Trading with every countrythat we have a Deficit with, which is most of them, we would make, at least, 1.5 Trillion Dollars a year.”Trump’s $5,000 pledge to voters is a shameless bribe | Steven GreenhouseRead moreNot only is Trump’s arithmetic childishly silly here, but any college student who took Econ 101 knows that if a trade-dependent nation like the US suddenly ended all trade with dozens of countries, that would lead to economic disaster. What’s more, it was worrisome that Trump views himself as almighty emperor with the power to singlehandedly halt hundreds of billions of dollars in trade.If Trump ordered the US to terminate all trade with every place with which it has a trade deficit – that includes China, Mexico, Taiwan and the European Union – many US manufacturers would quickly find themselves in desperate straits, unable to obtain critically needed computer chips, rare earths, auto parts, aluminum and much more. As a result, many factories would be forced to close. Not only that, many farmers would be crippled because they couldn’t import the fertilizer they need, while many homebuilders would have to stop work because they couldn’t import needed lumber.Those were by no means Trump’s only recent mind-boggling statements.Two days before the Federal Reserve raised its short-term interest rates to 3.75% to 4% to combat inflation, Trump was on a tear, badgering and bullying the Fed, telling it not only not to raise interest rates, but to cut rates sharply. “We should be at 1%or half a percent,” Trump said. Again, anyone who took Econ 101 knows that cutting rates so sharply and so low will push prices skyward at a time when the Fed and consumers already think inflation is too high. And let’s not forget that Trump was the guy who promised toreduce prices on day oneas president.With that statement, the self-described “stable genius” president showed his utter failure to understand one of the most basic teachings of Econ 101 – when interest rates are extremely low, like 1%, that heats up the economy and that revved-up economic activity fuels inflation. The University of Michigan economist Justin Wolfers called Trump’s demand for a 1% interest rate “the dumbest thing ever saidby a president”.Then there was this whopper. Trump said that if the Fed bowed to his demands and slashed interest rates, “we could have a GDP [growth] of 14, 15, 16 and 20.”Those numbers are absurd, fantastical. Considering that the US economygrew at a moderate 2.2% rate in this year’s second quarterand rarely grows faster than 5%, talk of 20% growth is delusional. Since the second world war, the US economy has grown at arate at 20% or higher just once. That happened in the third quarter of 2020 due to extraordinary circumstances – in that quarter, myriad businesses rushed to reopen after the worst pandemic in a century caused many to suddenly shut down during the previous quarter. (GDP plunged at a 28% rate that quarter.)Then there was this colossally wrong-headed statement about trade: “The word ‘Deficit’ is nothing more thana fancy word for LOSS.” Trump coupled that assertion with his misbegotten statement that the US would magicallybe $1.5tn richerif it terminated all trade with every nation with which it has a deficit.This shows an infantile understanding of trade – and a stunning blindness to its mutual benefits.To explain how inane Trump is being here, let’s hypothesize for a second that in the US-France trade relationship, the only goods traded are wine and bourbon. Under Trump’s ludicrous logic, if the US buys $2bn of wine from France, and the French import $1bn worth of Kentucky bourbon, the resulting $1bn trade deficit means the US is simply giving away $1bn to France.US ban on Canadian imports likely to weaken already fragile relationshipRead moreTrump bafflingly sees that as an outright $1bn loss. Blinded by ignorance, ideology or anidée fixe, Trump fails to see that that’s not a harmful $1bn “loss” – rather, Americans are getting $1bn worth of fine wine to enjoy. No doubt wine lovers across the US see that as a gain and certainly not as a $1bn loss.Bottom line, Trump’s delusional statements on the economy show that he is becoming more detached from reality and from rational understanding of how the world works. One can’t help but wonder why his economic advisers don’t stop him from making such ridiculous and at times dangerous statements. If Trump turns his absurd economic notions into reality, as he has done in his ugly, unnecessary trade war with Canada, that will be more bad news for Americans.Voters should realize that Trump, with his failure to grasp basic economics, is a danger to the economy. He has brought us higher prices, slower GDP growth, and constant economic chaos and uncertainty. His tariffs and disastrous war against Iran have hit the great majority of Americans in their wallets and pocketbooks.Tragically, Trump’s Republican supporters in Congress either cheer him on or remain dismayingly silent while Trump does serious damage to the economy and to the finances of millions of struggling families. Americans shouldn’t forget this when they vote in November’s midterm elections.Steven Greenhouse is a journalist and author, focusing on labor and the workplace, as well as economic and legal issuesExplore more on these topicsDonald TrumpOpinionTrump administrationUS economyEconomicsUS politicscommentShareReuse this content

title: It’s time to abolish ICE | Amy Fischer | The Guardian
description: Amnesty International is calling for an end to the agency, whose record of violating human rights dates back decades
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Amnesty International is calling for an end to the agency, whose record of violating human rights dates back decades
Content: ‘When a pattern of human rights violations is so undeniably occurring and completely embedded within an institution, for decades, and with pervasive impunity, the only solution is to start over.’Photograph: Bonnie Cash/UPI/ShutterstockView image in fullscreen‘When a pattern of human rights violations is so undeniably occurring and completely embedded within an institution, for decades, and with pervasive impunity, the only solution is to start over.’Photograph: Bonnie Cash/UPI/ShutterstockOpinionICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement)It’s time to abolish ICEAmy FischerAmnesty International is calling for an end to the agency, whose record of violating human rights dates back decadesMon 5 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 13.46 EDTShareICE must be abolished.That’s the conclusion we at Amnesty International have reached afterdocumenting the chilling patternof human rights violations across the US during immigration enforcement operations.ICE’s record of violating human rights has been documented for more than two decades, but our latest findings show that the abuses go well beyond a series of incidents. Instead, under the Trump administration, there is a clear pattern that has reached a new and dangerous scale.In large-scale immigration enforcement operations in Chicago, Minneapolis-St Paul, New Orleans and Washington DC, we documented federal agents repeatedly racially profiling and arbitrarily detaining people based on their perceived race. Agents also targeted workplaces and neighborhoods that they associated with Black and brown immigrant communities. I spoke with dozens of people – including Indigenous people, Black and brown US citizens, and people with legal immigration status who were also racially profiled, stopped and arbitrarily detained.The Guardian view on Trump’s immigration crackdown: who will have fewer rights next? | EditorialRead moreIn all of the cities, people told me about federal officers using intimidation and unlawful force, including lethal force, against people they were attempting to detain, as well as community members observing or defending their neighbors. Agents broke down doors with guns drawn, smashed vehicle windows without justification and threw people to the ground. They used teargas and pepper spray against protesters and observers in public places, often impacting children and the surrounding neighborhoods. They also used facial recognition technology, drones and helicopters to unlawfully surveil people and intimidate them at the same time. As a Washington DC resident, I remember the helicopters shaking the windows of my home.We documented abuses inside detention facilities as well. I heard harrowing stories from people who were held for prolonged periods in overcrowded and unsanitary facilities not designed for long-term detention, with minimal food, no access to healthcare, and severely restricted access to lawyers. We have concluded that these conditions constitute cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment and, in some circumstances, may amount to torture. We also documented unlawful incommunicado detention and possible acts of enforced disappearance, including cases in which families and lawyers could not locate people in ICE custody. I listened to panicked family members desperately seeking their loved ones who had been snatched by masked men in their communities, without a trace and no way to locate them.The significance of our findings is not simply the brutality of individual incidents. It is their consistency. These violations were committed across four cities, involving different communities, operations and agents, yet they were strikingly similar. They are characteristic of the Trump administration’s cruel mass detention and deportation machine, including an immigration enforcement system in which safeguards have been weakened, oversight dismantled and accountability having become nothing more than a buzzword.When a pattern of human rights violations is so undeniably occurring and completely embedded within an institution, for decades, and with pervasive impunity, the only solution is to start over. That’s why we are calling for ICE to be abolished.The Trump administration’s deliberately cruel and racist practices have left entire communities across the US living in fear. Families are being torn apart. My friends are being deported. People are afraid to leave home to go to work, take their children to school or seek medical care.The United States has an obligation to respect and protect the human rights of all of us. Immigration enforcement does not exempt any government from that responsibility. Yet the Trump administration has turned the country’s immigration enforcement system into a monster which repeatedly violates people’s rights.ICE is not an inevitable feature of the US government. It was created in the aftermath of 9/11 to turn immigration into a national security issue, and has been problematic since.ICE’s tactics look increasingly like torture | Judith LevineRead moreHowever, the scale and horror that we have witnessed since January 2025, fueled by billions of new dollars and persistent impunity, has reached new levels. It has become clear that no amount of defunding, training or disciplinary measures will be enough. The extent and scale of the abuses and failures we documented lead to only one possible road to justice: ICE must be abolished.But we can’t stop there. A future without ICE is not the end of the work. It’s a threshold step toward building an immigration system that complies with international human rights law and standards, centers family unity and compassion, and does not rely on cruelty and fear.In fact, across the four cities we investigated, communities have refused to accept cruelty and fear as inevitable. People have built rapid-response networks and hotlines. They walk neighbors to school and work. They provide food, financial assistance, legal support and medical care. They document abuses. They support families who have been torn apart. They protect one another. Their solidarity shows us what communities can do when people refuse to abandon one another.We don’t have to look farther than these communities to know that we can create a future where all of us are cared for, ICE agents don’t have free rein to terrorize our communities, where government power is subject to accountability, and where every person can enjoy their human rights.It is past time to build an immigration system grounded in human rights and human dignity. It starts by abolishing ICE.Amy Fischer is director of refugee and migrant rights atAmnesty InternationalUSAExplore more on these topicsICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement)OpinionAmnesty InternationalUS immigrationHuman rightscommentShareReuse this content

title: Australia’s housing market is definitely in a downturn – but let’s put that in perspective | Hal Pawson for the Conversation | The Guardian
description: While tax reforms and interest rate hikes have resulted in a slide in property prices across Australia, is the market truly in ‘freefall’?
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: While tax reforms and interest rate hikes have resulted in a slide in property prices across Australia, is the market truly in ‘freefall’?
Content: Property prices in capital cities have fallen, but in Australia’s capital cities, the largest falls have been at the top end of the market – out of reach for first home buyers.Photograph: Darren England/AAPView image in fullscreenProperty prices in capital cities have fallen, but in Australia’s capital cities, the largest falls have been at the top end of the market – out of reach for first home buyers.Photograph: Darren England/AAPOpinionHousingAustralia’s housing market is definitely in a downturn – but let’s put that in perspectiveHal Pawson for the ConversationWhile tax reforms and interest rate hikes have resulted in a slide in property prices across Australia, is the market truly in ‘freefall’?Mon 5 Oct 2026 19.38 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 19.49 EDTShareWith national property valuesdown by 5.2%in September from their March peak, Australia’s housing market is in a distinct downturn. This has sparked concerns voiced by the opposition leader, Angus Taylor, of a housing market “in freefall”.Translated into dollar terms, using theDomain property price series, the price of a typical home has dropped to about what it would have fetched one year ago.Let’s put that price decline further into perspective.What’s behind the change in sentiment?The fall in house prices is controversial partly because of the link to theproperty tax reformsannounced in the federal budget in May.Importantly, though, the current market down cycle was already well established in most parts of Australia before that, following the first official interest rate rise in February. Prices peaked in March and have now fallen for six straight months.Experts at Treasury estimated the tighter rules on negative gearing and capital gains tax unveiled in the budget would dampen pricesonly about 2%over “a couple of years”. That’s in line withearlier independent analysis. We should assume those expert judgments are valid.Is now a good time to switch banks for a better home loan rate? Here’s what to know after the latest RBA hikeRead moreMuch of the long-term run-up in house prices was fuelled by generally declininginterest ratesover three decades to 2020; each rate cut boosted buyers’ borrowing capacity. That suggests interest rate hikes have been the key driver of this year’s price drop.Prices have further to fallThe Reserve Bank of Australiaraised rates last weekfor the fourth time this year, and financial markets expect at least one more rate rise in November or in 2027.That being the case, many experts anticipate further house price falls. For example,Cotality’s research director, Tim Lawless, believes an overall reduction of 10% to 15% is “a fairly reasonable estimate”.While the current downturn is Australia’s fifth in only 20 years, a 15% price fall would – if realised – amount to a larger slide in values than in any previous downturn.Previous slumpshave generally seen peak-to-trough declines of 5% to 10%. By comparison,US national house pricesfell by more than 25% from 2006 to 2011.However, Australian price prospects need to be kept in perspective. According toone respected index, median national property prices (houses and units combined) have climbed by 78% since 2020. If the current downturn does reach 15%, that will see prices reduced only to their level in early 2024.First home buyers and negative equity risksIt’s true this would expose some recent first home buyers tonegative equity, where the outstanding mortgage exceeds the home value.Those most at risk would be first home owners who bought their property in 2025 with only a small deposit – for example, under the federal government’s5% deposit scheme. The RBAnoted this riskin last week’s Financial Stability Review.However, most first home buyers have until recently needed a 20% downpayment. And the bulk of Australia’s homes were already held by their current owners in 2024.The overwhelming majority of owner-occupiers and landlords would therefore continue to hold equity, even if prices fall 15%. Properties held since 2020 or earlier will be generally worth vastly more than their original price, even in that scenario.There’s an upside for (some) first home buyersFor aspiring first home buyers, of course, declining property prices are ostensibly a cause for celebration.Unfortunately for them, however, at least in our largest cities, the largest price falls have been at the top end of the market. Price declines have been smaller for entry-level homes.Why the horror warnings about Australia’s ‘collapsing’ housing market are absurd – and very much in bad faith | Greg JerichoRead moreCotality’s latest analysisshows the top quarter of Sydney properties have fallen by 5.3 percentage points more than the bottom quarter. For Melbourne the gap is 6.6 percentage points.Unfortunately, while rising interest rates depress prices, they also reduce the amount prospective buyers can borrow.For most first home buyers, therefore, slightly less expensive propertiesmay be no more affordable.But some of the biggest gainers from the current market downturn will be first home buyers substantially backed by the bank of mum and dad.If they can enter the market without a giant home loan, this lucky group will benefit from prices depressed by rising interest rates, while being insulated from mortgage cost pressures.Ripple effectsAs with previous downturns, the volume of sales is drying up as buyers hold back and wait for prices to recover. Westpac, for example, reports a17% year-on-year drop in transactions.In these market conditions, potential home buyers may also delay action in the hope of further price declines.The resulting hit to the real estate industry comes from the compounding effect of both reduced prices and fewer transactions. There are even reports of real-estate agents goingdoor to doorin the hope of rustling up a sale.More broadly, the downturn will also squeeze tax revenues for state and territory governments, which have become heavily reliant on stamp duty.InNew South Wales and Victoria, for example, stamp duty accounted for 18.5–22.5% of all revenue sourced within the state in 2022–23. The proportion is likely to have risen since then amid the market boom.Calls for the states to trim spending are likely to grow as a result. It can only be hoped this will remind Australian governments of the case, overwhelmingly supported by economists, for replacing stamp dutywith a broad-based land tax. The ACT hasalready moveddown this path.This would result in a more reliable revenue stream for state and territory governments, as well as reducing the disincentive for homeowners to move house when their circumstances change.More importantly, though, by discouraging land speculation and land banking, moving to a broad-based land tax system would contribute to a more stable property market less susceptible to booms and busts.Hal Pawson is an emeritus professor of housing at UNSW. He is also a non-executive director of Community Housing Canberra and a part-time unpaid adviser to Senator David Pocock. title: Manchester City’s spending and the fine margins of Premier League football | Manchester City | The Guardian
description: Letters: Responding to articles on the team’s breaches of financial regulations, Mike Alhadeff says Man City got remarkably little for their money, Ed Barrett says Liverpool were robbed of titles, while Neil Smith warns against triumphalism
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Responding to articles on the team’s breaches of financial regulations, Mike Alhadeff says Man City got remarkably little for their money, Ed Barrett says Liverpool were robbed of titles, while Neil Smith warns against triumphalism
Content: ‘By swelling City’s coffers, the owners allowed the club to expand their squad, building both strength and depth.’Photograph: Martin Rickett/PAView image in fullscreen‘By swelling City’s coffers, the owners allowed the club to expand their squad, building both strength and depth.’Photograph: Martin Rickett/PAManchester CityLettersManchester City’s spending and the fine margins of Premier League footballResponding to articles on the team’s breaches of financial regulations,Mike Alhadeffsays Man City got remarkably little for their money,Ed Barrettsays Liverpool were robbed of titles, whileNeil Smithwarns against triumphalismMon 5 Oct 2026 12.50 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 13.24 EDTShareAs the fallout continues from Manchester City’s industrial-scale cheating and we await their appeal (Building of the Pep supremacy is an era that will be defined by sham-ball, 30 September), it probably hasn’t been reflected upon enough how little they got for their money.Yes, you can look at the six league titles in seven years and the “Centurions” team in 2017-18, all under the aegis of Pep Guardiola. But take a closer look and they were run remarkably close on multiple occasions.Jürgen Klopp’sLiverpoollost out on the title by one point on two occasions (and in any other year would have won the title) and, barring a few last-minute wobbles, Arsenal could conceivably have won the title earlier than they did.This is testament not only to skill of the managers, but also to the tenacity of the teams they built. And let’s not forget that City won their first title only on goal difference, despite their huge spending (which we now know came from ill‑gotten gains).It only goes to highlight that you can cheat your way to glory with almost £1bn, but still only win by the finest of margins. And it perhaps goes to show why thePremier Leagueis still the most competitive league in the world. Just.Mike AlhadeffStoke Newington, LondonI must take exception when Richard Bryant says “Money did not enable [Manchester] City players to train harder or run faster” (Letters, 28 September). That’s precisely what itdiddo.By swelling City’s coffers, the owners allowed the club to expand their squad, building both strength and depth. This allowed regular squad rotation without weakening the team, giving players more rest than was the case at most other Premier League clubs. Rested players can indeed train harder and run faster. That’s pretty much the point.As a Liverpool fan, one of the things that galls me is that many Liverpool players ran themselves into the ground in order to compete withManchester City. In doing so, players have shortened their careers. With Manchester City beating us to the title once by two points, and twice by a single point, can there be any doubt at all that the Reds were robbed of the even greater success these efforts merited?As Bryant says, “City’s victories were paid for with effort”.But it seems pretty clear that a considerable portion of that effort was paid for by cheating, and the efforts to counteract that cheating were paid for by other clubs, players and fans.Ed BarrettBebington, MerseysideThe relentless rolling coverage of the Manchester City financial verdict across your sports section has taken on an uncomfortably triumphant tone. While the independent commission’s findings are historic, it is time for the media’s rhetoric to be toned down. The breathless calls from rival clubs and commentators for unprecedented, disproportionate punishments ignore the harsh human reality of such a sanction.Expelling a club from the top flight doesn’t just impact wealthy owners or multimillionaire players. It devastatingly threatens the livelihoods of hundreds of ordinary, non-playing staff – from matchday stewards to kitchen workers. In the rush to see a football giant cast down, the media should remember the innocent people who will actually bear the consequences.Neil SmithGlossop, DerbyshireHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? Pleaseemailus your letter and it will be considered for publication in ourletterssection.Explore more on these topicsManchester CityPremier LeagueFinancial fair playLiverpoolFinancesBusinesslettersShareReuse this content

title: Badenoch is trying to match Farage step for step – but it’s a dance of death for the Tories | Polly Toynbee | The Guardian
description: At conference here in Birmingham I found a small battalion of centrist remainers with a vision for the Conservative party to come, says Guardian columnist Polly Toynbee
Author: Polly Toynbee
Headline: At conference here in Birmingham I found a small battalion of centrist remainers with a vision for the Conservative party to come, says Guardian columnist Polly Toynbee
Content: Kemi Badenoch addresses the main hall audience on the first day of the Conservative party conference in Birmingham on Sunday.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianView image in fullscreenKemi Badenoch addresses the main hall audience on the first day of the Conservative party conference in Birmingham on Sunday.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianOpinionConservative conference 2026Badenoch is trying to match Farage step for step – but it’s a dance of death for the ToriesPolly ToynbeeAt conference here in Birmingham I found a small battalion of centrist remainers with a vision for the Conservative party to comeMon 5 Oct 2026 12.46 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 17.52 EDTShareYou can walk all the way from Somerset to Sussex without crossing a Tory-run constituency, if you wish. You could also travel through each of the counties of Wiltshire, Hampshire, Dorset and Surrey without setting foot in Tory lands. They are now mainly Liberal Democrat, and there’s not one Tory MP in all of Oxfordshire.Is Kemi Badenoch bothered? Everything she does seems cleverly designed to keep those places lost to her for ever as she woos Reform voters, unsuccessfully. The more she leans right, the more she repels home counties moderates. Those Reform voters are not coming back, psephologists say. Without reclaiming the old “blue wall”, there is no hope, ever, of a Tory majority, say both ProfsTim BaleandRob Fordand just about every political authority you care to ask.Shooting the breeze at the party’s Birmingham conference, you might never guess the Tories still poll four percentage points belowthe last election, the worst resultsince theDuke of Wellington was dismissedin 1830 for rejecting electoral reform and defending every rotten borough.Spot that Wellingtonian legacy inthe interviewBadenoch gave ConservativeHome. “I march to the beat of my own drum,” she says. Indeed she does, but out of step with the public, not condescending to care what it might be thinking and allowing no shade of disagreement. Removing theLords whip from Gavin Barwell, Theresa May’s chief of staff, was a deterrent message to anyone taking part in the “festival of ideas” here, a festival of one idea only. Barwell opposed Badenoch’s edict barring any candidate who supports net zero carbon emissions or staying in the European convention on human rights. “I haven’t left the Conservative party. It has left me,”Barwell tweetedplaintively. It has left a great many others, too.Margaret Thatcher, still holy here, never did that: she had“wets” in her first cabinetand never expelled them from the party. Her ideological obduracy over the poll tax only overcame her later on, and it did for her. But Badenoch is starting out this way. The adulation showered on her by Tories and their press must come from some alternative wonderland where they are notpolling in third place at 19%, while their leader, though improved, scores net -15 – compared withAndy Burnham on +7. In polling, more call her “nasty” or “rude” than “strong” or ‘intelligent”.What demographic is she for? Giving free childcare toparents earning over £100,000will strike most as a grotesque gesture. Only 4% make £100,000 or more:they don’t think themselves wealthy, but the other 96% of people do. The £700m cost of that policy should go to the dwindling number of deprived two-year-olds getting early years support, according to theInstitute for Fiscal Studies. Already, the children of the best-off are eight times more likely to benefit from funded childcare hours than the most disadvantaged,says the New Economics Foundation. Children arriving at school unready are tomorrow’s Neets (16- to 24-year-olds not in education, employment or training). This should have the education secretary, Lucy Powell, rampaging: it’s not about parents, it’s about children’s futures. Badenoch’s pledge to cutsome benefits to “subsistence” leveldeliberately implies the4 million children below the poverty lineare living the life of Riley.Her responses to Burnham are also out of touch with the times – and even withthe Times. While70% want closer relations with the EU, her party shockingly pledges torip up any agreement Burnham makes, sabotaging any trade pact on agri-foods or freedom for the young to travel across Europe. Negotiations are at risk of failure if the EU fears Europhobes might ever regain power and reverse it all.Austerity is still raw in public minds, with overflowing prisons, blocked courts, NHS waiting lists anda million Neets, alongside the housing crisis. What a time for Badenoch to propose£47bn in cuts, with her shadow chancellor now planning even more “in every part of government”.Instead of beckoning back those moderate-minded home counties, she competes punch for punch with Nigel Farage. Last week, she strippeddown the aid budget to £1bntoequal Farage’s policy. Look at their arms race to demolish the civil service: Badenoch started last year by pledging to cut132,000 civil service jobs, return it to pre-Brexit levels (before all the mundane EU agencies we quit – medicines, chemical safety etc – had to be replicated). Farage was due tocut a mere 68,500until Danny Kruger upped theante last month to 250,000in his “Storm and Sunshine” policy. The latest? The Tories just pledged to kill offthe Environment Agency, Natural Englandandthe Climate Change Committee. What do the home counties think of that?This contest for lowest taxes, smallest state, toughest stance on migrants, harshest welfare cuts and deepest loathing of young people will spiral downwards towards something new and dangerous. Modern British politics has never before had rightwing parties competing as equals. But locked in this dance of death, the politics of bile carries them further from most voters. Tories are dying out:63 is now the median ageof Badenoch’s voters, while Labour’s is 46.If nothing improves by next conference, the mirage of Badenoch’s rock-solid support will melt away. But what would replace her? Waiting in the wings there is a model of what a Conservative revival might look like –Prosper UK, launched in January.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIt tiptoes, praising Badenoch loudly, yet it is running seven events at this conference. That included a small Sunday night rally for electoral reform. It was addressed by former West Midlands mayor Andy Street, now co-chair of Prosper UK with Ruth Davidson It is backed by a formidable array of what was once the One Nation group, now defunct in parliament – or dormant under Badenoch’s rightwards march. No MPs back Prosper UK in public, but the group claims a third of them do secretly, alongwith 30,000 declared supporters. David Gauke, vice chair, has crept back into the party – he thinks by accident when the membership computer processing his re-application didn’t register he’d been ejected in 2019. In returning, he joined a battalion of remainer luminaries of the centre-right who’d had the whip suspended at the same time, including Kenneth Clarke and Dominic Grieve.Gauke travels the country speaking to Conservative associations and others. Prosper UK is pro-EU, pro-migration for skilled workers and foreign students, pro-net zero and against the pension triple lock – and Gauke says that “Conservatives should be truth tellers on all these”. But though socially liberal, he’s dry as a bone on fiscal discipline, campaigning for low business taxes, a smaller state and enticing back non-doms – all Hayek, no Keynes. “No one speaks for some 7 million people centre or centre-right,” he says.Indeed, the country needs a plausibly electable Tory party to put up a fight against Faragism, not a carbon copy of it. If Badenoch is not for turning, to survive it will need to turn her out.Polly Toynbee is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsConservative conference 2026OpinionKemi BadenochAndy BurnhamcommentShareReuse this content

title: What happens to a dog when its owner can’t leave hospital? | Ranjana Srivastava | The Guardian
description: Our relationships with pets matter to wellbeing. But concern for an animal’s welfare can also become a practical barrier to healthcare
Author: Ranjana Srivastava
Headline: Our relationships with pets matter to wellbeing. But concern for an animal’s welfare can also become a practical barrier to healthcare
Content: For many older people, an animal is their most constant companion, writes Ranjana Srivastava.Photograph: Eva Blanco/Getty Images/iStockphotoView image in fullscreenFor many older people, an animal is their most constant companion, writes Ranjana Srivastava.Photograph: Eva Blanco/Getty Images/iStockphotoOpinionHospitalsWhat happens to a dog when its owner can’t leave hospital?Ranjana SrivastavaOur relationships with pets matter to wellbeing. But concern for an animal’s welfare can also become a practical barrier to healthcareMon 5 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 18.22 EDTShare“Doctor, do you know I have a little dog?”My team exchanges a glance. It’s my turn today.“Tell me about your dog.”Her face lights up. “Well, he is just a lovely little thing. When I am knitting, he curls up on my lap and keeps me company. We are very happy, the two of us.”Complaining about healthcare can feel like an act of betrayal. But there is a real cost to silence | Ranjana SrivastavaRead moreIt is unlikely that our patient has knitted in the last year, during which a series of mishaps has brought her in and out of hospital. But the rest of her account rings true.For as long as possible, she stayed at home, managing miraculously well despite her cognitive impairment, with little help beyond an occasional carer. But now, a fall has brought her undone. For weeks, she has been waiting for residential care, one more statistic in the familiar story of “bed block”.From our medical perspective, she is waiting for a facility. But from hers, she is waiting to see her dog. She can recall very little about her life but, when it comes to her pet, her descriptions are unwavering. Her words paint a small brown dog, quietly following her around her apartment. Jumping into her lap when she settles into her armchair. Ready to do it all over again tomorrow.Sign up for a weekly email featuring our best readsThe paramedic who rescued her from her garden noted that the neighbour had offered to take the dog until the patient’s return. But this time, the patient is not going home.Seeing how much she enjoys the nurses fussing over her – and because she has never once asked to go home – we have not mentioned her living arrangement. But she longs for her dog – and our decision not to lie is far easier in principle than in practice.There is no easy provision to reunite her with her dog. The neighbour can’t bring the dog in. The hospital won’t let the dog in. (“Imagine the other patients.”)What if seeing her dog proved distressing afterwards? What if it created a safety risk? And if we made an exception for her, what would we do for the next patient who pined for her turn?The more frequently I encounter the problem, the more I see it as an emblem of the things medicine considers peripheral to patient care, even when they may not be peripheral at all.Our relationships with pets matter to wellbeing. They provide physical activity, psychological comfort and social connection. For some older people, an animal is their most constant companion.But concern for a pet’s welfare can also become a practical barrier to healthcare. Patients may delay seeking care, worry about coming to hospital, or discharge themselves because there is a pet at home.A recent essay in the New England Journal of Medicine onhuman-animal relationshipspoints to a perhaps delayed recognition of something we have understood for years: the wellbeing of humans and their pets is intertwined.When I was an intern, just two questions often formed the social history: Does the patient smoke? Does the patient drink?Today we do better. We ask: Where does the patient live? What services exist? Is there a history of falls? Is the family involved?skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFive Great ReadsEach week our editors select five of the most interesting, entertaining and thoughtful reads published by Guardian Australia and our international colleagues. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Saturday morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionPerhaps we should add another question: Are you concerned about a pet?It is a deceptively easy question to ask. Because what happens when the answer is yes?Who will feed the cat? Who will walk the dog? What if the patient cannot return home?The solution can’t be another mental responsibility casually added to the medical worklist. Yet ignoring the issue doesn’t obscure the problem.We have fact sheets for many health conditions.
