Why isn’t there one for ‘What to do on the day your loved one dies’? | Ranjana SrivastavaRead moreMore of us are starting to notice what we have traditionally neglected – not only where a patient lives but also which animal lives with them and what will happen to that animal if the patient doesn’t go home.For many people, pets are part of the social determinants of health.Hospitalscannot take on this responsibility alone. But it’s time to ask how hospitals can work effectively with community services and animal welfare agencies to care for the whole patient.Know thy neighbour – and thy neighbour’s dog.For as long as we cared for her, one doctor from our team sat down with our patient and heard her retell the story about her dog. We never let our interest drift, even when our hearts slightly broke each time. Every one of us would have brought in her dog – if only we could.One day, all of us rotated out. We left her in the hands of another team, hoping they would continue the ritual.Ranjana Srivastava is an Australian oncologist, award-winning author and Fulbright scholar. Her latest book is Every Word Matters: Writing to Engage the PublicExplore more on these topicsHospitalsOpinionPetsHealthcare industrycommentShareReuse this content

title: To state school alumni starting university, I say this: be proud of your background | Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett | The Guardian
description: Accusations of classism chime with my experience 20 years ago. So all hail the Bristol graduate awarding state schools red plaques, says Guardian columnist Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett
Author: Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett
Headline: Accusations of classism chime with my experience 20 years ago. So all hail the Bristol graduate awarding state schools red plaques, says Guardian columnist Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett
Content: Students at St Andrews University.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenStudents at St Andrews University.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianOpinionUniversitiesTo state school alumni starting university, I say this: be proud of your backgroundRhiannon Lucy CosslettAccusations of classism chime with my experience 20 years ago. So all hail the Bristol graduate awarding state schools red plaquesMon 5 Oct 2026 08.22 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 14.45 EDTShare“So, where did you go to school?” On the face of it, it doesn’t seem likea loaded question. I was mostly bemused when I first started university 20 years ago and found myself being asked it repeatedly by other students. Why were they so interested? Surely no one would have heard of the north Wales comprehensive I had attended? When they countered my baffled reaction with “Charterhouse” or “Marlborough”, how was I supposed to respond? When one student said, of another, “He went to Winchester, you know”, I stared blankly at him, not understanding why he was telling me about someone else’s day trip to a city in Hampshire (“Oh, did he have a nice time?”). It was strange, new territory.Asking someone where they went to school is often not an innocent question. It is a way of “placing” you on a social scale. As thousands of freshers settle in to their first terms at university, a significant proportion will be battling with this dawning awareness that Britain runs on a network of private schools whose alumni often seem to know, or know of, one another. State-school students might have been dimly aware of it before, but nothing puts it into sharper focus than freshers’ week. It’s clear that little has changed since my own student days. I was saddened to read recent reports ofclassism at St Andrews, which led to a student’s announcement that she would not return this academic year: “Working-class students have been made to feel ashamed of their home life at university,” she said.The pervasiveness of private school culture, as I suppose you could call it, remains nationwide and deeply embedded.It’s a shock, as a young person, to go from being the majority – state-educated – to suddenly feeling like the minority, and in some stark cases being made to feel “less than” as a result. It’s why I admireSophie Pender’s 93% Clubso much. Pender set up the initiative while she was at Bristol University, where she was mocked for her working-class background, to bring renewed focus to the fact that the vast majority of people educated in the UK – 93% in fact – attended state school, and to offer them a professional career mentoring and networking alternative to the “old boys” that is a de facto benefit of private school attendance.Pender’s new campaign, Made in State School, aims to shift attitudes by issuing red plaques to celebrate some of the nation’s finest state school alumni – from David Attenborough and Jacqueline Wilson to Jessica Ennis-Hill and Marcus Rashford. She evenpresented a plaque to Andy Burnhamat the Labour party conference last week. She is right when she says that state schools have a PR problem. They are often framed, in rightwing media especially, as dystopian, rough, a hardship that has to be overcome, as opposed to what they actually are: symbols of British excellence, innovation and creativity.So often the media conversation takes the default assumption that private schools are inherently better than state schools, and that it is always in a child’s best interests to attend one. When you hold opinions like mine – that in rejecting the local state school, you are choosing a form of segregation – they can sometimes feel uncomfortable to express. My industries, media and publishing, are dominated by people who went to private school (half of newspaper columnists are privately educated). Education is a sensitive topic, and this can sometimes have a silencing effect.So allow me to lay my cards on the table. Sending your child to private school encourages them to believe that they are better than other children.We have seen where this leads, in the behaviour of some of ourleading politicians.Thecultures of abusethat have been able to thrive at boarding schools that prioritised reputation and prestige over safety have left many victims in their wake.We should be lauding the benefits of state schools. Being moresocially mixed, they teach children openness and confidence. Being able to interact with people from a huge range of backgrounds is a vital life skill. State school kids are often hilarious – there is a unique sense of humour that comes from inclusion; from having seen it all. In the case of mixed-gender schools, they give you a far more developmentally appropriate understanding of the opposite sex. Perhaps due to a combination of socially repressed poshness or a lack of exposure to girls, the ex-public schoolboys at my university often seemed genuinely terrified of the working-class young women they were now expected to study alongside.I wouldn’t go as far to say that it’s impossible to be cool and to have gone to private school, but let’s be honest, it’s harder. University was the first place I went where privilege was a status symbol, and it was discombobulating to be treated with derision by someone who wouldn’t have lasted two minutes in the roasting competition that was your morning registration. Well, you might say, “cool” shouldn’t matter – but as the Made in State School plaques demonstrate, cool people often go on to do radical, groundbreaking, culture-defining things.I won’t rehash some of the toxic attitudes I experienced that first term, mostly from public schoolboys, but the scales fell from my eyes. Someone with less confidence and weaker politics might have put on a voice and tried to fit in. Which is why I want to say to any university fresher who feels that way now to hold their head high. These people’s parents chose to purchase educational advantage for their offspring – which was their prerogative – but that doesn’t make them better than you. You’ve still ended up in the same place, without the astronomical costs of private school tuition fees and largely off your own back! Being made in state school is something to be proud of. Become comfortable owning it, and using it to lift others up. We’re the 93%, after all.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionRhiannon Lucy Cosslett is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsUniversitiesOpinionPrivate schoolsClass issuesStudent experienceSocial mobilityFreshersHigher educationcommentShareReuse this content

title: ﻿The UK’s G20 presidency will push Andy Burnham to the centre of the global stage. What will he use it for? | Michael Jacobs | The Guardian
description: This is a chance for the PM to advance his progressive agenda and tackle urgent issues such as AI regulation and climate action, says economist Michael Jacobs
Author: Michael Jacobs
Headline: This is a chance for the PM to advance his progressive agenda and tackle urgent issues such as AI regulation and climate action, says economist Michael Jacobs
Content: Dried-up paddy fields in Jonggol, West Java, Indonesia, 17 September 2026. The El Niño-affected climate has caused extended drought conditions and increased the risk of wildfires across the country.Photograph: Mast Irham/EPAView image in fullscreenDried-up paddy fields in Jonggol, West Java, Indonesia, 17 September 2026. The El Niño-affected climate has caused extended drought conditions and increased the risk of wildfires across the country.Photograph: Mast Irham/EPAOpinionG20﻿The UK’s G20 presidency will push Andy Burnham to the centre of the global stage. What will he use it for?Michael JacobsThis is a chance for the PM to advance his progressive agenda and tackle urgent issues such as AI regulation and climate actionMon 5 Oct 2026 05.39 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 06.05 EDTShareAmong the many crucial decisionsAndy Burnhamhas to make over the next few weeks, one has gone almost completely unremarked: what Britain’s priorities will be when it assumes the presidency of the G20 next year.Burnham has said he wants to concentrate on domestic policy. But with the world in turmoil, chairing the group of the world’s largest economies will be one of his most important responsibilities.The last time the UK chaired the forum was in 2009, when Gordon Brown presided over the rescue of the global economy after the financial crash. Before the London summit in April 2009, the French president, Nicolas Sarkozy, had wrung his hands, saying that “none of us has a plan”. Barack Obama had a quick response to this: “Gordon has a plan.”He did. Brown got the G20 to agree to a$5tn fiscal stimulusamong its member states, increase International Monetary Fund lending to developing countries and create a new global coordinator for financial regulation, the Financial Stability Board.But 2009 was a rare year for the G20, in that it actually achieved something. In general, the long communiques issued at its annual leaders’ summits reflect only the lowest-common-denominator agreement on broad principles. The G20 rarely commits its members to doing anything they were not planning to do anyway, and only occasionally makes genuinely collective decisions. One of the most consequential was thesuspension of developing countries’ debtduring the Covid pandemic in 2020 and the subsequent establishment of a “common framework” for debt treatment.Indeed, for what is meant to be the effective executive committee of the global economy, the G20 is an oddly weak institution. Its 19 members (plus the EU and the African Union) have no HQ or staff and do not even have a standing website: if you want to know what the G20 has agreed over the past 20 years you need to go to a set ofunofficial webpageshosted by some enterprising academics at the University of Toronto.For most countries, hosting the G20 summit is a chance to impress its domestic audience by showing that its head of government bestrides the world stage. Last yearDonald Trump boycotted it; the South African president, Cyril Ramaphosa, was glad simply to get any kind of agreed communique. This year, the US is the host, with one of Trump’s own properties near Miami the summit venue in December: expect a show of personal and US power and very little attempt to achieve anything by way of multilateral cooperation.But that makes Burnham’s task next year even more critical. The UK needs to show that it is still possible for the world’s leading nations – including the US and China – to work together to meet the key challenges facing the world.So what should the UK’s presidency priorities be?View image in fullscreenAndy Burnham speaking at the Labour party conference in Liverpool last week.Photograph: Michael Bowles/ShutterstockFirst, agreement on the need for, and a process towards, a global treaty on the regulation of artificial intelligence. After the recent alarm over the existential risks of AI, the UK has a chance to lead the world towards a global agreement on its control. Even if Trump is unwilling to sign up, getting the rest of the world to do so, seeking a form of global “technological security”, would be a vital achievement. A future US president might well wish to accede later.Second, acknowledgment of the growing risk to food security and a plan to deal with it. The incoming“supersized” El Niñoweather pattern is combining with the climate crisis, soil and biodiversity loss, and the impact of the war in the Middle East on diesel and fertiliser costs to create a perfect storm for the world’s food system. Agricultural yields are falling and food prices rising, leaving millions of people at risk of hunger. The G20 needs to act to prevent it.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThird, acknowledgment of accelerating climate insecurity – the severe risks posed by the climate emergency to all countries’ economies and societies – and agreement on coordinated measures to improve climate resilience. Though the Trump administration does not support emissions reduction, it does accept the need to adapt to climate change, and this year’s extreme weather events have impressed on all governments how urgent this is. TheG20should agree to provide more support to the most vulnerable countries.Fourth, agreement on a debt restructuring programme for low- and middle-income economies whose debt – through no fault of their own, but because of rising global interest rates – has now become unsustainable. For too many countries the compounding of debt burdens with rising energy and food prices has made sustainable economic growth all but impossible.What connects these issues is that all are global problems that can only be tackled through international cooperation. They each address aspects of national and global security – technological, food, climate and economic. Importantly, the first three address problems that are highly visible and politically salient to the British public, enabling the government to demonstrate how international action benefits people at home. (And the fourth represents a vital contribution to global economic growth.) And all have a good chance of being agreed in the G20, despite the conflicts and tensions that in other areas divide the world’s leaders.G20 host countries always invent a slogan to express their presidency ambitions. In other contexts Burnham has said he wants to give people a sense of hope. That is something people all over the world need. For the G20 he might wish to try “national security through international cooperation”. It would not be a bad legacy to aim for.Michael Jacobs is professor of political economy at the University of Sheffield and a former energy and climate change adviser to Gordon Brown when he was prime ministerExplore more on these topicsG20OpinionAndy BurnhamForeign policyClimate crisisAI (artificial intelligence)Debt reliefLabourcommentShareReuse this content

title: Putin’s escalating bombing campaign won’t break Ukrainians’ resolve. History shows that it’s doomed to fail | Rajan Menon | The Guardian
description: As the fifth anniversary of Russia’s full-scale invasion looms, it’s worth remembering that this mode of warfare rarely crushes morale, says Rajan Menon, professor emeritus of international relations
Author: Rajan Menon
Headline: As the fifth anniversary of Russia’s full-scale invasion looms, it’s worth remembering that this mode of warfare rarely crushes morale, says Rajan Menon, professor emeritus of international relations
Content: Buildings heavily damaged following a Russian missile attack in Sloviansk, Ukraine, 16 September 2026.Photograph: Cameron Jones-Manley/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenBuildings heavily damaged following a Russian missile attack in Sloviansk, Ukraine, 16 September 2026.Photograph: Cameron Jones-Manley/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockOpinionUkrainePutin’s escalating bombing campaign won’t break Ukrainians’ resolve. History shows that it’s doomed to failRajan MenonAs winter approaches and the fifth anniversary of Russia’s full-scale invasion looms, it’s worth remembering that this mode of warfare rarely crushes moraleMon 5 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 11.22 EDTShareVladimir Putin’s army hasn’t made much headway in Ukraine this year, and his territorial goals – annexing four Ukrainian provinces – remain elusive, despite more than four and a half years of war. That explains his recent efforts to sap Ukrainians’ will to resist by launching relentless drone and missile strikes against their cities – targeting, among other sites, residential buildings, large open-air markets, shopping malls, the Dobrobut medical centre and the National Academy of Sciences,both in Kyiv.The capital has been hit the hardest, but other cities –Dnipro, Kharkiv, Kherson,Odesa, Mykolaiv,Sumy– haven’t been spared.Air-raid sirens pierce the quiet of night. People scramble to shelters (assuming there are any nearby) or, in Kyiv, race to below-ground subway stations. Even walking along city streets, shopping, or filling up your car at a garage forecourt – which are prime targets – can lead to injury, or even death.I got a taste of what these unremitting attacks are like during a September trip toUkraine. One night in Mykolaiv, I counted more than a dozen alerts between midnight and dawn. In Kopyliv, about 31 miles west of Kyiv, I was having dinner in a restaurant when a deafening bang made the walls shudder. A drone had hit a building about 500m away; orange flames engulfed its roof within seconds.Incidents like this are now part of daily life for Ukrainians, but are no less nerve-racking for that.During September, Russialaunched 3,177 jet-powered drones, mainly Geran variants, at Ukraine: nearly 12% more than in August, and a massive increase compared with 350 such strikes in June. Drones, jet-powered or not, are often supplemented by ballistic missiles such as the Iskander – devilishly difficult to intercept with its top speed of 5,600mph and ability to swerve in flight.The purpose of Putin’s escalating bombardment is to make life so unbearable for Ukrainians that they conclude that the only way out is to satisfy his unfulfilled annexationist ambitions: his army occupies almost all of Luhansk, but has yet to conquer the regions of Donetsk, Kherson and Zaporizhzhia completely.Putin would rather keep killing than admit he’s lost. As a winter of misery looms in Ukraine, Nato must step in | Simon TisdallRead moreBut his drone and missile campaign won’t force Ukraine to cave.In December 2025, aKyiv International Institute of Sociology pollrevealed that Ukrainians’ resistance to trading land for peace remains strong. Three-quarters of those surveyed rejected a hypothetical deal that included these provisions: Ukraine’s withdrawal from the unoccupied part of Donetsk, recognition of Russia’s legal ownership of Crimea and Donbas, and the abandonment of its Nato aspirations. Asked separately whether they would approve a settlement that required ceding the unoccupied parts of the two southern provinces, two-thirds said no. These responses are all the more significant because by the end of last year, Russia had begunattacking Ukraine’s power gridas abrutal winterapproached.Putin might nevertheless calculate that a massive bombing operation this winter that turns off the lights, disrupts heating and damages waterworks and sanitation systems will break Ukrainians’ willpower, creating conditions for Russia to conclude the war with additional territory in hand. His calculation isn’t unreasonable, considering Ukraine’s severe shortage of ballistic missile interceptors, whichreduced interceptionsfrom 70% in March to 20% in July. It’s collaborating with a European coalition to develop the cost-effective Freya ballistic missile defence system, and will acquire the Franco-Italian SAMP/T NG missile defence system, which provides far easier mobility to aid rapid relocation and is now under development. Neither, however, will be deployed in sufficient numbers any time soon.Still, the Russian leader’s strategy collides with some inconvenient facts, quite apart from Ukrainians’ proven toughness.Thehistorical recordshows that bombing campaigns don’t crush morale; they strengthen it. Ukrainians won’t be the exception. They regard resistance to Russia as essential for national survival. When I’ve asked them why they continue to fight, the reply, in one form or another, is that the alternative is to forfeit their independence. One can dismiss this as bravado, but what matters is that Ukrainians hold this view.Accompanying it is the widespread belief that Putin will use any deal to buy time and regroup before renewing his assault on Ukraine. This, too, makes Ukrainians wary of land-for-peace formulas, particularly those offered by Donald Trump and his two emissaries, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, whom they consider Putin partisans, rather than disinterested mediators.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBesides, Putin, too, is under pressure. According to the chief of the UK’s defence staff, his army has suffered1.5 millioncasualties. And though Ukraine has a military manpower shortage, so does Russia, despite a population that’s 3.5 times larger; hence its reliance onNorth Korean soldiersandAsian and Africanmercenaries. Moreover, the Russian army has barely gained any additional territory this year. During the first six months of 2026, it capturedonly 28% as much landas it did in the same period last year, and its troop losses nowexceed its monthly intake by 6,000.Furthermore, Ukrainiandrone attackson Russia’s roads and rail lines traversing Ukraine’s occupied territory in the south have left its troops in Crimea, Kherson and Zaporizhzhia short of critical supplies. Most recently,Operation Vivaldi, conducted by Ukraine’s 3rd Army Corps, caughtRussian troops by surprisein the Lyman sector of northern Donetsk, forcing them to retreat eastward.The war has harmed Russia’s economy. The army’s huge appetite for manpower has created severelabour shortagesthat have hurt businesses. The 2027 budget draft allocates35% of federal expendituresto defence. Ukraine’s strikes on refineries deep inside Russia had cut theirthroughput by about 30%, year on year, by June, creating chronic fuel shortages,widespread rationing, serpentine lines at petrol stations and a21% surge in petrol pricessince January.Taken together, Ukrainians’ opposition to sacrificing land, the historical failure of bombing campaigns to shatter civilian morale and Russia’s own assorted problems suggest that Putin’s drones and missiles won’t force Ukraine to accept peace on his terms – even under the stress of winter.Rajan Menon is a professor emeritus of international relations at the City College of New York and a senior research scholar at Columbia University’s Saltzman Institute of War and Peace StudiesExplore more on these topicsUkraineOpinionRussiaVladimir PutinEuropecommentShareReuse this content

title: Social care for disabled adults is in as much crisis as support for elderly people – so why is the government silent about it? | John Harris | The Guardian
description: Working-age adults such as my son, who is autistic, face an unreliable system, yet ministers talk only of a national care service for older people, says Guardian columnist John Harris
Author: John Harris
Headline: Working-age adults such as my son, who is autistic, face an unreliable system, yet ministers talk only of a national care service for older people, says Guardian columnist John Harris
Content: Illustration: R Fresson/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: R Fresson/The GuardianOpinionSocial careSocial care for disabled adults is in as much crisis as support for elderly people – so why is the government silent about it?John HarrisWorking-age adults such as my son, who is autistic, face a fragmented and unreliable system, yet ministers talk only of a national care service for older peopleMon 5 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 13.28 EDTShareSeemingly brilliant conference speeches are often followed by a hangover, and so it has arguably proved with Andy Burnham’s. It was, it has to be said, something of a triumph, but there is now a familiar sense ofnagging angstover how his big idea of a national care service is actually going to work. But equally, it doesn’t seem unreasonable to be more generous and patient. The policy issues are vast. The new PM’s commitment to serious change is clear. And having been urgently needed for years, the basics ofwhat he wants– personal, home-based care delivered free at the proverbial point of need – will be on their way if Labour wins the next election.Here, though, is a question that is much less finely balanced. NeitherBurnham’s speechnor themuch shorter address given by Yvette Cooper, the new health and social care secretary, contained a single mention of whatroughly halfof England’s social care budgets are spent on: provision for working-age disabled adults. Why not? I get the politics: fixating on older people’s care and the pensions triple lock makes everything clear and relatable. But England’s fragmented, unreliable system for younger disabled adults is in need of the same radical level of reform, and it’s the source of just as much fear and worry for the people who either depend on it, or eventually will do.I am one of them. In fact, I suffer from two sub-types of what we might call Care Dread. My mum is 83,my dad is 90, and they currently pay for visits from domiciliary care workers whose frequency is only going to go up.My son James– who is autistic and has learning disabilities – has just turned 20. He currently goes to a brilliant further education college, but my partner and I will soon face what special needs parents call “the cliff edge”: a switch from education to adult social care, which will bring on a bucket-load of questions. Could he be helped into employment? If he stays at home, what support and everyday stimulation is our local council going to pay for? If he goes into supported living, how do we guard againstwhat I have heard about from other mums and dads: long days spent plonked in front of the TV, the odd trip out, and the possibility of housemates with completely different needs?The list of fears goes on; it haunts all parents in our position. A new focus of worry, moreover, has just been added: proposals toaxe the health element of universal credit(which has already been almost halved this year to £217 a month) for young people with disabilities and health issues, and replacing it with new work schemes. To quote from the Guardian’s report, that plan comes with assurances about the measures not applying to “those with the most severe and debilitating disabilities”, which rather implies the grimly familiar official belief that you can easily grade disabilities from “mild” to “profound”, when lots of conditions show that you can’t (autism is one good example). But the proposals also underline why social care for disabled people has to be a big part of whatever detailed plan Burnham, Cooper and their comrades come up with.We know that the crossbench peer Louise Casey’sindependent commission on adult social carehas been convened to consider both older people’s care and support for working-age disabled adults. But evidently, the government is much keener on talking about the former than the latter. Indeed, when I contacted the Department of Health and Social Care, I was sent a comically bland and noncommittal response: “The prime minister has made clear that he wants to see rapid progress on adult social care reforms … Baroness Casey’s commission will outline what a national care service should look like, and as part of the review, the commission will explore and consider the options for supporting working-age disabled adults as well as older people in need of care.”Jim Kane is the CEO ofCommunity Integrated Care, a not-for profit that seeks to provide supported living and residential care for about 3,000 autistic and learning-disabled adults. “People who have disabilities absolutely have to be front and centre of everything that’s discussed,” he told me last week. “But I also want to be supportive of what the PM’s trying to do, because I don’t believe in my heart that he’s going to ignore disabled people.”There is so much to put right. Even in cases of disabled people who rely on benefits to live – the personal independence payment and universal credit, mostly – many councils’ care systems subject them to a means test. That means they snatch money as a contribution to the cost of care, whether that’s received at home and in what officialspeak calls “the community”, or through supported living. The learning-disability charity Mencap alerted me to theexperience of Fred– who has Down’s syndrome and autism and is deaf– and his mum, Annabel, who live in Somerset. “What many people do not realise,” says Annabel, “is that the local authority charges Fred £147.54 a week from his benefits to pay for his care. This leaves him with just £201.56 a week to live on, which amounts to £10,481 a year.”Two other issues were explained to me by Alison Bloomer, the editor of the expert online magazineLearning Disability Today. First, hundreds of thousands of disabled people are onwaiting listsfor the initial care assessments that councils endlessly evade and delay. At the moment, for people up to the age of 25, the special educational needs and disability (Send) tribunal – where decisions can be appealed – and education, health and care plans, which set out the support a young person is entitled to, offer some means of challenging councils’ decisions and conduct,though the government still seems set on degrading both mechanisms. And this is her second point: that dependence on the social care sector, by contrast, means the weakest kind of accountability. If you have a grievance, your only real hope is either the local government and social care ombudsman or your MP.In his speech, Burnham made moving reference to “the care we give to each other” via the state. But how do we define that? If my son starts to live within the care system, will he still get to indulge his passions: the Strokes, guitars,hillwalking? As Kane put it: “The social care system deals in safety. Have people got a roof over their heads? Have they got food? That’s about it, and it doesn’t even do those that well sometimes: we’ve all seenthe scandals. How does it help individuals build relationships? Can they even choose the people that they live with? You know, ‘Who are my friends? Can I have education? Can I pursue my hobbies?’”The chances of a system being able to consistently meet such fundamental needs are made slimmer by the appallingly low pay rates of care staff (the government is moving on this, although progress towards an adult social carefair pay agreementis still ongoing). Kane would like his employees to be thought of as the equivalent of Band 3 workers in the NHS. But there is now a28.6% gapbetween the two groups, and he cannot close it because of the dire financial position of just about all councils.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThese are the deep issues that any credible national care service will have to solve. Furious disabled people’s organisations are calling for a National Independent Living Service to be at the core of the reforms, but that will only happen if these issues are talked about – not just on conference podiums, but in the kind of Treasury circles where the best of intentions can too easily wither away. “If we want people to live genuinely fulfilled lives, there’s a price tag that’s different to the one we’ve got now,” Kane told me. Such is yet another quandary faced by this embattled but confident new government, and a vivid reason why so many of us have to keep on pushing.John Harris is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsSocial careOpinionLabourAndy BurnhamYvette CooperDisabilitycommentShareReuse this content

title: ‘I spat in Sean Connery’s face 16 times’: Ron Perlman on making The Name of the Rose | Movies | The Guardian
description: ‘When I couldn’t do the spitting scene, Sean took me aside and said: “Ron, if you don’t actually spit in my face, we’ll be here all day.” So I let one fly – and kept having to redo it’
Author: Chris Broughton
Headline: ‘When I couldn’t do the spitting scene, Sean took me aside and said: “Ron, if you don’t actually spit in my face, we’ll be here all day.” So I let one fly – and kept having to redo it’
Content: ‘I opened the door to find Sean there. He said, “Listen, boy …”’ Connery with Christian Slater in the medieval murder mystery.Photograph: Cinetext/Constantin Film/AllstarView image in fullscreen‘I opened the door to find Sean there. He said, “Listen, boy …”’ Connery with Christian Slater in the medieval murder mystery.Photograph: Cinetext/Constantin Film/AllstarHow we madeMovies‘I spat in Sean Connery’s face 16 times’: Ron Perlman on making The Name of the Rose‘When I couldn’t do the spitting scene, Sean took me aside and said: “Ron, if you don’t actually spit in my face, we’ll be here all day.” So I let one fly – and kept having to redo it’Interviews byChris BroughtonMon 5 Oct 2026 09.53 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 12.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJean-Jacques Annaud,directorI read an article about a curious book that had great reviews in Italy, a murder mystery about monks in the middle ages fighting for the fictional missing part of Aristotle’s Poetics. I said: “This is for me.” Since childhood, I had been fascinated with medieval and religious architecture, and Aristotle’s Poetics is my favourite literary work.I learned that Umberto Eco, the author, was going to be in France for one night and agreed to meet me at his hotel and that I would drive him to Charles de Gaulle airport. The first thing I saw was his shadow on the hotel staircase, which looked like the silhouette of Sherlock Holmes – Umberto was a man of great humour, and he met me wearing a deerstalker, with a pipe in his mouth. In the car, I asked questions: what sort of shoes would the Franciscans have been wearing? Would the monks have had beards? What colour would the pigs have been? He said: “I don’t know, I didn’t have to write any of that.” I ended up hiring medievalistJacques Le Goffand seven of his colleagues to make sure we got all the details right – costumes, architecture, liturgy and so on.double quotation markA big piece of timber fell on Feodor. ‘I’m 80 years old,’ he said, ‘I don’t mind dying. Was the take good?’I wanted an unknown to play William of Baskerville, the friar who investigates the deaths, and travelled the world to watch plays featuring great actors in their 50s. Meanwhile, agent Mike Ovitz kept calling, saying: “Sean Connery would love to make this movie.” Eventually, there was a knock on my door and I opened it to find Sean with the screenplay under his arm. He said, “Listen, boy …” and started reading. I had goose bumps. The way he said the dialogue was exactly what I’d been hearing in my head while reading the book.I flew to Vienna to look at paintings byBruegel the Elder. I wanted to be inspired by the real people of the period, people who had no dentists or doctors, but I did cast some good-looking monks, too. Christian Slater turned up to audition for the young novice, Adso, and said: “I didn’t learn the lines, I got drunk.” The casting director, Mary Jo, was furious and tried to send him away, but he was the one I wanted. He was only 16, but looked 14. It turned out he was Mary Jo’s son. I had three women selected to audition for the part of the nameless girl from the village, but Christian fell in love with the first, Valentina Vargas, as soon as he did a screen test with her, so I never saw the other two.We built a vast set on a hilltop near Rome for the monastery and village. During the scene at the end where the library tower burns, Sean’s cowl briefly caught fire, and a big piece of real timber fell on Feodor Chaliapin Jr, who played the blind monk, knocking him to the ground. “I’m 80 years old,” he said, “I don’t mind dying. Was the take good?” He went to hospital and we had to change the schedule because he then had a scar.After four months in Rome, I went back to my production office in Munich and couldn’t find it. I discovered the film’s producer, Bernd Eichinger, in the cellar with his feet on a table. He said, “JJ, I didn’t want to disturb you during the shoot, but I sold the building to help pay for the movie.”View image in fullscreen‘For my dialogue, I just went: eenie, meenie, miny, moe’ … Ron Perlman with Christian Slater in The Name of the Rose.Photograph: TCD/Prod DB/AlamyRon Perlman, playedSalvatoreMy very first film, Quest for Fire, was directed by Jean-Jacques. I played a caveman. Transforming myself into something completely foreign was an incredibly rewarding exercise and a phenomenal introduction to the world of cinema, so when I read that Jean-Jacques had attached himself to The Name of the Rose, I went through the book and found a character named Salvatore – an intellectually challenged hunchback who spoke in a jumble of seven languages – who would embody a similar challenge. I told Jean-Jacques that this part would be a dream come true.Jean-Jacques gave me complete freedom to figure out my dialogue. The Name of the Rose had been published in 80 languages, so I got copies in the seven thatUmberto Ecohas Salvatore referencing, and circled every time Salvatore spoke. Then I just went, “Eenie, meenie, miny, moe – OK, this word is Latin, this word is Spanish, this word is Italian …” and so on. That was the genesis of Salvatore’s communicative skills.I worked with a dialect coach who was also a historian with particular knowledge of the period. He suggested thelullabythat Salvatore sings when he’s burned at the stake. Jean-Jacques had this idea that Salvatore was so out of touch with reality that he was initially amused to be in that situation. The lullaby gave a sense of childlike wonder at the fact he’s involved in this ceremony, but doesn’t realise he’s about to lose his life.I only had to wear the prosthetic hump once, filming the scene where Salvatore is about to be tortured by F Murray Abraham as the inquisitor, Bernardo Gui. I was in the makeup chair for more than 13 hours and by the time I got to set, they had almost run out of time. My hair was shaved so it looked like I had mange. They said: “Good luck with your personal life, my friend.”I spent every moment I could with Sean Connery, watching him act and listening to his stories. He was my hero, the real deal. When it came to the scene where I had to spit in his eye, I just couldn’t do it. Sean took me aside, and said: “Ron, if you don’t actually spit in my face, we’ll be here all fucking day.” So I finally just let one fly. The problem was, you don’t film from just one angle, you have to recreate in profile, medium shot, closeup, over-the-shoulder … I must have spat in Sean Connery’s face 16 times that day.The Name of the Rose is available now on digital and limited edition 4K UHD and Blu-ray (Second Sight Films)Explore more on these topicsFilmHow we madeSean ConneryChristian SlaterRon PerlmanJean-Jacques AnnaudUmberto EcoFilm adaptationsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘If it’s too slick, it looks like a fashion mag’: Peter Zumthor on his £110m rammed concrete gallery | Architecture | The Guardian
description: It is one of the world’s finest collections, full of Monets, Miros and Picassos. But is the great Swiss architect’s extension for the Beyeler Foundation a worthy addition? Or is it a bit luxury boutique?
Author: Oliver Wainwright
Headline: It is one of the world’s finest collections, full of Monets, Miros and Picassos. But is the great Swiss architect’s extension for the Beyeler Foundation a worthy addition? Or is it a bit luxury boutique?
Content: ‘The stone of my youth’ … the gallery and a Louise Bourgeois spider.Photograph: Iwan Baan © The Easton Foundation / 2026, ProLitteris, ZurichView image in fullscreen‘The stone of my youth’ … the gallery and a Louise Bourgeois spider.Photograph: Iwan Baan © The Easton Foundation / 2026, ProLitteris, ZurichArchitecture‘If it’s too slick, it looks like a fashion mag’: Peter Zumthor on his £110m rammed concrete galleryIt is one of the world’s finest collections, full of Monets, Miros and Picassos. But is the great Swiss architect’s extension for the Beyeler Foundation a worthy addition? Or is it a bit luxury boutique?Oliver WainwrightMon 5 Oct 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 03.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn the early 1960s, when Peter Zumthor was a teenage apprentice in his father’s cabinet-making workshop, he designed his first cupboard. He later recalled the satisfaction of fitting the door so perfectly that it closed “with a special sucking sound”, saying his father instilled in him“the Basel pride in the well-built object”.Six decades on, with a fleet of globally celebrated projects to his name, the 83-year-old Swiss architect is back in Basel, beaming with the same local pride. He is gazing out at his latest well-built object, which is also his first project here: a monolithic new gallery that looks chiselled from the earth, its layers of pale crumbly concrete hammered into shape, its big oak and bronze doors – their handles wrapped with leather cord – closing with that same satisfyingly expensive Swiss swoosh.double quotation markThe glass lamps were blown by the only two men in Italy with the lung capacity“It was an old feeling,” Zumthor tells me, describing working in his home town to build the £110m addition to theBeyeler Foundation. “I encountered craftspeople who remembered my father, who had this special knowledge of how to make things. They weren’t surprised if something had to be custom-made.”View image in fullscreen‘Wooden womb’ … the pavilion is conceived as an open public lounge.Photograph: Mark Niedermann © 2026 Calder Foundation, New York / Artists Rights Society (ARS) New YorkIt was quite a change from his previous building site. Fresh from the recent opening of the tortuous, two-decade-long, $724maddition to the Los Angeles County Museum of Art, Zumthor is visibly relieved to be back on home turf. “The normal American architect is used to sourcing products, not looking for somebody who can make something custom-made,” he says, with a furrowed brow. “Their buildings are an assembly of products.”Not so inSwitzerland. From the pear wood handrails to the leather benches and blown glass lamps, every piece of his new gallery has been meticulously handmade. But is the sum of these bespoke parts a worthy companion to one of the country’s – if not the world’s – most beloved art museums?Designed by Italian architect Renzo Piano, the Beyeler Foundation washailedas a model of elegant restraint when it opened in October 1997 – the same month as Frank Gehry’s billowingBilbao Guggenheim– praised as a sober foil to the “iconic” tendencies of the time. Sited in Riehen, just outside Basel, in the grounds of an 18th-century villa, the museum was commissioned by Ernst Beyeler, Europe’s pre-eminent modern art dealer and co-founder of Art Basel, and his wife Hildy, to house their staggering collection of Monets and Mirós, Matisses and Picassos.A long, low, temple-like shed nestled in a garden, the foundation contains within its porphyry walls a luminous sequence of galleries, with daylight flooding through slender rooftop louvers. Piano took his hi-tech fetish and wrapped it in a luxurious stone skin, foreshadowing his bigger museums to come. But it was too small right from the day it opened. Two years later, it was extended by 12 metres and soon became the most visited art museum in the country, receiving 500,000 visitors a year. The challenge was how to extend a museum already deemed perfect by its art world patrons.View image in fullscreenPublic square of sorts … Zumthor’s Erlen Torhaus office and art-handling block, with fountain in the foreground.Photograph: Mark Niedermann“They wanted something completely different,” says Zumthor, who was selected from a shortlist of 11 architects in 2016, after 100 were approached for their ideas. “Renzo’s building is more industrial, whereas mine is almost domestic. It is the villa that this garden was missing.”The foundation acquired the Iselin-Weber park, a formerly private woodland adjacent to the museum campus, which now doubles its size, and where Zumthor’s gallery rises like a rocky outcrop. It is one of three new structures he has designed, along with a five-storey, timber-clad office and art-handling block, and an auditorium pavilion, conceived as an open public lounge – a particularly appealing space that can be accessed without a ticket. “Ninety per cent of the time,” says the foundation’s director, Sam Keller, “museum auditoriums are dead spaces. So we’ve turned it into a social space for people to come and hang out, read books, listen to podcasts or do some work, a real extension of the park.”The three buildings stand as an eclectic ensemble on either side of a lane, framing a public square of sorts, where a new drinking fountain trickles into a big stone trough, as in a traditional mountain village, welcoming art pilgrims to Zumthor-ville. Stone benches built into the museum facade greet weary wanderers. “A building is something you ought to be able to lean against every now and then,” says the architect, as Maurizio Cattelan’s unnervingsculpture of a drummer boyperches perilously on the parapet overhead, intermittently hammering his drum from the rooftop.The chance for Zumthor to finally build in Basel, a few kilometres from his birthplace, clearly brought back fond memories. In a schmaltzy new two-hour documentary by Wim Wenders called From Inside Out, the misty-eyed architect explains that this “intimate building” has “a lot to do with me growing up here”. He recounts that Jura limestone was “the stone of my youth”, describing how the village fountains and the cattle troughs “all glowed”. He wanted his own building to glow, too, so he mixed Jura stone into the concrete, and had workers tamp the dry mixture by hand, laying it at a rate of no more than 45cm a day. This is all filmed with a stirring musical backdrop. He wanted the wobbly joints between each day’s work left visible, like strata of sedimentary rock.View image in fullscreenBrighter upstairs … large picture windows framing pastoral views.Photograph: Mark Niedermann“I call it ‘farmer concrete’,” he says. “You see it everywhere in the mountains. They make it themselves, and they don’t vibrate the mixture, so it looks rough like this. You can see the building has a history, that hands have worked on it. It’s nice if you can see those traces. If it’s too slick, you just look like a fashion magazine.”Zumthor’s rugged brand of “rammed concrete” has become one of his highly published trademarks (and has indeedfeatured in fashion magazines). There is a sense of him bringing his greatest hits to the Beyeler ensemble. He used the technique for theBruder Klaus field chapelin rural Germany and aholiday house in Devonfor Alain de Botton’s Living Architecture company. The admin block, meanwhile, bears a distinct resemblance to hisatelier building in Haldenstein, also in Switzerland, its elegant oak facade (masking a concrete frame) crowned with a slender corrugated canopy.And the pavilion draws on yet another language. It’s like a warm wooden womb that’s been dug into the landscape, surrounded by walls of glass and topped with a low upholstered acoustic ceiling, full of armchairs encouraging visitors to lounge awhile. Zumthor had to wait so long for a commission in his home town, he has turned one project into three.View image in fullscreen‘It looks rough’ … the pharaonic staircase.Photograph: Oliver WainwrightThe galleries themselves are quite a departure from Piano’s top-lit white cubes. After the gleaming stone exterior, the interior feels almost cave-like, Monet’s waterlilies looking muddier than ever in the ground-floor gloom. Things get brighter upstairs, with large picture windows framing pastoral views in different directions as you ascend the three floors, looking towards the Black Forest on one side and the Jura mountains on the other. Limestone terrazzo floors, lime-washed walls and pale concrete ceilings create an all-encompassing world of beige, which somehow flattens the work on show, relieved only by dark timber-lined nooks for loos and lifts.Lozenge-shaped glass lamps (“made by the only two men in Italy who have the lung capacity to do it”, I am told) provide some ambient light, while spots highlight particular works. But you might find yourself pining for the celestial top-light of Piano’s galleries next door. Despite the architect’s protestations, it oozes the aura of a luxury boutique. As one visiting Angelino noted: “It feels like a newSkims store.”‘Starchitects go home’: what’s the truth behind Albania’s astonishing building boom?Read moreThe creamy promenade culminates in a roof terrace, with more views of pretty Swiss countryside, before visitors are shuttled down a pharaonic external stairway between the concrete walls, punched with triangular openings on one side, giving glimpses of the park and a mature ginkgo tree, around which the arms of the Y-shaped building extend. Questioned about the need for all this concrete, and its attendant carbon footprint, Zumthor is adamant. “I could not make a wooden museum,” he says. “I think it is not good for art. This kind of classical art needs more substance.”He might have questioned his own assumptions. When it first opened, the Beyeler was praised for its brave departure from the fashions of the time. Thirty years on, Zumthor, for all his talk of sensitivity to place, has created something that feels as globally ubiquitous as the Louise Bourgeois spider that crouches in the garden outside. Like the menagerie of buildings by noted architects at theVitra campusnearby, the foundation has succeeded in adding another familiar collectible to its haul of prized works.Explore more on these topicsArchitectureSwitzerlandMuseumsEuropeRenzo PianofeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Aphrodite review – a trashy way to treat the goddess of love | Exhibitions | The Guardian
description: She’s the ultimate female nude, a Greek goddess who inspired centuries of artists. Yet despite some world-class loans, her story here is jumbled
Author: Jonathan Jones
Headline: She’s the ultimate female nude, a Greek goddess who inspired centuries of artists. Yet despite some world-class loans, her story here is jumbled
Content: When sex goddesses ruled European art … Michelangelo Pistoletto’s Venus of the Rags.Photograph: Tate and Michelangelo PistolettoView image in fullscreenWhen sex goddesses ruled European art … Michelangelo Pistoletto’s Venus of the Rags.Photograph: Tate and Michelangelo PistolettoExhibitionsReviewAphrodite review – a trashy way to treat the goddess of loveAshmolean museum, OxfordShe’s the ultimate female nude, a Greek goddess who inspired centuries of artists. Yet despite some world-class loans, her story here is jumbledJonathan JonesMon 5 Oct 2026 10.58 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 10.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBotticelli’s Venus has parked her shell outside your house and come to pay a night-time visit. The glowing strands of her hair glitter against blackness as she looks past you at a mystery only she can see, while your eyes follow those river-like locks down to a hand that gathers a looping cascade between her thighs. She is, unmistakably, the goddess fromBotticelli’s The Birth of Venusin the Uffizi, Florence. This very similar painting from about 1490, also by Botticelli and his workshop, suggests his Uffizi masterpiece was already such an icon that someone commissioned this version without the zephyrs and green sea, just that goddess body.So it goes. Venus, in art, is just a word for “female nude”. Botticelli started a modern appetite that has never ended. From his hypnotic paintings a host of lush sex goddesses rose up, or reclined, to rule European art through to Michelangelo Pistoletto’s ironic 1967 assemblageVenus of the Rags, also here, in which a heap of old clothes overflow from a corner around a marble nude seen from behind, the mix of beauty and chaos resembling a rubbish-strewn Naples piazza.View image in fullscreen‘No exploration of its impact’ … Crouching Aphrodite.Photograph: Royal Collection Trust/The Royal Collection/ HM King Charles III © Royal Collection Enterprise/ British MuseumBut this exhibition is not called Venus. And it doesn’t tell her artistic story except in bits with vast lacunae. Instead, it sees Venus as a cheap Roman substitute for the original Greek love goddess Aphrodite, who in turn is exposed as a ripoff of a matriarchal deity once worshipped on Cyprus. The result is a mixture of world-class loans and an archaeological hobbyhorse.Both the quality and gaps hit you straight away with a classical marble Crouching Venus (sorry, Aphrodite), lent from the royal collection. There’s no exploration of its impact on later art. In fact, this Roman copy of an ancient Greek original was sold by Cromwell’s republican regime after the beheading of its royal owner, Charles I. It was acquired by the artist Peter Lely who painted his own mysterious, nude, anti-Puritan masterpiece Nymphs by a Fountain. After the Restoration he also portrayed Nell Gwyn nude – his interest in this Venus was perversely creative. Before that, Rubens saw this same statue and based his painting Venus Frigida on it.Which is another way of saying that the story of Aphrodite/Venus in art is massive, epic and complex. Perhaps the comparatively small size of the exhibition can’t hold all that, yet a lot of space is wasted. Still, it has to start somewhere and the first room displays the many ways Aphrodite was depicted in ancient Greece, including a Red-figure vase with a scene of her and rival goddesses, Hera and Athena, preparing for the beauty contest she will win, leading to the Trojan war. So many stories, and this room seems almost breezy with them. The marriage of Aphrodite to the smith-god Hephaestos and her adultery with Ares, god of war, is told in a yada yada way and illustrated by a minor 16th-century print. Then suddenly you are plunged way, way back to encounter what this show claims was the real, original Aphrodite.View image in fullscreenEgyptianised statuette of Aphrodite-Astarte Golgoi-Ayios Photios, Cyprus c. 600-550BC.Photograph: Louvre Museum/Musée du Louvre, ParisIn classical mythology, Aphrodite has a special relationship with Cyprus: it is to Cyprian shores that her shell wafts in The Birth of Venus. That is because the Greek Aphrodite, we’re told here, is an appropriation of a female deity who was once all-powerful on the island. Prehistoric totems with abstract bodies, and in one case a bird’s head, attest to the centrality of this cult. Terracotta figures of childbirth and motherhood may have been offered by women to this nameless deity. Other images mix her with Egyptian and Phoenician deities. But I wasn’t convinced that any of this explains the Greek and Roman love divinity. Either way, it is crushingly out of sequence – why didn’t they start here then go forward in time?What’s inescapable is that the ancient Greeks made nudity their thing. It embodied (literally) their sense of being different from other cultures. But you don’t want to be caught looking too long at the Capitoline Venus. This second-century AD Roman marble statue is a copy of a lost work that was an ancient scandal: the Venus of Knidos by Praxiteles. Before Praxiteles, the Greeks didn’t portray Aphrodite nude, so people were powerfully struck by its intimacy when it was unveiled in the fourth century BC. Aphrodite has stripped for her bath and is trying, failing, to cover herself with her arms. One besotted admirer allegedly entered her sanctuary by night and rubbed himself against the statue’s cold hard thigh, leaving a semen stain.It’s troubling to see this after you’ve encountered the evidence for the ancient Cypriot Aphrodite. It looks as if the Greeks took a matriarchal deity and turned her into a sex toy. The Romans borrowed that nude image and spread it throughout their empire: a raw, graffiti-like relief from a fort north of Hadrian’s Wall of a naked Venus bathing is a funny, fascinating delight.For me it’s Botticelli who is the true believer in Aphrodite/Venus. For 1,000 years, ever since the fall of the Roman empire, she was cast out by Christianity. Her worship was revived in the Renaissance. When you gaze at the unfathomable eyes of his Venus, you too believe that love is a holy thing that deserves its own deity.Aphrodite: The Making of a Goddess is atAshmolean museum, Oxfordfrom 8 October 2026 to 11 April 2027Explore more on these topicsExhibitionsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Post your questions for Sofia Coppola  | Movies | The Guardian
description: A new documentary by Eleanor Coppola goes behind the scenes on her daughter’s 2006 punk classic, Marie Antoinette. To mark its release, Sofia Coppola will be taking your questions
Author: Rich Pelley
Headline: A new documentary by Eleanor Coppola goes behind the scenes on her daughter’s 2006 punk classic, Marie Antoinette. To mark its release, Sofia Coppola will be taking your questions
Content: Brought up on screen … Sofia Coppola.Photograph: Stéphane Cardinale/Corbis/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenBrought up on screen … Sofia Coppola.Photograph: Stéphane Cardinale/Corbis/Getty ImagesFilm & Music reader interviewMoviesPost your questions for Sofia CoppolaA new documentary by Eleanor Coppola goes behind the scenes on her daughter’s 2006 punk classic, Marie Antoinette. To mark its release, Sofia Coppola will be taking your questionsRich PelleyMon 5 Oct 2026 07.20 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 07.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTo say thatSofia Coppolagrew up on screen would be an understatement. The youngest child and only daughter of filmmaker Francis Ford Coppola and documentary-maker Eleanor Coppola, she appeared in all three Godfather films: as the baby being christened in 1972’s The Godfather, as a child on the steamboat in 1974’s The Godfather Part II, and, aged 19, as Mary Corleone in 1990’s The Godfather Part III.In between came small roles in several of her dad’s films, including 1983’s The Outsiders and Rumble Fish, 1984’s The Cotton Club and 1986’s Peggy Sue Got Married, in which she played Kathleen Turner’s younger sister Nancy. She also popped up all over 1990s music videos, playing a wild-eyed Joan Crawford in Sonic Youth’s 1990 Mildred Pierce, a troubled drifter in the Black Crowes’ 1992 Sometimes Salvation, one of Madonna’s clubbing friends in 1992’s Deeper and Deeper, and an injured gymnast in the Chemical Brothers’ 1997 Elektrobank, directed by her then-boyfriend Spike Jonze.Although this brings up loads of questions you may well like to ask her already – what was it like growing up in the Coppola household, with Nicolas Cage as her cousin? – it’s probably what happened when she switched to behind the camera that will intrigue you most.Did she ever thank Sonic Youth’s Thurston Moore for accidentally kickstarting her screenwriting and directing career by recommending Jeffrey Eugenides’ 1993 The Virgin Suicides to her? How terrified was she that Bill Murray would even turn up in Tokyo to film 2003’s Lost in Translation with no contract? Why is there a pair of Converse trainers in 2006’s Marie Antoinette? What was the strangest thing she found while filming 2013’s The Bling Ring inside Paris Hilton’s actual house?And now she has returned to Marie Antoinette in the documentary Making Marie Antoinette, pieced together from more than 80 hours of behind-the-scenes footage shot by Eleanor, and finished by Sofia after her death in 2024. The 20th anniversary celebrations have already started too: there’s an exhibition at the Petit Trianon in Versailles full of costumes, props and bits from the film – and New Order even turned up to play a mini concert there last month.Get your questions in by noon this Wednesday 7 October and we’ll publish her replies in the Readers Interview section. Let them eat questions!Making Marie Antoinette is in cinemas from 23 October and streams on Mubi from 6 NovemberExplore more on these topicsFilmFilm & Music reader interviewSofia CoppolaFrancis Ford  CoppolacalloutShareReuse this content

title: Metallica review – metal titans on fine form in spectacular rarities-focused show | Metallica | The Guardian
description: The first night of a new residency is an immersive plunge into the band’s visual world that showcases the depth of their catalog
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The first night of a new residency is an immersive plunge into the band’s visual world that showcases the depth of their catalog
Content: Metallica at Sphere, Las Vegas, 1 October 2026.Photograph: Jeff YeagerView image in fullscreenMetallica at Sphere, Las Vegas, 1 October 2026.Photograph: Jeff YeagerMetallicaReviewMetallica review – metal titans on fine form in spectacular rarities-focused showSphere, Las VegasThe first night of a new residency is an immersive plunge into the band’s visual world that showcases the depth of their catalogSam Hockley-SmithMon 5 Oct 2026 09.21 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 14.27 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLas Vegas’s Sphere takes on the characteristics of whatever it’s advertising on its exterior. Depending on when you look, you might see Orbi, the Sphere mascot, winking at you, or an ad for one of their Wizard of Oz showings, or maybe a roiling mass of red flames and shocks of lightning announcing the arrival ofMetallicafor their residency Life Burns Faster. Looking at it feels like staring at the end times. It’s like a huge black hole, sucking in the jittery sun-blasted energy of Vegas and transmuting it into an ominous ode to the renegade titans of thrash, but, you know, an older, wiser, therapized version of the band.This is the first night of Metallica’s 24-show residency, and it features the return of their “no repeat” format, meaning they play twice a week without repeating a single song during that week. It’s a showcase of the breadth of their catalogue as much as it’s a reminder of just how many indelible classics they’ve written. It also makes for a more interesting show. It’s not especially difficult forMetallicato play hours of hits, but it’s more fun when they forgo a few obvious ones in favor of a larger narrative.‘Never fails to delight’: why Metallica: Some Kind of Monster is my feelgood movieRead moreThe implication of the unpredictable set list means that these shows are for the real fans. On night one, the band avoid a full nostalgia grab, playingHardwired … to Self Destruct’s marching Now That We’re Dead from 2016, the furious Lux Æterna from 2023’s72 Seasons, and the half-ballad-half-catharsis of The Day That Never Comes, from 2008’s Rick Rubin-produced return to thrash Death Magnetic. The loose, non-chronological album-hopping allows the band to track their progress through their relationship to those real fans, focusing on emotion over adherence to a rigid greatest hits timeline.Yeah, they do not play Enter Sandman on night one, but theydoplay Ride the Lightning’s instrumental The Call of Ktulu while a giant, slimy Cthulhu unfolds itself and plods through Vegas, mottled skin shimmering as it grabs a fighter jet and throws it at the audience. As much as I love that moment for the way it brings Metallica’s gruesome visual world into a twisted hyperreality, I can’t help but wish I am seeing the band in a tiny, sweaty venue without any visuals at all. They still hold so much kinetic energy and power.View image in fullscreenMetallica at Sphere, Las Vegas, 1 October 2026.Photograph: Jeff YeagerEveryone in Metallica is now in their early 60s, but it doesn’t seem like it. Lars Ulrich finds new pockets to expand his driving rhythm, James Hetfield can still move his voice from gravelly-metallic snarl to full and rounded ballad, Kirk Hammett’s guitar-work is intricate and unpredictable, swerving when you think he’ll just keep ascending – he’s undeniably one of the greatest living guitarists – and Robert Trujillo’s percussive work on the five-string bass adds depth to everything, gluing it all together.Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall review – Paul Thomas Anderson’s sumptuous recording is an immediate classicRead moreIn other words, Metallica don’t need the bells and whistles, but they’ve also long been a band that loves to experiment with their live show, and sometimes their entire identity: like when they invited a therapist to help them navigate interpersonal turmoil and then filmed the whole experience and released it as the documentary-cum-concert filmSome Kind of Monsterin 2004, or the time they performed a show they called Pandemica to virtually no one on an empty winery during those uncertain early months of the pandemic, and then toured a concert film of the event at drive-in movie theaters across the country.Most Metallica songs are built on constant forward-movement and simmering rage, but as they’ve gotten older they’ve peeled back the facade and revealed the self-awareness that allows them to avoid the nostalgia trap of seeming like faded versions of their former selves. Metallica’s whole thing – iron crosses and electric chairs, squealing guitar solos, obsession with mortality and death and war, skulls flaming and otherwise, the aforementioned Cthulhu – still works.View image in fullscreenMetallica at Sphere, Las Vegas, 1 October 2026.Photograph: Brett MurrayThe band bookend the show with two cuts fromMaster of Puppets, kicking things off with a furious rendition of Battery, an ode to their early thrash roots that is also about relentless destruction, and closing things out with the anthemic title track, which is about the all-consuming pain of addiction as the walls of the Sphere morph into an immersive version of the album cover’s military graveyard, with each member of the band projected on to one of the crosses. Heavy-handed? Sure, but Metallica have always been heavy-handed. That’s part of the appeal.One odd dynamic about the Sphere is that the bands that play there are forced to compete with their own visuals for attention. Metallica circumvent this by dialing into their visual world. During Ride the Lightning, a song about being wrongly executed in an electric chair, the audience stare out at the band from the chair itself, the headpiece crackling overhead as if we were the ones waiting to be killed. It was frequently overwhelming and occasionally awe-inspiring, but it never fully distracted from their very tight set. Ulrich is an elastic, fluid drummer, Hetfield’s voice is like a battering ram, and Hammett and Trujillo still look like there’s nowhere they’d rather be than up on that stage, masters of their respective instruments.In the middle of the show, Ulrich and Hetfield leave the stage, as the other two spend a few minutes jamming to the marching rhythm of a single kick drum. In this huge room, with sound bouncing off the curved walls, their guitar and bass tandem take on new textures, sounding full-bodied even when it gets a little indulgent or silly. While they are in a world of insular musical rapture, they are projected on to the Sphere, melting into viscous ocean waves. It feels like it’s happening upon a 3am public access live performance that you can’t tear your eyes away from because it is so weirdly compelling. A moment of warm humanity in the midst of a reckoning.View image in fullscreenMetallica at Sphere, Las Vegas, 1 October 2026.Photograph: Brett MurrayMetallica have survived this long not because they’re genre shapeshifters, but because their music is so rooted in the forever resonant concepts of injustice, mortality, human violence and mistrust. During each decade they’ve been active, the band has taken a look at the world they live in and come to the conclusion that there’s no escape, which is probably why they play like they’re trying to outrun something – time, death, love, reality, literal and figurative demons – but never can quite get away. Why would they want to? No other band at this level can make anger sound so good. During Nothing Else Matters, a ballad about love and loneliness that opened up the band’s sonic universe when it was released on 1991’s pivotal Black Album, Hetfield asks the crowd to sing the chorus back to him, and then after the final “and nothing else mattersssss” was belted out from the stands, he responds: “You’re absolutely right.” A guy a few rows in front of me clutches his head, staring down toward the stage in rapture or pain or both, or maybe he is just looking straight into his own soul.No one could terrify like Cronos, the black metal innovator who reignited rock’s hellraising attitudeRead moreToward the end of the show, Metallica go all the way back to the beginning with a tight, faithful version of the all-time classic Seek and Destroy, which is accompanied by footage of the band members in their early days. It’s always emotional to see titans of rock grow older, but there was another layer here, too. Metallica have been part of our musical landscape for so long that it’s easy to forget how innovative their early stuff was, and how Seek and Destroy in particular slashed its way through the then stagnant hard rock tropes of the 70s, giving way to the apocalyptic 80s, as a sound that was scuzzier and more nihilistic thrashed and clawed to the surface, taking hold of popular culture.Eventually the inside of the Sphere light up flat gray. The house lights come on, Hetfield greets fans, and Trujillo and Hammett throw cups full of guitar picks into the audience while Ulrich carefully hands out a few drumsticks, presumably to avoid pegging people in the head, before stopping to shake hands and admire signs concertgoers had written. The show is over, but Metallica are still here.Metallica’s Life Burns Faster residency is at Sphere,Las Vegas, until 13 March 2027Explore more on these topicsMetallicaMetalPop and rockLas Vegaslive music reviewsShareReuse this content

title: De Profundis review – Oscar Wilde brought alive with righteous rage | Theatre | The Guardian
description: Anguished monologue based on letter to jailed playwright’s ex-lover is gripping in its illumination of a tortured artist
Author: Arifa Akbar
Headline: Anguished monologue based on letter to jailed playwright’s ex-lover is gripping in its illumination of a tortured artist
Content: Anger is an energy … Jens Harzer in De Profundis.Photograph: Joerg Brueggemann/OstkreuzView image in fullscreenAnger is an energy … Jens Harzer in De Profundis.Photograph: Joerg Brueggemann/OstkreuzTheatreReviewDe Profundis review – Oscar Wilde brought alive with righteous rageCoronet theatre, LondonAnguished monologue based on letter to jailed playwright’s ex-lover is gripping in its illumination of a tortured artistArifa AkbarMon 5 Oct 2026 08.26 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 08.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOscar Wilde’s De Profundis really does belong to the depths. Written as a letter to his ex-lover after being jailed for homosexuality, it reflects soul-crushing torments.Its adaptation into a monologue rarely gets an outing, perhaps because it is so bleak, but is staged by the Berliner Ensemble with heaps of extra angst for good measure.It is dramatised with great anguished physicality by Jens Harzer and spoken in German with English surtitles. Only his face is lit up at first and the set-up looks Beckettian in its bare, black effects: Hansjörg Hartung’s lugubrious set design accompanied by Jörg Gollasch’s variously plangent or flighty musical compositions and Steffen Heinke’s well-crafted lighting. Harzer initially looks deathly, with a luminous outline around him suggesting a man speaking from his grave.The letter opens with Wilde’s pet name for Lord Alfred Douglas – Bosie – but this production only speaks in direct, accusatory address to “you”. Bosie is decried as something of an anti-muse to the suffering artist – a grasping, sybaritic parasite whose company sucked the creative life out of Wilde.View image in fullscreenBare and Beckettian …. De Profundis.Photograph: Joerg Brueggemann/Ostkreuz.Harzer does not overplay it or tip into melodrama but blasts the part with righteous rage. He spits or shouts some lines, speaks others with numbed forbearance. In between the anger are shafts of light: remnants of love for Bosie, flashes of his past celebrated glory as a writer. He cannot let himself be filled with hate, he says, yet this monologue is irredeemably bitter.Under well-paced direction by Oliver Reese, it is remarkable that none of it feels over-wrought or leaden. It is essentially a static piece of narration but does not feel it here. Harzeris sometimes curled into himself, like Franz Kafka’s insect-like Gregor Samsa, and sometimes stretching his arms in the air in Christ-like surrender.As an interval-free production just 10 minutes short of two hours, it is an accomplishment that a piece drenched in so much darkness is also so gripping in its illumination of an artist in full-throttle throes of despair.At theCoronet theatre, London, until 7 OctoberExplore more on these topicsTheatreOscar WildereviewsShareReuse this content

title: Tom Cruise’s Digger has flopped spectacularly – but I think it is a misunderstood masterpiece | Movies | The Guardian
description: This article contains spoilers for Digger: Alejandro G Iñárritu’s film may be about to become one of the biggest bombs Hollywood has ever seen – but it is destined to be re-evaluated with time
Author: Sian Cain
Headline: This article contains spoilers for Digger: Alejandro G Iñárritu’s film may be about to become one of the biggest bombs Hollywood has ever seen – but it is destined to be re-evaluated with time
Content: Tom Cruise as Digger Rockwell in Digger.Photograph: Courtesy of Warner Bros. Pictures/Warner Bros. Pictures/APView image in fullscreenTom Cruise as Digger Rockwell in Digger.Photograph: Courtesy of Warner Bros. Pictures/Warner Bros. Pictures/APMoviesTom Cruise’s Digger has flopped spectacularly – but I think it is a misunderstood masterpieceSian CainAlejandro G Iñárritu’s film may be about to become one of the biggest bombs Hollywood has ever seen – but it is destined to be re-evaluated with timeThis article contains spoilers for DiggerMon 5 Oct 2026 00.39 EDTShareIfeel for film critics, I really do. Tom Cruise’s latest film Digger put them in an impossible position: you can’t really talk about it without spoiling what makes it, in my eyes, a masterpiece. Or completely terrible–as many,manycritics have argued over the last week,without being fully free to say why.That is not their fault: media screenings around the world opened with a plea from Warner Bros to not spoil the film’s central reveal.This seems like it may have been a misstep, because curiosity and Cruise alone were clearly not enough to get bums on seats. Digger isnow projected to lose around $150m, after taking a paltry $20m globally in its opening weekend. Warner Bros is trying to make the best of a bad situation, first crowing about the stinker reviews – “insufferable” and “smug” have been repeated a lot – then pivoting to a new sell:the Yanks don’t get it, so it must be good.Which is a shame, because I thinkDiggeris a remarkable film and I am going to spoil the reveal to say why – so stop reading here if you don’t want to know.Despite the marketing, Tom Cruise isn’t really playing Digger Rockwell, a fictional, swaggering oil tycoon who is tasked with saving the world after his oil rig explodes in Greenland, causing an enormous glacier to hurtle towards Europe and guaranteed climate disaster. Cruise plays Curtis Markson, an actor who is portraying Digger onstage in a didactic, satirical play decades after the rig really exploded and left the world in ruins. The big-budget play, titled Fossil Fools, is directed and adapted by Hannah (Sophie Wilde) and funded by Rockwell’s nephew Kenny (Jesse Plemons), in what seems to be a tiny act of philanthropic penance to offset his family’s terrible legacy.I have seen Digger twice already, and I think it is brilliantly audacious. Alejandro G Iñárritu’s film is the best fictional work about the climate crisis that I have seen yet, because it is also about the inability of art to speak to this moment truthfully. It is about perception and reality. And it is about our inability to distinguish the two, and how that leaves us vulnerable to the loudest, most charismatic voices in a room.View image in fullscreenJohn Goodman in Digger.Photograph: Warner Bros Entertainment Inc/PACruise’s Curtis Markson is frustrated by Fossil Fools, complaining that he is being made to play a “cartoon” version of Rockwell so Hannah can “make some statement”. Fossil Fools is objectively terrible: the grotesque and pathetic US president (John Goodman) constantly moans about having “cancer of the asshole” for laughs, while his top brass, all gorillas, demand the chance to bomb the glacier and “blow that frozen cunt up”. One literally eats popcorn while watching Europe go underwater. And when Digger finally stands before the world to answer for his crime, he pins the blame on them; it was their demand for oil that lead to disaster, all so they could have “two-day delivery of shit you don’t need”. “You want freedom to live your unsustainable lives,” he shouts. “You love oil. Let’s cut the bullshit.”The real Digger Rockwell was a “composed, frightening, seductive psychopath”, but Curtis is being ordered to play him like a rootin’-tootin’ clown in a ten-gallon hat. “What the fuck is happening? What are we doing?” he shouts at Hannah. The two argue it out: is this meant to be a satire? Is it a farce? Is it revenge on Digger?
