Or is it just a bad telling of a true story, one that was never meant to go beyond the “shitty little theatre in London” where Kenny first saw it, then saved it with his big wallet and his guilty conscience?But then Kenny steps in to deliver a speech that, in my eyes, embodies the film’s true point. “It really doesn’t matter. Satire, comedy, farce, drama – it doesn’t matter,” he tells Curtis and Hannah. “You’re both right. We’re all right. Now what?”Tom Cruise unveils remarkable transformation in Digger trailer: ‘I’ve never had something that could challenge me in this way’Read more“Now what” is what stayed with me. I don’t think many of us need a film to tell us that climate change is a terrifying, maddening thing to live through, or that political bloviating will probably block viable solutions, or that greed is degrading us and the planet. But I do love that a blockbuster film packed with enormous stars has posed the question: what does art mean at the end of the world? And, if we are honest with ourselves, do we just want art that tells us the truth, or reinforces what we already think?Iñárritu’s answer is the latter; we’d probably settle for a middling play with a bad title if it gave us two hours of distraction and someone to blame. We like our US presidents stupid and laughable, not stupid and terrifying. A play written at the literal end of the world,aboutthe literal end of the world, would very likely be didactic, plodding and annoying. Did you see Don’t Look Up? We are not above Fossil Fools.Art will never be the thing that saves us from existential threat, Digger argues – but it can give us catharsis. In the end, Curtis plays Digger as a clown and gets a euphoric standing ovation. Then an alarm goes off, signalling some horrifying reality outside – and the audience put on their gas masks and file out the theatre.It is almost poetic that so many critics are arguing that all of Iñárritu’s metatextual postmodern faff is a lazy defence against the criticism they want to dish out: the acting/script/accent in Fossil Fools is supposed to be bad, so we can’t say Digger is bad! But I don’t think this is quite honest and it seems like every single critic has found plenty of creative ways to say Digger is bad. So many reviews seem unable to distinguish between what is Fossil Fools and what is Digger; perception and reality. Perhaps the one truth we can settle on is: you should probably go see it yourself.Explore more on these topicsFilmDiggerTom CruiseAlejandro González IñárritucommentShareReuse this content

title: Artist calls in lawyers after Tories use his Burnham portrait without consent | Conservative conference 2026 | The Guardian
description: Stanley Chow’s cartoon was put on water bottles at party conference with the slogan ‘Bottler Burnham’
Author: Helena Horton
Headline: Stanley Chow’s cartoon was put on water bottles at party conference with the slogan ‘Bottler Burnham’
Content: The bottles mocking Andy Burnham – and using Stanley Chow’s cartoon – were on view at the Conservative party conference in Birmingham.Photograph: Christopher Furlong/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe bottles mocking Andy Burnham – and using Stanley Chow’s cartoon – were on view at the Conservative party conference in Birmingham.Photograph: Christopher Furlong/Getty ImagesConservative conference 2026Artist calls in lawyers after Tories use his Burnham portrait without consentStanley Chow’s cartoon was put on water bottles at party conference with the slogan ‘Bottler Burnham’Helena HortonMon 5 Oct 2026 09.56 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 12.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAn artist is considering legal action after the Conservative party used his cartoon to mockAndy Burnham.Stanley Chow, aManchester-based illustratorwho works for the New Yorker magazine, created a cartoon of the prime minister for campaign material in the Makerfield byelection earlier in June.At theConservative conferencethis weekend, party workers handed out water bottles to journalists with the slogan “bottler Burnham” above Chow’s cartoon.He told the Guardian that theConservativesdid not ask permission before using his image: “I am taking legal advice, I may take legal action. It is copyright infringement, they are stealing my artwork to use for their own purposes.“An institution like the Tory party – there is no excuse for them not to do their diligence, and find out the rules of copyright. It’s amazing how it got signed off – that really disappoints me.”View image in fullscreenStanley Chow, who works for the New Yorker magazine, said he had asked the Conservatives for an apology.Photograph: Rebecca  Lupton/The GuardianChow first realised the cartoon was being used while watching Sky News. The presenters held the water bottles up to the camera and laughed at the joke slogan.“I was more shocked really,” Chow said. “When it appeared up on Sky News they were having a laugh and a joke about it, I thought, hang on, they have done this without telling me? I am peeved.”Chow said he had written to the Tories asking for an explanation but had not heard back. “It would be nice to get an apology out of them at some point.”Chow was also not a fan of the “bottler Burnham” joke: “It is very childish too, I think they should grow up.”He has also locked horns withReform UK, which used his cartoon in an attack advert on social media aimed at the prime minister. It was deployed for an anti-immigration message – a stance the artist does not endorse.Colin Bell, a partner at the law firm Brabners, said: “This is a clear case of copyright infringement. It’s important because an artists’ work, created with care and intention, has been used and edited without permission and without acknowledgment or remuneration.“That’s not acceptable. Stan is entitled to an injunction – or undertakings to cease and desist and take down the infringing works – compensation and a public apology.“We’re advising Stan in his pursuit of this claim to secure redress and to make clear that artists’ work, rights and reputations cannot be treated in this way without consent, including as leverage or collateral in political campaigns.”The Conservative party has been contacted for comment.Explore more on these topicsConservative conference 2026ConservativesAndy BurnhamIllustrationReform UKLabourBirminghamnewsShareReuse this content

title: Rowan Atkinson to bring Mr Bean, Blackadder and more to West End in new show | Stage | The Guardian
description: The actor will perform famous TV sketches – as well as new material created with Richard Curtis, Ben Elton and Howard Goodall – in Rowan Live, which opens in February
Author: Chris Wiegand
Headline: The actor will perform famous TV sketches – as well as new material created with Richard Curtis, Ben Elton and Howard Goodall – in Rowan Live, which opens in February
Content: ‘I thought it would be fun to perform again the sketches that began it all’ … Rowan AtkinsonView image in fullscreen‘I thought it would be fun to perform again the sketches that began it all’ … Rowan AtkinsonStageRowan Atkinson to bring Mr Bean, Blackadder and more to West End in new showThe actor will perform famous TV sketches – as well as new material created with Richard Curtis, Ben Elton and Howard Goodall – in Rowan Live, which opens in FebruaryChris WiegandStage editorMon 5 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRowan Atkinson will return to the stage next year to play Blackadder, Mr Bean and other comic characters from across his career in a West End show, Rowan Live. The production, which will have a short run of 30 performances, is to feature new routines as well as his famous sketches from TV shows including Not the Nine O’Clock News.“It is 40 years since I last did a comedy sketch show in the West End,” said Atkinson. “I thought it would be fun to perform again the sketches that began it all for myself and [writer]Richard Curtis, and in which my most well-known characters originated, alongside some surprise new material written especially for this show.” He and Curtis will be collaborating once more with Blackadder writer Ben Elton and its composer Howard Goodall.Atkinson created comedy stage shows with Curtis and Goodall when they were at Oxford University before his phenomenal success on BBC TV in the 1980s with the satirical series Not the Nine O’Clock News and in the various guises of the scheming Edmund Blackadder in the era-hopping historical comedy. He had a one-man show in theWest Endin 1981, at the age of 26, and another one five years later, which led the Guardian’s Michael Billington to report: “He can look like a damaged cherub, an establishment smoothy, a country vicar, but underneath you glimpse devilry, anarchy and rage.”View image in fullscreenRowan Atkinson in Quartermaine’s Terms in 2013.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/the GuardianMr Bean, an occasionally ingenious and mostly speechless ignoramus, brought him further success on TV and film in the 90s, proving Atkinson’s gift at physical comedy and even inspiring an animated version. Atkinson perfected the character of Mr Bean on stage in the 1980s before it reached the screen and he incorporated the character in a live comedy tour as well as reprising it for the 2012 London Olympic Games opening ceremony.Also in 2012, Atkinson performed at the Royal Albert Hall in a Prince’s Trust gala event,We Are Most Amused, that unveiled a new Blackadder sketch centred around the financial crisis. This time, Blackadder was the chief executive of a bank, with his series’ co-star Tony Robinson downtrodden as ever as Baldrick, appearing as Blackadder’s gardener. At that event, Atkinson also revived his routine as a priest who recounts how Jesus’s miracles lead him into a career as a magician. His priest’s vestments can be seen in a promotional image for Rowan Live, in a dressing-up box that also includes the mask of a gorilla. Fans of Not the Nine O’Clock News will recognise that as a nod to the sketch in which Atkinson, as Gerald the gorilla, argues with a professor played by Mel Smith, who says the animal was “completely wild” when he captured him for an educational experiment. “Wild?” retorts Gerald. “I was absolutely livid!”View image in fullscreenThe show will also feature sketches from Not the Nine O’Clock NewsAtkinson’s stage career has also included major West End theatre productions, with an Olivier-nominated role as Fagin inOliver!in 2009 and his appearance as the titular tutor and bachelor in Simon Gray’sQuartermaine’s Termsin 2013. Curtis said that it has been 50 years since he first saw Atkinson perform on stage: “It was instantly clear to all of us that we were watching a unique, once in a lifetime talent.” Over summer, they began to assemble the new show in front of a small audience. “All that magic, that unique accuracy and comic genius is still there for all to see,” said Curtis. “It’s such a joy and honour for me to be part of a show that will include the very best of Rowan on stage – all his voices, shapes, faces and characters. I hope it will make people very happy.”The show continues a recent theatrical trend for TV nostalgia, after stage versions ofFawlty Towers,The Good Life,Some Mothers Do ’Ave ’EmandOnly Fools and Horses.Rowan Live will be directed by Raz Shaw and runs at the Gillian Lynne theatre from 8 February to 13 March. That theatre is currently home toMy Neighbour Totoro, which ends on 3 January.Explore more on these topicsStageTheatreComedy (Stage)West EndRowan AtkinsonRichard CurtisComedy (Culture)newsShareReuse this content

title: Mary Beard suggests ‘tweaks’ to British Museum’s handling of queues to see Bayeux tapestry | British Museum | The Guardian
description: Classicist and museum trustee visited the line after people complained of waiting for hours, with some turned away
Author: Helena Horton
Headline: Classicist and museum trustee visited the line after people complained of waiting for hours, with some turned away
Content: The museum has announced new measures to make the viewing of the tapestry more accessible.Photograph: Amer Ghazzal/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenThe museum has announced new measures to make the viewing of the tapestry more accessible.Photograph: Amer Ghazzal/ShutterstockBritish MuseumMary Beard suggests ‘tweaks’ to British Museum’s handling of queues to see Bayeux tapestryClassicist and museum trustee visited the line after people complained of waiting for hours, with some turned awayHelena HortonMon 5 Oct 2026 07.55 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 21.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMary Beard has intervened in the row about excessively long queues for theBayeux tapestryby visiting the line and submitting a list of improvements to the British Museum.The Bayeux tapestry: a stupefying, thrilling, horrifying masterpiece that shakes the earthRead moreBeard, 71, is a trustee of the museum and inspected the queue herself after visitors to the tapestry complained that they had to wait for hours for their turn to view it, and some were turned away with no guarantee they would get another time slot.One visitor posted on social media that she had been waiting since she was seven to see the Bayeux tapestry, and had bought tickets only to be turned away after queueing.View image in fullscreenMary Beard, seen here at the announcement of the Booker prize shortlist last month, said she had some sympathies for the museum.Photograph: David Parry/ShutterstockThe museum has since announced new measures to make the viewing of the tapestry, which has returned toEnglandafter 1,000 years in France, more accessible. This includes longer opening hours to prevent queues, a new audio guide to help people move along the embroidery, and additional signage and seating.Beard, a celebrated classicist and TV presenter, told the Guardian she had visited to “chat to people in the queue”, adding: “The atmosphere was very good, with people who had come from everywhere. I thought some tweaks were necessary: more benches for old ladies like me, more guidance on wait times.”She said she had some sympathies for the museum: “We had to expect some teething troubles – this isn’t like an ordinary exhibition, everyone has come to see the same one object! The important thing is to put those teething troubles right.”Members of the public keen to see the Bayeux tapestry faced online queues of up to nine hours when tickets went on sale for the first time this summer. There were reports of 40,000 people queueing by mid-morning, with that figure ballooning to almost 80,000 by mid-afternoon. The next wave of public tickets for the tapestry will go on sale on 21 October at 10am.Adult tickets cost £33 during peak times and £27 at off-peak hours, compared with its usual €12 (£10) fee to see the tapestry in its home in Bayeux, Normandy.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFrom the Bayeux tapestry to Glastonbury: top tips and tricks to grab the hottest ticketsRead moreThe British Museum’s handling of the exhibition has come under scrutiny after the Guardian revealed that the controversial tech billionaire Peter Thiel was given a private viewing of the tapestry. The Trump-supporting businessman’s public software company, Palantir,plays a controversial role in the British state.Of the viewing, the museum’s chair, George Osborne, said: “It wasn’t like we expected anyone to know about it.” The museum’s director of development, Charlotte Appleyard, hosted Thiel at a VIP viewing of the tapestry before it opened to the public on 18 August.When asked what the museum might have received in return, Osborne said: “The short answer is [Thiel] hasn’t offered any money, and were he to offer money, the board would consider it and have to take into account the pros, you know, receiving more income, and the reputational risks.”ABritish Museumspokesperson said they were “delighted by the excitement” people had shown. They added: “We also know that some visitors have faced longer queues than we would have wanted, so we are introducing a series of measures to make the experience smoother and give more people the time they need to enjoy the tapestry.”Explore more on these topicsBritish MuseumMary BeardBayeux tapestryMuseumsLondonEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Gillian Anderson responds to backlash after telling ‘distracting’ fans to stop sitting in front row | Gillian Anderson | The Guardian
description: The actor, who is performing on the West End, was filmed telling theatre fans ‘you can’t come 20 times and sit in the front row, it’ll drive me mad’
Author: Emma Joyce
Headline: The actor, who is performing on the West End, was filmed telling theatre fans ‘you can’t come 20 times and sit in the front row, it’ll drive me mad’
Content: Gillian Anderson at the opening night of Who’s Afraid of Virginia Woolf? in London. The actor has issued a statement after telling a group of fans to stop sitting in the front row, saying ‘it can be a tad distracting’.Photograph: Dave Benett/Grant Buchanan/Getty Images for @sohoplaceView image in fullscreenGillian Anderson at the opening night of Who’s Afraid of Virginia Woolf? in London. The actor has issued a statement after telling a group of fans to stop sitting in the front row, saying ‘it can be a tad distracting’.Photograph: Dave Benett/Grant Buchanan/Getty Images for @sohoplaceGillian AndersonGillian Anderson responds to backlash after telling ‘distracting’ fans to stop sitting in front rowThe actor, who is performing on the West End, was filmed telling theatre fans ‘you can’t come 20 times and sit in the front row, it’ll drive me mad’Emma JoyceSun 4 Oct 2026 21.02 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 15.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGillian Anderson has come under fire after the actor was filmed telling a group of fans that they were “distracting” her by repeatedly sitting in the front row while she performs in London’s West End.The Sex Education and X-Files star was filmed outside the Soho Place theatre where she’s performing inWho’s Afraid of Virginia Woolf?, telling a group of fans: “You guys cannot sit in the front row. I do not care; you cannot sit in the front row. It’s so distracting.”Anderson, who is playing frustrated wife Martha in Edward Albee’s play about an unhappy marriage, then said: “You can’t come 20 times and sit in the front row, it’ll drive me mad.”The fans, who were not shown in the video, can be heard responding to Anderson’s comments with “I’m sorry” and “I know”.0:38Gillian Anderson confronts ‘distracting’ front-row superfans – videoAfter the video was uploaded to TikTok, the 58-year-old actor shared a statement on social media in an effort to clarify her position.“The video doing the rounds is me talking with women I go back over 20 years with – so please don’t say anything negative to or about them,”she wrote on X.“We’re thrilled to be doing this show but for people in the front row, please be aware that in such an intimate venue we can all see you and sometimes, it can be a tad distracting!”Who’s Afraid of Virginia Woolf? review – Gillian Anderson fights tooth and nail in marital meltdownRead moreAnderson signed off with: “That’s all. All good. On with the show and love to everyone and thank you to all of those coming.”It’s not the first time this year an actor has made headlines with comments about theatre etiquette. Last month, Cate Blanchett asked the audience of her National Theatre productionElectra/Personato put away their phones during curtain call.“I understand you like filming the curtain call – and it is kind of flattering in a way,” Blanchett said. “But for anyone who is filming the show, please don’t, because it spoils it for the next group of people who come in and are present with us.”Rosamund Pikecriticised an audience member for texting during her West End play Inter Alia in May. “I just wanted to say for anyone going to the theatre, it’s a huge thing that we’re trying to give you,” she told the audience at Wyndham’s theatre.“Somebody was texting in this part,” she said. “You know who you are … Maybe it was very important, and maybe you’re a doctor, and you’re saving someone’s life, and I hope you are, but we do see these, we do feel them.”In April, Wicked starCynthia Erivohalted her one-woman performance of Dracula – in which she played all 23 characters – at the Noël Coward theatre after spotting an audience member illegally recording the show.In May, The Pitt starIsa Brionestold fans to stop yelling references to the medical drama during her Broadway musical Just in Time. And Kristin Scott Thomas, who is due to perform in The Cherry Orchard at the Harold Pinter theatre this month, told theFinancial Timesshe witnessed an audience member eating “a ready meal in the front row once” – but said she still prefers theatre to screen acting, adding: “For me it is telling a story to live, breathing, coughing, eating people and trying to drag them along with you. Which I find incredibly thrilling.”Other actors, including Andrew Scott, Daniel Craig and Hugh Jackman, have spoken out about the decline in theatre etiquette. Lesley Manville told BBC Radio 4 earlier this year that she finds audience members who take photos during the curtain call “insulting”.“Clap or don’t clap, but don’t just stick up your phone in our faces,” she said.It’s not just the performers who have complaints either. Theatregoers at the Royal Shakespeare Company’sThe Tempest starring Kenneth Branaghtook issue with a baby cooing and gurgling through the first half of a performance in June. The mother and baby were asked to leave the Stratford-upon-Avon theatre for the second half after audience members asked for refunds.Explore more on these topicsGillian AndersonTheatreWest EndnewsShareReuse this content

title: Sass Jordan, Canadian rock singer-songwriter, dies aged 65 | Pop and rock | The Guardian
description: Musician who had hit albums with Racine and Rats later became a judge on six seasons of Canadian Idol
Author: Ben Beaumont-Thomas
Headline: Musician who had hit albums with Racine and Rats later became a judge on six seasons of Canadian Idol
Content: Sass Jordan performing in Toronto, 2009.Photograph: ZUMA Press, Inc./Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News.View image in fullscreenSass Jordan performing in Toronto, 2009.Photograph: ZUMA Press, Inc./Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News.Pop and rockSass Jordan, Canadian rock singer-songwriter, dies aged 65Musician who had hit albums with Racine and Rats later became a judge on six seasons of Canadian IdolBen Beaumont-ThomasMon 5 Oct 2026 05.22 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 05.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSass Jordan, the singer-songwriter who became a significant success in Canada’s rock scene in the 1990s before starring as a judge on Canadian Idol, has died aged 65.No cause of death has been given. A statement on social media said she died on 2 October “surrounded by her loving family … She remains in our hearts, an inimitable force of nature. An irreplaceable being of light and joy!”Born in Birmingham, England, in 1960, Jordan moved to Montreal as a child when her French academic father took a position at the city’s Concordia University. She began performing in her teens, and by her 20s was recording with a range of Montreal acts: she wrote a song for singer Michael Breen that became a Canadian Top 40 hit.By 1988 she was signed to Atlantic Records, who released her debut album Tell Somebody, with two singles – the title track and Double Trouble – charting just outside the Canadian Top 10. The following year she won a Juno (the Canadian equivalent of the Grammys) for most promising female vocalist.Her 1992 album Racine contained four Canadian Top 20 hits and, coupled with a move to Los Angeles, a new label in RCA, and an appearance on the bestselling soundtrack to The Bodyguard broke Jordan into a wider US market. Sun’s Gonna Rise, from 1994 album Rats, became her only US Hot 100 hit, and her biggest hit in Canada, reaching No 7. Taylor Hawkins, later the drummer for Foo Fighters, was her live drummer during this period.Her RCA deal ended and Jordan later voiced disappointment in the glossy sound of her next couple of albums, but her career received a boost from being a judge on the six seasons of TV talent show Canadian Idol, and she returned to recording with 2006’s You Get What You Give. In 2001 she also performed as Janis Joplin in the off-Broadway musical Love, Janis.She later embraced a bluesier sound, with 2020 album Rebel Moon Blues reaching the top five of the US blues chart, followed by her most recent studio recording, 2022’s Bitches Blues.In September, Jordan cancelled tour dates, citing “a serious medical condition”.Explore more on these topicsPop and rockCanadaAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: TV tonight: an essential film about the story of Damilola Taylor  | Television | The Guardian
description: John Boyega, who was friends with Damilola, speaks in this moving programme. Plus: David Harewood’s superb new legal drama. Here’s what to watch this evening
Author: Hollie Richardson
Headline: John Boyega, who was friends with Damilola, speaks in this moving programme. Plus: David Harewood’s superb new legal drama. Here’s what to watch this evening
Content: Love and hope … Damilola: The Untold Story on BBC Two.Photograph: BBC/Optomen TV/Tunde TaylorView image in fullscreenLove and hope … Damilola: The Untold Story on BBC Two.Photograph: BBC/Optomen TV/Tunde TaylorTV tonightTelevisionTV tonight: an essential film about the story of Damilola TaylorJohn Boyega, who was friends with Damilola, speaks in this moving programme. Plus: David Harewood’s superb new legal drama. Here’s what to watch this eveningHollie Richardson,Priya Elan,Ali Catterall,Alexi DugginsandSimon WardellMon 5 Oct 2026 01.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDamilola: The Untold Story9pm, BBC TwoIt’s been 26 years since 10-year-oldDamilola Taylorwas killed by teenagers. For the first time, the last people to see him alive create this essential account: from the actor John Boyega and Boyega’s sister Grace (Damilola’s mates who were at the library with him) to Guillermo Casal (the North Peckham Estate caretaker who found Damilola and cradled him as he died). His brother Tunde and the former Met officer Leroy Logan also revisit events, which eventually led to the conviction of two brothers, and take a wider look at why there were so many similar killings. The trauma and sadness remain palpable, but there is also a lot of love and even hope to be found in Damilola’s legacy.Hollie RichardsonPanorama: Cancer Before 50 – Why Is It Rising?8pm, BBC OneAccording to NHS data, rates of bowel and breast cancers are rapidly rising among much younger demographics. The reporter Hayley Hassall investigates the root causes, from ultraprocessed food to micro-chemicals, while speaking to patients and looking at the latest scientific research. She also asks if the government is doing enough to protect vulnerable people.Priya ElanClickbait Clinic With Stacey Dooley8.30pm, BBC OneNAD+ drips are the next viral “wellness claim” investigated by Dooley. Jennifer Aniston, Gwyneth Paltrow and the Kardashians are fans – and people who use them claim to be “ageing backwards”. But do they actually do anything? Dooley crashes a brunch where women are hooked up to the drips while sipping prosecco, before asking the health experts.HRPierre9pm, Channel 4View image in fullscreenCutting a suave figure … David Harewood in Pierre.Photograph: Channel 4This superb legal drama somehow pulls off being very funny and devastatingly compelling. David Harewood cuts a suave, wry figure as Pierre, a duty solicitor in London – but does his need to be a hero confuse integrity with vanity? It’s put to the test when a teenager he helps at the police station is later found killed and he swears to solve the mystery around what happened.HRMichael Palin in the Philippines9pm, Channel 5Palinheads deeper into the Philippines, from Palawan’s natural landscape to Moalboal’s extraordinary sardine shoals. Yet, as he observes, “there is darkness here”: the nickel mine threatening Indigenous communities; the fact that divorce is illegal. “I’m starting to wonder if there’s a price to pay for living in paradise,” he says.Ali CatterallPete Wicks: For Dogs’ Sake9pm, U&WThere’s a suspicious lump on a Maltese in this week’s reality star-hosted profile of the Dogs Trust’s work. Will it be bad news? It certainly doesn’t look good for the cane corso who continues to be investigated for a neurological condition, but things are on the up for a family of spitzes who are struggling in a new environment. Wicks is going to help “build their confidence”. Lucky them.Alexi DugginsFilm choiceAll We Imagine As Light (Payal Kapadia, 2024),10.20pm, Film4This exceptional Cannes-winning drama explores life in Mumbai through the eyes of three women. Senior nurse Prabha (Kani Kusruti) is married, but her husband is absent working in Germany. Her young colleague and flatmate Anu (Divya Prabha) is a Hindu secretly in love with a Muslim boy. And hospital cook Parvathy (Chhaya Kadam) is facing the demolition of her home by developers. As their intimate, involving stories unfold, Kapadia reveals a bustling, rain-soaked, ever-changing city – a place that draws migrants such as them but never truly feels like home.SWLive sportUefa Nations Leaguefootball: Northern Ireland v Georgia7.30pm, BBC Three.At Windsor Park.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionTV tonightDamilola TaylorJohn BoyegafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The Housekeeper by Rose Tremain review – a bloodless origin story for Du Maurier’s Rebecca | Fiction | The Guardian
description: The novelist has expanded her devastating 2014 short story about an imagined affair between Daphne du Maurier and a fictional Polish-Jewish housekeeper
Author: Clare Clark
Headline: The novelist has expanded her devastating 2014 short story about an imagined affair between Daphne du Maurier and a fictional Polish-Jewish housekeeper
Content: Lily James (front) as Mrs de Winter and Kristin Scott Thomas as Mrs Danvers in the 2020 film adaptation of Daphne du Maurier’s Rebecca.Photograph: Kerry Brown/PAView image in fullscreenLily James (front) as Mrs de Winter and Kristin Scott Thomas as Mrs Danvers in the 2020 film adaptation of Daphne du Maurier’s Rebecca.Photograph: Kerry Brown/PAFictionReviewThe Housekeeper by Rose Tremain review – a bloodless origin story for Du Maurier’s RebeccaThe novelist has expanded her devastating 2014 short story about an imagined affair between Daphne du Maurier and a fictional Polish-Jewish housekeeperClare ClarkMon 5 Oct 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe rollcall of notable novels that began life as short stories is surprisingly long and various. Two years before Clarissa Dalloway famously shopped for flowers in Virginia Woolf’s Mrs Dalloway she was shopping for gloves in Woolf’s short story Mrs Dalloway in Bond Street; Evan S Connell’s Mrs Bridge and Jeffrey Eugenides’s The Virgin Suicides began life as stories published in the Paris Review. Rachel Cusk’s story Project, which ran in the New Yorker in September 2025, serves almost word for word as the opening for her new novel, Life of M.The newest addition to that list is Rose Tremain’s 17th novel, The Housekeeper, which pays homage to Daphne du Maurier’s Rebecca by imagining the events that might have inspired it. Tremain first explored the idea in a 2014 story, also called The Housekeeper and included in her acclaimed collectionThe American Lover. Her protagonist, then and now, is Lilianne Danowski, a Polish Jew who fled the pogroms with her father as a child and who presides with reserved efficiency over a large staff at Manderville Hall near Fowey in Cornwall. When Du Maurier comes to lunch, it is Danowski, known to her employers as Danni (Danowski was “a mouthful of fishbones”), who is deputised to show her around the house, who proudly encourages Du Maurier to look through the clothes in her dead mistress’s fastidiously maintained bedroom and takes her down to the boat house. It is Danowski who, after a passionate year-long affair with Du Maurier, will be twisted into the malevolent Mrs Danvers.The married Du Maurier was violently attracted to women: her complicated, deeply closeted attitude towards her own sexuality lends Rebecca much of its darkly erotic charge. In the 2014 story, Tremain echoes that tension, offering, with her impeccable instinct for period, a masterclass in 1930s restraint. Danni is quite undone by Du Maurier, her careful armour torn away, yet bound, like the butler Stevens in Ishiguro’s The Remains of the Day, by the long habit of discretion; so she proves a tight-lipped narrator. Danni is the supplicant, the vessel; she knows she has no power. When Du Maurier, terrified of exposure, simply cuts her off, Danni scrabbles for ways to excuse her, to cling to what they shared. It is the discovery, more than a year later, that Du Maurier has immortalised her as the bitter and conniving Mrs Danvers, “ugly and diseased with jealousy”, that devastates her, smashing to pieces her passionately hoarded memories.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotiondouble quotation markTremain’s novel abounds with references to Rebecca and Du Maurier but its greater scope gives it none of Rebecca’s subversive complexityWhat moves a writer to return to a finished story after a decade, to rework it on the larger canvas of the novel? In Tremain’s case it was her story becoming a film. The Housekeeper, starring Anthony Hopkins and Helena Bonham Carter, is slated for upcoming release; Tremain wrote the screenplay.“Last night I dreamed I saw Daphne again,” Danni declares as the novel opens, recalling one of the most celebrated first lines in literature. Rebecca itself is, of course, part of a complex interplay of gothic novels, from Jane Eyre to Jean Rhys’s Wide Sargasso Sea, each book shifting the reader’s understanding of the others. Tremain’s novel abounds with references to Rebecca and Du Maurier – Daphne even confesses to Danni her fear that swooping gulls might take them for prey and attack them – but its greater scope gives it none of Rebecca’s subversive complexity. Instead, the story has fattened, its devastating reserve giving way to something softer and less substantial. Peripheral characters, evoked with discomfiting economy in Tremain’s original story, swell into caricature: Lord de Whithers, Danni’s terse, dismissive employer, becomes bumbling Lord Grenville-Whithers, kindly little boy lost, while his self-absorbed niece solidifies into a screaming harpy. Danni’s dead father is recalled in aphorisms more akin to fortune cookies than philosophy. More critically, the exquisite tension between Daphne and Danni, themselves echoes of the formidable Rebecca and the drab, shadowy second Mrs de Winter, fails to hold. With pages to play with, Tremain takes us deep inside their affair but, although this Danni tells all, the scenes remain curiously bloodless: hands and lips and tongues but no fire, no heart. Du Maurier famously called Rebecca “a study in jealousy”, but the lurching sense of malignity and darkness that gave that novel its vertiginous tension is missing here. Without it, Daphne’s final terrible betrayal of Danni feels like petty spite.“What am I to do with you, Danni? How am I to make you come alive?” Daphne demands teasingly in The Housekeeper’s opening pages. Du Maurier, of course, faced just that problem with Rebecca and pulled it off spectacularly, creating a woman of such toweringly vengeful, transgressive authority that, even in death, she rises up to dominate the book. Tremain has done the opposite. By stripping her Danni of her fierce, quiet dignity, she has robbed her of her power.The Housekeeper by Rose Tremain is published by Chatto & Windus (£20). title: The Yellow Tie review – John Malkovich gives major hauteur as legendary record-hating maestro | Movies | The Guardian
description: This biopic of Sergiu Celibidache, the renowned Romanian conductor who refused all recordings, is a sturdy labour of love directed by his son
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: This biopic of Sergiu Celibidache, the renowned Romanian conductor who refused all recordings, is a sturdy labour of love directed by his son
Content: Querulous … John Malkovich in The Yellow TiePhotograph: Adi MarineciView image in fullscreenQuerulous … John Malkovich in The Yellow TiePhotograph: Adi MarineciMoviesReviewThe Yellow Tie review – John Malkovich gives major hauteur as legendary record-hating maestroThis biopic of Sergiu Celibidache, the renowned Romanian conductor who refused all recordings, is a sturdy labour of love directed by his sonPeter BradshawMon 5 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 06.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHere is an old-fashioned biopic from central Europe that is also a labour of love on the part of its director: a little stolid and stately, yes, but robustly made, heartfelt and high-minded, with workmanlike performances and decent visual effects work. It is the story of the Romanian conductor and composer Sergiu Celibidache, a brilliant musician who became renowned among musical connoisseurs in the years following the second world war for his unique and uncompromisingly purist belief – derived from his Zen Buddhist studies – that music should never be recorded. He believed that LPs and CDs were inert and dead, and that music had to be experienced live, in the passionately authentic present.The director is the musician’s son, Serge Ioan Celebidachi, and as an older man in his rural French retirement, he is played with unsubtly querulous hauteur byJohn Malkovich, especially in the misjudged opening scene where he yells at Japanese executives for presuming to offer him a recording deal. Ben Schnetzer is the younger Celibidache, a prodigy whose musical ambition infuriates his old-fashioned father (Sean Bean), a well-regarded functionary who assumed that his son would follow him into public office. Celebidache Sr therefore demands the return of his birthday gift, a certain type of yellow tie that had been favoured by generations of the family’s menfolk, and which here becomes a fetish of the heartbroken young Sergiu’s need to please his father but also break away from him.Celibidache studies in Berlin in the 1930s as the Nazis take power, and is menaced and bullied as a Jew, but escapes the ultimate fate; he is sensationally installed as principal conductor of the newly denazified Berlin Philharmonic in 1945, where he astonishes the authorities with his no-recording views. He is finally forced out and begins a kind of wandering musical odyssey through Europe and Latin America.It is not easy to see what point exactly has been made by Celebidache’s stand; he did not appear to accumulate many followers, and the music world was filled with musicians at least as talented and principled as him who believed the exact opposite about recorded music. But there is a kind of lonely heroism here, and who can tell if, in this digitised world where recordings are so easily available, that his views might not come into fashion? A strong, unassuming picture.The Yellow Tie is in UK and Irish cinemas from 9 October.Explore more on these topicsFilmBiopicsPeriod and historical filmsRomaniaClassical musicJohn MalkovichSean BeanreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Exceptionally crafted’: why Little Shop of Horrors is my feelgood movie | Musicals | The Guardian
description: The latest in our series of writers’ favorite comfort films is a tribute to the lovably quirky 80s musical
Author: Juan A Ramírez
Headline: The latest in our series of writers’ favorite comfort films is a tribute to the lovably quirky 80s musical
Content: Rick Moranis with Audrey II in Little Shop of Horrors.Photograph: Warner Bros/Sportsphoto/AllstarView image in fullscreenRick Moranis with Audrey II in Little Shop of Horrors.Photograph: Warner Bros/Sportsphoto/AllstarMy feelgood movieMusicals‘Exceptionally crafted’: why Little Shop of Horrors is my feelgood movieThe latest in our series of writers’ favorite comfort films is a tribute to the lovably quirky 80s musicalJuan A RamírezMon 5 Oct 2026 10.44 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 14.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe key to afeelgood movie, beyond the necessary rewatchability, is familiarity – the real kind that lets you look away or fall asleep without doubting your affection. Musicals are perfectly suited to this particular subgenre since the majority of them, especially the classic ones adapted for film, atrophy with second-act problems. That’s where writers suddenly remember the plot they had introduced and drop all that singing and dancing to arrive at some type of conclusion.The first act of Funny Girl? A near-flawless parade of showstoppers,Barbra Streisandas Fanny Brice having the time of her life falling in love. I’ve probably seen it 200 times. The second act … well, who ever cared about her husband’s gambling addiction?At just 94 minutes, Frank Oz’s film of Little Shop of Horrors doesn’t suffer from that sharp of a drop-off. The cult 1982 musical that translates to the screen is already a pretty perfect piece; a hilarious send-up of B-movies with glorious songs by Howard Ashman and Alan Menken, the duo whose music would soon ignite the Disney Renaissance. The whole thing is a miracle of dumpster diving: adapting an almost-forgotten1960 movieby indie legendRoger Corman, who didn’t even bother to copyright his low-budget horror comedy.But enough history. Little Shop, the movie, begins, and you’rethere: Skid Row, the derelict, richly detailed cityscape with the lovingly obvious soundstage feel that most art departments left behind sometime in the 90s in favor of realism. The son of puppeteers and the first to perform both Yoda and Miss Piggy, Oz had individuality and scene-setting in his DNA.It’s there we meet Seymour (Rick Moranis), a perennially orphaned adult who works alongside the ditzy bombshell Audrey (Ellen Greene) at a run-down flower shop owned by the miserly Mushnik (Vincent Gardenia). Their dreams of a better life arrive quickly, when a mysterious plant Seymour has been secretly nurturing grows into a national sensation.‘Should have garnered the actor an Oscar’: why Liar Liar is my feelgood movieRead moreHis trouble, of course, is that the plant – named Audrey II, due to Seymour’s simping after his co-worker – feeds exclusively on human blood. In classicMichigan J Frogfashion, the anthropomorphic Audrey II (voiced by the Four Tops’ Levi Stubbs), only voices its carnivorous needs to Seymour, who’s left alone to decide whether success (and human Audrey’s love) are worth the carnage.In the simplicity of its plot and the spectacle of Oz’s puppetry, the film is sensational. Greene, a holdover from the original stage production, gives an all-time weirdo performance that is massive, intimate and memorable, with pipes to make the celluloid rattle. And she’s surrounded by heavyweight 80s funnymen, including Steve Martin, Bill Murray andChristopher Guest.A high concept horror-comedy with an all-star cast of comedians, Little Shop is a lot likeClue, released the previous year, and which also grew a devoted cult reputation over time. And here’s where I’ll get annoying again: both are intelligent critiques of capitalism disguised as kooky popcorn fare.“Disguised” might not be the right word for Little Shop, which never hides its thematic concerns. Menken’s score is a blend of doo-wop and rock’n’roll, but mostly Motown: a genre of romance, struggle and comfort. But even before that level of analysis, you’re hit with the original plot’s fable-like message, aided by Ashman’s cheeky anti-capitalist lyrics and, on film, Oz’s remarkable visions.View image in fullscreenVincent Gardenia, Rick Moranis and Ellen Greene in Little Shop Of Horrors.Photograph: The Geffen Company/AllstarThe movie’s first real number, Skid Row (Downtown), is a masterclass in placing its character’s individual desires against the backdrop of communal conflict. Every single shot is framed to acknowledge the individual’s involvement in the class struggle, which increases with each foot-stomp and angry face inincreasing desperation. Certain frames seem lifted straight out of classic Soviet propaganda.Do you see how excited I get talking about this? How all this spews out of me with such attractive, enviable ease due to how many times I’ve witnessed it? And do you feel how that breathlessness, upon an 857th rewatch, could easily tire itself out into a daze which, soon after the iconic Suddenly, Seymour climax, leads to a satisfied doze?What should convince any skeptics that this is a feelgood classic is that (a) one of its ardent fans can’t help but sound insufferable describing its merits and, (b) it is crafted with that Muppets-era showmanship, a remnant from an age where talent and individuality ruled, but acts would get caned off the stage if they weren’t pleasing the audience.Little Shop is exceptionally designed, performed and crafted, but there’s no whiff of spotlight-seeking to detract from the greater project. Tapping into that strain of communal excellence is why Oz delivered one of the finest movie musicals of all time, building on what Ashman and Menken fertilized from Corman and screenwriter Charles B Griffith’s seed of an idea. Clearly I’m not as good an analogist as all of these men, so don’t take my word for it. title: Forty years of the Phantom of the Opera - the show that wouldn’t die: ‘People come back to hear the impossible’ | Musicals | The Guardian
description: As Andrew Lloyd Webber’s enduring gothic melodrama celebrates its 40th birthday, producer Cameron Mackintosh and cast members from down the years recall what makes it so special
Author: Miriam Gillinson
Headline: As Andrew Lloyd Webber’s enduring gothic melodrama celebrates its 40th birthday, producer Cameron Mackintosh and cast members from down the years recall what makes it so special
Content: Spirit of the West End … Holly-Anne Hull and Jon Robyns in a 2023 production of The Phantom of the Opera.Photograph: Johan PerssonView image in fullscreenSpirit of the West End … Holly-Anne Hull and Jon Robyns in a 2023 production of The Phantom of the Opera.Photograph: Johan PerssonMusicalsForty years of the Phantom of the Opera - the show that wouldn’t die: ‘People come back to hear the impossible’As Andrew Lloyd Webber’s enduring gothic melodrama celebrates its 40th birthday, producer Cameron Mackintosh and cast members from down the years recall what makes it so specialMiriam GillinsonMon 5 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 05.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere is something about Andrew Lloyd Webber’s masterly musical The Phantom of the Opera – celebrating 40 years on the West End this month – which seems to take hold of its fans in a special way. For me, it was the show that first sparked my love of theatre and inspired me to work in the industry. Even today, Phantom is still the memory that gets my heart racing as I sit in the stalls, waiting impatiently for the curtain to come up, hoping for an experience just as intoxicating and all-consuming as that very first experience all those years ago.It’s not just the fans, either. When I talk to a cluster of key creatives, all of whom have a special working relationship with the show, each of them seems a little spellbound by Phantom. Sierra Boggess, who plays Carlotta in the 40th-anniversary production, talks tearfully about the lingering spirits of original director Hal Prince and choreographer Gillian Lynne. Jordan Donica, now starring as the Phantom in the West End, speaks passionately about the power of Lloyd Webber’s music (“It feels like heaven to me”), and John Owen-Jones, who has played the Phantom more than anyone else in the West End, talks tenderly about his long-term history with the show: “I’ve got a picture of me in full Phantom get-up holding my baby daughter. It’s an incredible thing to be part of.”Then there is producer Cameron Mackintosh who, if anything, seems even more enthusiastic about the show with each passing year. He just about stays sitting in his chair throughout our interview, yet gives the impression that he’s bouncing about the office as we discuss those early days working on Phantom: “Of all my productions, it’s the most beautiful show I’ve ever created, where every individual element contributed to its beauty.”View image in fullscreenWho scares wins … Michael Crawford and Sarah Brightman in the first run of The Phantom of the Opera in 1986.Photograph: Dennis Cooper/Rex FeaturesWhen Mackintosh and Lloyd Webber first started talking about Phantom in 1984, it was only ever meant to be a fun producing project. The two had enjoyed Ken Hill’s production at Stratford East theatre and, after rummaging around a few charity shops, tracked down a copy of Gaston Leroux’s original novel. They discovered a strange and sinister tale about a disfigured musical genius – with a face like a living corpse – lurking beneath a Parisian opera house (The Palais Garnier), seducing soprano Christine Daaé with the power of his music and causing havoc among the company performing above.As their research deepened, Mackintosh and Lloyd Webber began to unearth the unique characteristics of their new Phantom. Their new version absolutely wasn’t going to be a gothic horror story in the manner of Lon Chaney’s striking silent movie. And it definitely wasn’t going to be a Rocky Horror Show-esque pastiche. This Phantom was going to be lighter, more beautiful – and a lot more romantic.It also quickly became clear that the show was going to have to feature the music of Andrew Lloyd Webber. “The score was very much inspired by Sarah Brightman,” explains Mackintosh. “Andrew obviously had a very deep relationship with her at the time [the two were married] and it triggered something really special in her. Lots of people have attempted to do Phantom but Andrew’s music brought an emotional intensity to the show that had never been there before in any other version.”double quotation markThere’s something dangerous about the music. The vocal demand is so great and there’s a romance in thatThere was something exciting about the score from the start, but it wasn’t until late in the creative process that things came together: “The show only clicked on the first night of previews. I always describe it, up until that point, as a watch running really slowly. But on that night the audience was completely swept into another world. Maria Björnson’s incredible design, Hal Prince’s brilliant ability to shape pictures on stage; [choreographer and stager] Gillian Lynne inhabiting the real world of the opera house and giving it authentic style. It all came together and looked and sounded as one.”It is amazing to think of all the little tweaks that led to today’s production, revamped and revitalised during the Covid theatre closures, but still very much the same beast created more than 40 years ago. In the early days of rehearsals, there were big plans to include a lot more animals. Björnson was determined to have a white horse carry Phantom into the lair but perhaps unsurprisingly – despite the ingenuity of the props team – they just couldn’t make it work. At one point, Prince wanted scores of rats scampering beneath the stage, but the manufactured clump of glowing rats proved funny rather than frightening (“Those little red eyes had us in stitches!”). Prince also had his heart set on releasing white doves – played by a flock of seriously unpredictable pigeons – and having them fly up into the theatre boxes above. “It was a lovely idea,” says Mackintosh, his eyes sparkling, “except all they did was fly up to a perch and shit all over the audience.”View image in fullscreenJohn Owen-Jones as the Phantom in 2011.Photograph: Ken McKay/Rex FeaturesThe horse, the rats and the beautiful (but messy) white doves were all scrapped and the show was gradually finessed. Yet Phantom still opened to patchy reviews, with the Independent scoffing: “Starlight Express brought the form to the edge of the abyss. The Phantom of the Opera takes it back a few yards, but we’re not out of the woods yet.” Nothing about the first few weeks, months or even years working on Phantom screamed box-office gold: “We never tried to put together the most successful musical,” reflects Mackintosh. “I think if we had tried to do that it wouldn’t have succeeded. It was meant to happen the way it did.”The idea of something almost karmic behind Phantom’s success comes up throughout my conversation with Boggess, who first played Christine 20 years ago and went on to become a fan favourite. “For me, playing Christine was a dream come true,” she says. “It felt like I was supposed to be there, helping to tell this story. And now here I am playing Carlotta. It feels like it’s supposed to be.”For Boggess it’s the music, above all, that keeps the fans hooked: “There’s no other score in the world like this. People have to hear this music. It’s like it’s changing something on a cellular level.” The acute technical demands of the score are also part of the show’s appeal. “There’s something dangerous about the music,” she says. “The vocal demand is so great and there’s a romance in that. People come back to hear the impossible.”There is something about performing in Phantom’s first home, His Majesty’s theatre (formerly Her Majesty’s), that feels particularly special for Boggess: “After all the history I have with this show, I finally get to perform in the place where it all started. And there are ghosts here, too. The spirit world is all around us. I really believe that. They come and help us. It’s so much bigger than us all.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenCaught in the act … Peter Straker and Christine Collier in The Phantom of the Opera in 1991.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianOwen-Jones, who has played Phantom nearly 2,000 times, also believes that the venue itself has an important role to play in the production’s extraordinary performance history. He says the show was originally meant to run at the Palace theatre but Les Misérables – the only musical to have a longer West End run than Phantom – was refusing to close. So Phantom opened in the more intimate Her Majesty’s.“At the time, Her Majesty’s had the only functioning Victorian understage in London,” says Owen-Jones. “So the team were able to use that for things like the candelabra coming up through the floor. People hadn’t seen things like that in the West End for a long time.” Björnson’s design in this particular theatre is a huge part of Phantom’s enduring appeal: “When people watch Phantom they see this incredible set with all these old scenic elements. Flies from the top. Flies from below. Trap doors. Yet when the actors come on stage for their final bow, it’s just a black box. Maria has put all these incredible elements into the space but in the end there’s nothing to look at. It’s pure theatre.”Everyone I talk to mentions the simplicity of Phantom’s myth-like story, but also its flexibility. It’s a simple tale but a robust one too, which allows each actor – despite the powerful legacy of Michael Crawford’s haunting inaugural performance – to put his own stamp on the title role. For some that might mean imbuing the Phantom with an air of mystery, but for Owen-Jones the key was always about grounding him in reality: “In my mind the Phantom is a man. He’s not a magician. He’s not a wizard. He’s an incredibly talented engineer who can do all these magical things.”Donica, who began his stage career playing Raoul on Broadway, sees the Phantom through a very different lens: “I felt a kinship to Phantom my whole life. Being a mixed-race kid, raised by a single mum in the south and Indiana. Moving around all the time and being the new kid. The outsider. The person that’s always underestimated and made to feel unwelcome in a lot of spaces; having to show a talent that deems me worthy to be a part of society. All of these things and more, for me, very much relate to Phantom.”Andrew Lloyd Webber is ‘hot again’ – with help from new kids on musicals blockRead moreDonica describes the very first time he encountered the Phantom in the theatre, when a touring production came through Indiana. The actor had just turned nine and, in some strange way, he could literally see the power that Lloyd Webber’s music held over the audience: “We were sat in the orchestra level and you hear the Phantom before you see him. I remember hearing ‘Brava, brava, bravissima!’ and it was like a synesthetic response. I could just see the Phantom’s voice hovering over the audience and wrapping around them.”As we talk, Donica cannot help bursting into song. He talks to me about the frequencies contained in the score and, “from a hertz point of view”, the way that these frequencies connect with the audience. It’s an interesting and unusual way to think about the show; almost as if Lloyd Webber’s score is the result of some sort of physics experiment, designed to shock and move us: “The frequencies that Andrew uses in this show are what hit you to your core. You can sit there, being sceptical about the show, but when you hear those tones – ‘Da-da da-da daaaaa!’ – it automatically makes the hair on the back of your neck stand up. That’s why it works.”The Phantom of the Operais at His Majesty’s theatre, London, to 13 March 2027.Explore more on these topicsMusicalsAndrew Lloyd WebberTheatrefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Comédie Française review – pre-show bedlam plays theatrical chaos for laughs | Movies | The Guardian
description: French farce set in the tumultuous three hours prior to the opening night performance of Macbeth features comic-timing perfection from cast
Author: Leslie Felperin
Headline: French farce set in the tumultuous three hours prior to the opening night performance of Macbeth features comic-timing perfection from cast
Content: ‘Endearing portrait of French luvvies’ … Comédie Française.Photograph: Courtesy of Tull Stories/CharadesView image in fullscreen‘Endearing portrait of French luvvies’ … Comédie Française.Photograph: Courtesy of Tull Stories/CharadesMoviesReviewComédie Française review – pre-show bedlam plays theatrical chaos for laughsFrench farce set in the tumultuous three hours prior to the opening night performance of Macbeth features comic-timing perfection from castLeslie FelperinMon 5 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 08.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOne of Matt Groening’s Life In Hell comic strips from the 1980s,entitled How to Be a Clever Film Critic, sets out cinema’s greatest paradox: “The French are funny. Sex is funny. And comedies are funny. Yet no French sex comedies are funny.” Well, this film from Bertrand Usclat and Martin Darondeau proves that all commonly held certitudes must be disproved at some point, because here’s a French comedy, albeit one that’s not all that preoccupied with sex, that is a hoot.Set entirely inthe Parisian institution of the title, this frothy farce unfolds over the three hours before the opening night curtain goes up on a production of Macbeth, which is being directed by actor turnedmetteuren scèneNina (Pauline Clément). A series of catastrophes make it an open question as to whether the show will actually go on, starting from the moment Nina arrives at the entrance without her staff pass and has to try to get past the officious security team. Naturally, that’s just the beginning, and Nina must contend with superstitious actors, adulterous actors shagging while they rehearse (saying their lines between thrusts), a stoned grande dame (Danièle Lebrun), missing actors (Lady Macbeth is stranded in Brest while shooting a TV show on the side) and actors who understand their roles less than the usher (Sefa Yeboah), who is watching from the sidelines. Meanwhile, if there’s a technical problem, the stage manager (Christian Hecq) will tell you in tedious detail why it can’t be fixed, the wardrobe mistress (Florence Viala) discusses her colleagues’ bodily imperfections and the minister of culture is coming that evening to see the show.Not only must Nina take over the role of LadyMacbeth, her former partner also dumps their toddler on her before the show starts – prompting a whole debate about women trying to juggle careers and motherhood at the same time. This is a bit less persuasive, and some viewers may feel baffled as to why the production only seems to have six or seven actors on hand to mount what looks like a pretty traditional version of Macbeth. But try not to think about any of that too much, and just enjoy the performers’ immaculate comic timing and the endearing portrait of French luvvies ensuring the show must go on.Comédie Française is in UK and Irish cinemas from 9 OctoberExplore more on these topicsFilmComedy filmsTheatreMacbethFranceComedyEuropereviewsShareReuse this content

title: Barkouf review – Offenbach’s lost operetta is a quirky shaggy dog story | Classical music | The Guardian
description: Opera Rara revive the 1860 work in which a dog is appointed Sultan. A fine cast, the Hallé and ENO chorus, and impeccable rhyming narration from Alistair McGowan, ensure things fizz
Author: Clive Paget
Headline: Opera Rara revive the 1860 work in which a dog is appointed Sultan. A fine cast, the Hallé and ENO chorus, and impeccable rhyming narration from Alistair McGowan, ensure things fizz
Content: Gleaming coloratura… Anne-Catherine Gillet, with Valerie Eickhoff and Alistair McGowan in Barkouf.Photograph: David Hughes / The HalleView image in fullscreenGleaming coloratura… Anne-Catherine Gillet, with Valerie Eickhoff and Alistair McGowan in Barkouf.Photograph: David Hughes / The HalleClassical musicReviewBarkouf review – Offenbach’s lost operetta is a quirky shaggy dog storyBridgewater Hall, ManchesterOpera Rara revive the 1860 work in which a dog is appointed Sultan. A fine cast, the Hallé and ENO chorus, and impeccable rhyming narration from Alistair McGowan,  ensure things fizzClive PagetMon 5 Oct 2026 07.51 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAn operetta in which a dog is appointed Sultan of Lahore and, thanks to a resourceful market trader, ushers in a more enlightened despotism – what’s not to like? Plenty, to judge by the critical mauling doled out in 1860 to Offenbach’s Barkouf. Even Berlioz – a fine one to talk – accused the composer of crimes against harmonic convention. It duly sank without trace until unpublished bits and pieces resurfaced in recent decades. It’s fallen toOpera Rarato splice it back together again, fill in the odd blank and give us a chance to judge for ourselves.Barkouf followed hot on the heels of Orpheus in the Underworld, against which it must inevitably be considered a failure. Eugène Scribe’s workaday lyrics lack the divine silliness of the composer’s finest collaborators while blunting the story’s satirical potential. Offenbach, on the other hand, was never short of an idea and his energetic score has sufficient tics and quirks to suggest he was on the trail of something a little bit different. The orchestrations are original (there’s four horns) and a string of witty ditties go off like uncorked bottles of pop. Unfortunately, at other times it runs on a lower level of inspiration.View image in fullscreenSparkling music … Paul Daniel conducts the Hallé.Photograph: David Hughes / The HalleOpera Rara, the Hallé and the English NationalOperaChorus gave it their best shot under the idiomatic baton of Paul Daniel. The music sparkled, and a fine cast of French speakers was clearly enjoying being along for the ride (a few audibility issues aside). Anne-Catherine Gillet shone as Maïma, the feisty flower seller who translates the offstage woofs and growls of their canine overlord to her own advantage. Her gleaming coloratura was a perfect match for Valerie Eickhoff’s gutsy mezzo as her market colleague Balkis.Among the men, Mathias Vidal got some of the best tunes as Maïma’s boyfriend Saëb, including a sentimental ballad with a trio of cellos and a lilting habanera. Loïc Félix worked his socks off as Bababeck, the duplicitous vizier whose treachery ends in the shaggy sultan giving his life to save the city. Pulling the strands together was the tirelessly engaging Alistair McGowan delivering an impeccably crafted rhyming narration, care of the indefatigable Jeremy Sams.Explore more on these topicsClassical musicOperaEnglish National Opera (ENO)Hallé Orchestralive music reviewsShareReuse this content

title: Aditya Chakrabortty and Yanis Varoufakis dissect democracy: best podcasts of the week | Television & radio | The Guardian

Author: Alexi Duggins
Headline: The Guardian columnist and former Greek finance minister tackle big political questions in a hugely entertaining chat. Plus, why was actor Nkechi Simms placed in foster care?
Content: Deep thinking … Radical Thinking With Aditya Chakrabortty.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianView image in fullscreenDeep thinking … Radical Thinking With Aditya Chakrabortty.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianBest podcasts of the weekTelevision & radioAditya Chakrabortty and Yanis Varoufakis dissect democracy: best podcasts of the weekThe Guardian columnist and former Greek finance minister tackle big political questions in a hugely entertaining chat. Plus, why was actor Nkechi Simms placed in foster care?Alexi Duggins,Hollie RichardsonandHannah J DaviesMon 5 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 03.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePick of the weekRadical Thinking With Aditya ChakraborttyThisnew seriesfrom the Guardian columnist and senior economics commentator is a lively interview show that tackles politics’ big questions. First up, it’s former Greek finance minister Yanis Varoufakis for a hugely entertaining tour of his career, dissection of democracy and attempt to apply some long-term thinking to the UK. Or in his words: “How long do you think it’ll be before Andy Burnham is pushed out for someone else?”Alexi DugginsWidely available, episodes weeklyDeath of a PoetBeer, bellringing and bards in a lovely podcast about 19th-century poet John Nicholson – also known as “the Bingley Byron”. Peter: “I do random noises around the house. Do you hear them?” Emily: “Yes. You also scream in the shower.” There’s a surprising charm to this extremely in-depthfamily chatrecorded in their home – whether you’re a fan or not.ADWidely available, episodes weeklyCarelessActor Nkechi Simms has amassed some impressive TV credits, including Top Boy and PRU.
